The Gaida: Bulgaria’s traditional bagpipe and the voice of centuries
Sunday 18 October 2026 14:15
Sunday, 18 October 2026, 14:15
PHOTO Bozhidar Cholakov
Font size
From the village square to the grand concert stage, the Bulgarian bagpipe known as "gaida" has accompanied songs, festivities and rituals for centuries. Today, it is not only one of Bulgaria’s most recognisable folk instruments, but also a living tradition recognised by UNESCO.
Powerful, rich, resonant and deeply moving, the voice of the Bulgarian "gaida" is part of Bulgaria’s sonic memory. For Bulgarians, it symbolises home and the place where we come from. For centuries, its sound has been an integral part of our festive and ritual life. Today, the bagpipe is not merely part of the country's folk heritage, but one of the most vivid emblems of Bulgarian culture.
Part of the bagpipe ensemble from the "Hristo Botev-1869" Community Center in Kalofer at the Koprivshtitsa Festival, 2010
PHOTO Georgi Stoyanov
The craft of making a bagpipe and the skill of playing it are arts passed down through generations. Many Bulgarians think of it as a traditional Bulgarian instrument, yet it is by no means unique to Bulgaria. The most familiar form of the bagpipe has been widespread throughout Europe since the Middle Ages.
Almost every European nation has developed its own version of the instrument, and similar instruments can be found in other parts of the world.
Today, bagpipes are particularly popular in the Balkans, including Bulgaria, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece, Albania and Türkiye.
In Scotland, they are a symbol of national identity. Irish and Spanish traditional bagpipes are also well known. The instrument is found in North Africa, Western Asia and the Caucasus as well.
PHOTO Radostina Chernokova
The history of the bagpipe stretches far back into antiquity and is difficult to trace. It is believed that the first instruments of this kind appeared at least 1,000 years before Christ, although some sources place their origins as far back as the sixth millennium BC.
According to historical accounts, the Roman emperor Nero, a passionate lover of music and theatre, played the bagpipe. In Rome, however, the instrument had actually been introduced from Ancient Greece, and the Greeks may have borrowed it from the Hittites.
Some researchers believe that the bagpipe was part of the musical culture of the ancient Thracians. Even Herodotus, the “Father of History”, wrote that the Thracian people used the instrument “only for praise”.
PHOTO Ani Petrova
The Bulgarian bagpipe ("gaida") is a bag-powered wind instrument consisting of a leather bag ("meh"), a blowpipe ("duhalo"), a chanter ("gaidunitsa"), a drone pipe ("ruchilo"), reeds ("piskuni") and connecting stocks ("glavini").
Traditionally, the bag is made from treated goat or lamb skin and serves as an air reservoir. The piper blows air into it through the blowpipe and regulates the air pressure with the help of the elbow.
The chanter is the melodic part of the instrument. It has finger holes that allow the player to produce notes of different pitches.
The drone pipe provides a continuous, low fundamental tone over which the melody unfolds, giving the bagpipe its distinctive sound.
Particularly important are the reeds ("piskuni"), small vibrating components that turn the flow of air into sound.
PHOTO BNR
Making a bagpipe requires exceptional craftsmanship. Its wooden parts are traditionally made from dogwood, plum and other hardwoods, while tuning the instrument calls for precision and experience. A fine bagpipe is the result not only of good materials, but also of the maker’s skill.
Two main types of bagpipe are known in Bulgarian musical tradition: the djura gaida, which is smaller, and the kaba gaida, which is larger. A Macedonian bagpipe is also found in the southwestern regions. 
The djura gaida has a higher, clear and powerful sound. It is widespread throughout Bulgaria, from Moesia, Deliorman and Dobrudzha to the Balkan Mountains, Sredna Gora, Northern, Eastern and Western Thrace, Strandzha, the Shopluk region, Graovo, the Western Outlands and Pirin Macedonia. It is played both as a solo instrument and in ensembles, accompanying songs and dances.
The Macedonian gaida is found in the southwestern part of Pirin Macedonia, as well as in Vardar and Aegean Macedonia. Its tuning lies between that of the dzhura and kaba bagpipes, giving it a medium-high pitch.
The kaba gaida is the musical voice of the Rhodope Mountains. Larger in size, it has a lower, deeper, softer and fuller timbre, and is closely tied to the region’s folk traditions. Rhodope traditional round dances ("horo") are performed to its accompaniment, while the slow melodies played on the kaba bagpipe are among the most emblematic treasures of Bulgarian folk music.
A museum in the Rhodopes tells the story of the Bulgarian bagpipe
An ensemble of several kaba bagpipes creates a striking soundscape. Over the past half-century, the celebrated orchestra 100 Kaba Bagpipes has become a symbol of Bulgarian ensemble playing on this instrument. Founded in 1961 by folklorist Apostol Kisyov, the orchestra gave its first concert performance that same year at the Rozhen folk gathering, held in the village of the same name in the Rhodope Mountain in southwestern Bulgaria.
On 16 May 2012, in the National Palace of Culture in Sofia, 333 Rhodope kaba bagpipers, representing four generations of musicians from across Bulgaria, played fragments of traditional Rhodope melodies together for nine minutes and thirteen seconds. Their performance set an official mass-participation record recognised by Guinness World Records, surpassing the previous record held by 240 Scottish bagpipers playing simultaneously.
When "100 kaba bagpipes" play together, time comes to a standstill
The bagpipe is not merely an artefact of the past. Knowledge of how to make the instrument and the skills needed to play it are passed from one generation to the next, from master to apprentice, within families, at community cultural centres, in music schools and in folk ensembles. This living bond between generations has helped bring international recognition to the Bulgarian bagpipe.
In 2025, UNESCO inscribed “Bagpipes and Bagpipe Playing in Bulgaria: Transmission of Knowledge and Skills” on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The decision highlights the importance of the practices that allow the tradition to evolve and be passed on to future generations.
The Bulgarian bagpipe has also made its mark beyond the country’s borders. One of the most powerful symbols of the international reach of Bulgarian musical tradition is the song Izlel e Delyo Haydutin, performed by Valya Balkanska with bagpipers Stefan Zahmanov and Lazar Kanevski. The recording is included in the musical selection on the Golden Record carried aboard Voyager 1, the spacecraft launched from Cape Canaveral in 1977 and reported to have left the Solar System in 2004. The record, which contains images and sounds from Earth, was designed to preserve a part of our planet’s heritage for future generations and to serve as a message to extraterrestrial civilisations. In this way, the voice of Bulgaria's Rhodope musical tradition became part of a message from Earth to the cosmos.
PHOTO Facebook /gaidari.varna
A number of performers and teachers have helped popularise the Bulgarian bagpipe. Among them is Kostadin Varimezov from Strandzha, one of Bulgaria’s most celebrated bagpipers, known as the “king of the Bulgarian bagpipe” and “Saint Kostadin of folk music”. He was among the artists who brought the Bulgarian bagpipe into the world’s musical encyclopaedias.
He performed across Europe, Asia and America and was one of the first Bulgarian musicians not only to present the country’s folk music at concerts and festivals around the world, but also to live abroad for extended periods and teach Bulgarian folklore there.
Today, the bagpipe continues to sound out at folk festivals and gatherings, in community cultural centres and music schools, on concert stages and in contemporary musical projects. For Bulgarians, it is neither a museum relic nor simply an ancient instrument preserved as a keepsake. It is a living body of knowledge, continually passed on, developed and heard.
The bagpipe is made of wood, skin and air. But what makes it a symbol is human memory. As long as there are children learning to play, craftspeople making instruments and audiences who recognise and cherish this sound, Bulgaria’s bagpipe tradition will remain a vibrant part of the country’s cultural identity.

Tesla Roadster to gain ‘consciousness’ and learn to perform stunts, Musk says

Kremlin says Russian strikes aim to diminish Ukraine’s ‘offensive potential’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:08:33 UTC
21:08:33 KST

Kanyshai Butun
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Sunday that Russia continues to launch retaliatory strikes aimed at diminishing Ukraine’s “offensive potential,” the state-run news agency Tass reported.
Speaking to journalists, Peskov said Russia’s “systematic and massive” strikes in response to Ukrainian attacks were continuing.
“Some final signs of agony are being observed. The Kyiv regime is putting up resistance. But this cannot change the course of events,” he said.
His remarks came after a “massive” Ukrainian drone attack targeted oil facilities and an Ozon logistics center in St. Petersburg, as well as the data center of Russian social media company VK in the Leningrad region, according to Russian authorities.
The attacks killed one person and injured nine others in Russia, they added, while the Russian Defense Ministry claimed that air defenses destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian territory, the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014, and the Black Sea.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Moscow of launching strikes against residential buildings across the country, killing two people and injuring 12 others. He also said Russia hit substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions, leaving “tens of thousands” of families without power.

TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Iranian lawmakers on Sunday approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as the country's new defense minister in a vote of confidence, the official news agency IRNA reported.
During an open session of the parliament, lawmakers voted 237 in favor and 15 against, with no abstentions, to confirm Akhlaghi.
Iran's former Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed in U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. Following his death, President Masoud Pezeshkian appointed Seyed Majid Ebn Al-Reza as acting defense minister.
Akhlaghi previously served as managing director of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization.
On Feb. 28, the United States and Israel launched joint military strikes on Tehran and several other Iranian cities, killing Iran's then Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, senior military commanders and officials as well as civilians. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz. ■

Feature: Indian-controlled Kashmir's traditional musical instrument makers strive to keep vanishing craft alive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:06:13 CST
21:06:13 KST

by Peerzada Arshad Hamid
NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Inside the courtyard workshop of his two-story home, Mushtaq Ahmad Dar examines each chisel with meticulous attention. Holding one in his left hand, he runs his right index finger along the bevel, then reaches into a water-filled jug for a soaking whetstone. He hones the blade until a faint smile crosses his face, then braces another dull chisel and rubs it steadily across the stone.
"My father says that it is always the tools that work wonders," said Dar, a traditional Kashmiri musical instrument maker.
At 10 a.m., his apprentice places a half-done Kashmiri rabab, an ancient, plectrum-plucked stringed instrument carved from a single piece of mulberry wood, before him. Dar drives a sharpened chisel into the wood, hammering its butt with his adze as shavings curl away, gradually shaping the rabab's deep, concave bowl.
Dar tells Xinhua that he learned the craft as a boy from his father, continuing a tradition dating back to his grandfather, a locally renowned singer.
"Not only am I, but my three brothers are also well-versed in the craft," Dar said. "We live in a joint family, and I am hopeful our children too will carry forward this legacy."
Among his brothers, Dar has perfected the skill and now often discusses the instruments' intricacies with clients on behalf of his father, who, because of his advanced age, can no longer devote himself fully to the trade.
At Dar's workshop in Budgam district, a 25-minute drive northwest of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, traditional string instruments, including the rabab, santoor, sarangi, Kashmiri sitar, and Sikh rabab, are being made.
Dar spends months crafting a single instrument, carefully selecting mulberry and walnut wood and prioritizing quality over speed. His instruments are in demand across India.
"For most of the instruments, we use mulberry wood, but for santoor, we use walnut wood," he said. "I am lucky enough that I have a good clientele. This craft has given us everything we have today. People place orders at my workshop in advance for the instruments of their choice."
"The music runs in our blood, as our forefathers have been associated with it for generations," he said. "I know how to play every instrument that I make. These objects communicate with me."
Dar is seen as one of the torchbearers of a craft many feared would die with the Indian-controlled Kashmir's last santoor maker, 85-year-old Ghulam Mohamed Zaz of Srinagar.
Surrounded by the vibrant walls of his room, Zaz ran his frail fingers across the sharp edges of a newly fashioned, trapezoidal box of walnut wood. He checked its precision with a scale, his movements slow and deliberate.
"A craft doesn't simply die -- it endures," he said. "What kills a craft is the flood of fakes and inferior copies replacing the authentic work. I hold the line for this art today, but I do not know who will carry it into tomorrow."
He is the last of the eighth generation in his family to carve the classical instrument and claims that all the acclaimed artists of the region played on the santoors made by them.
The word santoor in Persian means "a hundred strings." The traditional Kashmiri santoor typically has 100 strings. Worldwide, santoor varieties differ mostly in their string count.
In his uptown Srinagar office, Nazir Ganaie, the founder of Kashmir Rabab Academy, an institute that works to preserve the region's musical heritage, is busy putting the final touches on an upcoming concert schedule. The event offers a rare chance to hear a performance played entirely on traditional Kashmiri instruments.
Driven by a passion to protect these indigenous folk traditions, Ganaie built this platform to bring local artists together and showcase their talents.
"For me, the rabab is not merely a musical instrument. It is an emotion deeply etched into our collective soul. The moment I strike its strings, I am transported to the mountains and valleys of Kashmir, where every note carries a story, a memory and a sense of belonging," Ganaie said.
His love for playing the Kashmiri rabab took him to Dar some years back to place an order in bulk for Kashmiri handmade rababs.
Ganaie often visits Indian-controlled Kashmir's master instrument makers to chronicle their personal histories and the resilient spirit driving them to preserve their craft.
"Today Kashmiri rabab, santoor, and sarangi stand distinct from their global counterparts," said Muzaffar Ahmad Bhat, a Srinagar-based musicologist. "They are now deeply woven into the region's folklore, defining the vibrant rhythm of folk songs and the spiritual depth of classical Sufiana Mausiqi, a centuries-old classical choral ensemble music. Far more than mere tools for performance, these instruments have become inseparable fragments of Kashmiri society, culture, and identity."
The traditional craftsmanship required to make these instruments is rapidly vanishing. At the heart of this decline is the loss of aging master craftsmen, with few apprentices stepping up to fill the void.
"Low financial returns and shrinking demand make it difficult for remaining artisans to earn a living. Ultimately, the shift toward electronic music and cheap, machine-made instruments has severely threatened a legacy that once thrived on human hands," he said.
Ganaie, however, feels the internet and social media have opened up avenues for the musicians as well as makers of the musical instruments to keep the art thriving and prevent it from vanishing into the thin air.
"It is heartening to see rabab and santoor makers and other traditional instrument artisans finding renewed hope as online orders and social media open up new markets for their craft. The growing visibility of these instruments in major productions of Bollywood and music platforms has also helped introduce the region's rich musical heritage to wider national and international audiences," he said.
Meanwhile, a young musical instrument maker Altaf Ahmad Sheikh is hard at work in another Srinagar neighborhood. His hands steady, engraving delicate floral and foliage designs that weave gracefully between the bird motifs on a sarangi. The design has transformed a plain wooden instrument into an ornate work of art.
He has spent months crafting this sarangi, an instrument that represents not just his devotion to the craft, but his very livelihood.
Sheikh, a school dropout, learned the craft from his father, a renowned sarangi maker.
"I am striving hard to keep the craft alive," Sheikh said as his young son sat in front of him, perhaps trying to imbibe the skill. ■

Lightning, strong wind gusts expected in eastern, western Japan through Tuesday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:05:53 CST
21:05:53 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Japan's weather agency on Sunday warned of lightning, violent wind gusts and sudden heavy rain in eastern and western Japan through Tuesday.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said a low-pressure system accompanied by a front is expected to move from the Sea of Japan toward the Sea of Okhotsk, while the front is forecast to linger over eastern and western Japan.
The JMA urged people to seek shelter indoors and take other safety precautions if they notice signs of approaching well-developed cumulonimbus clouds.
The warning comes after record-breaking rainfall in Chiba Prefecture near Tokyo in August left at least 13 people dead. The downpours caused widespread flooding, highlighting the risks posed by extreme rainfall in Japan. ■

Iran says its 7-day plan to reopen Hormuz Strait still on table
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:05:52 CST
21:05:52 KST

TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran-proposed seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is "still on the table."
Araghchi made the remarks in an interview with Iran's official news agency IRNA on the sidelines of the 52nd Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in the Iraqi capital Baghdad.
He said Iran's conditions for ceasing hostilities and reopening the strait were "completely clear" and had been submitted to the United States under the seven-day plan.
Washington has presented its views on the plan, which Tehran is reviewing, he added.
"Iran's plan is still on the table," Araghchi said. "If they (the United States) meet those conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the sixth day, and negotiations will resume on the seventh."
He said that Iran's conditions were neither extraordinary nor unusual, adding that they were the same commitments "the United States had already committed itself in the peace memorandum of understanding (MoU) and other negotiations."
Araghchi emphasized that Iran will not bow to threats and is prepared to defend itself, while remaining ready to pursue diplomacy.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program and the removal of sanctions. However, they failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal. ■

IMF raises Hong Kong growth forecast to 3.8 pct, HKSAR gov't even more optimistic
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:05:50 CST
21:05:50 KST

HONG KONG, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised Hong Kong's economic growth forecast for this year to 3.8 percent, with the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (HKSAR) government holding a more optimistic outlook than the projection, the local financial chief said on Sunday.
Paul Chan, financial secretary of the HKSAR government, wrote in his blog that during his visit to Bangkok, Thailand, last week for the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, discussions highlighted how the global economic landscape is being reshaped by the impact of high energy prices driven by conflicts, as well as the surging AI boom.
The IMF's latest forecast projected global economic growth to slow from 3.5 percent last year to 3.1 percent this year, with a widening gap of uneven development -- growth projections for economies affected by conflicts were sharply lowered, while those deeply anchored in the AI supply chain were upgraded, and growth across Asia as a whole continued to outpace the global average, with Hong Kong's growth forecast likewise revised upward to 3.8 percent.
Chan pointed out that whether supporting economic transformation through technology or bolstering economic momentum to sustain employment, the key lies in efficient financial support, and Hong Kong is playing an active role in driving efficient capital flows. ■

PARIS, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- More than 2,000 people have been arrested during violent protests across France on Saturday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday.
In a post on social media platform X, Nunez said that protests in some cities continued late into Saturday night, adding that investigations were underway to identify the perpetrators of the violent acts and bring them to justice.
More than 600 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters have been injured in the violence so far, he said, citing provisional figures.
Material damage was considerable, affecting several hundred businesses, he said.
"Demonstrating is a fundamental right. Causing disorder through coordinated violence is not," Nunez said.
Around 550,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday. Numerous attacks on public buildings, police stations and businesses were reported during the demonstrations. ■

Montenegrin president meets Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:05:19 CST
21:05:19 KST

CETINJE, Montenegro, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Montenegrin President Jakov Milatovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Cetinje, a city near Montenegro's capital, Podgorica, on Saturday, expressing Montenegro's willingness to deepen friendly relations and practical cooperation with China.
Milatovic asked Wang to convey his sincere greetings to Chinese President Xi Jinping, and welcomed the first-ever visit by a Chinese foreign minister to Montenegro.
Noting that this year marks the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Montenegro and China, Milatovic said the visit holds important symbolic significance.
Recalling his experience studying in China, Milatovic said he had gained a deeper understanding of China's economic and social development and the lives of its people, as well as the importance of cooperation with China.
Noting that European Union (EU) accession is currently a priority on Montenegro's foreign policy agenda, Milatovic said the country also attaches great importance to relations with China, with Montenegro firmly adhering to the one-China principle and remaining committed to friendly and mutually beneficial cooperation with China.
Over the past two decades, Montenegro-China relations have made significant progress across various fields, with infrastructure, economic and trade, and tourism emerging as three key areas, he said.
Earlier this year, Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic and Chinese Premier Li Qiang reached important consensus on further deepening cooperation during their meeting in China, Milatovic said, adding that Montenegro looks forward to maintaining political dialogue and deepening practical cooperation with China based on mutual respect, so as to bring greater benefits to the two peoples.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, conveyed Xi's cordial greetings to Milatovic, saying that despite the geographical distance, China and Montenegro have always respected each other and treated each other as equals, setting an example of friendly exchanges between countries of different sizes.
Wang said China appreciates Milatovic's rational and objective understanding of China and his active efforts to promote bilateral relations.
He said China has consistently maintained that all countries, big or small, are equal, and has always followed the path of partnership over alliance and dialogue over confrontation.
China appreciates Montenegro's firm adherence to the one-China principle, respects the path and governance model chosen by the Montenegrin people, and stands ready to be a reliable and trustworthy partner of Montenegro, he added.
Wang said China has engaged in practical cooperation with Montenegro in good faith, delivering tangible results. Describing Montenegro's north-south expressway as a landmark project of historic significance, he called on both sides to ensure the high-quality completion of its second phase.
Montenegro enjoys unique tourism resources and has a historical tradition of anti-fascism, Wang said, adding that China is helping restore the Tara River Bridge, which was featured in the famous Yugoslav film "The Bridge," and that more Chinese tourists are expected to visit Montenegro.
Wang said the two sides should take the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations this year as an opportunity to review successful cooperation, jointly discuss ways to elevate bilateral relations to a higher level, explore new areas of cooperation, and build an even brighter next 20 years.
On China-EU relations, Wang said China and the EU are comprehensive strategic partners and their relations have remained generally sound and stable.
China has always maintained that China and the EU are partners, not rivals, he said, noting that differences over economic and trade issues, which have emerged amid increasingly closer cooperation, can be resolved through dialogue and should not affect the overall development of China-EU relations.
Wang said China understands Montenegro's efforts to join the EU and its choice to pursue European integration, noting that the process is fully compatible with deeper cooperation with China.
China believes Montenegro will become another good friend of China within the EU after its accession, and hopes Montenegro will play a unique and important role in promoting regional peace and stability and advancing China-EU relations, Wang said.
The two sides also exchanged views on international and regional issues of mutual concern, including the Ukraine crisis.
Before the meeting, Milatovic and Wang jointly visited a photo exhibition marking the 20th anniversary of China-Montenegro diplomatic relations.
During his visit, Wang also met with Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic and held talks with Montenegrin Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic. ■

SYDNEY, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) model that analyzes DNA to identify genetic risk factors for stroke, paving the way for more personalized risk assessments and prevention.
The study identified 18 genetic variants linked to ischemic stroke, the most common type of stroke. People in the highest genetic risk group had a 22 percent higher chance of stroke than those in the lower-risk group, according to a statement released recently by Australia's University of Technology Sydney (UTS).
The team used a type of AI known as a transformer to train the model on thousands of genetic variations and identify links to ischemic stroke. Researchers tested the AI model using genetic and health data from the UK Biobank and a large U.S. database. The model was more accurate than previous genetic risk tools at distinguishing people who had suffered a stroke from those who had not.
The study also identified the gene EDEM2 in brain cortex tissue as a key contributor to stroke susceptibility, providing a target for further research.
Researchers are now developing a multimodal AI tool that combines genetic assessments with other modes of data, including health and lifestyle surveys, scans and imaging, to improve risk assessment for stroke and other diseases. ■

Brain iron levels in children with ADHD may depend on when they start medication
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:23 UTC
21:00:23 KST

Children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder who begin taking stimulant medications at a younger age may develop different brain iron levels than those who start treatment later. A new analysis of brain imaging data suggests that starting medication by age eight is associated with higher iron concentrations in dopamine-rich brain regions compared to starting at age nine or later. The research was published in the journal Brain Research.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. These symptoms often create challenges with everyday tasks and social interactions. The condition is closely tied to reduced signaling of dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate movement, attention, and reward. To manage symptoms, doctors routinely prescribe psychostimulants, which work by increasing the amount of dopamine available in the central nervous system.
Brain iron plays an essential role in this process because it is a necessary ingredient for the brain to manufacture dopamine. Tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme responsible for creating dopamine, relies entirely on iron to function properly. Iron also aids in the production of myelin, the protective sheath that insulates nerve fibers and speeds up communication between brain cells.
Because of this relationship, iron tends to concentrate heavily in dopamine-rich regions, such as the basal ganglia and the substantia nigra. These deep brain structures are heavily involved in motor control and learning. As a child grows into adolescence, iron levels in these areas typically increase alongside the maturation of the dopamine system.
Prior research has shown that children with ADHD who have never taken medication often have lower levels of brain iron compared to their peers without the condition. At the same time, some brain imaging research suggests that children treated with psychostimulants have iron levels similar to those of neurotypical children. This pattern raised the question of whether stimulant medications directly influence brain iron levels over time.
Hugo A.E. Morandini, a researcher at the Child and Adolescent Health Service in Perth, Australia, along with a team of colleagues, wanted to better understand how psychostimulant treatment relates to brain iron. They designed a study to track iron levels over a two-year period. They specifically looked at how both the duration of treatment and the age a child started taking medication might relate to iron concentrations.
To conduct the research, Morandini and his team used brain imaging data from the Oregon ADHD-1000 dataset, a public repository of clinical information. They identified 29 children with ADHD who were consistently taking psychostimulant medications and 38 neurotypical children with no psychiatric diagnoses. The children underwent magnetic resonance imaging scans at the beginning of the study and again two years later.
The researchers used a specific type of scan called functional magnetic resonance imaging. While this technology is often used to map blood flow, the team analyzed the data using a specialized technique that estimates the concentration of iron in brain tissue based on its magnetic properties. They focused their analysis on several brain regions rich in dopamine and iron, including the globus pallidus, putamen, caudate nucleus, thalamus, and substantia nigra.
First, the team compared the iron levels of the children with ADHD to the neurotypical children across the two-year period. The researchers adjusted their statistical models to account for variables like age, sex, and intelligence quotient. They found that differences in iron levels in the substantia nigra, thalamus, and most of the basal ganglia were not statistically significant between the two groups.
However, the children with ADHD had lower iron content in the globus pallidus. This structure is a key part of the basal ganglia that helps regulate dopamine circuitry and reward behaviors. The authors noted that a shorter average duration of medication exposure in their study compared to past research might explain why globus pallidus iron had not reached the levels seen in neurotypical children.
Next, the researchers looked exclusively at the 29 children with ADHD to see how their medication histories related to their brain iron. They calculated the total time each child had been taking psychostimulants and noted the age at which they first started the treatment. The researchers then tested whether these factors predicted iron levels across the different brain regions.
The length of time a child had been taking stimulants had almost no statistical relationship with brain iron. The researchers found a very small negative association between treatment duration and iron in the thalamus, but they noted this effect was so minor it is unlikely to have any clinical meaning. In all other regions, the models for treatment duration were not statistically significant.
The age at which a child began treatment showed a different pattern. The team split the children with ADHD into two subgroups based on when they started medication. One group began treatment at age eight or younger, while the other began at age nine or older.
The analysis revealed that children who started taking psychostimulants at an earlier age had higher iron content in the thalamus, caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. The researchers noted that the brain undergoes rapid developmental changes in iron and dopamine during childhood. They proposed that starting medication earlier in childhood might intersect with these developmental windows, making the dopamine system more sensitive to external influences.
The findings come with several limitations that affect how the results should be interpreted. The analysis relied on a relatively small number of participants, meaning the patterns observed need to be confirmed in larger populations. A larger study could provide more precise estimates of how medication timing interacts with brain development.
The researchers also had to rely on parent reports to determine when the children began taking medication and how long they had been treated. Parent recall can sometimes be imprecise, which could introduce errors into the timelines. The study also lacked information on the exact dosages the children were taking and how strictly they adhered to their daily medication schedules.
Because the researchers observed existing medication habits rather than assigning treatments, the results establish an association rather than a direct cause and effect. It is possible that children prescribed medication at a younger age have more severe symptoms, which could be tied to underlying differences in brain biology. The researchers could not measure the children’s brain iron before treatment started, making it difficult to isolate the exact impact of the drugs.
Future research will need to follow patients from before they start medication into adulthood to fully chart the effects of early treatment. Tracking these changes over a longer lifespan could help researchers understand whether the differences in brain iron persist as patients grow older.
The study, “Neurochemical impact of psychostimulants: Longitudinal MRI analysis of brain iron content in children with ADHD,” was authored by Hugo A.E. Morandini, Sjoerd B. Vos, Paola Chivers, Tim J. Silk, and Pradeep Rao.

Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.
The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.
Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.
The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.
Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.
The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.
His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.
Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.
He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),
Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.
He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.
This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.
“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.
The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.
Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.
His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.
In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.
“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

From overnight into Sunday, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit substations, homes, and industrial sites from Odesa to Volyn. They killed civilians and left tens of thousands of families without power.
Russia fights along the front line while hitting cities and the grid behind it with drones, missiles, and glide bombs. Ukraine says Moscow plans up to 1,000 such munitions against 60 key infrastructure sites this winter, and jet-powered drones partly free it to concentrate missiles on fewer targets, the Institute for the Study of War assessed. With Graham Act penalties on hold and US sanctions on Russian diesel suspended, Russia faces no new US cost for its strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Protecting and restoring the grid falls to Ukraine’s air defenses and repair crews.
Russia hit energy sites 76 times in a week
Zelenskyy counted 76 deliberate Russian strikes on energy and oil-and-gas facilities since Trump’s announcement. Overnight, Russia hit substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa oblasts, he said. In the past week, Russia fired almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, mainly to cause a blackout. His message was aimed at Washington.

Americans living abroad can often feel like they’re stuck on the political sidelines of their native land. With one of the most contentious midterm elections in US history coming up next month, we spoke with the Netherlands’ American community about how they’re getting involved in the race and the challenges they face.
For the past two years, Donald Trump has dominated headlines around the world. It seems like there’s little the divisive president and his administration haven’t disrupted within and well beyond US borders.
There’s no denying that much is riding on the country’s midterms on November 3 and that the result will have a defining impact on the course of global politics over the next few years.
As with prior elections, Americans living in the Netherlands may feel there’s little they can do besides mail in their absentee ballots – and even that is an often complicated process that many fail to complete.
Each state sets its own deadlines and decides whether ballots can go back by email, fax or post. A ballot posted from the Netherlands also has to cross the Atlantic in time to be counted.
Some don’t bother at all, and some feel they shouldn’t. “One of the reasons why many in the Netherlands don’t vote is because they’ve been here for a very long time,” said Tre’ Shawn Griffin-Noordermeer, vice chair of the Netherlands chapter of Democrats Abroad. “They feel like they shouldn’t be voting because they’ve lived outside the US for so long.”
In fact, federal law lets US citizens abroad keep voting in federal elections in the state where they last lived, however long they have been away.
To help get that message out, various groups here have been volunteering and hosting events in the days leading up to the midterms.
Reaching out to voters
Members of campaign group Democrats Abroad in the Netherlands have spent recent weeks running an email campaign and arranging “Vote From Abroad” gatherings on Zoom.
They’ve also been hosting lunches and other events in cities around the country to discuss the midterms along with putting up fliers and getting the word out on social media and via phone banking.
“We’ve got hundreds of volunteers here in the Netherlands who have been helping with this,” Griffin-Noordermeer told Dutch News. “A few weekends ago, we called over 13,000 people.”
Originally founded in 1964, Democrats Abroad serves as the Democratic party’s official organisation for American citizens living overseas. One of its primary tasks is encouraging its members and other voters, who are spread across 197 countries, to cast their ballots.
And that’s more difficult than it might seem.
Counting the voters
Nobody knows exactly how many Americans in the Netherlands can vote. The US does not require citizens to register with the government when they move abroad, and some states drop overseas voters from their rolls when they stop responding to election mail. That leaves neither the State Department nor voter lists with a reliable count.
The national statistics office CBS puts the number of US nationals living in the Netherlands at just over 27,000 in 2026 – though not all are old enough to vote, and Dutch-Americans with both passports are counted as Dutch, so aren’t included.
Worldwide, about 2.2 million Americans of voting age live abroad, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP), the US defence department office that helps military and overseas citizens vote. FVAP estimates only about 11% of them voted in the 2024 presidential election. Even fewer typically take part in midterms.
FVAP says 14.8% of eligible voters in Europe voted in 2024.
Preparing for the worst
Despite Trump’s low approval ratings, the path to a “blue wave” for the Democrats won’t necessarily be an easy one.
His administration also continues to meddle with the midterms. In August, the Pentagon, which runs FVAP, made last-minute changes to the Federal Post Card Application (the form overseas voters use to register and request ballots), removing the checkbox for US citizens who were born abroad and have never lived in the US. The Democratic National Committee has gone to court over the change.
That followed a March 2025 executive order in which Trump sought to add proof-of-citizenship requirements to the same form, parts of which federal courts have blocked. The order also aimed to stop states counting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.
In June, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that states can keep counting ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive later. That matters for voters whose ballots travel by international post.
Hayley Hughes, the co-founder of the Netherlands chapter of Indivisible, admitted she’s worried about how things might go.
She has already had discussions with the leads of other chapters about what to do if the administration interferes with ballot counts or sends government agents to polling stations.
Trump has said Republicans should “take over the voting” in at least 15 places, and his former adviser Steve Bannon has welcomed the idea of immigration agents at the polls.
“We’re already thinking we might have to mobilise,” Hughes told Dutch News.
“We’re looking at a protest here that week, if needed. In the US, there could be a mass mobilisation of peaceful protests and a general strike where people don’t go to work or school. We all hope that won’t be needed.”
The week of the midterms
Several midterm events are scheduled for the week of the elections. The Atlantische Commissie in The Hague is hosting an “American midterm election breakfast” on 4 November.
In Amsterdam, the commission is also helping with the John Adams Institute’s “Midterm Madness” event on November 6. It’s set to serve as an afterparty with a ‘festival-style experience’ featuring live music along with discussions and lectures about the results featuring Mark Leibovich, a staff writer at The Atlantic, and others.
Comedian Greg Shapiro is once again teaming up with Pep Rosenfeld for an Election Night Party at Boom Chicago. They’ve hosted these events since the ‘00s and are once again prepared to stay up late. The comedy club has vowed to remain open past 4:00 “if things get crazy.”
“How late, well, we’ll wait and see,” Shapiro told Dutch News. “I’ve got performances the next day. At some point I’ll have to get some sleep.”
Shapiro will be taking a break from his ongoing ‘KING ME: 250 Years of Donald Trump’ comedy tour for the Boom Chicago gathering. He’s worried about how much rewriting he’ll have to do for subsequent performances after the midterms.
“There’s no telling what could happen,” he said. “It could become January 6th on a national scale.”
If you’re an American living overseas and haven’t voted yet, there could still be time based on where you’re registered. Visit votefromabroad.org for further assistance.

How Israeli support could most effectively aid Saudi Arabia against the Houthis - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:50:52 UTC
20:50:52 KST

There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. If there is help, how might it take shape, and what might be most effective?
This also comes in the context of questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have persisted since the Accords began in 2020. However, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.
US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I do, I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments come days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.
This comes in the context of the Houthis increasing attacks on Saudi Arabia. The US has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence. The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.
On October 18, Israel’s Walla had a piece by Amir Bohbot, asking whether Israeli aid to Saudi Arabia would be an opportunity or a potential powder keg. “Security sources confirmed to Walla that the quality of Israeli intelligence is improving, but at the same time the Houthis are causing heavy damage. The security establishment is aware that there is an opportunity to strengthen relations, but is not addressing the issue for fear of inflaming the situation.”
Anadolu, a Turkish pro-government media outlet, noted on October 13 that “Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has rejected an Israeli push to join the military campaign against Yemen's Houthi group, despite efforts to secure Riyadh's approval through US mediation.” Anadolu said it based this on a report in Israel’s Haaretz. “Another source familiar with the matter said Israel hoped military cooperation with Saudi Arabia would strengthen bilateral ties and pave the way for a future normalization agreement,” the report said. “There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the report.”
Saudi Arabia needs Israeli aerial defense systems
Ynet noted on October 18, in a piece by Ron Ben Yishai, that “the Saudis urgently need early-warning radar systems and air-defense batteries capable of countering different types of aerial threats, including Iron Dome, David's Sling, and even Arrow 2 interceptors. The Houthis are attacking Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and explosive-laden drones, requiring a combination of defensive capabilities.”
The analysis also noted that “Trump sees a chance to revive Saudi-Israel normalization as the Houthis strike Riyadh; Israel is sharing intelligence, but Riyadh's demand for Palestinian statehood talks and Israel's need for its own defenses make a deal far from certain.” It also added that Trump may see an “opportunity for greater Israeli assistance, potentially generating enough goodwill in Riyadh to persuade the Saudis to abandon their longstanding condition for normalization: negotiations with the Palestinians toward a two-state solution. For now, however, there is considerable reason to doubt that Trump's comments signal a meaningful breakthrough in Israeli-Saudi relations.”
Walla noted that “security sources confirmed to Walla that as time goes by, the contribution of Israeli intelligence is increasing, with the Houthis in the background causing heavy damage to the Saudis throughout the country.”
The report went on to say that “as first published in Walla, the IDF is assisting Saudi Arabia on the intelligence front in the fight against the Houthis in aspects of warning, a target bank, and building a situational picture.” It added that “Israel sees this as a positive process that will intensify once the US decides how it will decide on the Iranian issue: If the US attacks Iran, the latter may attack the countries of the region, including Israel. If the Americans continue with the economic sanctions (there is a slim chance of a political agreement without further conflict), they could also lead to escalation in the region.”
Houthis targeted shipping they claimed was linked to Israel after Oct. 7
The overall story now points to potential increased Israeli involvement and support. It’s worth noting that the Houthis began attacks on Israel soon after the Hamas attack on October 7. The Houthis began by attacking ships they claimed were linked to Israel. The Iranian-backed group claimed that it was targeting Israeli ships and vessels linked to Israel, although many of the ships attacked had no direct Israeli ownership or operational connection.
One of the most prominent incidents occurred on November 19, 2023, when Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader, a vehicle carrier, in the Red Sea. Armed men boarded the ship from a helicopter and diverted it to Yemen. The vessel was operated by a Japanese company and linked through its ownership structure to Israeli businessman Abraham Ungar. None of its 25 crew members were Israeli nationals. They remained detained until January 2025, when the Houthis released them following the Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The seizure marked the beginning of a wider campaign against international shipping. The Houthis subsequently expanded their declared targets to include vessels traveling to Israeli ports and ships associated with American and British interests.
The Houthis also carried out ballistic missile attacks on Israel. Israel responded by striking dozens of Houthi targets in 2025. This illustrates how there has already been an Israeli campaign against the Houthis. The US has also carried out a campaign.
Saudi Arabia has also fought the Houthis since 2015. That means that all the players know the Houthi threat and capabilities. The Saudis have worked with Egypt, the UAE, and others in the past against the Houthis. It appears Riyadh will work with Egypt and the UAE again. Israel has ties with the UAE and Egypt via peace treaties. Israel also already works closely with US Central Command.
Any cooperation against the Houthis can increase the regional defense connections and defense infrastructure. This helps defend against Iranian-backed threats and Iran’s direct threats. For instance, when Iran carried out large missile attacks on Israel in 2024, many countries cooperated against the threat.

In France’s Limoges, the fire-ravaged town hall rekindles memories of Notre Dame
- Residents in Limoges were shocked as masked rioters burned the 19th century town hall, echoing memories of Notre Dame’s 2019 fire.
- The roof collapsed and much of the listed monument was destroyed, leaving only the west wing. Officials called it a “heritage catastrophe”.
- Mayor Guillaume Guerin said the attack was planned and police were too few. Locals demanded punishment and said violence had no place in protest.
AI generated
LIMOGES, France - Residents in Limoges recoiled in horror on Oct 18 at the city’s fire-ravaged town hall, an ornate 19th century neo-Renaissance building which survived two world wars but was torched by a masked mob during the worst unrest to convulse France in years.
Stunned onlookers had watched helplessly the previous evening as the blaze tore through the roof, felling the building’s clock tower in scenes that revived haunting memories of the collapse of Notre Dame cathedral’s spire in a 2019 fire.
“It broke my heart. I saw Notre Dame all over again, except this time it was our town,” said Francoise Faurie who witnessed the fire consume Limoges’ town hall.
Faurie’s family had been due to celebrate her grand-daughter’s baptism in the town hall in a month’s time.
“What kind of country are we living in? What are we leaving our children?” she said. “There’s no reason to touch that building. You can have demands, you have the right to protest, but not the right to violence.”
The local prefect, Maurice Barate, said the roof had caved in onto lower floors, sparing only the west wing, and that large parts of the exterior had been destroyed.
The destruction of the building, a listed monument that opened in 1883 and was inspired by Paris’ city hall, was a “heritage catastrophe”, he said.
Its central clock tower and belfry towered 43m over the square below.
“It’s inadmissible to have burned down the town hall!” one local resident, Gilbert, said. “Those who did this need to be punished. They need to pay out of their own pocket, it’s not for the state to pay.”
The town’s shaken mayor, Guillaume Guerin, described how the local police force had quickly been overwhelmed by several hundred-strong mob who he said smashed windows and used a battering ram to break down the main door.
“The logistics, the organisation, the premeditation behind yesterday’s attack on the town hall is something I find unbearable,” he told reporters.
Guerin said there had been insufficient police numbers to protect the building since officers from the national force had been deployed to the street protest.
“I had no single national police officer to protect the town hall,” the centre-right mayor continued. “This country is doing badly, this country is doing very badly, and it’s a small provincial mayor telling you so.”
Crowds gathered under blue skies as specialists surveyed the damage.
Edith Lorcen, a retired nurse, expressed her shock at the malice of those behind the attack.
“I’m disgusted. I’m hurting,” Lorcen said. “But it does nothing to add hate on top of hate.” REUTERS

Gov’t approves NIS 2.5 billion for defense, slashing ministry budgets ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

11:50:15 UTC
20:50:15 KST

The government approved on Sunday the allocation of NIS 2.5 billion for "urgent defense procurement," to be funded through across-the-board cuts to government ministries’ budgets, less than two weeks before the October 27 elections.
The funds will be allocated through across-the-board cuts of 4.9 percent to government ministries’ budgets, rather than coalition funds.
The cuts will affect key ministries such as the education, health, welfare and social affairs ministries, the proposal shows. 
A legal opinion attached to the government proposal warned of the implications of the cuts to government ministries and noted the need for the government to exercise restraint in making decisions during the election period.
The legal opinion also raised concerns that approving the funds so close to the elections could create an irreversible situation for the incoming government and risk prioritizing party interests over the public interest.
However, the document also acknowledged the need for the defense procurement, stating that it was required urgently.
Reason for urgency classified, will be presented to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement
The reasons for the urgency of the classified procurement, as well as the details of the security needs, will be presented as part of the classified proposals submitted to the Ministerial Committee on Procurement, the document added.
The government's decision on the funds comes after an additional NIS 3.5 billion was approved on Wednesday for further urgent defense procurement, including a roughly NIS 1 billion deal to purchase Apache helicopters.
The Finance Ministry told The Jerusalem Post that close to NIS 1 billion used for the Apache helicopter purchase would be diverted from funds earmarked for a five-year plan to develop Israel’s Arab sector. The remaining NIS 68 million would come from the 2026 state budget.
Lapid criticizes decision to cut government ministries
Opposition leader Yair Lapid on Sunday sharply criticized the defense procurement being funded by making cuts to government ministries.
"Defense procurement is essential, but it can be funded without cutting money for the poor or for our children’s education," he stated.
"There are billions of shekels sitting in coalition funds. Instead of the money going to the corrupt, draft dodgers, and deserters, it could be used to buy Apache helicopters."
"The cuts to the welfare and education budgets are yet another crime by the government against the productive, serving public," Lapid added.
MK Oded Forer (Yisrael Beytenu) accused the government of prioritizing political interests ahead of the elections.
“The Israeli government continues, even in its final days, to put political interests above the public interest," he stated.
"It is cutting the budget for the rehabilitation of the North, as well as health and welfare services in the periphery."
“But there is always money for draft dodgers and yeshivas. Netanyahu and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich will not touch their funding."
“Instead of harming essential services for Israeli citizens, it is time to cut the coalition funds that finance draft evasion and buy political loyalty," Forer added.

World leaders must wise up to threat of cyber-attacks or rogue fridges will be least of their worries | Heather Stewart
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:46:50 UTC
20:46:50 KST

Rogue French fridges were an unlikely talking point for the world’s leading economists, central bankers and finance chiefs meeting in a sultry Bangkok last week – helping to underline the spiralling cost of cyber-attacks.
Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, seized on news that supermarket chains across France had to chuck out piles of spoiled food after hackers accessed their fridge controls and turned up the temperature to 50C.
Speaking at the fund’s annual meetings in the Thai capital, she was keen to hammer home the importance of guarding against “bad actors” in a rapidly changing, interconnected world – especially now that AI was “putting the potential of digital fraud on steroids”.
Policymakers have been warning for some time that the AI boom could at some point threaten financial stability via a share price crash – a “correction”, as it is euphemistically called.
But a different, related threat came into sharp focus in Bangkok. Georgieva said she was concerned that cybercrime, turbocharged by AI, could undermine trust in the financial system altogether.
Social media feeds are rife with adverts using celebrity fakes to punt cryptocurrencies or gold, and even the old-school email-style scams can be generated far more prolifically.
Just as a sea of AI slop has the potential to undermine trust in fact-based reporting and send people down political rabbit holes, Georgieva fretted that cyber-fraud could knock consumer confidence in mainstream banks.
Recalling her own childhood behind the iron curtain in Bulgaria, she said many people did not trust the system, and kept their cash in a shoebox under the bed. “I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve … we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds,” she said.
It might not even take a cybercrime wave. This week the JP Morgan chief executive, Jamie Dimon, warned that the bank would not allow digital agents to operate on its customers’ behalf. “You don’t want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them,” he said.
AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, are starting to offer their users the opportunity to hand over their financial details. The agents will then scout for the highest savings rates and shift the user’s money accordingly.
Financial regulators fret about this for a number of reasons. One is that if such services become widely used, they could have destabilising herding effects. With deposits able to be moved around the financial system at a moment’s notice, it could accelerate a bank run in times of uncertainty.
A second worry is that highlighted by Dimon: who is responsible if your AI agent makes a financial decision on your behalf that turns out to be disastrous – or even criminal?
The answer is probably that we will need case law to find out, which will only come when something goes badly awry.
That is alarming because legal ambiguity about who owes what to whom when things go wrong can be an accelerant to financial instability.
We learned that lesson back in the 2008 financial crisis, when it turned out that some banks had built financial products with such fiendishly complex liability structures that they were effectively impossible to value – unleashing panic.
Speaking alongside Georgieva, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board of global central bankers, pointed to another arresting news story from this week – that Anthropic had warned AI models might soon be able to “self-replicate” in domestic devices. Who should bear the responsibility – and the costs – if your internet-enabled oven, or telly, blows up as a result?
One entirely prudent response might be for consumers to reject internet-enabled devices and stick to “dumb” appliances instead that can’t be hijacked by self-replicating bots. This month, some of those French supermarkets rushed to take their fridges offline to avoid the hack.
While it may not be much of a loss to society if internet-enabled kettles and fridges do not take off, the financial analogue to a dumb appliance would be Georgieva’s shoeboxes – and that would have costs for those consumers, and the smooth running of the economy as a whole.
As Bailey somewhat apocalyptically put it: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.”
Senior financial policymakers are genuinely disturbed at the collision between rapidly developing AI and the global financial system – which now extends well beyond heavily regulated banks – to embrace social media platforms, payments apps and other financial tools.
It is unfortunate this moment comes as the US – the crucible of the AI boom – is governed by a man whose main contribution to the debate has been to seek to rename AI “superintelligence”.
At the Bangkok meetings this week, Kevin Warsh, the chair of the US Federal Reserve, obediently used Donald Trump’s phrase on stage – as all US government agencies have been ordered to.
There has been some progress in acknowledging the risks. Trump’s superintelligence taskforce, chaired by the director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, is setting up mechanisms for AI labs to report “breaches, hacks, jailbreaks, and other issues” – although not, it seems, to submit their models for pre-launch testing.
The UK has pledged to take up the issue of AI safety as part of its agenda for the G20 presidency next year, and G7 finance ministers announced in Bangkok that they would carry out simulations to test the resilience of the global financial system to cyber-attacks.
That could help to highlight vulnerabilities, but the questions at stake are much wider and more complex than whether criminals can hack the banks – and are urgent now, just as the prospects for international cooperation seem bleak. Superintelligence will seem anything but super if its misuse becomes a trigger for financial chaos.

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into St. Petersburg, Setting Major Russian Oil Export Terminal on Fire

- Category

Ukraine Strikes Deep Into St. Petersburg, Setting Major Russian Oil Export Terminal on Fire
Ukrainian long-range drones struck one of Russia’s major oil export terminals in St. Petersburg overnight on October 18, igniting a fire at the facility as a large-scale drone attack targeted energy infrastructure across the city and surrounding Leningrad region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point on October 18, its FP-1 long-range attack drones were used to strike the Petersburg Oil Terminal, a major petroleum export facility on Russia’s Baltic coast. St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the terminal had been hit, with a fire breaking out in its oil storage area.
The Petersburg Oil Terminal is one of the region’s largest facilities for receiving, storing, and exporting petroleum products, with an annual handling capacity of approximately 12.5 million tons.
The complex contains 32 storage tanks with a combined capacity of approximately 442,000 cubic meters, making it an important component of Russia’s petroleum logistics and export infrastructure.
Footage published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ showed flames and smoke rising from the facility following the overnight strike. Reports indicated that the fire was still burning at approximately 7:30 a.m. local time.
The extent of the damage to the terminal’s storage infrastructure and its potential impact on petroleum exports have not yet been independently established.
The Petersburg Oil Terminal was not the only infrastructure facility targeted during the overnight attacks. Drones also struck a data center operated by VKontakte, Russia’s largest domestic social networking platform, near St. Petersburg.
The attack coincided with disruptions to VKontakte services and electricity outages in parts of the city and surrounding Leningrad region. The nearby 330-kilovolt Vostochnaya electrical substation was also targeted.

Drone Strike Hits Russia’s VKontakte Data Center, Knocking Services Offline as St. Petersburg Faces Blackouts
Russia’s digital infrastructure came under fire as an overnight drone attack reportedly hit a major VKontakte data center, exposing the vulnerability of the servers and power networks supporting one of the country’s most widely used online platforms.
A major overnight drone attack struck a data center belonging to Russia’s largest social network, VKontakte (VK), near St. Petersburg on October 18, disrupting digital services and coinciding with widespread power outages across parts of the city and surrounding Leningrad region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The attack targeted VKontakte’s data infrastructure alongside several other facilities in the region, including a major electrical substation and an oil terminal. Russian users subsequently reported significant disruptions to the social network and related online services.
The targeted data center is located in Novosergievka, in the Vsevolozhsky district of Russia’s Leningrad region, just outside St. Petersburg. The facility contains four server halls, approximately 640 server racks, and more than 20,000 servers, making it a significant component of VKontakte’s digital infrastructure.
The complex is located next to the 330-kilovolt Vostochnaya electrical substation, which was also reportedly struck during the attack.
Following the overnight strikes, parts of St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region experienced electricity outages, raising questions about the extent of the damage to the area’s power infrastructure.
At the same time, users across Russia began reporting problems accessing VKontakte and associated services. According to data from the Russian outage-monitoring platform Sboy.RF, complaints about VKontakte increased sharply between 3:00 a.m. and 5:00 a.m. local time on October 18.
The exact scale of the disruption remains unclear, and it has not been independently established whether the reported outages resulted from direct damage to the data center, interruptions to its electricity supply, or other technical failures.
VKontakte is Russia’s largest domestic social networking platform and a central part of the country’s digital ecosystem, serving tens of millions of users. Its parent company, VK, also operates a range of digital products, cloud services, and online platforms.
The reported attack on VKontakte’s infrastructure was part of a broader overnight wave of drone strikes around St. Petersburg. St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the Petersburg Oil Terminal had been hit, with a fire breaking out in its oil storage area.
The terminal is a major facility for handling and storing petroleum products, with 32 storage tanks and a combined capacity of approximately 442,000 cubic meters.
The reported strike follows earlier attacks on three Yandex data centers in Russia between October 8 and 11. According to Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, activity among suspected Russian disinformation accounts dropped by nearly 84% following the first strike, highlighting the potential impact of data center disruptions on Moscow’s online influence operations.

Better connectivity will boost India-Russia ties – Indian CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Better connectivity will boost India-Russia ties – Indian CEO
Improved connectivity, including more direct flights, could act as a catalyst for stronger bilateral trade between India and Russia, Manish Synghal, board member of the East-West Group of companies and chairman and managing director of Dimaz Group, has told RT India in an exclusive interview.
Speaking on the sidelines of the Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan, central Russia, Synghal said, “Easier travel procedures, subject to the respective governments’ policies, and more direct air links can stimulate tourism, business travel, investment and people-to-people exchanges.”
Officials in Tatarstan, of which Kazan is the capital, told the media they are in talks with the East-West Group and the Russian authorities about launching direct flights to India, including to its financial hub, Mumbai.
“A Kazan-Mumbai connection is worth exploring, provided a detailed assessment confirms sustainable passenger demand, commercial viability and the necessary regulatory clearances. With the right cooperation between governments, airlines and the tourism industry, such initiatives could create meaningful benefits for both sides,” Synghal said.
Asked about India’s efforts to diversify trade in response to tariff pressure from key trading partners, Synghal said diversification was “a strategic necessity for India,” adding that “our objective should not be to replace one market with another, but to build a broader, more balanced and sustainable network of international trade partnerships.” He said he sees potential in tourism, civil aviation, pharmaceuticals, agriculture and food processing, information technology, engineering, and transport and logistics.
Synghal emphasized that Russia’s regions offer major opportunities beyond the country’s main commercial centers. “For Indian businesses, the priority is to develop a deeper understanding of regional demand and local regulations, identify reliable partners, and establish commercially viable, long-term projects,” he said.
Trade between India and Russia reached $38 billion in the first half of this year and remains on course toward the annual target of $100 billion by 2030 set by the leaders of the two countries, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar told the media on the sidelines of the forum. “We think we are on the right path to achieve the target,” Kumar said, explaining that further focus areas would include boosting Indian pharmaceutical exports to Russia and expanding opportunities for India’s skilled workers, who are increasingly being hired by Russian companies.
