Pope Leo to gradually resume papal activities since removal of cancerous tumour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:40:25 UTC
20:40:25 KST

Pope Leo told a crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square on Sunday that he would “gradually resume” his activities, at his first appearance before the faithful since undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.
The Catholic leader, 71, was greeted with applause as he appeared unaided at the window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace to deliver his Sunday angelus. It was his first public appearance since making the shock announcement at the previous Sunday’s address that a small nodule had been found on his lung.
Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma – on Tuesday, after doctors removed part of his right lung to extract the tumour.
He thanked those who had prayed for him in recent days, saying that he appreciated the support while adding that the experience had made him feel especially close “to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity”.
“Now that this delicate phase has passed … I will gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” he said.
Leo left Gemelli hospital in Rome on Saturday, where doctors deemed him “fit for discharge” after undergoing blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning.
Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They said they were waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer had spread and if more treatment would be needed.
The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital.
The pope undertook some work duties in hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
There have been questions over whether Leo would be able to manage a gruelling 12-day trip to South America in November. However, his surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him from travelling.
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to fully recover from the operation “in another 10 days or so”.
Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.
The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

Egyptian parliament begins emergency session on possible troop deployment to defend Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:34:16 UTC
20:34:16 KST

Sahin Demir
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Egypt’s parliament began an emergency session on Sunday to consider possible measures to defend Saudi Arabia, including the potential deployment of Egyptian forces, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
The extraordinary session, held in Egypt’s New Administrative Capital, was chaired by Parliament Speaker Hisham Badawi following a request from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, according to the state-run Al-Ahram newspaper.
The session comes after Sisi said Saturday that Egypt was prepared to take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to defend its security and sovereignty.
“I call on parliament to hold an emergency session to authorize this move if we are asked to do so,” Sisi said.
Under Article 152 of Egypt’s Constitution, the president, as supreme commander of the armed forces, cannot declare war or send Egyptian troops on combat missions outside the country without consulting the National Defense Council and obtaining approval from two-thirds of parliament.
Parliament’s internal regulations also require such authorization to be considered during an urgent closed session convened at the president’s request following consultations with the National Defense Council.
Earlier Sunday, Egypt’s National Defense Council, chaired by Sisi, declared “full solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and decided to provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to defend the kingdom’s security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity, and safeguard Islamic holy sites.
The council stressed that Saudi national security was linked to Egyptian and Arab national security.
It also decided to intensify political and diplomatic efforts in coordination with regional and international parties to reduce tensions and peacefully resolve regional crises.
The developments come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, which has carried out missile and drone attacks targeting the kingdom.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government has intensified military operations against the Houthis in recent days, launching airstrikes on Houthi-held areas, including the capital Sanaa.
The Houthis have also threatened further attacks on Saudi territory, including oil facilities, as the conflict continues to escalate.

Royan Intl. Twin Congress slated for September 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Royan Intl. Twin Congress slated for September 2027
TEHRAN – Tehran will play host to the Royan International Twin Congress, including the 28th Congress on Reproductive Biomedicine, the 23rd Congress on Stem Cell Biology and Technology, and the 22nd seminar on Nursery and Midwifery, from September 1-3, 2027.
The three-day event aims to exchange knowledge and expertise, showcase the latest research achievements and novel technologies, and bolster interactions among researchers and experts, and lay the basis for scientific cooperation at national and international levels. The first two congresses will be held in English, and the last one in Persian, IRNA reported.
Over the past two decades, Royan International Twin Congress has provided an opportunity to display scientific findings, becoming a platform for the establishment of professional collaborations and the expansion of research cooperation among domestic and international researchers.
Faculty members, researchers, healthcare professionals, and students are invited to submit their scientific abstracts. The deadline for the submission of abstracts of the articles to the upcoming Royan International Twin Congress is April 20, 2027.
In 2026, a total of 447 articles out of 589 submitted articles were accepted to be presented, including 197 posters and 7 articles in the Reproductive Biomedicine Congress, 186 posters and nine articles in the Stem Cell Biology and Technology Congress, and 45 posters and three lectures in the Nursery and Midwifery Seminar.
The 27th Congress on Reproductive Biomedicine hosted 31 lecturers, including eight from England, Australia, Belgium, Russia, Italy, Germany, and Switzerland, who attended the event online. Out of 34 lecturers addressing the 22nd Congress on Stem Cell Biology and Technology, 14 were from Turkey, Russia, Malaysia, Canada, the US, and the Netherlands. Moreover, 19 Iranian scholars delivered lectures at the 21st seminar on Nursery and Midwifery.
Royan Institute
Royan Institute was established in 1991 by the late Dr. Saeid Kazemi Ashtiani and a group of researchers and physicians at the Iran University of Medical Sciences of the Academic Center for Education, Culture, and Research (ACECR) as an outpatient surgery center to provide medical services to infertile couples, as well as research and training in reproductive sciences.
Reproductive Biomedicine and Stem Cells Biology and Technology has been demonstrated to be one of the most successful experiences of scientific gathering in Iran and West Asia since 2000.
In 2002, the research fields at Royan Institute also extended into stem cell studies. Afterward, the research findings were adjusted for application in regenerative medicine and cell therapy approaches. After three decades, the Royan Institute focuses on increasing the success rate of infertility treatment alongside embryo health and the level of public health through cell therapy clinical services.
During these twenty years of active involvement in sharing and exchanging scientific knowledge and expertise with renowned scientific institutes and scientists, the Royan Congress has helped to form many shared scientific projects and exchanges.

Trump eyes reopening Europe to Russian gas – NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:32:18 UTC
20:32:18 KST

Trump eyes reopening Europe to Russian gas – NYT
The US plan for securing peace in Ukraine calls for Europe to increase its purchase of Russian gas, while Ukraine would consider reopening pipelines that once carried it to the EU, The New York Times reported on Saturday, citing people familiar with the talks.
The proposal is the latest in a series of steps by US President Donald Trump to broker peace between Moscow and Kiev. It follows an agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and the waiving of sanctions and tariffs mandated by the late American Senator Lindsey Graham.
Washington has reportedly pitched restoring Russian gas exports to Europe as part of a longer-term plan to offer Moscow economic incentives under a broader settlement. The proposed deal would also address relations between Russia and NATO, security guarantees for Ukraine and territorial issues, the sources told the newspaper.
US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly raised the idea of restoring Russian gas flows to Europe via Ukraine in talks with European and Ukrainian officials, including Vladimir Zelensky during a visit to Kiev in September.
Russian gas exports through neighboring Ukraine were only halted in January 2025, after authorities in Kiev opted not to extend the transit deal with Moscow.
Russia supplied around 45% of the EU’s gas imports before the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, but sanctions and damage to key infrastructure, such as Nord Stream 1, had cut its share to about 12% by 2025. The bloc nevertheless bought 36 billion cubic meters (bcm) of Russian gas last year, including pipeline supplies and liquefied natural gas (LNG). The latest estimates put the value of EU purchases of Russian LNG at €7.2 billion, nearly €1 billion more than in 2024.
Since the halt of gas transit through Ukraine, TurkStream has been the only remaining route for Russian pipeline gas to the bloc.
Brussels began phasing out gas imports from Russia under some short-term pipeline contracts in June 2026 and plans to ban Russian LNG imports from January 2027 and pipeline gas imports by September, with a complete phaseout targeted by the end of that year.
Meanwhile, Russia has shifted more energy exports to Asia, with deliveries of Russian natural gas to China reaching 38.8 bcm in 2025, up 24.8% from a year earlier. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow is ready to supply fuel to EU countries but needs a signal from Brussels. He said Russia would assess the feasibility and commercial viability of such exports rather than wait for Europe to “slam the door” on energy ties.

Gaza buries remains of 75 Palestinians recovered from rubble of homes destroyed by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:30:49 UTC
20:30:49 KST

Hundreds of Palestinians on Sunday attended the funeral of 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed by Israeli forces in Gaza City during the early months of Israel’s genocidal war, Anadolu reports.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza City.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defense, told Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighborhood in northeastern Gaza City.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defense’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told Anadolu on Oct. 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a ceasefire agreement in effect in Gaza since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

One person died and three others suffered serious injuries when a car veered off a motorway in southern Finland early on Sunday, police confirmed. The accident occurred at approximately 4.40am on Highway 4, also known as the Lahti motorway, near Orimattila in the Päijät-Häme region.
The vehicle was travelling south towards Helsinki when it left the road about three kilometres north of the Luhtikylä interchange.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
According to the Päijät-Häme rescue department, the car was travelling at high speed when it entered the central reservation and flew across a gap above an underpass before landing on the opposite side.
The vehicle sustained extensive damage but came to rest on its underside between the motorway carriageways, Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat reported.
Four people, including the driver and three passengers, were inside the car when the accident occurred.
Emergency services arrived at the scene and worked to free the occupants from the wreckage. Rescue personnel dismantled parts of the vehicle to assist medical teams.
Police confirmed that one occupant died and the remaining three sustained serious injuries.
The rescue department told Finnish broadcaster MTV News that driving conditions were normal at the time of the accident. Temperatures were slightly below freezing, but the road surface was dry.
The crash disrupted traffic heading towards Helsinki for several hours while emergency crews carried out rescue operations and investigators examined the scene.
Authorities initially closed the southbound carriageway before reopening one lane at approximately 7am.
Police have not established the cause of the accident or confirmed whether excessive speed contributed to the vehicle leaving the road.

The Dimple factor: Can she crack BJP's women-voter fortress &amp; deliver UP to Akhilesh?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:30:07 UTC
20:30:07 KST

NEW DELHI: Like many women who marry into political families, Dimple Yadav’s entry into politics was more a matter of circumstance than choice. She made her electoral debut in 2009 after her husband, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, vacated the Firozabad Lok Sabha seat, choosing to retain Kannauj after contesting from both constituencies.Despite a star-studded campaign, Dimple lost to Congress candidate Raj Babbar. Since then, however, she has contested five Lok Sabha elections, winning four.Yet, her electoral record did little to dispel the perception that she was a relatively passive player in politics. Within the Samajwadi Party, she was seen as a low-profile figure who complemented her husband from the background. In Parliament, she was often spotted sitting behind Akhilesh, thumping her desk in support of his speeches.For years, Dimple appeared unable (or perhaps unwilling) to step out of her husband’s political shadow.That may now be changing.With the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections approaching, Dimple, who has largely accompanied Akhilesh at party meetings and public gatherings, has been entrusted with an independent political responsibility. The move signals a possible shift in her role as Akhilesh prepares for another bid to return to power at 5, Kalidas Marg, after a decade out of office.
From Akhilesh’s shadow to SP’s second-in-command
Ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, Dimple Yadav is stepping into a more prominent role in the Samajwadi Party. Since Mulayam Singh Yadav’s death in 2022 and the decline of Shivpal Yadav’s influence within the party, she has increasingly emerged as one of its most visible campaigners and a key figure in its leadership.During the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, Dimple addressed rallies across more than a dozen constituencies. She also retained Mainpuri, the family stronghold, by a margin of nearly two lakh votes. Her media appearances and social media presence have grown considerably, reflecting a more assertive public role than in the past.
Her growing political visibility has extended beyond election campaigns. During the protests over the NEET paper leak in June and July, she emerged at the forefront of the party’s outreach to student protesters. She also led delegations to meet climate activist Sonam Wangchuk during his hunger strike, expressing support for his demands.On July 20, she joined the student-led “Sansad Chalo” protest in New Delhi and was seen tending to injured students after clashes with Delhi Police.While Akhilesh was inside Parliament, Dimple was out on the streets.She has also become a more vocal representative of the party’s position on issues ranging from women’s safety to the alleged embezzlement of donations made to Ayodhya’s Ram temple. Both inside and outside the Lok Sabha, she has sharpened her attacks on the BJP, challenging its claims on governance and social justice.Dimple has also accused the BJP of deliberately delaying the implementation of women’s reservation, despite Parliament passing the legislation in 2023.“When the Bill was tabled in 2023, all political parties supported it and it was passed, which explains that the opposition was in no way against the Bill. If the BJP’s sole intention was reservation to women, they would have implemented the Bill passed in 2023,” she said.“They have other motives behind moving the amendment Bill,” the Mainpuri MP added.Her latest initiative is the proposed Stri Samman Samriddhi Yojana, a scheme aimed at the economic and social empowerment of women that the Samajwadi Party says it will introduce if voted to power in 2027. The proposal promises eligible women an annual payment of Rs 40,000.“Women’s power will develop not merely by talking about it, but by giving women true representation. Respect and prosperity of every woman included in the PDA as ‘Aadhi Abadi’ (women) is our resolve,” Dimple said.
“She deserves respect simply because she is a woman. Social empowerment and strengthening her position require respect even before prosperity,” she added.The announcement also places the Samajwadi Party in direct competition with the BJP over women-focused welfare. It came amid reports that the Yogi Adityanath government was considering a direct cash-transfer scheme offering women Rs 50,000.
Why Akhilesh needs Dimple
The PDA formula — Pichada, Dalit, Alpasankhyak (backward classes, Dalits and minorities) — helped the Samajwadi Party stage a remarkable comeback in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections.After winning just five of Uttar Pradesh’s 80 seats in 2019, the party secured 37 in 2024, emerging as the state’s largest party in the Lok Sabha. It expanded beyond its traditional Muslim-Yadav support base by fielding candidates from non-Yadav OBC and Dalit communities.But replicating that success in an assembly election will require more than maintaining caste arithmetic. As Akhilesh prepares for the high-stakes polls scheduled for early 2027, he is looking to preserve the party’s momentum and widen its appeal further. Women, who cut across caste and religious boundaries, are central to that effort.
The scale of the opportunity is considerable. Women account for 45.46% of Uttar Pradesh’s electorate, with 6,09,09,525 registered voters, according to the figures cited by the state’s electoral authorities.They have also consistently turned out in greater numbers than men in recent elections. In the 2022 Assembly polls, women’s turnout stood at around 62.2%, compared with 59.6% among men. The pattern continued in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, when turnout among women was 57.22%, against 56.46% among men.Yet women voters have historically been a weak spot for the Samajwadi Party.According to the Lokniti-CSDS post-poll survey for the 2022 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, the BJP enjoyed a 13-percentage-point lead over the SP-Rashtriya Lok Dal alliance among women voters.The BJP has also repeatedly invoked the law-and-order record of previous SP governments to portray the party as insensitive to women’s safety. Recalling the period before 2017, chief minister Yogi Adityanath said during a public address in Gorakhpur: “A saying had become popular: ‘Dekh Sapayi, bitiya ghabrayi’.”He alleged that criminals and strongmen under the then government had created an atmosphere of fear, leaving families worried about their daughters’ safety.This is where Dimple could prove politically valuable.Her growing prominence gives the Samajwadi Party a recognisable woman leader who can take its PDA pitch beyond caste coalitions and make aadhi abadi — women, or half the population — a more visible part of its political strategy. She can serve as the face of its outreach to women, amplify its welfare promises and challenge the BJP’s claim to be the more women-friendly party.She also offers the SP a way to counter its longstanding image problem on law and order. Unlike the party’s male leadership, which continues to face the BJP’s allegations of mafia-gunda raj, Dimple has no comparable political baggage. Her public persona is less confrontational, potentially allowing the party to project a more measured and inclusive image without abandoning its attacks on the ruling party.Her role could also help the SP challenge the BJP on women’s representation and welfare on more equal political terms.Rather than relying solely on Akhilesh to make the case, the party now has a prominent woman leader with electoral credibility, national visibility and a place within its inner circle.Dimple’s Rajput background could offer another avenue for outreach beyond the party’s traditional support base. Whether that translates into wider support among Rajputs, however, remains uncertain.
How an SP win could reshape Dimple’s role
A return to power in Uttar Pradesh could further transform Dimple’s position, both within the Samajwadi Party and in national politics.If Akhilesh becomes chief minister, Dimple could assume a more substantial role in Parliament and potentially take on greater responsibility for coordinating the party’s parliamentary strategy. A stronger organisational position could also put her at the centre of the SP’s outreach to women and communities beyond its traditional support base.Such a shift would mark a significant departure from the role she occupied for much of her political career: a low-profile MP whose public identity was closely tied to her husband’s.But greater visibility does not automatically translate into electoral gains. Dimple’s prominence could help the SP soften its image, challenge the BJP’s women-centric welfare politics and give its promises on representation and economic empowerment a more credible public face. Whether she can materially alter voting patterns, however, remains an open question.Uttar Pradesh is expected to vote in February-March 2027 to elect a 403-member assembly, though the Election Commission has yet to announce the official schedule.
In the 2022 assembly elections, the BJP won 255 seats, securing a second consecutive term in power. The BJP-led NDA won 273 seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured 111, a significant improvement on its tally of 47 in 2017. The Congress was reduced to just two seats, down from seven in the previous election.For Akhilesh, the next election will be a test of whether the coalition he built in 2024 can be sustained and expanded. For Dimple, it could be an opportunity to establish herself as more than a trusted political companion and emerge as an independent force in the party’s bid for power.

Taiwan group urges tougher safety rules for large vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:29:37 UTC
20:29:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Higher-risk large vehicles should be considered for camera systems paired with audible and other active hazard warnings, the Consumers’ Foundation said Saturday.
The group, a public-interest watchdog, singled out public buses for priority consideration. Current rules let certain large vehicles meet visibility requirements with any one of three options: a surround-view display, side cameras with an in-cab screen, or a close-proximity mirror paired with front-right radar warnings, per UDN.
The foundation warned against new designs that create more work for drivers, arguing that cameras leave drivers with more to monitor while radars detect hazards more effectively. It urged audible warnings, saying more images do not guarantee better awareness of danger, per CNA.
The foundation called for full results from a transport ministry project that installed various active warning systems on 800 large vehicles, including missed-warning rates and changes in accidents and violations, according to UDN. Official figures have yet to show a clear improvement in accidents or violations. The group also wants serious crash records to show whether the equipment was working.
When a large vehicle turns, its rear wheels cut inside the path of its front wheels, putting people beside it at risk. The foundation linked that movement and blind spots to about 2,000 turning crashes and more than 2,000 casualties a year.
The group also urged slower turns and reviews of pedestrian signal timing at dangerous intersections. It sought equipment tests covering motorcycles passing nearby, image delays, rain and darkness.

Pope Leo says he will "gradually resume my activities" after cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.
The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.
''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
"This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are living with illness or infirmity," the pope said.
He told the crowd that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital," where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.
''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli Hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. He was discharged Saturday after the four-day stay. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared.
"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," said Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.
''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.
"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.
Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have urged Ukraine and European allies to consider resuming Russian natural gas transit through Ukrainian pipeline infrastructure as a key economic element of a prospective peace settlement, The New York Times reported.
According to officials familiar with the discussions, the proposal was presented by the Trump administration during high-level consultations with President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior European policymakers.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The initiative has encountered firm opposition across European capitals, particularly in Germany, where officials warn that reviving reliance on Russian hydrocarbons undermines continental energy security.
American negotiators argue that restoring Russian pipeline flows to Europe would provide the Kremlin with a commercial incentive to halt military operations, while generating valuable transit revenues for Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction. Washington also anticipates that sustained inflation and elevated energy costs will eventually prompt European consumers to demand cheaper supplies.
The proposal forms part of a broader, long-term settlement architecture being explored by the White House, encompassing future NATO-Russia relations, post-war security guarantees for Kyiv, and territorial arrangements.
Some Ukrainian and European officials briefed on the discussions suggested that Washington could seek a share of the commercial proceeds generated from the restarted gas trade.
US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
A White House spokesperson confirmed that the administration’s peace proposals incorporate economic incentives for both Moscow and Kyiv to encourage a durable armistice.
Backchannel references to Nord Stream 2
According to sources cited by The New York Times, discussions between American and Russian representatives have also touched upon the sabotaged Nord Stream 2 undersea pipeline across the Baltic Sea.
One source familiar with the backchannel contacts described restarting intact segments of Nord Stream 2 following a peace accord as the “simplest step” to stabilize regional gas balances.
However, White House officials formally denied that reviving the Baltic pipeline project had been actively discussed in recent engagements.
The gas transit proposal follows earlier economic inducements presented by Witkoff and Kushner during multilateral talks in Miami, which included unfreezing up to $100 billion in immobilized Russian state assets, authorizing a Middle Eastern buyout of Lukoil’s foreign operations, and easing sanctions on Belarusian potash.
German pushback and Berlin security warnings
The prospect of restoring Russian pipeline supplies has provoked decisive resistance in Berlin, formerly the largest purchaser of Russian natural gas in Europe prior to the February 2022 full-scale invasion.
During diplomatic consultations held in Florida, Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, pushed back forcefully against the initiative. German officials emphasized that Russian gas remains Russian regardless of whether transactions are structured through intermediary traders or third-party brokers.
Former German Economy Minister Robert Habeck warned against repeating past strategic mistakes, emphasizing that Germany has fundamentally adapted its energy architecture away from Moscow.
“Europe, and especially Germany, must never again become dependent on Russian gas. We saw how unreliable Russia was,” Habeck stated.
The diplomatic friction unfolds against intense domestic political debate within Germany. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has polled near 30 percent in recent nationwide surveys, has campaigned heavily on restoring direct imports of cheap Russian gas to curb consumer inflation and lower industrial electricity tariffs.
German and European officials maintain that restoring energy flows to the Kremlin would undermine European sanctions packages and generate billions of dollars in hard currency that underwrite Moscow’s defense industry, complicating ongoing transatlantic negotiations over post-war security frameworks.

Janno Jakobson: Speaking Estonian not the same as teaching Estonian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Janno Jakobson: Speaking Estonian not the same as teaching Estonian
Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background, but teachers can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide, writes Janno Jakobson.
The transition to Estonian-language education is one of the most significant changes in Estonia's education system. No one questions its necessity anymore, but are we, as adults, prepared to make enough of an effort to ensure its success? We are demanding increasingly better Estonian-language skills from students learning Estonian as a second language, but are we also creating the conditions they need to achieve this?
In discussions with colleagues from different schools, one point keeps coming up: The problem is not always a lack of skills among teachers, but rather how existing knowledge and skills are applied in everyday teaching.
Imagine a student who spends an entire school day in Estonian-language classes. The teacher speaks Estonian, the textbooks are in Estonian and the student completes exercises in a workbook. By the end of the day, however, the student has spoken only a handful of sentences in Estonian. Does such a school day do enough to support the student's language development?
To acquire a language, students must have opportunities to speak, ask questions, describe, explain their reasoning and make mistakes. Teaching subjects in Estonian requires teachers to set language-learning objectives alongside subject-specific goals and create opportunities to achieve them. Many teachers already have the methodological knowledge needed to do this. Yet when explaining more complex concepts, it may seem easier to switch to Russian. Students understand the material more quickly and the lesson can move forward.
But what happens when a teacher explains an entire topic in the students' native language, while the quiz or test must be completed in Estonian? Can we expect students to achieve a passing grade if they have not been taught the relevant Estonian vocabulary or given opportunities to use it?
In such cases, students may understand the subject matter perfectly well but struggle to understand the questions or formulate their answers. A poor result may therefore indicate a mismatch between the language of instruction and the language of assessment.
Are we grading knowledge of language proficiency?
Recent fourth-grade national assessments highlighted a contradiction in our education system. While the assessment of Estonian as a second language takes students' expected language proficiency into account, the same students faced significantly more complex vocabulary, lengthy texts and multipart questions in the natural science assessment.
Commenting on the linguistic complexity of the assessments, the Education and Youth Board (Harno) explained that the tasks are aligned with the curriculum and use the same terminology. If students' Estonian-language skills are insufficient, the agency recommends choosing the Russian-language assessment.
However, the Harno representative fails to consider that the students who took the natural science assessment have been studying subjects, including natural science, in Estonian for three years and may not even be familiar with the relevant terminology in Russian. I must admit that such a response is frustrating for teachers. Is recommending a Russian-language assessment really the solution to the challenges of transitioning to Estonian-language education?
Of course, students must also acquire subject-specific terminology in Estonian, but fair assessment means giving them an opportunity to demonstrate their actual knowledge and skills. That is precisely why, rather than simply recommending a switch of languages, we should also seek ways to make assessments in Estonian linguistically accessible to students.
Students cannot be responsible for adults' choices
A range of support measures have been established to facilitate the transition to Estonian-language education. Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) methodology centers operate at educational institutions, the Institute of the Estonian Language provides support through initiatives including the "Keelesamm" program and teachers in Tallinn can turn to the Tallinn Teachers' House and its methodology and competence center, MEKK. Teachers can attend training courses, receive guidance, explore teaching materials and learn from their colleagues' experiences. However, no trainer or methodology center can put what teachers have learned into practice in the classroom for them.
School leadership also has an important role to play. Schools must have a shared understanding of what Estonian-language education means and what principles should guide it. It is not enough for some teachers to consciously create an Estonian-language learning environment if others consistently switch to Russian during their lessons. Nor can the state's responsibility be limited to setting requirements. We need meaningful oversight that assesses whether Estonian-language education is actually working in practice.
Discussions about the transition to Estonian-language education often focus on students' lack of motivation, the language environment at home and parents' attitudes. These factors affect learning, but they cannot justify prejudging students' abilities.
Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background. Teachers, however, can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide. Students learning Estonian as a second language do not need lower expectations. They need high-quality teaching, consistent language support and teachers who believe in their abilities.
The transition to Estonian-language education is not simply about changing the language of instruction. Its goal must be to equip students with sufficient Estonian-language proficiency to continue their education, pursue their chosen field of study and compete on an equal footing with others in the future.
Achieving this requires effort from everyone involved. Students have a duty to learn, teachers have a responsibility to teach with clear intent, school leaders must establish shared principles and the state must ensure realistic expectations and meaningful oversight.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Albanian PM says mass protests a threat to EU membership, not government
TIRANA, Oct 18 - Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down from growing street protests, and said they were a threat not to his government but to Albania's progress toward joining the European Union.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks and pulled up paving stones to throw at police, who have responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests in the summer against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, pose the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office.
"I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook.
“Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
As Rama spoke, excavators were digging up and removing the paving outside his office in central Tirana as a new round of protests was expected.
Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU, and is aiming for entry by 2030.
Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week.
"God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand," he said.
Police said 388 people had been charged with criminal offences during the demonstrations. Scores of police officers and protesters have been injured. REUTERS

Iran, Iraq discuss boosting academic ties to meet domestic, regional priorities

Addressing the challenges and educational problems faced by the students in reciprocal countries was the other issue raised by the two sides.

FAO representative highlights livestock sector’s role in food security, rural employment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

FAO representative highlights livestock sector’s role in food security, rural employment
TEHRAN – The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Representative in the Islamic Republic of Iran Farrukh Toirov, has underscored the strategic importance of the livestock and poultry sector for the country’s food security, rural employment and agricultural economy, emphasizing the need to promote sustainable development through innovation, stronger animal health services and the conservation of indigenous livestock genetic resources.
He made these remarks during a speech at the 25th International Exhibition of Livestock, Poultry and Related Industries, held in Tehran on Sunday.
Highlighting Iran’s technical capacities, research institutions and private sector expertise in livestock and poultry production, the Representative described the exhibition as an important opportunity to strengthen partnerships, exchange knowledge and promote innovative solutions to improve productivity and resilience across livestock production systems.
According to the FAO Representative, meeting the growing demand for nutritious animal-source foods requires improvements in production efficiency, animal health, feed-use efficiency, food safety and environmental sustainability. The Representative also identified water scarcity, rangeland degradation, feed availability and costs, and animal diseases as major challenges facing the sector.
Referring to FAO’s longstanding cooperation with the Ministry of Agriculture Jahad and national technical and research institutions, the Representative highlighted the conservation and sustainable development of endangered indigenous livestock genetic resources as an important area of ongoing collaboration.
In this context, FAO is implementing a Technical Cooperation Programme project focused on valuable indigenous breeds, including Bactrian camels, Sarabi cattle, Mahabadi goats and Markhoz goats. The project aims to strengthen conservation approaches, promote community-based breeding programmes and support the livelihoods of livestock keepers.
Indigenous livestock breeds represent valuable genetic resources because of their adaptation to local climatic and environmental conditions. Their conservation not only contributes to agricultural biodiversity but also strengthens the resilience of livestock production systems under challenging environmental conditions, preserving options for future livestock development.
FAO has also previously supported the conservation of Bactrian camels in Iran and introduced mobile livestock biotechnology and reproductive services for livestock keepers in the country’s northwestern regions through its technical cooperation initiatives. These experiences provide a foundation for expanding community-based livestock services, improving access to specialized technical support and strengthening the productive capacities and livelihoods of rural and pastoral communities.
The FAO Representative also emphasized that animal health is a fundamental pillar of food security, public health and sustainable production. The One Health approach, which addresses risks at the human–animal–environment interface, is essential to tackling zoonotic diseases, transboundary animal diseases and antimicrobial resistance. Strengthening veterinary services, surveillance and early warning systems, biosecurity measures and the responsible use of antimicrobials was identified as critical to reducing economic losses, protecting livestock productivity and safeguarding public health.
In a further part of the address, the Representative referred to FAO’s emergency support for Iran’s fisheries sector following the impacts of the recent armed conflict. The emergency Technical Cooperation Programme project aims to restore essential fishing capacities, support affected coastal communities and strengthen household food security and livelihoods, particularly in the provinces of Sistan and Baluchestan and Hormozgan.
Referring to the United Nations’ designation of 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, with FAO serving as the lead agency, the Representative highlighted the importance of sustainable rangeland management, agricultural biodiversity conservation and support for pastoral communities.
Concluding the address, the FAO Representative called for stronger collaboration among government institutions, research centres, producers and the private sector, linking the future of livestock and poultry production to the theme of World Food Day 2026, “Innovate Today, Nourish Tomorrow.” The Representative stressed that combining scientific innovation with traditional knowledge and locally adapted solutions can improve productivity, enhance nutrition, protect the environment and strengthen rural livelihoods.

Iraq’s new Turkmen minister pledges co-op with Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

In addition to Iraq’s Turkmen community, Mohammed Samaan Agha’s appointment as a state minister in Iraq was also welcomed in Türkiye.
The minister, who also happens to be the leader of the Iraqi Turkmen Front (ITC) and serves as governor of Kirkuk, promised to work “for the benefit of Iraq and Türkiye” in remarks to Turkish journalists on Sunday in Baghdad.
He met Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Saturday as the latter was in Baghdad to attend a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
Fidan congratulated him on his appointment as minister and told journalists that Türkiye had long monitored the challenges facing Iraq’s Turkmen community. He said addressing those challenges required progress on Iraq’s broader political and social problems.
”They are loyal citizens of Iraq. They are also highly conscious of preserving their own identity, which is precisely what we want,” Fidan said.
He stressed that the Turkmen community had consistently played a constructive role in Iraqi society and politics. “Türkiye and Iraq are brotherly countries, extensions of one another geographically, culturally and historically,” Fidan said. He called for a more institutionalized framework for bilateral cooperation that would serve both countries’ interests.
Agha was elected governor of Iraq’s Kirkuk province in April by the Kirkuk Provincial Council, becoming the first governor of Turkmen origin in more than a century. Turkmens are a Turkic-speaking minority whose total population is estimated at around 3 million. Agha visited Türkiye on an official trip following his election.
The new minister told reporters that, as a minister of Turkmen origin, he would work on issues in the interests of the people of both countries.
Commenting on his meeting with Fidan, Agha highlighted the historical, geographical, religious and cultural ties between the two countries.
Noting that Türkiye and Iraq shared many common issues, Saman Agha said: “We discussed all issues of mutual concern to the two countries, particularly security, trade, oil exports, energy, water and the fight against terrorism. In the coming period, as a Turkmen minister, we will do our best to carry out work in these areas that will benefit both countries and their peoples. We have initiated this process. God willing, we will make very good progress.”
Stating that regional tensions were negatively affecting the Iraqi economy, he said developments around the Strait of Hormuz and tensions between Iran, Israel and the United States had seriously harmed Iraq’s oil exports.
Emphasizing that Türkiye was an important neighbor and economic partner for Iraq, Agha said the Development Road Project should be accelerated.
“The faster the Development Road Project is carried out and implemented, the more beneficial it will be for Iraq. Türkiye will also benefit from it, but Iraq’s gains will be greater because this project will connect the East with the Western world,” he said.
Unveiled in May 2023, the Development Road Project is a $20 billion regional infrastructure initiative designed to facilitate the transport of goods from the Gulf to Europe via the Grand Faw Port in Basra, southern Iraq. The port would be linked to Türkiye and subsequently to Europe through an extensive network of railways and highways.
In April 2024, Türkiye, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on joint cooperation on the project.
Noting that the issue of water was becoming increasingly important as winter approached, Agha said water and security had also been discussed during talks between Türkiye and Iraq.
Recalling that Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi had also recently raised security concerns, the minister stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation between the two countries in these areas.
“I believe that relations between Iraq and Türkiye will become much stronger in the coming period,” he said.
Commenting on the Iraqi Turkmen Front’s political goals and the representation of Turkmens in the new government, Agha said they attached importance to maintaining good relations with the country’s different social groups.
“First and foremost, we trust in God. Then, we trust in the votes of our people and the support they have given us and the Iraqi Turkmen Front. At a very critical and difficult time for Iraq, we have established very good relations with our Shiite, Sunni and Kurdish brothers. We maintain sound and sincere relations with everyone,” the Turkmen minister said.
Recalling the agreement on rotating the governorship of Kirkuk among Turkmens, Kurds and Arabs, Agha said it was also significant that Turkmens had subsequently secured representation at the ministerial level in the government.
Emphasizing that all social groups in Iraq should be represented in the country’s administration, he said: “I think everyone in Iraq has now come to the conclusion that, alongside Shiites, Kurds and Sunnis, Turkmens and Christians must also be represented. This would allow all segments of Iraqi society to feel that they are represented in the government Cabinet.”

Atlanta’s iconic tavern marks Georgia’s past with an eye on future as midterms approach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:15:04 UTC
20:15:04 KST

Atlanta’s iconic tavern marks Georgia’s past with an eye on future as midterms approach
ATLANTA, Georgia – Since it was established in 1956, Manuel’s Tavern in Atlanta has hosted legendary Democratic leaders while its founder played a key role in the city’s move from a Republican to Democratic stronghold. With the state’s Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff leading the polls in the midterms amid rumours of a future presidential run, the tavern is once more at the heart of the political action.
It’s TV debate time at Manuel’s Tavern, an Atlanta landmark that has hosted Democratic heavyweights for six decades, and the patrons are glued to the screens as Georgia’s incumbent Senator Jon Ossoff trades barbs with his Republican challenger, Mike Collins, in the second and final debate before the November 3 midterms.
The Republican contender this time is more biting and sharp after his lacklustre performance in the first debate. But the crowd here appears unimpressed. Between sips of beer and bites of burgers, they follow the political slugfest impassively. This is a Democratic watering hole, and their candidate, Ossoff, is leading in the polls. They’re also familiar with their senator’s special talent for getting under the skin of his opponents. At Manuel’s Tavern, they appear to know how the show will unfold.
Collins starts the debate with an opening salvo. “This is a race between Georgia and Georgetown,” he declares, referring to the historic Washington DC neighbourhood of Georgetown in a dig at Ossoff’s much-reported, but never confirmed presidential ambitions.
Ossoff, looking unfazed, declares he intends to keep his opponent on the defensive for the next hour. “We’re going to pick up right where we left off last week and ask him questions he refused to answer,” says the 39-year-old Georgia senator and only Democrat in the chamber seeking re-election in a state US President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election.
Watch moreGeorgia's Ossof-Collins showdown lies at the heart of the battle for US Senate
Nearly two years after Trump was elected to a second presidential term, Ossoff is at the centre of Democratic hopes to take back the White House in the 2028 presidential election. For many Trump critics, the opposition dream of regaining the executive reins and rolling back some of the current president’s most egregious policies rests on Ossoff, the fearless, articulate, handsome, young Democratic “Star of the South”.
At his final debate, Ossoff once again denied having presidential aspirations and reasserted his commitment to his Georgia constituency. But analysts are not willing to write off an Ossoff run for White House in the future. Georgia, they note, has previously given the country a Democratic president. Like Ossoff, he was a man not just of the South, but of America’s “Deep South”, the subregion of Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina, that has a distinct historic and cultural identity.
Fifty years ago, when Jimmy Carter, a former Georgia senator and governor, was elected 39th president of the United States, he was hailed as a product of a changing "Deep South". Carter’s death at the ripe old age of 100 sparked an intense examination of his legacy on the country. It’s a heritage that lives on at Manuel’s Tavern, where the walls host a virtual museum of photographs, paintings, memorabilia and mementos to Carter, Georgia’s “son of the South”.
The tavern also marks the state’s changing political colours from a reliably “red” Republican stronghold to a “purple” swing state, and the critical role Atlanta – the “capital city of America’s South” – has played in some of the darkest and brightest chapters of US history.
Above all, Manuel’s Tavern tells the story of a family’s journey from a remote valley in Ottoman-run northern Lebanon to the copper mines of Tennessee, the growth of Atlanta city, and a generational rise up political ranks. In short, it’s the story of the American immigrant dream – and it lives on with the chatter of clients debating televised debates.
Talking politics, life and art by the window
On December 29, 2024, when the Carter family announced the death of the former president – born in October 1924 in Plains, Georgia – many Atlanta locals immediately began arriving at Manuel’s Tavern to have a pint and pay tribute to a beloved statesman.
It was a logical gathering spot, according to Brian Maloof, the owner and son of the bar’s namesake, Manuel Maloof. Back in 1970, when Carter decided to run for governor, he chose Manuel’s Tavern to launch his Georgia gubernatorial campaign.
Maloof recounts that over the years, Carter developed a close friendship with his father. “I met president Carter ... I don’t know … dozens of times. His wife, his daughter, his son, his brother, Billy. I met them all. They were our neighbours at the Carter Center,” he explains, referring to the headquarters of the former president’s NGO down the road from the bar. “And before there was the Carter Center, president Carter – or governor Carter at that time – and my father had a friendship. So, the Carters have been a big part of the tavern for a very long time.”
Steven Pitts, the tavern’s longtime general manager, points to a lineup of photographs of the former president near a window, including one of Carter and his wife, Rosalynn Carter, at the 1976 Democratic convention. “Jimmy Carter and Manuel used to sit at the front window all the time, talking about politics and life and art and everything else that you could think of. And so, in general, we just became a big political hotspot,” he explained.
From ‘bedroom Republican’ to Democratic stronghold
For Georgia’s Democrats, as well as national party figures visiting Atlanta, Manuel’s Tavern has been an essential stop on the campaign trail.
Pitts moves from room to room in the sprawling establishment to provide a guided tour of the vast collection of photographs and memorabilia adorning the walls. “Bill Clinton's been here a couple of times,” he says, pointing to framed photographs on a wood-panelled wall. “Hillary Clinton has been here a couple of times. We had Al Gore, he was Bill Clinton’s vice president, of course, and we have several other pictures as well … John Kerry, who was a senator who ran for president in 2004, was here, amongst others.”
The roster includes Barack Obama, who dropped in while he was president. “There he is, throwing darts,” Pitts says, pointing to a photograph. “Obama was waiting for an interview, and he asked for some darts to throw. I was not here, but apparently he was very good at darts. This is not a surprise,” he adds with a smile.
Established in 1956 on the corner of North Highland and North avenues in the Poncey-Highland district of eastern Atlanta, Manuel’s Tavern attracted notable Democratic politicians and supporters not just because it was the place to be. In the late 1970s, its founder, Manuel, also entered local politics and gained a reputation as a man with a plan and the drive to make it happen.
By the time he died in 2004, aged 80, Manuel Maloof had served for decades in various elected positions in DeKalb County, a primarily suburban district of the Atlanta metropolitan area. An obituary in the city’s leading daily, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, noted, “Mr Maloof played a central role in the transformation of DeKalb County from bedroom Republican suburb to the urbanised Democratic stronghold it is today”.
‘First Amazon’ of oxcart deliveries
For the Maloof family, it’s been a long journey from the Qadisha Valley in northern Lebanon, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, where Gibran Maloof – Manuel’s father and Brian’s grandfather – was born.
“My grandfather immigrated to the US around the end of World War I,” explains Maloof. “He had an oxcart, and he travelled from Atlanta to Copperhill, Tennessee, delivering mining supplies. He worked that route every month, and along the way, he took orders from people living in small towns. He was like your first Amazon – a much, much slower, early Amazon,” he adds with a laugh.
The family’s history of running taverns began with the Tip Top Billiard Parlor right by the gold-domed Georgia State Capitol building in downtown Atlanta, which Gibran purchased and ran for three decades. “When the Georgia state legislature was in session, we were the closest place for those state legislators to have a drink and to discuss things,” explains Maloof. “My grandfather listened to what they were talking about. He heard them talk about making Atlanta a city as prominent as Paris and London. They wanted Atlanta to be as important as New York and Chicago.”
So when the legislators discussed plans to build Lake Lanier, a man-made reservoir in northern Georgia to supply Atlanta, Gibran promptly bought land in the area, Maloof explains. The Tip Top Billiard Parlor was purchased right before Prohibition, which lasted from 1920 to 1933 in the US. “There were people who thought he was an ignorant immigrant who didn't know that Prohibition was coming. But he saw it as an opportunity to buy something very inexpensively,” the grandson recounts.
Looking to the future with an eye on the past
Gibran’s son, Manuel, was born in the US and served as an Army Air Forces mechanic during World War II. He was deployed to England, where he met his wife, Dolly. When he returned to Atlanta to start his own enterprise, Manuel modelled his eponymous tavern after the British wartime pubs.
The family’s history lives on at Manuel’s Tavern, Pitts explains, pointing to the imposing wooden bar, which was originally in Gibran’s Tip Top Billiard Parlor and survived a fire.
As a politician, Manuel displayed his oxcart-driving father’s enthusiasm for infrastructural development, including a pugnacious push to expand Atlanta’s metro transportation system.
After he died in 2004, Manuel’s ashes were placed in the tavern. Pitts points to a wooden cabinet high on the memorabilia-cluttered bar wall containing an urn with a pennant of the Lebanese flag. “We joke that he’s watching the cashier,” says the tavern’s loyal general manager with a grin.
The ashes in the cabinet, photographs of legends, signed books on the shelves imbue the tavern with a sense of historical heft for the clients – and of responsibility for the current owner.
“Every day that I go in there, I'm reminded of all the people that were there before me, and how important it is that I do the very best job I can to keep this going. I have never, ever really viewed myself as the owner. I'm more of the historical preservation manager,” Maloof says.
“It's definitely a double-edged sword,” he confesses. “It's pretty amazing to be part of something that has been in Atlanta for so long and has a big history with my grandfather, my father, my uncle. That's tremendous. But it's also very difficult because you have to keep up with modern times, but people don't want the timer to change very much. So, it's very tricky.”
Read moreOssoff and El-Sayed: Two Senate races and what they say about the Democratic Party
Just weeks before the country goes to the polls in the 2026 midterms, the patrons at Manuel’s Tavern have finished watching their Senate candidates debate their future in an establishment that celebrates the past.
Caleb Scott, a policy writer who also works at a data collection centre, declares Ossoff the winner of the latest debate and says he was particularly interested in the senator’s position on artificial intelligence (AI), especially the hot-button subject of data centres.
“The issue I personally found interesting was when Senator Ossoff talked about AI. I think that we do need to lead the world when it comes to actually governing AI,” he says. “Georgia could lead the nation considering how many data centres are being built here. People see it as a problem, but it's already here, and if we don't learn how to govern it now, while it's still in the elementary phases, then we're not going to know what to do when it becomes the behemoth that it could be in the years to come.”
While Scott has been working on an AI governance policy paper, he says that when it comes to watching candidate positions, there’s no place like Manuel’s Tavern to follow the proceedings. “I enjoy the camaraderie that they have here. I met Senator Ossoff years ago, before he became our senator, right here actually. It’s a pretty cool place to be.”

NEW DELHI: At least 19 people died and 25 others were injured in a stampede at Kolkata's Chorbagan Durga Puja pandal on Saturday evening.The stampede occurred after a sudden downpour triggered a crowd surge, with hundreds of visitors rushing into the pandal for shelter and trapping those already inside.West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari blamed the incident on the organisers' callousness and appealed to puja committees across Kolkata to adopt safety measures.“It’s a painful incident and extremely heartbreaking,” Adhikari said.“As per initial information received, the incident happened due to an announcement made by the puja committee. Right now our priority is to treat the 25 people who have been injured. Among them, 24 are stable but one is critical. We are standing by the affected families. The Chorbagan puja pandal has been handed over to forensic teams, STF and fire brigade,” he added.Here's what we know so far about the incident.Locals blame sudden rain, narrow space and lack of police personnel for stampedeLocals, who were among the first responders, said sudden rainfall, narrow lanes, a heavy rush of visitors and a lack of adequate volunteers and police personnel for crowd management contributed to the stampede.
They said heavy rain forced people inside the pandal to wait for the weather to improve, while visitors outside grew restless and tried to rush into the already crowded marquee.Pramod Gupta, who lives near the Chorbagan puja pandal on Radha Madhav Lane, said the queue of visitors to the marquee had stretched to Mahatma Gandhi Road, about 700 metres away."Everything was fine till the rain started," he told news agency PTI."Standing in front of my house, I could hear screams as people rushed out. I and my daughters helped four girls and asked them to stay in our house till the situation eased," he said.Locals also said narrow lanes and a lack of police personnel and volunteers inside the pandal hampered the swift rescue of the injured."Ambulances could not reach the spot, and the injured had to be carried out to the main thoroughfare some distance away," a woman told PTI."We started the rescue work by breaking the bamboo structures and barricades of the pandal," another local man alleged.High-level committee reviews pandalsA high-level committee formed to review safety arrangements at major Durga Puja marquees across West Bengal began visiting community puja pandals on Sunday.The panel includes disaster management secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and director general of fire services Anuj Sharma.The panel members will visit several crowd-puller Durga Puja pandals across Kolkata to review safety and security norms and crowd management plans, sources told PTI.The administration has stressed the need for wider exit points, adequate lighting and the removal of bottlenecks caused by temporary rope enclosures.7 arrestedKolkata Police have arrested seven people, including organisers of the Chorbagan Durga Puja, a senior officer said.Police have also registered a suo motu case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder."We have arrested seven people. They were among the 14 detained last night. More arrests may be made," the IPS officer told PTI."Rajkumar Seoda and Shantanu Dubey were the secretary and vice-president, respectively, of the Chorbagan Puja committee. Biplab Mukhopadhyay was responsible for installing the bamboo structure at the pandal, while Kaushik Saha and Pintu De were in charge of crowd management," the officer said.Those arrested include the puja committee's secretary and vice-president, as well as two employees of a private security agency, among others, he said.Victims' bodies handed over to kinAuthorities handed over the bodies of those killed in the stampede to their family members on Sunday.Among the victims was a 27-year-old nurse whose mortal remains were taken to her native place in Hooghly. British police said Saturday they would take no further action against the wife of the government’s national security adviser over a social media post referencing the banned group Palestine Action, Anadolu reports.

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organization in July 2025. Expressing support for the group can carry a prison sentence of up to 14 years.

'Jews see us as Arabs, and some Arabs see us as traitors': SLA family's daughter becomes student leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:12:41 UTC
20:12:41 KST

In the living room of the Joubran family home in Nahariya stands a display cabinet filled with figurines of Christian saints, photographs of bearded Maronite clergymen, a depiction of the Last Supper and a Lebanese flag. Among these objects, which reflect the family's faith and origins, lies something you might not expect to find there: a booklet of teachings by Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.
But perhaps that should not be surprising. The family of George Joubran, a former artillery officer in the South Lebanon Army (SLA), navigates several identities. They are Lebanese, but also Israeli Christians who attend church while remaining deeply rooted in Jewish society.
Sometimes, those identities clash. "Jews see us as Arabs, and some Arabs see us as traitors," explains Sonia Joubran, 24, the eldest daughter of Adeline and George, who was elected chair of the student union at Kiryat Shmona University about three months ago.
Like her younger sisters, Lia, 22, and Joelle, 20, Sonia was born in Israel and has never visited her family's homeland. Yet she is convinced that peace is within reach.
"Most Lebanese want peace, and I believe that within a year I'll be able to visit. And who knows, maybe one day I'll be Israel's ambassador to Lebanon," Sonia told ynet.
We met Sonia and her mother ahead of the start of the academic year at Israel's northernmost, and newest, university.
George, 58, owns a company that brings workers from Jordan to Israel. He spends most of his time in Eilat and returns home every two weeks. He grew up in the village of Mazraat al-Mathaneh, near the Christian town of Jezzine. The Jezzine enclave was not part of Israel's security zone in southern Lebanon, but it was controlled by an SLA battalion that cooperated with Israel and fought Hezbollah.
Adeline, 48, a medical secretary at the Galilee Medical Center in Nahariya, grew up in Beirut. When she was 12, she moved with her family to the village of Burj al-Muluk (al-Khirbeh), along the road between Marjayoun and Metula. Her father worked as a cook, preparing meals for IDF and SLA soldiers, which made him, in Hezbollah's eyes, a collaborator with Israel.
'We thought we'd be back in two weeks. We've been here 26 years'
Adeline remembers May 24, 2000, the day the IDF withdrew from Lebanon, as though it were yesterday.
"I was 21, a psychology student and a teacher at a school in the village of Houla," she recalls. "In the middle of class, the principal came into the room and said, 'What are you doing here? Get out now! Hezbollah has entered the village.'
"I started fleeing on foot. My father picked me up along the way, and when we got home, he said, 'We're leaving for Israel.' I said, 'What do you mean, leaving? I have an exam at university.' And my father said, 'Forget the exam. We're leaving.' Hezbollah had threatened that the moment the IDF withdrew, they would enter our homes and slaughter us in our beds."
Just four kilometers separate Burj al-Muluk from the border crossing at Metula. "We waited there for seven or eight hours before they let us enter. We thought we'd be back home within two weeks, a month at most. And here we are, 26 years later."
Adeline met George at Kibbutz Shomrat, where she lived with her parents. Their eldest daughter was born in Nahariya, and when she was a baby, the family moved to Eilat. They returned north when Sonia was 4.
"There's an SLA community in Nahariya, and it was easier to adjust here. In Eilat, my kindergarten teacher didn't know how to deal with me because I didn't speak Hebrew," Sonia recalls. "Here, I learned the language, and my mother learned alongside me."
At elementary school, however, she once again felt like an outsider. "I was subjected to a kind of social boycott. I was the only SLA child in the class, and the other children didn't know what that meant. There was a Druze boy in my class, and they would always push us toward each other and shout, 'Arabs!' at us. Instead of dealing with it, the principal would remove both of us from the classroom."
In high school, Sonia studied Arabic in an intelligence-track program whose graduates are intended for IDF Unit 8200. "I also attended an 8200 preparatory program, but in the end I didn't enlist and received an exemption because I was the daughter of an SLA veteran.
"I have family in Lebanon, my paternal grandmother in Jezzine and an aunt on my mother's side in Beirut, and I was afraid that if Hezbollah discovered I had joined the IDF, they would harm them. Instead, I did national service at the hospital in Nahariya as a medical assistant," she said.
'They crossed out Israel and wrote Palestine instead'
After completing her national service, Sonia was accepted to study medicine at New Vision University in Tbilisi, Georgia, alongside students from around the world. She enjoyed her studies and made friends, but on the morning of October 7, 2023, during the second semester of her first year, everything changed.
"I found out about October 7 from an Instagram Story posted by an Arab Israeli student who uploaded videos of Hamas terrorists inside Israel and mockingly wrote, 'They're playing PUBG with them.' That's a game about shooting and killing. I'm not saying everyone is like that. There are extremists on every side."
The atmosphere on campus suddenly became hostile. "They turned the library into a mosque. There was a map of the world's countries at the university, and suddenly I saw that someone had put an X over Israel and written 'Palestine' instead.
"No matter how hard I tried to explain that our people had been massacred and murdered, they didn't understand. I had friends who were murdered, and I have friends who survived the Nova festival. It was difficult. I decided to stop studying and return to Israel," Sonia said.
Wanting to continue in a field involving care and treatment, she decided to enroll in psychology studies at Tel-Hai College, shortly before it became Tel-Hai Kiryat Shmona University.
Alongside her studies, she volunteered with the Rashi Foundation's Ma'aleh initiative, supporting the Ma'alot-Tarshiha municipality and helping develop strategic plans and programs for young people. She was also active in the Rothschild Foundation Ambassadors program, which trains young social leaders. Becoming involved in student leadership was therefore a natural next step.
Elections for the Kiryat Shmona University student union were held in June. "I decided to run at the very last minute and registered just a few hours before the deadline. I was stunned when I was elected because I hadn't run a major campaign, and I'm not Jewish," Sonia explains.
As chair of the student union at Tel-Hai Kiryat Shmona University, Sonia also serves on the general assembly of the National Union of Israeli Students.
Although she entered the race at the last minute, she has a clear vision. "It's important to me to work toward the rehabilitation, development and strengthening of communities in the Upper Galilee, especially Kiryat Shmona, after three difficult years of war. Twenty percent of our students are Arabs, Druze and Circassians, and it's important to me that minority populations feel part of the community and contribute to it.
"We met with Mayor Avichai Stern, and we're advancing social initiatives that will turn Kiryat Shmona into a vibrant city where young people choose to live."
One of the most significant days for Sonia in the past three years was September 27, 2024, when Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah was killed.
"We were so happy. We opened champagne and put up a sign downstairs for all our religious neighbors announcing that Nasrallah had been killed, because it was Shabbat. It was a moment of closure for my parents and the entire SLA community. But there's still a lot of work to be done to rid Lebanon of terrorist strongholds."
So far, Sonia has met her relatives from Lebanon mainly at the home of her uncle, who lives in Canada, or in nearby countries such as Jordan. But she believes that one day, and not in the distant future, visiting her aunt in Beirut will require nothing more than a 90-minute drive.
