JPMorgan Chase Bank subsidiary discriminated against conservative customers, US investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:55:29 UTC
19:55:29 KST

A JPMorgan Chase Bank subsidiary was found to have discriminated against political conservatives, according to a statement by the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) on Wednesday, alongside the release of its supervisory review of nine US banks following accusations that they were "debanking" customers for political or religious reasons.
Debanking refers to the limiting or refusal of services to a bank customer, such as closing accounts or refusing loans. While not inherently illegal, debanking becomes controversial when a bank's decisions are based on factors such as politics or religion rather than on an individual's financial or compliance risks.
Although not a judicial ruling, the review, conducted under US President Donald Trump's August 2025 executive order, "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans," aimed to identify and document specific instances the Trump administration would view as violations of the order.
The review examined nearly 100,000 complaints between 2020 and 2025 and over 50,000 documents; additionally, it targeted Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, US Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank, which, together with JPMorgan Chase, make up the nine largest banks under OCC supervision.
The findings showed multiple discriminatory practices at several banks, with JPMorgan Chase subsidiary WePay Inc. having closed accounts associated with pro-Trump merchandise, such as MAGA hats, which were categorized by the bank as hateful and intolerant.
In a September 2021 case, WePay closed a conservative customer's account after the subsidiary flagged items the customer was selling, including a Trump election-victory flag and a shirt describing former US President Joe Biden as illegitimate.
In an additional 2021 incident, the subsidiary initially halted payment processing for an event after the organizer's social media posts were found to include descriptions of Biden and former US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director Dr. Anthony Fauci as enemies, though the decision was eventually reversed.
Also in 2021, WePay closed a nonprofit's account after discovering its positions on LGBTQ issues, with bank employees describing the "right-wing religious conservative" organization as having "strong anti-LGBTQ rhetoric."
WePay shut down following findings, JPMorgan spokesperson says
A JPMorgan spokesperson responded to the findings, telling CBS News that the subsidiary has since been shut down as a result of the revelations.
WePay "did not meet our expectations," the spokesperson told CBS. "We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates."
The spokesperson emphasized that the bank's policies "prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views."
JPMorgan Chase staff were further found to have altered records of customers who were rejected because of their political views, including a case where a senior employee directed the removal of the phrases "right-wing" and "very tasteless, gun-centric videos" from records after a customer was denied commercial services multiple times between 2021 and 2023.
"As more far-right competitor(s) step in to take this company’s extreme clients, it may become more mainstream and more appropriate for JPM (JPMorgan) to bank," one redacted passage read.
In a further case of political discrimination, PNC Bank declined to extend a line of credit to a media company, in part because bank employees' personal politics conflicted with the business owners' conservative views, with an employee having written that "it becomes really difficult to justify aligning ourselves with a company whose owners have built very public personas around opinions very contrary to PNC’s beliefs/values."
Capital One denies services to groups across political spectrum
On the other side of the political spectrum, Capital One was found to have rejected Democratic pro-abortion organizations from opening accounts, though it did the same to a pro-gun group, a position generally seen on the political right.
Regarding religion, Wells Fargo terminated payment services for a religious nonprofit organization despite no violation of its agreement with the bank, according to an intermediary's initial determination.
Financial discrimination was also found across several banks investigated by the OCC, with small businesses receiving more stringent treatment than their larger counterparts, including instances in which wealthier companies faced negative publicity or even criminal proceedings.
Environmental aspects were also heavily considered for lending, as loans for non-renewable energy businesses were found to face stringent restrictions in several cases.
“Today’s report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation’s largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses,” said Currency Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould. “Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra; it is a mandate."
"Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," he added. "Accordingly, the OCC will be assessing further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework applicable to the largest banks to reduce the likelihood of these harmful practices recurring in the future.”
CBS reached out to other banks cited in the report beyond JPMorgan Chase, but they declined to comment, instead referring the news agency to a statement from a banking trade group.
"The banking industry supports fair access to banking services and has been working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers," said the Bank Policy Institute. "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk rather than reputational risk."

The language of extermination: NAZA, Artificial Intelligence and Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:51:04 UTC
19:51:04 KST

The 80-minute documentary NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is chastening. It examines the conduct of the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) during its ferocious, unremitting war in Gaza, drawing upon the interviews of 24 anonymised military and intelligence personnel. The interviews were filmed on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with profiles and voices appropriately altered. The name of the documentary draws on a Hebrew acronym for nezek agavi or collateral damage, an obscene term used when counting the estimated number of civilians who will perish in a military strike. Last month, the film won the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, receiving a standing ovation lasting 25 minutes.
The interviewees focus on the terrifyingly relevant role played by Artificial Intelligence (AI) targeting systems used in guiding the bombing campaign launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of 7th October 2023. In Abraham’s words, “the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanisation of Palestinians.”
One of the interviewed subjects speaks of the goal being “quantity, not quality.” Another notes the conscious decision to target Hamas members, some even in the lower echelons, when they would be at home even if it meant killing family members and neighbours.
In one recalled instance, the phone of a 12-year-old girl was hacked to learn when her father would arrive home. The subsequent strike killed her. The cold logic is revealed in the rhetorical question posed by one of the interviewees: “When people talk about ‘flattening Gaza,’ what do you mean if not executing people?’
Despite being placed in a “too hot to handle” category by prominent indie studios, the self-distributed documentary managed to pass the US$500,000 mark in the United States after two weeks of release. Eight days after premiering at New York’s IFC Center, it went on to earn US$125,000. A further 85 theatres across 30 cities across North America then showed the film. Michelle Goldberg, writing in The New York Times, was impressed by the drawing power of the production when attending Walter Reade Theater for a screening. The venue, seating 268, was at capacity. “This is, in my experience, very unusual for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like ‘NAZA,’ win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.”
Militaries specialise in euphemised killing. A dedicated process of terminology and assessment sanitises and exsanguinates: death and murder become justifiable, necessary measures against an enemy bloated with wickedness and venality. In that process, mock tributes are paid to the canon of international law, notably international humanitarian law and doctrines of targeting. The more honest generals do us a favour by boasting about high casualty figures and mass mortality: they are not hiding matters and lurking behind worn ceremonies and the emperor’s non-existent clothes. Take the remarks of a former head of Israeli military intelligence made in a leaked audio: “For every one person [killed] on Oct. 7, 50 Palestinians must die.” Those militaries with a heavily staffed legal department supposedly providing guidance in striking a target, largely to reassure the squeamish that they are not implicated in acts of murder, are always suspect. In that regard, the IDF provides a model example, always claiming to do things differently from other powers in the region, yet resorting to the selective language of exculpation.
The reception of the film in Israel has been markedly hysterical. This was to be expected: the film unmasks and discomfits. It demolishes shibboleths. The IDF chief of staff Eyal Zamir vowed to use “every tool at our disposal” against the production. The Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar thought the film treasonous.
Abraham and Szor were “willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world”. The irate minister was keen to “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” he thundered in a social media post. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also called upon the passing of legislation stripping the duo of their citizenship, a curious point given the existing provisions of Israel’s Citizenship Law. (Making German Jews stateless was a specialty of the Third Reich: that the Jewish state would consider this to its citizens is a distinct, bitter irony, yet sadly permissible in light of the Israeli Supreme Court ruling in 2022 validating revocation for acts done in “breach of loyalty to the State of Israel”.)
Activists and members of the far-right party Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir protested outside the parents of Szor’s house, with a speaker calling for both directors to be executed and the homes of their families to be demolished (collective punishment remains a great inspiration for tribal sentiment).
The IDF has marshalled its own response in a document accusing the filmmakers of presenting “a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process.” The narrative of the documentary drew upon “substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality.” Worth noting here is the lower register of critique that does not entirely repudiate the targeting practices of the IDF, dressed up in the apologetics of collateral damage. Concessions and confessions are always evident from those in and of power who resort to such dismissive language as “misrepresentative” and “disingenuous”.
Be that as it may, the agitated response is illuminating. The Lavender database, to take one objection, was apparently not one of targets, merely “a database that assists intelligence analysts.” This represents a distinction without a difference. The faith placed by militaries in the divinities of technology are hard to shake; there is nothing here to say that such analysts do not treat these data sets as unimpeachable. AI and religious deities serve to do the imagination for others; they discourage independent thinking and verification. Why bother when you have someone, or something else, doing it for you?
The response remains weak in claiming that the IDF believes itself “bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.” The staggering death toll in Gaza, always sneered and jeered at by the Israeli authorities and their defenders, would suggest otherwise.
NAZA serves to, as the Israeli American historian Omer Bartov points out, address a “state of denial” by “actually speaking about the issue of what happened in Gaza rather than refusing to speak about it.”

It’s dealmaking time: despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late Saturday to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm election campaign.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part on Monday in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries.
“This is an important relationship,” Rubio said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Friday that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill toward the “deepening partnership across Central Asia,” especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but only boasts a population of about 80 million people.
White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine -- with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia -- has repeatedly emphasized the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the secretary of state’s second official visit to India this year, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
Last February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fueled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by the Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani.

Zelenskyy Says Starlink Restrictions Apply Only in Ukraine While SpaceX Ignores Kyiv’s Inquiries
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of deliberately restricting Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, saying tests conducted in European Union countries showed that the same limitations did not apply outside Ukrainian territory. He also said the company had stopped responding to inquiries from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking to journalists in a group chat on October 17, Zelenskyy described the restrictions as a planned operation after Ukrainian officials tested Starlink terminals in moving vehicles across EU countries.
The President said Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine remain subject to a speed limit of approximately 161 kilometers per hour (100 mph). The restriction prevents Ukrainian forces from using certain drone interceptors against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, forcing them to rely on other air defense systems.
To determine whether the disruption resulted from technical problems or restrictions specifically targeting Ukraine, Ukrainian officials sent several vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into EU territory.
During the tests, the vehicles traveled at speeds exceeding 180 kilometers per hour (112 mph) where permitted, while their Starlink connections continued operating normally.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had documented the tests and collected evidence demonstrating that the restrictions applied inside Ukraine but not in EU countries.
He characterized the findings as evidence of a planned operation, although he did not publicly identify who had ordered the restrictions. The President also said Ukrainian military officials and diplomats were continuing efforts to contact SpaceX but had received no response through Defense Ministry channels.
According to Zelenskyy, explanations provided through other channels attributed the disruptions to technical problems. However, he questioned why those problems appeared to affect Ukraine specifically.
The accusations follow reports that SpaceX introduced new restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink, on October 14, without prior notification to Ukraine. The changes reportedly disrupted Ukrainian drone interception, strike operations, and frontline logistics.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk subsequently stated that Starshield was controlled by the US government, while the White House denied involvement and attributed the disruption to technical problems.
On October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported that Starshield connectivity during movement had resumed but said it was still investigating the restrictions.

Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:48:18 UTC
19:48:18 KST

Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
Smugglers in the Negev desert are increasingly using drones and helium balloons to transport narcotics across the border into Jordanian territory.
Amman, Jordan – Jordanians fear the country’s border with Israel is turning into a major drug-smuggling route amid a surge in high-tech operations by gangs using drones and helium-filled balloons.
Organised networks active in southern Israel’s Negev Desert have links to groups in Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, operating along one of the most heavily surveilled borders in the world, with Jordanian authorities increasingly concerned about the implications this could have for the kingdom.
This escalation coincides with changes in the regional drug trade, particularly after the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.
Elements in his regime were linked to the manufacturing and distribution of Captagon, an illegal amphetamine stimulant.
Syria became a hub for the distribution of Captagon to the Gulf, with Jordan a transit point and market for the drug. The Royal Jordanian Air Force carried out periodic strikes on drug manufacturing and smuggling points inside Syria, highlighting the huge security concerns Jordan had about the trade.
Since the collapse of the Assad government and the establishment of a new authority that views the Captagon trade as a national security issue, there has been a decrease in the drug trade from Syria into Jordan.
Although Druze militias in the Syrian province of Suwayda allegedly linked to Israel have been accused of continuing the drug trade, Jordanian security forces are increasingly focused on the Jordan-Israel border.
The use of quadcopter drones and balloons is reportedly among the new tactics used by gangs in Israel to smuggle hashish, crystal meth, and amphetamines into Jordan.
Jordanian security forces are said to be increasingly unhappy with the scale of the drug smuggling operations and have accused the Israeli army of not taking the issue seriously.
Initial data from Jordanian forces recorded 17 interception operations linked to drones during the first half of 2026 in Jordan’s southwestern border area with Israel.
They also recorded 231 smuggling and infiltration attempts and downed 56 drones across various borders during the same period.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al Jazeera that Jordanian forces were continuing efforts to prevent drugs from being smuggled into the kingdom. But they are evidently facing more complex activities by drug dealers.
“There is an increase in drug smuggling operations from Israel to Jordan using drones,” he said. “The number of seized drug cases during the current year reached 15,342 cases. Trafficking cases constituted about 28 percent of them, compared with 72 percent for usage cases.”
Israeli media reports indicate that gangs active in the Negev Desert are behind some of the smuggling operations into Jordan, where drugs can fetch higher profits.
There are estimates that 1kg of hashish can sell for approximately 7,500 pounds sterling (almost $10,000), according to the British newspaper The Telegraph, which recently uncovered the drug smugglers’ latest operations. Israeli security services believe that the price of hashish in Jordan is about 15 times higher than in Israel.
Due to widespread disenfranchisement and poverty, elements within Palestinian communities in Israel have been linked to the drug trade, according to reports. Multiple sources have accused Israel of allowing Palestinian towns and cities to become hotbeds of crime to create divisions and prevent calls for greater rights.
Ammar al-Qudah, a member of the Jordanian Senate and retired major-general in the Public Security Directorate, claimed that organised gangs in the Negev had obtained more than 1,000 drones that were originally used for agricultural and security purposes.
“The smuggling networks are linked to other gangs in Jordan, Sinai and the Negev, and rely on a route starting from Sinai, passing through the Negev, and reaching Wadi Araba, in addition to other routes including the Lebanese border with Israel and the Galilee region towards Syria,” he told Al Jazeera.
They are also using a range of sophisticated technology to bypass security on both sides of the border. This includes the use of helium-filled balloons equipped with GPS devices, drones capable of carrying about 50kg of narcotics, including black hashish and crystal meth, al-Qudah said.
He warned that a portion of the black hashish and crystal meth being smuggled into the kingdom is being sold domestically, with the rest going to other markets in the region.
With such high-tech operations, there are accusations that members of Israeli forces know about drug gang activities, based on past experiences in Egypt.
One West Point report said current and former trackers in the Israeli military in the Negev are being recruited by traffickers to provide intelligence to facilitate their operations in Egypt. In 2012, a number of Israeli service personnel were arrested on suspicion of collaborating with drug smugglers across the Egyptian border.
While there is no proof that the same situation is being repeated in Jordan, many have questioned how drones and balloons carrying drugs could cross a heavily surveilled and guarded Israeli border into Jordan.
Jordan’s counternarcotics department, in cooperation with the armed forces, has tracked such cases and made arrests.
Retired Brigadier-General Daifallah al-Daboubi, a strategic and military expert, said Jordan is witnessing a “reverse drug migration”, starting from the Sinai Peninsula, passing through the Negev region, and reaching the kingdom.
“Groups active in Beersheba and the Negev possess great financial capabilities and use advanced smuggling methods, most notably drones,” he said.
The Israeli army’s preoccupation with wars in Gaza, Lebanon and the occupied Golan Heights has provided smugglers with room to manoeuvre on the Jordan border, he added. But he ruled out the direct involvement of the Israeli political or military leadership in any drug smuggling.
Steps taken by Israel to boost security on its eastern border include the establishment of the 96th Division, which began operating in the Jordan Valley in 2025, and the construction of a controversial security barrier with Jordan.
But none of these measures appears to be designed to prevent drugs from leaving Israel; instead, they appear to be designed to prevent weapons and other illicit merchandise from entering the country from Jordan.

“We will make Türkiye a global center of attraction in health care,” Erdoğan said at the ceremony, adding that the country had become a destination for patients from around the world.
The president said Türkiye had made significant progress in expanding health care services through investments in public hospitals, city hospitals and private medical facilities.
He said two newly completed facilities — the Internal Medicine Hospital at Istanbul University’s Çapa campus and the Esenyurt Hospital — would be officially opened during the ceremony. Foundations were also laid for a new Orthopedics, Traumatology and Surgery-2 Hospital and the Deniz Abdal Mosque.
Reports from the event indicate that the Çapa hospital covers 44,000 square meters and offers a capacity of 186 beds, 39 of which are allocated to intensive care. Equipped with modern medical equipment, the center is tailored to advance medical training alongside patient treatment.
The Esenyurt Hospital has 200 patient beds and 50 intensive care beds, including neonatal intensive care capacity.
Erdoğan also announced that the government would launch a recruitment process for 38,000 non-physician health care workers before the end of 2026. The Health Ministry is expected to provide further details in the coming days.
The president thanked health care workers for their efforts to provide medical services across the country, saying investments in facilities and personnel would continue.
In a video message released earlier in the day, Erdoğan said Türkiye is opening a new chapter in its energy history with the deployment of the Osman Gazi floating production platform to the Black Sea.
“Today, we are opening a brand-new page in our energy history. We are sending Osman Gazi, essentially a floating industrial facility, off to its duty station in the Black Sea,” he said in a message sent to a ceremony marking the platform’s departure from Filyos port in Zonguldak.
“Osman Gazi is the first factory of the Blue Homeland, the maritime counterpart of our Century of Türkiye vision,” he said.
The president expressed his hope that the platform would provide beneficial services to the country and its people and wished success to the personnel who will work aboard it.
Equipped with 21 different units, the platform will process natural gas extracted from wells in the Sakarya Gas Field and transport it to Filyos through subsea pipelines.
“Natural gas production in the Black Sea will double to 20 million cubic meters per day, and starting in 2027, one in every three households will use our domestic natural gas,” he added.

TOKYO, October 18. /TASS/. For the first time since coming to power in October 2025, less than half of the Japanese -- 49.1% -- have expressed support for the government led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a Kyodo news agency survey said.
Over a third of the participants, or 33%, did not support Takaichi’s cabinet, while 17.9% of the respondents abstained from answering.
Almost 58% of the respondents believe that the prime minister was too late with dismissing Kazuo Yana, the minister of agriculture, forestry and fisheries, who found himself at the center of a scandal after threats to cut state funding for the local authorities, which did not support him in the latest general elections. He was also suspected of violating electoral legislation by providing free buses to transport his supporters during the elections.
At the same time, 54.7% of those surveyed believe that the Kazuo Yana scandal will have some degree of impact on the future political fate of the Takaichi government. According to Kyodo, this incident could become the main reason for the decline in the cabinet’s popularity.
More than 65% of the polled said they are concerned about the government’s plan to reduce the consumer food tax from the current 8% to 1% for two years, Takaichi’s pre·election promise, which was generally met with approval. However, the respondents now fear that the tax cut will undermine the country’s finances and will hurt other social spending.
The survey was conducted on October 17 and 18 across Japan by phone. The number of participants is not specified.

France reels from riots as 1,800 arrested and one dead
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
13:41:17 EEST
19:41:17 KST

France began clearing damaged streets and buildings on Sunday after protests over living costs and public services descended into riots, leaving one demonstrator dead, more than 500 emergency personnel injured and 1,800 people arrested across the country.
Around 550,000 people joined demonstrations on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris, as students, trade unions, teachers and former yellow vest protesters demanded action on prices, wages and public spending.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The demonstrations began peacefully in many cities before groups of masked individuals attacked police, looted businesses and set vehicles and public buildings on fire.
In Paris, police arrested 855 people, a record for a single event, according to Agence France-Presse. One demonstrator died after suffering a cardiac arrest during the protests.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters had suffered injuries. He accused far-left groups and criminals of organising attacks against public institutions and businesses.
“The Republic will yield nothing to those who seek to impose disorder and violence,” Nuñez wrote on X.
President Emmanuel Macron condemned the destruction and promised legal action against those responsible.
“No room for violence in our Republic,” Macron wrote on X on Saturday.
In Limoges, an arson attack destroyed much of the city's 143-year-old town hall. Firefighters contained the blaze after part of the building collapsed.
Haute-Vienne prefect Maurice Barate accused a group of masked individuals of deliberately setting the building alight.
In Marseille, rioters forced their way into city hall using a metal fence as a battering ram. Shops were looted, while authorities reported damage to businesses and public property.
Bordeaux Mayor Thomas Cazenave said as many as 100 shops had been looted. A group also entered the residence of the local prefect.
In Lyon, protesters set fire to the city's tourist office. Mayor Grégory Doucet described the situation as “total chaos in the city” in comments to BFMTV.
Police also reported attacks in Lille, Strasbourg, Rennes, Grenoble and other cities.
Across Paris, shopkeepers spent Sunday removing broken glass and clearing debris from their premises. Luxury retailers, restaurants and smaller businesses suffered extensive damage.
Police used tear gas and water cannon during confrontations in the capital.
The unrest followed weeks of student demonstrations that began in September over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating school buildings.
The movement subsequently attracted workers, parents, farmers and pensioners demanding higher wages, lower prices and greater investment in public services.
The CGT trade union backed Saturday's mobilisation, calling for higher wages and pensions and protection for public services.
A student interviewed by Al Jazeera said protesters wanted the government to address their demands.
“We are here because we want to take back our rights,” she said.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu blamed the violence on extremist groups and criminals, while Economy Minister Roland Lescure promised assistance for affected businesses.
The unrest comes ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, amid disputes over public debt, government spending and household costs.
Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan announced emergency financial assistance for businesses damaged during the disturbances.

Zack Polanski says application of Zionism is racist and no state has right to exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:39:14 UTC
19:39:14 KST

Zack Polanski has said Zionism in its current form is racist, that no country has a right to exist, and that the Green party motion on the issue was not controversial.
The leader of the Green party in England and Wales gave an unapologetic interview to the BBC on Sunday two weeks after his party approved a motion equating Zionism with racism.
Polanski did not attend the vote, prompting accusations of a lack of leadership, but he made clear he agreed with the broad thrust of it even if he felt it was unhelpful to have what he called a “debate about semantics”.
Asked by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg whether he thought Zionism was racist, Polanski said: “I don’t think this is actually controversial.
“What’s controversial is that 75,000 Palestinians have been murdered in the last few years, including more child amputees than ever in modern history. So when you take that to account, the fact that they’re being murdered because they’re Palestinian – that’s very obviously a racist ideology.”
He added: “I think Zionism is racism in the practical application of it. Now the conference had a debate about the motion, about the word. I said I think debates about words are unhelpful, and I still think that.”
Asked whether he believed Israel had a right to exist, Polanski, who is Jewish, said: “I don’t think any state has a right to exist under international law,” adding that the idea of a two-state solution was “for the birds” given Israel’s opposition to it.
The Green leader also insisted he had no regrets about the way he had handled the recent controversy, despite criticism from some prominent Jewish Green members, including Vivien Lichtenstein, the head of the Jewish Greens.
“I’m not sorry at all,” he said. “Vivien is someone I’ve had respect for and do have respect for, and partly co-founded the Jewish Greens together … Actually, when the Jewish Greens were surveyed about this motion, a majority supported it.”
Polanski’s defiant interview comes after the most difficult two weeks of his leadership of the party since he took over last September, during which he has endured the fallout from the conference vote and lost the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.
His strategy of shifting his party to the left, focusing on economically populist ideas and leaning into debates on Palestine and Gaza, initially paid dividends, with the party jumping from about 10% in the polls to 18% earlier this year.
In recent months, however, the party has tumbled, beset by questions over his tax affairs, a public spat with the police after the Golders Green attack and the recent row over Zionism.
He said on Sunday that he was confident voters would return to his party once they had seen more of Andy Burnham’s leadership of the country. “People more and more will see from Andy Burnham a change in rhetoric, but not a change in action, and know the Green party have been right all along,” he said.

Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:36:13 UTC
19:36:13 KST

Ukrainian officials sharply criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping planned sanctions against Russia, saying that it "sends the wrong message to the aggressor" and "helps only the Russians."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration needed up to 60 days to assess the potential economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs, while the White House argued that imposing them immediately could hinder efforts to negotiate a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
"If Russians are cheering yesterday's decisions in the US, it is certainly not about effective pressure to end the war," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on October 17. "Indecisiveness sends the wrong signal to the aggressor. It only prolongs the war."
He added that "Lindsey Graham understood this well," referring to the late senator of South Carolina for whom the sanctions legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- was named. Graham, who died on July 11, was a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine.
The bill passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and was signed into law by Trump in September. But in an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18.
The move prompted sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said removing the sanctions "definitely helps only the Russians."
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X on October 17.
The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions.
Rubio defended the White House's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia on October 17, saying Washington needed time to assess the economic consequences of additional penalties as conflicts across several regions strain global energy supplies.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a series of diplomatic and trade talks in Central Asia, Rubio defended the administration's efforts to balance pressure on Moscow against economic concerns.
The waiver followed a diesel deal Trump announced with Russia on October 9 that prompted criticism that Washington was prioritizing domestic fuel prices over efforts to constrain the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy called the waiver was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed."
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."
A senior envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, praised the waiver as "a truly historic moment."
Kirill Dmitriev, who heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, wrote on X late on October 16 that "economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations."
Energy Costs Complicate Russia Sanctions
Rubio said the administration needed 60 days to assess the effects of sanctions and tariffs, including their potential impact on countries such as India, which continues to rely substantially on Russian energy despite efforts to diversify its supplies.
He pointed to disruptions involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement, and the war between Russia and Ukraine as factors putting pressure on global energy markets.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," Rubio said.
The United States was paying higher prices than it wanted, he said, while some other countries were approaching a crisis over energy costs and availability.
Rubio also defended the administration's diesel deal with Russia -- which Zelenskyy called "a gift" to Putin -- arguing the fuel would have reached international markets regardless of whether the United States purchased it. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," he said.
Energy analysts have questioned whether the deal would significantly lower prices for American consumers, while warning that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with substantial economic benefits.
The waiver blocks additional sanctions and tariffs approved by Congress to discourage major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, although existing sanctions remain in place.
The decision drew sharp criticism from both parties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible," while Senator John Cornyn said the late senator Graham "would be appalled." Democratic lawmakers also accused Trump of helping Russia finance its war.

Japan readies Martian moon mission to uncover origins of life
The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration
Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the Solar System and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.
The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast-off from the Tanegashima Space Center Tuesday at 4.41am, according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).
“Being able to be involved in such a grand mission is incredibly exciting,” Makoto Arita, project manager of JAXA’s H3 rocket team, told reporters two days before the launch.

Turkish Cypriot President Erhürman (C) and Greek Cypriot leader Christodoulides (L) sit together at the festival.
The leaders of ethnically-divided Cyprus attended an annual bicommunal festival in the village of Pyla late on Oct. 17, marking a symbolic step as diplomatic efforts to resolve the island’s long-standing issues are ongoing.
Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman attended the event wearing a neck brace due to a recurrence of a cervical disc herniation but made no public remarks.
Seated alongside Greek Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides, Erhürman also joined in the folk dancing at the festival.
The event, aimed at fostering cultural ties and dialogue between Turkish Cypriots and Greek Cypriots, was also attended by Turkish Cyprus’ Republican Turkish Party (CTP) and the Greek Cypriot left-wing party AKEL.
Pyla, known as Pile among Turkish Cypriots, is one of the few villages in the U.N.-controlled buffer zone that continues to host both Turkish Cypriot and Greek Cypriot communities. The peace festival returned this year after a six-year hiatus.
“We are conveying a message of peaceful coexistence and underscoring the need to reunify our homeland once and for all,” Christodoulides said.
He added that, as he had recently told the Turkish Cypriot press, the island would undoubtedly be reunified if the decision rested solely with the two communities.
The Greek Cypriot leader also appeared to take an indirect swipe at the other side over the failure to reach agreement on a U.N. proposal concerning the opening of additional crossing points. He said U.N. envoy Maria Angela Holguin knew which side had immediately accepted the proposal and which had rejected it, without explicitly identifying either party.
Asked whether joint appearances with Erhürman at festivals and other events could become a regular feature, Christodoulides said he supported making such engagements routine, adding that this was precisely why he had attended the festival.
According to the media, Erhürman chose not to respond to Christodoulides’ remarks in order to preserve the positive atmosphere of the event.
Beyond their appearance at the festival, the two leaders are expected to attend upcoming meetings of the bicommunal technical committees on cultural heritage and youth, as well as the steering committee of the civil society consultative body. The two previously agreed to meet once a week.
Speaking to reporters on the second day of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 16, Christodoulides said the Cyprus issue would be discussed at a high-level meeting between the European Union and Türkiye scheduled to take place by the end of October.
Erhürman and Christodoulides are both expected to attend the U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31), which will be held in Turkish city of Antalya in November.
In a statement issued on Oct. 14, Erhürman announced that he had received an invitation to the summit from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and would be in Antalya on the scheduled dates. Christodoulides confirmed his attendance in a statement a day earlier.
Erhürman said he had learned through the media that Christodoulides would also attend the summit, adding: “As we have always said, diplomacy and dialogue are always good.”
It remains unclear whether the two leaders will meet on the sidelines of COP31.

Moscow’s defence ministry said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight.
Russian strikes kill two
In Ukraine, Russian forces struck residential buildings overnight, killing two people and injuring 12, including two children, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Sunday.
“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.
“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic.”

“Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions,” he wrote, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power as energy workers and repair crews worked round the clock to restore supplies.
Zelenskyy also said that the main targets of Moscow’s recent strikes were energy facilities, as the Russians were trying to “cause a blackout”.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.
Trump is also facing criticism in both Europe and the US after he signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump’s waiver would be a pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.
“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US.
“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

Ukraine’s Delta system proves NATO compatible at sea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:30:51 BST
19:30:51 KST

Ukrainian personnel ran maritime operations through the Delta combat system at NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal, integrating every asset transmitting data to NATO standards including uncrewed aerial, surface and subsurface systems and radars, according to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
The ministry said the exercise “again confirmed DELTA’s compatibility with NATO systems and brought Ukrainian solutions closer to standardization.” All assets transmitting telemetry in line with NATO STANAG 4817 were successfully integrated.
REPMUS, the Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems exercise, is run annually by the Portuguese Navy and is the largest international exercise focused on employing uncrewed systems in maritime operations. This was Ukraine’s third year taking part.
The ministry said partners and allies “practiced the joint employment of unmanned aerial, surface, and subsurface systems and tested interoperability within multinational forces”, with the Ukrainian team drawn from different services and branches and coordinating its activity through Delta.
Ukrainian specialists trained alongside allies in reconnaissance, maritime area monitoring, manoeuvring, and escort and simulated engagement exercises, and shared combat experience with partners on the employment of uncrewed systems in the maritime domain.
On how the system performed, the ministry said the Ukrainian team noted “DELTA’s uninterrupted operation under unstable connectivity, as well as the ease of streaming in the Vezha module compared with other platforms.” Delta served as the primary command and control platform at REPMUS 2025, when it integrated more than a hundred uncrewed systems across multiple domains.
Delta is the situational awareness and command system Ukraine built during the war, assembling a common operating picture from drone feeds, sensors, radar and reporting from units, and pushing it to commanders on ordinary devices through a browser. It has become the backbone of Ukrainian targeting, and the ministry has previously said it records more than six thousand six hundred enemy targets hit every day.
Running at a NATO exercise on NATO standards carries consequences well beyond the exercise. STANAG 4817 governs how uncrewed systems exchange command, control and telemetry data within the alliance, and a system that speaks it can plug into allied formations without a translation layer. Ukraine has been pressing for its battlefield software to be treated as an alliance asset and not merely a national one, and performing at REPMUS three years running builds that case in front of the navies that would have to adopt it.
The Royal Navy has been a regular participant at the Troia range where REPMUS runs, through NATO’s Dynamic Messenger exercise which follows it and which turns the experimentation into operational trials. British uncrewed maritime work has been moving in the same direction, with the Royal Navy’s autonomy programmes and the Atlantic Bastion effort both built on connecting crewed and uncrewed platforms into a single targeting network.

Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
DUBAI, Oct 18 - Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait.
"Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.
If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said.
A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war.
Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at [email protected] or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.
The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”
"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.
The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.
Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.
“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.
In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.
Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”
The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.
7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.
Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.
Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.
Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”
Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)
Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.
Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.
“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”
It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.
A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.
Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.
Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.
Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.
“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”
What We’re Writing
Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.
Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!
What We’re Reading
- Maine’s senate race was not on our data center midterms to watch, but apparently it should’ve been! Thursday’s debate between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson was interrupted by a protester yelling about the environmental impact of data centers. Collins tried to use the moment to score points as the more anti-data center candidate, though her finances might indicate otherwise.
- CoreWeave has been on a wild ride this week as the bonds it sells to finance its data centers have seen wild selloff and corresponding stock drop. Though there’s been a slight recovery to end the week, it reflects increasing skittishness around the data center buildout. Bloomberg also reports that CoreWeave’s founders have sold $3.3 billion in stock since the company went public.
- Westfield, Massachusetts, killed a $3 billion data center project, boston.com reports. The small western Massachusetts town’s planning board pilloried developer Servistar for missing deadlines and being slow to develop the project.

OnlyFans Creators Are Pissed That Meta Lets Muse Talk Dirty

The generative AI revolution hasn’t been kind to Vanniall, an OnlyFans creator who lives in New York City. She now constantly finds hyperrealistic deepfakes—AI-generated images and videos that copy everything about her—circulating online and often isn’t able to get them removed.
On top of that, Vanniall struggles to build an audience on popular social media platforms, like Instagram, without getting in trouble. “There’s always some sort of report or appeal that I'm going through with them,” she tells WIRED. Vanniall’s Instagram account, which has over 100,000 followers, is currently restricted and cannot be viewed without logging in.
So, when I tell her that Meta allows its AI agent, called Muse, to engage in explicit sexting with adult users, she seems frustrated by the decision: “It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent, but they won't let real people, real adults, engage in any sort of sensuality or sexuality.”
It’s a common refrain I heard from other adult content creators, who questioned why their accounts on Meta platforms often seem restricted, while Meta’s AI agent is now allowed to talk dirty with millions of adult users.
“A private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform,” Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED.
Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco. The Muse app is like a message thread; text the digital assistant, give it access to your personal data, like calendar and email, and have it proactively find ways to help, like canceling a workout class that overlaps with your dinner reservation. Meta’s large distribution network, through platforms like Instagram and Facebook, helped catapult the app to the top of the download charts during its first month, as millions of new users experimented with an agent for the first time.
In addition to having it organize your calendar, Meta says, it’s OK for users of the adults-only app to engage in X-rated AI conversations with Muse. A Meta spokesperson previously told WIRED the company wouldn’t “block legal adult behavior.” Meta’s Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos.
While Meta takes a different approach to moderation on Instagram, other social media platforms in the United States do allow sexually explicit content. X remains one of the most popular platforms for many OnlyFans creators to draw in new subscribers and connect with fans. Many adult performers have also migrated to Bluesky after Elon Musk took over the platform formerly known as Twitter, where users can also share adult content.
“I think we're already seeing AI being allowed to do more than humans would get away with,” says Jiz Lee, who runs an OnlyFans account and has worked for years behind the scenes in queer porn. Meta has previously flagged Lee’s Instagram posts for removal. Lee feels like queer and trans people are often treated unfairly by large social media companies, whether or not the person is an adult content creator.
Lee traces many online censorship issues back to FOSTA-SESTA, a law signed by President Trump in 2018 that impacted Section 230 protections for platforms, and many websites responded by censoring adult content. “If sex work was decriminalized, then a lot of these issues wouldn't be happening, a lot of the censorship wouldn't be happening,” they say.
Lee also wants to know more about how Muse was trained and who, if anyone, was compensated by Meta for their data. “We've been slow to react industry-wise,” they say. But Lee is starting to see more adult content companies clarify AI usage stances in official contracts. They want to protect performers from being gobbled up into AI training data.
“When we're at award shows, and companies do advertisements for AI agents, they literally get booed like crazy,” says Tony Genius, who also has an OnlyFans account and appears in adult films. He has concerns about fully AI-generated porn in the future potentially displacing human performers. He also sees current AI tools as helpful for some marketing tasks independent creators do, like using automations to clip video segments for social media.
For many OnlyFans creators, navigating Meta platforms is frustrating but critical to remaining visible online. Genius claims to be on his seventh Instagram account in the past five years.
When asked about Muse’s sexting ability, he questioned why Meta made one of its apps, Muse, gated for those 18 and over but doesn’t seem interested in creating another adults-only space on social media. “It could be: Instacam,” he says.
Muse generating adult content could offer explicit AI interactions to a wider audience. Genius says he would be open to collaborating with a tech company to create an AI-version of himself that fans could message. He wants to find ways for humans to keep making money as adult performers, ensuring they aren’t cut out or unfairly trained on. Right now, he sees his human-ness and authenticity as central to connecting with audiences.
Meanwhile, Vanniall is fervently against using any AI agent. Well, at least, Meta’s Muse. “Stop downloading that app,” she says. “You do not need to give Meta any more money or any more of your personal information. They have enough.”

Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:28:00 UTC
19:28:00 KST

Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
October 18, 2026
The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.
One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.
Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits
Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.
Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.
Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."
CDU and SPD divided on working hours
In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.
The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.
A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.
Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.
"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."
SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions
But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.
An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.
The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.
Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection
Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"
The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.
Why the reform stalled
At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."
It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.
In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.
From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.
This article was translated from German.
