France: Over 1,800 arrested after looting, arson during protests
October 18, 2026
More than 1,800 people were arrested across France following riots, looting and arson during cost-of-living protests, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said Sunday.
The unrest on Saturday has sharpened tensions ahead of France's 2027 presidential election, as anger over living costs collides with tight limits on government spending.
What happened during the protests?
Clashes, fires and looting broke out in several cities during Saturday's demonstrations. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 150 police officers had been injured and blamed what he described as a highly organized, violent far-left group.
Paris police reported 855 arrests, describing the figure as a record. Prosecutors said 517 people remained in custody, including 171 minors. Those figures were provisional, with arrests continuing until early Sunday.
Most arrests in the capital were linked to suspected handling of stolen goods, participation in a group intending to commit violence, and vandalism.
In central France, rioters set fire to Limoges' historic town hall, leaving much of it gutted. Mayor Guillaume Guerin condemned the destruction.
"There are no words to condemn what happened, so appalling is it," he told broadcaster LCI. "The country is in chaos."
Authorities reported attacks on public buildings and shops in Marseille, Lyon, Avignon and Grenoble. Police used tear gas, batons and water cannon in several cities.
Demonstrators were also reported injured. The newspaper Le Figaro reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand to a grenade fired by police in Saint-Etienne.
What have leading French politicians said?
President Emmanuel Macron vowed that those responsible would be prosecuted and punished.
"No room for violence in our Republic," he wrote on X, condemning attacks on government buildings, businesses and town halls.
The Elysee Palace said French President Emmanuel Macron would address the nation at 8 p.m. local time (1800 UTC) on Sunday.
Opposition politicians seeking to succeed Macron in presidential elections in April and May also responded to the unrest.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen accused the party of her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon of having "legitimized the violence." She pledged to protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left."
Melenchon, who had backed the demonstrations and preceding student protests, urged demonstrators to stay away from looting, calling it "contrary to our methods."
The demonstrations brought together grievances over fuel prices, low wages and problems facing farmers and firefighters. School and university students demanding better learning conditions also participated.
The interior ministry put nationwide turnout at 550,000, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union gave a higher national estimate of 800,000.
France's high debt and budget deficit limit the government's ability to meet demands for additional spending.
Online calls to revive the yellow vest movement have added to government concerns that student demonstrations could grow into broader unrest.
The yellow vest movement began in 2018 over planned fuel tax increases and grew into wider protests over living costs and inequality. Named after the high-visibility vests worn by demonstrators, it brought months of nationwide demonstrations, some marked by violent clashes with police.

Egypt to provide ‘necessary’ support to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks

The president’s office added that Cairo would also intensify diplomatic efforts for de-escalation.

Over 600 police officers, gendarmes, and firefighters were injured, Nunez said on US social media company X.
He said the injury toll remained provisional and investigations were underway to identify those responsible, while several hundred businesses sustained considerable material damage.
Alexandre Bompard, president of the Federation of Commerce and Distribution and chief executive of Carrefour, said 1,500 retailers had been affected, estimating damage at “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Saturday’s demonstrations drew 550,000 people nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry, while organizers put the turnout at around 800,000.
The mobilization brought together Yellow Vest collectives, trade unions, students, and farmers. While the main Paris march passed without any major incidents, violence erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations in several cities.
A demonstrator died after collapsing on Boulevard Magenta in Paris, with police reporting that the individual had suffered cardiorespiratory arrest. Le Parisien also reported that a 17-year-old lost a hand when struck by a police grenade in Saint-Etienne.
Paris police earlier announced 855 arrests, while prosecutors separately reported 720 arrests, including 517 people held in custody, adding that the figures had yet to be finalized.
In Limoges, a fire devastated the historic city hall. Shops were also looted and buildings damaged in cities including Marseille, Lyon, and Bordeaux.
Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire announced an emergency task force to assist affected businesses, assess damage, and facilitate administrative and insurance procedures.
He also announced a meeting Monday with business owners, chambers of commerce, insurers, and government agencies.
“This Saturday, numerous businesses were targeted by unacceptable violence and looting. The extent of the damage is considerable and unprecedented,” he wrote in an open letter.
“Nothing can justify such acts. No anger, no demand, however legitimate, can authorize attacks on those who work, who are driven entrepreneurs, and who keep our city alive every day.”
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will chair an interministerial crisis meeting at 7 pm on Sunday (1700GMT) to address the economic impact, insurance, and judicial follow-up. He will also meet with the mayors of Paris, Marseille, and Lyon, who demanded explanations over police resources and the handling of the unrest.
National Assembly President Yael Braun-Pivet is considering establishing a parliamentary commission of inquiry and will meet with parliamentary group leaders Tuesday, BFMTV reported.
Calls for renewed gatherings Sunday in Paris and other major French cities circulated on social media, including a rally at Place de la Republique at 2 pm (1200GMT), raising fears among shopkeepers of further violence.
Lecornu blamed the “ultra-left” for the violence, while opposition figures criticized policing tactics.
Green politician Marine Tondelier and lawmaker Alexis Corbiere called for Nunez’s resignation, while the far-right National Rally renewed its demand that he step down.

The Saudi-led coalition's more than decadelong war with the Iran-backed Houthis has reignited, with both sides reporting regular attacks.
Tenants of the Kingdom Centre, which towers over central Riyadh, include financial services giant Merrill Lynch, management consultancy McKinsey and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo pledged on Oct 18 to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter’s Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on Oct 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fuelling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Smiling from a window of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Oct 18, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule.
“Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers,” Leo said.
The pope, who was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 17, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual.
He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God “without compromise”.
Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock.
His doctors discharged him on Oct 17 after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough to return home.
They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.
Crowds in St. Peter’s Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Oct 18.
One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face.

Streets in ruins, France in shock: ‘It was an uprising,’ ‘The republic is dying,’ ‘I'm in tears’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:20:18 UTC
19:20:18 KST

France was surveying scenes of devastation on Sunday after a day of nationwide protests against the soaring cost of living descended into widespread rioting, with masked groups looting hundreds of shops, setting public buildings ablaze and clashing with police. In the most dramatic incident, a historic city hall that had survived both world wars was largely destroyed by fire, its tower collapsing as flames engulfed the building.
The unrest erupted on Saturday, October 17, on the sidelines of demonstrations attended by hundreds of thousands of people across France. Although most marchers protested peacefully against rising prices, deteriorating public services and the cost of fuel, groups of masked rioters attacked police, vandalized businesses and set fires in cities including Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Lille and Bordeaux. The violence quickly became the focus of a fierce political confrontation, with French right-wing figures accusing the radical left of encouraging the unrest and others seeking to blame immigration.
By Sunday, the number of arrests had risen to 1,800, while more than 500 police officers, gendarmes and firefighters had been injured, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had earlier described the violence as being of "extreme intensity" and warned that the financial damage would be substantial.
The full extent of the destruction remained unclear, but hundreds of stores were reported looted in Paris alone. Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said that entire streets had been systematically devastated. The French newspaper Le Parisien described extensive destruction in several neighborhoods, reporting that rioters had spared virtually no businesses around the Les Halles district in central Paris.
Tobacco shops, opticians, beauty salons, pharmacies, clothing stores and other commercial establishments were damaged. Dozens of additional stores were vandalized near Porte Saint-Denis in the 10th arrondissement, where piles of garbage and burned bicycles were left scattered across sidewalks, with smoke still rising from the wreckage on Sunday morning. Sanitation workers sent to clear the debris told Le Parisien that the cleanup would take days.
According to AFP, some looting appeared highly organized. Groups of approximately six young men, wearing masks and gloves, approached stores and first disconnected their security cameras. Only then did they smash the windows, break into the premises and steal merchandise. The businesses targeted included supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing stores, electronics retailers, cosmetics shops and opticians. In Paris, footage showed looters stripping mobile phone stores of their merchandise and throwing products to accomplices waiting outside.
One widely circulated video, said to have been filmed in Paris, showed a woman desperately trying to stop masked looters from breaking into a supermarket. "Why are you doing this?" she shouted as the intruders pushed through the entrance. One initially placed a hand on her back, apparently trying to move her aside gently, but others surged forward and forced their way into the store. "Stop! That's not the point!" she cried as she was pushed away. Her appeals failed to stop the looting.
AFP described scenes resembling an uprising, with some participants shouting "Revolution!" The agency reported that the scale and intensity of Saturday's unrest appeared to exceed previous waves of violence in France, including the riots of 2023 and the Yellow Vest protests that began in 2018.
The most shocking images came from Limoges, a city in central France, where masked rioters set fire to the historic city hall. The ornate building, inaugurated in 1883, had survived two world wars before Saturday's blaze devastated much of its structure. Videos circulated on social media showed flames spreading across the roof before the building's tower collapsed. Local authorities said the building had been largely destroyed.
François Vincent, a regional council member in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, described the destruction as a turning point for the country.
"I am shocked, and tears are streaming down my face," he told Le Parisien. "I have never felt such horror, such astonishment and such incomprehension as a regional representative of Limoges. This is a terrifying symbol for every resident of the city."
Despite the destruction, Vincent insisted that he had not lost hope. "Limoges, a city of workers' struggles and resistance, is in mourning. But our republic is still standing," he said.
The violence extended far beyond Limoges. In Marseille, Lille, Angers and Bordeaux, rioters broke into or attacked municipal buildings and regional administrative offices. In Lyon, the city's tourist information office was set ablaze, and footage showed a rioter waving a Palestinian flag near the burning building. Local police reported that hostile individuals obstructed firefighters attempting to extinguish the flames.
In Marseille, video footage captured what appeared to be street battles between police and large groups of masked rioters who hurled stones and other objects at officers and police vehicles. Security forces appeared overwhelmed at several locations as groups moved quickly between streets and carried out attacks.
Other footage from Grenoble showed a masked man taking control of a tourist road train and driving it recklessly past police officers wearing helmets and riot gear. The officers initially appeared to watch without intervening as the vehicle passed directly in front of them. A second video showed additional masked individuals aboard the train, some falling off while it was moving. The vehicle eventually approached another group of police officers who, according to the footage, deployed tear gas before the train came to a stop.
In Paris, an elderly couple were reportedly robbed and left in the street wearing only their underwear. Elsewhere, rioters set fire to vehicles and public property, leaving streets littered with shattered glass, debris and the remains of burned barricades.
Reports from across France described more than 1,500 fires involving vehicles and public equipment, along with approximately 60 buildings damaged by fire, including municipal offices, libraries, shops and restaurants.
The violence also left serious injuries among demonstrators and rioters. In Saint-Étienne, a 17-year-old boy reportedly lost his right hand after a crowd-control grenade exploded. According to initial reports, he had picked up the device after it was apparently thrown by police, in an incident resembling another serious injury reported about two weeks earlier. In Nice, a rioter was reportedly seriously injured by broken glass while attempting to smash a store window. The total number of injured protesters and rioters remained unclear.
Visiting security forces deployed in central Paris overnight, Lecornu said it was a "miracle" that the number of casualties was not higher. He expressed shock at the scale of the damage, warning that the financial consequences would be felt across France.
Alexandre Bompard, president of the French Retail and Distribution Federation, warned of severe economic and financial consequences for the retail sector. In Angers, Mayor Christophe Béchu pointed to the wider cost to taxpayers, arguing that money spent repairing the destruction would be diverted from more urgent public needs.
"Public money that will be used to erase the traces of this damage cannot be used for other, higher-priority needs," he said. The warning comes as the French government is already attempting to curb public spending to confront a growing budget deficit.
The nationwide demonstrations followed weeks of protests that began last month at schools in poorer suburbs north of Paris. Students complained of teacher shortages, deteriorating classroom conditions and insufficient educational resources. The movement gradually expanded into a broader protest against rising living costs, declining public services and higher fuel prices. High school students, university students, labor unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement joined Saturday's demonstrations.
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018 in opposition to President Emmanuel Macron's economic policies and subsequently became a broader expression of anger over inequality and the cost of living. France's Interior Ministry estimated that approximately 550,000 people participated in Saturday's marches nationwide, while the CGT labor union put the figure at 800,000. Most demonstrated peacefully, but the destruction carried out by smaller groups overshadowed the wider protest movement.
The violence immediately triggered a fierce political confrontation, with members of Macron's government and French right-wing politicians accusing the radical left of encouraging the unrest, which erupted just six months before the country's next presidential election. Some right-wing figures in France and abroad also sought to link the riots to immigration, although the scale of any involvement by migrants or their descendants has not been established.
Lecornu accused the far left of helping create the conditions for the violence and suggested that the unrest was being used as a show of political strength ahead of the election. He called on the party of far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, La France Insoumise (France Unbowed), to choose sides.
Mélenchon and senior figures from his party had participated in recent demonstrations by students and supported school blockades. Mélenchon himself joined Saturday's march in Paris before the violence escalated. Later, he attempted to distance himself from the destruction, writing on X that those who shared his political struggle had no place engaging in looting and robbery.
Nevertheless, Mélenchon continued to direct much of his criticism at the government, accusing the authorities of using excessive force and arguing that their response had contributed to the chaos. Lecornu responded sharply, accusing Mélenchon of trying to shift responsibility for the violence onto the police.
"Trying to blame the police leadership for the violence is a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibility," the prime minister wrote. "You cannot call for an end to violence while simultaneously providing excuses for those who commit it."
Mélenchon quickly fired back, accusing the prime minister of deliberately inflaming tensions.
"Mr. Lecornu, you played with fire," he wrote, claiming that the government's actions had united young people and labor organizations in opposition to it.
He accused the authorities of ordering harsh police repression and argued that Lecornu's political confrontation with him was deepening a broader crisis of government.
"You prove that you are not a statesman but merely an official whose actions provoke a political crisis," Mélenchon wrote, before asking whether the prime minister had nothing better to do than engage in political quarrels and moral lectures.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen also accused the radical left of hijacking legitimate demands concerning the cost of living and deteriorating public services. She argued that left-wing activists were legitimizing violence by portraying attempts to restore public order as repression and treating public disorder as a right. In her view, the approach was designed to create chaos.
Le Pen called on the French public to endure the remaining months before the presidential election, promising that her political camp would protect the country from what she described as Macron's harmful economic policies and violence encouraged by the radical left.
Other prominent figures on the French right expressed outrage at the scenes of destruction. Marion Maréchal, Le Pen's niece and a politician in her own right, accused the people she described as the children of Mélenchon's "New France" of destroying their country.
"The whole world is watching in amazement and disbelief as the children of Mélenchon's 'New France' destroy our country," she said.
Mélenchon has used the expression "New France" to describe his vision of a society in which immigrant communities are an integral part of the nation. Maréchal employed the phrase critically, reflecting the far right's opposition to demographic and cultural changes that it argues threaten France's future.
Éric Ciotti, the right-wing mayor of Nice, also reacted with alarm to the burning of Limoges City Hall, describing the images as a symbol of a republic in decline.
"This is an allegory of our republic going up in flames and dying," he wrote on X. "We will not allow our country to die without a response. Millions will reject chaos. We will win."
The turmoil also drew a sharp reaction from the United States. Vice President JD Vance shared footage of the burning city hall in Limoges and blamed France's immigration policies for the violence.
"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion," Vance wrote on X, accusing European leaders of neglecting questions of assimilation and cultural compatibility.
He said Western governments had been warned that such policies would lead to serious consequences but had ignored those warnings. He expressed hope that France would stop the violence before more of its historic landmarks were destroyed.
Vance also turned the unrest into a warning about American domestic politics, arguing that voters in the United States should pay attention to the events in France ahead of next month's congressional midterm elections. He claimed that the developments illustrated the future congressional Democrats wanted for the United States.
His comments followed earlier remarks by President Donald Trump, who had suggested that the French protests were connected to an attempt by Islam to gain control of the country, rather than being driven solely by demands for improved public services.
As France begins the difficult task of repairing burned buildings, clearing devastated commercial districts and investigating the violence, the destruction has intensified an already bitter confrontation between the country's political camps. The ruins of Limoges City Hall have become a particularly powerful symbol of the crisis: a landmark that stood for more than 140 years, survived two world wars and was reduced to wreckage in a single night.

Swiss cantons weigh lower social assistance for Ukrainian refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:17:21 UTC
19:17:21 KST

Swiss cantons weigh lower social assistance for Ukrainian refugees
Next year, 46,000 Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland will be eligible to receive social assistance for the first time. The federal government now wants to allow the cantons to decide for themselves on the level of these payments. Local authorities consider the change to be fair, while aid organisations warn of the social consequences.
If Asylum Ordinance 2 were not amended, people with protection status S – a special temporary protection status in Switzerland designed for people fleeing war – primarily Ukrainian refugees – would receive the same social assistance as Swiss nationals. This would mean a higher rate than the current social assistance for asylum seekers, explained Mathias Reynard, President of the Conference of Cantonal Social Directors (SODK), in response to a query from the Keystone-SDA news agency.
This would entail a significant increase in costs for the cantons, not least because, as part of Relief Package 27, the federal government’s lump-sum payment to the cantons for people with S status has been abolished where such status is linked to a residence permit valid for five years or more, the canton Valais member of the cantonal government went on to write.
The cantons had called on the federal government to allow them to determine the level of contributions themselves. This request had been incorporated into the consultation draft, Reynard stated. This would enable the cantons to pay lower contributions to those affected in future, right down to the level of asylum social assistance.
The municipalities welcomed the amendment to the Asylum Ordinance, but also want a say in the matter. After all, they would bear the main financial burden, according to the Swiss Association of Municipalities.
Those who pay less will make up the shortfall
The Social Democratic party, the Greens and aid organisations such as Caritas, Heks and Swiss Refugee Aid (SFH) fear that the cut in social assistance will lead to poverty and legal inequality. Ultimately, they also reject the draft because it hinders integration and social participation.
+ Switzerland extends Ukraine S status until March 2028
They warned that the proposed amendment to the ordinance also carries the risk of legal action. Depending on the ruling, the cantons might have to make back payments for the full amount of social assistance. The Radical Liberal party also pointed out to the federal government that the compatibility with the Refugee Convention is currently unclear.
The party called for the legal situation to be reviewed and for the amendment to the ordinance to be adopted this autumn, so that the cantons would have sufficient time to amend their social assistance laws by March 1, 2027.
The right-wing Swiss People’s Party concerns are quite different. The party welcomes the fact that persons in need of protection with S status will no longer be entitled to the same level of social assistance as Swiss nationals.
However, they argue that there is still considerable untapped potential for savings in the asylum sector. The party is therefore calling for the bill to be tightened up.

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Leaders' summit puts security, regional cooperation, finance at heart of upcoming COP17
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:16:32 CST
19:16:32 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Global efforts to halt biodiversity loss face a common test: whether conservation commitments can withstand the pressures of poverty, conflict and competing economic priorities.
At Friday's Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, those pressures brought the challenge of implementation into focus ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled to begin Monday in the Armenian capital.
The discussions underscored how closely biodiversity protection is tied to security and development, how much shared ecosystems depend on cross-border cooperation, and how implementation hinges on accessible finance and broad participation.
NATURE AS A SECURITY CONCERN
Speakers at the summit underscored how environmental pressures can compound security risks.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that pollution spreads beyond national borders, while Lebanese Environment Minister Tamara El-Zein cited World Bank estimates putting environmental damage from the Israel-Hezbollah conflict in 2023-2024 at more than 500 million U.S. dollars.
The security argument also extended to economic resilience. Britain's representative described nature as critical infrastructure supporting prosperity, security and resilience. European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera said 55 percent of global GDP was highly dependent on nature.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres linked biodiversity loss to conflict, climate disruption, food insecurity and disease, arguing that these crises could not be addressed separately.
With nature protection increasingly seen as essential to peace and security, Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu called for win-win cooperation and multi-stakeholder governance to strengthen biodiversity conservation and resilience for sustainable development.
GLOBAL GOALS, REGIONAL REALITIES
The summit's regional examples exposed another challenge: ecosystems cross borders, while policies and funding are largely organized nationally.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the Caspian seal population had fallen from 1 million to 270,000 over the past century, invoking the ecological disaster of the Aral Sea and urging action to prevent a similar fate for the Caspian. He reiterated Kazakhstan's proposal to establish an international water organization within the UN system, suggesting it could become a joint Central Asian initiative open to other countries.
The pressures extend beyond the Caspian. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon said his country had lost more than 1,300 glaciers in recent decades. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said only around 30 of the 101 rivers that historically flowed into Lake Issyk-Kul now flowed year-round.
Such changes threaten water supplies, ecosystems and livelihoods simultaneously, underscoring the need for cooperation on shared waters and habitats. Proposals included a regional center to combat desertification in Central Asia and an Armenian initiative for a Yerevan platform on biodiversity, mountain and freshwater ecosystems.
Yet regional cooperation must also deliver effective protection on the ground. International Union for Conservation of Nature President Razan Al Mubarak cautioned that simply meeting the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework's target of conserving at least 30 percent of terrestrial and inland water areas, and marine and coastal areas by 2030 would not guarantee lasting conservation outcomes. Protected areas also need effective management, equitable governance, ecological representation and connectivity.
Huang, the Chinese environment minister, called for advancing national biodiversity strategies and action plans and translating global targets into national policies and practical measures.
FINANCING DELIVERY
Even well-designed plans face a financial obstacle: money continues to flow overwhelmingly toward activities that damage nature.
Guterres said that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, 30 dollars were spent destroying it, with nature-negative financial flows reaching 7.3 trillion dollars in 2023. The challenge is therefore both to increase conservation funding and redirect investment and incentives that undermine it.
Speakers outlined several funding commitments. Ribera, of the European Commission, said the European Union was on track to double its international biodiversity finance to 7 billion euros (7.86 billion dollars) over 2021-2027. Britain said it would allocate around 6 billion pounds (7.98 billion dollars) in international climate finance over the next three financial years, with roughly a quarter expected to support nature.
For developing countries, however, the test is whether such commitments translate into predictable and accessible support. Indonesian Environment Minister Mohd Jumhur Hidayat stressed that other funding sources should complement, rather than replace, international public finance. Zimbabwean Environment Minister Evelyn Ndlovu highlighted the priority of delivering at least 30 billion dollars annually in international biodiversity finance by 2030.
Beyond funding, Huang said, technological and capacity-building support was also needed, pointing to China's contribution of 1.5 billion yuan (about 224 million dollars) to establish the Kunming Biodiversity Fund.
The summit's closing Yerevan Declaration called for political commitments to translate into measurable action and lasting results. As COP17 opens on Oct. 19, the challenge will be to turn that resolve into decisions that give countries the resources and support to deliver on their biodiversity promises. ■

The Ministry of Defence has refused to say when each of the seventy-eight Warrior infantry fighting vehicles removed from the fleet in the past year was disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the dates on which each vehicle was disposed of, following an answer of 7 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The answer to Question 23452 explained that the seventy-eight Warrior Infantry Fighting Vehicles removed from the reported fleet between 2025 and 2026 have been disposed of in accordance with Defence disposal policy. It would be inappropriate for me to provide exact disposal details, such as dates or variants as to do so could, or would be likely to, prejudice the capability of our Armed Forces.”
The number leaving the fleet has been confirmed, but not when they went or which variants they were, so the rate at which Warrior is being drawn down cannot be read from the published record.
The FV510 Warrior entered service in 1988 as the British Army tracked infantry fighting vehicle, carrying a section of dismounted infantry behind a two man turret armed with the 30mm RARDEN cannon.
A programme to rebuild the fleet around a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon, the Warrior Capability Sustainment Programme, was cancelled in March 2021 after more than a decade of development and around £430 million of spending, and the vehicle has been running down since.

Purses and other belongings left behind by devotees lie on the floor of a worship venue for the Hindu festival of Durga Puja following a stampede, in Kolkata, India, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (AP Photo)
A stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state has left at least 19 people dead, officials said on Oct. 18.
The stampede in the state capital of Kolkata happened on Oct. 17 night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga. According to police, some worshippers fell on the road, triggering the stampede.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment. He announced an investigation by a Special Investigation Team to be headed by a judge of the state’s High Court.
Police detained some pavilion organizers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Around 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions, known locally as pandals, have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures. In January of 2025, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.

Turkish police have arrested two foreign nationals in Istanbul after discovering 213 kilograms of synthetic drugs in a caravan allegedly used as a mobile laboratory, in an operation reminiscent of the U.S. television series “Breaking Bad.”

In the show, the two use a caravan as a mobile laboratory to conceal their activities and evade law enforcement.

Zelenskyy Says Russia Seeking 'Total Blackout' In Ukraine After Latest Onslaught On Energy Facilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:07:44 UTC
19:07:44 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian strikes overnight targeted power substations in multiple regions, leaving tens of thousands of households without electricity, as Ukrainian and Russian officials reported civilian deaths following overnight drone attacks on October 18.
Zelenskyy said Russia had carried out 76 attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors in the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy cease-fire. Trump said on October 11 that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to observe a weeklong pause in attacks on energy infrastructure amid freezing weather in Ukraine.
"Over the past week, Russia launched nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 66 missiles at Ukraine, most of them ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy wrote on social media on October 18.
Accusing Moscow of seeking to plunge Ukraine into a nationwide blackout, Zelenskyy wrote on social media: "Russia is not taking steps toward peace."
Zelenskyy said that power stations were targeted in the Vinnytsya, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskiy, and Odesa regions in the overnight strikes.
Russian attacks killed at least two people and injured several others in Ukraine, Ukrainian officials said.
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhya, a 27-year-old woman was killed and two people were injured, including a six-year-old girl, according to the regional military administration.
The attacks damaged two apartment buildings, 18 cars, and an educational institution, the administration said.
In the central city of Poltava, a Russian drone attack killed one woman and injured four other people, the head of the city's military administration, Vitaliy Dyakivnych, said on Telegram. Nine residential buildings were damaged, some by falling drone debris.
In the western Vinnytsia region, Russian drone attacks on critical infrastructure caused power outages, the regional military administration said.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 180 combat drones during the overnight attacks, of which 152 were intercepted. Impacts were recorded at 20 locations, it said.
Russia Reports Casualties, Infrastructure Damage
In Russia, one person was killed and five injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg, the city's governor, Aleksandr Beglov, said on October 18.
Fires broke out at the St. Petersburg oil terminal, an oil depot, and industrial warehouses, Beglov said. Twelve apartment buildings were also damaged.
Russian e-commerce company Ozon said a drone struck one of its logistics facilities in St. Petersburg, causing a fire. Employees were evacuated, and no one was injured at the facility, the company said.
The VK Internet company said its data center in the Leningrad region had also been targeted by drones, but its services remained available to users as normal.
A drone struck a cable-stayed bridge forming part of St. Petersburg's Western High-Speed Diameter highway. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
The attacks also caused power disruptions in parts of the region. Two transformer substations in Yanino were reportedly disconnected, while operations at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport were disrupted.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defense units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. The figure could not be independently verified.
Drone attacks also disrupted air travel across Russia. More than 350 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow's four airports overnight on October 17, as authorities imposed restrictions amid reported Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region.
The figures were based on airport departure and arrival boards reviewed by the independent Russian outlet Meduza.
Sheremetyevo was the worst affected, with 143 flights canceled and 53 delayed. Vnukovo recorded 55 cancellations and 113 delays, while Domodedovo reported 59 delayed flights. Some flights bound for Moscow were diverted to other cities, including St. Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Russian air defenses had destroyed 75 drones heading toward the capital. Russia's Defense Ministry said more than 600 drones had been destroyed or intercepted across the country overnight, Interfax reported.
Airports in Penza, Saratov, and Sochi also suspended operations.
Kyiv Says Starshield Connections Still Limited
The latest barrage on Ukraine came as disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, left Ukraine particularly vulnerable earlier in the week.
On October 17, Kyiv said the speed of Starshield connections across Ukrainian territory remained significantly limited, causing instability in battlefield communications, medium-range strikes, and the operation of interceptor drones.
"The shortage of air defense systems, combined with the lack of confirmation that Starshield's full operational capabilities have been restored, creates additional challenges for Ukraine in protecting critical infrastructure against Russian aerial attacks," Denys Sienik, Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the United States, told RFE/RL.
"With colder weather approaching and winter drawing nearer, we fully understand the deliberate nature of Russia's strategy: to systematically damage Ukraine's energy infrastructure and leave civilians without essential services," he added.
On October 17, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected claims that the United States had deliberately restricted Ukraine’s access to Starlink, the satellite Internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down Internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," he told reporters on October 17 as he prepared to depart for Central Asia, calling reports of US involvement "categorically false."
Rubio said his understanding was that Starlink's performance had returned to its previous level. Ukraine had used the commercial service to support drone operations.
He also questioned the Ukrainian president's account of the incident, saying he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about."
Rubio distinguished Starlink from Starshield, a separate defense-oriented satellite system used by the US military.
Ukraine does not currently have access to Starshield, he said, although Kyiv has requested it to conduct deep strikes inside Russia. The question of how the system might be used remains under discussion, Rubio added.
His comments highlighted the limits of Ukraine's access to US-linked military technology as tensions between Washington and Kyiv grow over the administration's approach to Russia.

Germany overtakes US as top destination for Turkish students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:06:13 UTC
19:06:13 KST

AA Photo
Driven by tuition-free education and lower living costs, Germany has surpassed the United States as the top foreign study destination for Turkish university students, according to the OECD’s Education at a Glance 2026 report.
The report shows that more than 5 million international students are enrolled in higher education across the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development nations, with the U.S., United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Germany among the largest host countries.
Türkiye has also emerged as a growing destination for international students, with their number rising from 71,000 in 2015 to 336,000 in 2024. Meanwhile, the number of Turkish students studying abroad increased from 44,000 to 77,000 over the same period.
In 2015, the U.S. was the preferred destination for 23 percent of Turkish students abroad, compared with 12 percent who chose Germany. By 2024, Germany had taken the lead, attracting 26 percent of Turkish students, while the U.S. accounted for 11 percent. Italy ranked third with 9 percent, followed by the U.K. at 8 percent and Poland at 5 percent.
Deniz Akar, general manager of IEFT International Education Fairs, said Germany and Italy appealed to Turkish students not only because of the quality of their education but also because of their lower costs.
Both countries offer options such as tuition-free education and scholarships, Akar said, adding that the U.K. and the Netherlands were also attractive destinations. The U.S. had fallen in popularity due to political and economic factors, he added.

Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition

Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
Some northern communities traditionally place a pumpkin under the wedding quilt as a blessing for future generations
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
In ancient China, welcoming autumn could involve stealing pumpkins, sitting on giant hanging scales and eating extra meat – rituals reflecting how people connected seasonal change with fertility, health and good fortune.
Historical records show that during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), groups of young people would gather on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival to sneak into fields and take pumpkins.
Far from being considered wrongdoing, the practice was often tolerated – and even welcomed – by farmers. By the Republican era (1912–1949), it had become particularly prevalent in rural communities.

World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models, which can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence.
While Silicon Valley big tech firms are focused on ever more sophisticated consumer products, Paschal Donohoe, the World Bank’s chief knowledge officer, said AI could also accelerate development for emerging economies – but only if it was adapted to local needs.
Small AI uses specialised models that are trained using narrower datasets for a specific purpose.
“We argue that economic development in the countries that we serve and partner with that could have taken centuries to make happen, the potential is there for that economic development now to happen within decades,” Donohoe said.
“Small AI would be available in a local setting, with low connectivity, and in the local language of the community – and tends to be available on your mobile phone.”
Donohoe, a former finance minister for Ireland, cited the example of Indian farmers engaged in the World Bank’s agricultural scheme, AgriConnect, who needed to access soil analysis in their own language.
“There’s not going to be enough scientists and agricultural experts to do that for every small farm in India. And this is where what we describe as ‘small AI’ comes in. Because small AI is AI that would be available on your phone, that can help deliver against those information needs.”
He suggested such products could emerge from collaboration between the World Bank, governments and the private sector.
The impact of AI on jobs and growth is a central theme of the annual meetings of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which are being held this week in Bangkok, Thailand.
Speaking on a panel about the impact of the technology on Monday, Kristalina Georgieva, the IMF’s managing director, called on governments to provide the preconditions for AI to succeed.
She said: “You need access to electricity. You need access to digital infrastructure. People have to be geared to adoption. And the government should be able to give some safety, protect against bad actors so that adoption can work.
“If we work hard to have the basics for it, [adoption] can be very democratic. As democratic as the cellphone.”
The World Bank’s annual world development report, published in August, hailed the potential benefits of AI. But it pointed out that, for example, almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lacked electricity and more than two-thirds did not have a consistent internet connection.
Georgieva warned that over time 40% of jobs worldwide were likely to be either augmented or eliminated by AI, with the impact particularly acute for young people at the start of their careers.
“When we look at this, what we recognise is that the people to worry about, first and foremost, are young people that are coming into the labour market,” she said. “Normally they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then go up the ranks. But if they’re gone, I don’t think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as a professional future.”
Under its president, Ajay Banga, the World Bank has made attracting private-sector funding into emerging economies a focus of its work.
Donohoe said the World Bank had mobilised $120bn (£90bn) of private capital in the past year using guarantees and other financial instruments, at a time when many countries, including the US and the UK, were cutting their aid budgets.
“We want to highlight the link between private capital mobilisation and jobs and economic development,” he said.

Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:45 UTC
19:00:45 KST

Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos
A thin white-concrete plane folds and steps down a hillside to enclose Bellavista 11, a minimalist home overlooking the sea in Ibiza, designed by Spanish studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos.
Bellavista 11 is the first villa to be completed in The Roca Views development, a cluster of six homes designed by the Valencia-based studio in the town of Roca Lisa on Ibiza's eastern coast.
The villas will be united by pared-back, rectilinear forms with thin white walls, designed by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos as a contemporary take on the island's traditional white-walled buildings.
"The project begins with a very simple question, 'Can we build on this hillside by placing a single element on it?'," studio founder Fran Silvestre told Dezeen.
"The aim is to create a continuous element that follows the topography and, through its different folds, gradually finds the best conditions offered by the site," he explained.
"It is an apparently very simple operation that allows many things to be resolved at once – adapting to the slope, organising the programme, orienting each room towards a different condition of the landscape and extending the architecture to generate shade."
Bellavista 11 is divided across three low-slung volumes, beginning at the top with a garage and access stair, moving through to a central social volume and ending in a block of five bedrooms.
The thin white concrete plane that defines the home is just 15 centimetres thick. As it steps down the site, it creates expansive roof terraces atop the lowest two volumes, folding around to create the interior floor plates and a series of lower terraces.
"We like to think in terms of an evolved tradition, learning from what works in Mediterranean architecture – shade, protection from the sun, clarity of materials – and resolving it through contemporary construction techniques," said Silvestre.
Alongside the open-plan living, dining and kitchen space is a swimming pool, while the bedroom block overlooks a seating terrace. Both are accessed via walls of full-height sliding glass doors with slender frames and hidden tracks.
The villa's interiors continue the deliberate simplicity of the exterior, with white walls, pale stone floors and timber carpentry chosen to emphasise the movement of light and shadow across surfaces throughout the day.
"White appears naturally because of its relationship with traditional Mediterranean architecture and because of its performance under intense solar radiation," Silvestre explained.
"At the same time, it allows light to transform the spaces throughout the day. This is something that particularly interests us, we understand light almost as another material within the project."
Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. The studio previously used a similarly singular geometric gesture for a home in Madrid, which is housed in a cluster of white cylindrical volumes.
Its other recent projects include the stepped Villa 95 in Andalusia and the winding Sabater House in Alicante.
The photography is by Jesus Orrico.

Psychopathy is the strongest predictor of frequent and malicious gossip among dark personality traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:17 UTC
19:00:17 KST

People with higher levels of socially aversive personality traits tend to gossip more often than others, though their underlying reasons for talking behind someone’s back vary depending on their specific personality profile. A new study published in Behavioral Sciences indicates that while psychopathy is the strongest predictor of how frequently a person gossips, Machiavellianism is uniquely associated with using gossip across a wide variety of social goals, from gathering information to protecting friends. The research also provides evidence that everyday sadism has its own distinct link to malicious gossip aimed at hurting others’ reputations.
In everyday conversation, gossip is often dismissed as trivial or mean-spirited chatter. In psychology, however, gossip is defined more broadly as the exchange of evaluative information, whether positive, neutral, or negative, about an absent third party. From an evolutionary perspective, talking about others is thought to serve important social functions, allowing people to learn about their community, build friendships, enforce social rules, and compete for status or romantic partners.
One widely used framework, which this study adopted, sorts the reasons people gossip into four motives. People may gossip for information gathering and validation, which involves finding out news about peers and checking if others share the same opinions about someone. They may also gossip simply for social enjoyment and entertainment, for group protection to warn friends about untrustworthy individuals, or for negative influence to intentionally damage a target’s reputation.
Because gossip can be used as a covert weapon to manipulate social standing, psychologists have examined how it relates to the Dark Triad of personality. The Dark Triad is a cluster of three distinct but overlapping socially aversive traits: narcissism, which involves grandiosity, entitlement, and a need for admiration; Machiavellianism, characterized by cynicism and strategic manipulation; and psychopathy, marked by callousness, impulsivity, and antisocial behavior.
Early investigations into these traits and gossip produced mixed results. For instance, a 2015 study of British adults found that all three Dark Triad traits were linked to gossiping to negatively influence others, while none were tied to gathering or validating information. In contrast, a 2019 study of German adults indicated that narcissism and Machiavellianism did predict information-related gossip motives, whereas psychopathy did not predict any specific reason for gossiping once the overlap among the three traits was accounted for.
In addition to these conflicting findings about why people with dark personalities gossip, prior work had not tested whether these traits actually predict how often people engage in gossip overall. Previous studies also omitted a fourth trait known as everyday sadism, which describes a tendency to derive pleasure from the suffering or humiliation of others in daily life. Researchers later added everyday sadism to the original three traits to form what is known as the Dark Tetrad, and a 2020 psychometric study produced a short questionnaire that measures all four traits together.
To clarify the ambiguous findings in past work and examine the role of everyday sadism, study authors Adam C. Davis, a professor in the Department of Social Sciences at Canadore College, Tracy Vaillancourt, a professor of counseling psychology in the Faculty of Education at the University of Ottawa, and Steven Arnocky, a professor in the Department of Psychology at Nipissing University who leads the Human Evolution Laboratory, designed a study examining how all four Dark Tetrad traits relate to both gossip frequency and gossip motives. Drawing on evolutionary theories of competition, the authors anticipated that individuals scoring higher on these four traits would gossip more frequently and would be more motivated to gossip both for fun and to harm others’ reputations, with differing patterns expected for the other two motives.
“To our knowledge, no researchers had investigated the links between gossip frequency (i.e., how often people tend to gossip) with ‘dark’ (i.e., sinister) personality traits,” Davis, Vaillancourt, and Arnocky told PsyPost. “We were motivated to explore these associations, specifically regarding a model of dark traits called the Dark Tetrad, which includes narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism.”
“Some had looked at the relations between some dark traits (e.g., psychopathy) with the motives for gossiping (i.e., why people gossip),” the researchers added. “But the work was limited and the findings were inconsistent. We wanted to build on this research to study a larger model of dark traits and to help clarify mixed results.”
The researchers recruited a final sample of 516 North American adults from the United States and Canada using Amazon Mechanical Turk. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 61 years old, with an average age of about 38, and just over half of the sample (53.1 percent) were women. Most participants identified as White (80.6 percent), and about a third held an undergraduate degree.
Participants completed an online survey containing three primary self-report questionnaires. To assess the Dark Tetrad, the researchers used the 28-item Short Dark Tetrad scale, which asks participants to rate their agreement with statements measuring narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism on a five-point scale. To ensure data quality, the survey included five attention-check questions, and the data were collected in 2021 before the widespread availability of artificial intelligence chatbots that can compromise online survey responses.
To measure gossip frequency, the authors provided participants with a standardized definition explaining that gossip involves sharing positive, negative, or neutral information about an absent person, either in person or digitally. Participants then completed a 13-item Gossip Frequency Scale, rating how often they talked about absent others across topics like work achievements, physical appearance, romantic relationships, rivals, and celebrities on a scale from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Participants also completed the 22-item Motives to Gossip Questionnaire, rating their agreement on a seven-point scale with four distinct reasons for gossiping: information gathering and validation, social enjoyment, negative influence, and group protection.
Before testing their main hypotheses, the researchers examined how age and biological sex related to the variables. On the five-point gossip frequency scale, women reported a slightly higher average score (2.61) than men (2.41), whereas men scored higher on everyday sadism (2.79) than women (2.33). Age was negatively associated with all four Dark Tetrad traits, overall gossip frequency, and the motives of social enjoyment and negative influence, meaning younger adults tended to score higher on these measures than older adults.
In initial correlation analyses looking at each trait individually, every Dark Tetrad trait was positively associated with gossip frequency and with all four gossip motives. Correlation coefficients (r) range from -1 to 1, with higher positive numbers indicating a stronger link between two variables. The traits’ correlations with gossip frequency ranged from 0.43 to 0.66, and their strongest links with any motive were for negative influence, ranging from 0.34 to 0.53.
Because the four dark personality traits overlap considerably with one another, the researchers next conducted a series of multiple regression analyses. This statistical technique allowed them to isolate the unique contribution of each individual trait while controlling for the influence of the other three traits, as well as age and biological sex. Exploratory tests also indicated that biological sex did not alter the relationships between the dark traits and gossip frequency or motives.
When predicting how often people gossip overall, age, sex, and the four dark traits together accounted for 52 percent of the variation in gossip frequency scores. Even after accounting for shared overlap among the traits, narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and everyday sadism each independently predicted higher gossip frequency. Psychopathy emerged as the strongest predictor of frequent gossiping, followed by sadism, narcissism, and Machiavellianism.
The researchers then ran separate models for each of the four gossip motives, revealing distinct motivational patterns across the traits. For the information gathering and validation motive, the overall model explained 14 percent of the variance, and Machiavellianism was the only trait to emerge as a positive predictor. Narcissism, psychopathy, and sadism did not show a statistically significant unique association with using gossip to gather or verify social information. This pattern differs from both earlier studies: the 2015 British study had found no Dark Triad links to this motive, and the 2019 German study had linked narcissism, along with Machiavellianism, to information-related motives.
For the social enjoyment motive, the model accounted for 16 percent of the variance. Both Machiavellianism and narcissism positively predicted gossiping for entertainment and fun, whereas psychopathy and sadism did not. This suggests that individuals with elevated Machiavellianism or narcissism tend to view talking about absent peers as a pleasurable, stimulating social activity.
When examining the negative influence motive, the model explained 34 percent of the variance in scores. Psychopathy was the strongest predictor of gossiping to damage someone’s reputation, followed by everyday sadism and Machiavellianism. This contrasts with the 2019 German study, in which psychopathy did not uniquely predict any gossip motive once its overlap with the other traits was accounted for. The finding aligns with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which similarly found that psychopathy was linked to more indirect aggression, a category that includes spreading rumors, though that study measured aggressive behavior among college-aged women rather than motives for gossip.
Although narcissism was linked to the negative influence motive when examined on its own, that link disappeared once psychopathy was added to the analysis. Follow-up tests indicated that psychopathy was statistically absorbing narcissism’s apparent contribution, a pattern known as suppression. As a result, it is hard to tell whether narcissism plays its own role in malicious gossip or whether its apparent link reflects the callous, antisocial tendencies it shares with psychopathy.
“Contrary to our hypothesis, narcissism did not predict the negative influence gossip motive in our regression model,” the researchers told PsyPost. “This seemed surprising given the nature of this dark personality trait and that it correlated positively with the negative influence motive. We conducted follow-up analyses and found that psychopathy was suppressing narcissism in our regression model; meaning that psychopathy was reducing the predictive power of narcissism and ‘downplaying’ its contribution.”
For the fourth motive, group protection, the model explained 16 percent of the variance. Only psychopathy and Machiavellianism positively predicted gossiping to warn or protect one’s social group, while narcissism and sadism did not. Earlier studies had linked narcissism to this motive; in the new study, its association fell just short of statistical significance. The researchers also tested whether sadism was statistically redundant with psychopathy in predicting group protection, and found that psychopathy contributed unique predictive power beyond sadism.
The finding that psychopathy and Machiavellianism predicted group protection may seem counterintuitive, given that both traits are associated with selfishness and low empathy. The authors suggest that people higher in psychopathy may still protect close allies, particularly within antisocial groups such as gangs, where protecting members and maintaining dominance can be advantageous. Similarly, manipulative individuals high in Machiavellianism may alternate between cooperative and aggressive tactics, protecting group members strategically for as long as those alliances remain useful to their own goals.
“Machiavellianism predicted each of the four gossip motives in our statistical models,” the authors explained. “It was the only dark characteristic to predict the information and validation motive, which makes sense given how cynicism (i.e., interpersonal distrust) is core to this personality trait. Machiavellians are expected to be manipulative and strategic; using both prosocial (e.g., cooperation) and antisocial (e.g., bullying) behavior depending on what will benefit them in each situation to gain power and status. So, it does make sense that a wider range of motives would underpin their gossip.”
“Among ‘dark’ (i.e., sinister) personality traits, psychopathy was the strongest predictor of gossiping more about a range of topics, including physical appearance, salaries and school grades, romantic relationships, friends, rivals, and celebrities (e.g., actors),” the researchers said. “It was also the strongest predictor of the negative influence gossip motive, which involves malicious gossip intended to hurt the reputations of others. Psychopathy also predicted the group protection gossip motive, describing gossip intended to defend and guard group members from the rule-breaking and exploitive actions of others.”
Standardized regression coefficients (β) measure the unique strength of each predictor after accounting for the others. Psychopathy’s coefficient of 0.35 for gossip frequency, for example, corresponded to roughly a quarter-point higher gossip score on the five-point scale for each one-point increase in psychopathy, holding the other traits, age, and sex constant.
The researchers also commented on the size of these effects. “In the regression analyses, where the shared overlap between the Dark Tetrad traits were statistically controlled for, medium-to-large effects were also found,” they noted. “In particular, large effects were found for psychopathy in predicting gossip frequency (β = 0.35) and the negative influence motive (β = 0.36), as well as for Machiavellianism predicting the information gathering and validation motive (β = 0.32). These results point to the practical significance of the findings, that are unlikely to be due to chance.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Beyond the statistical results, the researchers emphasized that everyday gossip is not inherently toxic or restricted to people with aversive personalities.
“There is a negative stereotype when it comes to gossip; people assume it is always malicious and that ‘gossipers’ are bad people,” the researchers explained. “The reality is that gossiping is a very common way that people communicate with each other, and most of our daily gossip is positive or neutral. With that said, some people gossip more than others, particularly when it comes to defamatory (negative) gossip. So, it is important to examine to what extent dark personality variables relate to different aspects of gossip (e.g., frequency, motives, etc.).”
Methodologically, the data were collected at a single point in time, so the study shows which traits tend to go along with more gossip, not whether the traits cause it. The study also relied entirely on self-report questionnaires, and people do not always have accurate insight into how often they talk about others. Some participants might underreport their behavior to avoid the social stigma of being labeled a gossip, though individuals high in callous traits like psychopathy and sadism may be less bothered by how they are perceived. That difference in candor could also make people high in these traits more willing to admit to gossiping, strengthening the apparent links.
The newly adapted Gossip Frequency Scale also combined positive, negative, and neutral chatter across many topics into a single score. Because of this design, the frequency measure cannot distinguish whether people high in dark traits are mostly sharing harmless news about celebrities or spreading cruel rumors about coworkers. Future studies could use naturalistic observation, daily diaries, or specific workplace scenarios to separate positive and negative gossip across different social settings.
Additionally, the Short Dark Tetrad questionnaire measures each personality trait as a single broad dimension, even though traits like narcissism and psychopathy contain multiple sub-facets, such as grandiose versus vulnerable narcissism. Future research could use more detailed personality inventories and track participants over time to better understand how specific facets of dark personalities shape everyday conversations.
“In the future, we would like to examine a wider range of gossip motives in connection with the Dark Tetrad personality traits,” the authors said. “More recently, researchers have proposed venting emotions and relationship-building gossip motives. It is unclear how narcissism, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and sadism might relate to these motives.”
While the current study analyzed how separate personality traits relate to gossip across the whole sample, the team also hopes to identify distinct profiles of gossipers. “In the current study we also used a variable-centered analytic approach,” the researchers noted. “In the future, we would like to use a person-centered analysis so that we can examine subgroups of participants based on similar response patterns.”
The study, “The Dark Tetrad Traits Differentially Predict Gossip Frequency and Motives,” was authored by Adam C. Davis, Tracy Vaillancourt, and Steven Arnocky.

Why Aren’t We Teaching Every Student CPR?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

In 2024, two Michigan high school students were sitting in the bleachers during a student-teacher basketball game when their physical education teacher collapsed from cardiac arrest. They had both recently learned cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) at a career-focused technical nursing center and rushed to help, beginning chest compressions and using an automated external defibrillator (AED) before emergency responders arrived.
Thanks to their actions, their teacher survived, and is one of approximately 350,000 Americans who experience an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest each year. Roughly nine out of ten will not survive.
We often describe the difference between life and death as a matter of speed: how quickly emergency services arrive and how fast a hospital can intervene. But in reality, cardiac arrest outcomes often depend on whether someone nearby begins CPR in the first few minutes, which rarely belong to emergency responders, but instead to whomever is standing closest: a classmate, teacher, stranger at a basketball game, or someone waiting for a train. Every minute without CPR sharply reduces the chances the patient will live long enough to reach a hospital.
Schools occupy a special role in public health. As a location most Americans pass through and one of the only places they may ever encounter CPR training, a high school classroom may be the best opportunity to prepare the next generation of lifesavers.
Schools already rehearse fire drills and lockdown drills for dangers that are statistically rare. Cardiac arrest is the reverse: far more common, and far less rehearsed. CPR skills can save lives years down the road when a cardiac arrest occurs at home, in a gym, at an airport, or at a university. Harnessing that opportunity requires both the resources to teach CPR effectively and the policies to ensure every student has the chance to learn it.
In Europe, Belgium, Denmark, France, Italy, Norway, Portugal, and England implemented school CPR education through national requirements or curriculum standards. Denmark offers a clear example of the positive impact. From 2001 to 2010, as Denmark introduced nationwide resuscitation initiatives including mandatory school CPR education, bystander CPR rates more than doubled, while 30-day survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest more than tripled.
A central challenge is how to implement CPR training at scale. The international KIDS SAVE LIVES initiative offers a practical blueprint. Endorsed by the World Health Organization, it calls for recurring, age-appropriate basic life support education beginning in childhood. Research from the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation shows children can learn the early links in the chain of survival from the young age of 4, perform effective chest compressions by age 12, and pass skills to family members and others.
Some may hesitate to perform CPR because of legal concerns over causing injury—like rib fractures—while administering CPR, but every state has Good Samaritan laws providing protections to people who render emergency aid in good faith. A 30-year review of U.S. litigation across all 50 states from 1989 to 2019 found no cases in which a layperson who provided CPR was held liable for causing harm.
The U.S. has also made significant progress in bringing CPR education into schools. In 1984, Alabama became the first state to require CPR instruction for high school graduation. Over the four decades since, communities have taken different approaches to bring CPR into the classroom. In West Virginia and Alaska, educators’ unions formally backed legislation requiring CPR education, while efforts in Washington and Illinois advanced in memory of students lost to cardiac arrest.
Today, 43 states require some form of CPR education before high school graduation. California, Colorado, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Hampshire, and Wyoming are the seven that remain. Several are already taking steps to expand CPR education. Massachusetts invested $425,000 to expand CPR education in public schools, while Colorado includes hands-on CPR and AED instruction in its statewide health education guidelines but stops short of requiring schools to provide it. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed a resolution directing the Instructional Quality Commission to include high school CPR in the state’s next health curriculum framework. San Francisco is taking an even broader approach, with paramedics and firefighters working to train 100,000 community members in CPR.
There is evidence that laws can translate into lifesaving action. A study of nearly 300,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests across 20 states found that patients had 12% higher odds of receiving bystander CPR in states with high school CPR education laws than those without them.
Other lifesaving education efforts can also offer a roadmap. In Georgia, Wesley’s Law, championed by Laura and Larry Gay after their son’s death, required public schools to stock overdose-reversal medication such as naloxone. In 2025, the state launched an opioid-settlement-funded initiative to provide overdose-reversal kits to public schools statewide, along with training resources for staff. In Indiana, emergency-response professionals helped expand Stop the Bleed training in schools, and the state’s Secured School Safety Grant program now offers funding for school bleeding-control programs and kits.
Both examples demonstrate how local champions and an existing source of funding can help turn a lifesaving idea into reality. Broadening collaboration among organizations such as the American Medical Association, American Red Cross, Project ADAM, and American Heart Association can also help expand CPR education nationwide.
After Buffalo Bills safety Damar Hamlin suffered cardiac arrest on the field in 2023, he became a leading advocate for the bipartisan HEARTS Act, which Congress passed unanimously in 2024. President Biden signed it into law later that year, supporting schools in expanding access to AEDs, CPR and AED education, and cardiac emergency response planning.
Cardiac arrest does not wait for emergency responders. The students who stepped forward when their teacher collapsed playing basketball in Michigan illustrate what becomes possible when CPR skills are taught before they are needed. Someday, every high school student in the U.S. could graduate prepared to step up and become a lifesaver.
