18:37:14 KST

Hundreds of Palestinians on Sunday attended the funeral of 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed by Israeli forces in Gaza during the early months of Israel’s genocidal war.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site on Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defence, told Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighbourhood in northeastern Gaza.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defence’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told Anadolu on October 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a ceasefire agreement in effect in Gaza since October 10 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90 percent of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

"Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility," Vance said on X.

It said officials made arrests overnight into Sunday, with most held on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence and vandalism.
Officials in Lyon said 160 people were in custody.
About 500 police officers, firefighters and paramedics were injured in the protests, Interior Minister Nunez said, adding the figure was provisional.
The violence occurred alongside nationwide cost-of-living protests, attended by 550,000 people according to the Interior Ministry, while the CGT union reported 800,000 participants.
Police used tear gas and water cannons against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.
A crowd-control grenade blew off a 17-year-old boy's right hand in the southern city of Saint-Etienne.
Analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group think tank said on X that Saturday's "terrible scenes were not political protest in any true sense. Most of the real demonstrations against high oil prices and failing schools were peaceful."
He added, "The violence came from a fringe of the ultra left. The looting by opportunistic gangs from the poor suburbs. All good news for Marine Le Pen."
During and after the demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty shelves.
France's Yellow Vest movement, which staged protests eight years ago against planned fuel-tax hikes by Macron's government, called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The primary grievance was the cost of living, which the war in the Middle East partly drove up, contributing to soaring inflation in Europe and elsewhere.

Feature: How Zhengzhou Marathon turns race into journey through Chinese civilization
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:27:10 CST
18:27:10 KST

ZHENGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- For most marathon runners, 42.195 kilometers is a test of endurance, discipline and will. In Zhengzhou, central China's Henan Province, the distance can also become a journey through thousands of years of Chinese civilization.
Held on October 18, the 2026 Zhengzhou Marathon offered a distinctive fusion of city running and cultural heritage.
"What surprised me most this year was the encounter between poetry and the marathon," said Tang Tao, a 35-year-old runner from Zhengzhou who has taken part in six consecutive editions of the event.
"Whether it was the ambience of the event or the on-site interactive activities, I felt surrounded by poetry," Tang said.
At the pre-race carnival, a specially designed "poetry corridor" drew visitors eager to photograph banners bearing famous Chinese verses. Lines such as "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step" and "Wildfires cannot burn it all away; the spring breeze brings it back to life" prompted spontaneous recitations, creating a fitting prelude to a race defined by perseverance and determination.
Together, these poems offered a fitting prelude to the marathon, where perseverance, uncertainty and the determination to keep moving forward are part of every runner's experience.
For Jong-May Urbonya, an American cultural influencer with nearly half a million followers who promotes Hanfu and Chinese traditions online, the poems struck a chord.
"The indomitable and forward-looking spirit depicted in the verses is precisely what marathon runners must possess," Urbonya said.
Poetry is only part of the story. As one of the cradles of Chinese civilization, Zhengzhou bears a long, continuous cultural thread beneath its layers of history. The 3,600-year-old Shang Dynasty city wall still stands in the city center , a reminder of the meeting of ancient and modern.
Zhao Hengkang, director of the Zhengzhou Sports Bureau, said the 2026 event wove four major local cultural elements - poetry, surnames, Henan Opera and kung fu - throughout the program.
Since its inaugural edition in 2018, the Zhengzhou Marathon has promoted a "Surname Marathon" concept rooted in Henan's kinship culture - the province is regarded as the ancestral home for many Chinese families and the origin of numerous surnames.
"For Chinese participants, a surname can evoke family history, ancestral origins and a sense of belonging. For international runners, the experience offers an accessible introduction to a cultural tradition in which a single family name may carry centuries of historical memory," said Ge Xiangyu, a runner who crossed the finish line carrying a flag bearing his surname.
Showing his medal, Ge added, "The symbolism goes beyond that of a souvenir," he said, noting that runners can personalize the design with magnetic stickers bearing their own surnames, making each medal uniquely their own.
Amid the hundreds of marathons held across China each year, culture is what sets Zhengzhou apart.
"We hope to make the Zhengzhou Marathon not only a competitive event for 25,000 runners, but also an immersive journey into the charm of traditional Chinese culture," Zhao said. ■

Interview: IMF official says China makes proactive efforts for maintaining multilateral, rules-based trading system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
17:27:02 CST
18:27:02 KST

Thomas Helbling, deputy director in the International Monetary Fund (IMF)'s Asia and Pacific Department, speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Bangkok, Thailand on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Rachen Sageamsak/Xinhua)
by Geng Lingnan, Liu Yang
BANGKOK, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China makes proactive efforts for maintaining a multilateral and rules-based trading system, and Chinese companies can play an important role in the diffusion of new technologies and in supporting their application through outbound investment, an International Monetary Fund (IMF) official has said.
The IMF has welcomed China's proactive efforts for maintaining a multilateral and rules-based trading system, Thomas Helbling, deputy director in the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, told Xinhua in an interview on the sidelines of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group held in Bangkok, Thailand.
"Ultimately, it will be important that countries resolve underlying tensions and differences behind trade disputes. For a large economy like China, it will be important for it to take on a leadership role in resolving some of these differences," he said.
Helbling also expects China to help deliver the benefits from new technologies to other countries through investment. Foreign direct investment by Chinese companies can play an important role in the diffusion of new technologies and in supporting their application in other countries, including in the digital and green energy sectors, he explained.
Helbling said the IMF remains concerned about risks from greater geoeconomic fragmentation and geopolitical tensions, which could obstruct trade and lead to greater trade frictions and more inefficiencies in the global and regional economy, as well as lower growth.
He stressed the IMF has long advocated that countries work toward resolution of the underlying issues behind trade tensions and toward an open, ideally multilateral trading system.
Speaking of economic resilience in China, and in Asia overall, Helbling noted that the impact of the energy shock has been more muted than expected earlier in the year, adding that in China's case, the government has mitigated the impact on end-user prices and mobilized other energy sources to partly compensate for the negative fossil fuel supply shock.
In addition, the AI boom is broadening and has broader positive spillover effects on the region, including China, he said.
In its latest Regional Economic Outlook for Asia and Pacific released on Thursday, the IMF raised Asia's 2026 economic growth forecast to 4.8 percent, up 0.4 percentage points from its April projection.
On the Asia-Pacific economic outlook, Helbling noted that while inventory buffers and measures such as energy subsidies or tax reductions have limited the impact of the energy supply shock, such measures are difficult to sustain over time.
He explained that if the energy shock lasts longer or intensifies, countries will at some point deplete their inventories, and the full price impact will affect the economy more severely. He recommended that countries rebuild buffers to ensure that they are in a position to effectively respond to another energy supply shock. ■

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:22:44 UTC
18:22:44 KST

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Sudanese are facing growing costs of medicine caused by the country’s civil war.
Hasanat al-Rashid, 48, has lived with diabetes for 15 years, and the three-and-a-half-year civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has worsened her situation. Finding the treatment she needs has become a daily struggle.
When the war broke out in April 2023, she was forced to flee south from her home in Haj Yousif in Khartoum North to Umm Daw Ban in Khartoum State.
During her displacement, she went for days without medication and was forced to eat foods unsuitable for her condition, such as asida, a traditional Sudanese porridge.
She underwent operations on her foot twice when she developed complications of diabetes, including a severe infection.
She moved between hospitals in Gezira State south of Khartoum, seeking treatment in Rufaa, Wad Madani and Al-Hasahisa. When fighting spread to these areas in December 2023, she fled again, arriving in Port Sudan, a city on the Red Sea that was less affected by the war.
Her condition has worsened to the point that she now has to use insulin every day and with this comes added costs, something that forces diabetes sufferers in Sudan to choose between medicine and other essentials, such as food.
“The doses vary depending on whether my blood sugar is high or low,” she told Al Jazeera.
The war has pushed income levels in Sudan back to those last seen in the 1990s, according to the United Nations Development Programme. This means Hasanat and other diabetes sufferers are struggling to afford the medicine they need to treat the condition.
Hasanat’s doctor recommended she use an insulin pen, a device used to inject insulin under the skin. She would need one or two of the devices a month, but the cost at 70,000 Sudanese pounds ($8) is more than she can afford up front, so she opts for a vial of insulin.
This is cheaper at 17,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.80), but there is the additional cost of buying ice every day to keep the insulin cool. She spends 180,000 pounds ($20) a month on ice to preserve the medicine. But she is able to spread these costs out through the month, making the vials her only viable option even if the overall costs are higher than an insulin pen.
“It may last a month or less, but the challenge is that I don’t have a refrigerator, so I struggle to store the insulin properly,” she said.
She also needs painkillers and vitamins on a regular basis to manage complications caused by the diabetes.
The rising cost of treatment
Fatima Adam, 75, is among the patients at Port Sudan Hospital struggling to afford the medicines she needs to manage her hypertension and a thyroid condition.
She was admitted to the hospital with complications caused by high blood pressure, which has started to impact her heart. Too unwell to speak to Al Jazeera herself, her daughter, Aisha, described how the rising cost of treatment has affected her whole family.
Before the war, Fatima received medicine through the National Health Insurance Fund. She paid a quarter of the cost while the fund covered the rest. But when the war started and the economy collapsed, the medicines she needed were no longer covered by the scheme.
“My mother takes six different medicines because hypertension has affected her heart in addition to her thyroid medication. The war has made things harder because the prices of these medicines have gone up,” Aisha told Al Jazeera.
The responsibility for paying for Fatima’s treatment and supporting her and her daughter falls on her son, who works as a casual worker. With no fixed income, he goes to the market every day in search of work but sometimes returns home empty without any luck.
“Sometimes, when my brother finds work, we buy enough medicine to last a month. Other times, we have to buy smaller quantities and take the medicines intermittently,” Aisha said.
She bought a month’s supply of her mother’s medication a few days ago for 160,000 Sudanese pounds ($17.80), a substantial expense for a family whose income depends on day labour but essential to treating Fatima’s condition.
War damage
The war has caused an estimated $500m in losses to medicine stocks, infrastructure and transport fleets, dealing a major blow to Sudan’s pharmaceutical supply system, the National Medical Supplies Fund told Al Jazeera.
The National Medicines and Poisons Board estimated that only eight of the 30 pharmaceutical factories in Khartoum that shut down during the conflict have resumed operations despite the security situation in the capital recently improving.
This has increased Sudan’s reliance on imported medicines, but the subsequent depreciation of the Sudanese pound has driven up the costs of pharmaceutical procurement and production.
Hossam al-Naeem, who works as a pharmacist in Port Sudan, said customers with diabetes and hypertension require regular painkillers and vitamins to help their overall condition.
“I feel deeply saddened when I see the expressions on some patients’ faces as they ask about the prices of medicines and discover how much they have increased because of the depreciation of the Sudanese pound,” Hossam told Al Jazeera.
The currency’s collapse has created added challenges for pharmacists. Before the war, a dollar traded for roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Now black-market currency traders are quoting rates of 9,300 pounds to the dollar, meaning higher costs for most goods in Sudan.
Sometimes Hossam incurs losses himself when he finds that the prices of drugs have risen sharply, and keeping essential medicines stocked is becoming difficult.
“I used to sell a strip of cold and flu tablets for 6,000 Sudanese pounds [70 cents]. But when I went to buy new stock, I found that the supplier’s price was also 6,000 pounds per strip. That means I made no profit, not even enough to cover the pharmacy’s operating costs,” he said.
The struggle to afford heart medication
Huda Mahmoud, 58, lives in el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state in south-central Sudan, where drone attacks and other violence remain a problem while the military is making advances towards the city.
Huda has lived with heart problems for more than 12 years and described the impacts of the war as being physical, financial and emotional.
“I take five different medicines. There was a time when they weren’t available, and I suffered a lot. Sometimes, I had to ask people in Wad Madani, Sennar or Port Sudan to send them to me,” she told Al Jazeera. “The medicines were extremely expensive, costing me 300,000 Sudanese pounds [$33.30] a month.”
Taking medication has become a carefully managed routine with each pill tied to a specific time of day.
“I’ve become tied to my pills: this one before eating, that one afterwards. If I forget one, my heart starts beating very fast,” she added.
In March, Huda was forced to travel from el-Obeid to Omdurman. Following her strict treatment regimen has become increasingly difficult during repeated periods of upheaval.
She has now returned home to el-Obeid, where her regular medicine is priced at 151,000 Sudanese pounds ($16.80) a month, something she can barely afford.
Her greatest fear is running out of medicine or being unable to afford her next supply, which would put her at risk of a blood clot.
“I’m afraid of becoming incapacitated. I used to be responsible for the whole household, but now I need help. I feel like I’ve become a burden on my family,” she said.

Houthis release video of Saudi AH-6i helicopter being hit
Unknown

2026-10-18

- The Saudi-led coalition said a National Guard AH-6i helicopter crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing both crew members.
- Houthi footage appears to show the helicopter being hit by a 358-family loitering munition, which the group calls Saqr.
Footage released by Yemen’s Houthis appears to show a Saudi National Guard AH-6i helicopter being struck by a loitering munition over Saudi Arabia’s Najran province, after the Saudi-led coalition said the aircraft crashed because of a technical malfunction, killing its two crew members.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said on Oct. 18 that the AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter, which belonged to Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of National Guard, crashed and was destroyed inside Saudi territory in the Najran area, near the border with Yemen. Both officers on board were killed. The coalition did not identify them or give further details.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree had said a day earlier that the group shot down a Saudi helicopter, which he described as an Apache, near Najran while it was attacking Houthi positions along the border. Al-Maliki responded on social media with a photo of a row of Apache helicopters, writing that the Houthis claimed to have shot one down but that it would enter the battlefield soon.
The video the Houthis later published appears to show a small helicopter consistent with the AH-6i being hit in flight. The weapon in the footage appears to be an Iranian-designed loitering munition from the 358 family, which the Houthis field under the name Saqr.
The 358 is a small, jet-powered surface-to-air loitering munition. Launched from a rail, it can circle over an area, search for low, slow targets such as helicopters and drones, and detonate near them. Iranian-made 358 components have been found in weapons shipments to the Houthis intercepted at sea, and the group has used the munition against drones over Yemen.
The AH-6i is a light attack and reconnaissance helicopter built by Boeing and based on the MH-6 Little Bird used by U.S. special operations forces. It carries a crew of two and can be armed with machine guns, rockets and guided missiles. The Saudi Arabian National Guard ordered about two dozen of the helicopters from the United States in the mid-2010s and uses them for reconnaissance and close air support.
Najran has come under repeated Houthi drone and missile attacks in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated. A week before the crash, Houthi strikes killed 13 people at Riyadh’s international airport, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:19:00 UTC
18:19:00 KST

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
October 18, 2026
Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.
The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.
Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made up Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).
The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.
How does the deal benefit Vietnam?
The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% to be tariff-free within seven years, the Norwegian government said in a statement.
According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.
Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.
It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:18:40 UTC
18:18:40 KST

There is no single interval for every part. Brake pads may be replaced according to wear, while timing belts usually follow a specific mileage or time interval.
Owners searching for kia spare parts sharjah, hyundai spare parts sharjah, or infiniti spare parts sharjah should match parts with the exact model, engine specification, and manufacturer requirements. Al-Miyar offers replacement parts matched to different vehicle specifications.
How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Every component experiences different stress. Some parts wear through friction, while others deteriorate because of heat, vibration, contamination, or age. As a result, car parts replacement intervals vary significantly.
Driving conditions also affect car parts replacement schedule. Heavy traffic, short trips, dusty roads, extreme temperatures, towing, and heavy loads can increase wear.
A practical plan should consider:
· Mileage and vehicle age
· Manufacturer recommendations
· Driving and road conditions
· Climate
· Visible wear or damage
· Changes in performance
· Maintenance history
This provides a more realistic way to determine how often to replace car parts.
Which Car Parts Usually Need More Attention?
Some components need regular inspection because they experience continuous wear or affect vehicle control. Understanding when to replace car parts is particularly important for brakes and tires.
Brake Pads and Brake Rotors
Brake components directly affect stopping performance. Brake pads become thinner through friction, but their service life varies with driving habits, traffic, vehicle weight, road conditions, and brake-system design.
Warning signs include:
· Squealing or grinding
· Vibration during braking
· Changes in pedal feel
· Longer stopping distances
· Reduced pad material
Brake rotors may also require replacement when excessively worn, damaged, or below the manufacturer's specified thickness. Inspection is more useful than relying only on mileage.
 
Tires
 
Tire replacement cannot be determined by mileage alone. Tread depth, uneven wear, cracks, age, damage, and handling changes can indicate that a tire needs attention.
 
Incorrect pressure and poor wheel alignment can accelerate uneven wear. Regular inspection helps maintain traction and handling.
 
Engine Oil and Filters
 
Engine oil becomes contaminated and may lose protective properties. Oil-change intervals depend on the vehicle, engine, oil specification, driving conditions, and manufacturer recommendations.
 
Oil filters are commonly replaced during an oil service. Al-Miyar offers parts for different vehicle models.
 
Parts With Longer but More Important Replacement Intervals
 
Some components remain in service longer, but their specified intervals are important.
 
Timing Belts
A timing belt synchronizes important engine components and may fail without an obvious warning. Replacement is generally based on the manufacturer's mileage or time interval.
 
On some engines, failure can cause significant engine damage. The car parts replacement schedule should account for both mileage and age when specified.
 
Batteries
 
A battery gradually loses its ability to hold a charge. Climate, driving patterns, electrical demand, battery type, and vehicle usage affect its useful life.
 
Slow cranking, dimming electrical systems, or starting difficulties may indicate that testing is needed. Unlike a timing belt, a battery does not have one universal replacement point.
 
Spark Plugs
 
Spark plugs are essential to petrol-engine combustion, but service intervals vary by engine and plug type.
 
Worn plugs can contribute to rough running, difficult starting, reduced fuel efficiency, or misfires. The vehicle-specific maintenance schedule is more reliable than a generic mileage figure.
How Driving Conditions Change Replacement Timing
 
Two vehicles with identical mileage can have different maintenance requirements. A vehicle driven on open roads may experience different wear from one driven the same distance in congested traffic.
 
Severe conditions include:
 
1.     Frequent short journeys
 
2.     Heavy stop-and-go traffic
 
3.     Extreme temperatures
 
4.     Dusty or poorly surfaced roads
 
5.     Heavy towing or loads
 
6.     Long periods of inactivity
 
Therefore, how often to replace car parts should be considered alongside actual vehicle use. Urban braking can increase brake wear, while dusty roads may require more frequent air-filter inspections.
 
A Practical Replacement Schedule
 
There is no universal schedule, but this framework identifies key items to monitor.
This table is a general framework, not a substitute for the maintenance schedule for a specific vehicle.
 
When Should You Replace a Part Before It Fails?
 
Waiting for complete failure is not always appropriate, particularly for braking, steering, suspension, tires, and engine timing components.
 
The useful question is whether the part still operates within its required limits. Replacing a brake pad at its specified wear limit is different from waiting until all friction material disappears.
 
Similarly, replacing a timing belt at its scheduled interval is different from waiting for failure. Understanding how often should car parts be replaced can help address wear before it becomes a larger mechanical problem.
 
The Maintenance Schedule Is a Starting Point, Not the Whole Story
 
A manufacturer's schedule provides a baseline for a specific vehicle and powertrain, but actual component condition also matters.
 
Drivers should notice unusual sounds, vibrations, warning lights, fluid leaks, braking changes, starting difficulties, or handling changes. Regular inspections can identify developing problems before they result in expensive repairs.
 
A vehicle-specific maintenance plan is the clearest reference for "how often do car parts need to be replaced", while inspections help account for actual wear and changing driving conditions.
 
Maintenance records are also useful for tracking time- and mileage-based services. For owners asking how often do car parts need to be replaced, the most reliable approach combines manufacturer recommendations, mileage and age, and the actual condition of each component.
 
Not sure whether a part is due for replacement or simply needs inspection? Start with the vehicle's maintenance schedule, then have the component's actual condition checked before deciding to replace it.
 
Conclusion
 
There is no universal answer to how often do car parts need to be replaced because components have different service requirements. Brake pads and tires depend heavily on wear and driving conditions, while timing belts and spark plugs generally follow vehicle-specific intervals.
 
The practical approach is to combine the manufacturer's schedule with regular inspections and attention to warning signs. This helps owners address worn components before complete failure.

Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens
Clashes between Yemeni forces and Houthis cause casualties on both sides as aid agencies warn of a deepening human crisis.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen amid a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
Eight soldiers loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government were killed during heavy clashes on the al-Maqatirah front in Lahij governorate, the government-affiliated Tur al-Bahah military axis said in a statement on Saturday.
In Taiz governorate, government troops said they killed 12 Houthi fighters in al-Aqroud, following days of fighting on the outskirts of Taiz city, where Saudi Arabia-backed government forces reported repelling Houthi advances and inflicting heavy losses on the group.
Elsewhere in Taiz, government forces said they broke a Houthi attack on the al-Shaqab front, while government-aligned Homeland Shield Forces reported destroying a Houthi supply vehicle with a drone in al-Wazziyah. The Southern Giants Brigades also said they targeted Houthi positions with precision strikes in al-Madaribah, near the Lahij border.
Meanwhile, government troops and allied Popular Resistance fighters pressed ahead with their offensive in al-Jawf and Marib.
Military officials reported using artillery barrages and drone strikes against Houthi military positions, barracks and troop assemblies in al-Jawf, while coalition aircraft bombed Houthi command hubs and supply depots.
Government artillery and missile units also targeted Houthi lines in Marib.
Yemen’s war has escalated sharply since the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive, and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, seized by the Iran-aligned group in 2014.
Saudi helicopter crashes
On the aerial front, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the group’s air defence forces brought down a Saudi reconnaissance drone over the governorate of Hajjah. He identified the aircraft as a Turkish-manufactured Lentatek Karayel drone, saying it was the fourth of its kind downed since the latest escalation began.
The Houthis also claimed they shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter in the kingdom’s border province of Najran.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki said an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter had crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing two crew members.
Houthi media also reported 10 Saudi air strikes targeting sites in Saada governorate.
Off the coast of al-Mukalla, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency reported that at least seven armed men on board a skiff attacked a liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker. They fired two shots at the tanker before the vessel’s onboard security detail returned two warning shots, forcing the attackers to change course and disengage.
Worsening humanitarian crisis
Meanwhile, the human cost of the conflict continues to rise, with humanitarian agencies warning of worsening conditions for civilians.
According to the International Organization for Migration, more than 233,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in Yemen, including about 121,000 in Taiz governorate alone.
The World Health Organization has also warned that Taiz city has become functionally isolated, with its 12 hospitals holding fuel for only four days, no surgical supplies, and facing critical shortages of oxygen and medicine amid a growing cholera outbreak.
The displacement crisis has spread to East Africa, with the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) confirming that more than 4,000 refugees have reached the region — 3,800 in Djibouti and roughly 200 in Somalia. The UNHCR also reported that health workers are treating a cholera outbreak at Djibouti’s Markazi camp, where 31 cases and one death have been recorded.

Summer drought drives up truffle prices in Switzerland

Summer drought drives up truffle prices in Switzerland
This summer’s drought has severely impacted the truffle season. The truffles are smaller than usual and scarce in the forests of canton Vaud, which has driven up prices. At the truffle market in the region La Côte, for example, the price per kilogram of truffles has risen by 30%, from CHF700 to CHF1,000 ($847-$1,210).
In the forests of Vaud, Joachim Fivaz and his dog Cita are searching for the prized mushroom. The dog’s nose is spot-on, but the haul is disappointing: the truffles are significantly smaller than usual. The reason? These mushrooms need moisture during their seven-month growth cycle, and the summer heatwave proved fatal for them.
+ Drought in Switzerland: Europe’s ‘water tower’ runs dry
At La Côte truffle market, the effects are being felt. This Saturday, there were only three vendors – half as many as last year. This scarcity is driving up prices: CHF1,000 per kilo this year, compared to CHF700 last year. A 30% increase that hasn’t deterred enthusiasts, however. “Chocolate is expensive, but we don’t deprive ourselves of it – and neither do we with truffles,” says one customer. “We can treat ourselves with just a few grams – no need to buy kilos,” adds another.
Rahman Dedic, president of the French-Speaking Switzerland Truffle Association, explains the price increase. “Given that there are fewer truffles and we have to travel farther to find them, it’s normal for prices to be higher than last year.” For those who make their living from truffles, he acknowledges that “it’s been a very difficult year”.
Several other truffle markets are scheduled for the coming weeks in French-speaking Switzerland.

‘The algorithm is a psychopath’: Why Israelis are trying to quit social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:11:34 UTC
18:11:34 KST

"Look, I don't have any other addictions. I'm not prone to getting addicted to things like cigarettes, alcohol or substances like that," says Ofra Miron-Lichter firmly. "But I'm very prone to screen addiction, and by screens I mean all of them. First I got addicted to Facebook, then Instagram, TikTok and news websites."
Miron-Lichter is a clinical psychologist who was supposed to talk about "the phenomenon." Instead, she offers a candid account of her own addiction to screens, social media and news updates, which turned her into a "junkie," as she describes herself. Her family even blocked her access to the Haredi news website Behadrei Haredim, where she had been getting her news after all the other websites had been blocked as part of a self-imposed detox program.
"I would look for it every spare moment," she adds. "And I'm a busy person with a lot going on, someone who knows it's bad and unhealthy, but that didn't change anything. I just kept looking for it, and I had no real motivation to change. Eventually, what happens to every addicted person happened to me: It got so bad that I had to do something about it."
What made you say enough was enough?
"It's a little personal, but people always talk about the body image problems it causes, beauty standards, anxieties that surface or wasted time. But we don't talk enough about the depressive states that screen addiction creates. And the depression isn't caused by some particular content you're exposed to on Instagram. It's not because everyone else is attractive and you're not. It's the passive scrolling itself. The very act of staring at a screen as time disappears.
"You don't need to see everyone else doing incredible things with their lives while you're not. The real mechanism that causes the harm is scrolling, the fact that you're sitting and watching rather than doing anything, just consuming content, even if it's educational, even if you're watching National Geographic or the History Channel.
"That's true of television too, but it's intensified on social media because the algorithm pushes all the addiction buttons, and you're constantly anticipating what the next video will be. It's a shutting down of the brain that creates depression. Not sadness, not a little dip in your mood because of comparisons we make, not a passing sense of feeling down. It creates real clinical depression and a significant drop in energy."
And when you're not looking at a screen, you're not entirely focused?
"Your attention becomes divided during every activity because you're wondering what you're missing on social media, or when you can finally go back or when it's acceptable to check your feed again. Or you're looking at a big screen and your phone at the same time.
"And yet, divided attention is a relatively minor problem compared with depression, which is a major problem and also causes anxiety and sleep problems. Willpower is no match for it. You can explain and understand the psychology of the algorithm and screen exposure, but all the knowledge in the world is no match for this habit.
"That's true even as awareness grows and schools no longer allow phones into classrooms, and it will remain true even when external regulation of social media is introduced. Only restrictions we impose on ourselves will help here. And that's very difficult, for children and adults alike.
"It's not easy for me to say this, but it's stronger than we are. The algorithm is a psychopath. It doesn't care what's in its way. It will do anything to get what it wants, and what it wants is you, your time, your attention, your clicks. You're facing a psychopath, and you have to protect yourself."
Miron-Lichter, 52, who also discusses the subject on her Hebrew-language podcast, "Sane Psychology in a Crazy World," recognized the symptoms in herself four years ago and took action. She completely cut herself off from every social media platform and news website, closing loopholes that had allowed her access through the family's laptop and iPad.
"There are lots of apps that block access to websites, send alerts saying, 'You've used up your time here for today,' or disable push notifications from websites, but they're a joke. You press 'skip' and keep going. Only ironclad blocks work, like when you don't know the password to reopen the gate to your feed and have no way around it.
"My husband had TikTok on his phone, and I would wait for him to come home so I could look at it. I completely wrecked his For You feed. I searched for what I wanted to watch, and his algorithm began changing what it showed to suit me. It learned who I was in seconds. Within an hour, it had been completely trained and had even tailored the ads to me.
"Eventually, I asked my husband to remove TikTok, and he did. The restriction extended to him too. My children were also limited in what they could have on their phones. When my son realized he was starting to get addicted too, he spent a while carrying an old-fashioned Nokia 'dumbphone', and we realized how complicated that was. Your credit card and Waze are all on your phone. It's very hard to go backward. But you have to find a very effective, very durable solution if you want to succeed."
Or self-discipline, perhaps?
"There's no self-discipline here. People need to understand that when it comes to screens, they really can't trust themselves. It's like taking a drug addict who's been clean for 10 years and putting heroin right in front of his face.
"Of course, there are people who manage to balance their time on social media and are less prone to addiction. My husband never got addicted to TikTok, but most of us do. Most people can't break this cycle."
What's life like on the other side, now that you've kicked your screen addiction?
"First of all, it frees up time. I'm more focused than I used to be. My mood is better. But the withdrawal symptoms are still there, like boredom and the feeling that you're out of the loop.
"I would search for any website where I could still get a little news, like looking for a cigarette butt on the sidewalk. That's how I discovered Haredi websites, which also carry news updates during wartime. During the war with Iran, my son blocked me from those too."
What about foreign news websites?
"Everything is blocked, everything! I don't have Google Chrome on my phone, iPad or computer. I look at minutes of screen time the way I'd look at a substance. And there are certain situations, like wars, that can make you relapse, just as people turn to alcohol or smoking during times of hardship and crisis.
"War sends many of us into a scrolling spiral that we can't escape even after it's over. We saw that during COVID too."
What do you do while waiting at the dentist? Just stare into space?
"I've gone back to reading books. I use Duolingo, talk to people on the phone and listen to music or podcasts. And look, I knew about what happened on the Flydubai flight, including everything that went on in the cockpit, without being connected to anything. You'd have to be on a desert island for important news not to reach you."
Miron-Lichter is a conservative representative of the growing movement of people disconnecting from social media. The most stringent among them even block themselves from niche news websites and retrain their thumbs to stop making the scrolling motion.
Others choose a middle path: Instagram installed only on an iPad rather than a cellphone, an app that blocks access to the feed at night, or a weeklong detox before returning. It's called "social cleansing."
They are of all ages and both sexes, united by a sense of disgust and a growing awareness of the price they are paying for endless scrolling, which has become an uncontrollable habit, performed like a motor tic dozens of times a day.
An article published this month in The New York Times examined fears that teenagers are trapped in "brain rot," a state of being hypnotized by an endless stream of mind-numbing TikTok videos and Reels featuring cats, dancing or "AI slop." But even adults consuming more intellectually demanding content are trying to put a finger in the dam to stem their compulsive hunger to scroll.
As with cigarettes, so with screens: Nobody quits smoking just because they see blackened lungs on a cigarette package. But a new wave of users is putting checks and balances in place.
Last July, influencer Liya Noga announced, on Instagram, of course, that she was deleting social media apps from her phone. "I realized they were making me focus far too much on how I look and compare myself to other women during five to seven hours of scrolling a day. I scrolled for hours without purpose, forgetting who I was and feeling bad about myself."
Young people on Reddit and Instagram describe switching to simple phones, including old-fashioned flip phones. In Instagram Stories posted after Yom Kippur this year, there were already quite a few declarations from influencers and ordinary social media users that disconnecting had actually been enjoyable, along with promises to try to incorporate it into everyday life.
Around the middle of the year, I also felt that something had to change. More than 15 years at the mercy of the algorithm began on the social network Mekusharim, moved to Facebook, then Instagram and TikTok, and now continue on Substack, a relatively new social network built around newsletters.
On almost every platform, the scrolling experience ends the same way: nausea after being force-fed information I didn't need, regret over 40 minutes that vanished, the feeling that I had fallen out of time, and an overwhelming urge to shop. Buy everything. Buy it now. Preferably with a coupon code.
My initial excitement over the magical algorithm that somehow knew I was one of millions planning a trip to Japan and delivered recommendation videos straight to me gave way to the feeling that someone had rummaged through my brain without my consent. And worst of all was the realization that I couldn't stop.
So I deleted the Instagram app from my phone and went one step further: I deliberately forgot my password so I couldn't log in from my computer either. I gained some peace, and more importantly, I gradually began forgetting the names of influencers' children. But I also felt as though I had thrown away an invitation to a class party and still wanted to know what was happening there.
Today, I'm still sticking to this arrangement, with planned two-hour lapses on weekends, after which I immediately delete the app again until the following week.
*****
"I've tried deleting Instagram twice: once for an extended period during pregnancy and again recently for a week," says Liraz Vazana, 27, from Beersheba, an occupational therapy student who has also recently started creating content for social media.
"I found myself constantly looking for the app. When you're sad, confused or don't know what you want, you open Instagram and it's just like a pacifier. It's emotional regulation in the most unregulated way imaginable. It makes you forget whatever feelings you had before, and you come away completely drained."
Why did you go back?
"When I was on pregnancy-related bed rest, I would catch myself scrolling through Instagram in the browser because I'd deleted the app. When I realized what I was doing, I said, 'Enough, you're just lying to yourself. You might as well download the app so at least it'll be convenient.'
"I now have a time limit set within Instagram, and it really doesn't help me. The overload is constant, every day, and so are the voices in your head. It's like a million people seeing you in the playground and telling you that you need to put socks on your child. Or a million hippies telling you about the quantum leap they've experienced and why you should try it too, and women showing off their beautiful homes.
"During the period when I wasn't on Instagram, I felt I needed that something, to open my phone and fiddle with it. I downloaded games and then tried to get rid of those too, but the overall feeling was that it was hard to fight.
"I would be sitting and breastfeeding, wondering what I was doing with my life, and find myself back on Instagram, then feel frustrated about it. Really, is the thing you need to do when you wake up in the morning catch up on the life of a woman you don't know? You're almost like her friend. You're sad with her, happy with her, excited for her and worried about her, and she doesn't even know your name."
*****
You might think people who create content for social media are protected from the mind-numbing passivity of scrolling, and can even make a living from it. But not really.
"They say it's better to be a creator than a consumer on social media, but when I post something, I also get caught up in who liked it, how much reach it gets in the first hour and what people wrote to me in direct messages," says Raen Hasbani, 27, from Tirat Carmel, a content creator who started on YouTube at 13.
"Nobody is immune to it. Even the people creating the content, who are supposedly on the right side because they're making money or gaining publicity from it, are trapped too.
"And to upload content, you also have to consume content. Ninety percent of my time is spent watching other people, and I even make excuses to myself that it's my job and I'm getting inspiration.
"People on social media don't care about one another. You scroll and stop at whoever gives you the most explosive line, the most sensational hook, a sound effect that grabs your attention, regardless of who they are or what they want to say.
"That's where I fall into the trap too. Instead of communicating messages differently, I also get sucked into finding that hook. I use the audience's familiarity with celebrities or well-known figures. I put a few seconds of them saying or doing something at the beginning of a video, then move on to talking about it myself. And of course I'm caught in a dopamine loop of highs and lows whenever I post something, and that's no less addictive than scrolling."
Doesn't that make you want to abandon the whole thing?
"It's mainly the moment you realize that if you don't have to pay money to be on Instagram, then this is the real payment: what you do there, your movements, your interest and your attention.
"Three years ago, I deleted TikTok and decided to divide my life between two phones, one for work and one personal phone with no social media apps. I don't have notifications from any apps on that phone, and I feel that I have control over my attention when I use it.
"If I want to open WhatsApp and answer or send a message, it's not because some guy named Itzik sent something and I have to reply right that second, even if I'm doing something else. I actively open it because that's the right time for me. And yet, I still manage to break the restrictions I've set for myself and spend more time there than I want or need to."
The desire to sink into the comfort of the feed grows when the need for community becomes stronger, even when people understand that it is a parasocial form of community, built around one-sided relationships.
"After a month without Instagram, I realized that what I was looking for was a feeling of togetherness," Vazana says. "I felt in my bones that I was missing it, and it took me time to understand what that feeling was. How is it that influencers make you feel you're their friend, even though you're not? In fact, that feeling actually makes you less likely to go out and form friendships in the real world.
"I see lots of friends around me trying to rethink their relationship with Instagram. They make rules for themselves, like not going on after 10 p.m., or they delete the app completely for certain periods. I'm now trying to stay away from social media on Fridays and Saturdays."
Hasbani links this to a shift in social media algorithms.
"They used to be a place to connect, where everyone was equal and consumed the same content. I clearly remember how, one year, everyone at my school, and maybe everyone in the world, knew the song 'Gangnam Style' from YouTube. The feed showed us the same things.
"Today, I sit with friends and the algorithm shows each of us something different. The experience of spending time on social media has become more personal and less communal.
"Even when I'm sitting with friends who all spend several hours a day scrolling Instagram, we haven't necessarily been exposed to the same people, and we don't understand one another's experiences the way we used to."
The growing desire among many people to distance themselves from social media raises the question of where they are now supposed to get their news and political information. Between an influencer's food Story and a cat video, Instagram and TikTok have also established themselves in recent years as places where people consume news and form opinions about it. A Reuters report based on a survey of 100,000 respondents of all ages found that 54% had consumed news on social media in the week preceding the survey.
Instagram, which according to the Israel Internet Association led social media platforms last year with an overall usage rate of nearly 80% among young people, is home to accounts trying, often successfully, to figure out how to deliver news to the scrolling generation, ages 18 to 35.
One example is the news outlet "Under the Radar," which has 177,000 Instagram followers. In recent months, it has been publishing content about the upcoming elections, including posts presenting political candidates as profiles on dating apps, a format dubbed "Politinder," and Reels explaining how much elections cost.
The major challenge is to attract likes without feeding the algorithm extreme, polarizing rhetoric.
"I admit I didn't understand anything I was reading in the news," says Ori Herzberg, 26, who founded Under the Radar about five years ago, when he was 21.
"Back then, Instagram didn't have news or accessible explanations of complex issues. When we asked young people where they consumed content, they repeatedly told us they didn't go to external news websites, so it was clear we needed to be where young people already were.
"We saw that a young Israeli spends almost four hours a day on Instagram and that most use all the social media platforms daily. This is absolutely the place where you decide what kind of coffee you drink, which shirt you buy and which ballot you put in the box."
Do many people on Instagram share political content, or do they consume it quietly?
"You share what you identify with and what you want to be part of your feed and the way people perceive you, or content that made you very angry, in which case you also write something negative about it. Of course, we prefer the identification option.
"We always try to ask how we can make the state budget interesting to you without wrapping the content in something populist or stupid. Instead, we ask why it's relevant to you as a young reservist who has completed 400 days of reserve duty."
But not everyone on these platforms operates the way you do.
"On social media, anyone can do whatever they want without any disclosure. There's an enormous amount of fake content and provocative headlines presented in quotation marks as though someone actually said them, when nobody did, except perhaps the person who wrote the item. It's designed to provoke reactions purely to generate traffic.
"Young social media users can no longer tell whether they're consuming fake content, and that further distorts the way they perceive political reality."
With so many young people wanting to break out of the cycle, some even switching to dumbphones, is there an effort to reach them offline?
"Yes, we've held quite a few in-person events around the elections, attracting 700 people. But put simply, social media is still the main way to reach an audience today."
*****
Watching a Reel telling you that you need to quit Instagram while you're actually on Instagram might sound funny, or suggest that all hope is lost. But amid growing demand to rethink our relationship with social media, content creators have emerged who do exactly that.
Linda Natan is a couples therapist and group facilitator who also found herself trapped.
"My business wouldn't look the same without Instagram, and it grew significantly thanks to that exposure," she explains. "Financially, too, there's a clear before and after social media in terms of what I earned. But I realized that when you don't know how to shape your technological environment to suit your needs, the benefits come with a million drawbacks. So you end up absorbing 90% disadvantages for 10% success.
"The point when I said, 'Enough, it's no longer worth it,' was when I noticed that I was scrolling while sitting next to people who matter to me and whom I want to spend time with, like my children. I was doing it even when I no longer wanted to, when I knew it didn't feel good, but I couldn't stop. Or when I found myself opening Instagram without consciously choosing to, because I hadn't really wanted to open it and scroll for 15 minutes. It just somehow happened."
Can you explain why that happens?
"It's a bit like driving a car without studying the theory, taking driving lessons or passing a test. You're given something powerful, but nobody makes sure you know how to use it properly or protect yourself from the harm it can cause.
"There's not enough awareness that we can change our phones' default settings instead of absorbing every notification from social media, like messages telling you someone liked your post or wrote you something. Those features were designed to pull you in, not for your mental well-being, and we don't do enough with our settings to avoid falling into those traps."
What traps have you personally eliminated to break your screen addiction?
"It came down to something as basic as where I put my phone charger. In our house, and this might sound extreme, there's no scenario in which we go to sleep with a phone in the bedroom. We know our hands will reach for it before we fall asleep and first thing in the morning.
"The conversation isn't about my willpower at all. I remove the temptation so I don't have to rely on willpower. We have a charging station in the farthest corner of the house, not in the living room or kitchen, where we spend our family time. I don't have notifications, not even on WhatsApp. Anyone who needs me calls. I've also stopped expecting people to answer the moment I send them something.
"It was a long process, both understanding why we were dealing with this at home in the first place and getting family and friends on board with these choices. Because part of the difficulty in disconnecting is the fear of having difficult conversations and telling the people around you that you won't be available to them on WhatsApp every moment.
"Nobody teaches us that you can receive notifications from just five important people on WhatsApp instead of being endlessly available."
Together with psychologist Rotem Kahani, Natan leads a challenge designed to encourage mindful screen use.
"It includes having a kind of 'Yom Kippur,' disconnecting completely to experience the effect on your time, attention and body. Then many people report withdrawal symptoms, a feeling that nothing has any value, irritability and a lack of motivation. It passes after a few days, but it's not an easy stage.
"For those who can't delete social media because of their business, we suggest practical ways to limit their use. Not in an open-buffet format where you can go on whenever you want, but in a smart way. Limit the number of days, the number of hours, decide what part of the day you want to be there, and maybe remove the app from your device.
"As strange as it sounds in today's world, you need to make it less convenient. We also say it isn't a choice between zero and 100% use, because that approach very quickly leads back to 100%."
What have you gained by putting your finger in the dam?
"One of the positive effects is being present with my children. I enjoy spending time with them more, rather than feeling it's a task. I've also discovered that I can enjoy a simple encounter without feeling overwhelmed all the time.
"The relentless mechanism of social media makes you feel that things that once brought you joy no longer do, because simple things, like sitting down for a meal and looking someone in the eye, reading a book or spending time with your children, require more attention and produce lower levels of dopamine, while the brain is constantly searching for more and more.
"You're also able to process emotions instead of just suppressing them, because the instinct is almost always to scroll and eat sugar when something is really weighing on you. It's very refreshing to feel frustrated and simply experience that feeling for a while, without shutting down your brain and looking at someone else's life."

Ukraine prepares two low-cost domestic missiles for combat use against jet-powered Geran drones
Two Ukrainian teams are preparing domestically developed surface-to-air missiles for combat use against Russian jet-powered drones.
Source: Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the Ukrainian defence-tech cluster Brave1, in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda
Details: "They are cheap and easy to manufacture. One of the requirements was to keep the cost of a missile below US$20,000," Hrytseniuk said.
The ambition of these projects is underscored by the average market cost of missiles, ranging from hundreds of thousands of dollars per shot for a Stinger to half a million dollars for an AIM-9X missile used by F-16 fighter jets.
Even using two or three such missiles against a Russian long-range drone is expected to be cost-effective relative to the value of the target. Various estimates put the cost of a standard Geran at around US$70,000, while its jet-powered version may cost tens of thousands of dollars more.
Hrytseniuk said Brave1 began funding the development of surface-to-air missiles in 2024. It took two years to produce the first prototypes. A total of 10 Ukrainian teams are working on such missiles.
Background: In May, it was reported that Ukraine is developing low-cost interceptor missiles and had already tested some solutions. Then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said there were plans to scale up their production dozens of times.

Iran's parliament approves Mehrdad Akhlaqi as minister of defence
DUBAI, Oct 18 - Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
Akhlaqi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.
Akhlaqi has spent decades in Iran's defence industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. He is subject to US and EU sanctions over his work in Iran's defence sector.
In a programme presented to lawmakers, Akhlaqi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate the development of defence technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies.
"If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran.
CNN reported this week that the US has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations.
The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal.
"The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlaqi said. REUTERS

Slovenian firm arms drone killer systems with Gatling gun
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:01:38 UTC
18:01:38 KST

- Valhalla Turrets announced a new Skythunder air defense system combining a 20 mm M197 Gatling gun, 70 mm laser-guided rockets and 360-degree radar.
- Company renders show the counter-drone system on an Oshkosh FMTV 6x6 truck chassis, the type used to carry HIMARS.
Slovenian turret maker Valhalla Turrets is preparing a new version of its Skythunder air defense system armed with General Dynamics Land Systems’ 20 mm M197 Gatling gun and 70 mm laser-guided rockets, designed to shoot down drones and protect critical infrastructure.
The company announced the system as “coming soon” in a social media post and released renders showing the turret mounted on a 6×6 Oshkosh truck chassis from the U.S. military’s Family of Medium Tactical Vehicles, the same type of truck that carries the U.S. Army’s HIMARS rocket launcher.
The three-barrel M197 is the cannon carried in the nose turret of U.S. Marine Corps AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters, and Valhalla says it will give the new Skythunder high-volume fire against drones and other low-flying targets. The 70 mm laser-guided rockets add a longer-reach option for targets beyond the gun’s effective range, giving the system what the company describes as layered kinetic effects across different distances.
According to Valhalla, the system will have full 360-degree radar coverage, use its sensors to find and track targets, and plug into wider layered air defense networks. The company describes it as mobile and modular, and says it is meant to provide cost-effective protection against large numbers of drones.
The new Skythunder adds a lighter gun option to a family Valhalla introduced this year. At Eurosatory in Paris in June 2026, the company showed the Skythunder 300 on a Mercedes-Benz Zetros 8×8 truck, armed with a Northrop Grumman MK44S Bushmaster 30 mm cannon, a separate rotating station with a 7.62 mm M134D Gatling gun and Arnold Defense laser-guided rockets. Valhalla also builds the MANGART 25 AD short-range air defense turret, which it unveiled on a Patria 8×8 vehicle for Slovenia in May 2026.
Its turrets are also turning up abroad. Azerbaijani defense company Zireh unveiled the HMS30 mobile air defense system at ADEX 2026 in Baku, built around a Valhalla Turrets turret with an electro-optical sighting system and two Russian-designed 30 mm 2A42 cannons. Zireh says the HMS30 can engage drones at about 1.5 to 2 km (0.9 to 1.2 miles).
Valhalla, based in Ljubljana, specializes in remote-controlled turrets and weapon stations and works as a development partner for several larger European defense companies. In August 2026, General Dynamics European Land Systems integrated a Valhalla turret into its ASCOD tracked combat vehicle.
Gun-based systems have become a major part of drone defense in Europe since the war in Ukraine showed how many cheap drones an army may need to shoot down, often with interceptor missiles that cost far more than their targets.

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Railway Bridge in Bryansk, Blasts Military Supply Depots Across Donetsk
Ukrainian forces struck a railway bridge in Russia’s Bryansk region and several Russian military logistics facilities in temporarily occupied Donetsk region during operations conducted on October 16 and overnight into October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 17, the strikes targeted infrastructure used by Russian forces to transport military supplies, store equipment, and coordinate drone operations.
One of the targets was a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near Sloboda-Seletskaya in Russia’s Bryansk region. Ukrainian military officials confirmed that the bridge had been hit but did not specify the extent of the damage.

Separately, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military supply depots in three locations across temporarily occupied Donetsk region.

Another strike targeted a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command post near Malynivka in Donetsk region. The Ukrainian military did not disclose the type of weapons used or provide an assessment of Russian equipment losses.
Earlier, on October 16, Ukrainian forces targeted a second Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in less than a week using a domestically produced VB140 Flamingo interceptor drone over Russia’s Belgorod region. Footage released by Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade showed the drone approaching the helicopter, although the extent of any damage remains unconfirmed.

Putin Claims 6,500 Square Kilometres Seized in Ukraine. The Reality Is 45 Times Smaller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:01:18 UTC
18:01:18 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Putin Claims 6,500 Square Kilometres Seized in Ukraine. The Reality Is 45 Times Smaller
Russian leader Vladimir Putin claimed that Moscow’s forces had captured approximately 6,500 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory and 310 settlements since the beginning of 2026. However, independent battlefield assessments suggest Russia’s actual territorial gains are roughly 45 times smaller than the Kremlin’s claims.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) in its October 16 assessment, Putin and Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov significantly overstated Russian advances across several frontline regions, including Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.
ISW estimates that Russia achieved a net territorial gain of approximately 144.5 square kilometers between January and September 2026. Russian forces also experienced periods of territorial losses, including a net loss of approximately 122 square kilometers since September 1.
Gerasimov separately claimed that Russian troops had captured more than 1,800 square kilometers and 92 settlements since September. ISW’s findings contradict those figures, indicating that Ukrainian counterattacks have reversed Russian advances in several sectors.
In Donetsk region, Putin claimed that Ukrainian forces controlled only around 10% of the territory. ISW instead estimates that Ukraine retains approximately 5,530 square kilometers, representing more than 20% of the region.
The institute also found no evidence supporting Russian claims of capturing Dobropillia or entering Druzhkivka. Russian forces remain at least 12 kilometers from Druzhkivka and nine kilometers from Kramatorsk, according to the assessment.
Similar discrepancies were identified in Zaporizhzhia region. While Putin claimed Ukraine controlled just 16.5% of the region, ISW assessed Ukrainian control at approximately 24.6%.
Gerasimov also claimed Russian forces were within five kilometers of Zaporizhzhia city. ISW placed their positions at least 20.95 kilometers away, or approximately 11.6 kilometers when accounting for limited Russian infiltration attempts.
In Sumy region, Russian commanders reported capturing more than 300 square kilometers during the summer and autumn. ISW estimated Russian territorial gains in the region at just 99.1 square kilometers since the beginning of 2026.
ISW assessed that the Kremlin’s exaggerated battlefield claims form part of a broader information campaign intended to portray Russian advances as inevitable and pressure Ukraine and its Western partners into accepting Moscow’s negotiating demands.
Earlier, Russia’s net territorial gains in Ukraine fell to their lowest monthly level since June 2023, according to the Finland-based Black Bird Group. Ukrainian counterattacks in northern Donbas disrupted Russian advances, while expanded drone operations further slowed Moscow’s offensive.
