====================================================================================================

Can Ken Paxton outrun a trail of scandal to win US Senate seat in ruby-red Texas?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Depending how you look at the situation, it is either predictable that Ken Paxton, Texas’s attorney general and Republican candidate for US Senate, is struggling in the polls – or impressive that he is not doing worse. Beloved by hardcore Maga voters and regarded with skepticism by the broader voting public, Paxton is also puzzlingly bland. Recently, Donald Trump told a crowd of supporters that the 63-year-old Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk exactly perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen”. The president was endorsing him.
Yet it is Paxton’s ability to attract – and somehow scrape through – scandal that makes him a less charismatic, perhaps, but still kindred spirit of “Teflon Don”: nothing sticks. He has survived state prosecution (on securities-related charges that he settled without admitting guilt), impeachment by the Republican-led Texas legislature (on abuse-of-office charges of which he was later acquitted), and so many controversies that it can be difficult to pin down the most outrageous.
There was the time in 2011 that God appeared to a tech entrepreneur in a red-roofed Dairy Queen in McKinney, Texas, and told him to give 100,000 shares of company stock to Paxton, then a state legislator, in what the entrepreneur called a gift and critics called an illegal commission. (Paxton and the entrepreneur denied that allegation.) There was the time in 2013 that Paxton allegedly stole a fellow lawyer’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (Paxton said that it was a mix-up while going through a security screening at a courthouse.)
Then there was the time in 2020 that eight of Paxton’s staffers asked the FBI to investigate whether their boss had, as attorney general, abused his office to help a real estate investor and political donor – in return for a free kitchen renovation and a job for a woman with whom Paxton was having an affair. (Paxton and the real estate investor denied those allegations; the investor was never charged with a crime and Paxton’s impeachment over the matter ended in acquittal.)
And there was the time in 2022 that Paxton’s wife, state senator Angela Paxton, allegedly helped him escape, in a Chevrolet truck, from someone trying to serve him with a subpoena for a federal court case. (Paxton said that the man was harassing him.) That screwball romcom ended sadly, however, when Angela Paxton filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds”. Ken Paxton’s scandal sheet includes two alleged extramarital affairs.
All of it may be catching up to Paxton – an ultraconservative Republican, in a diverse but still very right-leaning state, who has somehow found himself in a muddy political trench fight with a babyfaced Democratic state legislator, James Talarico, whom Republicans have likened to a “Coexist” bumper sticker in human form. Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and a seminarian affiliated with an arch-progressive mainline Christian church in Austin. (Trump has dubbed him “Talafreako”.)
Texas has not elected a single Democrat to statewide office since 1994 – the worst state losing streak, for either party, in the United States. But Paxton and Talarico are in a dead heat. Some polls even show Talarico leading.
“This is the closest race that we’ve seen in the state in three decades,” James Henson, a political scientist and pollster who directs the Texas Politics Project, said. Rightwing groups in “red-alert mode”, he added, are pouring millions of dollars into the state to prop up Paxton and other Republicans fighting for election next month.
Polls have, famously, been wrong before. But the fact that a Republican candidate in a Republican stronghold is struggling would be notable by itself even if this were not also one of the most high-profile of all the midterm elections. The race is critical to either party securing a Senate majority. It is already one of the most expensive of its kind in US history.
The situation has put Paxton – a hard-right Maga sycophant endorsed by Trump over the misgivings of some other Republicans – under a harsh and unflattering light. Paxton has repeatedly dodged opportunities to debate Talarico, enabling Talarico’s campaign to paint him as cowardly.
Less than a month before the election, Paxton’s woes keep growing. This week the Wall Street Journal reported that in 2024, he was filmed at a New Year’s Eve party in Dubai in the company of an extramarital girlfriend and two men who were under indictment for federal healthcare fraud and considered fugitives from justice. One of them had donated $190,000 to Paxton.
His campaign has shrugged off the new reporting. “Like President Trump, Ken Paxton has been politically persecuted for years,” a spokesman told the Wall Street Journal. “[A]nd every time, voters have seen through it and sent him back to office because they know he has always fought for Texas.”
Yet in a series of audio clips leaked to the news media by unnamed sources over the past several weeks, even Paxton could be heard admitting, in closed-room conversations with conservative allies, that he and other Republicans in Texas were struggling.
In one clip, he seemed to say that Trump’s recent midterm convention in Texas – where voters, as elsewhere, are furious about high fuel costs worsened by the Iran war – had hurt more than helped. (Trump’s approval numbers, according to recent polling, are at a dire low.) In another, he said, “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign … it’s all coming – you know – from DC.”
Were the tapes leaked by Republicans unhappy at the resources the party is expending to save the flailing Paxton? Or by loyalists of John Cornyn, the longtime Republican senator whom Paxton knifed in a party primary, earlier this year, and displaced as the Republican nominee?
Whatever the case, the tapes are embarrassing. “I thought that was a bad look for Ken Paxton,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a political scientist at the University of Houston, said. “It makes it look like he’s not grateful for all of the help that’s come to him. He needed all the attention that Trump can give. It may be that it comes with these caveats, and it’s not an unqualified good. But without Donald Trump, there would be no Ken Paxton.”
‘Scandal resilience’
As attorney general of Texas, Paxton sued the states of Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin and Georgia for, he claimed, voting irregularities that had stolen the 2020 presidential election from Trump. The lawsuit lacked evidence and critics on both sides of the aisle accused the lawsuit of being a political stunt and legal farce; some even speculated that Paxton was vying to win Trump’s favor in case his legal problems necessitated a presidential pardon. (Paxton’s campaign did not reply to an opportunity to provide comment for this story.)
Earlier this year Trump repaid Paxton’s loyalty when he endorsed him for Senate over Cornyn – the more bipartisan, respected and generally less scandal-prone politician who had represented Texas in the Senate, as a conservative Republican, since 2002.
Journalists, ex-employees, and political opponents have also questioned Paxton’s expensive and jet-setting tenure as attorney general, as well as the perks he has enjoyed and the energy he has often seemed to devote to building a national profile in the Maga movement, according to critics, instead of solving problems in Texas.
Of course, many Texans are well aware of Paxton’s alleged trespasses, some of which go back years, and have repeatedly elected him to office anyway. (The pen-theft allegation is less well-known, though the Talarico campaign – which did not respond to a query from the Guardian – recently began selling ballpoint pens marked “Not Ken Paxton’s Pen”.)
Jed Silverman, an attorney who prosecuted the state securities case against Paxton, noted that, in the eyes of the law, Paxton has a clean bill of health. “My opinion of him, my subjective belief one way or another, really doesn’t matter,” he said. “He made an agreement with the state, did what he was supposed to do, and got his cases resolved.”
For his part, Rottinghaus, whose recent research has studied politicians’ ability to navigate scandal, views Paxton’s career as “a textbook example of ‘scandal resilience’”. Political polarization, he noted, “has raised the standards for what a scandal breaking point is”. Voters in the Republican or Democratic bases are more likely to weigh their candidate’s alleged ethical lapses against a sense that their party “needs to win”.
Bill Miller, a Texas political consultant and lobbyist, made a similar point. “Baggage is something that the American public seemingly has learned to accept,” he said. Trump has “been elected twice, and everyone knows who he is and all that comes with that. I mean, people don’t expect squeaky clean. They hope they get squeaky clean, but they elect people who aren’t.”
Miller noted that he has known Paxton for years and is friendly with him; despite Paxton’s blotted public image and reputation as bumbling and less than charismatic, he described him as a savvy operator with a Bill Clinton-style facility for remembering people’s names and a history of being underestimated by political opponents.
Silverman, similarly, called Paxton a “political animal”.
The national political climate is overwhelmingly tough right now for Republican candidates, and strategists and pollsters are predicting that the midterm elections could be a bruising referendum on Trump’s second presidency. From that vantage, Paxton is facing uniquely fierce headwinds, or is uniquely ill-chosen for the moment, or both. His unorthodox opponent has benefited.
“The Democrats were looking for somebody who wasn’t a traditional politician,” Rottinghaus said. “Talarico fit that mold. He kind of looks like a youth minister, he talks like a choirboy and he’s committed to his values, which Democrats like and independents feel like they can trust. He’s a good candidate in that way. There’s baggage, though, that people are ignoring.”
Talarico has never held a statewide elected office. And, though he has tilted toward the center, he has a record of statements and policy stances that would be eyebrow-raisingly “woke” in Brooklyn, let alone in suburban Texas. Republicans are growing frustrated, Rottinghaus added, because they believe that he has been able to define himself to the public in a “way that isn’t the real James Talarico”.
Based on remarks Talarico made in the past about the environmental costs of eating meat, conservatives have even accused him of being a closeted vegetarian, a charge that he denies. In March, his campaign posted a photograph, hostage-style, of Talarico eating barbecue.
This month Talarico disappeared from the campaign trail for more than a week, prompting Democratic concerns as well as wild Republican rumors that he was secretly seeking mental health treatment in Ohio; his campaign has said that he had a bad flu, and had never been to Ohio. The campaign went so far as to provide the New York Times with time-stamped security camera footage from the days-long stretch that he was convalescing at home.
‘The hide of a rhinoceros’
Flipping a Texas Senate seat or governorship is a holy grail of the Democratic party: a seismic political victory that many hope could set the party on a path to winning the second-largest state in the union in a presidential election. The last time that happened was 1976.
For Republicans, losing to Talarico would be psychologically shattering – though there are those who might argue, perhaps with some credence, that Paxton was a uniquely flawed candidate.
Yet the memory of Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 longshot bid to unseat Senator Ted Cruz still haunts Democrats. O’Rourke attracted enormous Democratic enthusiasm and money but ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points. Democratic donors felt burned. After a short-lived presidential bid, O’Rourke ran again in 2022 – for Texas governor, against incumbent Greg Abbott – and lost by an even larger margin.
Despite Paxton’s tainted image and tight poll numbers, there are factors in his favor.
One is money. Nationally and in Texas – and even as Democrats are reporting impressive fundraising in key races – Republicans have a considerable advantage in campaign spending. To protect the seat of Governor Abbott, a Republican fighting for re-election against the Democratic state representative Gina Hinojosa, a conservative political action committee has been spending, by one estimate, nearly $1m a day.
“Paxton or any other Republican on the ballot is a beneficiary” of Abbott’s spending, Miller said, “because what that money does is find Republicans under every bush and rock and make sure that they’re motivated and they vote.”
And Elon Musk is personally bankrolling a Super Pac to back Paxton’s Senate bid.
Republican get-out-the-vote efforts, meanwhile, seem aimed less at reaching undecided voters, according to Henson, the political scientist and pollster, and more at “shoring up support and enthusiasm among a probably relatively small, but still crucial, band of Republican voters who might be considering either sitting this election out entirely or at least not voting for Paxton”.
Even Angela Paxton has now appeared in a political ad urging Republican voters to support the ticket. “Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team,” she argued. She did not mention her ex-husband, but the message was clear.
The other advantage Paxton holds is the political composition of Texas. Although the state’s major cities tilt Democratic and the state has become more diverse, urban and “purple” in recent years, a slightly higher percentage of its population is rural compared with other large states such as Florida and California. “Those small communities”, Miller said, were “not purple, they’re not orange, they’re blood-fucking-red”.
So far, according to polling, Democrats in Texas are seeing higher enthusiasm from their base than Republicans are seeing from theirs, Henson said, though Republican enthusiasm has begun to pick up. In a few weeks, Texas will find out the results. Even if Paxton loses, he will no doubt land on his feet somewhere in Maga political world.
“They say you need the sensitivity of a violinist and the hide of a rhinoceros to be good in this business,” Miller said. “Well, I don’t know if he has the sensitivity of a violinist, but he’s damn sure got the hide of a rhinoceros.”

More peas, please! 17 delicious ways to devour Britain’s most brilliant vegetable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:00:55 UTC
18:00:55 KST

It’s not good news for the pea farmers: pea consumption in the UK has fallen to a 50-year low. According to data from Defra, the average Briton ate just 37g of peas per week in 2025, down from 144g per week in 1975.
Though a classic British staple, peas are not for everybody. Apparently only 22% of gen Z associate peas with Britain at all (which is patently ridiculous: 90% of the peas we consume in the UK are grown here, while we produce about 160,000 tonnes for freezing alone each year).
But if I’m honest, I ate zero grams of peas last week; ditto the week before. I like peas – or at least I’m rarely offended by them – but as a suppertime option, they seem a little mundane. And while all the pak choi and purple sprouting broccoli in the fridge risks going floppy with age, frozen peas can be postponed indefinitely.
It shouldn’t be this way. Peas are healthy, versatile, sustainable and insanely available. If you’re like me, you don’t even need to buy peas to eat them: I’ve always already got some. But if you’re still in need of inspiration, here are 17 delicious ways to help keep the UK pea industry afloat.
Pea soup is a good place to start – especially if it’s Felicity Cloake’s perfect pea soup, an ideal distillation of this classic dish. As with all these recipes, frozen peas are called for at this time of year – but, as Cloake says, frozen and fresh are pretty indistinguishable in soup. In one sense frozen peas are fresher than fresh peas anyway – chilled within 150 minutes of picking, before they develop any starchiness. If you’re after something a bit fancier, Tori Haschka’s pea soup with almond and chorizo crumbs also contains courgette, broccoli, kale and a diced red apple – all blitzed smooth at the end and accessorised with crumbled chorizo on top.
Ravinder Bhogal’s easy pea and mint dip – which includes feta and a lightly pickled radish salsa – can be served with bread or crudites or both, and is allegedly even good on toast for breakfast. Simpler still is Jamie Oliver’s peas with broad beans, chilli and mint: all the ingredients are in the title, apart from a squeeze of lemon and a dash of olive oil.
Chorizo and pea risotto makes for a quick yet rather elegant midweek supper. Rukmini Iyer’s green pea pulao is another rice dish, topped with a fried egg and spiced with cardamom. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall mines a similar vein in a different genre with a dish featuring baby peas, bacon, garlic and risoni – a rice-shaped pasta more commonly known as orzo (although not in Italy, apparently).
Rachel Roddy’s peas and pasta offering uses ingredients you may well have on hand right now: peas, cream, onion, butter, lemon, some kind of hard cheese, a single tablespoon of cream cheese and pasta (macaroni, penne, fusilli or similar). A potato gnocchi with peas from Masha Rener is finished with ricotta salata – salted ricotta. If you haven’t got gnocchi, Rener says linguine can step in as understudy.
Many of us normally serve peas as a side dish with meat – as an afterthought, even – but Yotam Ottolenghi’s lamb shoulder chops with marinated feta and peas gives them a strong supporting role. You’ll struggle to secure the pea shoots he suggests at this time of year, but rocket makes a perfectly acceptable substitute. For Nigel Slater’s hake with pea salsa, the just-cooked peas are whizzed with coriander, parsley, mint, oil and vinegar.
Slater also has a recipe for pea, herb and mozzarella pie, which calls for leeks and courgettes too.
Rosie Sykes’s pea pav bhaji is a spreadable curry made with potatoes and eaten on bread rolls. This spiced green pea coconut curry from Maunika Gowardhan is yet another pea and potato pairing – this one using kokum petals, if you can find them, and tamarind paste if you can’t.
Should there be any peas left in the bag at the end of the night, here are three slightly weird desserts you can try. In the first, a pea sorbet from James Knappett, frozen peas are blitzed with sugar syrup, citric acid and salt before returning to the freezer, eventually to be served with sliced strawberries and mint oil.
This pea mousse combines a thin custard with gelatine, white chocolate and frozen petit pois. And odd as it sounds, Kate Hackworthy’s vegetarian pea cake is actually everything you would expect from an ordinary Victoria sponge, plus peas. And yes, it is green.

Seven striking buildings that make a statement with red
A timber-clad fire station and an arena with a zigzagging facade are among the projects that feature in this roundup of red buildings.
Liden's Brandstation, Sweden, by Kod Arkitekter
Stockholm studio Kod Arkitekter used bright red-stained cladding to distinguish this fire station in Liden, Sweden, as a local landmark.
Its concrete and glue-laminated timber structure is partially sunken into the site, which was selected for its close proximity to a nearby highway that will help ensure "rapid emergency response".

Jihlava Municipal Arena, Czech Republic, by Chybík + Krištof
A zigzagging facade made up of red aluminium panels was chosen to create a strong civic identity for this ice hockey arena in Jihlava, Czech Republic.
Completed by local studio Chybík + Krištof, the 5,650-seat Jihlava Municipal Arena serves as a cultural hub for the city as well as a home for a local ice hockey team – to which the red colour of the facade also nods.
Find out more about Jihlava Municipal Arena ›
Cucu, Ireland, by Studio Bucky
New York practice Studio Bucky used red-stained shingles to create a "sense of personality and wonder" at the off-grid Cucu cabin in rural Westmeath, Ireland.

Prostir Business Hub, Ukraine, by Aranchii Architects
Warehouse-like volumes cloaked in bright red metal panels form the Prostir Business Hub on the outskirts of Lviv, Ukraine, completed by local studio Aranchii Architects.

Magnesium May Not Reach Your Brain, Despite Supplement Label Promises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throughout the body, taking part in hundreds of essential chemical reactions, including building DNA and proteins and sending signals within our nervous systems and between our brains and the rest of our bodies.
But just because our cells—and especially our neurons—need magnesium doesn't mean that extra magnesium will make them function any better. Not only that, but ingesting more of the element doesn’t mean it’s reaching your brain or really any specific part of your body.
In supplement pills, magnesium isn’t just on its own but part of a compound usually called a “magnesium salt.” This must dissolve to release Mg²⁺, the ionic version that our bodies use. How much of this actually gets into your system—versus gets excreted—depends on a variety of factors including the dose, your stomach contents, and how much magnesium is already in your body. In other words, the higher the dose, the less magnesium gets absorbed.
That’s all if the supplement dissolves in the first place. Magnesium oxide, which is usually the basis of the cheapest pills offered, doesn’t break down all that easily. In reality, magnesium oxide supplements mostly act as laxatives, drawing water into the intestines to flush out the excess salt.
This is where the marketing comes in. There are other types of magnesium compounds that do dissolve better. Magnesium citrate, for example, has been shown to have the highest bioavailability in laboratory tests. Despite the fact that all these salts still break down in the intestine, some supplement labels also claim that their specific chemical blend targets the magnesium directly to certain parts of your body, like your muscles or your brain.
These claims are often based on experiments using rodents, and the animals are typically supplied with magnesium long-term at higher doses than found in a pill. One study in rats found that a salt called magnesium L-threonate increased the amount of magnesium in the brain and improved some manifestations of learning and memory. This is the basis of some of the more overzealous marketing in the supplement world, which proclaims that this special salt will take the magnesium right to your brain.
There are some human studies, but that’s not really what they say. A few small randomized trials reporting improvements in some cognitive tests or sleep have been conducted—but there are several important caveats. Some studies tested a mixture of substances, lasted for only a few weeks, or analyzed a very limited number of outcomes. Many of these studies can also not be considered independent, because they were funded by supplement manufacturers or led by their staff.
Moreover, the studies—for extremely understandable reasons—didn't measure magnesium content in the brain. So maybe a little more sneaks into your gray matter, but based on the scientific understanding of how these salts are processed, in all likelihood, a brain-focused magnesium supplement is still just an expensive laxative.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

The best AirPods cases are subjective, but luckily, you have thousands of options to match your style and mood. You can find a ton of novelty cases online, most of which are just fine. Rather than another case that looks like food or a licensed character, the recommendations below add some functionality or protection beyond the basics.

Featured in this article

Compatible with AirPods Pro (1st, 2nd, and 3rd generation) and AirPods (3rd and 4th generation).

How Can I Tell Which AirPods I Have?
How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) To find what you have, go to Settings > Bluetooth on the Apple device you paired them with. Tap the “i” icon next to your AirPods' name to see the model number. If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.
Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.
You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.
How We Test AirPods Cases
I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. I tested most of these cases with my AirPods Pro 3, but am hoping to check out more options for the AirPods 4 and the AirPods Max soon.

Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.
The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.
The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.
The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.
Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.
Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”
The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”
Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.
A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.
Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”
He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

Why Starlink is so important for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

How reliant is Ukraine on Starlink systems?
October 18, 2026
Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.
According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.
The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.
However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.
This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.
This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean
According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).
Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet
However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.
This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.
The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.
This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.
The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet
However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.
This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.
The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.
This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.
The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

Ramzi Mahmud and Sahin Demir
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Hundreds of Palestinians on Sunday attended the funeral of 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed by Israeli forces in Gaza City during the early months of Israel’s genocidal war.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza City.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defense, told Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighborhood in northeastern Gaza City.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defense’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told Anadolu on Oct. 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a ceasefire agreement in effect in Gaza since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.

Clashes, blazes and wide-scale looting in France during protests
Unknown

2026-10-18

Breadcrumb
Clashes, blazes and wide-scale looting grip France on day of protests
Clashes between police and protesters, massive looting and multiple blazes gripped France on Saturday, as nationwide marches against soaring inflation degenerated into street violence of "extreme intensity".
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty as the country readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris "have been devastated", the city's mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked many shops.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who earlier slammed the "violence of extreme intensity", said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.
The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.
Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.
Looting in many cities
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.
Scores of shops, supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.
AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men often attacking the shops in an organised way: wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.
The one in Limoges, more than 140 years old, was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region's top official. Protesters also broke into and vandalised two other buildings in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
Macron vowed on X that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting, even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished".
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in the April and May presidential elections seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, had "legitimised the violence".
She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left".
Mélenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests that preceded them, urged demonstrators to avoid looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods".
A 'revolution'
France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The main grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East, which has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons, the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution, we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
In the southern city of Montpellier, marchers unfurled a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" above a central square.
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.

It added that a cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods was hit at sea about 30 kilometers (19 miles) east of the port of Odesa.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 152 Russian drones during the overnight attack.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

Nighttime museum visits exceed 1.3 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:54:38 UTC
17:54:38 KST

The number of visitors to museums and archaeological sites in Türkiye under the nighttime museum program reached 1,326,590, a 32 percent increase compared with the same period last year, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
The program allows visitors to explore the country’s historical and cultural heritage after sunset, offering a different perspective on museums and archaeological sites.
Announcing the figures on social media, Ersoy said the program had attracted growing interest, adding that the ministry would continue working to bring cultural heritage to wider audiences and transform museums and archaeological sites into living spaces.
“We are delighted to bring the unique beauty of our history and cultural heritage together with visitors in the enchanting atmosphere of the night,” Ersoy said.
The total number of visitors rose from 1,008,080 last year to 1,326,590 this year, according to the minister.
Ephesus Archaeological Site in İzmir ranked first, welcoming 501,811 visitors, up 36 percent from 368,731 last year.
Istanbul’s iconic Galata Tower came second with 277,557 visitors, an increase of 35 percent from 205,344 a year earlier.
Hierapolis Archaeological Site in Denizli, also known as Pamukkale, ranked third with 190,910 visitors.
The Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology in Muğla followed with 62,071 visitors, ahead of Didim Archaeological Site in Aydın with 60,884 and Marmaris Museum in Muğla with 50,053.
Several other museums and archaeological sites also recorded substantial growth.
Visitor numbers at the Istanbul Archaeology Museums rose from 8,789 to 24,850, an increase of 183 percent.
At Didim Archaeological Site, the figure climbed from 27,846 to 60,884, representing a 119 percent increase.
Patara Archaeological Site in Antalya welcomed 28,021 visitors, up 98 percent from 14,141 last year.
At the Terrace Houses of Ephesus in İzmir, visitor numbers increased by 82 percent, from 10,718 to 19,541.
HH Nighttime visits extended at selected sites
The 2026 nighttime museum program ran from June 1 to Oct. 1 at 22 locations affiliated with the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums, comprising 11 museums and 11 archaeological sites.
Following public demand, the program was extended until Oct. 15 at Ephesus and Side, while nighttime visits at Göreme Archaeological Site in Nevşehir will continue until Oct. 31.
The program at Galata Tower in Istanbul will operate throughout the year.
The ministry aims to expand access to the country’s cultural heritage by extending visiting hours at museums and archaeological sites.

Veteran Turkish artist Süleyman Saim Tekcan dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:54:00 UTC
17:54:00 KST

Süleyman Saim Tekcan, the acclaimed Turkish artist and printmaker honored with the 2022 Presidential Culture and Arts Grand Award, has died at the age of 86.
His family announced his death on the artist’s social media account, expressing deep sorrow over the loss of “our beloved father, the great master of Turkish art, Süleyman Saim Tekcan.”
“Devoting his life to art, education and the transmission of cultural heritage to future generations, Tekcan left behind an invaluable legacy through his unique works, the artists he trained and his lasting contributions to Turkish art history,” the family said in a statement.
It added that people who placed human values above transient ones continued to live on through their works, the people they mentored and the lives they touched.
“We bid farewell with love and respect to the great master who devoted his life to serving art and humanity,” the statement said.
Born in Trabzon on Oct. 6, 1940, Tekcan was one of the pioneering figures in Türkiye’s original printmaking tradition. Alongside his artistic career, he was also known for his work as an educator and institution founder.
He graduated from the Department of Art and Crafts at Ankara’s Gazi Education Institute in 1961. He later expanded his artistic education through research into printmaking in Germany, combining his work in painting and engraving with his academic background and making significant contributions to the development of original printmaking in Türkiye.
One of the most enduring achievements of his career was the establishment of the Istanbul Museum of Graphic Arts (IMOGA) in 2004.
Bringing together production, archiving and exhibition facilities for original prints, the museum represented an institutional continuation of the workshop tradition Tekcan had developed over the years.

Sacred sites of the Eastern Rhodopes: The Wooden Mosque near Podkova
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:50:25 UTC
17:50:25 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
News
Sacred sites of the Eastern Rhodopes: The Wooden Mosque near Podkova
Sunday 18 October 2026 10:35
Sunday, 18 October 2026, 10:35
The Wooden Mosque above the village of Podkova
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
Font size
High above the village of Podkova, in the Kardzhali region of southern Bulgaria, rises the minaret of one of the country’s oldest mosques— the Wooden Mosque, also known as the Mosque of the Seven Maidens.
This sacred place is deeply revered by the local population, made up largely of Bulgarian Muslims and ethnic Turks who follow Islam. It is also included in tourist routes showcasing the cultural and historical heritage of the Eastern Rhodopes and draws many visitors every year.
Although the year of its construction is known-1428-little else is known about the mosque’s history. Tour guides, however, are eager to tell the legend that the Wooden Mosque was built by seven young women whose loved ones never returned from war. They sold all their dowries to buy the building materials and constructed the mosque in a single night. Afterward, they were never seen again.
It is believed that this happened on 6 May, during Hıdırellez, a spring festival celebrated by Muslims. Every year on this date, people from across Bulgaria, as well as neighbouring Greece and Türkiye, gather in the mosque’s courtyard. They recite mevlid (verses praising the life and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad), read from the Quran, and offer prayers. Guests are also treated to pilaf.
Tour guide Georgi Kyuchukov
PHOTO Krasimir Martinov
“As we mentioned, this is a legend in which the seven maidens lose their fiancés”, explains our tour guide, Georgi Kyuchukov. “But if we walk a little further, right next to the mosque, you will see seven unmarked graves. They were most likely built in their honour and are linked to the story we have just told. Perhaps this suggests that the story is more than just a legend. It is something the people here believe in.”
The mosque, which is nearly 600 years old, is also remarkable for its architecture. It is said that not a single nail was used in its construction. In 2009, the mosque was restored using traditional building techniques and designated a cultural monument. The 24-metre-high wooden minaret was built in 2018.
The village cemetery is located right next to the mosque and can be reached via its beautiful courtyard. The area is dotted with stones believed to possess healing properties.
''Local people believe that the stones give energy and have the power to heal. No one knows how long these stones have been here, but people revere them as places they visit to heal their ailments. You will notice pieces of clothing tied to the surrounding trees. This is based on the belief that you must leave something of yourself behind so that your illness stays here and does not follow you back home.''
One of the most remarkable is the “Pierced Stone”, known in Turkish as “Demitlikaya.” It is believed to cure various ailments, including infertility. The only condition is that visitors pass through the hole in the stone three times in a counterclockwise direction.
''People believe that the mystical healing powers of this place are strongest on the night of 5–6 May. Passing through the stone three times in a counterclockwise direction is said to bring forgiveness for your sins. One stone is used to relieve joint pain by kneeling on it. Another is believed to heal lower back pain, and a third that is believed to cure headaches. Each stone has a sign explaining what visitors should do at that particular spot.''
If our guide’s story about the Wooden Mosque near the village of Podkova has sparked your interest and you are already making plans to visit, here is a useful tip: the village, located just 15 kilometres from the Bulgarian-Greek border, is accessible by train as well as by car.
The journey aboard the “Rhodope Caterpillar”, as locals affectionately call the diesel train that crawls along the slopes of the Eastern Rhodopes, promises a unique experience. You can catch it in Dimitrovgrad, Haskovo or Kardzhali, and it will take you to Podkova railway station, the southernmost railway station in Bulgaria.

According to Herzog’s office, the two discussed strengthening the Abraham Accords and expanding regional cooperation. Herzog also met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev to discuss bilateral relations and regional security.
For Azerbaijan, an emerging middle power, the meetings reflect a diplomatic role that has developed over the years. The country maintains close relations with Israel while preserving strong ties with Turkey, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and other Muslim-majority countries. Its ability to work with governments whose interests sometimes conflict has made it a useful venue for sensitive discussions.
Azerbaijan’s diplomatic role allows for ‘reconciliation without a public stage’
Joseph Epstein, director of the Turan Research Center and a senior fellow at the Yorktown Institute, describes this approach as “reconciliation without a public stage.”
“Azerbaijan established relations with Israel in 1992 and has kept them intact through two Karabakh wars, the war in Gaza and years of pressure from Tehran and Ankara,” Epstein said. “The partnership covers security, trade, technology, and energy, and Baku built it without cutting a single tie to the Arab and Muslim world.”
According to Epstein, Azerbaijan’s relationships with Israel and Muslim countries gave it a diplomatic role well before the Abraham Accords were signed in 2020.
“Israeli and Arab officials could meet there years before because no one saw Azerbaijan as Israel’s enemy or as its client. Every side trusted the host,” he said.
That relationship has also helped manage tensions between Israel and Turkey. In April 2025, Israeli and Turkish security delegations met in Azerbaijan for talks aimed at establishing a mechanism to prevent military incidents in Syria, where both countries have strategic interests. The Prime Minister’s Office publicly thanked Azerbaijan and President Aliyev for hosting the discussions.
The talks did not resolve the broader disagreements between Jerusalem and Ankara, but they demonstrated the value of maintaining a direct channel even when political relations are strained.
“The same logic now applies to Turkey and Israel,” Epstein said. “Baku is Ankara’s closest ally and one of Jerusalem’s closest partners, and it uses that trust to keep the two from drifting into confrontation.”
After its victory in Karabakh, Azerbaijan took another step in this strategy, moving from military success toward normalization with Armenia. Negotiations over a peace treaty, border delimitation and the opening of transport links reflect Baku’s stated aim of consolidating its gains through a new regional framework rather than military force alone.
The process has also created opportunities for normalization between Armenia and Turkey. Without reduced tensions between Baku and Yerevan, progress between Armenia and Turkey would have been considerably more difficult.
Azerbaijan emerging as a middle power in the Middle East
Professor Ze’ev Khanin, head of the Post-Soviet Conflicts Research Program at the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies, sees Azerbaijan’s emergence as a middle power as a model distinct from the formal framework of the Abraham Accords.
Baku continues to develop relations with Israel despite the escalation of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and pressure from Iran and Turkey. For Israel, Khanin argues, this makes Azerbaijan not merely a partner but a rare example of a durable bridge between the Jewish state and the Muslim world.
Herzog’s visit also underscores Azerbaijan’s growing importance to the United States and the West. Washington’s recognition of the country’s role in regional stability was reflected in the strategic partnership charter the two governments signed in February 2026, which emphasized their shared interest in peace and security in the South Caucasus.
For Baku, this presents an opportunity to consolidate its position as a diplomatic intermediary. For Israel, Turkey, Armenia, and the Arab states, it highlights the availability of a venue for dialogue even during periods of regional tension.
Azerbaijani officials involved in the country’s foreign policy present Baku’s diplomatic approach as pragmatic rather than ideological. In this view, Azerbaijan does not require governments to endorse its political model or make public concessions as a condition for dialogue. Nor does it seek to turn diplomatic contacts into public propaganda campaigns.
This approach helps explain why Israel, Turkey, the Gulf Arab states, and Armenia can engage with Azerbaijan despite their sometimes conflicting interests, without necessarily turning such contacts into domestic political controversies.
This role is especially important as the Middle East faces continued tensions over Gaza and Iran and a wider crisis of trust among regional governments. The Abraham Accords demonstrated that normalization is possible, but their durability depends on more than formal agreements. It also requires countries willing to maintain relationships when political rhetoric hardens.
Azerbaijan has become one such country, preserving its partnership with Israel while maintaining contacts across the Arab and Muslim world.
Herzog’s meeting with the Bahraini foreign minister in Baku therefore carried significance beyond diplomatic protocol. Israel and Bahrain established diplomatic relations under the Abraham Accords in 2020, but their relationship came under strain following the outbreak of the Gaza war in October 2023.
The meeting showed that, despite a period of cooling relations, Jerusalem and Manama can still engage in direct dialogue, with Baku providing a venue for their talks.
For Israel, the encounter offered an opportunity to preserve and strengthen the Abraham Accords. For Washington, it underscored the importance of maintaining regional diplomatic channels. For Azerbaijan, it reinforced its growing status as a middle power and an independent center of influence.
As Prof. Khanin puts it, “Baku can offer a venue for dialogue between governments that have reasons to maintain contact despite their disagreements. As regional tensions continue, Azerbaijan’s experience suggests that diplomatic influence does not always depend on brokering a major peace agreement. Sometimes, maintaining relationships and providing a place where difficult conversations can continue is an achievement in itself.”

U.S. Army tests Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels as drone carriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:45:02 UTC
17:45:02 KST

- Ukrainian-built Magura drone boats took part in the U.S. Army’s Bayonet Quest 26 exercise in Michigan, launching aerial drones from a platform on the hull.
- The same boat family sank a target ship during Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines on April 24, 2026.
Ukraine’s Magura uncrewed surface vessels, the drone boats that have sunk Russian warships in the Black Sea, took part in a U.S. Army exercise in Michigan, where they were used as floating launch pads for aerial drones.
The boats appeared during Bayonet Quest 26, which the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, ran across Michigan from Sept. 26 to Oct. 6, 2026. The division said soldiers used the exercise to test autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft as it experiments with how new technology can extend sensing, reach and decision-making.
According to images and materials released by the division, the exercise included crewed-uncrewed maritime testing that paired a Mk VI patrol boat with autonomous systems, giving the U.S. Army a look at how the two could work together in complex terrain. The Magura boats, built by Ukrainian manufacturer UFORCE, carried a dedicated platform on the front of the hull from which aerial drones took off.
The 7th Infantry Division did not say how many Magura boats took part, which model was used, or what type of aerial drones they carried.
The Michigan exercise is the second publicly known use of the Magura family by U.S. forces this year. During Balikatan 2026, the largest annual U.S.-Philippines military exercise, Magura boats destroyed a decommissioned target ship in a live-fire maritime strike off Itbayat in the Batanes islands on April 24, 2026. UFORCE confirmed on June 8 that its vessels had taken part, after The Defence Blog reported that U.S. special forces had sunk a ship with Ukrainian-designed drone boats.
Magura boats became one of Ukraine’s best-known weapons after its military intelligence used them to strike Russian Black Sea Fleet ships near Crimea, forcing much of the fleet to move away from the peninsula. Ukraine has since developed versions armed with missiles and machine guns, and in 2025 Ukrainian military intelligence said Magura boats armed with air-to-air missiles had shot down Russian fighter jets over the Black Sea.
Using a drone boat to carry and launch aerial drones extends how far a small craft can see and strike without putting a crewed ship close to the target. Ukraine has used drone boats in a similar way to carry smaller strike drones toward Russian-held coastlines, and the U.S. Army has been looking at uncrewed boats for its units in the Pacific, where many operations would play out among islands and along coastlines.
The 7th Infantry Division, based at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, was reorganized under Multi-Domain Command-Pacific as part of the U.S. Army’s efforts to prepare for operations in the Indo-Pacific region.

Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks during an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
 
Huangqihai Lake in Ulanqab was once on the verge of drying up due to climate and other impacts. After years of comprehensive conservation, its water body has gradually been restored and expanded.
 
During the inspection trip, Xi visited the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve, where he was briefed on Inner Mongolia's efforts to strengthen ecological conservation, and inspected the lake's shoreline and mudflats and observed birds inhabiting the area.
 
He stressed the need to fully implement the country's wetland protection law, firmly uphold ecological red lines, and safeguard biodiversity. For degraded wetland ecosystems, he called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, and carrying out restoration in a scientific and sound manner.
 
Xi also visited Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, and learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in advancing the construction of a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of the green computing power industry.
 
Noting that implementing the "East Data, West Computing" project and building a national integrated computing power network is an important decision made by the CPC Central Committee, Xi stressed the need to ensure the efficient operation of completed projects and finish the construction of follow-up projects on schedule.
 
He called on all parties to earnestly implement the requirements for efficient, green and safe development, actively promote the development of the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces.
 
Xi also viewed displays of local agricultural and livestock specialties, encouraging local authorities to better align production with sales to help farmers and herders increase their incomes.

Huanggang busy on first long weekend travel rush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:37:42 UTC
17:37:42 KST

Secretary for Security Chris Tang on Sunday said authorities have stepped up on-site management at the Huanggang port to cope with higher passenger traffic.
This came as the redeveloped port saw crowds at its departure hall heading into its first travel peak – the long Chung Yeung Festival weekend.
The Security Bureau noted that the port was busiest between 1pm and 2pm with more than 9,700 departures – nearly nine times more than previously.
During the peak, travellers needed to wait for 30 to 45 minutes for crowd diversion arrangements on the second floor of the port building, and within 30 minutes at the departure hall on the fifth floor, it said.
The bureau said departure traffic began to ease from 2pm.
Writing on his social media page, Tang said the port had seen an "obvious" rise in passenger traffic.
He called on cross-border travellers to follow the instructions of on-site staff members and register for the automated channels in advance for faster crossings.
Tang added that people should plan their trip early and avoid crossing the border during peak hours.
The Immigration Department, for its part, said outbound passenger traffic was heavy between 10am and 2pm on Sunday, with departures topping 30,000.
The department said it had deployed extra manpower and opened all clearance channels and counters to cope with the crowds.

Yang stars with 20 points in Flames' WNBL win
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:37:41 CST
17:37:41 KST

Yang Shuyu (R) of Sydney Flames breaks through against Shay Ciezki of Adelaide Lightning during the round 1 game between Sydney Flames and Adelaide Lightning at the 2026-2027 Women's National Basketball League in Sydney, Australia, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Gong Bing)
SYDNEY, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese basketball player Yang Shuyu showcased her long-range shooting skills after scoring an equal game-high 20 points in Sydney Flames' crushing 95-68 victory over Adelaide Lightning on Sunday.
In her first WNBL home game at the Quaycenter, Yang hit 4-of-6 from three while teammate Jazmin Shelley also scored 20 points.
The 24-year-old Yang had launched her WNBL career on Friday night with 11 points in the Flames' 77-73 season-opening victory against Southside Melbourne Flyers.
In that match, she went toe-to-toe with Chinese player Wang Siyu, who scored 11 points off the bench in her WNBL debut for Flyers.
The Flames were determined to continue their unbeaten start to the season and Yang made a steal in the opening minute, prompting loud cheers from a large contingent of Chinese fans in the crowd.
Yang's first three-point attempt rimmed out, but she made no mistake on her next from the right corner. She ended a see-saw first quarter with a sublime layup through traffic to give the Flames a 17-16 lead at the break.
The Lightning hit back in the second quarter before Shelley lifted the home side, who finished the first-half strongly with Yang showing off her dribbling prowess as she drew the foul at the rim.
The Flames threatened to pull away in the third quarter, with Yang nailing her second three-pointer to stretch their lead to 65-56.
She hit another from the left corner early in the last quarter as the unstoppable Flames built an unassailable lead.
"This is the second game we've played together, and we solved a lot of the problems from the last game. The team is getting better. We'll also have another key player returning soon, so there's a lot to look forward to," Yang told Xinhua after the game, adding that the win was a team effort.
"I came to this team to learn. Australia has always been a powerhouse in world basketball, and I hope to learn from their physical, fast and accurate style of play," she said.
"She played really well, and I'm excited for her," Renae Garlepp, Head Coach of the Flames, said. "I think she slots in really well with the rest of the character we have. I think she's quite selfless, like the rest of them. She works hard, and she wants the best for the team."
"She's the best. She is so involved in our team. She wants everyone to score. She's unreal off the floor, and we just want nothing but success for her. And she wants the same for us. So it's really cool to play with someone like that," said Shelley.
The Flames next play UC Capitals on Friday night at home. ■

Yemen gov't forces launch fresh offensive against Houthis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
16:37:40 CST
17:37:40 KST

SANAA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Fierce fighting erupted near Yemen's strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait on Sunday as government forces launched a fresh offensive against Houthi positions in the area, a government military official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said units from the Giants Brigades and Nation Shield Forces advanced from several directions to seize key Houthis-held positions overlooking approaches to the strait.
Heavy clashes were raging as Houthi fighters resisted the advance from fortified positions and trenches, the official said, adding that extensive minefields had complicated the government forces' push.
"The fighting is among the fiercest we have seen in the area," the official said. "The Houthis are heavily entrenched, and our forces are trying to break through their defensive lines."
The official said the Houthis also deployed fiberoptic-guided first-person-view kamikaze drones known as "Shawaz" against the advancing government troops.
Several people on both sides were killed or wounded in the fighting, the official said, without giving specific figures.
The outcome of the offensive remained unclear as clashes continued, with no confirmation of significant territorial gains.
The latest push follows previous attempts by government forces to break through Houthi defenses in the area. Bab al-Mandab, separating Yemen from the Horn of Africa, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and serves as a vital passage for international trade. ■

Casualties reported in serious incident at Canadian military base
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

17:37:19 KST

OTTAWA, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty confirmed Saturday night that a serious incident occurred earlier in the day at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright in western Alberta province, causing casualties.
Speaking at a press conference in Ottawa, McGuinty said the Department of National Defence is closely monitoring the situation and will release more details as they become available.
The minister did not provide a specific number of fatalities, saying that it is still a "very active and delicate situation."
"We will have more to say in the coming hours and days," he said.
The base has not yet issued a statement on the specific cause of the incident or any casualties.
Local media reported that an explosion and subsequent fire at CFB Wainwright killed at least seven people and injured dozens of others. The report said live-fire training exercises were underway at the base when munitions may have struck a natural gas pipeline or gas well, triggering the explosion.
According to local media citing health officials, hospitals in Edmonton, the provincial capital, have been placed on Code Orange alert to handle a mass influx of incoming patients.
Located about 200 km southeast of Edmonton, CFB Wainwright covers over 600 square km. It is one of the busiest Army bases in Canada, and home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, according to the government website.
High winds were reportedly spreading the fire rapidly toward adjacent areas following the incident. The fire burning south of the town of Wainwright is now being held, according to the Municipal District of Wainwright. ■

NANCHANG, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China Jingdezhen International Ceramic Expo opened on Sunday in Jingdezhen, a city in east China's Jiangxi Province famed as the "porcelain capital," attracting more than 1,000 professional buyers from home and abroad.
The five-day event showcases several facets of the ceramic industry, including the entire industrial chain, its domestic and international markets and its application of digital technology, all within an exhibition space of 140,000 square meters.
It has brought together exhibitors from over 19 countries, including Spain, Germany and Japan. Themed zones feature creative design, smart ceramic manufacturing, international brands, and ceramic-producing cities.
The 2026 standards for the "Jingdezhen Made" regional brand and the city's digital culture and tourism platform were unveiled at the opening ceremony.
On July 25, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, filling a long-standing gap in the list for porcelain heritage and becoming China's 61st World Heritage site.
The heritage sites represent the handicraft porcelain industry system that developed in Jingdezhen from the 10th to the 19th century.
Today, Jingdezhen's ceramic industry chain employs over 100,000 people, and the comprehensive division-of-labor system that once underpinned its historic success continues to thrive.
First launched in 2004, the expo has not only continued to broaden its international reach but also gradually built a comprehensive platform integrating exhibition and trade, cultural exchange, and investment cooperation.
With a population of over 1.6 million, Jingdezhen recorded a net population inflow of 136,000 over the past decade. Among those who have started long-term businesses in the city, more than half come from outside Jiangxi Province, with a notable number from overseas. ■

Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as the country’s new defense minister on Sunday, the state broadcaster IRIB reported.
Akhlaqi received 237 votes in favor and 15 against, with no abstentions, out of 277 votes cast during a parliamentary session held via video conference.
Lawmakers voted after hearing arguments from supporters and opponents of Akhlaqi and reviewing his plans for the Defense Ministry.
Akhlaqi replaces Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was killed in the initial US-Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. Majid Ebn al-Reza had served as acting defense minister following Nasirzadeh’s death.
In his first remarks after securing parliamentary approval, Akhlaqi said Iran had taken measures to counter the possible use by the US of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, known as the “Mother of All Bombs,” against the country.
“We have taken the necessary measures to counter such an action and are continuing our work with confidence,” he told reporters.
Akhlaqi also warned that US President Donald Trump should be concerned about getting American forces out of the region safely.
“If he drops one bomb, he should see how many of his forces he will have to take out of the region horizontally,” he said, apparently referring to potential US military casualties.
He claimed Iran’s preparations were among the reasons Washington had so far refrained from using the bomb, adding that the situation would be different if US threats were turned into action.
Addressing lawmakers before the vote, Akhlaqi warned that Iran would deliver a “surprising and extensive” response if the US and Israel launched another attack against the country.
“If the American-Zionist enemy once again makes a miscalculation, the response of the Iranian nation and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive,” he said, adding that Washington and its allies would bear responsibility for any regional and international consequences.
Akhlaqi also said he had been on what he called his enemies’ “assassination list” for 35 years and pledged to further strengthen what Iran calls the “resistance front.”
He said his priorities would include expanding defense production across Iran’s industrial network, boosting research and adapting the Defense Ministry’s structure to current security threats.
Akhlaqi, a longtime senior Defense Ministry official, previously headed Iran’s Aerospace Industries Organization and has been subject to US sanctions over his involvement in Iran’s missile-related activities.
