Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:59 UTC
16:32:59 KST

Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Relations between the two countries are dominated by policy complexes shaped by a history of hostility.
Since the start of the war, there have been several negotiation initiatives between the United States and Iran. Only one – the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad on June 18 – was concluded, but it collapsed within days.
While prevailing analyses tend to explain this failure through the details of the provisions, this article proceeds from a different premise: that the diplomatic stalemate between the two sides is shaped by a syndrome that has governed US-Iranian relations for years.
In international relations, psychological syndromes can arise as a result of deep crises that leave their mark on political consciousness and memory, potentially obstructing efforts at rapprochement and negotiation between countries.
In the case of Iran and the US, the syndrome is comprised of two complexes: the complex Washington developed as a result of the 1979 siege of the US embassy in Tehran and the complex Tehran developed as a result of historical US hostility and its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018.
The roots of the rupture between the two countries go as far back as August 1953 when US and British intelligence agencies helped overthrow the nationalist government of Mohammad Mosaddegh after it nationalised the oil industry in 1951. Since then, a perception has become entrenched in Iranian consciousness: that Washington does not accept an independent government in Tehran and it is prepared to sabotage it if it goes against its interests.
From this perspective, Washington’s decision to host Shah Reza Pahlavi, who had just been overthrown by his people, for medical treatment in October 1979 was read in revolutionary Tehran as a prelude to a second coup.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy on November 4 that year and held 52 Americans for 444 days. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed and have not been restored to this day.
While the incident is portrayed in the Iranian narrative as a defence of the revolution, in American consciousness, it established the image of Iran as a state that does not respect international norms, whose word cannot be relied upon and whose behaviour should not be rewarded.
That is the embassy siege complex. It is not about the incident itself so much as the informal rule it produced in US decision-making: that Iran must concede first and its concession must be verified before it receives anything in return.
The Iranian complex was shaped by this history as well, but it reached its peak in May 2018 when US President Donald Trump withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) despite the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) confirmation that Tehran was complying with it.
Just two weeks later, US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced 12 demands for a new deal, only four of which were related to the nuclear file. Seven of them were related to Iran’s regional behaviour in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, Afghanistan and the Gulf. In other words, Washington did not merely revoke an existing agreement; it also raised the ceiling of its conditions for any future agreement.
The knot then deepened in June 2025 when the US took part in the Twelve-Day War and struck the nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at a time when a new round of indirect negotiations was scheduled in Muscat. It then reached its furthest point with Washington’s participation alongside Israel in the current war.
Accordingly, a conviction became entrenched in the Iranian consciousness that an American signature guarantees nothing, that any agreement can be overturned with a change of administration and indeed that negotiation itself may be a cover for war rather than an alternative to it.
The informal rule this has produced in Iranian decision-making is that there will be no step taken before binding guarantees and no concession before pressure is lifted.
Thus, the two complexes stand at opposite ends: The first requires Iranian action before an American quid pro quo while the second requires an American guarantee before Iranian action.
A reading of the recent negotiation initiatives shows that every US initiative bears the imprint of the embassy siege complex. The 15-point plan put forward in March demanded the dismantling of the Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow facilities; an end to uranium enrichment; the suspension of Iran’s missile programme; and the abandonment of its allies in exchange for promises to lift sanctions later.
The May draft by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner linked the release of Iran’s frozen funds to the suspension of enrichment first. The American response in September also stipulated the freezing of enrichment and the entry of inspectors throughout the negotiation period.
What remains constant in the American initiatives is that Iranian action precedes the quid pro quo and verification precedes trust.
The imprint of the JCPOA withdrawal complex in the Iranian initiatives is also a constant. The five-point response in late March demanded guarantees that war would not be repeated. The 10 points put forward in April demanded a binding UN Security Council resolution shielding any agreement from being overturned. And the 14 points in May demanded a nonaggression pledge that includes Israel.
Meanwhile, the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran last month stipulated the lifting of sanctions and the US naval blockade on Iran before the opening of the Strait of Hormuz on the sixth day and the start of nuclear negotiations on the seventh. What remains constant in the Iranian initiatives is that guarantees precede action and the lifting of pressure precedes Iranian concessions.
All these initiatives were dialogue between two complexes with each side drafting its text to protect itself from a repetition of its historical experience with the other, rather than to meet the other halfway. This may explain why the gap in substance has narrowed, but the gap in trust has not.
The Islamabad memorandum represents the exception that proves the rule as it was the closest moment to a settlement because it was formulated to reassure both sides over their core concerns. To reassure Washington, it stipulated the dilution of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium and made the lifting of sanctions and unfreezing of funds conditional on Iranian implementation.
To reassure Tehran, it provided for an end to hostilities, respect for mutual sovereignty, a mechanism to monitor implementation and UN Security Council approval of the final agreement. Ballistic missiles were also entirely absent from the text.
But this agreement did not hold. Tehran suspended its participation in the Geneva round of talks because of the absence of a ceasefire in Lebanon, which had been a consistent demand in every Iranian initiative since March. In the Iranian reading, Washington’s inability to rein in Israel confirmed that an American signature was not enough. The JCPOA withdrawal complex immediately kicked in, and the two sides returned to square one.
By late September, the dispute appeared to have shifted definitively from substance to sequencing. Informed sources indicated that it now revolves around the order of steps rather than their content and the stated goal has become a return to an enhanced version of the June memorandum.
Here the two complexes appear in their clearest form: Washington wants the Strait of Hormuz opened and enrichment frozen first because it does not trust Iran while Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted first because it does not trust the US.
A comparison between Pompeo’s 2018 conditions and the June 2026 memorandum shows that US demands have retreated from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear file and the Strait of Hormuz while Iranian demands have shifted from compensation to be paid by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties.
In other words, the substantive gap between the two sides has narrowed considerably – something that would have been unimaginable eight years ago.
However, the two complexes have not diminished; indeed, they may have deepened because of the war. Each complex feeds the other until together they have become a single syndrome, and diplomatic deadlock has turned from a passing condition into a stable structure.
Accordingly, any new formula for sequencing the steps, however precise, will remain unable to break this deadlock unless it addresses both complexes at once – something that requires a third party capable of guaranteeing both the action and the reciprocal action simultaneously.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

CURE Art Gallery opens in Bursa with works by Oran, Yalçındağ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:18 UTC
16:32:18 KST

AA Photo
CURE Art Gallery opened in the northwestern province of Bursa’s Balat district on Oct. 15 with an inaugural exhibition featuring recent works and previously unseen pieces by Turkish artists Ahmet Oran and Ekrem Yalçındağ.
Running through Nov. 12, the exhibition brings together two distinct approaches to contemporary painting, exploring color, texture, repetition and abstraction.
Oran builds layered surfaces by applying paint in different colors onto canvas and selectively scraping away sections with spatulas and scrapers. The technique reveals underlying layers, creating lines and bands of color across the surface.
Yalçındağ incorporates recurring botanical motifs and circular compositions into his paintings. His dense application of paint through small brushstrokes creates a raised, textured surface. Both artists have exhibited in Türkiye and abroad.
The gallery’s founders said the initiative establishes a dedicated space in Bursa where audiences can regularly engage with contemporary art and interact directly with artists.
Beyond its exhibition program, CURE Art Gallery plans to develop long-term relationships with artists, collectors, art writers and other professionals in the art world.
The opening exhibition was held with the participation of Oran and Yalçındağ, in collaboration with Lexus Nilüfer. The works remain on display at the gallery until Nov. 12.

Drones Hit St. Petersburg Oil Terminals, VK Data Center, and Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:22:00 UTC
16:22:00 KST

A Ukrainian drone attack early Sunday morning, Oct. 18, struck fuel transshipment infrastructure, a major enterprise data center, a logistics warehouse, and a highway bridge across St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region, sparking multiple fires and knocking out power to 20,000 residents.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed that the municipality came under attack by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, resulting in blazes across four city districts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Beglov acknowledged impacts at the Petersburg Oil Terminal (PNT) alongside damage to additional infrastructure sites, while claiming that emergency responders had been dispatched to contain localized fires.
According to independent Russian outlet Astra, municipal emergency warning systems failed to notify residents ahead of the strikes, with alerts transmitted either after impacts had occurred or with substantial operational delays.
Open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis conducted by Astra verified that fires erupted at the Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Baltic region’s primary petroleum transshipment hub.
Concurrently in the city’s Krasnogvardeisky district, drone debris ignited a blaze at the “Ruchyi” oil depot. The Ruchyi fuel depot maintains an operational capacity of 3,900 cubic meters, functioning as a bulk storage and loading facility for AI-92 and AI-95 gasoline alongside commercial diesel.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
Hits on VK data center, substation, and Ozon logistics depot
The overnight assault extended across the administrative boundary into the Leningrad region, targeting corporate digital backbones and electrical distribution facilities.
In the village of Novosergievka in the Vsevolozhsk district, strike drones hit a large server data center owned by Russian technology giant VK (VKontakte).
Although VK company representatives claimed corporate services continued operating normally, users across Russia reported widespread connection dropouts and outages affecting the VKontakte social media platform and its integrated ecosystem.
Astra’s OSINT analysts established that an electrical substation located adjacent to the VK data center was also damaged during the strike.
Leningrad Region Governor Alexander Drozdenko confirmed that damage to electrical distribution installations triggered emergency power cuts, leaving approximately 20,000 residents in the area without electricity.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon confirmed that an aerial impact sparked a fire at its fulfillment center in St. Petersburg’s Kolpino district on Sofiyskaya Street.
Operating as one of Ozon’s busiest logistics facilities in northwestern Russia, the hub spans up to 79,000 square meters.
The company reported that emergency brigades contained the blaze and confirmed no personnel were injured.
Strike on Western High-Speed Diameter bridge
Drone impacts were also recorded on municipal transport arteries. According to Astra, a drone struck the cable-stayed bridge spanning the Korabelny fairway in St. Petersburg, located roughly 4.5 kilometers from the Petersburg Oil Terminal.
The bridge forms a critical section of the southern viaduct of the Western High-Speed Diameter (WHSD), a multi-lane toll expressway connecting northern and southern sectors of the metropolis.
Municipal engineering teams were deployed to evaluate structural damage to the suspension cables and road deck.
The multi-site strikes in St. Petersburg and Leningrad region reflect an expanding Ukrainian asymmetric campaign to degrade Russian rear logistics, petroleum transshipment, and corporate digital logistics.
The incident follows consecutive strikes on Russian technology hubs earlier in the month, including attacks that disabled Yandex data centers in Vladimir, Ryazan, and Kaluga regions, alongside reported strikes on a Sberbank data center facility in Saratov region.

Eisenkot leads Netanyahu in four polls, but neither bloc secures Knesset majority - poll

With just nine days left until the election, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party has maintained a consistent lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud in four recent election polls, but neither political bloc comes close to securing the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority, according to surveys published by Maariv, Channel 13, Kan News, and Channel 12.
The four surveys paint an almost identical picture: the Zionist opposition averages 51.25 seats, compared with 51 for Netanyahu's bloc, a virtual tie that leaves the Arab parties and smaller factions hovering around the electoral threshold in key positions ahead of election day.
Maariv poll: Winter below electoral threshold, Eisenkot leads
The Maariv poll shows the Arab parties each gained one seat over the past week, bringing their combined total to 14 seats. By contrast, Likud has lost two seats, falling to just 18.
Despite Likud's two-seat decline, the coalition bloc loses only one seat, dropping to 51. This follows United Torah Judaism's gain of one seat, bringing it to eight, and People of Israel’s success in crossing the electoral threshold with four seats.
However, Yisrael Beytenu also lost one seat, falling to eight, which reduced the Zionist opposition bloc to 51 and tied the two blocs.
Channel 13 poll: Netanyahu bloc loses four seats
Channel 13's election poll gives Netanyahu's bloc just 51 seats, compared with 55 in the previous survey. Likud dropped two seats to 18, while Eisenkot's Yashar party maintained its lead with 20 seats.
Eisenkot's bloc remains unchanged at 50 seats. The Arab parties, which are not affiliated with either bloc, receive a combined 15 seats.
KAN News poll: Winter fails to cross electoral threshold, Bennett gains a seat
A poll published by KAN News showed that Eisenkot's Yashar party continued to lead Netanyahu's Likud, although the distribution of seats between the political blocs gives Netanyahu the advantage.
At the bottom of the list of parties crossing the electoral threshold are People of Israel, which receives four seats, and the joint Reservists/Economic Party led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, which also received four seats.
The key finding in the survey concerns the balance between the blocs. Netanyahu's bloc receives 53 seats, compared with 50 for Eisenkot's bloc, giving the political camp aligned with the prime minister a three-seat advantage.
Channel 12 poll: Eisenkot leads Netanyahu, People of Israel remains out
Channel 12's poll placed Eisenkot's Yashar party in first place with 23 seats, compared with 20 for Likud under Netanyahu.
Winter's People of Israel fell below the electoral threshold, receiving 1.8% of the vote.
Meanwhile, the balance between the blocs remained unchanged, with 54 seats for the opposition parties, 49 for the coalition, and 13 for the Arab parties. Hendel and Zelekha's party received four seats.
Polling average: Eisenkot holds narrow lead, blocs remain virtually tied
The average of the four polls presented an almost symmetrical picture of the two political blocs. The opposition averages 51.25 seats, compared with 51 for Netanyahu's bloc.
In other words, among the Zionist parties, neither side has a decisive advantage.
The gap widens when the Arab parties are included. They average 13.75 seats, while the Hendel-Zelekha party stood at four seats and remained outside the two-bloc division.
Together, the Zionist opposition and the Arab parties average 65 seats.
Eisenkot also holds an advantage among the largest parties. Yashar averages 21.5 seats, compared with Likud's 19, while Bennett trails significantly with 12.5.
The overall picture is of an extremely close election within the Zionist political camps, in which the Arab parties and smaller factions could become decisive factors.
The average is based on the distribution of Knesset seats in four separate polls and does not constitute a new survey or a forecast of the election results.

The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order didn't specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump chose a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Trump's decision draws criticism from Zelensky, Republican senator
Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia."
Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

====================================================================================================

Nearly one in three Israeli students considers leaving country as living costs soar - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:20:11 UTC
16:20:11 KST

The average Israeli student's monthly expenses have reached NIS 6,907, nearly half rely on financial assistance from their parents, and 29% are considering leaving Israel after graduation, according to the National Union of Israeli Students' 2026 survey, released ahead of the academic year's opening on Sunday.
The survey reveals the financial and emotional toll of higher education in Israel.
Alongside the financial difficulties, the survey highlights the impact of the war on students who served in the reserves, with 64% reporting emotional and social difficulties upon returning to their studies. Meanwhile, 38% of all students believe their academic institutions are not adequately preparing them for the age of artificial intelligence and changes in the labor market.
The findings were published ahead of the opening of the new academic year on Sunday, October 18, amid a complex economic and security situation.
Working, relying on parents, and still struggling to make ends meet
According to the survey, 81% of students work while pursuing their studies, compared with 79% in 2024. Working students are employed for an average of 97 hours a month and earn approximately NIS 6,235 gross. Despite juggling work and studies, only 49% are employed in fields related to their academic programs.
The average monthly expenses of a student in Israel stand at NIS 6,907, up NIS 28 from the previous year.
Housing and household maintenance constitute the largest expense, averaging NIS 3,155 a month. This is followed by groceries for home consumption at NIS 1,463, entertainment at NIS 751, and transportation at NIS 724.
Regional disparities are also evident. The Central District recorded the highest average monthly expenses at NIS 7,258, compared with NIS 6,392 in the Haifa District.
Nearly half of students (49%) receive financial assistance from their parents, up from 46% the previous year. The average monthly assistance is NIS 2,252, up NIS 100 from the previous year.
In addition to family assistance, one in five students has taken out a loan during their studies. Among borrowers, 61% took out loans exceeding NIS 20,000.
The average loan amount reached NIS 49,849, up NIS 1,716 from the previous year. Half of borrowers said the loan helped them to a great or very great extent to complete the academic year.
Financial difficulties are also affecting students' ability to plan for the future. Some 67% cannot save money regularly each month, while 38% believe they will never be able to buy a home.
Nevertheless, this represents an improvement over the previous year, when 42% believed they would be unable to buy a home.
The housing situation is also affecting living conditions. Some 22% of students reported having to compromise on the quality of their accommodation because of the cost of living or rental prices, while 14% moved back into their parents' homes.
Half of respondents live in rented apartments or sublets, while 31% live with their parents.
One of the survey's most notable findings concerns the risk of students dropping out of higher education.
Some 33% said they had considered dropping out in the past year, as Walla first reported. Among those who considered leaving their studies, 50% cited financial difficulties as a primary reason, 41% pointed to difficulties coping with their academic workload, and 22% reported mental health difficulties.
Reservists return to campus but struggle to resume normal life
The war continues to affect students' academic lives. Some 27% of respondents reported being called up for reserve duty during the academic year, compared with 23% in the previous survey. Another 16% said they were spouses or partners of reservists.
Among students who served in the reserves, 64% reported that returning to their studies was emotionally and socially challenging to a great or very great extent.
Nearly half (47%) felt a sense of distance, alienation, or lack of understanding from students who did not serve in the reserves.
The difficulties extend beyond emotional and social challenges.
Only 43% of student reservists said the academic accommodations they received, including extended assignment deadlines, attendance exemptions, and special examination dates, helped them catch up on missed coursework to a great or very great extent.
Another 26% said the accommodations helped them only to a small extent or not at all.
Student reservists have also faced financial difficulties related to their reserve service, including disputes over eligibility for municipal tax discounts.
The issue of equality in military service also weighs heavily on reservists.
Some 68% reported significant feelings of frustration, burnout, or anger over the unequal distribution of military and reserve service obligations.
Another 38% said this inequality significantly or very significantly undermines their motivation and willingness to report for reserve duty in the future.
Half of student reservists said financial compensation was a significant consideration or positive incentive in their decision to report for duty or extend their service, beyond their sense of mission.
Some 22% said they had to postpone one or more courses until the summer semester or the following academic year, while 58% completed the year as planned.
Concerns over artificial intelligence and future employment
Alongside financial and emotional difficulties, students are expressing concerns about entering the workforce.
More than 40% of respondents are considerably concerned about finding their place in the job market after completing their degrees.
Some 38% believe their academic institutions are not adequately preparing them for the age of artificial intelligence and technological changes in the labor market.
The findings come as efforts to introduce artificial intelligence into Israel's education system continue, including cooperation between the Education Ministry and technology companies.
Despite these concerns, students' salary expectations keep rising.
The average monthly salary students expect to earn about two years after graduation is NIS 16,657, up NIS 631 from the previous year.
The nature of academic studies is also changing.
Some 49% of students attach great or very great importance to maintaining in-person learning and a physical presence on campus, although most do not wish to attend classes in person every day.
Some 27% prefer coming to campus two days a week, 23% prefer one day, and another 23% prefer three days.
Only 3% want to attend campus five days a week.
Nearly three in 10 students consider leaving Israel as trust in government declines
The economic and security situation is also influencing how students view their future in Israel.
Some 29% of respondents said they would consider moving to another country after completing their studies, compared with 26% the previous year.
Another 56% said they were not considering leaving, while 15% remained undecided.
Among students considering emigration, 79% cited the cost of living as one of the main reasons, 46% pointed to the security situation, 20% cited their employment prospects, and 20% identified the political and diplomatic crisis.
Trust in the government has also declined.
Some 63% of students believe the current government does not look after their interests at all or does so only to a limited extent, compared with 57% the previous year.
Meanwhile, the proportion of students who are highly or very highly optimistic about Israel's future has fallen from 37% to 31%.
When asked which issues would most influence their votes in the next Knesset elections, 67% selected the cost of living and the economy, 37% chose internal security and personal safety, and 35% identified foreign and defense policy.
Another 27% cited education and social policy, while only 15% selected the identity of the prime minister as one of the two issues most important to them.
Students with disabilities and student parents face additional challenges
The survey also examined the circumstances of students with disabilities.
Among respondents in this group, 62% said their academic institutions were physically accessible to a great or very great extent, while 12% reported limited or no accessibility.
Nevertheless, concerns about life after graduation remain significant.
Some 47% of students with disabilities are highly or very highly concerned that their disability will constitute a significant obstacle to entering the workforce.
Another 26% expressed moderate concern, while only 27% reported little or no concern.
Students who became parents during their studies also face difficulties.
Only 39% said the support they received from their academic institutions after the birth of their child was adequate to a great or very great extent.
Another 30% felt the support was limited or entirely inadequate.
The National Union of Israeli Students' 2026 survey was conducted among approximately 12,000 respondents ahead of the new academic year, which began on Sunday, October 18. Conducted for the 17th year in its current format, the survey examined students' financial circumstances, integration into the labor market, satisfaction with their academic institutions, and the impact of the war on their lives.

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European nations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:19:33 UTC
16:19:33 KST

AFP Photo
Vietnam and four European nations outside the EU signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi yesterday, seeking to diversify their markets as US tariffs disrupt global commerce.
The deal, between Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which includes Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland, eliminates or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
The deal was signed in the capital in the presence of Vietnam's top leader To Lam and representatives of EFTA governments.
Vietnam and EFTA concluded negotiations in July, more than a decade after the free trade talks officially began in 2012.
The parties relaunched negotiations in September last year, after they had stalled since 2018.
The agreement covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Bilateral trade between the EFTA and Vietnam last year was valued at 4.8 billion euros ($5.4 billion), according to the association.
Electrical and mechanical machinery, fish and pharmaceutical products were the EFTA nations' top exports to Vietnam last year.
Machinery, footwear and apparel were manufacturing hub Vietnam's major exports to the EFTA.
The association was created as a counterpart to the European Economic Community, precursor of the European Union which its four member states are close to but have not joined.

IMF chief says has 'optimism' and 'worry' after Bangkok annual meetings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:15:37 UTC
16:15:37 KST

AFP Photo
International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva said on Oct. 17 this year's Annual Meetings with global policymakers were marked by "optimism and worry" as the event winds down in Bangkok.
Meetings in the Thai capital this week brought together finance ministers, central bank chiefs and other top officials from around the world.
"[The meetings] were marked by both optimism and worry," said Georgieva.
"Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia. But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry, and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks."
All week, the IMF has warned that high levels of debt and spiking bond yields are tightening financial conditions just as central banks need to focus on bringing inflation down, likely by increasing interest rates.
Global energy prices have spiked since late February, when the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran. The price increases have rippled across the globe, fuelling inflation in economies across a range of income groups.
The most vulnerable to the shock, the IMF has said, are low-income oil-importing countries that are not exposed to the boom in AI investment that has propped up growth in many advanced economies.
"I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, they don't like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor," said Georgieva.
She said such countries needed to set spending targets such that they prioritised growth and protecting the most vulnerable people, adding that the Fund had a "relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries".
Higher global interest rates and bond yields, however, were driving up debt repayments for low-income countries, she said.
The share of debt repayments as a percentage of government revenue had gone up from eight to 14 percent for low-income countries in recent years, the IMF chief said.
She said her organisation had a responsibility to help countries to restructure debt if needed; to assist with domestic resource mobilisation; to bring in international finance; and to create conditions for private investment.
"When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people."

Taiwan lawmakers pass health insurance subsidies for seniors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:13:33 UTC
16:13:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The legislature on Friday passed an amendment to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act requiring the central government to fully subsidize National Health Insurance premiums for eligible people aged 65 and older.
The subsidy applies when a senior or their legally obligated supporter has an income tax rate below 20% or income for the most recent year below the tax filing threshold, per UDN. The amendment to Article 22 passed its third reading 60–39, with support from the KMT and TPP.
The legislation sets a national subsidy standard for qualifying seniors, shifting responsibility for their premiums to the central government from local subsidy programs with varying eligibility rules.
The KMT and TPP legislative caucuses submitted proposals to amend the law in 2024. The draft completed its initial committee review on June 13 that year, followed by cross-party negotiations on June 27, but lawmakers failed to reach a consensus.
After the bill remained stalled beyond the one-month negotiation period, Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) announced that it would proceed to a plenary vote. The amendment passed despite opposition from DPP lawmakers.
The TPP legislative caucus said the measure would increase annual government spending by approximately NT$39 billion (US$1.21 billion), based on a monthly subsidy of NT$826 per eligible senior. The party argued that the additional expenditure would account for about 1% of the annual government budget and would not create an insurmountable fiscal burden.
The proposal has also raised concerns about fairness and the long-term finances of the National Health Insurance system.
DPP Legislator Wang Cheng-hsu (王正旭), a physician by training, said an estimated 4 million seniors could qualify. He warned that providing benefits based primarily on age and income tax brackets could undermine the principle that people should contribute to the health insurance system according to their ability to pay.
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said the cost would ultimately be borne by other contributors or taxpayers. If the additional expenditure were passed on to people aged 15 to 64, the main contributors to the insurance system, each person could face more than NT$3,000 in additional annual costs, he said.

AFP Photo
Sri Lanka suffered a nationwide electricity blackout on Oct. 17 after the national grid tripped, possibly because solar power generation exceeded consumption, officials said.
The country was without grid power for more than two hours. State-run Electricity Distribution Lanka (EDL) said suspected excess solar power had caused the breakdown.
said authorities hoped to restore supplies "stage by stage."
"We request rooftop solar system owners to disconnect their systems until further instructions in order to support the restoration efforts," Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka said in a brief statement.
The entire grid shut down in February 2025, when solar power generation exceeded consumption on a bright, sunny Sunday. It took more than six hours to restore supplies.
Sri Lanka has an installed solar power capacity of just over 3,000 megawatts, while daytime demand ranges from 2,000 to 2,500 megawatts.
Tax concessions have encouraged consumers to switch to solar and sell their surplus electricity to the grid, creating imbalances that the utility provider is struggling to manage.
The government aims to increase solar power generation capacity to nearly 4,400 megawatts within three years, a 388 percent increase from 2024.

At least 7 killed, dozens injured in explosion during live-fire drill at Canadian military base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

At least seven people were killed and dozens more injured Saturday in an explosion and massive fire at a Canadian military base in Alberta, according to military sources cited by Global News, in what officials described as an exceptionally serious disaster that overwhelmed nearby hospitals and sent flames spreading beyond the base's perimeter.
The explosion occurred at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, about 200 kilometers southeast of Edmonton, at approximately 4 p.m. local time. Multiple Canadian Armed Forces sources told Global News that a live-fire training exercise struck a gas pipeline or gas well on the base, triggering the blast. Canadian authorities have not officially confirmed the cause.
The explosion sparked a large fire that spread rapidly amid powerful winds, with gusts reaching 100 kilometers per hour. About three hours after the incident began, local authorities reported that the flames had crossed the base's perimeter fence, prompting firefighters from several jurisdictions to join efforts to contain the blaze.
Ambulances and medical helicopters were dispatched to the base, and casualties were transported to hospitals in Edmonton after medical facilities in the nearby town of Wainwright became overwhelmed by the number of patients requiring treatment.
Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency physician at Edmonton's Royal Alexandra Hospital, told Canadian public broadcaster CBC that the scale of the emergency was extraordinary.
"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Thirsk said. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."
Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed that the incident had caused fatalities and injuries but did not provide an official casualty count.
"I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory," McGuinty said Saturday night, describing the situation as "very, very active and delicate."
The minister said authorities had launched an investigation to establish the circumstances of the disaster, with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police involved alongside military personnel and emergency responders.
Prime Minister Mark Carney also addressed the incident in a post on X, calling it a serious emergency.
"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," he wrote. "We are working closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities."
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it had affected many Canadian military personnel.
By late Saturday night, local authorities reported that firefighters were holding the fire and that property and critical infrastructure were being protected. No evacuation order had been issued for residents of the nearby town.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training installations, used to prepare soldiers and military units for operational deployments.
The base houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, where military units train to operate together under realistic battlefield conditions, as well as the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides basic infantry and other military training.
The disaster has prompted a large-scale emergency response, with federal, provincial and local authorities working together as investigators seek to determine how a routine military training exercise could have ended in such a deadly incident.

Japan to launch space mission to bring samples from Martian moon to Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:08:38 UTC
16:08:38 KST

Aamir Latif
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Japan is set to launch a space mission on Tuesday to bring samples from a Martian moon to Earth, state media reported on Sunday.
The Martian Moons eXploration mission, or MMX, will be launched from the southwestern prefecture of Kagoshima on Tuesday, state-run NHK reported.
The mission, which will lift off on an H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center, is designed to become the first in the world to land on the Martian moon Phobos, collect samples from its surface, and deliver them to Earth.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency led the project to develop the three-module mission. The total development cost for the mission is 55.3 billion yen (nearly $350 million).
The exploration module carries sampling equipment, various observation instruments, and two super high-definition cameras.
The mission is expected to reach the vicinity of Mars about one year after launch. It will then spend three years conducting observations.
The return module will likely deliver the samples to Earth during the fiscal year ending in March 2032.

Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that?
European condemnation of Netanyahu is mounting, but analysts say Israel’s election offers little prospect of a material change for Palestinians.
While marking Israel’s 75th anniversary, Ursula von der Leyen offered solidarity.
“Europe and Israel are bound to be friends and allies,” the European Commission president said on April 23, 2023.
That friendship reached beyond diplomacy. Israel played international football in Europe, competed in Eurovision and shared intelligence with European governments. Its weapons industry was woven into European production lines.
Those ties still exist, but have since become battlegrounds after Israel’s systematic destruction of Gaza, which has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians.
European countries have withdrawn from Eurovision over Israel’s participation. European footballers have refused to play the Israeli team. Some declarations of friendship have been recast as condemnation.
Ireland and Spain have long led criticism of Israel’s oppression of Palestinians.
At the recent UN General Assembly, Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin said Israel’s actions in Gaza “will shame the world”, while Spain’s Pedro Sanchez spoke of “condemning unequivocally the genocide that Netanyahu continues to perpetrate in Gaza”.
Recently, in a sign of how much has changed in three years, Britain, whose Balfour Declaration helped lay the foundations for Israel’s creation, imposed a ban on goods from illegal settlements, while its foreign secretary accused Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing.
On Saturday, a group of settlers attacked European diplomats and officials from Belgium, France and Poland who were visiting Palestinian olive harvesters near the village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank. The assault, which came a day after settlers attacked a United States journalist north of Ramallah, drew widespread international condemnation.
Scarred relations between Europe and Israel may never fully repair, experts said as Israel heads to an election on October 27 that is too close to call.
Will the result affect Europe-Israel ties?
Yossi Mekelberg, a Middle East analyst at Chatham House, said if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returns with the far right, “certain things will become irreversible. The damage caused by this government is deep”.
Nicola Perugini, a senior lecturer in international relations at the University of Edinburgh, warned that the re-election of the leader, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC), would see Gaza’s population continue to struggle under “unliveable” conditions.
A Netanyahu coalition with more liberal parties might slow settlement expansion. But having a premier wanted by the ICC at the helm would likely lead to a continued deterioration of the Israel-Europe relationship. Replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a break with the policies driving European criticism, experts said.
For instance, Gadi Eisenkot, former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, viewed as Netanyahu’s main challenger, has opposed Palestinian statehood.
An annual public opinion survey by Israel’s Mitvim Institute last year showed that 67 percent of Israelis regarded the EU more as an adversary, compared with 14 percent who saw it as a friend.
Mekelberg sees potential for a different relationship under a more liberal government.
“The conversation with Europe would be more reasonable and rational,” he said, but warned that the picture would not change overnight.
More humanitarian aid could be delivered to Palestinians and the rate of settlement expansion could slow, analysts said. The E1 settlement plan could be abandoned.
But Julie M Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, said that may not be enough for European governments to make amends.
Rather, Europe would look for concrete moves towards Palestinian statehood and ending the occupation.
“But so far, we’re not seeing that under the current government and probably not under the next,” she said.
‘Ruling elite in several countries trying to align with the public’
At the beginning of Israel’s war on Gaza, Western leaders supported Israel’s campaign.
But sustained pressure from groups demanding action to stop the onslaught in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank – from civil rights organisations, international courts, trade unions and professional bodies to millions of protesters across the world – forced governments to act, analysts said.
“Now the ruling elite in several countries is trying to align itself with the public,” Neve Gordon, an Israeli professor of human rights law at Queen Mary University in London, told Al Jazeera, adding that the pro-Palestine movement had changed the “common sense” position of governments.
Pew Research Center polling in the UK found that the proportion viewing Israel unfavourably rose from 61 to 69 percent between spring 2025 and spring this year, from 66 to 75 percent in Italy and from 64 to 73 percent in Germany, one of its strongest allies.
Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist, linked that pressure to recognition of Palestinian statehood, moves towards suspending the EU-Israel association agreement and bans on settlement imports.
“If anything has had any impact on European policy towards Israel, it is precisely the wave of protests over the last few years,” she said.
Norman at Chatham House said European states have shifted from targeted measures, such as sanctioning far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, towards “broader structures, in terms of scrutiny of the Israeli state itself”.
But support for Israel persists in parts of Europe, noted Oxford University professor Janina Dill.
Two successive German governments have been “utterly unwilling to act on justified public criticism of Germany’s diplomatic and material support for Israel”, she said.
With support generally on the decline, Israel has cultivated ties with Europe’s far right, finding common ground in nationalism and hostility towards Islam, despite historic and current ties to anti-Semitism.
Menachem Klein, a senior lecturer at Bar-Ilan University, told Al Jazeera, that the current government has caused “huge damage to relations with friends and allies” – and scars will take time to heal.
Mekelberg added that improving relations requires concrete steps towards a peace process and a different future for Palestinians. Even then, the damage will endure.
Israel’s isolation
The election debate in Israel has focused on security, rather than the morality of the continued killing of Palestinians or the country’s international standing.
Israel’s wars abroad appear to have widespread domestic support.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey in April found that 92 percent of Jewish Israelis highly rated the military’s management of the Iran war. Eighty percent supported continuing the fighting against Hezbollah, even at the cost of friction with Washington. In September, Jewish People Policy Institute polling found that 72 percent of Jewish Israelis would not accept withdrawal to Gaza’s border without retaining an Israeli security perimeter inside the territory.
Israel’s diplomatic isolation might therefore seem an obvious election issue. Instead, “it is barely discussed”, Yaakov Katz, cofounder of the Middle East American Dialogue Forum, wrote in an article for Chatham House.
Rather, the main talking points are the degradation of Hamas and the weakening of Hezbollah and Iran, while the opposition promises to lower living costs, investigate the failures surrounding October 7 and draft members of the ultra-Orthodox community into the military.
“It is not that Israelis are unaware of the campus protests, the arms embargoes, growing European sanctions and recognition of a Palestinian state, and the International Criminal Court arrest warrants,” Katz wrote. “The 7 October attack has shaped public opinion in Israel to such an extent that when a foreign government criticises Israel … Israelis see only two viewpoints: that the criticism is either antiSemitic or it is ignorant.”

Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
October 18, 2026
The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.
The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.
The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.
What happened in the Czech Senate elections?
Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.
The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.
Babis called the result "catastrophic."
"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.
That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.
His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.
Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact

Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that President Donald Trump had signed an executive order waiving the imposition of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act for 60 days to assess how they might affect the US and global economies.
Source: Marco Rubio speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "The problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries – India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy.
I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies."
Details: Rubio said that global energy prices have been affected not only by the situation in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, but also by Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and, supposedly, the war between Russia and Ukraine, "where energy infrastructure is being hit".
He noted that the administration needs 60 days to "take all of that into account and weigh it against each other".
Rubio cited India as an example, saying that the country has voluntarily diversified its supplies but still obtains a significant share of its energy resources from Russia.
When asked by a journalist whether the decision amounts to a gift to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, the secretary of state said Russian diesel fuel "was going to be sold one way or the other".
Quote: "The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they will make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get. But this is not unprecedented. If you recall, a few months ago, we also did a 60-day waiver on Russian oil when Hormuz was being challenged."
Details: Rubio noted that conflicts around the world are now interconnected and could therefore create uncertainty in global energy markets.
"So all of these things have to be managed delicately because they're all coming together now. It's not just the Strait of Hormuz anymore. It's what's happening with Saudi Arabia and the uncertainty that that's creating. It's also what's happening between Russia and Ukraine and the constraints that's putting on global energy supplies," he added.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump signed an executive order waiving the application of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act. He said the decision was in the US national interest. The deadline for Trump to impose new sanctions on Russia expires on 18 October.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Graham Act could still put pressure on Russia despite Trump's decision not to introduce new restrictions under it for the time being.
- Senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the Graham Act, sharply criticised Trump for refusing to take further steps to put pressure on Russia under the law.

‘Keep away from the doctor’: a visit to an influencer’s wellness event, where the advice could kill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:00:54 UTC
16:00:54 KST

A roar of laughter erupts from a crowd inside a large conference room at the De Vere Cranage Estate hotel. The joke? The idea that visiting the doctor could help treat a serious illness.
On stage the controversial Australian proponent of natural remedies Barbara O’Neill is taking part in a question-and-answer session during a five-day wellness conference, where science mixes uncomfortably with Bible verse and potentially deadly pseudo-scientific practices.
She is advising people attending at the event in Cheshire on a variety of medical ailments, and dismisses the use of antibiotics, vaccines or scientifically proven cancer treatment.
Tickets for the residential retreat can cost up to £1,300. An undercover reporter for the Guardian attended for one day, observing four sessions covering topics including the immune system and one titled Barbara Under Attack.
The audience’s rapturous laughter is prompted by a woman asking O’Neill if there is anything that could help her lupus, which she says has not responded well to the doctor’s treatments. “Yes, keep away from the doctor,” quips O’Neill.
O’Neill tells the audience that she is “just a little lady”, but she is an incredibly influential one, with 3.6 million Instagram followers and 1.7 million on Facebook. Many of her videos rack up millions of views.
Having initially found success promoting alternative treatments in Australia, in 2019 O’Neill was banned from providing any health services in her home country, where authorities found she was responsible for “misleading vulnerable people”. They said she “made dangerous claims not supported by evidence and posed a risk to public safety”.
She has since taken her unregulated services overseas, most recently with a string of appearances in the UK and Ireland which prompted concern from experts in both countries. A number of prominent doctors and scientists have told the Guardian her advice is “dangerous”, with some warning it could kill.
O’Neill appears regal sitting on stage in an armchair offering audience members softly spoken advice on endometriosis, varicose veins and constipation.
The 73-year-old is dressed in a long skirt with a woollen wrap, which she later switches for a soft cardigan, creating a look that sits somewhere between Queen Elizabeth II at Balmoral and Claudia Winkleman in The Traitors. The Highlands-inspired attire is a nod to her Scottish heritage, which the Australian mentions on multiple occasions.
She carries an air of authority to her devoted followers, many of whom seem confident that her doctrine could improve their health.
Much of her core teaching aligns with established scientific health advice: few doctors would dispute that a balanced diet, regular exercise, hydration and plenty of sleep are important factors for good health, while it is advisable to avoid alcohol, caffeine and smoking.
During some of the lectures, O’Neill draws diagrams on a whiteboard while issuing long scientific-sounding explanations.
She talks about the glycocalyx lining of the endothelium cells, which provides anticoagulant effects and releases nitric oxide, a vasodilator.
But she also makes some highly unscientific and potentially deadly recommendations.
During the Q&A session, a woman says that while she recently underwent tests, doctors found a stomach tumour, which she says two specialists have advised her to have surgically removed.
“Sometimes scans are not right,” replies O’Neill, who advises the woman to treat the tumour with a castor oil compress – kitchen roll soaked with high viscosity oil from the castor plant – on the outside of the body.
That day O’Neill recommends the same remedy for nasal polyps, endometriosis, carpal tunnel syndrome and bile duct stones. Medical experts told the Guardian there was no evidence castor oil compresses did anything to improve any of those conditions.
She suggests using castor oil with a pinch of cayenne pepper in the eye to an audience member with glaucoma and high blood pressure.
Prof Gus Gazzard, a leading glaucoma expert, says: “There is absolutely no evidence to support these claims, and unfortunately, there’s the possibility that they might indeed cause harm.”
The questions continue, read out by her husband, Michael, who gives some of his own lectures during the retreat. The pair stumble over long names of medical conditions, while the audience laughs along.
O’Neill advises a pregnant woman against taking folic acid, which randomised controlled trials have shown can protect against neural tube deficits in babies. To someone else, she claims antibiotics are “the worst thing to give” for infections.
To a woman who says she does not have a functioning thyroid, she recommends slowly stopping her dose of thyroxine, which is prescribed for thyroid dysfunction, to “see what the body does”.
Medical experts say this would lead to fatigue, hair loss, weight gain, a slow heart rate and low mood. Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, says: “Someone without a functioning thyroid cannot make thyroid hormone, so stopping thyroxine to ‘see what the body does’ really makes no sense and risks serious, potentially life-threatening illness.”
A woman who says she has diabetes tells O’Neill she is hoping to come off metformin, a drug used to lower blood sugar levels. Metformin is typically used to treat type 2 diabetes, which can respond to a change in diet, while type 1 requires daily insulin injections. Both types require blood glucose monitoring. O’Neill advises her to stop testing her blood sugar because it would “balance right out with the change in diet”.
This advice is “very dangerous”, according to Gill Livingston, a professor of psychiatry of older people at UCL. “Untreated diabetes means the body is bathed in bloodstream high sugar and increases the risk of multiple physical illnesses, such as loss of eyesight, loss of peripheral sensation, dementia and sometimes death.”
Refusing medical tests is a regular theme in O’Neill’s teachings across her publications, her social media and her public appearances. “It’s amazing how many tests are creating illnesses,” she says at the Cheshire event.
At another point, not long after encouraging a follower to ignore her oncologist’s recommendation to take a drug, and without any clarification about the type of cancer the woman was being treated for, she says: “They give you a label and then they give you a drug.”
Interspersed throughout the day are claims that people have recovered from illnesses after taking her advice. She cites a man who had suffered a stroke, and had “no adverse effects at all” when he stopped taking medication prescribed by his doctor, including statins and blood thinners, on one of her retreats.
“It’s outrageous what medicine will do. We have to start saying ‘no, thank you’,” she says. “It doesn’t matter what they say to you, what fear they put into you, say no.
“The body, it’s got an inbuilt ability to heal itself.”
Prof Liam Smeeth, director of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, calls her claims “extraordinary”. He says: “Most disturbingly, many of these – if followed – will cause substantial harm, and this could include death.”
It is clear some of her followers have a lot of trust in her. Speaking to the Guardian’s undercover reporter at the end of the day, one audience member says O’Neill’s answer to her question was “very helpful” and she now has the confidence to go against specialists’ advice for surgery for a health condition.
In other conversations during breaks, some people attending say they have lost trust in western medicine after side-effects or failed treatments.
One woman in her 60s explains that she and her family refused masks and vaccines during the Covid crisis, had gatherings and “actually washed my hands less than normal”. She says her husband went into hospital in early 2020 with pneumonia and died two days later. She blames the medics for his death.
“You know they’re satanists, don’t you?” she says, of the government and those who run major global institutions. “The elite are all flesh-eating paedophiles.”
Some at the conference wear amulets they claim protect against 5G signals and a stall selling them proves popular. There is no evidence that 5G signals cause harm and yet O’Neill advises those working at a computer to invest in a device to protect against damage she says is caused by electronic devices and “balance the body after exposure to an electromagnetic field [EMF]”.
Dr David Robert Grimes, an expert in biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin, says fear of modernity is a common pseudoscience trope.
“The canard that EMFs are ‘damaging’ us is a tired one that exploits our ignorance of technical terms to instil fear,” he says. “There is no device that ‘balances’ you after exposure, because the central conceit is nonsense. We live in a world with light, heat, radio waves, and the sun, so EMFs are all around us. The idea of balancing is really meaningless.”
He adds: “The evidence is clear that patients seduced by the false allure of complementary medicine fare objectively worse than those that stick to conventional treatments. These patients are typically convinced by dubious healers to delay or reject life-saving treatments until it’s too late, with often tragic consequences.”
Before O’Neill’s most recent tour, senior doctors and medical experts, including Grimes, wrote to some of the venues hosting her conferences urging them to reconsider holding events that would “spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience”.
O’Neill’s husband, Michael, co-runs her company and is the engine behind her tours. In an afternoon session titled Barbara Under Attack, he describes her “persecution” by authorities, the scientific community and the media . “There is a war against us,” he tells the audience.
After an approach from the Guardian to O’Neill for comment on her claims at the conference, a video of the couple appears on her Instagram and Facebook pages warning their followers of “disgusting” reporting. Michael reads out the statement issued to the Guardian.
“The complaints against Barbara are purely speculative, based on an ideology that the only legitimate way to health is through the medical profession,” he says.
Michael claims the couple have not received complaints about O’Neill’s work and highlights statistics about medical mistakes in the NHS.
He adds: “The campaign against Barbara by the media, and academics is a modern-day witch-hunt that has no substance in facts, but purely an ideology that supports the most corrupt organisation in the world; the pharmaceutical industry.”
The pair have vowed to continue holding events. O’Neill says she is driven by God, who she believes spoke directly to her.
“It would be wrong of me to stop.”

Condé Nast’s UK profits drop by more than a third as sale of Vogue publisher ruled out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:00:53 UTC
16:00:53 KST

Profits at Condé Nast’s UK arm slumped by more than a third last year, according to figures published shortly after the billionaire family that owns the luxury magazine group and titles from Vogue to GQ ruled out a sale.
The publisher, which enjoyed a bumper 2024 after booking £64m in proceeds from the sale of its UK headquarters Vogue House in London, saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items tumble 36% from £28m that year to nearly £18m last year.
Revenues generated in the UK fell 7% from £75.9m to £70.6m, newly filed accounts showed. However, an 18% increase in international revenues, to £29.7m, helped keep the company’s total revenues almost flat, at £100m.
“Condé Nast remains profitable in the UK for another year,” a spokesperson for the publisher said. “The change in the exact level of profit reflects a period of planned investment in customised client solutions.”
Restructuring costs at the company, which publishes glossy titles and brands including Vanity Fair, House & Garden and Tatler, more than doubled year on year, from £1.9m to £4.3m.
Condé Nast said the latest restructuring charge was “primarily due to severance costs”. Despite the hefty restructuring bill, staff numbers remained almost flat, dipping from 466 to 461 between 2024 and last year.
“There were no large restructures in the UK business in 2025. There were isolated instances of redundancy, but headcount remained flat as hiring continued across the business,” the spokesperson said. “In addition, there have been changes to the pension scheme projections and wage inflation, which also impacted profit for this year.”
Last week, Steven Newhouse, the chair of the Newhouse family holding company Advance that controls Condé Nast, ruled out a sale of the publishing giant. There had been speculation that the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, who owns the Washington Post, could buy the business.
Newhouse made the comment after the abrupt departure of the chief executive Roger Lynch, hired in 2019 to turn around the business, to become the boss of the toymaker Mattel.
“Maybe for a certain class of non-media owner, there’s a prestige to owning media properties,” he told the Financial Times. “But we’ve been a media owner for 100 years. So we’re not in it for the glamour.”
Earlier this year, Lynch described the introduction of Google’s AI Summaries – which often negate the need to click through to source material – as “another sort of death blow” to the way consumers have traditionally searched online and reached media outlets. He said Google searches were “no longer a meaningful driver” of Condé Nast’s business, accounting for only about a quarter of visits to its websites last year.
Globally, seven of Condé Nast’s largest brands – Vogue, GQ, the New Yorker, Wired, Vanity Fair, Architectural Digest and Condé Nast Traveler – account for 85% of the company’s revenues.
Newsstand sales and other subscriptions account for about 14% of total revenues, with advertising and “other services” accounting for about 86%.
The publisher’s accounts filed at Companies House show that the highest-paid director - Natalia Gamero del Castillo Calleja, the company’s most senior executive outside the US who resigned last August - took home more than £1.3m.
Earlier this year, Condé Nast announced plans to shutter Self, its women’s health magazine, after 47 years.

Attacked from the sky: Sudanese goldminers count deadly cost of eking out a living on the Egypt border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:00:52 UTC
16:00:52 KST

Torches still fixed on their heads but tools cast aside, the Sudanese goldminers of the North Valley had already mounted an impromptu rescue operation by the time Ammar* arrived at the site of a suspected Egyptian airstrike.
At least 114 were killed, according to the Sudanese rights group Emergency Lawyers, in the strike on Saturday 10 October on an artisanal goldmine brimming with young Sudanese trying to eke out a living in a country where the economy has been shattered by three years of war.
There has been anger in Sudan among those who accuse Egypt of being behind the strike, furious at what they see as aggression by their northern neighbour against workers who produce much of the gold consumed regionally and at the country’s inability to defend itself.
“These are people who have just come here to earn a living, through their own hard work,” says Ammar, a gold trader who worked at a different site and responded to calls to help the survivors.
“Their families are scattered by the war and they send them what they earn,” he says. “Sudan doesn’t have jobs, so they go to the mountains and dig with their hands to live.”
When Ammar arrived, he found chaos at the scene after the strike. The green bags used by the miners to carry excavated materials littered the ground as they abandoned their work to rescue the injured. They made stretchers from blankets, loaded the wounded into pickup trucks to be rushed to nearby towns, and began digging graves for the dead.
The strike was immediately attributed to Egypt by the miners, whose military later confirmed they had carried out operations as part of their push to end “illegal goldmining in the eastern desert”, though they did not address the airstrike.
Egypt reportedly struck the same site in June, killing at least 15 people, according to Sudanese media, and has carried out raids, arresting miners and confiscating equipment.
Egypt said it had distributed leaflets warning civilians to leave before launching the operation. Photos on social media appear to show a leaflet stating: “Surrender yourselves and your equipment. Your lives are more important than any equipment.”
Mohamed Salah, director of Emergency Lawyers, said there were scuffles before the bombing between miners and Egyptian security forces trying to force them out of the area.
“While Egyptian authorities have sought to curb illegal border trade for a long time, locals did not anticipate an escalation involving military aircraft,” says Salah.
He says most of the miners have dispersed since the attack but does not expect them to stay away.
“The miners say they will return – artisanal goldmining in these border areas is the only source of income for them,” he says.
Many come from conflict-hit parts of the country, such as the Darfur and Kordofan regions, he adds, and have slowly made their way through the country’s interior until finding themselves try to make a living prospecting for gold on the Egyptian border.
While Egypt has framed its operations as an attempt to curtail illegal mining, it has been a beneficiary of the informal mining sector, receiving an estimated 60% of the gold produced and smuggled from parts of northern Sudan that border Egypt.
Despite a three-year war between the Sudanese military and rebel paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, gold production has continued in areas controlled by both sides, with artisanal mines proliferating because of rising poverty in the country.
The mines rely on manual labour and expose workers to health risks because of the chemicals used to process the gold, such as mercury and cyanide.
The human rights campaigner Hala al-Karib says the airstrike reveals the vulnerability of the prospectors.
“They are blocked from any other means of livelihood with the collapse of the education system [and] the high rates of unemployment. What other options do they have to survive?” says Karib, who leads the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa network.
“They are at the bottom of the chain because they are subject to the exploitation of big traders. So it is quite painful that on top of that they are exposed to this terror, being killed randomly. It’s a crime and there is nothing to justify it.”
* Name changed to protect his identity
