Why Marco Rubio’s visit to Mumbai has ruffled feathers in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:16:49 UTC
14:16:49 KST

Why Marco Rubio’s visit to Mumbai has ruffled feathers in India
The US secretary of state is skipping New Delhi on his second trip to India in six months, and opposition leaders say the arrangements are humiliating.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is to visit India in the coming week, but he will not set foot in the capital, New Delhi.
Instead, on Monday, Rubio will hold talks with Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai, India’s financial hub, and then visit an oil refinery in Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat, according to a statement from the US Department of State.
His itinerary sparked a political storm after the US ambassador to India said Washington expected Jaishankar to travel to meet Rubio, prompting opposition leaders to accuse the government of allowing India’s top diplomat to be “summoned” on home soil.
The spat comes as relations between the two countries are strained over trade, tariffs and India’s purchases of Russian oil.
So why is Rubio avoiding New Delhi, and why has it caused such upset? Here’s what you need to know:
What is Rubio doing in India?
He plans to discuss trade, energy and investment.
Rubio is arriving on Sunday from Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he has been meeting with five Central Asian states at the C5+1 summit.
In India, he is due to meet senior officials to discuss the US-India strategic partnership and energy cooperation and hold talks with business leaders, the State Department said.
Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal appeared to confirm the agenda, stating on Friday that the Mumbai talks would cover energy, trade and investment, defence, and critical and emerging technologies.
In Jamnagar, Rubio is to visit the world’s largest single-site refinery, operated by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, and attend a reception hosted by the Ambani family, according to The Hindu newspaper.
Why isn’t Rubio going to New Delhi?
No official reason has been given.
Rubio was in the Indian capital in May for a meeting of foreign ministers of countries in the Quad, a group consisting of the US, India, Japan and Australia.
The State Department has framed his upcoming trip around energy and investment, and the second stop on Rubio’s India visit, Jamnagar, is one of the world’s most important energy hubs.
The visit also comes as fuel prices bite in the US before next month’s midterm elections.
Reliance, an energy, retail and telecommunications conglomerate, also sits at the centre of Washington’s wider oil diplomacy.
Business Standard, an Indian financial daily, said the Jamnagar stop was significant because Reliance is the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude oil besides the US at a time when Washington has been urging India to buy more.
Since US forces seized Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January and took essential control of the country’s oil industry, the US government has marketed Venezuelan oil to buyers abroad.
Reliance is also investing in a new refinery in Texas, the first to be built in the US in 50 years, which Trump hailed as a $300bn deal when he announced it in March, Business Standard reported.
What did the US ambassador say, and why has it caused upset?
Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Thursday, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said Rubio would meet Indian government officials in Mumbai, and Washington “expected” Jaishankar and others from New Delhi to travel there to see him.
Earlier in the week, however, Jaiswal had not confirmed the trip or explained why Rubio was skipping New Delhi, telling reporters the Indian government would announce it “at the appropriate time”, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Jairam Ramesh, a general secretary of the opposition Indian National Congress party, wrote on X that the ambassador’s statement was “quite extraordinary”.
Rahul Gandhi, leader of the opposition in parliament’s lower house, also took to X to comment, writing on Friday that Rubio had “summoned his employee to Mumbai”.
Congress MP Pawan Khera went further.
“A foreign government summoning India’s External Affairs Minister on Indian soil is a new low, even by the Modi Government’s standards,” he wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Why are US-India relations strained?
Mainly because of Trump’s tariffs and Russian oil.
In August last year after a round of trade talks broke down, the US hit most Indian goods with a 50 percent tariff. Under a framework the two sides agreed in February, that rate fell to 18 percent, however.
Since then, negotiations have stalled.
This month, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks had “plateaued”, according to The Hindu.
On Thursday, Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said the “first tranche” of a deal was in its final stages but India would not sign until its exporters had an edge over rivals such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Indonesia, according to the Reuters news agency.
Other points of friction have emerged.
Last week, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling announced that his department was suspending eight companies – including the Indian IT giants Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL – from a labour certification scheme that is a key step for employers seeking green cards for their foreign staff.
Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote this week that Indian public opinion of the US has hit a record low, citing US engagement with Pakistan and the US-Israel war on Iran, which he said had pushed India back towards Russian oil.
Despite that, he argued, defence and technology cooperation has quietly deepened, and bilateral trade grew by almost 12 percent in 2025 to nearly $240bn.
In his view, “perceptions of the political relationship have deteriorated faster than its strategic foundations.”
A sanctions law had threatened to make matters worse.
Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which could impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas.
India, one of the world’s biggest buyers of Russian oil, had warned Washington that new tariffs could hurt bilateral ties. Trump signed an executive order seeking to waive the sanctions on Friday as he tries to ease high oil prices before the November 3 US elections.

Russia attacks Ukraine with missile and 180 drones: 152 UAVs downed by air defence
Russian forces have attacked Ukraine with one Iskander-M ballistic missile and 180 attack drones of various types since the evening of 17 October. Air defence has downed 152 drones, but strikes were recorded at 20 locations. The attack is ongoing.

Quote: "Early reports indicate that as of 08:00, air defence shot down or jammed 152 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (16 jet-powered), Gerbera drones and loitering munitions of other types. Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.
As of 08:00, the attack was ongoing, with around 10 Russian drones still in Ukrainian airspace.

In pictures: Orangutans rescued from Indonesia blazes as species faces extinction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:13:11 UTC
14:13:11 KST

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in recent weeks from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia, conservation groups said.
The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions both among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.
Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world's top five most polluted major cities as fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands, intensified by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, keep emitting smoke.
In Indonesia, groups are working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.
On Saturday, the West Kalimantan conservation agency and Indonesian non-profit YIARI said a team evacuated 51 orangutans from locations in the province from August 6 to October 19.
And figures from Indonesia's forestry ministry suggested this week that the number rescued over recent months in Kalimantan could be as high as 96.
Officials could not be immediately reached to clarify the number.
The latest rescue came on Saturday, when three conservation agencies rescued a 20-year-old male orangutan in Hampangen village in Central Kalimantan, on Borneo island.
"The evacuation process was carried out with great caution," the agencies said.
"After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the... rehabilitation center," it said.
Indonesia's transport ministry also said around 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since mid-August.
"Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations. Every operational decision is made with safety as the top priority," the ministry said.
All three orangutan species face a critical risk of extinction due to deforestation, wildfires, habitat loss and illegal hunting.

Israel's opposition will not defeat Netanyahu by focusing on October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:48 UTC
14:11:48 KST

The clock is ticking toward October 27, and tensions are running high. The central question is whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will manage to hold on to power, although most polls suggest that his chances are slim. Yet a closer look at the election campaigns of Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu reveals that each side has its own interpretation of why the 2026 election is critical to Israel’s future.
While Eisenkot and his fellow leaders of the center-left bloc, including Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan, have placed the October 7 failure and the question of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at the center of their campaign, Netanyahu is seeking to highlight the achievements of the War of Redemption [the multifront conflict following Hamas’s 2023 attack] while downplaying his responsibility for the October 7 failure.
Alongside allegations that Netanyahu received two warnings of an impending attack, from the Emiratis and the Egyptians, the statements made by his former military secretary, Avi Gil, are regarded by the opposition as compelling evidence of Netanyahu’s failure.
Eisenkot’s camp has also continued to emphasize that Netanyahu’s inner circle is tainted by corruption and a lack of integrity. In addition to the alleged attempt to falsify the official record, Netanyahu presented a selective account of the State Comptroller’s Report on the October 7 failure.
The opposition’s claims are certainly open to debate, and a closer examination of Gil’s statements only reinforces the conclusion that the security establishment failed on that terrible night. Nevertheless, several questions arise when we analyze the arguments put forward by both sides.
Analyzing the arguments
First, although Netanyahu pursued a failed policy toward Hamas, motivated in part by a desire to avoid a confrontation that could derail efforts to normalize relations with Saudi Arabia, the fact remains that he received intelligence indicating an impending attack only after it had begun.
Unlike the hours preceding the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War, when then-prime minister Golda Meir was involved in the decision-making process and could have ordered a preemptive strike against Egypt, Netanyahu was not even given an opportunity to influence events that night.
Second, questions also arise regarding the claim that the alleged criminal attempt to change the time of a phone call in the official record, from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m., was intended to reinforce the bizarre conspiracy theory that a generals’ revolt had taken place. Netanyahu’s opponents argue that members of his inner circle sought to create the impression that the generals had deliberately failed to wake him.
An alternative explanation, however, is that the change was intended to demonstrate that Netanyahu had not been asleep while Hamas terrorists were infiltrating communities near the Gaza border. If Netanyahu’s associates had wanted to emphasize that the generals had kept him in the dark, it would have made more sense to leave the call time at 6:40 a.m., allowing them to argue that he had been informed only 11 minutes after the attack began.
Third, Netanyahu’s strained relationship with the security establishment’s leadership was shaped in part by his insistence, during the judicial reform debate, that the phenomenon of military refusal be confronted rather than tolerated. Critics argue that Netanyahu chose to disregard the security chiefs’ warnings about the implications of the proposed judicial legislation and the threat it posed to national security, as well as their less specific warnings of a possible war.
Others, however, argue that had the IDF responded to military refusal as it did during the Disengagement from Gaza, Yahya Sinwar and Mohammed Deif might have thought twice before launching their attack.
This raises another question: If the security establishment’s leaders had warned of an impending war, why was the IDF so unprepared on that fateful day and caught so completely off guard?
In conclusion, Netanyahu has effectively been campaigning continuously since the 2022 election, particularly in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, massacre. Yet focusing on the alleged falsification of official records and the conduct of Netanyahu’s inner circle is unlikely to be the key to defeating him in the 2026 election.
Israel’s political history repeatedly demonstrates that corruption is not necessarily a decisive issue for voters. Arye Deri, for example, led Shas to 17 seats in the 1999 election despite having been convicted of bribery. Ariel Sharon led Likud to 38 seats in the 2003 election despite the cloud of suspicion surrounding the Cyril Kern affair.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, has consistently secured more than 30 seats in elections held since he became a criminal defendant. Rather than dwelling on the past, the opposition would be better served by persuading the public that Israel has a better future beyond Netanyahu’s leadership. That is how elections are won!
The writer is a lecturer and research fellow at the University of South Wales in the United Kingdom. He is the author of Collapse: The Israeli Labor Party, 1992–2024.

Israel’s election puzzle: Why are so many voters still backing Netanyahu? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:25 UTC
14:11:25 KST

I thought that after living here for 32 years (this week marked our “aliyahversary”), I finally understood Israelis. But perusing the pre-election polls, I realize how little I know about my neighbors outside our insular Anglo bubble.
How is it that, three years after the Oct. 7, 2023 failure of the entire military and political establishment, the current coalition is, in some polls, tied with the opposition parties and, in Channel 14’s pro-government poll, scoring a resounding win? That is not what I hear from friends and acquaintances in the ’hood.
On October 8, it was widely predicted that the coalition would fall – imminently. Indeed, the depravity of the massacre spurred a kind of dark hope for the future among those of us opposed to the relentless proliferation of hate and divisiveness that has been Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s key strategy to stay in power.
Yet, not only did the coalition serve its full term, but the narrative has been so twisted that Netanyahu’s Likud party has regained much, if not all, of its support.
Adding to this turnaround, inexplicable in southern Jerusalem, the anniversary of Oct. 7 doesn’t seem to have moved the dial a bit. Voters made up their minds long ago. There’s little chance of committed Likud voters changing sides, even as new examples of corruption and disregard are disclosed daily.
How did we get to this place? The answer, sadly, at least from where I’m sitting, seems to be racism. You only have to look at the giant election billboards with the rhyme “Yamin or Palestine” (in Hebrew, “yamin” means “right”), or the horrifically insensitive AI ad with the opposition party Yashar’s leader Gadi Eisenkot running to greet his dead son in a field, only to bypass him to embrace Ra’am (United Arab List) head Mansour Abbas.
That message is outrageous on so many levels.
Equality at Hadassah-University Medical Center
I spent two months hospitalized at Hadassah-University Medical Center, in Ein Kerem this summer. The institution epitomizes equality in this country. Some of the best doctors and nurses who cared for me were Arab Israelis. Fifty percent of all pharmacists in Israel are from the Arab sector. I never felt I was getting anything but the right treatment from the entire staff, even as they were pricking my tired fingers to make sure my glucose wasn’t spiking.
Earlier this year, I went to hear Naftali Bennett, who leads the opposition B’Yachad (Together) party, speak at an English-language event at Jerusalem’s Begin Heritage Center. When asked if the opposition should include an Arab party like Ra’am in a coalition, as he had done previously during the short-lived “change government,” he danced around a direct answer.
He would consider any party that affirms the right of the Jewish people to a state of their own in Israel, he implied, among other criteria. Ra’am has done this – and gone one step further, by adding a Jewish Israeli, Yoav Segalovich, as the party’s number two, with the specific mandate to fight crime in the Arab sector, an issue about which there should be consensus.
Eisenkot, pressured by right-wing goading, has stated publicly that he would not include any Arab parties in a future coalition, but if it’s between bringing in Ra’am again or returning to elections, I wouldn’t believe everything that’s said on the campaign trail.
At this point, I’ll reveal who I’m voting for: Bennett. His won’t be the largest party among the opposition. But Bennett has put together a series of detailed working plans to fix what’s wrong with this country, covering everything from transportation to education to the military.
His list includes skilled technocrats who have run ministries in the past and can hit the ground running. I hope that, if Eisenkot gets enough seats and is able to form a coalition, he’ll put some of Bennett’s team in place as ministers.
And yet the opposition can’t seem to decide on a consistent strategy. Should it hammer away at government corruption and the threat of a renewed judicial coup? What Netanyahu knew, or didn’t know, on Oct. 7? Should establishing a state commission of inquiry be the main talking point? Or can it harness the overwhelming fury of the non-haredi population by doubling down on a proposed law to draft ultra-Orthodox yeshiva boys into an army that is tens of thousands of soldiers short.
Compare that to Netanyahu, whose anti-Arab messaging is unwavering.
One last indelicate thought: Why is Netanyahu still around? He’s 76 and presumably in ill health. He has a pacemaker and cancer (supposedly in remission, but he hid his treatments from the public, so why should we believe him?).
I’ve seen pictures of Netanyahu lately. He’s so thin. I know, I should give him the benefit of the doubt (he must be exercising more). But I know better than many that when you’re faced with grave health challenges, you can shed a lot of weight quickly.
If Netanyahu lost the election, would that prompt him to accept a plea bargain in his criminal trial and leave politics to avoid jail? If so, why couldn’t he have done that already?
I’m not planning to leave Israel, regardless of the outcome. But my children might. My doctors might. Our tax-paying techies and overburdened reservists might. According to a Channel 12 survey, 23% of Israelis have developed contingency plans to emigrate if the current coalition continues its drive toward totalitarianism.
I pray that, in arguably the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, there will be a surprise surge that will shake the public out of its status quo slumber, so we can begin to repair this country we all love so much.
Maybe then I’ll finally understand Israelis.

Paris's cost of living protests spiral into France's worst violence, riots in decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:23 UTC
14:11:23 KST

Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiraled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Some 1,200 people had been arrested during the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated the protesters at 800,000.
President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks.
"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X.
Protests rage across Europe amid rising living costs
Belgium, Portugal, and Italy also saw smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, job shortages, and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president, and the wealthy.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks, and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques, and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fueling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending, and living standards.
In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office.
Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Police tactics criticized after demonstrators injured
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.
Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
"Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

Türkiye’s Embassy in Baku on Oct. 17 rejected media reports that Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held a “secret meeting” during his recent visit to Azerbaijan.

The Qafqazinfo news site had reported that Fidan visited a foundation established by Turkish philanthropists in Baku, where he allegedly held a secret meeting and issued various instructions. The report was later removed from the website.

SOPOT, Poland, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China and Europe should strengthen dialogue and mutual understanding to promote practical cooperation in a changing world, a Polish expert on China has said.
Bogdan Goralczyk, a professor at the Centre for Europe at the University of Warsaw, told Xinhua in a recent interview on the sidelines of the 15th European Forum for New Ideas that Europe needs to better understand China, which has become a major global economic and technological power.
Goralczyk called for closer dialogue between China and the European Union (EU) to manage differences, while highlighting electric vehicles and artificial intelligence (AI) as potential areas for practical cooperation.
"Europe is still a rich market and interesting for China," he said. He added that Europe's desire to play a greater role in AI could present opportunities for China.
Beyond government talks and economic cooperation, Goralczyk emphasized the importance of strengthening mutual understanding between Chinese and European people.
Goralczyk, who visits China almost every year, praised China's visa-free policy for citizens of some European countries, saying it has made it easier for Europeans to visit China and learn more about the country firsthand.
Europeans visiting China will discover a country different from the one portrayed in some media, he added.
Goralczyk also noted growing interest in China among younger generations in Europe. He said young Europeans visiting China are witnessing its modern society and technological advances, which inspire them to learn Chinese.
He called for closer academic exchanges between China and the EU, including more Chinese participation in Erasmus+, an EU program supporting education, training and youth exchanges. ■

Students perform during the awarding ceremony of Myanmar Chinese Song Competition 2026 at the National Theater in Yangon, Myanmar, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Melodies of Chinese songs and graceful dance performances filled the National Theater in Yangon on Saturday, as the Myanmar Chinese Song Competition 2026 held its awarding ceremony, bringing together Chinese song enthusiasts from across Myanmar.
Organized by the Chinese Embassy in Myanmar, the competition attracted growing interest, with nationwide participation reaching 27,000 this year.
For Kaung Khant Aung, 16, who won first prize in the youth category, the competition marked a rewarding milestone. Having learned Chinese since he was six, he said he practices singing every day.
"This is my second time participating. I didn't win a prize in my first competition, but this time I won first prize," he said.
"Through Chinese songs, we can learn about Chinese history, traditions and arts. Songs connect people around the world and help them relax," he said.
Aye Nant Thar Aung, 28, who won second prize in the adult category in her first competition, said she had studied Chinese for about two years.
Although learning Chinese can sometimes be challenging, she finds songs and dramas helpful in improving her language skills.
"If you don't feel like studying, listen to songs and watch dramas," she said, adding that learning Chinese could open up more opportunities for young people and help strengthen friendship between the two countries.
Ah May, 22, who traveled from Shan State to compete for the first time, won third prize in the adult category. Despite transportation difficulties, she said the experience allowed her to meet people from different regions and learn from other performers.
"Beyond singing, the competition offers Chinese language learners an opportunity to learn, share and build friendships. So, I am very proud to be part of this event," she said.
Founded in 2024, the Myanmar Chinese Song Competition aims to showcase the charm of the Chinese language, foster mutual understanding and friendship between the people of Myanmar and China through singing events and cultural exchange. ■

Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:05:43 UTC
14:05:43 KST

Rubio heads to Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
WASHINGTON, Oct 18 - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
The top US diplomat is scheduled to land in Samarkand on Sunday to meet with leaders from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.
Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly last September.
Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign-policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.
For instance, Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state. He was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.
Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.
Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots.
Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment."
US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM
One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region are wondering to what extent the US will continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say.
In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows.
But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to import Russian diesel, a move to lower domestic fuel prices before the congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump waived all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan.
India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia.
Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia.
A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip.
Separately, the US has talked to additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that could in theory continue in Samarkand.
More than 200 business executives will accompany Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.
The trip to Uzbekistan was largely organized by Sergio Gor, the US ambassador to India, the Central Asian diplomat said. Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan and is a friend of Rubio, also serves as the US special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs.
After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago.
The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday. REUTERS

Istanbul demolishes streambed buildings after deadly floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:01:00 UTC
14:01:00 KST

AA Photo
As rescue teams continue searching for missing residents following severe flooding, Istanbul officials have begun tearing down streambed structures in Ayazağa and preparing a broader urban renewal plan to prevent future flood disasters.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gül said the demolition of 16 shops in Ayazağa Square, a sports field, stadium stands, a Quran school and adjoining residential quarters would be completed by Oct. 18. The structures obstruct a 1,700-meter stretch of the stream where rehabilitation work is planned.
Officials say clearing the area is necessary to allow the Istanbul Water and Sewerage Administration to carry out stream rehabilitation.
Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum identified the covered stream and unplanned urban development as major factors behind the flooding in Ayazağa. Following an inspection of the affected area, he said the Ayazağa and Cendere streams would undergo rehabilitation, alongside a wider urban transformation initiative coordinated by the Urban Transformation Directorate.
The proposed project aims to create a more resilient neighborhood with buildings designed to withstand earthquakes and climate-related disasters. Residents will be offered options including the “Half Is on Us” urban renewal campaign, which provides financial support for rebuilding eligible homes, or redevelopment through the state-run Housing Development Administration (TOKİ).
Kurum said an urban transformation office would be established in the neighborhood to collect residents’ requests and coordinate the process.
Trade Minister Ömer Bolat said 80 million Turkish liras ($1.6 million) in cash support would be provided to flood-hit tradespeople. Gül said more than 5,000 people had received emergency payments of 10,000 liras each, with separate compensation for damaged belongings scheduled to begin on Oct. 19.
The measures follow torrential rainfall on Oct. 14 that set an 84-year precipitation record in Istanbul, killing 5 people, inundating roads, underpasses, homes and businesses and sweeping away vehicles. Water levels in parts of Ayazağa reportedly reached 2.5 meters, while around 300 businesses in the neighborhood were rendered unusable. One fatality was also reported in Kocaeli, bringing the death toll from floods to 6.
Gül said three people remained missing in connection with the flooding, including two Turkish nationals and a Turkmenistan citizen.
Elsewhere, heavy rain overnight caused the Göçbeyli stream to overflow in Pendik, on Istanbul’s Asian side, sweeping a car carrying three people into the water. One passenger escaped and was taken to hospital, while search teams continued looking for the other two.
Flooding also affected Ağva, where the Yeşilçay stream overflowed, inundating homes, businesses, roads and farmland. In Pendik, residents of an apartment building were evacuated as a precaution after nearby ground subsidence.
Schools closed from Oct. 15 were expected to reopen on Oct. 19. Kurum announced orange weather alerts for 10 provinces and yellow alerts for 26 others for Oct. 18, as authorities continued responding to the aftermath of the flooding.

Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:58 UTC
14:00:58 KST

Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers
Furniture brand Karimoku New Standard has announced the global release of its KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which repurposes upcycled foam from unused ASICS trainers as cushioning for two seating designs.
The KNS x ASICS Collaboration uses deadstock and sample footwear from ASICS that would have otherwise been discarded.
Karimoku New Standard, a sub-brand of Japanese manufacturer Karimoku, used the same technique that ASICS has utilised for its upcycled Neocurve trainers to create the material for the collaboration.
The ASICS footwear is dismantled, sorted and crushed to extract Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) foam, a flexible, light material commonly used as cushioning for midsoles, outsoles and footbeds.
After the foam has been extracted, it is blended with cotton and paired with a three-millimetre condensed foam sheet to create a hybrid structure, according to Karimoku New Standard.
The material is then used as cushioning in the brand's Castor Lobby Sofa and Polar Lounge Chair, which also feature an embroidered tag as a symbol of the collaboration.
The KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which was introduced in Japan earlier this year before the recent global launch, came about after Karimoku New Standard was working on seating for the meeting spaces in ASICS' Tokyo office.
"Through rigorous sessions with ASICS – leveraging their expertise in sports science – and a meticulous adjustment process for real-world office use, Karimoku repeatedly prototyped to transform an unfamiliar material like shoe waste into true furniture comfort," Karimoku New Standard said.
"This uncompromising, hands-on exploration led to the creation of the innovative hybrid structure," the brand continued.
"Beyond merely reusing materials from a sustainability standpoint, it turns them into a functional added value."
Karimoku has previously collaborated with brands including Zaha Hadid Design.
ASICS recently released the "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers with fashion brand Issey Miyake and has also designed pastel-coloured trainers with Danish brand Hay.
The images are courtesy of Karimoku New Standard.

====================================================================================================

Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala.
The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10.
Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died.
By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing.
The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders.
While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war.
The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, has noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.
The recent loss of life, he suggests, has been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.
The profile of vessels being attacked – that is, ships trading with Ukraine – had not changed, he added. “The Russian intent is clear, which is to degrade the export of Ukrainian grain and agricultural products.”
The result has been a precipitous fall in the number of vessels visiting Ukraine. Insurance rates have soared, and seafarers and operators have become increasingly reluctant to operate in the Black Sea basin, even on ships unconnected with Ukrainian cargoes.
The vast majority of the more than 60 fatalities of seafarers in the Black Sea since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 have occurred in the past year. In September the Joint War Committee, representing the London insurance market, moved to extend the high-risk areas of the Black Sea to include the whole of the basin, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia.
The threat is not confined to the Black Sea itself. Attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have also increased sharply in the past year.
A number of factors are driving the expansion and escalation of the conflict towards the shores of Nato countries, say experts. Russia has responded to a geographical expansion of Ukrainian strikes on its shadow fleet of oil tankers by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian agricultural cargoes – a key component of Kyiv’s economy.
As ships sought safer passage further from the coastlines, so the threat has changed: from naval mines to drones, with ever longer ranges.
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said after the sinking of the Alfa Watan: “Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea.”
In a statement at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, Col Joby Rimmer, a senior British military adviser, said: “Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN convention on the law of the sea.
“Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.”
Operators have warned of the wider impact on trade in the Black Sea, including from Bulgarian ports. In a recent interview on Bulgarian television, the shipping agency owner Todor Georgiev warned the Black Sea was in danger of becoming a “dead zone”.
“Whenever the Russians are caught having struck a ship with one of their drones, they claim the vessel was carrying weapons,” he said. “Weapons are not being transported to Ukraine via the Black Sea.”
Rumen Radev, Bulgaria’s prime minister, has described the attacks in the vicinity of his country’s territorial waters as “absolutely unacceptable”.
Bulgarian officials are calling for the EU and Nato to support the efforts to enhance security, while working with Turkey and Romania on increased regional security.
Although they have refused to attribute blame to Russia, officials have said there is “no logic” for Ukraine to attack its own shipments.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side,” said Radev. “However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
As Russian strikes on shipping move ever closer to the borders of Nato members, they pose mounting security challenges to the mutual defence organisation, which is already confronting Moscow’s growing hybrid warfare across Europe. There is speculation that the affected Nato countries may be forced to invoke article 4 of the organisation’s treaty, a step below the article 5 invocation of mutual self defence.
Triggered twice already around the Ukraine war – in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and by Poland in 2025 after Russian drones violated Warsaw’s airspace – it calls for formal crisis discussions on a security threat.
On Thursday Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, met Radev and Nicușor Dan, Romania’s president, to discuss security in the Black Sea. Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Another consequence of the escalating attacks is the renewed danger of a global food crisis. Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.
“We’re looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery,” said Oana Toiu, the Romanian foreign minister, at a security conference in Warsaw last week. “It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence.”
Damien Chevallier, the director of maritime safety at the UN’s International Maritime Organization, warned last month of the long-term impact on shipping caused by attacks linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
“With rising casualties across the Black Sea, Red Sea and strait of Hormuz, being a seafarer has become a genuinely dangerous profession,” he said. “Seafarers are not trained to deal with threats from actions which are linked to wider security issues or geopolitical situations.
“What makes this moment genuinely unprecedented is not just the number of incidents, but the pattern behind them. Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage.”

‘There’s a lot of racism, a lot of hatred’: Far right gains predicted as Israel heads to the polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

Four decades ago, when the extremist rabbi Meir Kahane won a single seat in Israel’s Knesset, other legislators passed a law to prevent him running again, left the chamber when he rose to speak and worked together to block discussion of his ethnonationalist proposals.
These ranged from mass expulsions of Palestinians to apartheid provisions such as segregated beaches and the criminalisation of sex between Jews and gentiles.
This month, Kahane’s political heirs may claim more Knesset seats in national elections than the remains of the once mighty Labor party, home of Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres and Golda Meir.
At an election rally this week, Israel’s national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, mixed calls for ethnic cleansing and jokes about starving Palestinian prisoners with a proud anecdote about his conviction in 1998 over bumper stickers that read “Rabbi Kahane was right”.
A poll for the Israel Hayom newspaper, published on Friday, forecast his Jewish Strength party would win nine seats in the 27 October election. The Democrats, successor to the Labor party led by former general Yair Golan, were predicted to claim eight seats.
Ben-Gvir’s rise is one of the more extreme manifestations of a broad shift to the right among Jewish citizens of Israel. It is particularly pronounced among the young and will shape the country’s next government, regardless of who becomes prime minister after closely fought elections.
More than 500,000 Israelis have reached voting age since the last election in 2022, and three-quarters of first-time Jewish voters define themselves as right or centre-right, a recent poll for Channel 12 television found (it did not survey Palestinian citizens of Israel).
The generation voting for the first time came of age after the Oslo process collapsed, when the prospect of negotiating a political resolution to the Israel-Palestine conflict seemed to be fading.
They were teenagers during the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians. Militants took 251 living hostages and dead bodies to Gaza, leading to a two-year hostage crisis.
“There’s a lot of people, especially young people, who think that there is no solving the conflict, that we’ll always be at war. There’s a lot of racism, a lot of hatred, but most of all, there’s fear,” said Erez Uzan, vice-chair of the Young Democrats.
Bucking global trends, young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations and are likely to vote in a new Knesset with more rightwing members than the current chamber, said Dahlia Scheindlin, a political analyst and public opinion researcher.
Consistently rightwing ultra-Orthodox and nationalist religious communities make up a growing proportion of Israel’s Jewish population but still account for only around a quarter of the electorate, so demographics alone do not explain the growing age gap on political issues.
“All Israelis, and particularly younger people, have been living in a political environment where not only is the government rightwing but the general terms of debate are really populist and ultra-nationalist. That’s all they know. They’re socialised into it,” Scheindlin said.
“There’s been a real downplaying of anything to do with democracy, universal values or human rights. Those are seen as weak, if they’re discussed at all, possibly as bad as betrayal. And very few politicians talk about peace, concessions, negotiations, Palestinian self-determination, or even Palestinian wellbeing.”
A consistent majority of Israeli polls show prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc with the ultra-Orthodox and the far right will fall well below the threshold of 61 seats needed to form a government.
The opposition has a clear path to power through an alliance with parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, known as Arab parties inside the country. But the political shift right means most of the Jewish-led parties have ruled out such a coalition, although similar promises have been broken after past elections.
Particularly when it comes to Palestine, most offer little challenge to Netanyahu’s claim that security can only be pursued through military domination and annexation of territory from Gaza to Syria and Lebanon.
The peace deals that secured Israel’s borders with Jordan and Egypt, once seen as no less an existential threat than Iran is today, do not feature in political debate as an alternative path.
Their campaigns focus on other issues, from promises to tackle corruption and bring accountability for the 7 October attacks to improving schools and stopping ultra-Orthodox draft dodging.
The man leading the field to replace Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot, is a former head of the Israeli military who formulated the notorious Dahiya doctrine of using “disproportionate force” to cause damage and destruction.
Naftali Bennett is a former prime minister and former chair of the settler council, who supports annexing much of the West Bank. Avigdor Lieberman wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and replace it with an Israeli-Jordanian confederation (though apparently he did not consult the Jordanians about this plan).
No Jewish-led party backed a future Palestinian state and only the Democrats opposed settlement expansion, the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper reported, after seeking all parties’ positions on the future of the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party pledged to strengthen and expand settlements, which are legal under Israeli law. All settlements are illegal under international law.
The Democrats, the only remaining political home for Israel’s Zionist left, are led by Golan, a former general and deputy head of Israel’s military who personally rushed to border communities under the Hamas attack on the morning of 7 October to rescue civilians.
Golan rejects a two-state solution and is campaigning on a policy platform that would be solidly centrist in much of Europe. Yet even so, Israel’s political shift to the right is so pronounced that the party’s campaigners have been repeatedly attacked – physically and verbally – as a radical fringe.
Last week, rightwing thugs assaulted Democrats volunteers manning a stand at Jerusalem’s historic Mahane Yehuda market, kicking, hitting and spitting at the group and stealing a phone while police stood by and watched.
The scale of abuse prompted the party to train campaigners in non-violent direct action, “so they know how to handle themselves in a situation where they can keep safe and de-escalate,” said Uzan of the Young Democrats.
The far right is on the rise globally, but Israeli politics that “revolve round constant conflict” heighten the appeal of ethnonationalist messages, Uzan said.
“We grow up in fear, seeing war all around us – and that leads to a certain perspective. In the last 20 years, our leadership in the centre-left camp has avoided talking about security issues,” Uzan said, adding they had ceded that ground to the right.
Now he and fellow campaigners are trying to tackle that failure at a grassroots level, including speaking to young people about the peace agreements with Egypt and Jordan that were unpopular when signed but have brought lasting stability.
The process is slow but effective, he says, pointing to an active young membership several thousand strong, well above parties who attract more young voters.
Comedian turned activist Lior Schleien has been trying to have similar conversations with groups of young Israelis about the deadly futility of pursuing “total victory” in endless wars. He posts footage of some of the most shocking exchanges, featuring smiling teens advocating on camera for the mass killing or expulsion of Palestinians.
“Lots of Arabs live here. They were born here, they are citizens like you and me. What will you do with them?” Schleien asks one group.
“Kill them … give me a knife and I’ll murder them,” says one young man.
Ben-Gvir is particularly adept on social media, where posts like a recent AI video laying out plans for ethnic cleansing have helped build more engagement with young voters than any Israeli politician except Netanyahu.
But he is not an outlier for extremism among allies of the prime minister. Finance minister Bezalel Smotrich is a messianic settler who recently called to “wipe out Gaza”, and has vowed to “bury” a future Palestinian state.
For this election, Smotrich has joined forces with Moshe Feiglin, a fundamentalist who has long called for the mass expulsion of Palestinians and the construction of a biblical Jewish temple where the al-Aqsa mosque compound now stands.
The rise of the far right and religious fundamentalism, combined with Netanyahu’s assault on institutions protecting Israel’s partial democracy (Palestinians living under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of citizens), mean many Israelis on the centre and left see this vote as existential.
David Harel, the president of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, says the country’s current path leads towards a bleak future as a corrupt, impoverished pariah state, dominated by messianic fundamentalists maintaining a “violent, cruel occupation”.
“We are already in ‘stoppage time’. If we lose this time, there will be no second chance. The country we love so dearly will breathe its last. Plain and simple!” he told a rally in the northern city of Haifa.
“That is why I have come here today, to ask and to implore. And if necessary, I will get down on my knees and beg. Please, please, please! Just go out and vote!”

Buvette, London WC2: ‘It’s actually rather lovely’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

A faux-French, cult-hit New York brasserie has opened in Neal’s Yard, deep in the hairy armpit of Covent Garden among alleyways where holistic therapy rooms, walk-in back rub spaces, Neal’s Yard Remedies and 26 Grains cafe are its immediate neighbours. The windchimes and the whiff of patchouli part the air round these parts, and the footfall is yoga pant-clad and hungry for hummus. Buvette, meanwhile, has brought a touch of Gallic glam to the neighbourhood, and is clearly aimed at the Emily in Paris generation with its totalement français menu featuring croque monsieur with roast mushrooms and gruyere, rillettes de saumon or salade niçoise with haricots verts and a mollet egg; there’s also a Macvin champagne and muscadet spritz, pastis on the rocks, warm scones with jam, and almond croissants.
This is the London arm of Jody Williams’ West Village gastrothèque, and its menu is a pretty card listing 25 dishes to choose from, none of them above £18. It clearly thinks it’s a hot, fresh, new thing, but I’m not sure it’s anything new at all. We used to call places that looked like this Café Rouge: that is, recognisably French, and by that I mean recognisable if you have a working GCSE knowledge of La Rochelle cafe life. It’s that version of French dining that won’t scare the horses, or at least the horses that the French haven’t minced coarsely and served in their own gastroduodenal canals with an exemplary homemade moutarde.
Buvette’s cute red frontage gives way to something heartstoppingly pretty inside: marble-topped tables, bentwood chairs, a zinc bar, good-looking, chipper staff – though, let’s be honest, that latter chipper bit would never happen in a lunchtime Paris tourist spot. It’s all very charming and ought to be packed, but on this midweek lunchtime there are plenty of seats to spare in this 80-cover space. In fact, almost all of them are empty. This is Buvette’s second attempt at cracking London – the first, in Notting Hill in 2020, came and went within four years.
As I peruse the gorgeous little cut-card menu, 12 northern ladies with pull-along suitcases sit down at the next table, read it, confer briefly and leave sharpish. Mais pourquoi, Julie? This is a quick café au lait and a freshly squeezed orange juice joint (though they’ve missed a trick not serving Orangina), or a longer saumon grillé with betteraves (beetroot salad) on the side and a mousse au chocolat for pudding kind of place. Nobody is being asked to sit a GCSE French oral exam, which is a blessing, because the memory of being dragged into a room in Carlisle in 1991 and being expected to discuss Scottish devolution in French still wakes me at night.
And maybe that’s Buvette’s problem. It’s so coy and cool that it scares away the normals, but it’s not cool enough to ensnare foodies who’d rather be chucking money at Fergus Henderson’s wine bar just across the way; the local yoga brigade, meanwhile, would rather be queuing outside a clandestine juice shack to hand over £28 for juiced turnip and echinacea. Even so, and to make a plaintive case for Buvette, it’s actually rather lovely.
 
We order the croque madame, which is a classic construction: thick, white toasted bread, melted cheese, all draped in thin ham, snowed over with more grated cheese, topped with a vivid egg yolk and garnished with a flourish of tiny, crunchy cornichons. It is a noble and considered attempt. That grilled salmon comes dressed in sauce ravigote, a sharp, herby, caper-spiked vinaigrette, and with dressed green beans and a petite salade verte alongside. The skin is crisped correctly and the fish moist, and it’s clearly been cooked as if someone downstairs truly cares. We share a copper pan filled with pommes frites and pick at a meaty, sharply dressed salade de poulet. As for those betteraves, these chunky, sweet, glossy roast beets with horseradish creme fraiche are the kind of thing you don’t get as a side any more, and you find yourself wondering why not.
The set lunch menu at £23 is ridiculous value: salmon, green beans and green salad, or burger, fries and salad, or a croque and two salads, all with a coffee to finish. And this in Covent Garden, where you usually have to sell a kidney to afford a crepe. Buvette isn’t reinventing the wheel, but it’s somewhere to pop in for lunch and end up lingering over pots of fresh mint tea and a rather incongruous offering of warm scones with raspberry jam and cream, or almond croissants hot from the oven. Cafe Rouge lasted for years because it wasn’t terribly French, or terribly hot, but it was fantastically useful. Perhaps Buvette needs to reposition itself as a pit stop rather than an Instagram backdrop. Then more people might want to mange tout.
- Buvette 2 Neal’s Yard, London WC2, 020-3540 4989. Open all week, lunch 11.30am-4pm, dinner 4-9pm (10pm Thurs-Sat). From about £40 head à la carte; formule set lunch (main, two sides and coffee) £23, all plus drinks & service

Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.
In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.
This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.
Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.
But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.
Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.
Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.
It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.
In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.
There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.
Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.
The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.
For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.
The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.
Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.
Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.
The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.
Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.
And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.
Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.
- Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer
