‘Mr Fix-It’: How Romas Šležas helped bring America’s civil rights history to the screen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Romas Šležas, a Lithuanian-born documentary filmmaker who helped capture the early American environmental movement and later contributed to an award-winning series on the civil rights struggle, believed in exposing injustice wherever he found it.
During the 1960s, when environmental activism was still taking shape in the United States, Šležas and his filmmaking partner Holly Fisher produced three films examining the tension between economic development, traditional ways of life and the natural world. One premiered at a prestigious National Geographic Society event in Washington.
Šležas, who died in 2019, later joined Blackside Inc., one of the pioneering minority-owned film production companies in the United States. There, he helped shape Eyes on the Prize, a documentary series about the American civil rights movement that won Emmy, Peabody and other awards.
His career reflected a lifelong commitment to truth and fairness, said his wife, Birutė Vaičjurgis-Šležas, a translator who lives in Boston and regularly visits Lithuania, and Fisher, his former filmmaking partner.
“Romas was fundamentally searching for truth and justice,” Vaičjurgis-Šležas told LRT RADIO. “I think that is reflected in his films: both those about environmental protection and his later work about Black people experiencing social injustice. It simply reflected his values.”
Fighting to save a Florida river
Born in Klaipėda in 1938, Šležas fled with his parents to Germany during World War Two, living in refugee camps before the family moved to Boston in 1949. He remained in the city until his death.
He initially studied history at Tufts University near Boston. A film course he took toward the end of his studies changed the direction of his career. In 1965, he earned a master’s degree in film arts from Boston University and began working at a local public television station.
Through his cousin Marytė Kavaliauskaitė, he met Fisher, whom he taught filmmaking. The pair established the Fisher-Šležas film company and went on to make three films together.
Their first, Progress, Pork-Barrel and Pheasant Feather, was released in 1966 and took aim at a proposed barge canal across northern Florida. The project, revived after being abandoned as economically unfeasible following World War Two, was intended to connect the Gulf of Mexico with the Atlantic Ocean, shortening the route for oil shipments by about 600 miles.
But the canal would also have dammed and effectively destroyed the Ocklawaha River, one of Florida’s last natural rivers and a habitat for alligators, birds and other wildlife.
Local residents organised against the plan, seeking not only to preserve the river but also to challenge the political favouritism and corruption they believed lay behind the project.
The film’s title refers to “pork-barrel politics”, a term for politicians exchanging support for spending on projects in their respective districts.
“In Congress, it is customary to help one another: If your colleague from Florida wants funding for a local project, you support it, hoping that when you want something for your own constituents, they will support you,” Vaičjurgis-Šležas explained. “One hand washes the other.”
The filmmakers portrayed a state senator promoting the canal while presenting himself as a lover of nature.
“What we depicted in this film is still happening. Nothing has changed, only the projects are bigger,” Fisher said.
Environmental activism was still relatively new in the 1960s, she recalled. In one scene, a woman uses a roll of wallpaper to collect signatures against the canal, an illustration of how grassroots political campaigning was developing.
“We really wanted to make people angry,” Fisher said, describing the film as the most overtly political of the three she made with Šležas.
The filmmakers faced threats from people who supported the canal. On one occasion, they were left waiting in Florida’s alligator-filled wetlands for a local contact who had agreed to collect them at the end of the day. As darkness fell, they feared they had been deliberately abandoned to intimidate them.
The film also faced obstacles to distribution. According to Fisher, the pair struggled to find audiences and suitable venues for screenings. A politician featured in the documentary reportedly helped prevent it from being shown at Florida’s state universities after his daughter watched it and told him about its contents.
Despite its limited reach, the project attracted considerable criticism, and the canal was never built.
Recording a vanishing way of life
Two years later, Fisher and Šležas released Watermen, a documentary funded by the National Geographic Society. Its premiere took place at a society event in Constitution Hall in Washington, which can accommodate 3,700 people.
The film followed one of the last captains of a sailing fishing vessel and his crew on Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary on the US East Coast.
Rather than approaching the fishermen simply as workers, the filmmakers examined their lives and beliefs from an anthropological perspective. The documentary also captured a conflict over plans to introduce artificial oyster farming, which threatened to displace traditional fishing practices.
The fishermen, Fisher recalled, often spoke about their religious faith. They believed God had created oysters and that harvesting them for a living was therefore justified. Oyster farms, in their view, would interfere with that natural order.
The farms were eventually established.
“I think we captured the end of that belief system,” Fisher said. The film recorded a period when traditional livelihoods and religious convictions were coming under pressure from rapid modernisation.
The filmmakers’ environmental concerns were shared by a growing number of Americans. Vaičjurgis-Šležas said her husband, like many people of his generation, had been influenced by Rachel Carson’s 1962 book Silent Spring, which exposed the environmental damage caused by pesticides and helped inspire the modern environmental movement.
By the early 1970s, mass protests against pollution had helped build momentum for major environmental reforms, including the Clean Water Act, the Clean Air Act and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency. Lithuanian-American Valdas Adamkus, who later became president of Lithuania, worked for more than 20 years at the agency in senior positions.
The duo's third film, “Psssht,” released in 1968, took a more humorous approach. The short fiction film followed a couple who relied heavily on aerosol sprays around the house. Its closing line delivered the punchline: “A couple that sprays together stays together.” Šležas himself appeared as an intruder who is sprayed with a canister.
It was their final film together. Fisher, inspired by the experimental filmmaking of Lithuanian-born artist Jonas Mekas, turned toward avant-garde cinema. Šležas became increasingly interested in racial issues and joined Blackside Inc.
“We thought our films were not an effective way to protect the environment. Romas became interested in questions of race. I started becoming interested in structural problems,” Fisher said.
The man who could fix anything
At Blackside, Šležas became vice president and worked with the company’s chairman, Henry Hampton, helping turn ambitious ideas into finished films.
His technical expertise earned him the nickname Mr Fix-It.
One of his most significant contributions came on Eyes on the Prize, the acclaimed documentary series examining the history of the US civil rights movement from 1954 to 1965 in its first season, followed by a second season covering 1965 to 1985.
The first version of the series’ pilot had failed to attract television networks. Šležas and his colleagues reworked it, adding new material and changing its structure. The revised film received a much stronger response, Vaičjurgis-Šležas said.
The series, broadcast from 1987 to 1990, won major awards, including Emmys and Peabodys, and continues to be used for educational purposes.
Šležas also remained active in the Lithuanian-American community. During the 1970s, he spent five years producing an English-language radio program about Lithuania with his wife and friend Perkūnas Krukonis. Called Garso bangos, or Sound Waves, it aired on Boston public radio.

Deaths, injuries after fire at Alberta military base: Canada minister

‘Serious incident’ at Canada military base causes deaths, injuries
Defence Minister David McGuinty says people were killed and injured after an incident caused a major fire in Alberta.
A major fire at a military base in the province of Alberta has caused several casualties, Canada’s defence minister said.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night on Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright, one of the busiest military training bases, and into the surrounding rural area.
“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” Minister of National Defence David McGuinty said.
“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said, adding that the situation was “very, very active and delicate”.
The Canadian broadcaster Global News said at least seven people were killed and dozens were injured, citing unnamed military sources.
Global News reported that a gas line or a gas well was hit during a live-fire training, causing an explosion that sparked the blaze.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said a “serious incident” had caused the fire, writing on social media: “Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected.”
A doctor at a hospital in Edmonton, 180km (112 miles) northwest of the base, told Canada’s national broadcaster that the casualties were being taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base were “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.
“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News.
“It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15-to-25-year disaster.”
The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire crossed the base’s fence and spread rapidly in high winds.
Canadian armed forces and federal, provincial and local authorities are coordinating the emergency response, McGuinty said.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the fire “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.
Opposition Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre said he spoke to Carney and McGuinty to offer support. “Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” he wrote on social media, urging people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire comes two days before Albertans vote on whether the province, home to about five million people, should begin the legal process towards a binding referendum on seceding from Canada.
Carney used his Thanksgiving message last week to call for national unity.

UK police rule out probe into Palestine Action post by PM adviser’s wife

UK police rule out probe into Palestine Action post by PM adviser’s wife
Officers determine post by Sarah Helm, seen to endorse Palestine Action, does ‘not meet the criminal threshold’.
Police in the United Kingdom have determined that a social media post by the wife of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s national security adviser that appears to endorse Palestine Action, a group proscribed in the country as a “terrorist” organisation, does not merit a criminal investigation.
A Metropolitan Police spokesperson on Saturday said that officers looked at Sarah Helm’s post and ruled that it “did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.”
The police had said on Friday that Helm’s post was “being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.
Helm, an author and journalist who is married to National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, wrote on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”
Helm made the comment after publisher Faber said this week that its Irish author Sally Rooney could not sell her books in the UK, after she announced her plans to use the royalties to support Palestine Action.
“Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher,” Faber said in a statement on its website.
“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format,” the British publisher said, adding that it would continue to sell her work in other countries and regions.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism, a British NGO, had responded on X that Helm’s post was “gobsmacking” and “clearly, the police need to investigate and Ms Helm must face the full force of the law”.
After being asked for comment on Friday, a government spokesperson said Helm’s comments did “not represent the government in any capacity”.
Palestine Action has been proscribed as a “terrorist” organisation since a July 2025 vote by UK lawmakers.
Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested in the UK for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since it was banned last year, many of them for holding up placards.
Palestine Action challenged the government’s decision to ban the group, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that the proscription was lawful.

Ministers protest sweeping defense cuts as coalition funds remain untouched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:44:04 UTC
13:44:04 KST

Just four days after the Israeli government approved the allocation of 1 billion shekels to the Defense Ministry for the purchase of Apache attack helicopters, another major budget cut is on the agenda. The government is expected to approve an additional 2.6 billion shekels in cuts on Sunday to finance what officials describe as "urgent defense procurement," with civilian ministries again bearing the burden while funds earmarked under coalition agreements remain untouched.
Unlike the previous cut, which drew the entire 1 billion shekels from a multiyear development budget for Israel's Arab communities to purchase 12 Apache helicopters, the new measure will impose across-the-board reductions on government ministries. In both cases, not a single shekel will be taken from coalition funds, the allocations earmarked for projects and priorities agreed upon by the governing parties.
The latest cuts will amount to approximately 5% of each ministry's development and procurement budget. As a result, just nine days before Israel's October 27 election, the government is preparing to approve substantial reductions in funding for major civilian ministries already struggling with budget constraints.
The Education Ministry will lose 285 million shekels, the National Security Ministry 225 million shekels, the Health Ministry 150 million shekels and the Welfare Ministry 140 million shekels. The proposed reductions come despite a recommendation from senior Finance Ministry professionals to draw the money required for urgent defense procurement from coalition funds instead. That recommendation was rejected, and the proposed decision would leave those allocations entirely intact.
The additional reductions will affect approximately 4% of ministries' flexible budgets, meaning funds not already committed to employee salaries or other binding government obligations. In practice, this means that future programs and planned initiatives will be among the main casualties.
Following angry objections from ministers over the planned cuts to their departments, senior Finance Ministry officials said Saturday evening: "Several government ministries asked to avoid cuts to budget items they considered urgent. The government therefore decided on an equal, across-the-board reduction for all ministries. We have already warned that enormous budget increases for the defense establishment would come at the expense of citizens, and that is exactly what is happening."
Education Ministry: 285 million shekel cut
The Education Ministry has been instructed to cut 285 million shekels from its overall budget of approximately 97 billion shekels.
About 90% of that budget is allocated to teaching hours in kindergartens and schools, effectively covering salaries for teachers and kindergarten staff. Those funds will not be affected. The ministry's management has therefore been asked to examine other areas where reductions could be made and submit recommendations to Education Minister Yoav Kisch.
The options under consideration involve spending items over which the ministry has greater flexibility, particularly supplementary programs whose funding is determined annually rather than guaranteed in the permanent budget. These include informal education activities such as youth movements, external educational programs, teacher training in schools, professional training at ministry headquarters, funding for nonprofit organizations and joint educational initiatives with local authorities. Streamlining operations at the ministry's headquarters is also being considered.
The Education Ministry said it was "examining the options and will present them to the minister for consideration regarding implementation."
Health Ministry: 150 million shekel cut
Health officials have expressed serious concern about the proposed reduction and its potential consequences for an already strained healthcare system.
In a strongly worded letter to Finance Ministry Director General Israel Malachi and budget commissioner Maharan Frozenfar, Health Ministry Director General Moshe Bar Siman Tov called for the healthcare system to be exempted from the cuts.
Bar Siman Tov warned that the additional across-the-board reduction would bring cumulative cuts to the healthcare system's budgets since the beginning of the year to approximately 600 million shekels and would "inevitably cause severe harm to public healthcare services."
Israel's healthcare system has faced successive crises in recent years, beginning with the COVID-19 pandemic and continuing through three years of war. During that period, hospitals and healthcare providers have faced unprecedented pressure, including treating large numbers of wounded patients and responding to a significant increase in demand for mental health services. These challenges have been compounded by persistent staffing shortages and other operational difficulties.
Officials warn that another cut could further reduce access to healthcare services for Israelis, some of whom already face limited availability and lengthy waiting times. Mental health services could also be affected, along with the ministry's ability to recruit additional healthcare professionals.
The cuts could also undermine emergency preparedness, efforts to protect hospitals against attacks and the healthcare system's preparations for the needs of an aging population.
"In 2026 alone, approximately 20% of the ministry's current operating budget, amounting to some 500 million shekels, has already been cut, in addition to numerous reductions since the beginning of the war that have directly and severely harmed the healthcare services that should be provided to the public," Bar Siman Tov wrote in the letter, copies of which were also sent to Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Health Minister Haim Katz.
He also criticized the government's broader budget policy.
"The notion that security needs can continue to be financed through the systematic and relentless erosion of Israel's civilian systems and public services, by imposing indiscriminate across-the-board cuts, fails to take account of all the components of national resilience," he wrote.
"Israel's resilience does not rest on military strength alone, but also on the ability of all its civilian systems to function, provide support and serve citizens in routine times and during emergencies."
Welfare Ministry: 140 million shekel cut
The Welfare Ministry faces a reduction of 140 million shekels, raising concerns about the impact on services for survivors of domestic violence, people with disabilities and women involved in prostitution. Hundreds of millions of shekels have already been cut from the ministry's budget, leaving it struggling to address needs arising from the war.
The ministry has submitted an urgent request to the Finance Ministry seeking an exemption from the planned across-the-board reductions.
A senior Welfare Ministry official warned that the proposed cut could directly affect essential social services.
"This would deal a devastating blow to the ministry's ability to provide services to the most vulnerable populations in Israel," the official said.
Among the initiatives at risk are new facilities for women affected by domestic violence, planned services for women involved in prostitution and programs intended for people with disabilities as part of the implementation of Israel's Welfare Services for People with Disabilities Law.
The ministry was already subjected to a 3% reduction in its flexible budget in March to finance war-related expenses, amounting to approximately 90 million shekels. That was part of a series of across-the-board cuts that have totaled around 450 million shekels in the ministry's 2026 budget.
Even before the latest reductions, the ministry had limited room to maneuver in developing new programs. Of the approximately 1 billion shekels originally allocated for new services, nearly half was earmarked for expanding services for people with disabilities, an obligation established under legislation passed by the Knesset in 2022.
The successive cuts now threaten to bring the ministry's ability to develop new services to an almost complete standstill, even as demand continues to grow because of the war and broader social needs.
National Security Ministry: 225 million shekel cut
The National Security Ministry, which oversees the Israel Police and other law enforcement and security agencies, faces a reduction of 225 million shekels. However, a ministry official said the cuts were not expected to affect the operational budgets of the bodies under its authority.
According to the official, the reduction would be taken from an emergency reserve held by the ministry rather than from funds allocated to the agencies' routine operations.
The official emphasized that the measure was not expected to affect operational capabilities, day-to-day activities or the ability of the organizations to continue carrying out their duties.

‘It’s family’: Lebanese villagers dread looming UN peacekeeper pull-out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:40:00 UTC
13:40:00 KST

‘It’s family’: Lebanese villagers dread looming UN peacekeeper pull-out
IBL AL-SAQI, Lebanon – From his shop in south Lebanon near the Israeli border, Mark Diab says life in his village will be turned upside down when a decades-long United Nations peacekeeping force pulls out in 2027.
“UNIFIL isn’t just business. To us, it’s family,” said Diab, 59, whose sister is among residents of Ibl al-Saqi who have married peacekeepers from the UN Interim Force in Lebanon over the years. She now lives in Spain.
“We’re basically open because of the UN. We started when I was young,” Diab said from his shop, just down the road from a UNIFIL base, selling clothes along with other items including alcohol and headphones.
The force’s withdrawal will hurt the local economy and “will impact our relationships... and we’ll lose security and stability”, he said, as the sound of an explosion rang out in the distance.
“I’m very sad they’re leaving... We’ve spent a lifetime with them.”
UNIFIL has served as a buffer since Israel first invaded Lebanon in 1978.
It has become part of the fabric of south Lebanese villages like Ibl al-Saqi after decades spent monitoring border hostilities and supporting local communities, including with humanitarian assistance.
But after pressure from Washington, the UN Security Council in 2025 voted to end the force’s mandate on Dec 31, 2026.
In a narrow garden in Ibl al-Saqi called Norway Square, tattered Norwegian and Lebanese flags flew near plaques paying tribute to peacekeepers from the Scandinavian country whose arrival decades ago forged ties that run deep.
A street sign points to a town in Norway about 5,200km away.
Nearby, an Indian flag flew at Mahatma Gandhi Park close to a statue, posters and plaques set up by Indian peacekeepers.
‘Positive mark’
Ibl al-Saqi is located just outside an Israeli-declared “security zone”, which runs around 10km deep in Lebanese territory along the border. It was established after the latest war between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah group erupted in 2026.
Israeli troops operate nearby, and locals advised AFP journalists to avoid southern parts of the otherwise quiet, peaceful village, nestled among hills covered in olive groves.
From his municipal office near framed UNIFIL pictures and paraphernalia, mayor George Rahhal said the peacekeepers had brought stability and reassurance to villagers over years of conflict and uncertainty.
“They’ve left a positive mark on everybody’s hearts, first through security, then the economy, healthcare, supporting schools, the sick,” said Rahhal, who like others in the village also has Norwegian citizenship and speaks the language.
“At some point, the UN has to leave... but not in these circumstances.”
Lebanon has called for UNIFIL’s mandate to be extended, fearing a security vacuum at a time when hostilities prevent the Lebanese army, whose resources are limited, from deploying across the country’s south.
Rahhal said many Ibl al-Saqi residents were UNIFIL employees or contractors.
Almost “the entire community will be impacted” economically by the withdrawal, directly or indirectly, he said.
“We can live after the international force (leaves), but how and where and who will be responsible for us?”
UNIFIL now counts about 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.
Spokesperson Kandice Ardiel told AFP it also “has around 400 national staff” and works with numerous local companies providing contracted services.
‘Stayed in our village’
Peacekeepers are stationed in many Israeli-occupied areas now off-limits to most Lebanese after the most recent war. Many border villages have seen heavy destruction.
More than 4,300 people have been killed in Lebanon since March, including seven peacekeepers caught in the crossfire.
Israel still carries out strikes and demolitions despite a lull in hostilities since late June.
Andrea Tenenti, who served as UNIFIL spokesperson for almost 20 years, told AFP that the force’s presence “was not simply about maintaining peace and security”.
UNIFIL “has long been the second-largest employer and economic contributor in southern Lebanon, after the Lebanese state”, he said.
“Its economic footprint, however, extended far beyond its direct workforce,” he added, with associated activities “supporting a much wider network of businesses and livelihoods”.
Its withdrawal “risks creating a significant vacuum... at a particularly critical time”.
At a workshop in Ibl al-Saqi, labourers supervised clattering embroidery machines sewing customised items including banners and tags for peacekeepers stationed nearby.
Shelves were packed with colourful souvenirs and keepsakes for UNIFIL personnel – the business’s main market after Lebanon’s economy collapsed in 2019.
Co-owner Khaled Nahra, 48, said the workshop had been running for some 25 years and had around a dozen employees, but would be forced to close when UNIFIL leaves.
“We’ve stayed in our village... this was the best thing about working with the UN,” he said.
“There are people who’ve been working here for 15... 20 years. They’re like me. They don’t know what to do.” AFP

AI cuts job demand in exposed occupations by nearly 10% across Asia: IMF report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:37:27 UTC
13:37:27 KST

As Job Placements Near, India Inc Taps Old IITs for AI Roles
NEW DELHI: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping labour demand across Asia, with employer demand falling by nearly 10% in occupations more exposed to the technology since the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, according to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) October 2026 Regional Economic Outlook: Asia and Pacific.The report, based on approximately 40 million online job postings across 19 Asian economies, highlights the challenges facing countries such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines as they seek to create productive jobs for growing working-age populations while AI transforms the sectors expected to absorb new workers.However, the decline in demand for workers in AI-exposed occupations appears to have stabilised, suggesting that the technology’s impact on employment is not limited to job displacement.AI creates demand for new skillsThe IMF report points to the emergence of new employment opportunities requiring specialised AI skills, including prompt engineering, retrieval-augmented generation and AI agent development.Employers are increasingly seeking workers who can integrate AI into business processes, improve productivity and translate technological capabilities into practical applications.
Firm-level adoption of AI, however, remains uneven. Around 6% of firms in Asia explicitly seek AI skills in their job postings, the report said.Businesses adopting AI are experiencing stronger labour demand growth than those that have not adopted the technology, including in occupations highly exposed to automation. This suggests that AI can complement human capabilities even as it reduces demand for certain tasks.India faces jobs and skills challengeThe implications of AI differ across Asian economies. Emerging economies such as India may initially be less exposed to the technology because a large share of their workforce remains employed in agriculture and other sectors less affected by AI.However, this could pose a longer-term challenge if AI makes it harder for workers to transition into higher-productivity manufacturing and services, the report said.For countries with expanding working-age populations, the challenge is to generate enough productive employment while ensuring that workers have the skills required by an increasingly technology-driven economy.Education, reskilling key to managing AI disruption
The report emphasises that the response to AI must go beyond encouraging technological adoption. Education reform, reskilling programmes, digital infrastructure and stronger labour-market institutions will be essential to prepare workers for changing occupational demands.Businesses will also need to invest in workforce development alongside AI adoption to help employees adapt to new roles and changing skill requirements.The report suggests that AI need not become a barrier to inclusive growth. With timely investments in skills and preparedness, Asian economies could use the technology to boost productivity, encourage innovation and support sustainable employment.

Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

Marco Rubio says Trump's Russian oil sanctions waiver is a '60-day pause,' denies restricting Starlink access
Speaking with reporters on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio detailed U.S. President Donald Trump waiving sanctions on the sale of Russian oil and addressed issues surrounding Ukraine's access to Starlink services.
When asked to respond to criticisms of Trump waiving sanctions that restrict the sale of Russian oil, Rubio said the waiver was a temporary measure to study the policy's impact on the global economy.
"I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," said Rubio.
Noting high energy prices around the world as a result of the U.S's war with Iran and the global need for oil, Rubio said that "we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is."
The Secretary's comments come following widespread outcries that Trump's move will create a windfall for Moscow, helping it continue attacking and killing Ukrainians.
"Unfortunately, I don't think this is a way to stop (Russian President Vladimir) Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy that he has such support," President Volodymyr Zelensky said about Trump's actions amid a falling out between the two leaders.
Rubio also addressed rumors that the U.S. had a role in limiting Ukrainian access to vital Starlink systems.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," Rubio said.
Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink, a satellite internet network operated by SpaceX, for battlefield communications and drone operations, including its campaign against Russian forces and logistics, and interceptor drones used against Russian long-range attack drones.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starlink systems on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky claimed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
Multiple media reports have alleged that the issues with Starlink stem from U.S. leadership.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, the Telegraph reported on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
Conflicting reports about the reason for the cutoff — and who was responsible — have left Ukraine with questions even after Starlink service stabilized on the front lines.
"I don’t know what their theory is, but nothing to do with the White House," said Rubio. "I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false."
When asked to respond to Zelensky's comments, Rubio pushed back.
"I don’t know what Zelenskyy said," said Rubio. "I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that."

Around 550,000 join protests across France, nearly 400 arrested
Nearly 550,000 people joined protests across France on Saturday, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, as demonstrations over rising living costs and public policy issues led to widespread disruptions and clashes with police, Qazinform News Agency cites Xinhua.

French President Emmanuel Macron denounced the violence, saying those responsible for acts of destruction, attacks on public institutions and looting would face prosecution and punishment.
Macron also expressed support for law enforcement officers, pledging to stand against those seeking to undermine public order while emphasizing citizens' right to express their grievances peacefully.
At least eight education staff members were injured in France on Monday amid high school student protests, as school closures declined but violence intensified, the Education Ministry said.

Tunisia’s economic crisis deepens as the promise of a better life fades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:14:42 UTC
13:14:42 KST

Tunisia’s economic crisis deepens as the promise of a better life fades
Joblessness, failing services and rising costs deepen hardship across the country.
Tunis, Tunisia – Like many Tunisian university graduates, Cherine Ghanmi believed a degree would offer her family a way out of poverty.
Growing up in the marginalised town of al-Mazzunah, in the central Sidi Bou Zid governorate, Ghanmi had walked 5km (3.1 miles) to the school her parents struggled to put her through. They hoped she would eventually find a job and support them financially, easing their burden after years of sacrifice.
But more than a decade after graduating in 2012, she remains unemployed. Instead of supporting her parents, she says, she continues to rely on them.
“We studied and graduated believing we had finally found a way out of poverty,” she said. “We thought that once we found jobs, we could make up for all that hardship, repay our parents for their sacrifices and make them happy.”
“Unfortunately, reality was a big shock for us,” she added. “Instead of helping them, we have burdened them even more.”
For Ghanmi and thousands of other unemployed university graduates, the struggle to find work has become a symbol of Tunisia’s wider economic crisis, marked by limited opportunities, mounting financial pressure and growing frustration with successive governments.
The ‘Dignity March’
On September 27, unemployed university graduates began a roughly 300km (186-mile) march from Menzel Bouzaiane in central Tunisia towards the capital, Tunis, to demand jobs and the implementation of legislation intended to provide a clear path to public-sector employment.
Known as the “Dignity March”, it began with 23 participants, according to organisers. More graduates joined along the route, with the coordinating committee later estimating that the number had grown to more than 120.
The journey was physically demanding. Participants paused at points because of exhaustion and injuries before continuing towards the capital.
On October 6, police blocked the group from moving forward in the town of Borj Cedria, south of Tunis. Participants said they were told they could travel individually, but not as a group. The marchers had hoped to reach the Tunis suburb of Carthage, where the presidential palace is located, to press their demands.
For Ghanmi, “the Dignity March was not just a march”, she said, describing it as an expression of the hardship and disappointment experienced by graduates who had spent years searching for work.
Many protesters say they have waited years for promises of public-sector recruitment to translate into real opportunities.
Their demands came amid broader discontent over Tunisia’s economic and political direction.
On October 17, thousands gathered in Tunis to protest against President Kais Saied’s government, deteriorating living conditions and restrictions on freedoms. The demonstration, led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), opposition groups and civil society organisations, was among the largest against Saied in years.
Participants voiced frustration over unemployment and the difficulties many households face in meeting their basic needs.
Saied, who has concentrated power since 2021, has presented his political project as a response to corruption and the failures of the established political class. Critics say the concentration of power has weakened democratic checks and balances while doing little to resolve the country’s economic problems.
Stalled promises
The unemployment figures reflect the scale of the challenge. According to Tunisia’s National Institute of Statistics (INS), the overall unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Among university graduates, it was 26.6 percent. The rate for women graduates was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent for men. Among those aged 15 to 24, unemployment reached 35.4 percent.
“Almost all the governments that succeeded one another after the [2011] revolution did not make the economic situation, development and the treatment of social issues real priorities,” Cherif Khraifi, spokesperson for the Tunisian Union of Higher Education Graduates, told Al Jazeera.
“Their biggest concern was ensuring they stayed in power.”
Attempts to address graduate unemployment have repeatedly raised expectations. The 2022 Law No. 38 intended to establish an employment pathway for long-term unemployed university graduates, but the law’s implementation stalled amid financial constraints.
Khraifi said measures intended to address the crisis have too often served as “tools for letting off steam” rather than resolving the problem.
The 2025 Law No. 18 provides for the exceptional recruitment of long-term unemployed university graduates into the public sector and civil service. It calls for a digital platform to register eligible applicants and sets out criteria for prioritising candidates. Recruitment is to take place in phases over no more than three years from the law’s publication.
The law was dated 22 December 2025 and published in Tunisia’s Official Gazette on 23 December 2025, when it entered into force. Article 6 provides for recruitment in phases over a period not exceeding three years from the date of publication.
The graduates taking part in the Dignity March have demanded a clear process for implementing the law, including practical arrangements and a timetable for recruitment. For people who have already spent years out of work, another promise offers little reassurance without concrete steps towards employment.
Ghanmi is also sceptical of Saied’s community-based companies programme, which aims to promote local development and employment through projects established by people in their communities.
“The authorities insist on promoting community companies as a solution for jobs and development, yet none of these companies managed to do that,” she said.
Public-sector recruitment alone cannot resolve a problem of this scale, Khraifi argued. Tunisia also needs investment and businesses capable of expanding and hiring. In disadvantaged regions, where employment is scarce and access to capital is limited, starting a business can be difficult.
For graduates such as Ghanmi, the central question is whether government policies will translate into actual jobs.
An economy struggling to create opportunities
Anis Ben Said, a tax adviser and university professor, said Tunisia’s “problem is not a lack of skills, but the economy’s inability to turn skills into production, investment and job opportunities”.
Weak investment has constrained the creation of businesses and jobs, he told Al Jazeera. Poor infrastructure and unreliable public services also make it harder for businesses to operate, particularly in regions already struggling to attract investment.
According to the INS, Tunisia’s economy grew by 2.7 percent in 2025 and by 2.4 percent in the first half of 2026. In September, the World Bank projected growth of 2.3 percent for the full year.
But economic growth does not necessarily create enough jobs for those who need them. For unemployed graduates, the figures offer little reassurance unless growth translates into accessible employment opportunities.
“The financial crisis explains part of the problem, but it does not justify all of it,” Ben Said said.
He pointed to shortcomings in investment and the management and maintenance of public infrastructure as barriers to economic activity.
“Infrastructure investment is not just a public expense, it is a productive economic investment,” he said
This summer, extreme heat coincided with electricity cuts and water shortages in several parts of Tunisia. Disruptions to these basic services affected businesses and added to public frustration.
The Reuters news agency reported that recurring power and water cuts were among the grievances raised at the October 17 demonstration.
For small businesses, interruptions to basic services can mean lost customers and income. Where jobs are already scarce, such disruptions make earning a living even harder.
In L’Aouina, a northern suburb of Tunis, 20-year-old barber Khalil said he was waiting for an opportunity to leave the country by boat.
“There’s nothing worth staying for in this country. Dying at sea would be a relief,” he said.
“I’m going to leave as soon as I can, and let them figure out the solutions on their own. Our generation has borne the brunt of all these crises, and nothing is left for us.”
Others struggle to keep their business afloat.
Khalil’s neighbour, a grocery shop owner who asked not to be named, said persistent problems with the water supply had become exhausting.
“I think the only solution is for someone to take over this shop. I cannot keep up with these crises any more,” he said.
For Ghanmi, the years without work have brought more than financial hardship.
“The wound on the body heals, but the wound in the mind and heart does not heal,” she said. “It really does not heal.”

Feature: As tigers return, technology protects wildlife and people who share their habitat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:13:49 CST
13:13:49 KST

CHANGCHUN/HARBIN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A tigress moved through the forest, followed by five cubs, their small bodies weaving through the undergrowth.
This rare scene was captured by an infrared camera in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park (NCTLNP) late last year. It was the first recorded footage in China of a wild Siberian tiger accompanied by an unusually large litter of five cubs, offering a glimpse into the recovery of these endangered big cats.
Transmitted to the park's monitoring center in real time, the footage became part of a growing body of data that helps conservation workers identify individual animals and track their movements without having to follow them deep into the forest.
Latest monitoring shows that three of the tigress's five cubs have already left their mother's side, while the other two are still with her.
Siberian tigers, also known as Amur tigers, along with Amur leopards, are flagship species for biodiversity conservation and important indicators of a healthy ecosystem. Following a pilot phase launched in 2017, the NCTLNP was officially established in 2021 as one of the first five national parks in China.
Leveraging new technology, this park has built an integrated monitoring system that combines satellite remote sensing, ground-based infrared cameras and aerial surveillance involving drones, covering most of its 14,100-square-kilometer area across Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces in China's northeast.
A major challenge in building such a system is network coverage. The park has established 95 wireless communication base stations and deployed around 30,000 cameras, according to Sun Pengyu, the person responsible for the forestry and grassland sector at Jishi Media, the main constructor of the system.
Wireless data transmission covers more than 80 percent of the park area, allowing footage to reach the park administration within roughly a minute of being captured, Sun said.
Empowered by artificial intelligence, the system can identify more than 30 wildlife species and make preliminary identifications of individual tigers and leopards based on their distinctive coat patterns, said Chen Xiaocai, head of the park administration's comprehensive office.
Researchers then cross-check the initial identifications against other biological features, including facial contours, to verify each animal's identity and build individual profiles for further research and conservation work, Chen added.
The park has also restored forest habitats and improved ecological connectivity. Along the China-Russia border, more than 290 sections of fencing in areas frequented by tigers and leopards have been removed, helping reopen cross-border routes for wildlife.
The latest monitoring data show that the number of wild Siberian tigers in the park has risen from 27 in 2017 to 72, while the wild Amur leopard population has grown from 42 to 115. Sightings of other wildlife, including deer and roe deer, offer further indications of an ecosystem supporting the return of its top predators.
For Li Gang, deputy head of Chaoyanggou forest farm in Dongning, Heilongjiang Province, the changes brought by technology are tangible.
Li has worked at the forest farm, also a core conservation area, since 2009. In the early years, maintaining infrared cameras meant trekking into the mountains to replace batteries and retrieve memory cards.
This process not only delayed access to information but also exposed staff to risks posed by rugged terrain and encounters with large predators.
"On one occasion, I walked 17 kilometers carrying about 200 batteries and spare cameras," he recalled.
Now, cameras equipped with wireless transmission can send images and video directly to a central platform. Satellite imagery helps workers assess habitat conditions across large areas, while drones can inspect remote terrain, check for suspected forest fires and investigate possible illegal activities.
Li has also seen changes in the wildlife around him. "Sika deer were scarce in the area when I began working here, but during a recent outing, I saw more than 100," Li said.
As tigers and leopards reclaim more territory, protecting them also means keeping people safe. In parts of the national park, villages and wildlife habitats overlap, making early warnings an important part of conservation.
Cameras near settlements can detect tigers, leopards, bears and wild boars entering designated risk areas. Alerts are then sent to patrol teams and nearby residents, giving people time to avoid potentially dangerous encounters.
In Dongning, information can also be shared via local chat groups, allowing rangers to warn residents when a tiger is spotted.
For Li and his colleagues, such technology does not replace fieldwork for rangers, but it helps make patrols more targeted, reducing unnecessary journeys into sensitive habitats.
"We want to give people and wildlife room to live without disturbing one another, for the benefit of both," Li said. ■

World Insights: LatAm journalists explore drivers of China's NEV industry
China

2026-10-18
12:13:44 CST

by Xinhua writers He Yixuan, Xi Yue, Zhao Yanchao
CHANGZHOU, China, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Cameras clicking and smartphones raised, a group of Latin American journalists moved through the production workshops of a Chinese new energy vehicle (NEV) maker in Changzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, capturing robots at work and vehicles taking shape on the assembly line.
For some, the scene offered a glimpse into the technology behind Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) they had already seen on the streets back home. Thousands of kilometers away, Chinese-made EVs are becoming part of everyday life in Latin America, while charging facilities and power transmission projects are opening up new avenues for green cooperation.
During the 2026 Belt and Road Journalists Forum, dozens of journalists from Latin American countries visited Changzhou, known as China's "capital of new energy," to explore the industrial strengths behind China's green development and discover opportunities for cooperation with Latin America.
FROM FACTORY FLOORS TO EVERYDAY MOBILITY
For Rody Olivera, president of the Uruguayan Press Association, the visit was more than a tour of a manufacturing facility. Having purchased a Chinese NEV in May, he was eager to see how it was made. Inside the welding workshop at Li Auto's manufacturing base in Changzhou, he said the visit had confirmed that he had "made the right decision."
"The factory is impressive in terms of its size and productivity. Electric vehicles offer many advantages, as they provide a quieter driving experience, numerous driver-assistance features and greater comfort," Olivera said.
In his view, China's progress in the sector stems from both policy support and industrial capabilities. "China is a pioneer in this technology," he said, attributing the country's achievements to its innovation capabilities and the development of a complete industrial chain.
At the exhibition hall of Segway-Ninebot, a renowned electric two-wheeler maker, Angel Sanchez, president of the Federation of Journalists of Peru, recognized the company's electric scooters, saying they could offer a convenient transportation option for young people and office workers in Peru.
"They have many advantages, including quick responsiveness, flexible center-of-gravity control and a portable design," Sanchez said, adding that China's development of new energy and other emerging technologies ultimately aims to improve people's lives.
Such products offer a glimpse into the broader industrial ecosystem that has taken shape in Changzhou. Its industrial chain spans five areas: energy generation, storage, transmission, consumption and distribution networks. In 2025, the scale of the city's new energy industry exceeded 1 trillion yuan (about 150 billion U.S. dollars).
CONNECTING INDUSTRIAL STRENGTHS WITH LOCAL NEEDS
The city's industrial strengths extend from NEVs and key components to charging infrastructure and power transmission equipment, creating opportunities for cooperation across different stages of the energy transition.
At the exhibition area of charging infrastructure operator Star Charge, Virgilio Arias, president of Mexico's Front Page Club, stopped in front of a photograph showing an electric-bus charging station in Mexico City.
"I've just learned that this Chinese company has provided charging facilities for three Bus Rapid Transit lines in Mexico City and Monterrey, supporting the operation of more than 150 electric buses," Arias said.
The example highlighted how Chinese technologies are being applied to local transportation systems in Latin America. As Mexico and other countries in the region accelerate their energy transitions, cooperation in charging infrastructure and electric mobility could help address practical needs while advancing shared sustainable development goals, Arias said.
Green cooperation also extends beyond transportation to the infrastructure needed to transmit clean energy over long distances.
For Samira de Castro, president of the National Federation of Journalists of Brazil, a visit to NR Electric brought an unexpected connection to a project she had covered years earlier.
In 2012, she wrote a report on Brazil's Belo Monte hydropower project. During her visit in Changzhou, she learned that the company's technology had been used in the project's second-phase ultra-high-voltage transmission system.
Now operational, the transmission project helps deliver hydropower from northern Brazil to distant consumption centers, including areas serving Rio de Janeiro. Castro said the advanced technology had made a significant contribution to Brazil's electricity supply and changed the lives of local residents.
TURNING SHARED GOALS INTO GREEN COOPERATION
"There is an ecosystem of companies here that are collaborating to advance clean energy. Renewable energy is the future, and it is happening right here, right now," said Geraldo Cantarino, a member of the Brazilian Press Association, during his first visit to China.
For Latin American countries with diverse energy resources and growing demand for cleaner development, cooperation with China could create further opportunities in equipment manufacturing, infrastructure construction and the application of new energy technologies.
For the journalists visiting Changzhou, the trip offered a closer look at the industrial capabilities underpinning China's new energy development and their potential relevance to Latin America. From EVs and smart mobility products to charging networks and power transmission systems, the examples they encountered demonstrated how green cooperation can take shape across an interconnected industrial chain.
As the visit drew to a close, the journalists took away more than photographs of production lines, electric scooters and power transmission equipment. They had also gained a firsthand understanding of how technologies developed in a Chinese industrial hub could connect with the green development ambitions of countries across Latin America.
For Castro, the next step was to share these observations with a wider audience.
"As a journalist, I hope to tell more people the stories of China-Latin America cooperation in the new energy sector, so that the world can see China's commitment to high-quality development, openness and cooperation," she said. ■

Exclusive: Documents Show How Israel Steered Qatari Payments to Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:01:09 UTC
13:01:09 KST

As Israeli voters prepare for elections on Oct. 27, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tried to defend and distance himself from one of his government’s most controversial policies: allowing Qatar to funnel nearly $2 billion into the Hamas-controlled Gaza Strip for more than a decade. Previously undisclosed documents obtained by TIME, including letters from senior Israeli security officials to Qatari leaders, reveal that Israel encouraged and played a direct role in a payment program that was more extensive than Netanyahu has publicly acknowledged.
Beginning in 2012, Netanyahu’s government helped to facilitate Qatari payments to Gaza that had begun after Hamas seized control in 2007. By 2018, Qatar had sent roughly $1.1 billion into the Strip, according to an analysis provided to Israeli ministers, the Israeli daily Haaretz reported, with the funding designated for humanitarian assistance, fuel, and government salaries. That year, after Israeli officials castigated Qatar for allegedly financing Hamas, the Qataris began demanding formal documentation of an arrangement the two governments had agreed was meant to provide relief to citizens of the beleaguered enclave.
The extent of Israel’s cooperation with the payments was reflected in a 2020 letter from Yossi Cohen, then director of the Mossad, Israel’s intelligence agency, to Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. “It is indeed a great opportunity to express our gratitude and appreciation for the humanitarian aid efforts that the State of Qatar has provided the last few years to the Gaza Strip,” Cohen wrote. “Undoubtedly, these humanitarian efforts have played a crucial role in improving the humanitarian situation within the Gaza Strip, and ensuring stability and safety in the region.”
The payment arrangement had the support of successive Israeli governments, the Palestinians, the Trump and Biden Administrations, the United Nations, and European powers, according to officials who served in both the Trump and Biden Administrations. The flow of money from Qatar into Gaza has taken on new significance since October 7, 2023, when Hamas terrorists stormed southern Israel, murdered some 1,200 people, and took 251 more hostage. The worst security failure in the country’s history raised troubling questions about whether the financial lifeline helped to sustain Hamas’s grip on power and, in turn, enabled it to carry out the assault.
Since then, Qatar has been frustrated by allegations leveled by Israeli political leaders that its payments to Gaza had helped finance the deadliest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust. “All of Qatar’s financial assistance in Gaza has been directed to Palestinian citizens through mechanisms coordinated with the Israeli authorities and international partners. Under previous aid mechanisms, all financial assistance, as well as goods such as food, medicine and fuel, passed through Israel before entering Gaza,” a spokesperson for Qatar’s International Media Office tells TIME. “Nothing was delivered directly by Qatar; we provided the aid, while delivery was carried out by the United Nations’ organizations in coordination with the Israeli authorities. If any funding reached Hamas, as alleged by individuals and groups with political agendas against Qatar, the responsibility lies with Israel, which oversaw the delivery and created the mechanism.”
Critics have long argued that Netanyahu sought to sustain Hamas rule in Gaza to keep the Palestinians divided between the Islamist terror group and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, foreclosing the prospect of a unified Palestinian leadership capable of negotiating a two-state solution. Netanyahu’s wager, according to these critics, was that the aid would give Hamas something to lose and would therefore help contain the group while Israel pursued normalization with the Arab world without resolving the Palestinian question. Instead, as Israel moved closer to a historic agreement with Saudi Arabia, Hamas launched an assault that upended the region, plunging it into war.
The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment for this story.
The documents now give Israelis a fuller accounting of a policy that preceded the catastrophe, as they prepare to render a verdict on the man who presided over both. “It was a policy failure on our part born of good intentions that multiple prime ministers kept going,” says one former Israeli defense official. “But Netanyahu was unquestionably at the center of it. He was the one who championed and accelerated the program, his government was in charge of the way it was run, and now we know as a society that we can never afford to make a mistake like that again.”
Ehud Olmert was still prime minister when Qatar began sending money to Gaza in 2007, after Hamas won control of the coastal enclave. At the outset, the Israeli government was not directly involved in the transfers. That changed under Netanyahu. By 2012, his government had approved a system that gave Israel a direct role in facilitating Qatari assistance: delivering food and medical supplies, determining which Palestinian families qualified for financial aid and disbursing the funds, and enabling Qatari financing to expand Gaza’s electricity supply, according to Israeli and Arab officials, as well as official documents obtained by TIME.
At first, the arrangement was informal. Qatar supplied the money with Israel’s approval, even as Israeli officials publicly criticized Doha for financing Hamas, according to sources familiar with the negotiations. The contradiction aggravated the Qataris, a senior official in the first Trump Administration tells TIME: Israeli officials would denounce the payments in public, then privately ask Doha to renew them.
Qatar, a gas-rich monarchy in the Persian Gulf, is accustomed to walking a fine line. It plays host to both the U.S. Central Command and to senior Hamas officials. The country set up a Hamas political office in Doha at the request of the U.S. in 2011. In contrast to other Gulf monarchies, especially Saudi Arabia, Qatar sees no threat in the Muslim Brotherhood, the political movement that spawned Hamas. After Oct. 7, Qatar's government emerged as the go-between in negotiations among Israel, Hamas and Washington, where Biden Administration officials privately praised the Qataris as honest brokers.
By 2018, Qatar sought written documentation of the Israeli government’s role in the aid agreement. It was subsequently formalized through a trilateral mechanism involving Qatar, Israel, and the United Nations, designed to administer the aid with international and Israeli oversight. On October 2, 2018, Israel and Qatar, together with the United Nations, signed an agreement to finance fuel deliveries into Gaza.
A spokesperson for the United Nations declined to comment for this story but referred TIME to statements the body’s special coordinator for Middle East peace, Tor Wennesland, made in 2021 acknowledging the arrangement. “These efforts are vital to improving the dire socioeconomic and humanitarian situation in Gaza,” he said at a UN Security Council briefing.
In August 2021, Qatar signed another agreement committing $40 million to a cash assistance program that would give nearly 100,000 Palestinian households $100 per month for four months. The arrangements were subsequently extended. American officials were brought into the discussions as well. According to a diplomat briefed on the process, who asked for anonymity to divulge details because they were not authorized to comment publicly, Qatar wanted Washington to understand precisely how the system worked, fearing that Israeli officials might later accuse Doha of financing Hamas without acknowledging Israel’s own role. “The Israelis kept insisting on doing it this way, so that they can control what goes in and out,” the official told TIME, rather than establish “something more regular and something which goes directly to the people.”
Under the system, according to U.S. and Israeli officials, Qatar paid for fuel and electricity purchased from Israel to increase the number of hours Gaza received power, a structure coordinated with Israeli security services. It transferred money through the United Nations for projects in the Strip. And it provided monthly $100 payments to some of Gaza’s poorest families. According to diplomats familiar with the system, Israel vetted the recipients and oversaw the distribution mechanism, with funds transferred through the World Food Programme and eligible families notified by text message before collecting their assistance at designated locations. “If the money ever got in the wrong hands, it was because of the Israelis,” the diplomat said, “because they were the ones overseeing the whole thing.”
Netanyahu’s government was so committed to the policy that when Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas cut payments to government workers in Gaza in 2018, Israeli security officials shuttled Qatari cash into the Strip in suitcases, U.S. and Israeli media reported at the time. Naftali Bennett, then Netanyahu’s education minister, publicly opposed the transfers, denouncing them as “protection money.” Netanyahu briefly suspended the payments in January 2019 amid renewed violence along the Gaza border, using the prospect of their resumption as leverage to pressure Hamas to stop firing rockets.
But while critics on the Israeli right railed against the deal, Netanyahu’s deputies worked behind the scenes to preserve it, according to correspondence obtained by TIME. In July 2019, according to one letter, Qatar notified the Netanyahu government that it was transferring $6 million to 20,000 beneficiaries in Gaza, with each receiving $300. It is unknown how many of those beneficiaries, chosen by Israel, were connected to Hamas or had family members who belonged to the group. Over the last two decades, Hamas has been deeply embedded in Gaza, operating not only as an armed militant organization but also as a political movement and governing authority, employing civil servants responsible for the territory’s public services and infrastructure.
In 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic swept through Gaza, R. L. Maoz, a member of Netanyahu’s National Security Council, urged Qatari officials to maintain the payments despite the Israeli government’s public criticism. “We reiterate the importance of continuing to transfer the Qatari humanitarian financial assistance through the existing mechanism,” Maoz wrote. “We ask that Qatar’s financial assistance not be transferred through mediators or countries other than the ambassador, Mohammed Al-Emadi,” he added, referring to the chairman of the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza. “We greatly appreciate your cooperation and open discourse to safeguard stability and security in the region and to bring our countries and peoples closer together.”
The program survived Netanyahu’s departure from power. His successor, Bennett, had been among its fiercest critics, raising the prospect that the arrangement might finally end. At that point, Qatar prepared to halt the program, a former Biden official tells TIME. Instead, after taking office in 2021, Bennett ended only the delivery of cash-filled suitcases, not the broader flow of Qatari assistance to Gaza, the Associated Press reported. According to people familiar with discussions about the policy, Bennett’s prior objections were a message intended for his domestic political constituency. “There’s no issue,” an Israeli representative told a Biden envoy, according to an official present. “We want to continue with it as is.”
To some of the officials involved, the compact contained a fundamental flaw: both the Israeli government and Hamas retained control over aid intended for ordinary Gazans. “Bibi and Hamas hold the tap, essentially,” one of the officials told me. Hamas could restrict the system to exert pressure internally, the official said, while Netanyahu could restrict it to pressure Hamas. “We knew this was not something that was beneficial for the long term. We need to have something that’s sustainable, that empowers the civilians.”
By 2023, with tensions mounting between Israel and Hamas, Qatari officials pressed for a different model, one that would deliver assistance to Gazans without making civilians dependent on either Hamas or the Israeli government. But Netanyahu’s government wanted the existing framework kept intact, according to multiple sources who spoke to TIME, including an Israeli official and an international diplomat.
Two weeks before October 7, Mossad director David Barnea traveled to Doha and asked Qatar to renew the funding, the New York Times reported in 2023. The Qatari officials agreed but warned Barnea that it would be the last renewal. With tensions rising between Israel’s far-right ministers and Hamas, the arrangement had run its course, Qatar believed. Barnea asked for two more months. The rationale, according to the officials familiar with the conversation, was that continuing assistance to Gaza’s civilians gave Hamas something to lose and therefore gave Israel a measure of leverage over the group. After two months, the parties could reassess Hamas’s behavior and devise a more durable mechanism for delivering aid.
They never got the chance. With the brutal Oct. 7 attack on southern Israel, the Qatari aid arrangement that successive Israeli governments had spent years helping to build, modify, and preserve was over.
Ever since, Netanyahu has faced accusations that he deliberately strengthened Hamas to keep the Palestinians divided—between Hamas in Gaza, and the secular Fatah party that under Abbas governs the West Bank—and forestall a peace agreement. Critics point to remarks Netanyahu allegedly made at a 2019 Likud Party meeting. “Anyone who wants to thwart the establishment of a Palestinian state has to support bolstering Hamas and transferring money to Hamas,” he said, according to a report in the Jerusalem Post. “This is part of our strategy—to isolate the Palestinians in Gaza.”
In a 2024 interview with TIME, Netanyahu denied making the statement, insisting that the payments were meant to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe. “The reason that successive governments agreed to that is that we wanted to make sure that Gaza has a functioning civilian administration to avoid humanitarian collapse,” he said. Without the money to maintain sewage systems, water supplies, and schools, he argued, the territory could have descended into chaos and disease. Netanyahu claims that Iran supplied Hamas with weapons through separate channels, including suspected smuggling routes across Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.
Netanyahu’s dealings with Qatar have also become a source of controversy in Israel. Netanyahu has been under intense scrutiny in recent weeks over the so-called Qatargate scandal, in which former and current aides to the Israeli premier allegedly received payments to conduct a public relations campaign to cast Qatar in a favorable light for more than a year after the Oct. 7 onslaught.
Now, as international diplomats contemplate Gaza’s reconstruction, they face a version of the same dilemma: how to provide essential assistance without strengthening Hamas or another militant organization. Trump Administration officials, led by envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are working with Qatar and other Arab governments on a framework that would restore basic services while eliminating Gaza’s dependence on Islamist armed factions. “We want to ensure that the civilians are reliant on themselves and not on anyone else,” an international diplomat tells TIME. “So it’s providing actual opportunities for civilians to make money and be sustainable.”
The question confronting Israel and its international partners is not simply whether money should flow into Gaza, but also who controls it—and whether the next arrangement will avoid the failures of the last.

‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:00:50 UTC
13:00:50 KST

An Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content.
Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online. When she opened the links, she found herself staring at images from one of her first ever press conferences – but the images had been digitally altered to remove her clothing.
It was a shocking twist on a defining moment of her career. “I felt disgusted,” she said. “I remember how nervous I was and how much I had prepared for the press conference. And then to see someone using this image in a way aimed at harming and humiliating me was really hard to grasp.”
Schilling is one of 50 MEPs – 46 of them women – who have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes, according to a report by Agora Digitale Transformation (ADT).
The Berlin-based thinktank, which alerted Schilling to the presence of the images online, said the finding laid bare how deepfake pornography had become a “systemic threat to women in European politics”.
An earlier ADT report found that 138 female parliamentarians from 22 EU countries had been affected, and that women were 33 times more likely than their male colleagues to be depicted in or associated with deepfake pornography.
Schilling described the images as a form of “digital violence against women” piled on top of the already disproportionate amount of sexist abuse, harassment and violence that women in politics faced.
The result was a potent threat to democracy, she said: “These things make going into politics even harder than it is already. Just imagine what would happen to our society if more and more women disappear from public life.”
Schilling said she had spoken to some of the other female MEPs targeted, but they had expressed fears about coming forward. “But there’s nothing to be ashamed of. People misused your photos, you did nothing wrong,” she said. “And I think that’s the moment when you say: ‘OK, this has to stop.’”
The sentiment was captured in a recent letter to the EU initiated by Schilling and the German Green MEP Terry Reintke. Signed by 119 MEPs, it called on officials to ensure that a forthcoming ban on apps and websites that use AI to undress women, scheduled to take effect across the EU on 2 December, would be paired with mechanisms capable of enforcing the prohibition.
“A ban on paper protects no one until it is enforced,” the letter said, pointing to the widespread use of “nudifier” apps in which photos of women can be undressed with just one click.
“Its purpose is humiliation and control over women’s bodies, and its effect is to make public life more hostile for female politicians,” the letter said. “Every young woman considering a political career now must factor in that this could happen to her.”
Schilling said the aim was to push national authorities to close any loopholes or workarounds that would allow the apps to continue to function in the EU. “We were stripped naked without our consent,” she said. “This cannot become the new normal.”
The call for action was why she had decided to speak up, she said, in the hope that sharing her story would convince member states to crack down on tech companies for which this sort of digital violence could be a viable business model.
“It’s quite simple,” she said. “Every woman who wants to run for office should be able to do so without being afraid of being undressed against her will.”
