Why is Hong Kong hosting the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting? There is another agenda
Decision for Hong Kong to host this week’s meeting is part of a broader strategy to bolster the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub, experts say
As Hong Kong hosts the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part one, Simpson Cheung and Alfred Lam explore how the event could elevate the city’s status as an international financial centre at a pivotal moment.
Beijing’s decision to have Hong Kong host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting this week is a deliberate move to galvanise the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and showcase it as a safe harbour amid continuing geopolitical tensions, analysts have said.
About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which Hong Kong will host for the first time. It will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.
Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Beijing’s choice of venue showed it deliberately intended to promote Hong Kong’s international status, especially as a financial centre. The event would bolster its standing as an offshore renminbi hub and a wealth management capital, support the city’s economic development and underscore its importance to China’s development, he said.

China's Zhang wins world junior badminton women's singles title
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:57:28 CST
09:57:28 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Yixin came from a game down to defeat Japan's top-seeded Saki Matsumoto and win the women's singles title at the Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Junior Championships in Cairo on Saturday.
Zhang recovered from losing the opening game 9-15 to win the next two 15-10, 15-9 in a hard-fought 47-minute final, securing China's only gold medal in the five individual events.
"I'm extremely happy and excited because this is my first time competing at the World Junior Championships, and I've managed to win the title," Zhang told Xinhua.
"I think getting through this match was indeed very difficult. But I had prepared thoroughly beforehand, and my coach and teammates also gave me a lot of confidence and encouragement," she said.
She approached the final against the top seed as a challenger and remained calm under pressure. "I think it was mainly my mental strength. I had a very strong desire to win this gold medal for the Chinese team," Zhang said.
Matsumoto said she was able to dictate play in the opening game. "But in the second and third games, my opponent started getting used to my shots, and I was the one who made mistakes first. I think that's something I need to work on in the future," she said.
Yin Yiqing of China and Ip Sum Yau of Hong Kong, China shared bronze in women's singles after losing their semifinal matches on Friday.
In the mixed doubles final, Indonesia's Muhammad Luthfi Habibi and Dian Ramadhani Mukti defeated China's Feng Yilang and Li Menghan 17-15, 8-15, 16-14 in a closely contested 50-minute match, leaving the Chinese pair with silver.
Habibi explained that training with senior players had helped refine his playing style, adding that he wants to become a world champion at the senior level and an Olympic champion in the future.
"I think my performance today was fairly good overall, but I didn't make the most of some crucial points toward the end of the match," Li said, adding that Chinese players in all five disciplines had given their all and would continue to improve.
Chinese Taipei's Lee Wei-Ting and Chen Yu-Hsi, along with Indonesia's Raihan Daffa Edsel Pramono and Atresia Naufa Candani, shared the mixed doubles bronze medals.
Indonesia secured its second gold medal in men's singles, where Radithya Bayu Wardhana defeated compatriot Fardhan Rainanda Joe 15-9, 11-15, 15-8 in 47 minutes.
France's Mady Sow and India's Jagsher Singh Khangurra shared bronze in men's singles.
In women's doubles, Malaysia's second-seeded Genevie Lim and Low Zi Yu defeated Japan's Nijika Kamata and Shizuku Kashio 15-7, 9-15, 15-12 in a 41-minute final.
China's Shi Sichen and Xiang Yujin, along with South Korea's Choi Ye-da and Kim Min-chae, took bronze in women's doubles.
In the men's doubles final, Chinese Taipei's top-seeded Chen Ping-Hsuan and Lee Wei-Ting defeated Japan's Mahiro Oku and Masato Yamashiro 15-10, 15-9 in just 23 minutes.
Feng and Wei Jianzhen of China shared bronze in men's doubles with Njoto Michaelangelo and Yu Zhirui Jerry of Hong Kong, China.
Indonesia topped the individual-event gold medal standings with two titles, while China, Malaysia and Chinese Taipei claimed one each. China finished with one gold, one silver and three bronze medals, while Japan collected three silvers.
The individual championships followed the world junior team event, which China won earlier this month. ■

NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The death toll in Saturday's stampede in India's eastern city of Kolkata rose to 19, with 25 injured people receiving treatment in different hospitals and one in a critical condition, confirmed West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Sunday.
Most among the dead were women and children, he said while admitting that there were "some shortcomings" in the arrangements made by the organizers. Kolkata is the capital city of India's eastern state of West Bengal.
The stampede occurred at a religious event, locally called "Durga Puja", amid the ongoing annual festive season in the country. Thousands of people had gathered to take part in the celebrations when the stampede occurred. The mishap was partly blamed on heavy rains.
"This happened partly due to the rains, and there were also some shortcomings in the arrangements made by the event organizers," said the chief minister.
Meanwhile, media reports said that around 10 people, including the organizers and private security personnel, present when the mishap occurred were detained by the Kolkata Police for questioning. "Whoever is found negligent will face legal action," the chief minister said. ■

Crowd, rain or misleading announcement: What led to Kolkata stampede tragedy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
00:51:06 UTC
09:51:06 KST

Several people reportedly fell down a flight of stairs near the exit and were trampled by those behind them
NEW DELHI: A sudden surge of people, heavy rain and alleged confusion over announcements and entry-exit routes are among the factors being investigated after a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in Kolkata killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others on Saturday evening.The incident occurred around 7.15pm on Maha Saptami, when a large crowd waiting on the narrow Radha Madhab Saha Lane to enter the pandal reportedly surged forward as a downpour began. Those already inside were caught in the rush, with people unable to move towards the exit as visitors ahead blocked their way. Several people reportedly fell down a flight of stairs near the exit and were trampled by those behind them.
A misleading announcement by the puja committee is also suspected to have added to the confusion, while the blowing of whistles by private security guards may have triggered a rush among visitors, according to CM Adhikari.
Crowd management and security under scrutiny
Kolkata Police are investigating whether lapses in crowd management, confusion over entry and exit routes, and heavy rain contributed to the tragedy, a senior officer told PTI. Eyewitnesses alleged that announcements about entry, exit and crowd movement were improper, leaving visitors confused during peak hours.Locals also questioned the police deployment at the venue, claiming that personnel were largely stationed near the VIP entrance.
"I have not seen adequate police presence this year. This resulted in the mismanagement," Chorbagan resident Sanghamitra Bhowmik told PTI.Another concern raised by locals was the alleged lack of administrative assistance in taking the injured to hospitals."There must be some lapses, but these should be probed. Whether lapses were on the part of the organisers or they had flouted the rules to erect the pandal will be checked," the police officer told PTI.A forensic team visited the site late on Saturday to collect evidence. Police are questioning the organisers and examining CCTV footage, while also seeking details of the security guards and other personnel deployed to manage the crowd. Officers who were posted at the venue will also be questioned as part of the investigation.
State orders safety review of pandals
Adhikari, who visited the injured at Kolkata Medical College and Hospital, said the incident had raised concerns about safety arrangements at crowded Durga Puja venues. According to hospital sources, 11 injured people were shifted to SSKM Hospital. The deceased included 13 women and a child, a source at the medical college said.The chief minister announced a high-level committee to inspect prominent pandals across West Bengal and review crowd management, exit routes, lighting and structural safety. The panel will be led by Disaster Management Principal Secretary Rajesh Sinha, Fire Services Director General Anuj Sharma and Additional Director General of Police (Law and Order) Javed Shamim.
Adhikari urged organisers to follow official safety recommendations, warning against elaborate themes that compromise visitors' safety. He also called for wider exits, better lighting and the removal of bottlenecks created by temporary rope enclosures. Where complex structures obstruct movement, organisers may be advised to restrict rituals to the inner sanctum and use LED screens outside.The state government has announced Rs 25 lakh in compensation and a Group D government job for the family of each deceased victim. A toll-free helpline, 18003455678, has also been set up to help people seeking information about those affected.

Across the US, ‘No Kings’ events seek to boost early voting for midterms

Unknown Publisher

Across the US, ‘No Kings’ events seek to boost early voting for midterms
WASHINGTON – Carrying an umbrella painted with the words “vote, power, people”, retired teacher Sabine Carlson said the plan for the Oct 17 “No King” marches was clear.
“It’s great to voice your anger and we have long lists of complaints, but the most important thing of all is to go and vote,” said the 66-year-old Democrat from Washington’s suburbs.
At the demonstration near the country’s Capitol, Carlson joined one of the estimated 3,000 events organised by the prominent anti-Trump movement across the US on Oct 17.
Rather than holding massive marches, the latest “No Kings” events varied across the country – with honking convoys, concerts and neighbourhood gatherings.
It was the fourth iteration of the demonstrations since US President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025.
The stated goal of the event was to fire up voters just as Americans begin casting ballots in the midterm elections, where Republicans, who hold the majority in Congress, face fierce opposition.
Democrats are seeking to take control of Congress by campaigning on cost of living issues and an unpopular war in the Middle East.
Focused on early voting ahead of election day on Nov 3, the events ranged from New York, Los Angeles and other blue stronghold cities to small towns across the nation.
“It’s one of the most important votes and it’s really important to make people aware, and make sure they’re registered correctly,” Carlson said. “Don’t go to the wrong polling station.”
‘An act of joy’
Most areas of the US allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.
Alma Couverthie, who oversees grassroots-organising efforts for democracy watchdog Common Cause, said the point of the “No Kings” rallies was “reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service, and an act of joy”.
Trump has openly criticised the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results – especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is likely.
By advocating for voting early, “No Kings” organisers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance.
“The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question,” Couverthie said.
‘We want our country back’
One 52-year-old military veteran who joined the Oct 17 protest did so seeking catharsis from the current state of American politics.
“I am so disillusioned by what I thought I was serving versus what this country has become,” said the Virginia resident, declining to give his name.
“Over the last 18 months – I finally came to this conclusion about six months ago – I’ve been mourning my country.”
Carrying an umbrella with the message “Vote for humanity. End this circus now. We want our country back”, he said he hoped to see “a robust response come Nov 3 from the American people”.
Beyond Washington, like-minded Americans echoed his hopes and fears.
Outside a church in Gastonia, North Carolina, women carried signs that read “Honk for Democracy” and “Make a plan to vote!”
In Portland, Maine, demonstrators bundled up against the autumn chill waved the American flag and carried signs reading “Your Vote is Your Voice” and “No Kings, No Cowards Collins”, in reference to Republican incumbent Senator Susan Collins, who faces a tough re-election race.
In Wilton Manors, Florida, demonstrators were out in the sun, dressed in shorts and sunglasses and carrying signs reading “Enough is enough”.
“Trump is destroying America” and “Democracy not Autocracy” read some signs in Atlanta, Georgia.
A man dressed as Uncle Sam at a protest in Kansas City, Missouri, stood near a sign reading “Uncle Sam Says Make American What Was Promised”.
In Houston, a large crowd marched through city streets carrying a banner that said “Resist All Corruption” and handmade signs reading “War Crimes Don’t Hide Sex Crimes” and “Rein in the Mad King Vote Blue”.
All across California – from San Diego to San Francisco and many points beyond – crowds filled the streets, including in Los Angeles, where protesters marched to city hall carrying signs declaring “No Kings” and at least one that added “No Idiots Either”. AFP

Trump’s Russia sanctions waiver called mistake by Republican Party allies
- Trump’s waiver of the Graham law on Russian diesel has angered Republican allies, who say it helps Putin and weakens sanctions on Moscow.
- Senators led by Ted Cruz and Thom Tillis urged Trump to keep pressure on Russia, saying the deal will not cut US prices much and may fund the war.
- Ukraine and Democrats also opposed the move, while Congress is unlikely to act soon because it is out of session until the midterm elections.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Republican lawmakers blasted Donald Trump for waiving new tariffs and sanctions on Russia, prompting the President to defend himself against members of his own party.
Republican Party critics said Trump’s decision trampled on the will of Congress, which overwhelmingly passed a sanctions law in September championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, and would aide Moscow’s war effort against Ukraine.
Trump issued the waiver shortly after cutting a deal with Russia on diesel exports aimed at lowering high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections, in which the cost of living is voters’ dominant concern.
“It’s a very good decision. And it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country and I think good for the world,” the President told reporters on Oct 17.
The decision by Trump threatens to open up a new rift between the White House and its congressional allies with Republicans in grave danger of losing their majorities in the House and Senate in the Nov 3 elections.
Earlier in the day, Senator Ted Cruz, a Texas Republican closely allied to Trump, said the administration should have found other ways to lower fuel costs, such as importing more from Canada or waiving renewable-fuel requirements.
“I wish the President hadn’t done it. I think it was a mistake,” Cruz said on Fox News, referring to Trump’s executive order late on Oct 16 waiving the Graham law. “The current path, unfortunately, just benefits Putin.”
At least eight Republican senators, along with several of their House counterparts, have spoken out against Trump’s diesel deal with Russia or the sanctions waiver.
“What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisers not understand?” Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican retiring at the end of his term, wrote on Oct 17 in a social media post.
He said Trump could lower energy prices by addressing Iran rather than “doing a solid for Vladimir Putin”.
A bipartisan group of 12 senators sent Trump a letter earlier this week urging him to rescind his diesel deal with Russia and enforce the Graham law.
The Republican signatories included Tillis, Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Susan Collins, Alan Armstrong and Lisa Murkowski.
“Allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans,” the senators wrote in the letter, arguing that the revenue would help finance Russia’s war in Ukraine and deepen Moscow’s cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea.
Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother’s seat and is running for a full term, said she is proud of the Bill named after Lindsey Graham and plans to speak to Trump when he visits South Carolina next week.
“The President and I share the same goal, which is to end the war and get gas and diesel prices down. The sanctions Bill is one of the tolls he can use to do that. It’s up to him whether or not he choses to do so,” she told local reporters on Oct 17.
“Personally, I would keep the pressure on Russia to end the war and get the gas prices down because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
While Ukraine has broad support on Capitol Hill, Congress is out of session through the midterm elections, so there is little prospect of immediate action to block Trump’s diesel deal.
His plan to return Russian diesel to US and global markets is expected to have little immediate effect on prices. A sustained resumption of Russian exports by year-end, however, could help shrink global supply deficits, provided Moscow can meet its commitments despite Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries.
Jeanne Shaheen, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, joined with six other senators earlier in the week on a letter opposing the decision, saying Congress “explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine”.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the US runs directly counter to that law,” Democratic Senators Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden, and Republican Senators Collins, Murkowski, Tillis and John Curtis said in a statement on Oct 18.
House lawmakers are also moving against the deal.
A group of Democrats and one Republican introduced legislation on Oct 16 to block Russian diesel imports, though passage would be difficult in the Republican-controlled Congress and could require overcoming a Trump veto.
Representative Don Bacon, a retiring Nebraska Republican, co-sponsored the Bill.
Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican facing re-election in a contested seat, has separately said he would propose legislation barring purchases of Russian oil.
“Many of us won’t fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator’s invasion and throwing an ally under the bus,” Bacon wrote in a social media post on Oct 17.
French Hill, a Republican lawmaker from Arkansas, said he has requested a classified briefing on the rationale behind the decision, arguing the US should be increasing economic pressure on Russia.
Democrats have almost unanimously opposed Trump’s overtures to Putin. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said in a social media post on Oct 17 that “there’s nothing America First” about the new diesel deal and criticised it for giving the Russian economy “life support” while “Americans need relief from skyrocketing prices”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also criticised the waiver, saying it could mark the beginning of broader sanctions relief for Moscow.
“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law,” Zelensky wrote on Oct 17 in a social media post.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have risen since Trump announced the diesel deal last week.
Ukrainian defence officials said this week that connection speeds on Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service, had been slowed. A US official said on Oct 16 that Trump had not ordered any limits on Ukraine’s access to the satellite technology.
“A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelensky said. BLOOMBERG

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect, will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 17, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” Zelensky wrote on X. “It definitely helps only the Russians.”
An executive order issued by Trump on the night of Oct 16 waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs – including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas – that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law in September.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the US.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming towards Moscow while publicly criticising Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelensky said the latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people,” wrote Zelensky, who said Russia struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites on Oct 16. “This certainly does not stop the war.”
He accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. “Is Russia preparing for this? I think so,” Zelensky wrote.
Russian envoy praises waiver
Russia’s investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, called the Trump waiver “a truly historic moment”, posting on X on Oct 16 that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before US midterm elections in which Trump’s Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely due to the US-Israeli war with Iran, analysts said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation’s primary backer in Congress was the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican. It would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to fill his Senate seat after he died in July, and Trump endorsed her for a full term heading into the midterm elections. At a campaign stop on Oct 17, she did not directly criticise Trump for waiving sanctions, but said she would not have made that choice.
“Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia,” she told reporters, according to multiple news outlets. “Because I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia.”
China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing said it “consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law”, while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. The Oct 16 executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that “further action is appropriate”.
US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
“Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression,” Beyer said in a statement on Oct 16.
Lindsey Graham, who died in July, strongly supported US assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope of continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelensky.
But with Graham gone, the US under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond the Oct 16 waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier in October, the Ukrainian leader predicted.
“I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” wrote Zelensky, who lamented Graham’s absence. “It’s unfortunate because we all had great respect for Lindsey... It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest.” REUTERS

Assistant treasurer knew about ATO's credit card ban plans months ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:58:19 UTC
08:58:19 KST

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino concedes he knew of ATO's credit card ban plans in July
In short:
The assistant treasurer says the government knew in July the tax office was considering a credit card ban following the Reserve Bank's surcharge changes.
Outrage about the change from the business community forced the prime minister to step in.
What's next?
The issue has exposed tensions between the prime minister and the treasurer.
Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino has conceded the government knew the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) was considering banning credit card payments in July, months before the decision was made public.
The ATO's decision in late September to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1 sparked backlash from the business community.
That outrage eventually forced an intervention from the prime minister and the treasurer to underwrite the costs and allow credit cards to be accepted by the tax office until mid-2027.
Mr Mulino today said he and Treasurer Jim Chalmers were first made aware of the ATO's intentions months ago.
"In July, the government became aware that the ATO was looking at options and that at that point their preference was to not accept credit cards," Mr Mulino told ABC's Insiders.
"The indication we gave to the ATO was that they should continue to engage with the credit card companies, and that there should be a transition period."
The admission comes after the Australian Financial Review yesterday revealed the ATO had privately informed the government about its credit card ban and presented the government with options.
The ATO's decision followed changes from the Reserve Bank of Australia to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank has said was "in the public interest" and was costing consumers about $1.6 billion a year.
Mr Mulino was asked why the government did not push for the ATO to continue accepting credit card payments from small businesses back in July.
"So, accepting credit card payments going on indefinitely, would have very serious fiscal ramifications for the budget, and that's why we always said that there should be a transition period,"
he said.
Small businesses were informed of the ATO's decision on September 30, a day before it was made public, and given a two-month grace period.
"But the transition period, as it turned out, from stakeholder feedback, wasn't enough. And so that's where the government stepped in," Mr Mulino said.
He was asked if he had any regrets about not stepping in earlier.
"We've changed our position. So I've listened to stakeholder feedback, as has the PM and the treasurer," he said.
"So, obviously we've changed tack and we've listened to feedback. And that's a sign of a government that is putting in place important big reforms."
Earlier this month, Mr Chalmers said he was informed by the ATO ahead of their decision, but did not give a specific timeline.
"The ATO made this decision late in September, not to accept credit card payments. Obviously, we were aware before then that they were grappling with this issue," he said.
Opposition says
Mr Mulino denied the government had a "hands-off approach", saying they "didn't get into all of the details" but insisted that the ATO should continue to negotiate with credit card companies.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson slammed the government, saying they "had three months to fix this" and "only stepped in when the backlash got too loud to ignore".
"At every point the Albanese government has failed to understand the implementation consequences of their higher taxes," he said.
He questioned Mr Mulino's assertion that the ATO made the call as an independent agency, only for the government to then fund the transition period for credit card payments.
"You can't claim it's somebody else's decision while you're the one paying for it," he said.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) chief executive Andrew McKellar said it was concerning these discussions were happening in July when businesses were only informed the day before it became public.
"Business wasn't made aware until just hours before the surcharge ban took effect in October," he said.
"This looks like a completely deficient policymaking process that took small business for granted."
The ATO initially defended its decision, saying it was not tenable for the agency to absorb the $200 million cost and that it would result in less revenue being collected and therefore less funding for government services.
Taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but that credit card companies did not offer a low enough rate.
Small businesses felt the move was a double standard, since they were expected to wear the costs of the RBA's surcharge changes themselves, and they also feared losing the ability to use credit card payments to the ATO as a tool to manage their cash flow.
Issue hints at leadership tensions
The debacle, and its timeline, has also exposed some tension between the treasurer and prime minister.
Mr Albanese said he intervened after receiving a text from ACCI's Mr McKellar the day before.
"My door is always open. Andrew did text me last Thursday morning, and by Friday morning we had an announcement," he said.
Mr Chalmers denied he was "rolled" and said he and Mr Albanese discussed the issue on the Wednesday prior.
Mr Wilson on Sunday suggested the prime minister "enjoys humiliating his treasurer" and described the relationship as a "psychodrama".
Industry Minister Tim Ayres denied there were underlying frustrations between the pair, and told News24 that Mr Albanese was "a remarkably collegial prime minister".
"This is a cabinet-style government that's working very well, it's very stable," he said.
"It's a real contrast to not just what's happening around the world, but a real contrast to what's happening on the other side of politics, which is a total mess."
Mr Ayres was asked if the government might permanently waive the ATO's credit card decision.
"I don't think that there's any prospect of this issue being managed that way. We've made a big decision to defer this question to allow credit card payments to continue being used," he said.
"There's a significant budget cost to that. It's the right call to make in these circumstances."
Mr McKellar said ACCI wanted a "permanent outcome".
"We think that will most likely involve a long-term solution for credit card payments to continue to be accepted, but let's not pre-empt those discussions," he said.
He said a key question was how that cost would be funded, and added it would be a welcome step if credit card companies lowered their fees.
"We don't want small business to be left carrying the can for this decision," he said.

Since Yemen’s conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh’s airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Oct 17 that it had “intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in Riyadh, the Eastern Province and the South”.
The interceptions came as the President of Egypt, which is a member of the coalition, said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was “harmed or its security and stability threatened”.
“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said. “We are speaking only about defence.”
Though Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has mostly concerned Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen. It and Saudi Arabia are historically close and have strategic economic ties.
Egypt’s Parliament will hold an emergency session on Oct 18 at Sisi’s request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens not to use Saudi airports or not to visit the country altogether.
The Saudi Education Ministry on Oct 17 announced the extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.
Residents of the Saudi capital received a mobile phone alert on Oct 18 warning of a “hostile aerial threat” and to stay away from windows and doors. It was lifted after a few minutes.
‘Political process’
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis’ recent escalation, a charge Tehran denies.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 17 that Tehran supported a “comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve” the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He repeated Iran’s offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh had not responded to Iran’s overture. But Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected Iran’s offer in a statement on X on Oct 17, saying “the Tehran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator”.
The Houthis are part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” against Israel and the US, but both they and Tehran insist the group acts independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily air strikes on the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to roll back gains the group made in a lightning offensive in September.
On Oct 17, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Riyadh had conducted 53 strikes on the Yemen capital Sanaa and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, with “numerous dead and wounded”.
A Houthi-affiliated news agency had earlier accused Saudi warplanes of targeting “civilian residences” in Dhamar and Taiz provinces, killing 12 people and wounding more than 30. It alleged that the strikes were carried out “using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally”. AFP

Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

News analysis
Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
- EU leaders backed new trade defence tools against China, including a possible “killer switch” to impose tariffs or quotas fast. The move follows a trade deficit of more than €360 billion and rising Chinese exports.
- The plan is still vague. There is no legal text, trigger or scope yet, and the European Commission is expected to propose ideas by the end of 2026. Many states may resist giving Brussels such wide powers.
- Support is growing in Brussels as chemicals, machinery and wind turbines face pressure from Chinese imports. The European Parliament called Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”, showing the hardening mood.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – European Union leaders ended their summit in the late hours of Oct 16 with no deal on the Union’s future budget, but with a new and surprisingly strong resolve to adopt new defence tools to tackle a ballooning trade deficit with China.
Heads of state and government of the EU’s 27 member-nations approved a trade deal concluded in Beijing earlier in October, under which China voluntarily agreed to cut by almost half its exports of electric vehicles to Europe.
But the member-states still deemed this Chinese concession insufficient in addressing bigger trade questions, and they authorised the European Commission, the EU’s executive, to create “without delay” a toolbox of new trade defence instruments. That included a so-called “killer switch” provision that will enable the Commission to impose quotas and tariffs on products at a moment’s notice.
The Commission is expected to come forward with such proposals by the end of 2026. There is, as yet, no legal text, no defined trigger, no agreed scope and no answer to the question of what a trade “cut-off” would mean in practice.
Still, should the Commission gain such “killer switch” powers, the entire structure of Europe’s trade with the world could be revolutionised. And a trade war with China will be almost inevitable.
China loomed large at the EU leaders’ summit, as the European bloc faces a trade deficit of more than €360 billion (S$519 billion) with Beijing in 2026, or about €1 billion each day. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has long warned the Chinese authorities that such deficits are “unsustainable”.
Yet the latest EU statistics indicate that Chinese exports to the Union expanded by a further 25% during the first eight months of 2026. Europe’s car industry is no longer the primary concern; the continent’s chemicals and industrial machinery are now the latest sectors acutely vulnerable to what is described as a Chinese export onslaught.
A decade ago, the EU registered a yearly deficit of €71 billion in industrial machinery trade with China but enjoyed a surplus of €6 billion in trade in chemicals. Today, the machinery deficit has grown to €206 billion, while a gaping trade deficit has developed in chemicals, to the tune of €24 billion a year.
At the latest summit in Brussels, the seat of the European Commission, Belgium, Denmark, France and Germany backed the Commission’s determination to move fast on seeking to protect these sectors. EU anti-dumping investigations into chemicals, pharmaceuticals and machinery are expected within weeks, and an investigation into Chinese-manufactured wind turbines is not far off either.
In a joint letter released on Oct 5, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued that the Commission should be granted powers to, in the authors’ phrase, “cut off access to the European single market if needed if another trading nation deliberately ignores calls for the restoration of fair trade conditions”.
The proposed weapon could be deployed not only if trade in a particular commodity suddenly balloons and no action is taken, but also if another country were to use other coercion instruments – such as a cut-off in supplies of critical raw materials – in an effort to avoid serious discussions about trade imbalances.
If that happened, “the EU must be able to inflict damage comparable to that being done to us”, a German government official explained soon after the Franco-German proposal was released.
Challenges of a ‘switch’
EU officials are refusing to identify any country to which such a provision may apply.
Still, it is a legal necessity dressed as diplomatic courtesy: A China-specific regulation would be indefensible at the World Trade Organization and awkward for many European nations still hoping to maintain friendly relations with Beijing.
Yet nobody is fooled. The entire discussion about this “killer switch” provision – from subsidies and non-tariff barriers to overcapacity and dumping – amounts to the EU’s longstanding gripes against Beijing.
Currently, the EU’s powers of dealing with trade problems are cumbersome.
The Commission must start an investigation into alleged fair-trade distortion. The findings must be substantiated. And any measure taken against a nation exporting to the EU must be approved by a majority of the Union’s member-states.
Until now, China had little problem in rendering such European measures irrelevant, either by launching its own trade distortion investigations into European products entering Chinese markets, or by dangling economic favours to a number of individual European nations, in return for their pledge to veto Commission measures against Chinese trade.
But if the “killer switch” proposal is adopted, that will transform the entire trade debate.
The Commission will be able to dispense with most of the elaborate investigation procedure. And incoming goods in a particular sector could be immediately subjected to tariffs or blocked altogether without first asking for the approval of the EU member-nations.
This is, to all intents and purposes, a revolution in the way Europe does business.
Beijing seems to have understood the significance of this proposal; this is assumed to be the main reason why China offered a highly unusual voluntary concession on future exports of electric vehicles. However, the trade debate in Europe was never principally about cars; it was a template for broader discussions on China’s trade volumes.
So, while Beijing thought that its concession on cars was a one-off gesture to silence the debate, the agreement to limit the volumes of Chinese EVs sold in Europe encouraged EU member-states to believe that it was precisely the discussion about the “killer switch” that forced China into giving way.
The question now is whether a consensus really exists over the adoption of such a measure, and how quickly it can be implemented.
While the EU’s biggest economies support the “killer switch” suggestion, many governments may yet baulk at the idea of granting the Commission wide powers; the idea that the Commission can make such critical decisions without prior authority from member-states is controversial. So, all that has been agreed at this stage is that the Commission will come back with its proposals.
Then, there is the question of how quickly such measures could become legally enforceable. The guess in Brussels is that, even if new powers are adopted, the Commission will not be able to use them until the second half of 2027 because the necessary legislation will take time to be enacted.
Still, the anti-China mood is growing in Brussels. The European Parliament approved on Oct 7 by 454 votes to 86 – with 110 abstentions – a resolution calling Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”.

Western leaders back a two-state solution, but do Palestinians even want one? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:13:28 UTC
08:13:28 KST

You’d think that British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who just happens to be Jewish, would have heard the “From the river to the sea” chant, shouted by many of his citizens, at one of their almost daily anti-Israel protests.
The phrase, which represents the entire State of Israel, from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea, means that any officially approved Palestinian state, to those protesters, would have to comprise that full area, including Judea, Samaria and Gaza.
That unnegotiable demand is not just coming from the shouters on the street. It is the final goal of Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran, and anyone who assumes leadership of Palestinians.
While some might be tempted to point to PLO head Mahmoud Abbas, arguing that he has advocated for a two-state solution, that contention is contradicted and completely undermined by the educational indoctrination given to Palestinian children who are taught, from an early age, that Israel is occupying Arab land and that the enemy must be eradicated.
So, for all intents and purposes, the spoken commitment of “From the river to the sea” wholeheartedly negates a two-state solution.
Nonetheless, for whatever reason, Miliband has said that “when it comes to the attempt to destroy the two-state solution, this party, this movement, this government says, ‘we will not let you succeed.’”
My question is, how do you square those two things – a growing protest movement that insists the State of Israel must be entirely replaced by a Palestinian one, with no Jewish presence, and a government minister who assures everyone that no one will succeed in extinguishing the aspiration of a two-state solution?
Unless I’m wrong, each of those concepts is diabolically opposed to the other. One supposes the good will of both sides, endeavoring to commit to peaceful coexistence and ready to make whatever compromise it takes for the sake of ending the long-standing conflict.
While the other immediately dispenses with all pretense, publicly declaring that there will be no compromise, no attempts at sharing the geographic area, and no getting along with those they clearly despise.
So, where do you go from there? Because Miliband and his government are, essentially, pushing a policy that’s being drowned out by the voices on the street who are, in no way, supportive of the idea.
Of course, Miliband is not alone. He shares the company of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, along with an overwhelming majority of UN member states.
Leaders from France, Canada, and Australia are also on board with the two-state solution. And shockingly, the official policy of the US agrees with that position.
Needless to say, many Arab states, such as Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Morocco, the UAE, Qatar, and Egypt, support the idea as well. Those Arab League members base their assumption on pre-1967 borders, with east Jerusalem as the capital of a Palestinian state.
So what we’re witnessing is a stalled status quo, paralyzing the possibility of all progress, because while a significant part of the global leadership still promotes a two-state solution, the ones who would be instrumental in approving such a deal are laser-focused on the whole pie, and not just one piece.
How can there be any resolution to one of the world’s biggest conundrums when two sides are dug in deeply, believing that their particular philosophy is the only proposition that is acceptable?
That leaves us with only one conclusion. This falls into the category of unsolvable problems that are simply too complex and too emotionally charged to figure out.
When coming to that obvious reality, it’s tempting to ask ourselves why, then, would someone like Miliband, and all the others, continue to back a losing proposition, knowing, in advance, that the likelihood of its implementation is zero?
Here is a speculative answer. The whole concept of a two-state solution is very compatible with the social construct of virtue-signaling. That is because the idea of two states for two peoples sounds reasonable, moral, ethical, and even noble. It plays into the idea that there can be an equitable solution for both sides, resulting in a real win-win situation.
The cost of indoctrination
What is missed by those leaders, who are clearly attempting to inflate their own goodness, is the vast reservoir of hatred and contempt, welling up inside of the individuals who have been part of a centuries-long experiment of indoctrination, from cradle to grave.
The toxic and lethal education they received, both at home, in school, and at their mosques, did the trick, painting Jews as demons who must be eradicated at all costs. Losing one’s life for the sake of diminishing their numbers is the greatest sacrifice that can be made.
Consequently, it’s no wonder that such a society, dedicated to the end of another one, cannot build anything productive or contribute to others through its own achievements and accomplishments.
Because when you are obsessed with destruction, the thought of rising to greatness is completely counterproductive and immaterial to the goal of finally doing away with an avowed enemy. It’s the reason that their youth will never live to inherit the realization of their dream, if that were possible.
Everything is secondary to eliminating the evil in their backyard, and that is the tragedy completely missed by world leaders who have spent decades trying to fit a round peg into a square hole.
So, if you think about it, the thing that is standing in the way of “peace in our time between Jews and Arabs” is the personal need of those in power to appear virtuous, magnanimous, and the ones who possess the highest moral standards.
By forcing the rest of us to cling to a losing prospect, precious time is wasted, young lives are snuffed out, and nothing moves forward. It is the ultimate prolonging of conflict, almost deliberately designed to remain the world’s thorn in the side, as useless and feigned efforts are expended to resolve the mother of all unescapable quagmires.
Don’t even bother asking the question of why they can’t see this for what it is, because they clearly are deeply invested in playing the game of who can appear the most civilized and principled exemplary figures, each vying for that top honor.
Yet, they are outed by the continuing conflict, which will only result in more bloodshed. And, sadly, there’s absolutely no honor in that!
The writer, a former principal of Jerusalem elementary and middle schools, was a member of Kibbutz Re’im from 1994 to 1999. She is the author of Mistake-Proof Parenting, based on the time-tested wisdom found in the Book of Proverbs, available on Amazon.

American Democratic establishment figures’ criticism of Israel has gathered around one name: Benjamin Netanyahu.
Party leaders, activists, and editorial boards repeat it until the alliance itself slips out of the sentence.

The objection had already left one man’s calculations and landed on the government as such. Policy, coalition, and character were folded into a single charge.
Activist groups had been writing that indictment for months. In June 2023, Jewish Voice for Peace described the Israeli government as “the most extremist, racist, homophobic, and far-right in Israel’s history.” The sentence does the work these campaigns need. It implies the problem can be voted out. Attaching a superlative to one government leaves the door open for a later government to be welcomed back.
That implication is the hedge. Leaders can tell older voters and traditional donors that they still support Israel and object only to its present prime minister. They can tell campus organizations and the progressive wing that they have broken with the man those organizations have spent years branding as the obstacle to justice. The two assurances occupy the same week and different rooms. Each audience hears what it came to hear.
The arrangement holds only as long as Netanyahu remains available as the villain. His coalition partners supply ready language about extremism. His long tenure supplies a story about one politician clinging to power. A Democrat can point at Jerusalem and say the difficulty sits there, in a single career, and that a different Israeli government would restore the old terms.
Many Democrats still expect those old terms to return. Criticize the government of the day. Vote for aid. Affirm the alliance in a speech. Move on. The formula belonged to a party whose disagreements with Israel concerned settlements, timing, and tone, and whose voters still treated a Jewish state as a settled fact. Support came with arguments. It did not come with a question mark over the state’s existence.
Rejection of the Jewish state
A large and growing part of the Democratic base has left that settlement. For many activists, the objection is Israel; it is Zionism; it is the idea that a Jewish state should exist in any form. Encampments after October 7, 2023, made the demand public. Chants rejected a Jewish state “between the river and the sea.” Organizations that began with a cabinet ended with a country. The prime minister’s name remained useful. The country has become the target.
Surveys have tracked the same movement for years among younger Democrats, whose sympathy for Israel has fallen well below the levels their parents reported. Party leaders know the numbers. They also know that saying them aloud costs a coalition that still includes pro-Israel voters, Jewish communities, and members of Congress who will not abandon the alliance. Silence about the shift, paired with volume about Netanyahu, has been the working compromise.
So the Netanyahu frame continues and postpones the admission. Support that remains intact only until the loudest faction demands something more extreme is support on a timer. The faction has grown more maximalist with each cycle.
Conditional language about occupation gave way to language about an illegitimate state. Calls for a ceasefire gave way, in some quarters, to calls for the end of the state conducting the war. Each step was described as a response to the current government. Each step survived the news cycle and hardened into doctrine.
The choice will come. A party either grounds its support for Israel in principle, in the legitimacy of Jewish self-determination and in the reality of a democratic ally under attack, or it ties that support to the mood of a wing that has turned uncompromising. There is no stable third position in which leaders condemn a prime minister forever and never answer the people who condemn the country. Coalitions can delay a reckoning; they cannot cancel one.
Netanyahu will not be prime minister forever. Israeli politics has removed him before and can remove him again.
His departure will not retire the argument; it will end the postponement. A successor will still lead a Jewish state. That state will still control territory won in wars it did not start, still face groups sworn to its destruction, and still elect governments that American activists dislike. The adjectives will transfer. They already moved from earlier prime ministers to this one, with barely a pause for the difference between their records.
On that day, Democrats will have to answer a plain question. Were they drawing a line around one man, or were they moving, quietly and for years, toward a break with the alliance itself?
The voters who treated Netanyahu as a convenient objection will still be in the coalition. The voters who want the alliance intact will still be there, too. Neither group will accept the old double message once the named obstacle is gone. A new prime minister cannot do the work a party declined to do with its own base.
The Jewish state will remain after this prime minister, as it remained after the ones before him. American leaders who spent the Netanyahu years treating him as the whole issue will then have to say what they actually support.
The delay is the policy. The day Netanyahu leaves office, the policy expires. What remains is the argument they have been postponing, and it will be harder to hide.
The writer is a certified interfaith hospice chaplain in Jerusalem and the mayor of Mitzpe Yeriho.

Roundup: Firefighters battle multiple wildfires in Southern California under red flag warnings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:09:57 CST
08:09:57 KST

Firefighters put out hot spots along Avenida Calita during the Norte Fire in San Juan Capistrano, Orange County, California, the United States, on Oct. 17, 2026. Firefighters are battling multiple wildfires across Southern California on Saturday as red flag warnings remain in effect amid critical fire weather conditions. (Photo by Qiu Chen/Xinhua)
LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Firefighters are battling multiple wildfires across Southern California on Saturday as red flag warnings remain in effect amid critical fire weather conditions.
A fast-moving wildfire, dubbed the Norte Fire, has burned 570 acres (about 2.3 square kilometers) near San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano as of Saturday morning, with only 5 percent contained, according to the Orange County Fire Authority.
"Crews worked throughout the night to attack the fire and strengthen containment lines," the agency said in an update on X.
Six homes have been damaged or destroyed, the agency said, adding that the cause of the fire remains under investigation.
Evacuation orders were issued for multiple neighborhoods in the area, affecting approximately 16,000 residents as of Saturday.
The Henderson Fire, the largest of the four wildfires currently burning in Southern California, has scorched 3,132 acres and is 35 percent contained, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (Cal Fire).
The blaze was first reported Thursday afternoon in San Diego County.
Overnight, firefighters constructed handline along the southern portion of the fire in the heavily vegetated riparian area of Las Pulgas Canyon and worked to extinguish hot spots, Cal Fire said in an update on Saturday morning.
Crews will focus on the northern portion of the fire, extinguishing hot spots along the perimeter and within the interior, it added.
Relative humidity is expected to recover this evening, helping reduce fire activity. However, grasses and other vegetation remain extremely dry and will continue to pose a fire risk until significant, soaking rainfall occurs, according to the agency.
The Bryson Fire, which started on Thursday, has burned 147 acres in Malibu, Los Angeles County, with 52 percent contained.
Fire officials said that more than 700 personnel had been assigned to the fire as of Friday night. Crews will focus on mopping up hot spots identified during an infrared flight, reinforcing existing containment lines and building additional ones.
The smaller Peak Fire has burned 43 acres so far in Los Angeles County and is 41 percent contained.
A heat advisory issued by the National Weather Service remains in effect until 8 p.m. local time Saturday for parts of Southern California.
Red flag warnings across much of the region prompted Southern California Edison, the area's primary electric utility, to implement public safety power shutoffs, leaving more than 90,000 residents in Los Angeles and Ventura counties without power, local television reports said. ■

SC: No need for nod to prosecute govt official seeking bribe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:00:01 UTC
08:00:01 KST

The court stressed that the statutory protection is meant only to prevent persecution of officials for decisions made in discharge of their duties
NEW DELHI: In a significant ruling relating to Prevention of Corruption Act, Supreme Court has said that the shield of prior sanction from higher authorities to prosecute a public servant is not available if they are caught demanding bribes. The court stressed that the statutory protection is meant only to prevent persecution of officials for decisions made in discharge of their duties.The ruling was given by a bench of Justices SVN Bhatti and N V Anjaria while interpreting Section 17A of the Act, which was inserted in the statute in 2018 and prohibited police or investigating agencies from conducting without official approval any inquiry or investigation into alleged offences committed by public servants while discharging their duties.Dismissing an appeal by a Rajasthan police constable challenging an FIR and chargesheet against him for allegedly demanding a bribe of Rs 1.5 lakh, the bench said the Section 17A shield cannot have an omnibus application to all public servants facing prosecution for criminal offences.
“The act of demanding a bribe is a pure criminal act, not connected with official functions and not relatable to or having any linkage with recommendation or decision of the appellant in his capacity as public servant,” the bench said, accepting the arguments of Rajasthan additional advocate general Sansriti Pathak.
Writing the judgement, Justice Anjaria said, “In the facts and circumstances of the case, therefore, the act of the appellant does not fall within the protective umbrella of Section 17A of the Act. It could not be said that the proceedings were vitiated for want of sanction.”

The settlers smashed a window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian consulate and asked the diplomats and passengers to show their identification documents, Palestinian local and security sources told Xinhua.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said in a statement that the diplomats' tour had not been coordinated with the military and that no IDF soldiers were present at the time of the attack, because the call was routed to a divisional operations room handling reports from security personnel rather than civilians.
Israeli police said that they had opened an investigation and notified the Israeli Foreign Ministry to help locate the diplomats who were attacked, collect statements, and identify the attackers.
"Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will pursue these investigations to their conclusion, bringing to justice everyone involved in such incidents," the police statement said.
The IDF condemned the attack as a serious act of violence against diplomatic representatives, saying that police and forensic investigators entered the area under military protection to collect evidence and question witnesses.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar condemned in a statement "the serious acts of violence committed by Israeli rioters in the Taybeh area," saying his ministry is in contact with the ambassadors of the countries concerned to assist law enforcement authorities, which are working to identify the assailants and bring them to justice.
Yet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers as he sought to cast doubt over the circumstances of the attack.
"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge," his office said, using the biblical name for the West Bank.
Meanwhile, settlers across the West Bank attacked Palestinian olive harvesters and farmers, beating and shooting several people, stealing agricultural equipment, and forcing farmers off their land, according to local sources.
Israeli forces were also reported to have fired tear gas, while a settlement guard fired live ammunition, sparking a fire. Settlers also established a new outpost targeting olive harvesters.
The Palestine Liberation Organization's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission reported 40 attacks by settlers and Israeli forces against farmers, their land, and crops.
Palestinian Authority Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh condemned the attack on foreign diplomats, calling the perpetrators "colonial terrorist gangs."
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates held the Israeli government responsible and called for accountability.
More than half a million Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in 1967, alongside about 3.4 million Palestinians.
Also on Saturday, Palestinian police officer Abdul Jawad Joudah was killed in an Israeli airstrike on a police post in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Palestinian sources.
Since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel took effect in October 2025, Israeli attacks have killed 1,511 people, bringing the total death toll since Oct. 7, 2023, to 74,469, according to Gaza-based health authorities on Saturday. ■

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 18, 2026
Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, as Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and in Lyon protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview
The captain of a flydubai flight whose co-pilot attacked him with an axe in an alleged bid to bring down the plane said one thought kept running through his head as the harrowing ordeal unfolded: “You can’t die like this.”
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar recounted the “traumatic” experience to Sky News Arabia in his first interview since the incident late in September in which he, passengers and other crew members were credited with averting disaster on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
With his head and one hand bandaged and glasses perched on his nose, Machchhar spoke from his hospital bed in the UAE.
Haaland brace extends Man City’s winning start in Premier League
Erling Haaland struck twice as Manchester City defiantly extended their blistering start to the Premier League season with a 3-2 win against Ipswich on Oct 17.
Phil Foden put City ahead in the first half at the Etihad Stadium before Daizen Maeda grabbed a shock equaliser for Ipswich.
Haaland netted before the interval and struck again after the break to take his tally for the season to 12.
It was City’s second win since the club were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial regulations in September.
A reporter who saw Covid-19 coming has died
Helen Branswell, a leading reporter on infectious diseases who wrote with foresight, urgency and clarity about the emerging danger of the Covid-19 pandemic, ahead of the vast majority of journalists and even many medical experts, died on Oct 13 in Ottawa. She was 69.
Her death, at a hospital, was from complications of a recurrence of breast cancer, her sister Brenda Branswell said.
Branswell “saw the pandemic coming well before anyone was paying attention,” Ashish Jha, the White House Covid-19 response coordinator in 2022 and 2023, said on social media.
Alberta support for Canada rises ahead of separation referendum
Support for Alberta remaining in Canada gathered pace ahead of a referendum on whether the province should begin a legal process to separate from the country, according to a poll from Abacus Data.
The survey of 1,021 eligible voters, released on Oct 17, found 68% of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, up from 64% last month. Support for beginning a legal process that could ultimately lead to separation was unchanged at 24%, while the share of undecided voters or those planning not to vote in the Oct 7 to 13 poll fell to 8% from 12%.
Albertans will decide on Oct 19 whether to remain a Canadian province or to set the stage for a second, binding vote on secession. At stake is the future of Canada’s largest oil-producing province, which pumps more than 4 million barrels a day, most of it for export to the US.

Prices of 137 cancer drugs to fall by up to 70% from November 9
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:02:18 UTC
07:02:18 KST

This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients
In good news for cancer patients, prices of 137 drugs are set to be reduced by up to 70% from Nov 9, with govt capping trade margins by 30%. Drug prices regulator National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) Saturday notified the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs to address the issue of excessive trade margins, invoking Paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. Significantly, patented drugs are also included in the list.The trade margin rationalisation at 30% of MRP, excluding GST, corresponds to a mark-up of 42.9% on price to stockist/price to distributor (PTS/PTD), according to the minutes of the NPPA meeting accessed by TOI. Simply put, PTS/PTD is the first point of sale of the drug.
This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients, in certain cases of 10 times.The MRPs of certain drugs — including pertuzumab + trastuzumab, atezolizumab, teclistamab, inotuzumab ozogamicin and daratumumab — are up to Rs 5 lakh per vial/pack.All manufacturers will be required to inform NPPA of their revised prices within seven days of publication of the gazette notification. Manufacturers will be req-uired to display the price lists on their website and widely disseminate them to all retailers and hospitals, with the latter also required to display the revised prices on their websites prominently.
The authority approved the calculation of the revised MRP based on PTS/PTD for March 2026 as the reference month.NPPA said patient assistance programme quantities may be excluded from the calculation of PTS/PTD and MRP for trade-margin capping only. These programmes, where drugs are supplied free of cost, are typically run by MNCs.As a substantial supply of anti-cancer drugs is directly made to hospitals and medical institutions, they shall be responsible for ensuring revised prices of such drugs from the date of implementation, NPPA said. State drug controllers will take necessary steps to ensure compliance by manufacturers, dealers including retailers, hospitals and medical institutions, it added.In a bid to tighten rules further, NPPA said uninterrupted availability of the covered formulations needed to be ensured. Any manufacturer intending to reduce monthly production levels would have to obtain permission.
Consumers can use the Pharma Sahi Daam app and NPPA website to check revised prices of drugs, an official release said.In 2019, the MRP of 526 brands of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was reduced by up to 90%, NPPA said. The present exercise extends this approach to a larger set of drugs, based on the list recommended by an expert committee under Directorate General of Health Services.
