====================================================================================================

Mothers and fathers may pass along different kinds of sexism to their kids, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:00:34 UTC
07:00:34 KST

A new study published in Sex Roles suggests that 8-year-old children’s views about women tend to mirror their parents’ sexist attitudes. Fathers’ hostile sexism and mothers’ benevolent sexism were most consistently linked to their children’s views, hinting that mothers and fathers may play different roles in passing these beliefs along.
Psychologists often divide sexism into two distinct categories: hostile and benevolent. Hostile sexism involves openly negative feelings toward women, particularly those who are perceived as challenging male power. Benevolent sexism is more subtle, as it involves idealizing women who conform to traditional gender roles and believing that they are delicate and require men’s protection.
Research suggests that benevolent sexism, despite its polite surface, can reinforce an unequal division of household labor and limit women’s career ambitions. Parents appear to be one source of children’s ideas about gender: a 2002 meta-analysis found that parents with more traditional views about gender tended to have children with more traditional views.
Studies of whether parents pass on hostile and benevolent sexism specifically have mostly involved teenagers. A 2012 study, for example, found that mothers who endorsed more benevolent sexism tended to have teenage daughters who did too. Some theorists had argued that benevolent sexism only emerges in adolescence, but a 2020 study co-authored by Hammond, which introduced the stuffed-toy task used in the new research, found that children as young as 5 already agree with both hostile and benevolent ideas about women.
Parental sexism may also show up in everyday interactions: research covered by PsyPost in 2023, led by Overall, found that mothers and fathers higher in hostile sexism were less responsive toward their young children during family interactions.
To build on this line of inquiry, researchers Oksana S. Voznyuk, a PhD candidate at the University of Auckland, Nickola C. Overall, a professor at the University of Auckland, and Matt Hammond, an associate professor at Victoria University of Wellington, set out to test the direct intergenerational links between parents and children. They wanted to see if mothers’ and fathers’ specific sexist attitudes predict their children’s agreement with similar statements.
“In the big picture, we wanted to investigate why gender gaps persist worldwide, even as generations of women and men have been fighting for gender equality,” Voznyuk, Overall, and Hammond told PsyPost. “We thought that an overlooked process that may contribute to this slow progress toward gender equality could be the transmission of sexist beliefs intergenerationally – from parents to their children.”
The research team collected data from 175 family groups, each consisting of a mother, a father, and their 8-year-old child. The families lived in New Zealand and were part of a larger study that began when the children were 4 or 5. The children were fairly evenly split by gender, with 51 percent being girls and 49 percent being boys. Parents filled out standard questionnaires designed to measure their levels of hostile and benevolent sexism.
To assess the children’s attitudes, the researchers used a specially designed laboratory activity that young kids could easily understand. An experimenter introduced each child to a stuffed toy named Feppy, explaining that the toy was a visitor from far away. Feppy then made a series of statements about men and women.
Some of the toy’s statements reflected hostile sexism, such as saying that women get upset easily over jokes. Other statements reflected benevolent sexism, such as claiming that men need to protect women from danger. The children were asked to indicate whether Feppy was “sort of” or “really” right or wrong about each statement. On average, children rated Feppy’s hostile statements as sort of wrong and its benevolent statements as sort of right, and boys and girls gave similar answers.
When the researchers analyzed the responses, they found distinct patterns connecting the parents’ views to their children’s views. Because both parents’ attitudes were analyzed together, each link held even after accounting for the other parent’s views. Fathers who expressed higher levels of hostile sexism tended to have children who also agreed more strongly with hostile gender attitudes. This link was present regardless of whether the child was a boy or a girl.
A different pattern emerged for benevolent sexism. Mothers who endorsed benevolent sexist beliefs were more likely to have children who agreed with benevolent gender attitudes. Just like the link between fathers’ and children’s hostile views, this connection applied to both sons and daughters. Fathers’ benevolent sexism, by contrast, was not linked to their children’s benevolent attitudes.
The researchers also found that a mother’s hostile sexism was linked to her child’s views, but only for sons. The authors note the reason is unclear, but one possibility is that mothers higher in hostile sexism parent boys differently, for example by being more controlling with sons.
“The big takeaway from our findings is that children learn from the attitudes, behaviors, and everyday conversations they see at home, and the messages we send about expectations for women and men, or girls and boys, likely have a lasting impact,” the researchers noted. “This matters because those beliefs can shape everything from career opportunities to romantic relationships later in life.”
“One surprising outcome was that mothers and fathers may play unique roles in passing along sexist beliefs,” the researchers explained. “These differences may be about the roles that fathers and mothers play. Fathers who agree with hostile sexism believe that they should be the authority in the family, and they may use more controlling parenting behavior and express hostile sexism by behaving aggressively toward mothers. These behaviors can show children that men should have power and authority and therefore socialize children’s hostile gender beliefs.”
The authors suggest that mothers who endorse benevolent sexism might actively teach these values to their children, as these beliefs often appear socially acceptable or positive on the surface. “Mothers who agree with benevolent sexism may be more likely to hold traditional homemaker and caregiver roles,” the team added. “This may give them more opportunity to model and teach children ideas about protecting and valuing women who fit traditional expectations of what good girls and good women should be like.”
To ensure these links were not driven by other factors, the researchers adjusted their statistical models for the parents’ education levels, employment status, perceived socioeconomic status, and whether the mother or father was the primary caregiver. They also controlled for the children’s age and their “theory of mind,” which is the psychological term for a person’s ability to understand that other people have their own separate thoughts and feelings. Even with these adjustments, the connections between the parents’ and children’s sexist attitudes remained, and incidentally, parents’ hostile sexism was linked to lower theory-of-mind scores in children.
“The most important note is that this research is not about blaming parents, but about recognizing that we all play a role in transmitting and reinforcing gender beliefs,” the researchers emphasized. “Small changes may make an important difference. Many of us have internalized sexist attitudes to some extent, and often we don’t even know what they are, their impact, or how we display them. This research is a good reminder that the little things we say and do can shape how children think about women and men.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The links were modest: the correlation between fathers’ and children’s hostile attitudes, for example, was about 0.29, on a scale where 1 would mean a perfect match.
“As with most research about beliefs and attitudes, the effect size of parents’ sexist beliefs on children’s beliefs is relatively small,” the researchers pointed out. “Children are likely to have many experiences that contribute to their beliefs about women and men, but as children’s first and often most long-term role models, parents are likely to be particularly impactful influences in children’s development of sexist attitudes and an important intervention point.”
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot establish a direct cause and effect. There is also a possibility that children influence their parents’ views over time as they express their own ideas about gender. Additionally, the stuffed-toy task was developed with U.S. children, and one hostile item had to be dropped for poor fit with this New Zealand sample. All of the families were mother-father couples in New Zealand, so the patterns may differ in other family types and cultures.
Future research will need to explore these dynamics in single-parent households, families with LGBTQ+ parents, and across different cultural contexts.
“We believe two main directions are important for the next steps in this research,” the researchers said. “The first is to investigate whether children’s gender attitudes are related to negative outcomes for children’s wellbeing and their social, emotional and educational development.”
They suspect these attitudes could affect how children see themselves, how they do in school, and how they get along with peers. “The second is to investigate how parents are passing down their beliefs – are parents modeling traditional gender roles at home, treating sons and daughters differently, or shaping how children dress and behave in a way that communicates these gender beliefs?” they added.
The authors argue that because children’s early beliefs about gender may shape their later interests, schooling, and relationships, efforts to reduce gender stereotypes in childhood will likely need to engage parents as well as children.
The study, “Intergenerational Links Between Parents’ and Children’s Hostile and Benevolent Sexism,” was authored by Oksana S. Voznyuk, Nickola C. Overall, Matthew D. Hammond, Rachel S. T. Low, Annette M. E. Henderson, Valerie T. Chang, and Myfanwy Christensen.

Internet is fundamental right of all, even children: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:54:56 UTC
06:54:56 KST

It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.
NEW DELHI: Raising citizens’ right to access and use of internet to the level of fundamental right, Supreme Court has held that even children are entitled to that right and said it does not endorse imposing in the name of safety a blanket ban on children accessing internet. At the same time, it favoured restricting access to content that is inherently harmful to kids.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Chandran said that right to access and use of the internet is part of Article 21 (right to life and liberty) and Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression). The internet is “priceless” as it provides access to information and education to all in even remote areas, where it is often the only source of learning for many children. Noting that the SC had earlier refrained from expressing a definitive view on whether the right to access the internet is, by itself, a fundamental right, the bench said, “...we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.”
SC: Internet’s value priceless, efficacy of curbs not provedSC said, “Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or freedom of speech worth expressing.”
The order was passed on a public interest litigationfiled by NGO ‘Just Rights for Children Alliance’, which highlights continued lapses by intermediaries in tackling child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) despite SC’s 2024 judgment in this regard.
Agreeing with its plea, SC said there has been “no progress worth the name” in the last two years.Acknowledging that there has been “a growing yet short-lived tendency across the globe in the recent past to limit the access of children below a certain age to the internet, more particularly to social media platforms,” SC said, “we too gave this our anxious consideration, and only thereafter, we decided consciously not to endorse the same”.It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.“... Children do not cease to use the internet merely because the law prohibits them from doing so ... They move to other platforms and websites that are unregulated and even more unsafe,” SC said.“All that we are trying to say is that any blanket restriction on access to internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality. No jurisdiction has, so far, been able to demonstrate that children are any safer on account of such measures,” it said.It said some age-based restrictions and safeguards should exist for the safety of children online.

Paulson’s donation a 'profound expression of confidence in Israel’s human capital'

Israeli charity Save a Child's Heart marks 30 years, 9,000 children treated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:40:53 UTC
06:40:53 KST

The Talmud teaches that whoever saves a single life is as one who saved an entire world. If that’s the case, SACH (Save a Child’s Heart) can be credited with saving some 9,000 worlds.
SACH is Israel’s leading practitioner of medical diplomacy.
Founded in 1995 by the late Dr. Ami Cohen and headquartered in the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital at the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, it provides free cardiac surgery for children with heart ailments regardless of their religion, ethnicity, or nationality. This includes children from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, and youngsters from countries that are sworn enemies of Israel. To date, over 9,000 children from more than 75 countries have been brought to Israel for treatment. Each child is accompanied by a family member or nurse from the child’s home country.
In addition, medical personnel from third-world countries are brought to Israel to train in all aspects of cardiac surgery, so that children with heart problems can be treated closer to home. SACH teams frequently travel abroad to evaluate children with congenital and rheumatic heart diseases, and often perform urgent surgeries when the child’s condition is so serious that immediate treatment is required.
SACH volunteers and supporters met last Friday with President Isaac Herzog at his official residence to celebrate the 30th anniversary of SACH’s founding.
Along with the above were medical personnel, ambassadors and other diplomats from some of the African countries from which children have been brought to Israel for surgery, representatives of African hospitals whose pediatric cardiology teams were trained in Israel, representatives of international foundations which help fund SACH, and mothers with children who recently underwent successful surgeries and who will soon be returning home.
'We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds'
SACH Executive Director Simon Fisher described the children who came under SACH care over the years as “living miracles,” adding, “We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds.”
Fisher emphasized that SACH had grown from a small group of dedicated professionals to global proportions.
In explaining this, Fisher said, “A child in need is part of our collective responsibility.
Herzog, who has long been familiar with SACH's work, said that the organization deserved a Nobel Peace Prize and pledged to do everything he could to bring that about.
He declared that he was honored to host a milestone anniversary of “a remarkable Israeli humanitarian organization of which we’re very proud.”
Herzog characterized SACH’s achievements as “the triumph of human kindness which connects a wide heart of human effort.”
But it is more than simply healing a diseased heart, he pointed out. “From Iraq to the Palestinian Authority, all have been welcomed with wide open arms - simply because they are children in need.”
Herzog saw the effects of this a year ago when he paid a state visit to Zambia, and met with adults who as children had been healed in Israel, and were leading fruitful and meaningful lives.
“Few things leave me prouder to be Israeli,” he said.
“This is the essence of doing good in the world. This is something the international community should bear in mind when they accuse us of something else.”
In closing Herzog implied that SACH received its inspiration from the Biblical Noah - “one man who braved the current and ultimately saved the world.”
SACH co-chair Robert Baruch noted that over the years, SACH has given thousands of children a second chance at life, and has not been deterred by the child’s place of birth. Children come to Israel as the hope of families who cannot find treatment at home, he said. “It’s a reminder of what can happen when people decide to act. The impact of SACH is far greater than its size.”
Mega philanthropist Sylvan Adams, who, together with a group of other philanthropic families living in Israel, established the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital within the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, shared some of his own SACH experiences.
The first time he visited, more than a decade ago, he was on a tour, and SACH staff asked whether he would like to spend a few minutes watching open-heart surgery. He agreed and was so fascinated by what he saw that he sat for hours and instantly became a donor. The children’s hospital that bears his name came into being because there was no children’s hospital in Holon before then. Since its inception, he has visited many times.
On that first occasion, he saw the surgeon being assisted by a doctor from Tanzania. What amazed him was that the two were conversing in Hebrew.
One per cent of all children are born with heart defects
Adams was shocked to learn that one per cent of all children are born with heart defects, which makes SACH’s work all the more vital.
During his visits, he has witnessed children from Gaza arriving with their parents and sometimes accompanied by their physicians. They were always treated with dignity - even after October 7, he said.
\In relation to the attitude toward Gazan children being treated in the same friendly manner as children from anywhere else, Adams is certain that there are people in Gaza who do not bear hostility toward Israel.
Along the entrance to the main building in the presidential compound, there were tall round tables bearing enlarged photographs of children who came with hope and left healed. Alongside each photograph was a round vase filled with white tulips. When the petals of a tulip first open, they form the shape of a heart. The message, though subtle, was clear.

Hundreds of thousands take to the streets for separate demonstrations, putting pressure on governments across the EU.
Hundreds of thousands of Europeans have taken to the streets in separate, uncoordinated demonstrations to protest against the rising cost of living in their countries.
Saturday’s wave of unrest in Belgium, France, Italy and Portugal has put pressure on governments across the European Union.
France experienced one of its most turbulent days of protests in decades, with more than 550,000 people joining demonstrations, according to the Ministry of Interior, and police facing off with protesters across the country.
The marches, which followed weeks of student protests, degenerated into clashes, looting and fires after violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 1,200 people were arrested and 150 police officers were hurt. “It’s a miracle the toll wasn’t higher,” he said as he visited officers deployed in central Paris.
Dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg, the French news agency AFP reported.
Whole streets in the capital “have been devastated”, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said.
A fire set by masked protesters in Limoges largely destroyed the more than 140-year-old town hall, while city halls in Marseille and Lille were broken into and vandalised. In Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
President Emmanuel Macron said on X that those responsible would be “prosecuted and punished”.
In Belgium’s capital, Brussels – which has already seen weeks of protests by students against university registration fees – police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters, whom they accused of launching missiles at them and setting fires.
In Liege, a smaller city east of Brussels, police also deployed water cannon to break up demonstrations. Police did not say how many people attended.
Meanwhile, in the Portuguese capital of Lisbon, an estimated tens of thousands of protesters marched against the cost of living crisis, low wages and an inability to access housing in major cities. House prices in Portugal have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have increased nearly as much.
Portuguese Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Friday that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street”. Protesters said their leaders are “out of touch” with the problem.
Italy
In Milan, rioters clashed with police, looted stores and set property on fire in the city centre, emptying Piazza del Duomo and a luxury arcade that would usually be full of shoppers.
A march against wars and rising living costs began peacefully, but masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Police used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
At least two police officers were injured, and about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained, the Italian LaPresse news agency reported.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the violence.
“Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not,” she wrote on X, blaming “hooligans who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos”.
Milan’s centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said “the reasons for the protests were understandable. The violence against law enforcement and serious damage to the city are not justifiable.”
In Bologna, police also reported that, alongside peaceful rallies, protesters threw stones and clashed with officers.
French protests spill over
Although protests in the other countries did not reach the same scale as the rallies in France, they may be a sign of discontent spilling over, Alberto Alemanno, professor of EU law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera.
“France is the epicentre of this movement … and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France,” Alemanno said.
He said Saturday’s protests may not be the last in many of these countries and new hotspots could emerge.
In Greece, Germany, and Austria, the “early stages” of a movement are emerging, with mobilisation expected “in the coming week”, he said.
They are not a single movement, he explained, but several protests happening at the same time, with some “shared grievances”: underfunded education, rising living costs and, for students, uncertain prospects after graduation.
The unrest comes at a crucial time for Europe, Alemanno said, as the continent prepares for an “unprecedented super-cycle of national elections” in the coming 12 months, with votes scheduled in Spain, France, Italy and Poland.
“Inevitably, all these protests, all these mobilisations, are going to be at the centre of the political conversation,” Alemanno said.

Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
- Mass protests over rising living costs and poor public services turned violent in France, with attacks on city halls, shops and police, and about 1,200 arrests, said Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu.
- Macron and Lecornu vowed to punish the rioters and said violence would not change policy, while protesters said most marches were peaceful and blamed troublemakers for the damage.
- The unrest spread across Europe, and France’s police response faces scrutiny after injuries, including a teenager who lost a hand, and claims that officers are under severe strain.
AI generated
FRANCE – Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, as Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and, in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence, and blamed the unrest on the “far-left” and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
“To those who clearly want to use this violence as a ‘warm-up’ before the presidential election, I say clearly – We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence,” he wrote in a post on X.
Some 1,200 people had been arrested as part of the protests, Lecornu said while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, he said. The CGT union estimated protesters at 800,000 people.
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had performed such attacks.
“We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so,” he wrote in a post on X.
Belgium, Portugal and Italy also faced smaller-scale protests on Oct 17 as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president and the wealthy.
“We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest, and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Tear gas, fire and looting
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques, and looted a mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fuelling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
French police response under scrutiny
The protests in France began in September, at high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
In Paris on Oct 17, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked French President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term in office.
The protests on Oct 17 eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron’s pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France’s efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in the Oct 17 protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.
Nunez said one person lost his hand in clashes with police on Oct 17. French media reported he had tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
“Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes,” the union said. “Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum.” REUTERS

Prominent Guatemalan anti-corruption lawyer killed in shooting
GUATEMALA – Guatemalan lawyer Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa, known for his high-profile fight against corruption in the Central American country, died after being shot on Oct 17 by two men while visiting a sports centre, a crime condemned by President Bernardo Arevalo.
Solorzano Foppa, 43, was a former prosecutor who denounced wrongdoing by some of Guatemala’s most powerful politicians, business leaders and companies, and in 2023, briefly joined the defence team of a prominent journalist.
Shortly after the attack, Guatemalan police reported that they had detained two men and seized a carbine-style firearm and a motorcycle. Police said the arrests and weapon seizure were in connection with the case.
“I strongly condemn the cowardly murder of former prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa. Both the direct perpetrators and those who ordered the crime must face the full weight of the law,” Arevalo posted on his official X account. He said he had instructed the government to coordinate with the relevant authorities to solve the crime.
“Those who believe that terror can intimidate the people of Guatemala and the government I lead are mistaken. In honour of Foppa, in honour of our homeland, in honour of justice.”
Foppa was known for his anti-corruption work as head of the Criminal Investigations Directorate in the Public Prosecutor’s Office, and later as head of Guatemala’s tax authority, the SAT, from 2016 to 2018, when he helped prosecute dozens of powerful Guatemalan business figures and recover unpaid taxes.
In 2025, Foppa alleged a connection between the Barrio 18 gang and the National Unity of Hope party, as well as links between criminal gangs and the judicial system.
In 2023, he briefly joined the defence team of Guatemalan journalist Jose Ruben Zamora, who has become an international symbol of resistance to the criminalisation of journalism and erosion of judicial independence in Central America.
Foppa had to leave the Zamora case after being accused by the Public Prosecutor’s Office of obstructing the proceedings and destroying or concealing information, a charge he denied but ultimately accepted as part of a plea agreement, saying he did not believe he would receive a fair trial.

tob.studio’s timber bike station in germany resembles stacked log pile
the bike station integrates e-bike charging stations, repair facilities, and digital information, as well as public amenities including an accessible toilet and shower.
prefer designboom on google
LOG PILE GEOMETRY SHAPES TIMBER CYCLING HUB by ToB.Studio
Designed by ToB.Studio, the Burgsinn Cycling Rest Station establishes a public service hub along the D9 cycle route in Germany, positioned at the transition between the town and surrounding landscape. Drawing visual cues from local forestry history, the compact building reinterprets the form of stacked timber logs. Its solid volume features carved-out niches that accommodate sheltered seating areas, entrances, and service points beneath a broad overhanging green roof.
rough-sawn larch cladding wraps bike station’s exterior
The station, designed by ToB.Studio architectural practice, provides a range of amenities for cyclists, pool visitors, and local residents, including e-bike charging stations, a repair and wash area, digital information displays, and an accessible toilet and shower. The structure is built using a prefabricated timber frame according to Design for Disassembly principles, utilizing reversible mechanical connections to facilitate future maintenance and material-specific recycling. Constructed with locally sourced untreated larch cladding, wood-fiber insulation, and a membrane-free wall assembly, the building rests on a single reinforced-concrete slab that functions as the foundation, flood barrier, and finished floor surface.

Adhikari added that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident
NEW DELHI: West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday announced a compensation of Rs 25 lakh and a government job for the family of each person killed in a stampede at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata.The state government will also bear the entire cost of medical treatment for the injured and provide Rs 5 lakh to each of them, Adhikari said, adding that a fact-finding committee would be constituted to investigate the incident."This is a tragic incident. 19 people have lost their lives, 17 of whom died on the spot... 25 people have been injured; 24 of them are out of danger, while one remains in critical condition," the chief minister said. He added that the government was making every possible effort to assist the affected families and that he had personally met relatives of the deceased.
'Appropriate measures against those who failed to manage crowd'
Adhikari said the state government would seek the intervention of the Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court to constitute a fact-finding committee, which would include special task force (STF) and forensic teams. The investigation would examine the circumstances leading to the stampede and identify those responsible for the crowd management arrangements.
Kolkata Police's Anti-Rowdy Section (ARS) has collected CCTV footage from the site, which will be examined as part of the investigation."We will check the footage and take appropriate measures against those who failed to manage the crowd. That could be a member of the puja committee, a homeguard, a temporary worker, a policeman, or a private company security guard. Nobody will be spared," Adhikari said.He said the state government was making arrangements for postmortems in accordance with the law and that six of the deceased had been identified so far. Officials were also coordinating with the families of the victims.The chief minister said the families who had met him had expressed faith in the state government. He added that the Prime Minister's Office had sought a report from the chief secretary, which had been submitted, and that the Centre and the state were working together to provide assistance.
'Some attempting to politicise this, but it will be to no avail'
Adhikari also criticised the previous state government over its handling of past tragedies, accusing some people of attempting to politicise the current incident."Everyone is well aware of the role of the previous government in similar incidents that occurred in the past. Some are attempting to politicize this, but it will be to no avail. I have met with the families of the deceased, and they have explicitly stated that they have full faith in the Chief Minister and the government... The PMO also requested a report from the Chief Secretary, which we have submitted. The Prime Minister has announced relief and compensation. The central and state governments are working together on this..." he said.Referring to other incidents, Adhikari said 13 people had died due to electrocution during the 2025 Puja season amid heavy rain. He also referred to a devastating flood in north Bengal that killed 100 people, questioning the previous chief minister's response to those tragedies.
'An announcement by the organisers' led to the rush
The stampede occurred on Saturday evening, on Maha Saptami, at the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durga Puja pandal in north Kolkata. At least 19 people died and 25 were injured after a crowd surge amid rain, according to officials.A police officer said people waiting outside the pandal rushed forward as it began raining, causing some to fall on the road and triggering the stampede. Adhikari said an announcement made by the organisers of the community Durga Puja had led to a rush among revellers, resulting in what he described as a "painful incident".Officials of the organising club, private security guards and personnel on duty were detained for questioning, he said. The administration also advised several crowded theme-based puja pandals to temporarily close following the tragedy.
Union home minister Amit Shah, who had arrived in Kolkata and was scheduled to visit pandals on Sunday, cancelled his programmes following the incident. President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Shah and former chief minister Mamata Banerjee expressed condolences over the deaths.PM Modi announced an ex gratia payment of Rs 2 lakh for the next of kin of each deceased person and Rs 50,000 for each injured person. The state government has also launched a toll-free helpline to provide information related to the stampede.

Dramatic footage from France on Saturday showed the historic city hall in Limoges engulfed in flames before much of the building collapsed, as violent riots spread across the country, leaving dozens of police officers injured and hundreds of people under arrest.
The 143-year-old municipal building, one of the city's most recognizable landmarks, was set ablaze by rioters during nationwide protests against the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services. Built in 1883 and inspired by Paris City Hall, the landmark was almost completely destroyed.
According to local authorities, "the roof collapsed onto the lower floors, except in the western wing, and two-thirds of the facade have already disappeared."
In Paris, police reported another disturbing incident in which a couple in their 80s was robbed by rioters near Place de la République. According to law enforcement officials, the elderly victims were left standing in the street wearing nothing but their underwear.
Just 400 meters from the Élysée Palace, the official residence of French President Emmanuel Macron, violent clashes erupted after rioters took control of a temporary structure at a construction site. Police stormed the structure using stun grenades, in scenes French media described as resembling "urban guerrilla warfare."
Elsewhere in the capital, audience members at the Théâtre de la Madeleine found themselves trapped inside the building because of heavy concentrations of tear gas in the surrounding streets. They were eventually evacuated.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced that 60 members of the security forces had been injured during the day's unrest, including two who were hospitalized unconscious. One of the officers was injured after being struck by a stone.
Authorities also reported 400 arrests nationwide, with the number expected to rise as police continued confronting rioters in several cities.
The violence erupted during a nationwide day of demonstrations against the rising cost of living, declining public services and increasing fuel prices. Participants included supporters of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in France in late 2018. Critics of the demonstrations, however, accused radical far-left groups of using the protests as a violent show of force ahead of next year's presidential election.
In Paris, Lyon and Marseille, masked rioters, some wearing Palestinian keffiyehs, clashed with police, who deployed tear gas and stun grenades in attempts to disperse the crowds. Footage from the French capital showed burning cars and a bus shelter engulfed in flames, while groups of rioters confronted security forces in the streets.
In Marseille, dramatic video captured a prolonged street battle between police and a crowd that hurled stones and other objects at officers and police vehicles. The confrontation lasted several minutes, with scenes resembling urban warfare.
Widespread looting was also reported, particularly in central Lyon, where masked rioters smashed the windows of a North Face store before breaking inside. A hotel was also targeted, while another group of masked looters raided a store selling Apple devices.

That could potentially reduce the need for spin and provide the option of a fourth quick in Scott Boland, with extra grass also left on the St George's Park wicket.
But Cummins gave every indication that Lyon would remain as a key part of the attack.
"We always look at all options," Cummins said when asked if it was conceivable that they could go in without a specialist spinner.
"We love playing with Nath. We saw last week, a couple of key wickets in the first innings.
"And even the control he gives. It makes the rest of us fast bowlers be able to function around him."

====================================================================================================

Two styles of meditation eased depressive symptoms in a four-week trial, possibly through different routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:00:58 UTC
05:00:58 KST

A randomized controlled trial found that two different styles of meditation, one centered on focused attention and one on self-inquiry, reduced depressive symptoms over four weeks compared with a wait-list control group in adults without a depression diagnosis. Exploratory analyses suggested that the two practices may work through partially different psychological processes. The paper was published in Mindfulness.
Meditation has long been studied as a way to ease depression. However, an important question is why meditation works, and whether all forms of meditation work in the same way. Depression is often maintained by rigid negative beliefs about the self, habitual patterns of thinking, and a tendency to interpret experiences as threatening or personally damaging. Meditation may interrupt this cycle through cognitive decentering, which helps people observe thoughts and emotions without immediately treating them as facts or as reflections of who they are.
This shift may also contribute to a broader psychological state sometimes described as selflessness, in which the self is experienced as less rigid, less isolated, and less central to every experience. The idea has roots in Buddhist traditions, which regard attachment to a fixed and independent self as an important source of suffering.
Modern psychology has begun to translate this idea into measurable processes such as connectedness to other people and nature, along with the ability to adopt a more detached perspective on one’s own thoughts and feelings. However, meditation is not a single technique. Different practices may influence these processes in different ways.
Study authors Céline Stinus of the University of Navarra in Spain and Sophie Berjot of the University of Reims Champagne-Ardenne in France conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing the effects of two types of meditation on depressive symptoms and several related psychological characteristics. They expected the self-inquiry practice, which targets rigid beliefs about the self more directly, to produce larger benefits.
Focused-attention meditation involves sustaining attention on a chosen object, such as the breath, noticing when the mind wanders, and repeatedly returning attention to that object. Self-inquiry meditation is a practice in which people examine their thoughts, beliefs, and sense of self by asking questions about where these mental experiences come from and how they shape emotions and behavior. The self-inquiry program used in the study was secular and did not include Buddhist teachings.
The final sample included 147 adults recruited in France through social media, university campuses, and the researchers’ professional networks. People were not eligible if they were taking psychiatric medication, had previously been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, or were experienced meditators.
Participants were randomly assigned to focused-attention meditation, self-inquiry meditation, or a wait-list control group, with 49 people in each group in the final analysis. The average age was about 49 in the focused-attention group, 46 in the self-inquiry group, and 44 in the control group, and each group was mostly made up of women.
Participants in the meditation groups were not told which type of meditation they had been assigned to, while those in the control group were told they had been placed on a wait-list. Each meditation program lasted four weeks and included five 60-minute online group sessions, all led by the study’s first author, plus 20 minutes of individual practice a day, five days a week. The two meditation groups attended sessions and practiced at home at similar rates.
Participants completed assessments a week before the programs began and within seven days after they ended. The assessments included measures of depressive symptoms (the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), dysfunctional attitudes (the Dysfunctional Attitudes Scale), identity threat, or the perception that one’s sense of self is being undermined or devalued (the Threat Appraisal Subscale of the Cognitive Appraisal Scale), cognitive decentering (the Metacognitive Processes of Decentering Trait scale), connectedness to nature (the Connectedness to Nature Scale), and connectedness to humanity (the Connectedness to Humanity scale).
Both meditation programs led to greater reductions in depressive symptoms and identity threat than the wait-list condition, with moderate effect sizes, and both increased cognitive decentering. There were no reliable differences between the two meditation programs on these outcomes. Contrary to the researchers’ expectations, only the focused-attention group showed a reduction in dysfunctional attitudes relative to the wait-list group; the self-inquiry group did not.
The meditation programs did not differ reliably from the wait-list group in their overall effects on connectedness to humanity or nature. However, exploratory analyses found that only the self-inquiry group showed increases in both forms of connectedness from before to after the program.
Exploratory analyses of the processes behind these changes suggested that, in the focused-attention group, increases in cognitive decentering fully accounted for the reduction in depressive symptoms and partly accounted for the reduction in dysfunctional attitudes. In the self-inquiry group, increases in connectedness to humanity partly accounted for reductions in identity threat. Unexpectedly, increases in connectedness to nature in this group were linked to smaller reductions in identity threat, and none of the measured processes explained the self-inquiry group’s reduction in depressive symptoms. Because these analyses were run separately within each group, they do not allow a direct statistical comparison of the two practices’ mechanisms.
“Attentional and deconstructive meditation practices yield comparable benefits for depression-related outcomes but operate through partially distinct mechanisms. Cognitive decentering played a central mechanism in attentional meditation [the focused-attention meditation procedure] while deconstructive practice [the self-inquiry meditation procedure] showed exploratory associations with connectedness [to nature and to humanity], warranting cautious interpretation,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the mechanisms through which meditation practices might affect depressive symptoms. However, it should be noted that participants in the control group knew they were not receiving treatment, and all outcomes were based on self-reports, which leaves room for expectancy effects and self-report bias. Participants had not been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, and their average depression scores were low and within the nonclinical range.
Both meditation programs were delivered by the same instructor, who was also the study’s first author, leaving open the possibility that instructor-related effects influenced the results. In addition, 20 participants dropped out of the wait-list group compared with four or five in each meditation group, the study was not preregistered, and there was no long-term follow-up. Participants were also mostly women who signed up for a meditation study and may have been especially receptive to it.
The paper, “Preventing Depression through Selflessness: Effects and Mechanisms of Attentional vs. Deconstructive Meditation in a Three–Arm Randomized Controlled Trial,” was authored by Céline Stinus and Sophie Berjot.

Pope's surgeon details operating on the "ideal patient" after lung cancer discovery "entirely by chance"
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have shifted dynamics, expectations, and assessments of whether the conflict could restart.
The high oil prices come amid a decline in stock prices on Wall Street, amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the United States, and thus also affecting Israel.
That is because the United States has been working hard to keep diesel and oil prices from skyrocketing. There has been a lot of messaging that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that other energy sources exist, but the question is whether the global market will accept those assertions.
Recent videos showing ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress are certainly not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
What will the Houthis do?
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group there. All this could continue to disrupt global trade. For example, when attacks hit pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, repairs can take weeks. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting policy regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Meanwhile, Iran continues to be blockaded, but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. As a result, we see potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the United States; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India
Incident took place at festival in Kolkata, in India’s West Bengal state, amid large crowds and rainfall, police say.
A “stampede” during a Hindu religious festival in eastern India has killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others, officials said.
The stampede in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state, happened on Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga.
According to police, some worshippers fell on the road and were trampled.
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment.
Among the dead was a seven-year-old girl, Adhikari told reporters.
He announced that a special investigation team to be headed by a judge of the state’s high court would look into the disaster.
Police detained some pavilion organisers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Police said the injured were taken to hospital from a Durga Puja pandal, a temporary pavilion housing idols of the goddess Durga at a festival which attracts thousands of devotees.
A police statement said the stampede happened in the evening due to “heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall”.
A senior police official at the scene told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal [pavilion] was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the incident as “saddening”.
“Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery. The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families,” Modi wrote on X.
Modi’s office announced compensation of 200,000 rupees ($2,106) for the next of kin of those who died and 50,000 rupees ($527) each for the injured.
Interior Minister Amit Shah said the “administration is ensuring that all possible medical facilities are being provided to the injured”.
About 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Deadly crowd incidents happen frequently at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, often due to poor management and safety lapses.
Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others. In Bengaluru, 11 fans were crushed to death during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
In southern Tamil Nadu state, 36 people were killed in a stampede at a campaign rally for a popular actor-turned-politician.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.

Salman refused to stay silent. His brother paid the price
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:39:45 UTC
04:39:45 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Salman Shabbir was having breakfast at his Sydney home when his phone rang in the pre-dawn hours of 15 March 2024.
On the other end of the line, in Pakistan, his sister-in-law was in a panic.
"They're here. They're asking for you. They're taking your brother," she told Shabbir.
Then an unfamiliar man came on the line and asked Shabbir to confirm his identity.
Shabbir says he could hear his sister-in-law screaming in the background, pleading with the men not to take her husband. Then the screams fell silent.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He was in Australia, thousands of kilometres from his family in Pakistan, a country he left 11 years earlier.
Hours later, Shabbir says, the callers demanded that he stop posting about Pakistan's politics on his X account.
SBS News has contacted the High Commission for Pakistan in Canberra for comment but did not receive a reply by the deadline.
The episode raises a disturbing question: can speaking out against a government from abroad put the people you love at risk? It is a question at the heart of transnational repression in which governments or their alleged proxies seek to silence critics beyond their borders.
Shabbir, his activism and his family
In the hours after the call, Shabbir tried to piece together what had happened to his brother.
He says several uniformed men arrived in a black ute known locally as a Vigo Dala. One was from the local police; the others wore commando-style clothing and carried what Shabbir describes as "huge guns”.
"They were sent by the [Pakistani] military," he alleges.
"I have no doubt."
Shabbir runs an X account called Citizen Action, which he initially used to advocate for overseas voting rights. He later turned to criticising Pakistan's elections and the treatment of former prime minister Imran Khan.
Shabbir alleges that, days before his brother was taken, Pakistan's then-information minister, Attaullah Tarar, criticised a petition he had launched. The petition addressed bodies within the European Union and highlighted the alleged mistreatment of Khan, arguing it breached human rights expectations embedded in trade agreements. Shabbir says the petition attracted more than 3,000 signatures.
Khan has been jailed since 2023 following a string of convictions and charges. He and his party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, maintain the cases are politically motivated and aimed at keeping him out of power.
"I tweeted out that they have taken my brother, and the tweet started going viral," Shabbir says.
He says he also contacted Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT), the National Security Hotline, the Australian Federal Police (AFP), and Pakistan's then-high commissioner to Australia, seeking help. He also spoke to a Pakistani media outlet.
Within 12 hours, Shabbir received a second call. The caller asked where Shabbir was and whether he had an Australian passport. He demanded Shabbir's X username and password. Shabbir says he refused.
The caller then warned they would continue to hold his brother if Shabbir wouldn't comply, before ending the call.
Shabbir says he received a third call about half an hour later. SBS News obtained a recording of the calls, first published by Drop Site News.
The callers demanded that Shabbir stop posting on X about Pakistan's politics, initially for three months. When he refused, he says they reduced the demand to one month and then five days.
At one point, Shabbir alleges, the men tortured his brother during the call.
"The conversation got really heated.
They tortured my brother on the call, and he made sure that I heard his screams.
Not an isolated incident
Shabbir's experience is not the only alleged case of transnational repression involving people in Australia.
In recent years, allegations have included death threats linked to the Cambodian government, requests to spy on a neighbour allegedly made on behalf of the Chinese government, and stalking orders attributed to the Iranian government. Other reports have involved India, Myanmar, Rwanda, South Sudan, Vietnam and other countries.
Australians have also reportedly been targeted overseas. Melbourne-based Tran Hiep is currently being detained in Vietnam on terrorism and sabotage charges, which the United States-based pro-democracy group Viet Tan, designated as a terrorist group by Vietnam, alleges are unfounded.
In another case, last year, an Australian journalist was arrested in Thailand at Malaysia's request over a criminal defamation complaint, prompting criticism from human rights groups.
In September, a Senate inquiry was launched to examine the nature, scale and methods of transnational repression, including its impacts on diaspora communities and democratic processes. The inquiry was established by a Greens motion with support from the Coalition.
Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge tells SBS News: "The purpose of this inquiry is to surface this and force parliament to confront the reality that there are foreign governments, bad actors in other parts of the world that are actively trying to silence and stifle political discussion inside Australia."
Shoebridge says perpetrators can be "incredibly bold" and make little effort to hide their actions.
They're making the phone calls, they're sending the social media messages, they're having, sometimes somebody who's a consular official, turn up or attend a community rally and start taking photos and observe what's happening.
"Sometimes it's quite overt and there is a potentially quite significant evidentiary thread."
He says he's spoken to many Australians who've experienced transnational repression, including Shabbir, who contacted him after his brother was taken.
How transnational repression works
Transnational repression occurs when states or their proxies seek to control, intimidate or punish people for their activities beyond their own borders.
Tactics range from threats, surveillance and physical violence to pressure on relatives and the misuse of legal or law enforcement systems. They can also include denying passports or consular services, refusing re-entry into the country or revoking nationality. Some acts are criminal offences, while others can foster fear and mistrust within diaspora communities.
The issue has drawn growing concern from the United Nations. More than 100 UN special rapporteurs and mandate holders expressed "deep concern" over the "growing challenge" in a statement published last month.
At the 56th session of the UN Human Rights Council in June 2024, Australia joined with more than 45 other countries in a statement condemning transnational repression as a threat to sovereignty, democracy and human rights, and calling for stronger protections for those at risk.
For people living in exile, the effects can extend well beyond their own safety, reaching family members who remain in their country of origin.
Naung Naung, a refugee from Myanmar who studies transnational repression, says Myanmar people in Australia have reported threatening phone calls, surveillance, intimidation at pro-democracy events and restrictions on passports, as well as the alleged misuse of Australian law.
In 2021, the Myanmar embassy in Canberra was accused of transnational repression after it wrote to students demanding they pledge loyalty to the military junta.
Naung says his brother was doxed because of his alleged friendship with figures from the National Unity Government, an opposition administration formed after the 2021 military coup, in their hometown. He says a photo his brother had posted online was shared in a pro-military Telegram channel with calls for arrest.
"My parents had to move to a different town, and they have not been able to come back since then to my hometown," he tells SBS News.
For years, Naung used a pseudonym online, despite living in Australia.
He remains too worried about his family's safety to connect with his parents on social media.
I don't want to be a victim of the transnational repression. I don't want to be a victim of the subject I'm studying.
In a statement, the Embassy of Myanmar in Canberra denied all allegations it has engaged in transnational repression or foreign interference, calling them “entirely groundless” and saying it acts in accordance with Australian law and relevant diplomatic rules and regulations.
The embassy said it has never threatened, surveilled, or intimidated members of the Myanmar community in Australia, and that it has handled passport-related matters in accordance with applicable rules and regulations.
“It is a globally widespread phenomenon for individual with differing point of views to criticize and target one another on social media,” the embassy said.
How widespread is transnational repression in Australia?
The scale of transnational repression in Australia is difficult to establish, partly because there is no comprehensive public data tracking reported cases, according to Shoebridge.
"One of the reasons is when you go to, for example, the Australian Federal Police — and I've put many complaints in front of them about foreign interference — after a rudimentary review of it, they will say, 'Well, actually the core potentially criminal action is happening in another country and therefore they won't undertake a police investigation and therefore they don't gather the data,'" he says.
In recent years, the AFP has pursued several cases involving alleged transnational repression.
In one case, three Chinese nationals have been accused of covertly collecting information about a Canberra Buddhist association on behalf of a Chinese public security bureau.
The Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) has also documented attempts to intimidate or harm critics living in Australia. In his 2024 annual threat assessment, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess said the Counter Foreign Interference Taskforce, established in 2020, had conducted more than 120 operations to mitigate threats to communities, Australia's political system and classified information.
The operations covered a range of foreign interference threats, Burgess said at the time.
"One involved an individual working on behalf of a foreign government who wanted to physically harm an Australian-based critic of the regime, including attempts to identify the target's home address and bank details, hiring a subcontractor to photograph the house, and requesting a quote for 'severe action' against the dissident.
"Even more recently, a foreign intelligence service tried to find an Australian who would be willing to make a different dissident quote 'disappear'."
When fear follows you abroad
Mubashar Hasan is a Sydney-based researcher on transnational repression whose work draws on both his own experience and accounts from diaspora communities. He was a political science professor in Bangladesh before relocating to Norway and later moving to Australia in 2020, after being forcibly disappeared by Bangladesh's military in 2017.
I remember on the first day of kidnapping when they blindfolded me, they were beating me. They put me in handcuffs.
"I heard people crying. I heard people begging. There was no freedom to even drink water as you want. There was a 24-hour high-voltage light," he tells SBS News.
Hasan says he was held at a secret detention site for 44 days, but after his release, he could no longer feel safe in Bangladesh.
"I became a kind of refugee in my own country, because the police, the intelligence, the judge, everyone knew there was a crime against humanity that took place against me, but no-one was doing anything," he says.
SBS News tried several times to contact the Bangladeshi embassy for comment but did not receive a response.
After relocating to Norway, Hasan began hearing similar accounts from other people, some of whom were living in exile.
He later turned to researching transnational repression, taking care with how he wrote about the subject because he feared attracting the attention of authorities back home. He has since moved to Australia, where he studies the issue and works with diaspora communities.
"In my experience of engaging with the community members from Myanmar, Iran, Rwanda, South Sudan, and a few other countries, we've found mistrust within the community," he says.
Some people fear they are being watched by others in their own community; others avoid community gatherings or posting on social media, worried about intimidation or harassment.
Hasan says more needs to be done to address the effects of transnational repression on migrant communities.
"Communities here need to find confidence in the authorities that yes, if I believe that I'm facing repression, I could go somewhere, and that could be a government department, an agency or even a counselling support system where I can go and talk about it and people will listen."
Calls for reform
In July, Independent National Security Legislation Monitor Jake Blight completed a statutory review of Australia's foreign interference laws.
He says evidence from ASIO, AFP, civil society and academics convinced him transnational repression is a "very serious and growing problem".
Blight says it can be addressed using diplomatic pressure, sanctions, and the visa system, as well as through criminal law.
"Many types of these actions are already crimes. Assaulting people, stalking people, using a telecommunication service to menace or harass: these are all offences," he tells SBS News.
"And while I found a few gaps in the offences, it's very challenging when you're talking about prosecuting people who are acting offshore."
Those who are outside the country are very difficult to prosecute under Australian law.
Blight's review identified four areas for reform: creating a new offence for coerced repatriation; extending an existing foreign interference offence concerning democratic and political rights from Australians to anyone in Australia; increasing penalties for people paid to commit crimes on behalf of foreign governments; and extending protections against foreign interference to judicial proceedings, royal commissions and independent inquiries.
A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs told SBS News the government takes the "persistent, evolving and increasingly complex threat" seriously.
They said the government is carefully considering Blight's recommendations and "is committed to ensuring Australia's robust criminal offences remain fit-for-purpose to address the risks posed by espionage and foreign interference, including transnational repression".
In May, the government launched the Counter Foreign Interference Community Support Hub, providing online resources in more than 23 languages to help recognise and respond to foreign interference.
But Shoebridge wants the law to go further.
"I think if somebody in a third country is threatening to harm somebody's relatives, threatening to potentially destroy their house, to coerce them, to change someone's behaviour in Australia, and if you can establish that causal connection, then I think it should be a crime on the Australian statute books," he says.
Shabbir encountered the limits of Australia's response firsthand when he tried to get help after his brother was taken.
"On the day I called DFAT, they asked me to call the National Security Hotline, who asked me to call AFP, who asked me to call DFAT," he says.
"It was a bit of ping-pong, to be honest, but in the end, I was forwarded a flyer that was made by Senator [David] Shoebridge's office, and it had guidelines on how to register such a case, and something called the category called foreign interference."
Eventually, Shabbir says he got a call from NSW Police, who discussed the case and conducted a risk assessment. An officer gave him a case number and told him to call if anything changes.
His brother was ultimately released within a day, and Shabbir continues his online activism, but he wants to see greater action to protect Australian citizens from alleged transnational repression.
Like Shoebridge, he wants Australian authorities to recognise what he calls the "extraterritorial proxy loophole" — where threats made through relatives overseas fall outside the reach of Australian law because the conduct occurred offshore.
They have to recognise it as a criminal offence because ultimately the target was an Australian citizen.

European diplomats say they were attacked by Israeli settlers in the West Bank; Israel urges caution before drawing conclusions

"The Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will pursue these investigations to their full extent, ensuring that everyone involved in such incidents is brought to justice," the statement said.

Netanyahu alleges reports come amid concerns of a smear campaign against Israel
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office condemned the reports of the attacks on the diplomats and urged caution against drawing conclusions, as it tried to cast doubt over the circumstances surrounding the attack.

Baudoux said he did not suffer serious injuries. He said the attackers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, and threw him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
Netanyahu's office, in its statement, said Baudoux previously raised the Palestinian flag over the Aulnoye-Aymeries municipal building, "prompting French authorities to order its removal."

Activists say authorities do little to stop it, particularly during this year's annual olive harvest.
Netanyahu, in the past, has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.
Human rights groups and critics say the government is complicit in the attacks and that Netanyahu's condemnation appears to be posturing since the Israeli military often intervenes on the settlers' side and the perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.
