‘A sudden blow to my head’: Flydubai captain recalls cockpit attack that nearly downed the jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:29:12 UTC
04:29:12 KST

Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar, who was seriously wounded when his Omani co-pilot attacked him during a flight to Israel, has spoken publicly about the terrifying moments inside the cockpit and his desperate efforts to prevent the aircraft from crashing.
In interviews published Saturday by the Emirati newspaper The National and Sky News Arabia, Machchhar described how he managed to reach the cockpit door despite severe injuries, allowing Israeli passengers and crew members to enter and help stop the attacker.
Both interviews were conducted at his hospital bedside in Abu Dhabi, where he remains under medical care. His head was still bandaged, although he appeared stronger than during an earlier televised conversation with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi several days after the September 30 attack. Neither interview devoted much attention to the significant role played by the Israeli passengers in preventing the disaster.
Machchhar described his brief interactions with the attacker, Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, before the assault, saying there had been nothing unusual about his behavior. The two had never flown together before.
Asked about Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayun, who made international headlines as the "plumber who saved the plane," Machchhar said he had little recollection of his involvement.
"To be honest, I don't know the plumber's story," he said. "But I do remember someone senior on the flight saying that the captain was in control. I didn't see him."
He then laughed when asked whether a plumber could land an aircraft. "Can a plumber land a plane? I don't want to speculate. All my memories and energy at that moment were focused on staying alive," he said.
Machchhar explained that he was drifting in and out of consciousness and that his vision had been severely impaired by the repeated blows he suffered.
In his interview with The National, Machchhar recalled initially believing that the violent blow to his head had been caused by a technical malfunction or an object falling from the aircraft's ceiling. "It was such a hard blow that I nearly fell onto the controls," he said.
The captain said he had met al-Hammami for the first time that morning. "We exchanged some small talk, but nothing particularly deep, just like on other flights. There was never anything that made me think something was wrong."
When the attack began, his first instinct was to release his seat belt and try to defend himself. "The first thing I did was free myself from the seat belts and try to block the blows as much as possible," he recalled. "The blows were directed at my head. After the first few, my vision narrowed dramatically, and I could only make out outlines."
Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to reach toward the mechanism that opens the cockpit door. "My hand went to the handle that opens the door, and I shouted for my colleagues. That's when I believe I lost consciousness for the first time. I heard the door opening," he said.
The most frightening moment came when he realized the aircraft was losing altitude. "The scariest thing was hearing the engines slow down and feeling the nose of the aircraft dive," he recalled.
He said he repeatedly tried to reach the door, desperate to let others into the cockpit. "I kept looking for the door. People ask me whether I opened it. I tried to get to it. I pushed, tried to reach out. But the next thing I remember is lying face down. And thank God, the cockpit door was open."
Machchhar said he did not know whether he would survive the ordeal but refused to give up. "I wasn't sure I would come out of it alive, but I didn't give up. I thought about my son and daughter. It was as though a survival instinct had taken over, and fortunately it saved me and all the other passengers and my colleagues. I would say a higher power was involved."
Speaking separately to Sky News Arabia, Machchhar provided further details about the moments immediately preceding the attack. He said al-Hammami had indicated that he wanted to pray inside the cockpit.
"He wanted to pray, so he stood up and started praying," Machchhar recalled. "On our 737, the aircraft I fly, the cockpit isn't particularly large. Out of respect for someone who is praying, I try not to look at them."
The captain continued working, checking flight information on his computer. "I was doing my job, sitting there and checking the timings and everything else on my computer, when suddenly I received a very hard blow to the back of my head," he said.
"It was an extremely strong blow. I felt that whatever struck me was very hard and solid. At that moment, I had no idea what had hit me. As the incident continued, I kept losing and regaining consciousness."
Machchhar said the attacker appeared to say something while striking him, but he could not understand the words.
Asked by the Sky News Arabia interviewer whether there had been a moment when he thought he might not survive, Machchhar acknowledged that he was still struggling to process what happened. "I'm trying to get over it now, but yes, there was a moment when I realized I had to tell myself: Do something. You can't die like this," he said.
He stressed that he had not resigned himself to dying. Instead, he felt an overwhelming need to act before it was too late. "It wasn't that I had accepted my death. It was more a feeling that I had to do something. There was a moment when I realized that if nothing was done immediately..."
Then the cockpit door opened, and the situation changed dramatically. "When the door opened, the scene was completely different. I remember lying face down. There was panic, of course, and screaming," he said.
Machchhar reserved particular praise for the colleague who eventually took control of the aircraft.
"What happened afterward, the fact that another colleague of mine took over the controls and saved the situation, deserves enormous praise," he said. "It's something I will carry with me until the day I die."

Albanian police fire rubber bullets as protests against Rama escalate
Five days of clashes rock Tirana as students join a wider movement demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation.
Police in Albania have fired rubber bullets at antigovernment protesters in the capital, Tirana, as violent clashes intensify over demands for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The clashes continued on Saturday for a fifth consecutive day after high school and university students joined a broader movement against Rama, whose governing centre-left Socialist Party has held power since 2013.
The unrest has brought growing anger over education, unemployment and alleged corruption into a wider confrontation with the government.
Protesters threw stones, petrol bombs and fireworks at police near Rama’s office and elsewhere in central Tirana.
Some set cars and rubbish bins alight, creating burning barricades across streets.
Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and baton charges as demonstrators pushed against security lines.
The AFP news agency reported that officers used rubber bullets for the first time since the demonstrations began.
National police chief Skender Hita confirmed their use at a news conference on Saturday, saying they had been deployed “in a limited manner”.
The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare said nine protesters and four police officers received medical treatment on Saturday.
Hita said 167 people had been arrested over five days of unrest, while 132 officers had been injured.
Seven police officers were also suspended pending investigations into allegations that they had exceeded their authority.
Rama, who is serving his fourth term and has refused to resign, visited businesses damaged during the unrest on Saturday. He promised to listen to students and protect their right to demonstrate, while warning against further destruction.
He also accused his conservative political opponents of encouraging the violence.
Growing discontent
The students have complained about expensive university fees, poor educational facilities and limited employment opportunities, alongside allegations of government corruption.
At the start of Saturday’s demonstration, protesters set fire to a suitcase and threw it into the Ministry of Education’s courtyard. AFP reported that the gesture symbolised their determination not to leave Albania in search of better opportunities.
“We are demanding our rights, our future and a better country,” journalism student Sinan Billa told AFP.
The student demonstrations have added to months of antigovernment rallies organised by the Flamingo movement, which began as a campaign against a luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast.
The project is linked to an investment company founded by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
The movement has since widened its demands to include Rama’s resignation amid allegations of corruption against his government.
The unrest has also spread beyond Tirana. Local media reported that protesters in the coastal city of Durres damaged a post office and blocked roads with burning barricades, extending the confrontations beyond the capital.

Poland asks EP to waive immunity of ex-CEO at state oil giant
Poland submitted on Thursday a request to the European Parliament (EP) seeking to waive the immunity of MEP Daniel Obajtek, a former CEO of state oil conglomerate Orlen, as well as to authorise his pre-trial detention, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek announced on X.
The request relates to an investigation into the artificial lowering of fuel prices in 2023, a period during which Obajtek served as CEO of Orlen, said Zurek, who is also the country's Prosecutor General.
Investigators allege that Obajtek, while serving as CEO of Orlen and "acting on grounds unrelated to economic considerations", instructed subordinates to lower wholesale and retail fuel prices. The objective was to ensure that, between October 1 and October 15, 2023, the price of a litre of fuel would not exceed PLN 5.99 (EUR 1.4) at the pump.
The prosecution asserts that Obajtek acted in violation of established procedures and, "despite mounting problems and losses, personally monitored the operation and issued ongoing directives to maintain the artificially low rates", according to Zurek's post.
He argued that Obajtek's decisions led to a fuel shortage at over 600 service stations, causing damage to Orlen exceeding PLN 4.1 billion (EUR 938 million).
Zurek added that the acts covered by the request to lift immunity carry a potential sentence of up to 25 years in prison.
In early October, five current and former Orlen managers were charged in connection with the suspected manipulation of fuel prices.
Daniel Obajtek is currently a member of the European Parliament representing Poland's ex-governing socially-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. He served as CEO of Orlen from 2018 to 2024. (PAP)

What Trump’s Waiver of New Russia Sanctions Means for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:17:33 UTC
04:17:33 KST

President Donald Trump signed an executive order Friday that waives many of the sanctions in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Congress passed in the late senator’s name last month. The waiver, coming a week after Trump announced a diesel deal with Russia, also underscores fraying relations between the U.S. and Ukraine.
The law, which was set to take effect Oct. 18, called for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and other entities, alongside tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported into the U.S. from major buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. Those measures were intended to restrict the financial resources supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Read More: Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
The U.K.’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office estimated in June 2025 that international sanctions had deprived the Russian state of at least $450 billion in war funds since February 2022, including through lost oil tax revenues and immobilized central-bank reserves.
While Trump’s waiver leaves existing sanctions in place, it blocks the additional pressure the new measures were intended to exert.
Trump has also pushed Ukraine to scale back its own campaign against Russia’s energy sector, repeatedly urging Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure and suggesting that those attacks are driving up U.S. fuel prices. But Ukrainian strikes are only one factor affecting fuel prices; disruptions linked to the war with Iran are largely responsible for constraining global supplies, while reduced Russian refinery activity has added pressure to diesel markets.
On Oct. 11, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire.” But Ukrainian officials reported Russian strikes on energy infrastructure hours after his announcement, and Zelensky said the purported agreement was news to him.
That same day, Trump called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky. Withdrawing sanctions within a week of those statements, and thereby improving Russia’s financial position, points to an increasingly uneven display of support from the U.S.
Jeff Colgan, a professor of political science at Brown University, tells TIME that the decision is basically “is like trading [Ukrainian] democracy for diesel.”
A diesel deal with Russia, announced Oct. 9, is one of the many recent actions Trump has taken in an effort to reduce fuel prices for Americans ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. The deal came with an easing of sanctions as the Treasury Department issued a temporary license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel, including imports into the U.S., through April 7, 2027.
In his announcement of the deal on Truth Social, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply global markets with more than 4.8 million tons of diesel, claiming that it would bring diesel prices down “IN RECORD NUMBERS.”
But experts question whether the deal would actually have any material impact on the price of fuel for American consumers.
“There could be a modest short-term effect on wholesale prices, but only a small and delayed benefit, if any, would reach consumers at the pump,” says Tatiana Mitrova, a fellow at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.
The waiver signed Friday, in comparison, could potentially prevent additional disruption to the global energy market. It allows Russian oil to continue flowing to importers like China and India, preventing further market volatility.
“The broader sanctions waiver may prevent additional market disruptions, but it does not itself create new supply,” Mitrova says. “The potential economic benefit to American consumers looks rather modest compared with the geopolitical cost of weakening sanctions pressure.”
Reducing that pressure—which has widely been interpreted as a component of the diesel deal, though it has not been explicitly identified as such—likely benefits Russia more than the monetary value of the diesel deal itself, Mitrova points out.
“The much bigger financial benefit for Moscow is avoiding additional sanctions that could have undermined its much larger crude oil export revenues,” she says.
And while Trump has touted the benefits of the deal, Colgan questions whether they will be tangible to any country other than Russia itself.
“Easing the sanctions probably won't move global prices very much (big market), but could mean substantial extra revenue for Russia,” he says.
But the potential consequences extend beyond Russia’s balance sheet. The waiver also raises questions about Washington’s commitment to Ukraine as relations between the two countries deteriorate.
How might the sanctions waiver affect Ukraine?
Beyond its impact on global diesel prices, Trump’s sanctions waiver could deepen a growing rift between the U.S. and Ukraine—raising further questions about Washington’s support for Kyiv.
Konstantin Sonin, a Russian economist and a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, reads the move as a symbolic gesture of support for Russian President Vladimir Putin. He suggests that it could send a message to U.S. allies that extends beyond economic considerations.
“I think this will be read by Ukraine and Ukraine leadership—and European leadership—as another step in the United States withdrawing from being an active European player,” he tells TIME.
In addition to bolstering Russia’s finances and giving it latitude in its invasion of Ukraine, Sonin says that the waiver of additional sanctions could also “boost morale” for Putin.
“It’s another bit of signaling that the United States is not as supportive of Ukraine as they were historically,” he adds. “You still cannot say that the United States is on Putin's side, but it is another bit of diminishing support for Ukraine.”
Mitrova agrees that the biggest benefit to Russia might be more strategic than financial.
“For Putin, the most valuable outcome may not be additional diesel revenues but the perception that Washington is increasingly prioritizing domestic energy prices over sustained pressure on Russia,” she says. “That could reinforce the Kremlin’s belief that it can outlast Western support rather than make meaningful concessions.”
Zelensky criticized the decision to block the new sanctions.
“The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me,” the Ukrainian President wrote on X on Saturday. “And it definitely helps only the Russians. It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people. This certainly does not stop the war.”
Mitrova argues that in easing sanctions, the U.S. also compromises its position with European leadership that has continued to align closely with Zelensky and Ukraine.
“Europe is still tightening sanctions against Russia, while Washington is now moving in the opposite direction,” she says. “By suspending sanctions that were designed to discourage major countries from buying Russian energy, Washington risks undermining a central pillar of the Western strategy toward Russia.”
Why Republicans and Democrats are criticizing the waiver
Trump’s waiver earned a flood of criticism from both sides of the aisle, particularly since it undermined a widely supported act of Congress. The Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 cleared Congress on Sept. 16 with overwhelming bipartisan support: a vote of 86-11 in the Senate and a vote of 262-159 in the House.
North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who is leaving office in January, called the decision “beyond irresponsible” on Saturday.
Suggesting that the Trump Administration is overtly snubbing the will of the legislative branch, Tillis wrote on X: “It’s unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine.”
Texas Republican Sen. John Cornyn reacted by saying “Lindsey would be appalled,” referencing the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham—a staunch Ukraine supporter after whom the sanctions act was named. Graham had spent over a year petitioning for the move before his death on July 11.
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, said in a statement that Trump was “enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer released a statement Saturday saying that “by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump’s deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier.”
Trump was able to waive the sanctions through a safety valve provision embedded in the legislation. The law allowed Trump to waive its sanctions and tariffs after submitting a written certification to Congress that doing so was in the national interest, along with a report explaining that determination. In Friday’s order, Trump said he had submitted both.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump wrote in the order. “I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States.”
Trump has not yet publicly disclosed how the move served national interests, and the White House did not reply to TIME’s request for comment.
Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to fill his seat in South Carolina and is running for election this November to keep it, said at a campaign stop on Saturday that the decision was Trump’s to make; however, she voiced disapproval, saying that she would prefer to “keep the pressure on Russia.”
“I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” she said.

Aoun's remarks came as he received a French delegation headed by Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.
Lebanon seeks to extend UNIFIL’s mandate and welcomes any arrangement that ensures a continued international presence in the country’s south to prevent power vacuum, he said.
Barrot expressed French solidarity with Lebanon and its continued support across all sectors, the statement said, adding that he also reaffirmed readiness to mobilize resources to address urgent humanitarian needs in the Arab country.
Israel began its deadly attacks in southern Lebanon in early March, and has continued the bombing unabated despite a U.S.-sponsored framework agreement in June paving the way for Israeli withdrawal and the disarmament of Hezbollah.

====================================================================================================

They were about to break up before October 7. Then Hamas captivity changed their love story forever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:05:02 UTC
04:05:02 KST

The conversation about the future of their relationship that Sasha Troufanov and Sapir Cohen had planned after a year together never happened. Instead, they found themselves somewhere neither could have imagined, though not particularly far from each other. He was being held in a hideout in the Gaza Strip, while she was underground in a tunnel.
"Our relationship wasn't very good in the months before we were kidnapped, and you could even say we were about to break up just before October 7," recalls Sapir, who was released from Hamas captivity after 55 days and is now sitting on a sofa beside Sasha, who was freed after 498 days.
"I think that if October 7 hadn't happened, we would have had a conversation after the Jewish holidays along the lines of, 'Listen, I don't think this relationship is going anywhere. We've tried everything, including moving in together and opening up to each other, but it's just not working. We're too different, and for both our sakes, I think it's better if we break up,'" Sasha says.
Who would have initiated that conversation?
"Probably Sapir. She was almost 29, and I was 27. She wanted a serious relationship and marriage, while I'd just moved to central Israel after finishing my studies in the south. Marriage was the last thing on my mind. That's why, when I was in captivity, I never expected her to wait for me. Logically, she had absolutely no reason to."
But she did wait. For more than 400 days after her own release, she joined the campaign to bring him home and became a source of support for his mother, Lena.
"I didn't even know where I should wait when they told us he was coming back," Sapir recalls. "I thought it wouldn't be appropriate for me to be at the first reception point in Re'im, which is usually reserved for family members. I didn't want to surprise him, and I knew he wasn't expecting me. I didn't want him to feel obligated. But Lena was absolutely insistent, and I felt I deserved to see Sasha reunited with his mother after such a long struggle, regardless of what happened between us."
"From my perspective, she completely invited herself," Sasha jokes.
"We practically threw ourselves at him, and after that, I barely remember anything because I was so overwhelmed," Sapir says. "He told me he'd found faith during captivity, and I immediately saw in him qualities I'd always hoped he would have. Still, I tried to give him space and stayed out of his room. But when they asked whether he wanted to sleep alone, with his mother or with me, he called for me."
"I'd already spent enough time sleeping alone, and sleeping with Mom would have been strange," Sasha says. "At first, the whole interaction was awkward. You're having these intimate conversations with someone you've already broken up with in your head and never expected to see there. Then you discover she was a major part of what had become your most important goal in captivity: making sure your mother stayed alive.
"There was enormous gratitude, but also a need to understand where our relationship stood. And I discovered that we had both changed."
Their journey culminated in a wedding in July, attended by 500 guests who could scarcely believe the moment was real. Among them were Israel's president and Nitzan Alon, who headed the military's hostage headquarters. "They were invited by Lena, because they really helped us throughout the way," Sapir recalls. "We felt they deserved to be part of our happiness. I saw this wedding as a moment of national joy, not just a personal celebration."
"Sasha greeted the guests, while I stayed out of sight until the ceremony. As I left the bridal suite, I caught a glimpse of everyone through a glass door. I thought about how unimaginable this moment had seemed when we were both being held underground."
Sapir walked down the aisle to "MiMa'amakim" ("Out of the Depths") by Israeli musician Idan Raichel, a song Sasha had heard while in captivity. 
"A terrorist guarding me once left his radio with me," Sasha recalls. "I listened at a very low volume so I wouldn't drain the battery. I remember being desperately hungry and hearing all those radio commercials for supermarket chicken and grilled-meat restaurants. Then this song came on, and I thought about Sapir."
"There was also 'Shir LaMa'alot,' the song Sasha walked down the aisle to," Sapir adds. "I used to hear it in my head when I thought about him in captivity."
"For me, being able to walk down the aisle at my own wedding after everything my legs had been through in Gaza was extraordinary," Sasha says. "Back on October 7, when they were using broomsticks as makeshift splints for my injured legs, I could never have imagined a moment like that. I was a different person then."
"During our final slow dance, I suddenly noticed that everyone around us was crying, just crying tears of joy," Sapir says. "I told Sasha, 'Look what's happening here.' And he said, 'Sapir, I'm crying too.'"
‘I decided I had to break up with him’
Today, after the adrenaline of two separate experiences of captivity, the struggle to bring the hostages home, speaking tours around the world, a marriage proposal in the Caribbean and a wedding, the couple are a little less emotional.
They are the first to acknowledge that their relationship is a miracle, much like their survival after countless moments in which they believed they were about to die.
But returning to ordinary life is another matter. They are now two people in their 30s who lost a substantial part of their 20s and were left with trauma instead.
We meet in an apartment in central Tel Aviv, about a 10-minute walk from the sea, which friends have temporarily lent them.
"We're between temporary apartments right now," Sapir explains. "We came back from a speaking tour abroad, and we're living out of one suitcase of clothes I took with me, not realizing those would be all the clothes I'd have. Everything else is in storage until we move permanently to Herzliya soon."
Sasha has returned to his engineering job at Amazon on a part-time basis. "We don't really talk about captivity in our day-to-day lives, but we're not at the point where we can joke about it either," Sapir admits. "Sometimes I forget, or find it hard to believe, that I was actually held hostage. There were moments during captivity when I imagined I was being tested for a job with the Shin Bet security agency, and that any minute a recruiter would walk in and say, 'You're hired.'
"I can watch an interview with former hostages on television and think, 'Wow, what they went through was terrible,' and Sasha, sitting beside me, can't believe what he's hearing. It still hasn't fully sunk in that we went through it too."
"I look around and see that everyone has moved forward while I was gone, and you realize you're a step behind," Sasha says. "It's hard for me to have fallen out of the race. I feel as though I've been held back a grade, and I could have been somewhere else in my career. But then I remind myself of all the ways I grew during that time, and the picture changes.
"Before everything happened, all I cared about was making as much money as possible. I wanted to reach 10 million shekels as quickly as I could, have enough financial security to stop worrying about money and then become a teacher.
"After captivity, I can't wait that long to find meaning in my life. I need it now. I want to feel that being taken hostage and surviving isn't the greatest thing I'll ever accomplish."
"I was a software engineer before I was kidnapped, and even before that I'd been wondering whether it was right for me," Sapir says. "I didn't have the courage to leave, but when I came back, sitting in front of a computer working on some feature felt so far removed from who I was. Now I'm searching for what comes next."
They met on a dating app, and the beginning was hardly promising. "We were together for a year before the kidnapping, but it wasn't a year in which the relationship was getting better," Sasha says.
"I used to show my brothers pictures of guys from the app," Sapir recalls. "They'd say things like, 'Nah, boring,' or 'Wow, handsome!' With Sasha, everyone agreed he was good-looking.
"We talked for about two weeks before meeting, and it was genuinely fun. Then we met, and the first date wasn't great. I took the train all the way from Kiryat Ata to Sarona in Tel Aviv, and of course he didn't make the effort to come to me.
"When I saw him, I couldn't believe my eyes. It was like Hercules was walking toward me. But once we started talking, things just didn't click. The conversation felt awkward, and there was no chemistry.
"I headed back to the train station feeling disappointed, convinced we'd never speak again. But then he texted to ask if I'd gotten home all right."
"Neither of us thought there would be a second date," Sasha says. "On the way home, I thought about how little I'd enjoyed the date itself, but I remembered how much fun it had been talking to her for those two weeks beforehand. So I decided to cast a line."
"I replied, 'Good night, sweetie,' the way I'd written to him before our date," Sapir says. "When he asked, 'What, am I still sweet?' I told him yes. And that's how it continued."
The following dates were even stranger. 
"On our second date in Yarkon Park, a jackal picked up my bag in its mouth, and I had to chase it," Sasha says. "It also ate the cheese pastries she'd brought me. On our third date, a thief stole my phone without me noticing."
"He used my phone to call a service that helps locate lost phones," Sapir says. "The representative asked him, 'Wait, which phone are you calling from?' And he replied, 'Um, my girlfriend's phone.' I remember thinking, wow, this guy is serious about us."
"On another date, we were cuddling on a beach chair when someone came over, stood next to us and simply took my bag with my laptop inside," Sasha recalls. "At that point, with everything happening on our dates, I started wondering whether it was a sign that something wasn't right."
"And then, on our last date, they took him from me," Sapir says. "And they took me too."
When did things finally start to turn around between you?
"They didn't!" they answer in unison.
"As the months went by and I felt our relationship wasn't going anywhere, I pushed for us to move in together," Sapir says. "I felt like I still didn't really know him. Eventually, I told him, 'Your lease is ending. Let's move in together, or we break up.' Everything was an ultimatum.
"Somehow, he agreed. It was only after six months together that I first went to Nir Oz to meet his family and friends. Even after we moved in together, we struggled to communicate. We argued a lot and just couldn't understand each other."
"In a relationship, you have to be willing to give as well as receive," Sasha says. "Back then, I didn't want to give anything. Without realizing it, I kept pushing her to see how much she could take before she'd finally break up with me, because I couldn't bring myself to end things. Meanwhile, she wanted me to be the one to do it. I knew she was a good woman and that I'd be losing something valuable, so I didn't want to be the one who made that decision."
"I grew up in a family where achievement was everything. Then I served in military intelligence in southern Israel, where you feel enormous pressure to do your job well because you're protecting your own home. After that, I studied engineering at Ben-Gurion University.
"Everything in my life had been demanding and highly structured. Then I finally moved to central Israel, and suddenly I was in a relationship, another commitment with its own expectations. I wanted her to understand that I simply wasn't ready for that kind of commitment. Maybe I would be someday, but not yet. And she had to decide whether she wanted to stay."
"I was exhausted," Sapir says. "I was constantly traveling to see him in central Israel and initiating dates. That Saturday, when we were already living together and it was a holiday, I wanted to go somewhere. I knew that otherwise he'd spend the entire day playing PlayStation, and what was I supposed to do?
"So we could either visit my parents or his. I convinced him to go to the kibbutz, even though he kept saying he didn't want to. It was a real negotiation, and the winning argument was that it was the last day the kibbutz swimming pool would be open until Shavuot."
"I thought about that a lot in captivity," Sasha says. "Why was I so reluctant to go to the kibbutz that Saturday? I deliberately started taking my time, and we missed at least two buses."
"We argued on the bus on the way to the kibbutz," Sapir recalls. "I remember he said something that made me cry, and I decided I had to break up with him after that weekend."
‘I was certain they were going to execute me’
After that weekend, they really were separated, but not in the way Sapir had imagined.
When they arrived at Nir Oz, they settled into a guest room opposite Sasha's parents' house, planning to give their relationship one last chance.
"It was the guest room my mother always liked giving us because she could look out of her window and try to figure out where things stood between us," Sasha says. "On October 7, that turned out to be a less-than-ideal arrangement."
"I remember sitting with his friends on the evening of October 6," Sapir says. "I think Shani Goren was there, along with her sister Shira, Arbel Yehoud, and maybe Ariel joined us later. Everyone who grew up with Sasha."
"We had a great time, as always," Sasha recalls. "A little smoking, playing Jenga. We went to sleep around 1:30 or 2 a.m., and at 6:30 we woke up to chaos. Sapir woke me and said there was a rocket alert."
"I was in shock," Sapir says. "I wasn't used to anything like that. We waited, but there was no quiet, and it went on for about an hour. Then terrorists started entering communities, first Be'eri. I remember someone messaging Sasha that terrorists had infiltrated a kibbutz. Ynet was already publishing headlines with quotes like, 'Terrorists are murdering us, nobody is coming.'
"At that point, terrorists began entering our kibbutz. We could hear screams in Arabic and gunfire in the background. There was no safe room in the apartment, so we hid under the bed. Sasha was using his phone a little. I didn't touch mine. I didn't want to say goodbye to anyone, and I didn't send any messages."
Were you able to talk to each other under the bed?
"I was sure we were about to die, and I kept thinking, what am I supposed to say to him? Say goodbye? Tell him I love him? But after everything we'd been through that year, I didn't feel like I loved him at that moment. And yet, were we really going to die without me saying anything? Those were the thoughts racing through my mind as we hid under the bed."
"I was also a little angry that he couldn't protect me. We were both curled up like sardines, pressed against the wall, and he kept telling me to be quiet. All I could feel was anger."
"At one point, they started banging on our door," Sasha recalls. "The kind of banging that tells you someone is about to break it down and tear apart whoever is inside. By then I knew there was nothing I could do. It wasn't one or two terrorists, and I was helpless in a tiny room. The best thing I could think of was staying under the bed and hoping they'd miss us and leave.
"Sapir was having a panic attack. Pure panic. She wrapped herself in blankets, shaking and saying, 'Hug me, hug me.' But that wasn't the moment to start fumbling around under the bed trying to hug. It was the moment to figure out what was happening and how we might save ourselves.
"Then we saw the beam of light as the door opened, and it was as though death itself had entered the room. I saw uniforms and weapons. A terrorist came in and started overturning the beds. I was wearing boxer shorts, and Sapir had on a little pair of pajamas. I raised my hands, and he looked almost surprised. I shouted in English that we were civilians.
"About 10 terrorists came in carrying machetes, clubs and guns. They started approaching us and pulling Sapir out of all the blankets she'd wrapped herself in. I was trying to understand whether they intended to rape her in front of me or something like that. I started shouting in English, 'Give her pants!'
"From my military service, I had some idea of what was happening in Gaza and what they were capable of. I understood they could slaughter us, and worse. I just wanted them to put some clothes on her. One terrorist threw me a pair of jeans, thinking I was the one who needed something to wear. I kept insisting until one of them came over and punched me in the face.
"I started panicking because they were becoming violent. They grew angry and began rushing us. They took me out with my head down, on my knees. From that point, I couldn't see anything. I was certain they were going to execute me."
"I saw a burned-out tank as they were leading me toward a motorcycle," Sapir says. "And all I could think was, 'A Holocaust is happening, and the trees are still green, and the sun is still shining in the sky. How can that be?'"
‘The terrorist said, “Of course we're humane”’
Cohen was abducted by Hamas terrorists and held in apartments and tunnels alongside other hostages from Nir Oz. Troufanov, meanwhile, was kidnapped by Islamic Jihad terrorists and spent most of his captivity alone.
His entire family was either kidnapped or murdered in the attack. His mother, Lena, and grandmother, Irena, were abducted and held for 55 days, while his father, Vitaly, was killed and buried without family members present. Their home in Nir Oz, where the family had settled after immigrating from Russia more than 25 years earlier, was completely burned down.
"I arrived in Gaza completely broken," Sasha recalls. "At one point, after they'd already taken Sapir, I tried to escape. It was a matter of life or death because I imagined they'd take me into Gaza, torture me, try to extract military information from me and then kill me. When I tried to run away, my punishment was being shot in the legs from about a meter away. The bullets shattered my bones." He points to his legs, now resting on the sofa, with scars running along them.
"At the border, we fell off the motorcycle. I couldn't stand because of my leg, and I just collapsed with the bike. Then a group of Gazans started kicking and punching me. They took me to an apartment with a bag over my head. At first, they placed broomsticks around my leg to immobilize it, using an improvised elastic bandage. They also put an oven grill rack against my leg to keep it straight. I still have marks from it on my skin."
One of the hardest moments came when he began to comprehend his new reality and realized he might not be rescued anytime soon. "In those first days, I really gave up on everything," Sasha says. "I'd lost so much blood. I was physically and mentally exhausted. They kept moving me from one house to another, and I just lay down on a mattress and fell asleep.
"I woke up in the middle of the night because the medication had worn off. I wanted to believe it was all a dream. Then I woke up a little more, saw a dim light in the room and realized two terrorists were sitting there watching me. I pulled back the blanket and saw that the entire mattress was covered in blood. My whole body hurt, and I could barely move.
"The following day, they took me to a celebratory meal for everyone who had participated in the kidnapping. There was a large tray of chicken and rice in the middle, and everyone was delighted. The terrorists kept saying, 'Ta'al, ta'al,' meaning 'Come, come.' Everyone who saw me wanted to take a picture with me. It was as if someone had brought in a giant tuna, like in Japan, to show off the catch."
Did they talk to you?
"They started interrogating me about who I was and what I did for a living. From what I knew about Gazans during my intelligence service, I understood that many were religious. I was afraid that if I said Sapir was only my girlfriend, not my wife, they'd see her as a woman who had been with a man outside marriage.
"I didn't know what had happened to her, but I thought that if she was also being held hostage, I wanted them to understand that she was someone's wife and that they weren't allowed to touch her."
Did you both realize that you needed to build relationships with the terrorists, perhaps even some degree of trust, to survive?
"Yes, and it wasn't easy," Sasha says. "You have to swallow your pride and absorb endless insults about who you are as a people, where you grew up, things you never did. You have to put your ego aside. The instinct to ask, 'Why are you letting them treat you like this?' only reduces your chances of survival if you become insolent or violent.
"I had to keep reminding myself what my goal was: getting out of there. And I understood that my one purpose was to return home, not so I could play PlayStation or go back to work, but so I could be with my mother and father again and bring them happiness."
Sapir found her own way to build a relationship with one of her captors. "The owner of the house where I was being held was a religious man, and I managed to connect with him partly because the others couldn't stand him," she says.
"I started asking him questions in English about what he was reading. I thought that if I brought up the Quran, he might engage with me. He began explaining the Quran to me. Gradually, I asked more questions, and he became completely absorbed in our conversations.
"At a certain point, he'd open the shutters in the morning and say, 'Sabiro,' which is what he called me, 'Let's talk. Wake up, let's talk.' He always wanted to talk. Eventually he started suggesting that maybe I should become Muslim. He saw potential. I said, 'Why? I don't understand. Is Islam a good thing? Prove to me that you're humane.' He said, 'Of course we're humane. The Quran says that whenever a captor eats, he must give food to his prisoner.' So I said, 'Well then, go ahead.'
"The next day, I saw him eating and said, 'What's going on? Didn't we agree the Quran says it's fifty-fifty?' And he'd bring me another pita. I'd compliment him when he cooked. I'd say, 'Smells very good. You are a good chef.'
"He was a family man with two wives whom he'd sent away from the house. They didn't know what he was doing with the apartment while they were gone. He understood that if he allowed me to move around the house freely, without having to ask permission to use the bathroom, our conversations would continue. So he went along with it."
Did he gradually become more sympathetic toward you?
"One day, he drew a memorial candle on a piece of paper and wrote my name on it. I thought he was hinting that they were going to kill me soon. He had a Hebrew-English dictionary, and I tried opening it to words I thought he might want to say.
"I opened the dictionary to the word 'enemy,' and he said, 'Yes, this is you.' Then he added, 'But when you're here, everything is full of light.' I looked at him strangely. I couldn't understand how a terrorist could say something like that. Then he tore up the drawing and threw the paper away."
Sasha also learned to navigate the complicated relationship between a hostage and his captors. "Look, there were too many of these terrorists for every single one of them to be a psychopath," he says. "Most were doing it for ideological reasons and what they regarded as their values, not because they were insane.
"There were moments when I broke down crying in front of them, when I sensed they might be about to put a bullet in my head. They'd look at each other, confused, and say, 'He's in pain.'
"When they listened to the radio, I'd ask them what was being said so I could understand how the war was unfolding. They could easily have lied to me. When I heard my mother's and Sapir's names mentioned on the radio, for example, they could have told me they'd been killed instead of released. They could have done it just to torment me, to watch me suffer, if they'd hated me and hadn't cared about me at all.
"On October 7, I felt they saw me as an animal. But over time, some kind of connection developed. One of them began translating the news for me accurately. I also managed to make him laugh and learned how to create situations where he needed me."
What did you know about your father during captivity?
"I had some indication that he'd been kidnapped, based on a fragment of information I received from them during the first month. But their accounts contradicted each other. My father was alive in my mind throughout captivity. Whenever things were hard, I'd say to myself, 'I hope he isn't suffering as much as I am, or that he's somewhere better.'
"One thing I realized was how important family is. I wanted to repair my relationship with my parents. I'm an only child, and our relationship wasn't particularly good. I'd speak to them occasionally, but the conversations were superficial, not emotional. I never really shared anything significant about myself.
"My father had great emotional intelligence and a good heart, but I somehow missed that because I saw the version of him at home, the tough Soviet father who pushed you to achieve. In captivity, I promised myself I'd strengthen our relationship. I imagined us traveling around Europe together, the way he wanted. But as time passed, the realization that he might no longer be alive grew stronger."
When did you finally learn what had happened to him?
"Officially, only when I was released. In the first few minutes at Re'im, a social worker came up to me and said, 'Your mother and Sapir are waiting for you.' And I understood that if I'd come out before my father, he probably wasn't with us anymore.
"I broke down crying. I can still see him in front of me when I make decisions. His voice continues to guide me, even on days when I try not to let the loss consume me."
‘I was in a cage in Rafah. One day they came to film a video’
The person who helped rebuild Sapir and Sasha's relationship, even while he was absent, was his mother, Lena. The bond between the two women deepened while they were still being held in Gaza's tunnels. 
"At first, I asked them to deliver a letter I'd written to her by hand in Hebrew," Sapir recalls. "The terrorist who had drawn the memorial candle agreed to take me down to the tunnel where Lena was being held. As soon as she saw me, she said, 'Sapir, I can't believe you're alive.'
"She was incredibly emotional. She had thought Sasha and I were dead because she'd looked out of the window and seen what happened in the guest room next to her house that Saturday."
Sapir later made another arrangement with one of her captors. "I had an agreement with another terrorist that he'd take me to Lena's group on Sasha's birthday, November 11. Lena was being held with Danielle and Emilia Aloni. She'd taken several sleeping pills and was terribly depressed that day.
"The moment I walked through the door, she jumped out of bed in tears. She couldn't stop crying. We sat together, and I told her, 'Do you know how long I've wanted to talk to you alone, without Sasha around, so I could ask you all kinds of things about him? And now I can!'
"Emilia drew a picture of Sasha and me getting married, with a wedding canopy in the background. She said she'd make us orange juice when we got married.
"A week before our release, they moved Lena into my group, and we caught up on everything. We talked endlessly. I told her all about Sasha's antics, and she asked, 'So how did you put up with him like that?'"
"My parents always thought I'd never find a partner," Sasha interjects.
"Lena told me so many stories about what he was like as a child," Sapir continues. "I felt that I got to know him better during those few days with her in captivity than I had during our entire year together.
"She told me, 'Sapir, I can't bear the thought of going back to Israel and facing whatever awaits me there. I need you to be released with me.' I stayed with her at the Kfar Maccabiah Hotel for almost two years, until Sasha came home. She was struggling with some very dark thoughts. She'd say, 'He's my only son. I have nothing else left in this world.'
"I kept trying to reassure her that he would be home soon. In her mind, she'd already married us off, and I played along. I even picked out names for the granddaughters she imagined Sasha and I would give her. My parents became close to her too, and we all grew into a family. We observed Shabbat together."
But were you perhaps idealizing Sasha while he was away? Weren't you afraid that he might return as a different person, or as the same man you had wanted to leave, making the future you had imagined impossible?
"I'd say to his mother, 'Yes, yes, a wedding.' But over time, I couldn't keep lying to her. As our relationship grew closer, I told her the truth: that Sasha and I had differences that might never be resolved. We came from different worlds. I'm a person of faith from a traditional Jewish home, and Sasha wasn't religious. That affected many aspects of our lives and habits.
"I tried to think about how long I could wait for him, and when I'd have to move on and find the person I was meant to be with, someone with whom I could fulfill my greatest dream of building a family. But I still felt I had to wait because I couldn't imagine dating someone else, especially someone who hadn't experienced what I'd been through. I felt we owed ourselves closure. He'd be released, we'd talk about everything, and then we'd either separate or stay together."
At some point, Sasha stopped mentioning you in the hostage videos released by his captors.
"I was surprised he mentioned me at all in the first video they released," she says. "I was happy he did. But when he didn't mention me in the second video, I was convinced he'd given up on us. I thought that if he'd believed there was still a chance before, he was now letting me go, as if to say, 'Move on with your life and find someone else.' I knew how much he hated feeling like a burden."
Meanwhile, Sasha was going through some of the darkest periods of his captivity. "I was held in a cage in Rafah, where they interrogated me about my military service. I was also in Khan Younis during the bombardments," he recalls.
"I kept going for my mother's sake. I knew that if I did something to end my life, she might do the same, or spend the rest of her life consumed by grief.
"One day, they came to film a video of me. They brought me clean clothes and someone who spoke very formal Hebrew. He started asking me questions. They filmed several videos for different factions involved in their internal politics.
"Then they filmed a video intended for Israel. The terrorist dictated exactly what I had to say, sentence by sentence. He even included Sapir's name, which he pronounced 'Sabir,' and insisted that I say I missed her.
"I tried explaining that I didn't think it was appropriate. In my mind, she'd already been free for five months and was getting on with her life. Maybe she'd even started rebuilding her life and looking for someone else."
"We took the first video, the one in which he mentioned me, to a body language analyst," Sapir recalls. She told me, 'Sapir, he loves you, but with his head rather than his heart.' And I hadn't told her anything about our relationship beforehand."
"My feelings for Sapir developed after I came home," Sasha says. "As far as I was concerned, the day I returned was the day we started from zero. Back in November, during captivity, I'd already buried myself emotionally. I wanted her to move on, partly because I genuinely didn't feel any romantic longing for her.
"I pushed people out of my mind during captivity because thinking about them only made me feel lonelier. I never imagined Sapir would be there for my mother. Why would she feel any obligation toward her? Her family also stood by my mother and gave her strength. They're a big part of the reason she's still alive today."
Troufanov was released in February 2025. The couple's relationship underwent a rapid transformation, culminating in a marriage proposal just five months later. "We came back as genuine, open people," Sapir says. 
"Before captivity, I felt I was constantly walking on eggshells. I was afraid of ruining what we had, afraid he'd feel pressured by things I wanted. I hid my emotions, and that created a relationship that wasn't authentic. 
"I came out of captivity a different person. I asked myself, 'What were you so afraid of all that time?' It feels so good to be direct, to feel confident about who you are and what you need. I promised myself that when he came back, I'd put everything on the table. I'd tell him I observe Shabbat and that it wasn't up for negotiation. I'd tell him all the things that might make him run away and see whether he stayed. And he came back suddenly able to open up emotionally too."
"We talked all night when I got back," Sasha says. "I suddenly saw someone with extraordinary strength in Sapir, someone with wisdom and warmth."
"That first night was one long conversation," Sapir recalls. "I felt that I hadn't waited all that time for nothing. This was my man. I was on cloud nine."
‘You could see the ring box from miles away’
The couple returned to Kfar Maccabiah, where former hostages had been staying, and initially lived in separate rooms. "I knew I needed my space, and she needed hers," Sasha explains. "Our relationship wasn't yet at the point where we were ready to share a room.
"I had all kinds of physical problems when I came back, from head to toe. After eating canned food for a year and a half, your digestive system isn't the same. My stomach would swell up. My skin would itch and turn red from soap because I wasn't used to showering. I couldn't sleep properly or get back into a routine. Even today, I still struggle with sleep and have recurring dreams."
"Before captivity, he always tried to appear strong and tough," Sapir says. "But when he came back, he was able to open up to me about his dreams and struggles. The fact that he now feels comfortable sharing those things with me has brought us closer."
"Sapir made it clear that we'd reached the point where I had to decide whether to propose," Sasha says. "At first, I wanted to wait because I felt that my friends were still in Gaza. Ariel and Arbel were still being held hostage."
Sapir, how did you know he wanted to propose for the right reasons, and that your relationship had a solid enough foundation beyond the emotional needs you were fulfilling for each other?
"I was afraid he wanted to make his mother happy. I didn't want him to propose because he felt he owed me something. I'd tell Lena, 'Don't say things to him like, "Sapir is the reason I'm alive," because it puts pressure on him.' But I also wanted to know where things were going. I needed reassurance."
Much of their renewed connection developed during speaking tours they began giving to Jewish communities around the world shortly after Sasha's release. "We built shared experiences during those trips abroad," Sapir says. "During our first year together, we'd been two strangers who met on an app."
"You could say we feel as though we grew up together," Sasha adds. "That's something couples often look for, the feeling that they've developed as people alongside each other, rather than confronting two fully formed versions of one another, with each person trying to change the other.
"We became a good team. "We went on a speaking tour in the United States, and I knew I'd propose during that trip. We'd decided that the Caribbean would be our final destination. I started trying to convince her to wear something she wouldn't regret being photographed in, and to hurry so we'd make it in time for sunset."
"He was wearing tight shorts," Sapir recalls, laughing, "and you could see the ring box sticking out of his pocket from miles away. I remember thinking how sweet it was that he genuinely believed nobody could see it."
Both recognize that the transformation in their relationship has taught them lessons about communication and expressing their needs, beyond the extraordinary story of personal growth following trauma.
"Most of the questions we get during our talks are about our relationship," Sapir says. "We realized we wanted to talk about what took us from being a couple on the verge of breaking up to a couple who went through captivity and came back stronger."
Sasha, would you return to the Gaza border area to raise your children?
"I still haven't gone back, not even for a visit. All I have left are memories. I remember the kibbutz as it was on October 6, because on October 7 I was taken out of it with a bag over my head. Nothing has contaminated my memory of Nir Oz. That's why I don't go back. I want it to stay that way in my mind.
"It's difficult to admit, but there's an unwritten agreement with people who live in Israel's periphery. They benefit from relatively affordable living, in terms of taxes and prices, but they serve as a human shield. People who live in central Israel have the opposite arrangement. They enjoy relative security but pay a higher cost of living.
"I'd rather contribute enough to the country's economy to be able to live in central Israel, so my family won't be part of that unwritten contract that says, 'You'll be the first to absorb enemy fire. Sorry, my friend.' My mother, on the other hand, goes to Nir Oz three times a week to feed the cats."
You've had contact with politicians during the most critical period of your lives. How do you feel about the upcoming elections?
"There was a politician who told Lena and me, 'If it were up to me, you wouldn't be here either, and you wouldn't have come back,'" Sapir recalls. "I noticed Lena smiling out of the corner of my eye. When I asked why she was so happy, she said, 'Now I finally understand that only God can help me.'"
"There's a wonderful side to this country, but the politicians' hearts weren't in the right place," Sasha says. "They're in it for the money, the power and control over budgets."
"I'll probably vote for someone different from the person I voted for before October 7," Sapir says. "But they're all equally focused on looking good on Instagram, and I can't see myself voting for any politician with complete conviction."
"You see Ben Gvir having his picture taken with prisoners," Sasha says, referring to Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir. "As someone who was in the opposite situation, I know how much nonsense that is, because those are people who will say whatever he wants them to say.
"It's pure propaganda for the cameras. There's no candidate today whom I want to support publicly. I simply think that anyone who wants to be elected owes the families affected by October 7 a concrete plan explaining what they intend to do."

'American Intellectual Antisemitism': Shai Davidai exposes universities’ deep-rooted antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:01:29 UTC
04:01:29 KST

In 1919, my grandmother applied for admission to Barnard College of Columbia University. The notoriously antisemitic dean at the time, Virginia Gildersleeve, told her she would not be notified of her acceptance until after the start of freshman year, in an attempt to encourage her to choose a different school. My grandmother stood her ground and entered the graduating class of ’23 only a few days late.
In ousted Columbia Prof. Shai Davidai’s exposé, American Intellectual Antisemitism, I learned that Gildersleeve, who supported Nazi Germany’s expulsion of Jews from academia, was taking her cue from the higher-ups at Columbia.
“After Jewish enrollment reached 40% of the incoming class of 1919… the university implemented a series of exclusionary policies explicitly designed to curb the presence of Jews on campus,” he writes.
Jew-hatred is nothing new in the Ivy League. It just takes on new forms.
“American Intellectual Antisemitism” is the term Davidai coined for what he defines as “a modern and insidious form of Jew-hatred that cloaks itself in progressive jargon and academic rhetoric,” using the “language of social justice” to disguise bigotry as intellectual virtue, and constitutes “a direct assault on Western liberal values.”
Davidai became known throughout the world after he posted a long letter on social media on October 18, 2023, in reaction to vile and violent post-October 7 events – and top-tier American university leaders’ shocking support, or at least lack of condemnation, of those pro-terror, anti-Jewish incidents.
'We cannot protect your child[ren]'
“I want this message to get to every parent who sent their kids to Columbia University, entrusted their kids and their children’s safety with us. I want this message to get to every parent in America who sent their kids to New York University, to Harvard, to Stanford, to Berkeley, and I want you to know one thing: We cannot protect your child[ren],” he wrote, calling Columbia University President Minouche Shafik “a coward.”
Over the following year, he organized rallies, appeared on prime-time television, and testified before Congress.
Davidai paid dearly for his ongoing peaceful activism on behalf of beleaguered Jewish students, organized with “a small but dedicated group of Jewish students, postdocs, faculty, staff, and alumni.” He and his family received death threats, and he was barred from teaching his award-winning business course. He was derided by detractors as a “genocidal maniac,” “a hate-mongering charlatan,” and an “extremely dangerous” professor.
A year after the Hamas-led massacres in Israel, when Davidai’s video of the unchecked disruption of a campus memorial service for October 7 victims garnered over a million views in a few hours, Columbia’s administration suspended him – not the perpetrators – from campus.
“The decision’s timing told me everything I needed to know about Columbia’s priorities,” he writes.
Blending a firsthand account with broader analysis, his book exposes the radical politics, ideological indoctrination, institutional indifference, leadership failures, and moral unraveling of American academia.
The timing of the book’s release coincides with the beginning of another school year. “Across the nation, more than 1.5 million new students are stepping into lecture halls for the first time, joining student organizations, and attending campus events where the dogmas of American Intellectual Antisemitism are paraded as moral virtue,” he writes.
“Adopting their professors’ radical ideology, 18-year-old students – many of whom could not even point out Israel on a map – quickly discovered that condemning Israel’s existence and ostracizing dissenters became an easy route to social acceptance and community,” he says.
Having studied or worked at higher education institutions, including Cornell, Princeton, and The New School, before joining Columbia in 2019, he saw how “college students have realized that sowing chaos and disruption is an effective way to silence speakers with opposing views.”
University administrators across America have “capitulated to student protests, letting the loudest and most aggressive voices dictate which conversations were considered ‘acceptable’ on campus,” he writes.
Davidai delves into a variety of factors supporting “the open embrace of terrorism” in higher education. For example, “Columbia has taken an estimated $300 million from Qatar; Carnegie Mellon, $750 million; and Georgetown University, $1 billion. Cornell University alone has received close to $2 billion from Qatar.”
Jewish students at Columbia told Davidai they felt like outcasts and were negatively affected socially and academically by the relentless pro-Hamas drumbeat set by students and faculty alike. Administrators offered “no meaningful reforms, no accountability, nor a shred of remorse… bent rules to appease the mob, overlooked misconduct, empowered those who spread hate, and actively nurtured the very chaos they were supposed to stop.”
Many students lamented “that they were paying tens of thousands of dollars to attend a school that showed no concern for their well-being.”
Davidai concludes with a list of action items following his doctrine of countering fanaticism through “radical moderation.” For instance, parents “must insist on concrete guarantees of physical safety for Jewish students, publicly support their children when they speak out and are targeted for it, file formal complaints when universities violate their own professed values and mission statements, and leverage their financial resources, professional networks, and social capital to engage outside civil rights and legal organizations when internal channels fail.”
He uses the words “naive” or “naively” seven times in the book to describe himself, such as: “I naively believed that I had joined an institution that shared my commitment to intellectual rigor and open disagreement.”
His suggestions seem largely naive as well, considering that in the book he has amply proven an entrenched, ever-worsening anti-Jewish problem on college campuses: “By intentionally rebuilding learning environments where intellectual courage is rewarded, and dissent is treated as a civic virtue rather than a moral failure, American higher education can gradually earn back the public’s trust and reclaim its role not merely as a professional credentialing system but as a true training ground for democratic citizenship,” he writes.
That statement is pure naivete. Davidai could have questioned the prevalent “Ivy League or bust” attitude among many American Jews. He could have encouraged Jewish parents to put their “tens of thousands” – it’s actually hundreds of thousands – toward a quality education at, say, Yeshiva University or at institutions of higher learning in Israel that cater to English-speakers, rather than continue to bankroll schools that tolerate extremist ideologies while disrespecting their children’s views, beliefs, and physical safety.
Yes, it would be nice if American colleges heed his cry to “reclaim the educational mission of teaching people how to think, not what to think.” But as American Intellectual Antisemitism makes excruciatingly clear, the odds of that happening are rather poor.
AMERICAN INTELLECTUAL ANTISEMITISM: 
THE ANTI-JEWISH MOVEMENT  TEARING THROUGH OUR UNIVERSITIES
By Shai Davidai 
Wicked Son/Post Hill Press
352 pages; $30

Harriet Jackson finds belonging in Israel after fighting campus antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:01:25 UTC
04:01:25 KST

‘I was in a state of shock after Oct. 7,' says Harriet Jackson. “As the daughter of a Holocaust survivor, I could not imagine or accept another massacre of Jews. Antisemitism has been on my radar since I was a child. I believe in ‘Never Again.’”
At the time, Jackson worked as assistant director of research at Teachers College, Columbia University.
“I was immersed in a university culture that was predominantly anti-Zionist,” says Jackson. “A loud minority of faculty and students became intoxicated by Hamas propaganda and condemned Israel.
“What I heard on and off campus was silence in response to the pro-Hamas chants and the call for the annihilation of all Jews. I understood that extremist anti-Israel ideology, under the guise of being pro-Palestinian and financed by Iran and Qatar, has long been infiltrating educational and political institutions.
“My aliyah began at Columbia University.”
Jackson, an independent scholar, historian, educator, and Zionist crusader, joined forces with kindred spirits to combat antisemitism on campus, the irrational hatred, and disconnect from facts.
A few days after Oct. 7, 2023, Dr. Shai Davidai, now a former Columbia Business School professor, called out university president Minouche Shafik at a student vigil for not publicly condemning the Hamas massacre. The videographed outcry went viral. Soon Davidai became a vocal presence. Eventually, he left the university.
Anti-Jewish hatred on campus
In his forthcoming book American Intellectual Antisemitism: The Anti-Jewish Movement Tearing through Our Universities (Wicked Son, October 2026), Davidai describes his life-changing experiences and examines how “radical politics, ideological indoctrination, and institutional indifference have transformed campuses into incubators of anti-Jewish, anti-Israel and anti-American hatred.”
Recalls Jackson: “Prof. Gil Zussman introduced me to Columbia Faculty and Staff Supporting Israel (CFSI), which works to ‘support the inclusion, safety and voices of Jews, Zionists, and Israelis.’ I also joined Prof. Ran Kivetz’s informal, influential group of senior faculty, and had the opportunity to meet with Columbia presidents.
“I tried to explain to an interim president that our 4,000-year Jewish history has taught us to believe our enemies when they say they want to kill us.”
In the summer of 2024, Jackson joined the CFSI mission trip to the Gaza border communities, sponsored by Columbia Hillel. It was a gift to the activists.
“Our mission was to bear witness in Gaza, to visit the kibbutzim and the centers of rehabilitation. I stayed for a month afterward to travel through the country. I felt an infusion of light and sanity, and I made the decision that this is where I belong,” she says.
Jackson has felt drawn to Israel since her childhood visit to her mother’s family.
“I was born and raised in Queens, New York. My sister, Diana, and I grew up in a French-speaking home,” she explains. “My mother was Moroccan. My father was a German-Jewish Holocaust survivor who had relocated and recreated his life many times. He fled Nazi Germany to the US after being interned in a slave labor camp run by Vichy France in Morocco.”
After graduating from high school, Jackson earned certification in French civilization from the Sorbonne University. She then studied history at Stony Brook University and later received a master of philosophy in history and French studies from the Institute of French Studies at New York University.
Her graduate work took her back to Paris, where she attended classes at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales, and the Institute d’etudes politiques de Paris. Jackson’s graduate work focused on the impact of World War I on the development of state benefits for injured soldiers and their families in France between the wars, and the anti-Jewish bias in the media in France before World War II.
But when her mother became seriously ill, Jackson was compelled to put aside her passion for research. She and her sister became their mother’s full-time caretakers.
Perhaps it was destiny when a chance encounter in 2005 with a Lubavitcher woman on a flight from Paris to New York led Jackson to an archival position at the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research, and to a transformative experience. Founded by a group of Jewish scholars in 1925 in Vilnius, Lithuania, YIVO, now situated in New York, is one of the largest pre-war Jewish archives and libraries to have survived the Holocaust.
“YIVO hired me to process a collection of documents from wartime France, and specifically the archives of the Association des Israelites Pratiquants, (Association of Practicing Jews), under the direction of the Lubavitcher Rabbi Schneour Zalman Schneerson (1898-1980),” Jackson recalls.
In her article, “The Rescue, Relief, and Resistance Activities of Rabbi Zalman Schneerson: Does it count as rescue when a Jew saves a fellow Jew?” (French Politics, Culture, and Society, 2012), Jackson writes: “A descendant of the distinguished Schneerson dynasty from the Lubavitcher sect of hassidim, he was a Soviet émigré in France between 1936 and 1946.
“Schneerson’s personal experience of communist repression and arrest, his participation in clandestine activities and spiritual resistance in the Soviet Union, as well as his fierce anti-communism, placed him in a better position than many of his French brethren to deal with the authoritarian regime of Vichy and its anti-Jewish policies.”
Reflecting on Schneerson’s activities, she notes: “I have been a new immigrant for only five months. It amazes me that within one year of arriving in Paris, Schneerson set up a kosher soup kitchen, providing 400 meals a day. He also tended to the physical, emotional, and spiritual needs of traumatized children ripped from their parents, emphasizing their Jewish identity.
“That Schneerson and his family were able to house, feed, and educate more than 80 children, save at least 53 children from deportation, help smuggle at least 35 children to Switzerland, and find creative ways to release people from internment camps demonstrates that he participated in an international and interfaith network of rescue and resistance.
“In documenting his life, I had two objectives: to integrate Schneerson’s resistance work into a larger scholarship by historians, and to demonstrate a broader definition of resistance that does not only mean a taking up of arms.”
TWO YEARS after witnessing the devastation of the Gaza border communities, Jackson made aliyah in 2026, a month before the ceasefire of April 28. 
Reflecting on her life in Jerusalem, Jackson notes: “I came to Israel to begin a new chapter in my life – to continue advocating for Israel and fighting antisemitism. I am looking to collaborate with innovative organizations that are seeking new solutions, such as cultivating interfaith allies of the Jewish people.
“I am half German and half Moroccan, Ashkenazi and Sephardi, raised in a home that was primarily German, French, and Middle Eastern. Not at all American.
“I often felt invisible in the US, suspended between siloed Jewish communities. In Israel, these cultures are not contradictions but threads in a larger tapestry. I recognize the tastes, the sounds, and the traditions of my home.
“Making aliyah is a form of spiritual resistance against the fragmentation of my experiences. It is a declaration of strength, coherence, and wholeness.
“It connects me to generations of Jews who have drawn resilience from Jewish values and Jewish history: from the observant to the non-observant, from my parents and Rabbi Zalman Schneerson to the many known and anonymous Zionists who have stood up for Israel on US campuses and beyond.
“Israel allows all the disparate threads of my identity to weave a beautiful tapestry and become whole and healed.”
Harriet Jackson
From New York
to Jerusalem, 2026

Police brutality at nationwide protests in France continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:55:59 UTC
03:55:59 KST

Demonstrators attempted to march on government buildings in Paris on Saturday during a nationwide day of protest against the high cost of living that saw hundreds of arrests, Germany's DPA reported as cited by Yahoo News.
The Interior Ministry said police secured the government buildings and blocked the protesters, adding that police remain on high alert to contain violent groups, protect public facilities and prevent looting.
At least 272 arrests had been made nationwide by the afternoon, the ministry added.
In the morning, police had used tear gas and batons against protesters in the cities of Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg.
In Marseille, protesters repeatedly tried to break into a police station, gained access to the town hall and looted shops, the ministry said.
In Lyon, a tourist information centre was set on fire and shops were damaged. The ministry said the fire brigade was prevented from intervening by rioters.
In Avignon, rioters forced their way into the courtyard of the prefecture, and in Grenoble, damage was caused to the town hall.
According to the Paris police prefecture, around 100 people were arrested in the capital for carrying weapons and other prohibited items.
Various groups joined the day of protest, which had been planned for some time, including school pupils and university students who have been demonstrating for weeks for better learning conditions.
The call to protest was spread on social media, and also addressed high fuel prices, low wages, the large number of people in low-paid jobs and problems in agriculture and the fire service.
There was also a call for a renewed yellow vest movement, feeding government fears that the demonstrations could spark broader protests.
The yellow vest protests roiled France in 2019, spreading from demonstrations against a planned increase in fuel taxes into a nationwide movement against high living costs and social injustice, which caused President Emmanuel Macron serious problems during his first term in office.

Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defense ministry said.
The drones were brought down days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO's eastern flank.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.
NATO member Romania shares a 614-km border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Romania started shooting down such drones earlier this year.
Origin of drones not yet specified
The defense ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively.
The ministry did not specify the origin of the drones.
The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still searching for seven missing crew members.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighboring Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters.
