Is New Zealand holding back women's Test cricket?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:39:59 UTC
03:39:59 KST

For years fans and players have been crying out for more women's Test cricket.
Yet by the time Australia's women next don the whites at Headingley to kickstart the 2027 Ashes, 15 months will have passed since their last red-ball match.
Much of this comes down to the team's limited opposition. Just four of the top-ranked women's teams have cricket boards willing to commit to Tests.
Australia, England, India and South Africa have been pushing forward the past five years.
They've played 13 Tests since 2021, either as a standalone or part of a multi-format series, a significant improvement on the five years prior when two Tests were played worldwide.
Both of these fell in the 2017 and 2019 Ashes. The biennial contest has safeguarded tradition for England and Australia at a time when governing bodies have been hell-bent on growing the women's game through the shorter formats.
In fact, the Ashes points-based system used to determine the better side across three T20Is, three ODIs and a single Test, has widely been suggested by administrators and players as the best way to increase women's Tests overall. Enticing those on the fence to give it a go.
Tacking on a four-day Test match to a tour that already features six white-ball fixtures sounds like a no-brainer.
Unfortunately, two countries have knocked back that idea this year.
Australia missed out on a chance to face the West Indies in a Test for the first time in 50 years in March when their plans to play a multi-format series in the Caribbean fell through.
Then New Zealand declined to play a Test against Australia later in the year.
The three T20Is and three ODIs scheduled between the trans-Tasman rivals were originally supposed to run through February and March, but when the ICC's inaugural Champions Trophy shifted on the calendar, the tour had to be split.
Instead the three T20Is will now be played at North Sydney Oval, starting Sunday, while the ODIs will still be played at the end of the summer.
As close neighbours, the White Ferns would be ideal opponents for regular Test match cricket. Both in proximity and habit, the sides already meet most seasons for the Rose Bowl series.
Sadly, New Zealand Cricket doesn't share that view.
Despite being one of the first three nations to play women's Test cricket in the 1930s, it now refuses to play the longest version of the game.
Limited overs prioritised
The summer of 1934–35 saw the birth of women's Test cricket, when Australia and New Zealand hosted England on its first overseas tour.
Now, the White Ferns haven't played a Test since 2004.
After the governance of the men's and women's sides of the game were amalgamated, the frequency of Tests for the White Ferns gradually decreased and have now been non-existent for 22 years.
It also appears New Zealand Cricket is unwilling to budge on the matter, as per their previous statement in the media:
"The limited-overs formats have proven to be very effective in terms of attracting and retaining young players, which is a significant factor in the health of the women's game here.
"In time, this will provide a bigger base from which talented players will emerge to ultimately play for the White Ferns.
"Focusing on formats which include ICC global events, such as World Cups, is our preference for now."
ABC Sport requested a fresh response and more clarification but did not hear back.
That means retiring Kiwi legends Sophie Devine, Suzie Bates and Lea Tahuhu never got to experience red-ball cricket internationally.
At the end of the T20 World Cup the trio retired.
Various Australian players told ABC Sport it was an "atrocity" and a "real shame" that after 15 to 20 years of service the trio weren't offered the opportunity.
"Those girls are absolute icons and to think that they've never played a Test match and never will, knowing that they want to, that's tricky," Australia captain Sophie Molineux said.
"Hopefully one day we can play another Test against New Zealand, that would be really special."
"It's a tragedy that they won't get a baggy black cap," Beth Mooney said.
"I feel really sorry for them," Ellyse Perry added.
"They've had amazing, decorated international careers and never got to experience it."
Equal pay to blame
In 2022, New Zealand Cricket was heralded for a groundbreaking pay deal that granted men and women equal match fees.
From then on, when representing their country, both sets of athletes would be paid $NZ4,000 ($3,245) per ODI and $NZ2,500 per T20I.
Although this five-year agreement, due to expire next year, was a positive step in the recognition of female cricketers, it seems to have put the final nail in the coffin for Tests. Requiring a fee of $NZ10,250 per player, it pushed the dream further out of reach.
Especially in light of New Zealand Cricket's latest budget update, which predicted a $NZ7.3 million deficit for the past financial year.
New chief executive Geoff Allott started in the role in July and has indicated the organisation will need "to be prudent" as it looks to get back on track and "ensure long-term sustainability" of the game.
White Ferns head coach Ben Sawyer recently finished up a four-year tenure where he took the team to its maiden Women's T20 World Cup victory in 2024 and a bronze medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.
Speaking with ABC Sport, Sawyer highlighted the financial burden and the recent news that the England and Wales Cricket Board is considering footing the bill for its April Test match against the West Indies in order to ensure their 2027 multi-format series goes ahead.
"The reality is that it's a very expensive venture because of the equal match payments in New Zealand, and the cost is a huge part of it," Sawyer said.
"I'm assuming that's over $NZ150,000 in match payments and there are other priorities for them.
"Their domestic structure isn't full-time, and so it's my opinion that they think that money could be better used elsewhere."
Sawyer has previously held a range of coaching roles in women's cricket — as an Australian assistant, the head coach of the Sydney Sixers and the head coach of the Birmingham Phoenix.
He explained that New Zealand's top players are only contracted from October to March for eight hours per week. They train individually in the off-season and with teammates in-season at night after work.
When Sawyer first took on the White Ferns job, he recommended the national sporting body copy England's county system and gradually build their numbers the same way; starting with two to three professionals in each county, before eventually signing five to seven and then making the entire team full-time.
Since then, he hasn't seen any progress in this regard.
"I've always respected the vision that Cricket Australia have for five to 10 years down the track and the money they're willing to invest; that's what makes them the best in the world," he said.
If New Zealand Cricket was to change its mind and green-light a women's Test, Sawyer believes it'd be better to play someone with a lower ranking and a similar part-time domestic structure.
"They'd need a good lead in, and I wouldn't necessarily want to play Australia first.
"Maybe that's where two countries like New Zealand and Sri Lanka get together and say let's play one.
"I've got no doubt it'd be tough and hard the first time, but it's the only way to get better."
This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview
DUBAI – The captain of a flydubai flight whose co-pilot attacked him with an axe in an alleged bid to bring down the plane said one thought kept running through his head as the harrowing ordeal unfolded: “You can’t die like this.”
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar recounted the “traumatic” experience to Sky News Arabia in his first interview since the incident late in September in which he, passengers and other crew were credited with averting disaster on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
With his head and one hand bandaged and glasses perched on his nose, Machchhar spoke from his hospital bed in the United Arab Emirates.
“My vision was restricted to a few inches,” said the pilot, describing the effect of being struck in the back of the head with an emergency axe by his co-pilot, who had positioned himself behind Machchhar’s seat.
Thinking that a part of the airplane’s ceiling had come loose, he then received several more blows and was wounded in the hand as he tried to shield himself.
Machchhar recalled struggling to open the cockpit door so another pilot who was travelling on board could get inside.
“So I was screaming his name, and I was trying because the switch that was very close to me to open the door, I was trying to just get help in,” he said.
“But I remember being able to open the door,” he went on, only for it to shut again.
“And at that point, I felt all the blood, you know, everything rushing down, my energy, everything, I was just, I was barely staying in consciousness.
“Soon after that, that was the time when I heard the engine sounds going down. And then immediately after that, I felt the aircraft going into a dive.”
According to findings released by the Emirati attorney-general, Machchhar’s 29-year-old Omani co-pilot had planned to use the plane to carry out a suicide attack on the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, inspired by the Sept 11, 2001 attacks in New York.
He claimed to have acted alone, something investigators are still working to verify.
The prosecutor found that the other pilot on board, having seen the cockpit door open and close “in an unusual manner”, entered the flight deck and with the help of another crew member and passengers, subdued the co-pilot and regained control of the aircraft.
The jet, which plunged violently during the fray, was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar said the way his colleague was able to intervene and safely land the plane was “commendable”.
“It’s something that I’ll keep with me till I die.” AFP

He is YouTube's spiciest music analyst but Rick Beato loves the backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Rick Beato on interviewing music icons, YouTube backlash and Australian tour
He has interviewed some of music's biggest names and his videos regularly attract millions of views on YouTube.
So, how did Rick Beato become one of the internet's biggest music personalities?
"I always tell people that my channel was just one video at a time," the 64-year-old says.
"I didn't have any grand strategy. I just made videos on things I was interested in."
That curiosity began in 2016, when Beato was just a proud dad showcasing his young son Dylan's perfect pitch. A clip challenging him to identify complex chords by ear swiftly went viral.
Today, his channel Everything Music has 5.8 million subscribers, sharing not only his hot takes on contemporary music and the perils of AI, but thoughtful dives into instrumental technique, technology and trends.
His popular What Makes This Song Great? segment dissects the production, songwriting and music theory of iconic records; everything from Nirvana and Fleetwood Mac to Adele.
Beato's passion and expertise has earned him the trust of huge talent. Sting and Flea have personally requested to be interviewed, adding to a star-studded CV that includes Billy Joel, Seal, Sheryl Crow, Josh Homme and super producer Rick Rubin.
His golden rule? "I never talk about myself. I always think … I'm here to talk about music and about them. That's my job."
Beato thoroughly enjoys it. You can see a "pinching himself" grin creep across his face as he basks in awe of a jazz great's improvisational skill or soaks up a rare showbiz anecdote.
A pandemic interview with Brian May was a turning point, helping him appreciate that rock stars are human beings, too.
"He was so nice! It was really disarming because he was like, 'Rick, I can't believe I'm talking to you. I've seen you in that same spot all the time.' And I was like, 'Same to you, Brian!'
"He made it easy to talk to these incredibly talented, gifted people after that," he continues.
"Even though a lot of them have written the most famous songs of all time … when it comes down to it, they're like you and I. Except, when they put their pants on, they make gold records, as Christopher Walken would say," he says, quoting a classic Saturday Night Live skit.
There are still plenty of names on Beato's bucket list:
"Paul McCartney, Angus Young, Jimmy Page, Keith Richards, Eddie Vedder, Dave Grohl," he says.
A few may be ticked off already, but "I never say it before it happens because I don't want to jinx it."
The Australian connection
Beato took his video content to the live stage a few years back. Facing an audience instead of a camera was "a little strange at first" but public speaking was "no big deal" thanks to his background as a college professor.
He's "super excited" for his first visit to Australia this month. His fans feel the same, selling out shows in Melbourne and Brisbane and prompting a venue upgrade in Sydney.
Beato's first major label gig was producing an Australian singer, the late, Perth-born American Idol contestant Michael Johns.
"He was one of my closest friends. I produced a band he was in before he got signed [The Rising], then we did demos and co-wrote a bunch of songs together," he explains.
Beato took Johns's death, in 2014 at age 35 from a blood clot, really hard. "Tragic," Beato reflects. "He was an incredibly talented guy. One of my favourite singers."
Becoming Beato
Born in Fairport, New York into a musical family, Beato played cello and double bass as a child before teaching himself guitar at age 13.
He earned degrees in classical music and a master's in jazz guitar in 1987. He would go on to lecture at several music institutions, including the prestigious Berklee College of Music and his alma mater, Ithica College.
In the 90s, he inked a songwriting deal and was a member of rock band Billionaire. He moved to Atlanta in 1995 and bought Black Dog Sound Studios, which he operates to this day.
Unafraid to voice his distaste on popular music or the financial fallout of streaming, Beato divides opinion. To some, he epitomises "old man yells at clouds" clickbait. For many, it's never just "this sucks", it's always "this sucks because …"
How does he cope with backlash?
"I think it's funny. I enjoy when people criticise my opinions," Beato says.
"As a matter of fact, I have friends that made videos critical of videos I've made, and I'll text them, 'I thought it was great.' I don't take it personally. I think it's really flattering."
And what do his three teenage children think of their dad being internet famous?
"They make fun of me all the time: 'Why did you do that rage-bait video?'"
Whenever strangers approach him for a selfie or chit-chat, his kids are there to deflate his ego. "And they're good at it."
Audience vs algorithm
It's clear the YouTuber has a thicker skin than most of the creatives he interviews.
"It's hard for a lot of artists that I talk to, they can't read any critiques of their music or get into the comments section. And I always tell them, 'Look, the comments are about the people that are writing them. They're not about you.'
"Don't take it to heart because it's literally a reflection on them, as is the algorithm on these platforms are a mirror for people. It just feeds back exactly who they are to them over and over.
"That's the problem with algorithms, because it only shows them things that they want to see.
Before his son's viral video, Beato was a producer, session player, label boss and educator who preferred to keep out of the spotlight.
He recognises the irony of finding success in putting his face to addressing an audience of millions.
"I couldn't have imagined it. I just wanted to give back and teach people things."
Rick Beato's Australian tour begins on October 29 at Sydney's Enmore Theatre, then heads to Melbourne's Thornbury Theatre on October 30 and Brisbane's Princess Theatre on October 31.

In central Gaza, staff at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital reported one person killed and another injured in Deir el-Balah.

In an update covering the preceding 48 hours, the ministry reported six deaths and 43 injuries across the strip.
It said 74,469 Palestinians had been killed and 175,492 injured since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023.
The continuing toll on children was highlighted on Friday by UNICEF, the United Nations children’s agency.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, spokesman Ricardo Pires said more than 340 children had been killed since the ceasefire began.
He said seven children had died in attacks over the previous two weeks, with at least 33 others seriously injured.

Mapping published by Al Jazeera on October 12 showed Israeli forces control or restrict access to about 65 percent of the territory.
The “Yellow Line”, initially established to mark Israeli military positions after a partial withdrawal under the “ceasefire”, has been pushed further into Palestinian areas, the report said.
The remaining accessible area is home to 2.1 million people.
On Friday, Gaza’s Health Ministry warned that more than 1.4 million Palestinians were projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse for the rest of the year.

'Do something. You can’t die like this': flydubai pilot Capt Smit Machchar recounts cockpit attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:25:17 UTC
03:25:17 KST

'It went on like a normal day till it wasn’t,' Smit recalled
MUMBAI: Two hours into the flight from Dubai to Tel Avivi, flydubai commander, Capt Smit Machchar was checking landing time and fuel figures on the computer when something struck hard at the back of his head. He thought part of his Boeing 737’s cockpit roof had broken loose. Seconds later, as more blows rained in, he turned and saw it was his co-pilot. Bleeding, his vision shrunk to a few inches, he drifted in and out of consciousness during those fateful minutes when the aircraft went into a rapid descent, while the attack continued. “There was a moment I told myself, Smit, do something, you can’t die like this,” said the flydubai pilot, recounting the Sept 30 terror attack on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, which was diverted and landed in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.The pilot said his memory of what followed is fragmented, a gap he is still working through with doctors and psychologists. In his first extended account since the incident, given to Sky News Arabia on Sat evening, Machchar said an ordinary flight, with a co-pilot he was flying with for the first time, turned violent minutes after the man stood up to pray.
It was a route he had flown many times. An augmented crew was on board, and the relief captain was to take over operating duties after landing.
“Normal flight,” he told the channel. “It went on like a normal day till it wasn’t.”About two hours in, the relief captain had dropped by the cockpit to chat about rosters and flying hours when the co-pilot, who had stepped out for a toilet break, returned. A few minutes into their conversation, he said he wished to pray and asked the relief captain to step out. Machchar said such requests are accepted in the region when the flight is stable.The co-pilot asked the other Captain to step out, stood up behind him and began praying. “Out of respect, I did not look back. I was checking the landing time and fuel figures on the computer, the routine background tasks of the monitoring pilot. Suddenly there was a very hard hit at the back of my head,” he said. “It was something very strong and hard. I didn’t know at that point what had hit me.” He fell forward, and his mind reached for training. “My first thought was, okay, something has broken from the aircraft roof, and it has been a catastrophic damage. I was planning to regain my composure and check my systems.”The blows kept coming. Within seconds his vision had narrowed to a few inches, he said. When he glanced back, he understood. “He was saying something while hitting me, but I could not understand.” Machchar unbuckled and tried to shield himself, taking a blow on his hand. “That’s when something flipped,” he said. He screamed for the relief captain and, since the door switch was within reach, managed to open it. He lost consciousness for the first time soon after. He recalled hearing shouting between the co-pilot and the other crew before the door shut again, with the co-pilot threatening to hit them too.It was after this, he said, that he heard the engines spool down and felt the aircraft pitch into a dive. “I don’t have to see the instruments, I can have my eyes closed and still know the engines are spooling down and the aircraft is going down. Every pilot will tell you this.”Drifting in and out of consciousness from blood loss, he said, he reached a point of decision. “I told myself, Smit, do something. You can’t die like this. I’m not saying I accepted my death. It was like, do something, otherwise...” The pilot added his memory of what followed is fragmentary, a gap he is still working through with doctors and psychologists. He said he remembers locking his legs against something and pushing toward the door. He said he remembers then lying face down between the cockpit and the galley, the door open, passengers panicking.Machchar credited his colleague for taking the controls and recovering the aircraft, calling it something he will carry “till I die.” Asked about the speculation over how the plane was saved, he declined to single anyone out.
“Everyone did the best in their capacity,” he said, including crew and passengers.He said he knew he was out of danger only when the aircraft touched down. Until then a doctor on board and his crew kept him conscious. “At that point, what I was more focused on was to not give up on life. You say you see flashes and stuff like that (speaking about death). You just remember the person who matters the most,” he said. The first call he made was to his 2-year old son. In the days that followed the incident, he continued to get flashes of the first blow. The commander added that he has been getting better with each passing day and can now sit and have conversations.

Cosmic Breath: Global calls to prayer answer rising Islamophobia in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:24:03 UTC
03:24:03 KST

Tucked away just a stone’s throw from the relentless hum of Oxford Street, a new sonic sanctuary has taken root in central London. Joe Namy, an American-born Lebanese artist and composer whose practice encompasses sound, its history, and its physical impact on the built environment, has brought his multi-channel sound installation, Cosmic Breath, to the UK capital, Anadolu reports.
The work is reimagined for Ibraaz’s Musalla, a space dedicated to spiritual practice as both lived experience and creative expression.
Composed of recordings of the adhan—the Islamic call to prayer—the installation brings together historical and contemporary calls from different geographies, amplified through horn speakers like those mounted on mosque minarets.
Played simultaneously, each speaker softly emits a different adhan recording, inviting the audience to lean in and listen closely. At prayer times, the volume increases, making the calls clearly audible throughout the room, creating a congregation of calls to prayer.
‘Interested in collective sound experiences’
The work forms part of Namy’s wider exploration of sound systems, community, and spirituality.
First commissioned for the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah in 2023 by its artistic director and architect, Sumayya Vally, the installation explores collective auditory experiences and public sound landmarks.
“A lot of my work deals with the politics of sound, and deals with the spirituality of sound as well, how it affects us in different ways,” Namy explains. “So, I’m interested in sound system cultures (and) collective sound experiences as well, and how they impact our lives.”
Developed in close collaboration with Vally, who designed the installation’s spatial scenography, the artwork grew out of a poetic reflection on time and geography.
Namy was moved by the idea that “at any moment in time on Earth, there is an adhan happening somewhere on this planet, which I think is such a really powerful and beautiful gesture.”
Approaching the adhan through a sociological lens, Namy examines how an ancient oral tradition has transformed alongside modern technology, amplification, and recordings.
Bringing the piece from Saudi Arabia to London reshapes its meaning dramatically, particularly given the current social atmosphere in the UK.
READ: UK security adviser’s wife faces scrutiny over Palestine Action post
From Jeddah to London: A different political soundscape
“Showing it for the first time in Jeddah was a very different experience than showing it here in London, which … situates the work very differently than how it was situated there,” Namy underlined.
He pointed directly to the heightened hostility surrounding the current political landscape: “Especially now today in the current kind of political climate here in London… there’s just a more heightened kind of Islamophobia, xenophobia, prejudice… all these things that we’ve been experiencing and has been increasing.”
For Namy, installing the piece in the heart of London serves as a sanctuary and an antidote to that hostility.
“I feel like it’s a more powerful gesture to be able to show it here in the center of London, you know, just off of Oxford Street, and to be able to have this space for people to be able to come, relax,” he said.
He notes how rare it is in contemporary art spaces to engage with faith so openly: “I think, what I really enjoy is the fact that it’s thinking about the spirituality in relation to art, which you don’t always get a chance to explore, but also providing a kind of third space for people to explore more.”
A London memory born during lockdown
To ground the exhibition in its current environment, this iteration at Ibraaz features a local recording. “So, this recording is from London,” Namy notes.
“Actually, it was important to bring in something that was local as well, and so this was actually one of the first recordings of a public adhan in London that happened in Walthamstow during COVID. It was again a time (when) everyone was social distancing, and so it was a way for the community to be able to kind of — although they were distant — to feel closer together, so it was important to bring in a local element into the setting as well, so that we have some a more closer connection to where we are here in London.”
The recording captures the historic call performed by the Waltham Forest Islamic Association in 2020, offering a sonic expression of shared experience when physical gathering was impossible.
Adhans from Mecca to Singapore, Tbilisi to Khartoum
The audio selections in Cosmic Breath span more than a century and cross vast physical and acoustic terrains, revealing how each call carries a unique character shaped by local traditions, acoustic environments, and regional histories.
“The selections that we included within this installation each represent a certain aspect, or have a unique aspect for the adhan,” Namy says. “Part of it is thinking about spaces (where) you normally wouldn’t encounter the adhan, spaces in which recordings of the adhan are kind of historically significant as well.”
Among the archival highlights is what is considered the first recording of the adhan at the Haram Mosque in Mecca, dating back to the late 19th century. “I think this one is the first recording that was ever done of the adhan from the late 1800s in Mecca. You can kind of hear the grain of the recording. It’s not a really great recording, but it’s interesting to hear it in context of all the other ones,” Namy reflects.
From Asia, the piece gathers landmark history and geography.
“From the Philippines, (there is) an archival recording from the 1950s. It was one of the first recordings of the adhan in the Philippines,” Namy points out.
Contemporary and historical selections also feature the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem and Singapore’s Sultan Mosque, thought to be the first mosque to adopt loudspeakers in the 1930s.
READ: Protest outside Azerbaijan’s embassy in London against hijab ban in schools
“This one is from Singapore, and this was recorded at the first mosque that actually used speakers to amplify the call to prayer. The mosque is still there, and that was important,” he adds.
Other field recordings offer stark contrasts in style and setting—from the ornate to the stripped-back.
“This one is Georgia Tbilisi, and this one is probably the most flowery, I think. You really hear the improvisation and the embellishments and how the voice gets extended in the recitation,” Namy says.
In contrast, “one is from the Sahrawi refugee camp in Algeria, and it’s one of the only ones that’s not recorded, that’s not amplified,” Namy explains saying, “It’s somebody who is old school-style, kind of just reciting it without any speakers or anything like that, just their voice.”
The installation captures deeply intimate acts of faith as well as distinct colloquial traditions.
“I think this one is from Japan,” Namy shares, explaining that similar to the recording mentioned before, it was “somebody just kind of reciting it into the forest for themselves, basically, which I thought was a really beautiful gesture. So, it’s a very personal personal recording reflection.”
A call to prayer from Khartoum highlights regional identity: “This one is Khartoum. It’s recorded in Sudan, and again, you hear the colloquial differences and how the adhan is recited. It’s very different in the recitation. It’s very Sudani in its style, which I really love.”
Not every place could be captured on audio.
Namy recalls attempting to record the first mosque built in South America, located in Brazil. Because the building is reserved for special occasions, “you don’t hear the adhan there, so we recorded just kind of like the empty space from that room, just to have that kind of gesture,” though it ultimately remained unreleased alongside seaside field recordings from Egypt.
From South Africa, a protest becomes the seed of Cosmic Breath
The initial impulse for Cosmic Breath traces back to a pivotal moment of civic resistance in South Africa. During the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, rising social tension, Islamophobia, and xenophobia in Durban led to a local ban on publicly broadcasting the adhan.
In response, an act of interfaith solidarity emerged. “This protest was actually organized by a Hindu community member. He wasn’t Muslim, but he organized this protest in solidarity with the Muslim community there,” Namy recalls.
Sumayya Vally shared the link to the event with him, sparking the broader concept.
Restricted by social distancing rules, residents adapted: “How do you protest at a time when you can’t congregate and gather together? And so they asked everybody to bring their cars and made this huge parade. Everybody tuned their car stereo systems to one of the channels that was broadcasting the adhan.”
The resulting soundscape of hundreds of car speakers reverberating through the streets of Durban provided the foundation for the entire project. “This is the recording from that experience as well,” Namy reflects.
“And that was kind of the first recordings that really made me think about the piece… and bring everything together.”

"It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia on Friday struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites. "This certainly does not stop the war."
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskyy wrote.
Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Friday called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before U.S. midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."
U.S. Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Graham, who died in July, strongly supported U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope that there would be continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented the late senator's absence.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," Zelenskyy posted on Saturday.
The Ukrainian leader predicted that the U.S. under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month.
"I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," Zelenskyy wrote.

Alberta support for Canada rises ahead of separation referendum
CALGARY, Alberta – Support for Alberta remaining in Canada gathered pace ahead of a referendum on whether the province should begin a legal process to separate from the country, according to a poll from Abacus Data.
The survey of 1,021 eligible voters, released on Oct 17, found 68% of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, up from 64% last month. Support for beginning a legal process that could ultimately lead to separation was unchanged at 24%, while the share of undecided voters or those planning not to vote in the Oct 7 to 13 poll fell to 8% from 12%.
Albertans will decide on Oct 19 whether to remain a Canadian province or to set the stage for a second, binding vote on secession. At stake is the future of Canada’s largest oil-producing province, which pumps more than 4 million barrels a day, most of it for export to the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to reject separation at a rally in Edmonton on Oct 16, warning that a vote against Canada would bring “years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities”. An increasingly divided world makes national unity more important, he said.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged longstanding grievances towards the federal government, saying frustrations over Ottawa’s treatment of the province’s resources and energy industry were “real”.
His government has made a number of policy moves to address tensions in the province of 5 million people, by easing restrictions on oil and gas development and promising to financially back a new oil pipeline, known as Pacific Link, capable of carrying 1 million barrels a day to the west coast for export to Asia.
Carney on Oct 16 cast the pipeline as part of the case for remaining in Canada, saying it would help reduce Alberta’s dependence on the US, open new export markets and generate more than 140,000 jobs.
“Canada is where we can build bigger, faster and better than we ever could alone,” he said. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome.” BLOOMBERG

Weaker inputs to a key emotion hub are linked to more depressive symptoms in healthy young adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:00:57 UTC
03:00:57 KST

Weaker incoming connections to a key emotion-related brain region were associated with greater depressive symptoms in a study of 890 neurotypical young adults published in the International Journal of Neuropsychopharmacology. Patterns in these incoming connections sorted participants into groups that differed in depressive symptom severity, although the results do not establish a diagnostic test for depression.
The subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) is a small region near the front of the brain involved in regulating emotion and bodily responses. Altered activity in this region and its connections has been linked to depression, and the area has been a target of brain stimulation treatments for depression. However, conventional brain-imaging measures usually show whether two regions are active together without indicating which region’s activity may influence the other.
To examine this distinction, the researchers used a statistical technique called Granger causality analysis. This method looks at the timing of fluctuations in brain signals to estimate whether activity in one region tends to precede and predict activity in another. Applied to brain scans that track blood flow, it provides an estimate of directional influence rather than proof that one region drives another.
Led by Huey-Ting Li of Yale University School of Medicine, the researchers analyzed resting-state functional MRI scans from 890 neurotypical young adults in the Human Connectome Project, a large study of healthy adults. The sample included 459 women and 431 men aged 22 to 35. Participants completed a questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and other emotional and behavioral symptoms.
The researchers examined connections between the sgACC and 268 other brain regions, separating connections estimated to run toward the sgACC from those estimated to run away from it. They then used a clustering method to sort participants into groups with similar connectivity patterns and compared the groups’ symptoms. For comparison, they repeated the analysis using conventional measures of which regions were active together.
Many regions showed connections running toward the sgACC, including frontal and parietal regions (involved in planning and attention), the anterior insula (which helps process bodily and emotional information), temporal regions and the cerebellum. The orbitofrontal cortex, which contributes to decision-making and emotion, showed connections in both directions. The sgACC, in turn, appeared to send signals mainly to movement-related areas, the brainstem and the cerebellum.
Clustering based on the incoming connections divided participants into five groups, with depression scores rising from the first group to the fifth, although only the group with the lowest scores differed reliably from the three highest-scoring groups. Participants with weaker inputs from several frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital areas tended to fall into groups with higher depression scores, with the strongest links involving the superior frontal gyrus and the temporal poles. Because participants were not a clinical sample, the absolute differences were modest: the gap in depression scores between the lowest- and highest-scoring groups was small to moderate in size.
The differences were not limited to depression. The clusters also varied in anxiety, physical complaints, attention problems, aggression and rule-breaking behavior. The group with the highest depressive symptoms also showed the greatest overall burden of internalizing problems (difficulties directed inward, such as depression and anxiety) and externalizing problems (difficulties expressed outwardly through behavior, such as aggression and rule-breaking).
The groups also differed in their mix of women and men, and men scored higher than women on some behavioral problems within certain groups. However, the link between the groups and depression held after accounting for sex.
A machine-learning model using the incoming connections sorted participants into the correct groups with about 87% accuracy, and a more rigorous tuning procedure raised this to about 92%. However, because the groups were themselves defined from the same connectivity data, these figures describe how cleanly the groups could be separated within this dataset, not how accurately the model would identify depression in new people.
In contrast, clustering based on outgoing connections produced two groups that did not differ in symptoms, and conventional measures of regions being active together did not produce meaningful groups. The authors caution that this difference may partly reflect how reliably each type of connection was measured, rather than showing that the sgACC’s inputs matter more for mood than its outputs.
Li and colleagues wrote that the findings “highlight an outsized role of sgACC inputs in distinguishing individuals’ depressive symptom severity in a neurotypical population.”
The study has important limitations. The participants were not recruited based on psychiatric diagnoses, and most had relatively low symptom levels, so the analysis cannot show that these connectivity patterns identify major depressive disorder or predict treatment response.
The findings also come from a single dataset with no independent replication, and the data were collected at one point in time. In addition, Granger causality applied to fMRI data estimates directional patterns in blood-flow signals rather than establishing that one brain region actually drives another.
The study, “Functional inputs to the subgenual cingulate cortex differentiate levels of depressive symptom severity in neurotypical young adults: Granger causality and clustering analyses,” was authored by Huey-Ting Li, Yu Chen, Shefali Chaudhary, Jaime S. Ide and Chiang-Shan R. Li.

Being pregnant can still cost women their jobs in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

How pregnancy discrimination is pushing Australian women out of the workforce
When Abby McCawley found out she was having a girl, she sent a message to her coworkers to share the exciting news.
"Everyone around me was so happy, including the people I worked for and the people I worked with," she said.
Abby was five months into her role as a rental property manager at Ray White Brunswick in Melbourne's inner north.
After taking two days off work to manage morning sickness, Abby returned to her desk in the office and discovered something odd.
She couldn't log onto her computer.
Moments later, Abby's boss called her into his office and terminated her employment.
"I burst into tears," she said.
"I was shocked, I was upset … I thought about the baby.
"I just thought, 'I haven't done anything wrong, why am I being let go?'"
Abby said she had never received warnings she wasn't performing.
"It had to be because I was pregnant,"
she said.
More than 100 women have told Four Corners they lost work after becoming pregnant or having a child.
Some were employed at Australia's biggest companies, and nearly a quarter worked in the public sector.
Together, the cases reveal the problem is far bigger than a few bad bosses.
After analysing dozens of cases, Four Corners has established a collection of tactics used to push mothers out of the workforce, revealing an unwritten playbook used by employers.
Fired after being publicly praised by the company on social media
In the weeks before Abby was let go, she had no idea her job was at risk.
Then, in her first trimester, she asked to work remotely for a few hours to manage morning sickness.
Her request was denied by the office manager.
Instead, Abby was told a new policy required employees to give a day's notice to work from home.
"It [was] quite disappointing, because it's obviously not something that you can predict," she said.
Still, Abby felt secure in her job and wasn't worried.
A week before Ray White Brunswick terminated Abby's employment, the real estate agency publicly praised her on Instagram.
When she was fired, Abby said she was told it was partly due to a company restructure.
She took her employer to the Fair Work Commission seeking compensation, but mediation failed, so she is now suing Ray White Brunswick in the Federal Court.
Her lawyer, Laura Blandthorn from Solidarity Solicitors, alleged Abby had experienced "very clear, direct discrimination based on her pregnancy".
She said Abby was initially told her employment was terminated due to an "office restructure", then was later advised it was due to "performance reasons".
"There was a shift in the alleged reason for the dismissal,"
Ms Blandthorn said.
Ray White Brunswick's director Jamil Allouche declined an interview with Four Corners.
In a statement, he said: "Abby's employment was terminated for the reasons that we discussed with her at the time her employment ended.
"Those reasons related to her behaviour in the workplace, reported to me by other employees and observed by me as the decision-maker.
"As the matter is currently before the court, I am not able to comment further, and I will allow the process to take its course."
Mr Allouche did not respond to further questions about what that behaviour was.
Lawyer Susan Price, from the Working Women's Centre NSW, has represented women facing pregnancy discrimination for decades and said in other cases, criticism of a new or expectant mother's performance in the workplace was common.
"You do see what I describe as a real shift in attitude towards a worker once they've come into the workplace and announced they're pregnant," she said.
"It's almost like that worker has now been identified as a problem and things that were absolutely fine before, start to get criticised, their performance gets managed."
Twenty-one women told Four Corners they had been let go after becoming pregnant, only to find someone else had taken their job, and in some cases under a different title.
It's a practice lawyers call a "sham restructure".
Zana Bytheway, executive director of employment rights legal centre JobWatch said it could sometimes happen to women on maternity leave.
"They may find their job has been made redundant, but it's often a construct," she said.
"Often they found that their actual position … is still there."
Melbourne mother highlights vulnerability of casual workers
The experience of factory worker, Challis, who asked to keep her surname private, shows casual workers can be especially vulnerable to pregnancy discrimination.
For two years, Challis worked in a Melbourne warehouse for NewCold, one of the world's largest refrigerated food companies.
She worked 40 hours a week in regular evening shifts, arranged through labour hire firm OzStaff.
After she fell pregnant, OzStaff insisted on three separate medical certificates confirming that she was fit to work in the warehouse freezer.
Doctors repeatedly cleared her for all her duties, but Challis was left without work and chasing shifts.
When she was eventually rostered back on two weeks later, her hours were cut to 24 hours a week, reducing her pay.
"[The message] was, you take what you're given or you get nothing," she said.
In her second trimester, Challis requested morning shifts because she had developed pelvic pain in the evenings.
Challis said she offered to continue to work in the evening if that was not possible, but after working one more shift, she was never rostered again.
"Not being able to work and make an income for myself and to save money to have a child was really, really hard," she said.
Catherine Hemingway, associate director of Victoria Legal Aid's equity law program, which is representing Challis in a mediation, said casual workers were protected under anti-discrimination law.
"It's not lawful to treat someone less favourably because they're pregnant or because they have caring responsibilities," she said.
"This applies to all workers."
Challis and her lawyers are taking her employers to the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC).
NewCold told Four Corners it was committed to providing a "respectful" workplace but would not comment further given the ongoing legal action.
"[NewCold] takes all allegations of discrimination, including pregnancy discrimination, very seriously," a company spokeswoman said.
OzStaff declined to comment as the matter was before the commission.
Research shows very few women take legal action in response to pregnancy discrimination, and those who do face a long wait for their cases to be heard.
New figures obtained by Four Corners reveal nearly half of Sex Discrimination Act complaints resolved in 2025-26 took more than a year to be finalised, up from 1 per cent in 2020-21.
Last year, the commission received the highest number of pregnancy discrimination complaints in more than a decade.
Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody acknowledged the long waitlist was difficult for complainants because it stopped them from being able to find another job or to move on.
"We have sought additional funding to deal with that [and] so far, we haven't been successful," she said.
Construction worker leaves industry she once loved
The construction industry has been vocal about struggling to hire women, launching support groups and glossy campaigns to get them onto worksites.
Katelyn Dower was one of them.
She developed the skills to operate cranes and eventually landed a job at Allied Crane Hire in the NSW Hunter region.
"I loved the challenge and just being at a different job and doing a different thing every single day," she said.
After Katelyn fell pregnant with her twin boys, she said she told her manager she could do anything but work on a Franna crane.
"It kind of swings around belly height and there's a lot of pulling and pushing," she said.
"Ligaments, when you're pregnant, all loosen up and it's not as easy to do that sort of work."
Katelyn said there was other work that was safe for her to do, but she was still rostered on the Franna crane.
Text messages show Katelyn raised concerns with her employer on multiple occasions.
She said she was then threatened with termination, which the company denied.
"I gave birth to the twins … [prematurely] at 35 weeks," she said.
"I had a very traumatic birth [after] all the stress from the whole work situation."
Katelyn started legal action with the help of her union, arguing a woman is legally entitled to a safe job, but the company went into liquidation.
"At the time, Allied Crane Hire disputed the allegations made by Ms Dower," a company spokeswoman said.
"The matter was never finalised, and the allegations were not the subject of a final determination against the company."
Katelyn said she has since quit the construction industry.
"I don't think I'll ever go back, and it's robbed me of a career that I used to love a lot," she said.
Women pursuing legal action face 'daunting' hurdles
The Fair Work Commission (FWC) is one of the agencies that handles employment claims involving pregnancy discrimination, but it is overloaded with cases.
The FWC said ongoing funding cuts had forced it to constrain some operations, including limiting settlement conferences to one hour.
Ms Price said the new processes could disadvantage women alleging pregnancy discrimination, especially if they were fighting major companies with legal teams behind them.
"I think it can be really daunting and a factor that makes that woman go, 'You know what? I don't think I want to put time and effort into pursuing my claim,'" she said.
Advocacy groups, lawyers, academics and other organisations are now calling for more legislative protection.
Abby agreed.
She's heavily pregnant and remains unemployed after losing her job with Ray White Brunswick.
It's unlikely she will finalise her matter before her daughter is born.
"[I hope] she never has to deal with something like this," Abby said.
"[I hope] she can work in an industry or have a career she loves and she's good at, and she can thrive, and that she never has to experience another male getting rid of her because she's having a baby."
Watch Four Corners' full investigation, The Pregnancy Penalty, on Monday at 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.

Patience of Labor MPs is beginning to wear thin as mid-term blues bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Patience of Labor MPs is beginning to wear thin as mid-term blues bite
For years, Anthony Albanese's ability to maintain discipline within Labor has been one of his greatest political strengths.
His MPs have largely kept their complaints private, accepted decisions made by a small group of senior figures and trusted the prime minister's judgement.
But political loyalty is easier to maintain when a government is winning, and the patience of some Labor MPs is beginning to wear thin.
Albanese told his caucus colleagues this week that despite Labor's current struggles, its political fortunes would improve as the next election drew closer.
He revisited a favourite refrain, telling MPs the party would be "kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter".
It was the same self-assured confidence he projected when Labor was in the grips of a political slump at a similar point in the last parliamentary term.
Frustration builds for MPS
Having been vindicated so emphatically at the last election, Albanese has reason to trust his instinct.
But while the Voice referendum defeat and controversies over Qantas upgrades and the PM's Copacabana house were politically damaging, they were not as deeply felt by households as the economic pressures confronting them today.
High inflation was a major factor in Labor's previous mid-term woes, but now the financial strain has become more entrenched and the political challenges harder to overcome.
Labor MPs and senators are hearing all this and more as they move around their communities, and they are not happy about it.
The extent of caucus rancour cannot be exclusively judged through complaints aired anonymously through the media. But in recent weeks there has been a noticeable uptick in the frankness of private commentary volunteered by an increasingly broad cross section of Labor figures.
Their frustration is palpable and the subjects of the ire are varied.
Neither Albanese nor Treasurer Jim Chalmers fare particularly well, and there is widespread concern about the government's economic predicament.
There remains strong internal support for Labor's attempt to tackle the inequity in Australia's housing market where older home owners and investors have long held the advantage.
But anxiety about the impact of inflation and rising interest rates is at an all-time high.
Problems of Labor's own making
Labor has spent years acknowledging Australians are struggling with living costs and offering a raft of measures to ease their burden, from cheaper medicines and bulk billed GP appointments to income tax cuts and energy rebates.
Now, despite the public experiencing the same pressures, the government is asking voters to accept a very different economic prescription.
Labor is increasingly emphasising the need to restrain spending to help ease inflation, with Chalmers using a speech this year to reaffirm there would be "another new savings package by year's end".
Current petrol and diesel prices are about the same as they were in March this year when Labor temporarily halved the fuel excise.
Rates were lower, albeit inflation was substantially worse, when Labor introduced energy rebates and various other supports in its 2023 budget.
The economic rationale for restraint may be sound, but it is a much harder political argument for a government that has spent years presenting itself as the answer to household financial pressures.
But the caucus doldrums go beyond the persistent cost-of-living issues.
It's the problems that are of the government's own making that are considered the most infuriating.
Labor's fix for the Australian Tax Office decision to ban credit card payments for tax was only temporary, with the government still under pressure to find a permanent solution.
Stacked up with the capital gains tax changes, the minimum tax on trusts and the card surcharge issue, a picture is emerging of a government repeatedly being caught on the back foot.
There is internal anger at Chalmers, disbelief at some of the messaging and concern the government lacks a clear "agenda" for the remainder of the term.
Opponents face their own battles
Some Labor MPs view the level of caucus angst as disproportionate to the reality of the party's position.
The Coalition remains in disarray, One Nation is yet to face the scrutiny that comes with being a serious electoral contender, and the Greens are grappling with their own internal tensions.
Even if Labor's opponents manage to get their act together, the government still has time to recover.
There is a sense that the recent internal rumblings are the result of pent-up frustration that has built over the last year spent being a loyal backbencher.
Many MPs were willing to accept their largely powerless roles as "team players" when things were going well.
They are less inclined to sit quietly when they believe the government is making avoidable mistakes.
Loading
Punishing end to the year
The caucus knows last year's election result, where Labor did not lose a single seat, was exceptionally rare in Australian politics.
There is almost no chance that happens again, which means there are Labor MPs currently in parliament starting to consider the very real prospect of being out of a job in 18 months' time.
Albanese is attuned to these internal rumblings and has consistently proven adept at managing the forces that shape the caucus' mood.
The PM prizes orderly process, but the danger is in mistaking stagnation for stability.
A frontbench reshuffle is not only inevitable, but also necessary to reinvigorate the cabinet and bring new talent through the ranks.
Labor can ill-afford any malaise and is in dire need of fresh ideas to kick start productivity and capture voters' attention.
Not everyone can be winners, which means some on the frontbench will also have to embrace the role of "team player" and step back.
Albanese now faces a punishing end to the year, with little prospect of relief from the economic and political pressures weighing on his government.
The prime minister may be confident the conditions will favour Labor in time to secure victory, but his teammates out on the field are impatient for a clearer game plan.

'He kept on hitting': Indian flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar reveals what happened mid-flight as he was stabbed

Indian pilot Smit Machchhar who was attacked by his co-pilot aboard a Flydubai flight has recalled how a routine journey turned into a fight for survival, describing the repeated blows to his head, his attempts to call for help and the moments he lost consciousness as the aircraft went into a dive.after he was stabbed by his Omani copilot Hamam Al Hammami who was allegedly trying to crash the plane.In an exclusive 1st news interview after being stabbed, with Sky News Arabia, Captain Smith Machchhar said there had been nothing unusual about the flight until about two hours after take-off. He was carrying out routine checks in the cockpit when the attack began, initially mistaking the first blow to the back of his head for damage to the aircraft.
Giving out details as he remembered he said, "when I was just in in the checking my computer for the timing and everything, uh suddenly there was a a very hard hit at the back of my head, right here. And uh it was quite hard and felt that it was something which was very strong."He said he initially thought something had broken off the aircraft's roof and hit him, causing catastrophic damage. Drawing on his training, he tried to regain his composure and check the aircraft's systems. “My thought process went on that track, that oh, there is a big damage in the aircraft which has hit me at the back,” he said.But within seconds, he realised he was being attacked. “He kept on hitting,” Machchhar said.
He recalled turning around and realising what was happening, although the impact had severely restricted his field of vision.“Immediately, I would say in the next few seconds, my vision was restricted to like few inches,” he said, adding that he learnt about the extent of the impact from doctors later.His first response was to protect himself from further blows. He quickly unbuckled his seatbelt, turned around and tried to block the attack, sustaining an injury to his hand. “At this point, it was very obvious what was going on,” he said.
‘Smith, do something. You can’t die like this’
Machchhar said he immediately tried to get help from another captain who was on board and was expected to operate the return flight. “I was screaming his name and I was trying because the switch was very close to me to open the door. I was trying to just get help in,” he said.He lost consciousness amid the commotion but remembered managing to open the cockpit door. He could hear shouting as the other crew members confronted the co-pilot. “The door shut immediately after that because he threatened to hit them as well,” Machchhar said.By then, he was struggling to stay conscious and could feel his strength fading because of blood loss. Soon afterwards, he heard the engine sounds change and felt the aircraft go into a dive. “Since I’ve been flying for such a long time, I don’t have to see the instruments to figure out or hear the engine to know what’s happening,” he said.Machchhar said he repeatedly drifted in and out of consciousness but realised he had to fight to survive. “There was a moment where I realised and I told myself that, ‘Smith, do something. You can’t die like this,’” he said.His memories of what happened next remain fragmented. He recalled trying to reach the door, bracing his leg against something and pushing himself forward.“The next memory that I have is the door’s open and I’m lying between the cockpit and the galley,” he said. He remembered being face down as panic and shouting continued around him.
‘Everyone did their best’
While Machchhar was fighting to survive, another captain took over the controls and helped save the aircraft. “The other thing, how my other colleague who took over the controls and saved the day again is commendable. It’s something that I’ll keep with me till I die,” he said.Asked what he wanted people to understand about the incident amid speculation over how the plane was saved, Machchhar said everyone on board had done what they could.“I think everyone in world everyone in world did the best in their capacity to save the day,” he said. The pilot said the first blow continued to haunt him in the days after the attack.“Immediately after the event, I used to get flashes of the first hit. And trust me, it shook me up for the first few days,” he said, describing how the memory would return suddenly and leave his heart racing.But what stayed with him most was the determination of those on board. “One thing that I would take away from that day was the determination, the sheer determination of everyone to survive,” he said.Machchhar said he felt out of danger only when the aircraft touched down in Saudi Arabia. By then, a doctor was attending to him in the galley, while crew members worked to keep him conscious.
Asked whom he thought of first, he replied: “My son.” His two-year-old son, wife and daughter live with him in the UAE.Machchhar also expressed gratitude for the medical treatment he received in Saudi Arabia and after being brought back to the UAE. “From the first day onwards, the way I was taken care of, the way I was brought back to the UAE, even the care that I was given in Saudi is something I would never forget in my life,” he said.Still recovering from the traumatic incident, he said he felt grateful for the care and support he had received over the preceding two-and-a-half weeks.“Grateful is the word I would say right now,” he said.

ANU – Museum of the Jewish People in Tel Aviv will celebrate Aliyah Day on Sunday, October 18, beginning at 5 p.m., with an evening of food, films, music, and conversation dedicated to immigrants and their contributions to Israeli society.
Aliyah Day, established by the Knesset in 2016, recognizes the importance of Jewish immigration to Israel and honors immigrants’ contributions to the country.
Now in its third year, the museum’s “Oleh Oleh” initiative is organized with Nefesh B’Nefesh, the Nadav Foundation, local authorities from around Israel, and organizations that support immigrants.
New arrivals and longtime residents are invited to participate in activities in English, Spanish, Russian, and French.
This year’s theme is the Jewish and Israeli dining table, exploring how food connects people with their memories, traditions, and communities.
ANU offers guided tours, film screenings
A market featuring kosher food stalls, games, and activities will run from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m. Classic films and rare archival footage documenting immigration journeys, drawn from the museum’s Oster Visual Documentation Center, will screen from 6:30 p.m. to 8 p.m.
Two rounds of guided museum tours, offered between 6:15 p.m. and 7:45 p.m. in Hebrew, English, French, Russian, and Spanish, will explore the connections between Jewish food, memory, culture, and identity.
From 8 p.m. to 9 p.m., immigrants from different countries and generations will gather around tables to share their experiences of making Israel their home.
A live performance and folk dancing will conclude the evening from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m.
ANU CEO Oded Revivi said the event recognizes immigrants as partners in shaping Israeli society.
Rabbi Yehoshua Fass, co-founder and executive director of Nefesh B’Nefesh, emphasized that integration continues beyond arrival, through friendships, social connections, and opportunities to develop a sense of belonging.
Admission includes all activities. Food at the market is sold separately.
For more information, go to the ANU website at anumuseum.org.il/he/events/olim-event

LUMAGICA light festival returns to Tel Aviv's Hayarkon Park after 160,000 visitors in first edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:47:52 UTC
02:47:52 KST

Following an initial season that drew an estimated 160,000 visitors, the international light exhibition LUMAGICA is scheduled to return to Hayarkon Park (Ganei Yehoshua) starting November 12.
The upcoming iteration features an updated thematic concept developed specifically for the local venue by global design teams and local artists.
Produced by MK Illumination, the installation utilizes approximately three million LED lights, kinetic sculptures, and interactive elements.
Logistics began nearly a year in advance, involving production across four facilities in six countries and the maritime transport of 15 tons of equipment. The scale of the prior event earned the Tel Aviv location a placement within the organization’s top 10 European parks last year.
The global production framework required simultaneous coordination across multiple manufacturing sites, using 12 shipping containers and specialized gear air-freighted directly to Israel to meet the complex infrastructure demands.
Key features at LUMAGICA Tel Aviv
Key features of the upcoming layout include a field of roughly 30,000 illuminated artificial tulips. The centerpiece consists of a 30-meter-wide water screen displaying video art, accompanied by an original musical score composed by artist Misha Anton.
The venue will also accommodate a European-style winter fair, incorporating two dining spaces, food stalls, and a carnival games sector.
Designers have structured the layout to prioritize the active visitor experience, aiming to move attendance away from passive observation. Visitors are invited to physically step inside the light environments, becoming an integrated component of the illuminated installations, flower fields, and technological displays.
According to the production team, the objective is to leverage color, movement, and sound to immerse the public directly into the nocturnal journey.
Standard admission tickets cost NIS 109. The exhibition will operate from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. on weekdays and Saturdays.

TMoCA cinematheque to review 6 films by Stanley Kubrick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:45:28 UTC
02:45:28 KST

TMoCA cinematheque to review 6 films by Stanley Kubrick
TEHRAN – The cinematheque of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art (TMoCA) will review six films by Stanley Kubrick on Sunday.
The films will be examined from a philosophical perspective in a session titled “Kubrick and the Cinema of Machines,” Mehr reported.
In this program, Farzad Karimi, a postdoc in interdisciplinary studies of literature and philosophy, will analyze the works alongside screening excerpts from six films by the late filmmaker.
The event will feature excerpts from the films “Dr. Strangelove,” “2001: A Space Odyssey,” “A Clockwork Orange,” “The Shining,” “Full Metal Jacket,” and “Eyes Wide Shut”.
Attending this program is free and open to the general public.
Stanley Kubrick (1928 – 1999) was an American filmmaker and photographer. A prominent figure of the New Hollywood era, Kubrick is regarded as one of the greatest and most influential filmmakers. His films spanned a number of genres and gained recognition for their attention to detail, innovative cinematography, extensive set design, and dark humor.
Kubrick's “Dr. Strangelove or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the Bomb” (1964) was a satirical black comedy. Kubrick became preoccupied with the issue of nuclear war as the Cold War unfolded in the 1950s, and even considered moving to Australia because he feared that New York City might be a likely target for the Russians. He studied over 40 military and political research books on the subject and eventually reached the conclusion that "nobody really knew anything and the whole situation was absurd".
A perfectionist who assumed direct control over most aspects of his filmmaking, Kubrick cultivated expertise in writing, editing, color grading, promotion, and exhibition. He was famous for the painstaking care taken in researching his films and staging scenes. He frequently asked for several dozen retakes of the same shot, often confusing and frustrating his actors. Many of Kubrick's films broke new cinematic ground and are now considered landmarks. The scientific realism and innovative special effects in his science fiction epic “2001: A Space Odyssey” (1968) were a first in cinema history; the film earned him his only Academy Award (for Best Visual Effects) and is regarded as one of the greatest films ever made.
While many of Kubrick's films were controversial and initially received mixed reviews upon release—particularly the brutal “A Clockwork Orange” (1971), which Kubrick withdrew from circulation in the UK following a media frenzy—most were nominated for Academy Awards, Golden Globes, or BAFTA Awards, and underwent critical re-evaluations.
With the horror film “The Shining” (1980), he became one of the first directors to make use of a Steadicam for stabilized and fluid tracking shots, a technology vital to his Vietnam War film “Full Metal Jacket” (1987). A few days after hosting a screening for his family and the stars of his final film, “Eyes Wide Shut” (1999), he died at the age of 70.

Researcher calls for greater understanding between religion and music in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:45:05 UTC
02:45:05 KST

Researcher calls for greater understanding between religion and music in Iran
TEHRAN- A deeper understanding of the relationship between religious institutions and the arts is essential to addressing longstanding challenges surrounding music in Iran, cultural sociologist Hossein Sarvi says, emphasizing the need for informed dialogue and a reassessment of institutional relations.
Speaking to Mehr News Agency, Sarvi, whose book “Religion and Music in Contemporary Iran” examines the historical and social dimensions of the subject, said some of the tensions between religion and music stem not necessarily from fundamental conflicts but from insufficient understanding of the nature, functions and sensitivities of the two fields.
“One of the main objectives of this research has been to help improve what I call ‘mutual institutional literacy’ between religious institutions and the arts,” Sarvi explained.
The concept refers to the ability of each institution to better understand the other's internal logic, functions, requirements and concerns, creating opportunities for more informed and realistic interaction.
Sarvi argued that the relationship between religion and music in Iran remains an important subject for cultural and social debate. Questions concerning the relationship between religious and artistic institutions, cultural policymaking on music, and the scope and methods of official intervention continue to require reflection and scholarly discussion, he said.
According to the researcher, examining these issues solely through a historical lens would overlook their continuing relevance to contemporary Iranian society. He believes that a more comprehensive understanding of the two fields could help move discussions beyond oversimplified interpretations and encourage more constructive engagement.
Sarvi also stressed that academic research should not be evaluated solely by conventional publishing-market standards, noting that specialized scholarly works generally address a narrower audience than popular literature. For him, the more significant measure of a study's impact is its ability to enter academic discussions, attract the attention of researchers and contribute to sustained intellectual debate.
He expressed hope that his book would reach a broader audience, particularly university students, researchers, cultural policymakers and those interested in interdisciplinary studies. He added that further discussion of the issues raised in the research could contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between religion and music in Iran.
Sarvi also highlighted the role of institutions responsible for introducing and promoting scholarly publications, saying that producing and publishing research represents only part of the process of generating and disseminating knowledge. Efforts to make such works accessible to wider audiences are equally important in helping them gain a stronger presence in academic and cultural life.
Sarvi holds a PhD in cultural sociology and specializes in cultural studies and the sociology of art. He has experience in research, teaching and cultural administration and is currently conducting postdoctoral research in the Department of Music Studies at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens.
His book, “Religion and Music in Contemporary Iran,” has recently reached its second edition following interest from researchers, academics, scientific and research centers, and readers interested in cultural and social studies.

26th Tehran Auction realizes over $4.6 million

26th Tehran Auction realizes over $4.6 million
TEHRAN – The 26th Tehran Auction, dedicated to modern and contemporary Iranian art, grossed more than $4.6 million. In this edition, Parviz Tanavoli’s bronze “Heech” sculpture was sold as the most expensive artwork in the history of the auction.
Held at the Parsian Azadi Hotel in Tehran on October 16, the 26th Tehran Auction presented 100 works by 93 modern and contemporary Iranian artists, celebrating the diversity of artistic expression and the enduring value of Iran’s art scene, Honaronline reported.
The total estimated value of the artworks in this edition was announced at $2.941 million. Ultimately, amidst intense competition among art buyers, all 100 offered works were sold for a total of $4,603,500.
The most expensive work of this auction was a bronze sculpture titled “Heech” by Parviz Tanavoli, which had a base price of $750,000 and was hammered down at $1.77 million. This work broke the sales record across all editions of the Tehran Auction.
Following Tanavoli’s “Heech” sculpture, an untitled mirror mosaic work by Monir Farmanfarmaian, with a base price of $377,000, was sold for $461,538, setting the second-highest record in the auction’s history.
The third landmark artwork in the Iranian art market was a piece by Kourosh Shishegaran titled “Inside and Outside,” which had a base price of $204,000 and was sold for $252,800.
The other best-selling artists whose works were offered at the auction include Abolghasem Saidi, Mohammad Ehsai, Hossein Zenderoudi, Mansour Ghandriz, Aydin Aghdashloo, Farideh Lashai, Wahed Khakdan, Manouchehr Yektai, Massoud Arabshahi, Sadegh Tabrizi, and Shahriar Ahmadi, among others.
The first of its kind in Iran, the Tehran Auction was launched in 2012 as an independent and private initiative to introduce the best in Iranian art, ranging from established and emerging Iranian artists to art collectors and the global audience.
It aims to address the increasing interest in modern and contemporary Iranian art and facilitate the acquisition of quality works in reliable ways.
Photo: From left: “Heech” by Parviz Tanavoli, untitled mirror mosaic work by Monir Farmanfarmaian, and “Inside and Outside” by Kourosh Shishegaran were sold as the most expensive artworks of the 26th Tehran Auction, respectively.

Iran's FM says Tehran ready for dialogue based on mutual respect, credible guarantees
