Tens of thousands march in Lisbon over housing and living costs
LISBON – Tens of thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Oct 17 to protest against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis in Portugal, increasing pressure on the centre-right government.
Portugal’s biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “tens of thousands” packed one of the capital’s main avenues. Police gave no crowd estimate.
Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet in the European Union and NATO member state.
The demonstration followed days of growing unrest, including a tent camp set up by housing activists in the northern city of Porto that police cleared in a pre-dawn operation on Oct 12.
It coincides with protests in France against rising costs and declining public services, and smaller protests in Belgium. There are also mass protests in Albania, where protesters are demanding the prime minister’s resignation.
Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6% in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15% year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.
House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s worst housing affordability crises.
The squeeze is most acute in major cities.
Protesters’ concerns
Carolina Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher earning about €1,300 (S$1,870) a month on a scholarship, may lose her home as her rental contract nears expiry.
She and her partner pay €716 monthly for a flat in the Lisbon area, but renewal could push the rent above €1,200 – far beyond their means.
“I’m the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I’ve done, I still can’t make it... Right now, housing in Lisbon is the problem,” Cruz said.
Pedro Penilo, 62, a teacher, said Portugal’s leaders were “out of touch with reality”.
“Life is incredibly expensive… it’s going up brutally. I need to see how my mortgage is going to turn out in the coming months when it’s adjusted. I’m very worried,” he said.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Oct 16 that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street” and that concrete measures to address the concerns were already being rolled out. REUTERS

The revered Sabarimala Lord Ayyappa temple was opened on Saturday for the rituals of the Thulam month, drawing numerous devotees eager to pay their respects.
The Sabarimala Lord Ayyappa temple opened on Saturday for the Thulam month rituals, with Kerala Chief Minister V D Satheesan and several other dignitaries visiting the hill shrine to offer prayers.In the presence of Tantri Kandar Brahmadathan, head priest Prasad E D opened the sanctum sanctorum and lit the ceremonial lamp. The sacred fire was then kindled in the Aazhi, located below the 18 holy steps leading to the shrine.

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:04:04 UTC
02:04:04 KST

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together
Iran's FM tells OIC US has deepened distrust after two years of good-faith talks, making new talks impossible without credible guarantees.
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi told the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad that lasting security in the region is indivisible: either states build security together, or they will endure insecurity together.
Speaking on Saturday at the OIC ministerial meeting hosted by Iraq under the theme "Dialogue and solidarity, two fundamental pillars for promoting peace and sustainable development," Araghchi laid out Iran's position on the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, Palestine and Yemen.
Araghchi arrived in Baghdad to attend the 52nd session, and was welcomed at the airport by Iraq's Deputy Foreign Minister. Upon arrival at Baghdad International Airport, he paid tribute at the memorial of resistance commanders Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis.
He opened his address by thanking the Government and people of Iraq, "our neighbor and brother," for hosting the meeting, congratulating Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed on his appointment, and thanking Türkiye for its successful chairmanship of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers.
The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice, he said, recalling that its Charter, like the UN Charter, rests on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and refraining from threat or use of force. Those principles, he stressed, "belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value."
Aggression instead of diplomacy
Araghchi said Iran has remained steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy over the past two years, while "the United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law."
About 5,000 Iranians have been martyred, including hundreds of women and children, he said. He accused the United States and the Israeli regime of assassinating Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, calling it a grave violation of international law.
Citing documented cases, he listed the killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak in Sirik. The U.S. and Israel, he said, "cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor."
He thanked those member states that expressed solidarity with the Iranian people and called on the Organization as a whole "to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member."
Iran, he added, defended its people, sovereignty and legitimate interests and will continue to do so by any means. "We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the U.S. military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately located in our neighborhood."
There is no contradiction between defending rights and pursuing peace, he said: "We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace. Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all."
"This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation," he added.
Hormuz open until Feb. 28, reopenable in seven days
On the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's commitment to safe and secure navigation in the waterway vital to the energy and trade of many OIC members.
"Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States," he said.
"Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal."
He revealed that diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on June 17. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to facilitate safe movement of vessels and immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman. Within two weeks, he said, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level.
Subsequent unilateral U.S. measures and military action blocked implementation and bypassed the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged, Araghchi said.
Over two years, Iran negotiated in good faith and repeatedly was met with military action rather than diplomacy, creating deep distrust about renewed talks without credible assurances, he said.
"Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," Araghchi told the ministers.
Palestine and Yemen
Araghchi called Palestine the central cause of the Islamic world. "We cannot speak of peace while ignoring it," he said, describing Gaza as a victim of genocide and a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians.
Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence, he said, urging the OIC to make ending the killing and blockade and protecting civilians a shared priority backed by practical and coordinated action. He endorsed the proposal by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to designate a Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.
On Yemen, he said the people have endured almost a decade of devastating conflict, prolonged blockade and restrictions on civilian infrastructure, with undeniable U.S. and Israeli roles. Iran supports the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of both Yemen and Saudi
Arabia, he said, and backs a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only sustainable solution.
"There is no military solution," he said. "Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion."
Iran, he added, is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to assist dialogue between the parties on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.
Build security together
Closing his speech, Araghchi delivered his central message to the Islamic world in a direct appeal:
"No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former."
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees," he concluded.
On the margins of the Baghdad session, Araghchi held a series of bilateral meetings to explain Tehran's positions on Hormuz, Palestine and the Arabian Peninsula.
U.S. broke its word two weeks after Islamabad MoU
In his meeting on Saturday morning with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Araghchi, recalling the founding philosophy of the OIC, described Palestine as still the most important issue of the Islamic world, and stressing the genocide and crimes in occupied Palestine, underlined the need for urgent and joint action by the Islamic Ummah to end occupation and genocide and end the impunity of the Zionist regime.
On the region, he said the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime that began on Feb. 28 and have continued in various forms.
Emphasizing Iran's commitment to diplomacy and peace, he noted that the Islamic Republic has always responsibly adhered to diplomacy to reduce tensions, but the American side has repeatedly broken its promises, and in the latest case violated its commitment only two weeks after signing the agreement on ending the war.
He also briefed his Egyptian counterpart on the latest diplomatic consultations through mediators.
On the Arabian Peninsula, Araghchi announced Iran's readiness to provide any assistance to stop clashes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, stressing that the experience of 12 years of tension and conflict showed there is no military solution or military approach to Yemen.
Hormuz developments reviewed with Fidan
In his meeting with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, the two sides discussed bilateral ties and the latest regional developments, particularly Palestine and the continued genocide.
Referring to the summit theme of dialogue and solidarity, Araghchi stressed the need for Islamic states to focus on Palestine and take practical measures to stop Israeli crimes and help realize the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Both sides, emphasizing stronger cooperation among Islamic countries, also consulted on using OIC capacities to confront challenges facing the Islamic world, including Islamophobia.
The latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz were also reviewed, with Araghchi briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing trends.
Stability in Libya is prerequisite for North Africa
In a meeting with Taher al-Baour, acting Foreign Minister of Libya, both sides reviewed Tehran-Tripoli ties and stressed strengthening consultations.
Araghchi repeated Iran's principled position in support of national sovereignty and territorial integrity and unity, and the need to stop any foreign interference, and stressed that security and stability in Libya is a prerequisite for peace and stability in North Africa.
Both sides also consulted on developments in the region and the Islamic world. Araghchi, pointing to continued occupation and genocide by Israel in Palestine, called Palestine the greatest priority of the Islamic Ummah and the international community and called for urgent and serious OIC action to end the genocide in Gaza and end Israeli impunity.
Araghchi also met his Lebanese counterpart Youssef Raji on the sidelines in Baghdad for talks on bilateral ties and regional developments.

Meta denies favouring Bolsonaro as Brazil court orders equal treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:02:58 UTC
02:02:58 KST

Meta has denied favouring Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro after a court ordered the company to treat him and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva equally ahead of their October 25 runoff.
The company said on Friday that problems affecting Lula’s accounts stemmed from global technical glitches, anti-fraud measures and regulatory compliance, rather than political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it said.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported, citing internal messages it reviewed, that Meta employees acknowledged restrictions had hindered Lula’s Instagram accounts while the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and WhatsApp channel.
Lula’s campaign alleged that some of his posts lacked sharing options, had reduced reach and suffered technical problems affecting audio and user interactions.
The campaign also said it would file a complaint with the Organization of American States, accusing Meta of manipulating social media during the election.
Meta said the technical issues were already public and that the internal discussions concerned their severity, not political interference.
The company cited two global disruptions earlier in October: one froze Instagram Reels view counts across more than 100 countries without affecting content distribution, while another temporarily prevented users from creating advertisements from existing Instagram posts through one of its tools.
Its response did not address why Bolsonaro’s Instagram profile and WhatsApp channel had received algorithmic recommendations.
Court orders equal treatment
On Thursday, a justice at Brazil’s top electoral court ordered Meta not to unjustifiably restrict the reach of political content related to either candidate during the runoff campaign.
The ruling also required the company’s chatbot, Meta AI, to avoid favouring either candidate in election-related content.
Meta said it would continue to defend itself in the case.
The dispute follows Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected first-round performance, which secured him a place in the runoff against Lula.
Lula’s administration has pursued tighter regulation of technology platforms, including measures targeting illegal content and misinformation.
Irregular political ads
Separately, a study by researchers at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro found Meta allowed at least 1,613 irregular political advertisements between July and September.
The ads, funded primarily from the United States, generated 171 million views and approximately two million reais ($400,000) in revenue, AFP reported, citing the study.
Marie Santini, a communication professor involved in the study, said only political parties, candidates and coalitions were permitted to purchase electoral advertisements in Brazil.
“It is not the first time that Meta is negligent with the electoral law, not the first country. It is a systematic behavior of the company,” she said.

Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:00:11 UTC
02:00:11 KST

Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
New York architect Diana Kellogg has renovated her historic Tribeca residence, highlighting materials repurposed from its industrial past.
Kellogg and her family have occupied the home on Staple Street for 25 years, which is close to the studio that the architect shares with her filmmaker husband.
The building originally served as cold storage for neighbouring produce distribution facilities, then became a plumber's supply storefront and eventually a residence around 50 years ago.
Kellogg has renovated and updated the structure gradually over the years, and when her kids moved out, she decided to undertake a more comprehensive overhaul.
An old freight elevator was removed and replaced with a space that Kellogg refers to as the Green Room.
The glass-wrapped nook is lined with cushioned seating and used for intimate catch-ups over drinks, or private video calls.
The salvage from the elevator and other elements around the building were repurposed to create structures for the kitchen, bookcases, and a staircase that connects the four levels.
"Throughout the house there were old glass and steel doors, and windows and stuff," Kellogg said. "I just moved them around and repurposed them."
In keeping with the architecture, the decor remains industrial and spare, highlighting key elements like the fireplace and the 25-foot-long chestnut beams that span the ceiling.
"It was a massive pain in the neck to strip those, but one of the best decisions we made, because they add so much warmth and character," said Kellogg.
During the most recent renovation, the upstairs bedrooms with vaulted brick ceilings were reconfigured as neutrally decorated spaces separated by sliding mahogany doors.
On the ground floor, the children's former playroom – complete with climbing ropes and a swing – was converted into a comfortable TV room, featuring a large L-shaped sofa and a variety of midcentury furniture pieces.
Matching those on the level above, Noguchi pendant lights hang from the steel beams that Kellogg added to suspend the "jungle gym".
"There's still one climbing rope down there that people think is an art piece, which I love," she said.
Key artworks include a pair of photographs by Ljubodrag Andric, which he produced to sit either side of the first-floor fireplace and "give the place so much depth and warmth," said Kellogg.
Downstairs, the walls are adorned with images of The Rajkumari Ratnavati Girl's School that Kellogg completed in 2021 in India's Thar Desert.
The roof terrace was relandscaped with planters and a variety of wooden outdoor furniture that forms dining and seating areas with views of a historic bridge between the adjacent buildings.
"I really wanted an oasis up there, and to have it be a second living room," said Kellogg. "And there's the fabulous bridge, which we have kind of great views of from our house – which is, in my opinion, better than actually being inside it."
Many of Tribeca's former industrial buildings are now residential, housing large lofts and penthouses, while others contain galleries and creative spaces.
Examples of other homes in the neighbourhood include a penthouse in the American Thread Building updated by Crina Arghirescu Rogard and a loft that Andrea Leung renovated to conceal "secret spaces".
The photography is by Andrew Brinka.

Merz warns EU irregular migration battle far from over despite drop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned Friday that the European Union still faces significant challenges in managing migration, despite a decline in arrivals and the adoption of new asylum rules aimed at overhauling the bloc's migration system.
"By now almost every head of state and government in the European Union sees it that way: We have a massive problem that places a considerable burden on our societies," Merz said at the EU summit in Brussels.
He said he expressly agreed with this view. "Irregular migration is one of the biggest problems we have in Europe," he added.
Merz commented on the issue on the sidelines of a debate about the lessons from the migration crisis in Ceuta.
At the end of July, an estimated 80,000 migrants had entered the Spanish exclave from Morocco. According to the government in Madrid, most of the arrivals returned voluntarily to Morocco within a very short time. At least 140 people died trying to reach Ceuta. Aid organizations put the figure significantly higher.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker demanded at the EU summit that there should be more legal options to respond to mass arrivals like those in Ceuta, in particular a right not to have to accept asylum applications under such circumstances.
Greece's government is also pushing to create the legal basis for this option. Greece has suspended the examination of asylum applications twice in the past, most recently in 2025 for three months because of a sharp rise in boat arrivals from Libya to Crete and Gavdos.
The EU migration rules do not actually provide for a full suspension of the right to apply for asylum. The principle of non-refoulement states that a state may not turn back or deport a person to a country where they face persecution, torture or another treatment that violates human rights.

Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?

Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?
A wave of new Latin American leaders reverses measures meant to isolate Israel after its genocidal war on Gaza.
When Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced on October 8 that Colombia would be moving its embassy to Jerusalem, he made sure to point out how important the development was for his country’s diplomatic narrative, and that it heralded warming relations with Latin American governments.
“We will work hard because this is the diplomatic battle over the truth,” Saar said. “And the truth is, Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation.”
Brazil, Saar went on to say, might soon join Colombia and the growing list of Latin American countries that had moved their embassies to Jerusalem, the disputed city claimed by Israelis and Palestinians as their capital.
Latin America’s relationship with Israel is shifting, as right-wing parties come into power in the region and pro-Israel politicians use their support for the country to rally voters.
Brazil, the largest country in the region, is in the midst of a presidential election campaign in which the relationship with Israel has become a key talking point.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a left-wing ardent supporter of Palestine, is locked in a close contest with right-wing rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. He has sported Israeli flags at campaign rallies and played up his friendship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The pair are scheduled to take part in a run-off election after Bolsonaro performed surprisingly strongly in the first -round, apparently raising hopes for a detente with Israeli officials like the foreign minister.
Last month, for instance, Colombia and Israel began allowing their citizens to travel visa-free between their countries, yet another signal the newly inaugurated government of Abelardo de la Espriella wants to restore ties that were cut in the wake of Israel’s war on Gaza.
Experts say the realignment with Israel is driven, in part, by new leaders trying to signal they have joined a regional alignment with United States President Donald Trump. But it’s also being fuelled by a massive lobbying effort in which Evangelical Christian groups and Israeli-government-backed organisations in the region have pushed Latin American countries to support Israel.
“It’s not one factor or the other, but a convergence,” said Marta Tawil Kuri, Research Professor at the Center for International Studies at the College of Mexico. “Right-wing leaderships seeking validation from Washington, evangelical bases giving them electoral and ideological grounding, and an Israeli diplomatic offensive that finds fertile ground in Latin America precisely as its image deteriorates elsewhere.”
“The most Zionist president in the world”
Colombia’s last leader, Gustavo Petro, severed ties with Israel over what he said was the genocidal war on Gaza. He stopped exporting Colombian coal to Israel, cut military and security cooperation and planned to open a Colombian embassy to Palestine. The former left-wing fighter seemed to take every public opportunity to criticise Israel, even using a trip to New York City for a United Nations summit to take part in a protest against Trump and the war on Gaza.
His successor, de la Espriella, has rapidly reversed Bogota’s stance on Israel since coming to power in August, announcing plans to move his country’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, re-appoint ambassadors and even recognising Israeli control over the occupied Syrian territory of the Golan Heights.
Strong presidential systems and weak, unprofessional diplomatic corps allow new heads of state to quickly pivot on issues such as ties with Israel, said Kuri.
“Unlike the US, where support for Israel has stayed relatively stable across administrations thanks to more consolidated institutions and bipartisan consensus, in much of Latin America foreign policy can swing sharply from one election to the next because that institutional buffer doesn’t exist,” Kuri said.
In 2023, Argentina elected right-wing populist Javier Milei as president, who pledged to move the embassy to Jerusalem, refused to recognise a Palestinian state at the UN and said he was “proud to be the most Zionist president in the world.”
In Bolivia, the leftist administration of Evo Morales, who was president from 2006 to 2019, had refused to have full diplomatic ties with Israel. This continued under the presidency of Luis Arce, who joined other regional left-wing leaders in recalling their ambassadors from Israel after October 7, 2023. When Arce was voted out last year, his replacement Rodrigo Paz promptly reversed that policy.
Soon after coming to office this August, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast undid his leftist predecessor’s actions against Israel as well, appointing an ambassador to Israel who describes himself as a “proud Zionist”.
Over in Honduras, the left-wing government was replaced by a right-wing leader this January. New President Nasry Asfura, the grandson of Palestinian immigrants from Bethlehem, similarly reappointed an ambassador to Israel this year.
In August, Venezuela announced it would restore consular relations with Israel, undoing nearly two decades of an antagonistic stance towards Israel under previous leaders Nicolas Maduro and Hugo Chavez.
Besides deciding where to put their embassies, Latin American governments have also sometimes lent support to legal efforts against Israel over the Gaza war. Mexico, Bolivia, Colombia, Brazil, Chile, Belize, Cuba and Nicaragua are among governments that at one point backed South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
Signalling in the Trump era
When Flavio Bolsonaro launched his Brazilian presidential campaign last July, he did so standing beside Argentinian President Milei. Some in the crowd waved Israeli flags and watched as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a video message calling Bolsonaro a friend and a “great champion of the friendship between our peoples”.
Giving foreign leaders such a prominent role in an election campaign is “unheard of in Latin America,” said Alexander Main, Director of International Policy at the Washington-DC-based Center for Economic and Policy Research. “This did not happen before, at least not so overtly.”
Bolsonaro’s campaign, experts say, is seeking to make itself part of a larger political camp that is led in the hemisphere by Trump and internationally includes Israel. Some received direct endorsements from Trump, such as Colombia’s de la Espriella and Honduras’s Asfura.
They’ve joined new right-wing umbrella groups led by the US, such as the Shield of the Americas, a counter-narcotics security alliance bringing together Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago. The effort is part of Trump’s policy for the Western Hemisphere that seeks to keep out the influence of other global powers like China.
Members of this Trump-led bloc have helped facilitate controversial US policies to deter migration, such as El Salvador, which is housing third-country deportees for the US. They’ve also chosen to frame their war on narcotics as a new kind of war on terrorism, a zero-sum conflict that is inspired by Israel’s war on the Palestinians, according to Main.
“They find common ground with Israel on a lot of these things,” Main said.
“Before, you had left-wing politicians in these regions that have seen what has happened in Gaza and called that war crimes and human rights abuses,” Main said. “Now you’ve seen, on the other hand, sectors seeing this as an existential fight against a deep-rooted enemy and that merits a kind of war on terror framing.”
Having good relations with Israel could translate into access to key military and security resources as well, Main said, including the use of sophisticated spy software such as Pegasus – which was developed by an Israeli software company – and sales of military jets or training of forces.
Isaac Accords and evangelical lobbying
The rally in August in Brazil that featured Netanyahu’s video message was also an attempt to win support from a large and influential voter bloc there who see protecting Israel as part of their religious worldview.
The Evangelical Parliamentary Front, a caucus of pro-Israel evangelical legislators, includes more than 40% of the Chamber of Deputies and more than a quarter of the Senate. If they formed a party, the loose alliance would become the third-largest in the country.
“Those constituencies have become increasingly politicised in recent years, to the point it is beneficial for politicians to court them and one of the ways they can do that is rallying behind Israel,” Main said.
Brazil is not the only country seeing this evangelical push to build ties with Israel.
“Evangelicalism — particularly Christian Zionism — is a real and growing factor in countries like Honduras and Guatemala,” Kuri said.
Around 40 percent of the population in those countries are evangelicals and both governments have moved their embassies to Jerusalem.
Groups from the US have also been lobbying on Israel’s behalf.
The Latino Coalition for Israel, led by Florida-based evangelical pastor Mario Bramnick, sends delegations throughout Latin America and has met with leaders in Guatemala, El Salvador, Brazil, Panama, Chile, and Costa Rica.
“Our support for Israel is first and foremost rooted in the Bible, where it was clearly established that God gave the Land of Israel, with Jerusalem as its undivided capital, to the Jewish people as an eternal covenant,” the group says on its website. A spokesperson for Bramnick declined to comment for this story.
In 2025, the Genesis Prize – an Israeli nonprofit launched with a $100 million endowment and Israeli government backing – awarded $1m to Argentinian President Milei for his “unequivocal support of Israel during one of the most difficult times since the founding of the Jewish State”.
Milei took the money and established the Isaac Accords, modelling the effort after the Abraham Accords, a Trump-backed effort to restore diplomatic and economic ties between Israel and the Arab world. The initiative gives grant money for pro-Israel civil society groups in Latin America. It also keeps meticulous track of many of the signalling moves right-wing governments are making in recent months to show their new stance on Israel, from moving embassies to Jerusalem to how they vote on Israel-related resolutions in the United Nations.
The initiative’s latest push? At the end of Netanyahu’s trip to the UN General Assembly in late September – where most of the audience walked out of his speech in protest – he and the leaders of Bolivia, Panama and Paraguay held their own summit. The Israeli leader urged them to join the Isaac Accords, writing on X that he sought to “expand the circle of friendship and partnership with Israel”.

Kenya confirms four more Ebola cases, bringing total to seven

Kenya confirms four more Ebola cases, bringing total to seven
Three health workers who treated the country’s first Ebola patient are among the latest confirmed cases.
The Kenyan government says four new patients have tested positive for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus, bringing the total number of confirmed cases in the East African nation to seven.
Three of the new cases were among health workers who treated the country’s first patient, Kenya’s Ministry of Health said in a statement posted on X on Saturday.
The fourth case is a relative of that same patient, who died from the disease, it added.
The relative had been in quarantine since October 6, the ministry said.
This comes a day after Kenya confirmed three cases in the country. The patient identified on Friday was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, the Health Ministry said.
Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which has recorded more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.
Kenya’s index patient died on October 5 after being ill in the DRC for a month and then flying to Nairobi on October 3. The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya.
Of the first patient’s 130 contacts, the Health Ministry said 128, or 98.5 percent, had been quarantined – above the global benchmark of 85 percent to break the chain of transmission.
The ministry says it has traced and quarantined nearly all of the first patient’s contacts and there is no evidence that the virus is spreading in the community.
Kenya has reacted quickly by strengthening screening and establishing a hotline for anyone who suspects they may have been in contact with an Ebola patient, but some observers have questioned how the index patient managed to bypass health screenings upon returning to Kenya and make contact with so many people.
Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing.
The dominant strain in this outbreak is the Bundibugyo strain, for which there are currently no vaccines or treatments. This has complicated efforts to control the spread of the disease.
Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain, and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.

The navy and the coast guard are acquiring 292 units of MQ-35A V-BAT vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) surveillance drones manufactured by US-based defense technology company Shield AI, making Taiwan one of the largest buyers of the drone.
The Coast Guard Administration budgeted NT$1.2 billion (US$37.1 million) to buy 12 drones, which have been delivered, Shield AI said in a report on Oct 13.
The navy is planning to spend NT$36 billion under a four-year program code-named Project Yuan Xiao (遠鴞) to acquire 280 V-BAT drones, the Ministry of National Defense’s fiscal 2027 report showed.
Photo: EPA
The combined procurement is expected to cost NT$37.2 billion.
The navy’s order alone would exceed the 250 V-BAT drones that Shield AI had sold to the US and other NATO countries as of 2024, the ministry’s report said.
The US military and coast guard combined are estimated to operate about 300 V-BAT drones, while the Netherlands, Armenia, Poland and other countries each operate fleets of several dozen drones, it said.
Taiwan could become the largest operator of V-BAT drones outside the US once deliveries are complete, it said.
The drones are intended to help maintain operational capability if Chinese attacks disrupt Taiwan’s command structure, the report said.
Of the navy’s planned procurement, 212 drones are earmarked for the Coastal Combat Command and Hsiung Feng anti-ship missile units. The package also includes 140 control systems and 82 ground transport vehicles, allowing missile units to use drones for reconnaissance and maintain precision-strike capabilities even when relocating or if their radars are destroyed, the ministry’s report said.
The navy cited the V-BAT’s performance during the war in Ukraine, saying that it had completed 130 successful reconnaissance missions despite strong Russian electronic interference.
At a briefing in Taipei on Oct 2, Shield AI president and cofounder Brandon Tseng (曾國光) said the share of V-BAT components supplied by Taiwanese companies was expected to rise to 25 percent from 16 percent.
Aerospace Industrial Development Corp will handle logistics, maintenance and training for Taiwan’s drones, he said.
The procurement is expected to bolster Taiwan’s defense capabilities in peacetime and during conflict, while giving Taiwanese companies a greater role in the supply chain for advanced US-made drones, he said.

Military to enlist civilians to map coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:14 UTC
01:48:14 KST

The navy plans to use civilian ships and aircraft to map beaches China is likely to use in an invasion, in a first-of-its-kind initiative, a senior military official said yesterday.
The Ministry of National Defense’s Defense Innovation Division plans to employ civilian fishing boats and aircraft to conduct high-precision hydrographic surveys and beach terrain mapping at potential Chinese invasion landing sites, known as “red beaches,” across Taiwan, the official said on condition of anonymity.
“Red beaches” are locations where the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is most likely to attempt amphibious assaults in the event of a conflict across the Taiwan Strait.
Photo: CNA
Four to 20 potential landing sites have been identified by the ministry, US think tanks and the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, including Zhuwei (竹圍) in Taoyuan, Wazihwei (挖子尾) in New Taipei City’s Bali District (八里) and Sishu (喜樹) in Tainan.
In the past few years, the concept has expanded to include “composite red beaches,” which combine port facilities with environments suitable for airborne operations.
In the past, crucial hydrological data were gathered independently by the navy’s 192nd and 151st fleets during training exercises.
However, given the dynamic near-shore topography shaped by dramatic seasonal and typhoon-driven changes, the capabilities and flexibility of traditional naval survey vessels have proven inadequate.
The military is adopting mature commercial off-the-shelf technologies with civilian and military applications.
Under the plan, the military would contract private survey companies to deploy vessels such as civilian fishing boats as asymmetric maritime sensors.
Equipped with advanced multibeam echo sounders, the boats would survey coastal waters up to 3m deep, where larger vessels cannot operate and smaller boats would otherwise take too long to map, generating high-density bathymetric data.
The military would also charter civilian aircraft to conduct large-scale aerial surveys of beach environments using light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology.
By directing laser pulses through the water’s surface, the aircraft can rapidly produce integrated 3D models of terrain above and below the waterline.
The data could help plan for PLA amphibious landings and provide a basis for defensive mine-laying operations, the official said.
They could identify deep channels in which to lay mines and reefs where obstacles could be placed, concealing mines to make them difficult to detect and blocking landing routes used by Chinese vessels and amphibious vehicles including hovercraft, they added.
Addressing concerns over national security risks associated with outsourcing sensitive military data to the private sector, including potential information leaks to China, the official said that security measures have been built into the mechanism.
Civilian fishing boats and aircraft would only collect raw physical data at the initial stage, the official said, comparing the information to meaningless fragments of a code.
Processing, including noise reduction, data integration and the most sensitive tasks — linking the information to military tactics and planning coordinates for counter-landing operations — would happen behind closed doors at military units, including the Naval Meteorological and Oceanographic Office, they said.
This decentralized approach would harness the efficiency of civilian technology while protecting national security, they added.
Faced with a possible cross-strait conflict, the navy has discarded a decades-old policy of relying solely on warships for military hydrological surveys by embracing private-sector partnerships and asymmetric warfare thinking to defend Taiwan’s coasts, they said.
The military would be able to gather critical intelligence on coastal operating environments dozens of times faster than before, the official said, calling it a major milestone.
The initiative demonstrates Taiwan’s determination to follow the US military’s Defense Innovation Unit’s example in developing asymmetric capabilities, they added.

Rennie vows expansive game at Cup

New Zealand coach Dave Rennie yesterday said his team would be sticking to their expansive style at next year’s Rugby World Cup after the All Blacks thrashed the Wallabies for a second successive week with some sensational attacking rugby.

More Taiwanese traveled to China this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:12 UTC
01:48:12 KST

Taiwanese made 2.492 million trips to China in the first eight months of this year, up 19.63 percent from a year earlier, even as the government kept its orange travel warning in place for China, Hong Kong and Macau, the latest statistics from the Tourism Administration showed.
China was the second-most popular overseas destination for Taiwanese travelers after Japan, the data showed. Trips to China have exceeded 300,000 every month since March, with March recording the largest year-on-year increase at 32.34 percent.
Taiwan has maintained the orange warning for China, Hong Kong and Macau since June 27, 2024. Orange is the second-highest warning level in Taiwan’s four-tier travel advisory system and advises the public to avoid nonessential travel to the affected destinations.
Photo: EPA-EFE
The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) said the increase in trips to China was part of a broader rise in outbound travel, which grew 15.24 percent year-on-year over the same period.
It attributed the trend partly to Taiwan’s economic growth and rising stock prices, which have boosted people’s wealth and made them more willing to spend on overseas travel, it said.
The MAC urged people planning to visit China to carefully assess the risks and keep up with official travel safety updates, citing changes to China’s national security laws and entry-exit regulations.
The rise was in line with overall growth in outbound travel, and business trips might also have contributed to it, Providence University Department of Tourism associate professor Huang Cheng-tsung (黃正聰) said yesterday.
Some Taiwanese might judge the risks based on previous visits, said Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), director of the Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience at the University of Taipei.
However, past trouble-free trips do not guarantee the same experience in the future, he said, citing cases in which Taiwanese have been questioned, detained or had their freedom of movement restricted in China.
The government faces challenges in communicating travel risks, as the orange warning has been in place for more than two years and might have limited influence on people who need to travel across the Taiwan Strait, Hung said.
He called for more specific information tailored to travelers’ backgrounds and purposes, including guidance on seeking help if they are questioned or prevented from leaving.

Small spenders beat rich teams as World Series looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:11 UTC
01:48:11 KST

When the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the mighty, monied Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday, it set up the first World Series between two of the MLB’s smallest spenders in 35 years — just as team owners are arguing that such clubs need a salary cap to compete consistently.
Milwaukee face either the Cleveland Guardians or the Tampa Bay Rays in a best-of-seven series for the title beginning on Saturday, ensuring that two clubs in the bottom half of big-league payrolls will play in the World Series for the first time since 1991.
Game 4 of the playoff series between the Guardians and the Rays on Friday was postponed due to rain.
Photo: Ken Blaze / Imagn Images
The Dodgers, the New York Mets and the New York Yankees will watch from home with payrolls this season that each cost more than the Brewers’, Guardians’ and Rays’ rosters combined.
The low-budget World Series showdown is to start six weeks before a likely management lockout, a work stoppage that threatens next year’s season as owners and players battle over the sport’s lack of a salary cap.
Speaking at the All-Star Game in July, Major League Baseball commissioner Rob Manfred made his case for a cap while saying exceptions did not reflect parity.
“Our view of the world is that over a very long period of time there’s a very strong relationship between who gets into the playoffs and who proceeds, notwithstanding the exceptions we’ve got,” Manfred said.
Milwaukee, who won the National League pennant with a four-game sweep of the Dodgers, had MLB’s 19th-highest payroll as of Aug. 31, while Tampa Bay were 25th and Cleveland 30th.
The last time both pennant winners were among the bottom 50 percent in player spending was when the Minnesota Twins (15th of 26 teams) beat the Atlanta Braves (19th) for the 1991 championship.

IMF head flags ‘optimism,’ ‘worry’ at meetings in Bangkok
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:11 UTC
01:48:11 KST

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva yesterday said that this year’s Annual Meetings with global policymakers were marked by “optimism and worry” about the global economic outlook as the event wound down in Bangkok.
Georgieva also said her organization had a “responsibility” to help low-income countries struggling with price shocks stemming from the US-Israel war on Iran.
Meetings in the Thai capital this week brought together finance ministers, central bank chiefs and other top officials from around the world, with surging inflation, spiking bond yields and economic growth driven by artificial intelligence (AI) at the top of the agenda.
Photo: EPA
The meetings “were marked by both optimism and worry,” said Georgieva, who was speaking at a press briefing alongside Saudi Arabian Minister of Finance Mohammed al-Jadaan.
“Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia. But AI is also recognized to be a source of worry, and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks,” she said.
All week, the IMF has warned that high levels of debt and rising bond yields in advanced economies are tightening financial conditions just as central banks need to focus on bringing inflation down, likely by increasing interest rates.
Global energy prices have spiked since late February, when the US and Israel launched the war on Iran, with Tehran’s retaliatory actions targeting Washington’s Gulf allies and curtailing oil and gas supplies.
The price increases have rippled across the globe, fueling inflation in economies across a range of income groups.
The most vulnerable to the shock, the IMF has said, are low-income oil-importing countries that are not exposed to the boom in AI investment that has propped up growth in many advanced economies.
“I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, they don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said.
Such countries needed to set spending targets such that they prioritized growth and protecting the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF had a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries.”
However, higher global interest rates and bond yields are driving up debt repayments for low-income countries, she said.
The share of debt repayments as a percentage of government revenue had gone up to 14 percent from 8 percent for low-income countries in the past few years, she said.
Her organization had a responsibility to help countries to restructure debt if needed, to assist with domestic resource mobilization, to bring in international finance and to create conditions for private investment, she said.
“When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” Georgieva said.
On the AI investment boom, she said that member countries had recognized its value in propping up growth, but “when we are dependent on one particular driver of growth, it is like we stand on one leg.”
A key debate at this year’s meetings has been on whether the technology’s most advanced frontier models require regulation and guardrails.
The question has grown more urgent after recent revelations of security incidents involving autonomous AI agents.
Georgieva said she was “impressed” by the spirit of cooperation between AI companies, governments and other stakeholders that she witnessed in Bangkok on the issue.

A call a day keeps the phone company away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:10 UTC
01:48:10 KST

An 88-year-old bakery owner in Changhua has found an unusual way to preserve a piece of Taiwan’s telecommunications history: by making a daily phone call from the public payphone outside his shop to his own home phone.
Li Tien-an (李添安), owner of the Hsing An Chen Bakery (興安珍餅行), now only sells mooncakes for 15 days each year during the Mid-Autumn Festival season due to his age, but he still carries coins to use the payphone outside his store every day to ensure it remains in use so that it would not be removed.
Li said he opened the bakery in 1962 and moved to a location on Minsheng Road in 1967. The next year, he applied to have a public payphone installed outside the store.
Photo: Liu Hsiao-hsin, Taipei Times
Before the construction of the nearby Minsheng underpass, the shop stood just one railway crossing away from the Changhua Railway Roundhouse, and the area was busy with foot traffic, making the payphone highly popular, he said.
At the time, mobile phones did not exist and payphones were heavily used, he added.
In the early days, the Directorate-General of Telecommunications, the predecessor of Chunghwa Telecom, paid commissions to businesses that hosted public payphones, he said.
He recalled receiving NT$300 a month, which provided a useful supplement to his income.
The payphone remained busy during the pager era, when people receiving messages while outdoors would search for a public phone to return calls, he said, adding that people frequently came to his bakery to exchange money for coins.
However, after mobile phones became widespread, payphones use fell off sharply, he said.
“In the past, people sometimes had to line up to use a payphone,” he said. “Nowadays, everyone has a mobile phone. A payphone’s main function is providing free access to emergency calls.”
After learning that payphones with insufficient usage could be removed, Li took steps to prevent it.
Every day, he inserts coins into the payphone and dials the family’s home telephone inside the store, hanging up as soon as he hears it ring.
“In the old days, having a payphone earned me money, but now I have to spend money to keep it from being removed,” he said.
The payphone has remained outside his store for 58 years and has been replaced with several different models across the decades, he said.
Li said he plans to continue making his daily calls to ensure the phone remains outside his shop.

====================================================================================================

Reading Taiwan in Indonesian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:05 UTC
01:48:05 KST

A few days ago, Indonesian social media were filled with photos of something unexpected in Taiwan: public notices written in Indonesian.
One widely shared image showed a no-smoking sign in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area. Alongside Chinese and English, the warning appeared in Indonesian, saying that smoking was prohibited outside designated areas. Another image showed a notice in Indonesian inside a shop asking customers not to open products before paying.
The posts quickly attracted comments. Some Indonesians reacted with embarrassment. The implication was uncomfortable, but easy to understand. Indonesian-language warnings would hardly be necessary, unless Indonesian visitors or residents had repeatedly been associated with the behavior being discouraged.
There is a lesson here that should not be avoided: Indonesians living or traveling abroad carry not only passports, but also a representation of their country. Smoking where it is prohibited, littering and disregarding other local rules might look like individual behavior, but it can easily become attached to a nationality.
The appearance of Indonesian on warning signs can be read as a reminder of civic responsibility. Living abroad requires more than adapting to a new workplace. It also means understanding how public space is regulated and how everyday behavior is judged by society.
The same signs also reveal how deeply Indonesians have become part of Taiwan’s social landscape. According to the Ministry of Labor, there were 329,586 Indonesian migrant workers in Taiwan at the end of March, making them the largest group of foreign workers in Taiwan.
The Ministry of Education said that more than 19,300 Indonesian students were studying in Taiwan last academic year. These numbers are large enough to transform everyday life.
Indonesian caregivers look after Taiwanese elderly people. Factory workers contribute to manufacturing. Fishers work in an industry vital to Taiwan’s maritime economy. Students study in Taiwanese universities. Indonesian shops, restaurants and community gatherings have become familiar parts of life in Taiwanese cities.
This is why an Indonesian-language sign means more than a warning. A city translates its everyday instructions into a language, because speakers of that language have become visible.
Indonesia and Taiwan do not have formal diplomatic relations. Indonesia maintains its “one China” policy, while practical relations are managed through representative offices. On paper, the relationship has political limits. However, at the level of society, the relationship is remarkably dense.
Formal diplomacy might be limited, but everyday diplomacy is flourishing. It happens in factories, classrooms, nursing homes, fishing ports, convenience stores and train stations. Daily encounters rarely make diplomatic headlines, but they create something diplomacy often struggles to produce: familiarity.
For Indonesians in Taiwan, greater visibility brings greater responsibility. Community organizations, recruitment agencies and Indonesian institutions should pay more attention to civic orientation.
For Taiwan, Indonesian should not appear only when something has gone wrong. If the language is useful for saying “do not smoke” or “do not open this product,” it is equally useful for explaining labor rights, health services, emergency procedures, public transportation and other forms of public information.
Language can discipline, but it can also welcome. Perhaps that is the most interesting meaning of these signs. They reveal friction, certainly, but they also reveal proximity.
Taiwan and Indonesia might not exchange ambassadors, yet their societies encounter one another every day. Sometimes, the reality of an international relationship is written not in a treaty, but on a signboard.
Najamuddin Khairur Rijal is an associate professor in the International Relations Department at the University of Muhammadiyah Malang in Indonesia.

People urged to make advance healthcare plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:48:05 UTC
01:48:05 KST

The public should make an advance healthcare directive and discuss it with their family or significant others, Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Chuang Jen-hsiang (莊人祥) yesterday said.
Echoing World Hospice and Palliative Care Day, observed on the second Saturday of October annually, the Ministry of Health and Welfare-affiliated Taiwan Organ Sharing Registry and Patient Autonomy Promotion Center yesterday held a charity run at Daan Forest Park in Taipei to help raise public awareness.
This year’s theme was “Advance directives: Let’s make an agreement first,” supporting a peaceful and dignified end of life. Alongside making an advance directive, people are encouraged to tell family or significant others the plan ahead of time.
Photo: Chiu Chih-jou, Taipei Times
The center’s chief executive officer, Fan Hsiu-lung (樊修龍), said that, as a doctor, he has seen many patients’ families bearing the burden of making medical decisions for their loved ones, as well as the hope for a second chance at life of those waiting for organ transplants.
“Advance care planning is not only an act of self-love that honors one’s own dignity, but also an act of love and consideration for one’s family, and a commitment to the greater love for life itself,” he said.
Chuang, who is also center chairperson, said a survey by the center found that almost 78.8 percent of respondents agreed that talking about end-of-life issues is important, and 79.8 percent believed people should decide their own path during their terminal stages of life.
However, while 82.7 percent did not want their family to bear the stress of making important medical decisions for them and 79.4 percent said they were willing to discuss their end-of-life arrangements with their family, 51.8 percent said they had not actually discussed it with their family or significant others, he said.
The survey showed that 46.8 percent thought advance directives meant denying all treatment, Chuang said, adding that an end-of-life plan is not about giving up.
Through advance planning, people can talk with their family and medical team about their wishes while they are still conscious and capable of making decisions, he said, adding that the advance directive can be withdrawn or adjusted at any time even after signing.
Having experienced severe illness, Chuang said he came to realize that he should discuss his healthcare preferences with his family while he still had his faculties, so that they know what he wants and provide the medical team with clear guidance in the future.
He and his wife signed advance directives before he took up the post as head of the center last month, he said, adding that taking charge of these decisions in advance is a way of being responsible to oneself, and it offers comfort to their family.

Recently, many young people are suffering from “notriphobia,” a fear of having no future trip arrangements, or “travel dysmorphia,” an insecure feeling that they haven’t seen as much of the world as their peers.
These anxieties are especially common among “Gen Z,” whose members were born between the late 1990s and early 2010s. Having grown up in a digital environment, they are more prone to FOMO, or the fear of missing out, and thus often feel the pressure to present an exciting lifestyle online.
A 2025 survey showed that 55% of Gen Z in the US feel they are falling behind after viewing other people’s travel posts online. Moreover, 47% say travel vlogs make these feelings even worse. Constant exposure to carefully edited content may encourage unhealthy comparisons with others. The emergence of terms such as travel dysmorphia and notriphobia shows how strongly social media now affects people’s attitudes toward travel and lifestyle expectations.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
近年來，許多年輕人因「無旅行焦慮症」或「旅遊失調症」正飽受折磨（前者指的是因未來沒有出遊安排而憂慮，後者則是覺得自己不如同齡人見過那麼多世界的不同面貌而感到不安）。
這些焦慮在出生於 1990 年代末至 2010 年代初的「Z世代」中尤其普遍。在數位環境成長的他們更容易產生錯失恐懼症（即害怕錯過），他們因此常常覺得自己要在網路上表現出精采的生活方式而感到有壓力。
2025 年的一項調查顯示，五成五的美國 Z 世代瀏覽他人的網路旅遊貼文後，會感覺自己很落後。此外，四成七的人表示，旅遊 vlog 會加劇這種感覺。持續接觸精心剪輯的影片內容可能會助長與他人之間不健康的比較。旅遊失調症和無旅行焦慮症這類詞彙的出現，顯示社群媒體現今深深影響人們對旅遊和理想生活樣貌的看法。
Words in Use
1. insecure a. 不安的，缺乏安全感的
Some people will become insecure in new environments. 有些人在新環境中會變得不安。
2. peer n. 同儕，同輩
Teenagers often compare themselves to their peers. 青少年常常拿自己和同儕比較。
3. exposure n. 接觸（常與介詞 to 並用）
Early exposure to music can improve a child’s creativity. 早早接觸音樂可以提升孩子的創造力。
4. content n. （影片、文章等的）內容
The editor reviewed the content of the online article before publishing it. 編輯在審閱內容後才發布這篇網路文章。
5. emergence n. 出現
The emergence of online banking changed the daily habits of many customers. 網路銀行的出現改變了許多客戶的日常習慣。
Practical Phrases
1. suffer from. . . 受……所苦
People suffering from depression may find it difficult to concentrate or enjoy daily life. 深陷憂鬱的人可能難以專注，也不太能享受日常生活。
2. miss out 錯失（表錯過樂趣、機會等）
I didn’t go to the party, so I felt like I missed out. 我沒參加派對，所以覺得自己好像錯過了很多樂趣。
3. fall behind 落後
Jason always compares his life with others’ because he worries about falling behind. 傑森總是拿自己的生活與他人比較，因為他常擔心自己會落後。

Building friendships is the best education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:58 UTC
01:47:58 KST

In my classroom, you can find students from Vietnam, the Philippines, India and Thailand sharing the same space. I am from Guatemala. Just like the 140,417 international students reported by Study in Taiwan for last academic year, we came for a degree or an exchange program. The first big surprise in Taiwan for me was not eating with chopsticks or using an EasyCard; it was finding myself in a classroom full of young people from many parts of the world.
Taiwan has become a hub offering world-class education, attracting people from diverse continents. This is partly thanks to scholarships and funding opportunities provided by the government and other institutions to connect the world with Taiwan.
Beyond scholarships, there are other elements that make Taiwan and its education system special. According to a study published in 2012 on international students’ perceptions in Taiwan, 36 percent of international students chose to study in the nation because it had a “surrounding suitable for learning.”
In terms of a conducive environment, some people might simply imagine quality infrastructure, modern technology or innovative approaches. However, there is something rarely discussed that is also important for effective learning: collaboration, diversity and inclusion.
The same study identified three main aspects that international students recognized as part of classroom and campus norms in Taiwan. One was that they felt cultural differences were respected at school. The other two aspects were related to academics and their initiative to encourage interaction and efforts to support international students.
After 14 years, I can affirm that this sense of respect, safety, and above all, teamwork remains active and tangible. I was surprised when one of my professors set aside an entire morning just to get to know me and my international classmates, learning where we came from, what we had previously studied, and even identifying what we truly hoped to learn in Taiwan.
On the student side, if there are 30 people in a classroom, I can guarantee that I have heard perhaps up to 12 different accents. In addition to the Asian touch I mentioned earlier, one can distinguish those who come from France, some Caribbean tones from the Americas, and others from Africa. Coming across such an environment proves that these values are not merely reflected in statistics or studies, but are part of the daily language in the country.
Another data point mentioned in the study was that 40 percent of international students wished to have a Taiwanese friend. This remains a significant challenge for those of us who have come to this country. Popping the bubble of feeling like a foreigner is not so easy. Saying “hello” and “thank you” in Chinese is not enough to make friends.
One day, a Taiwanese classmate asked me, in Spanish, whether I spoke Spanish, and I said: “Yes.”
He told me he had learned some words on Duolingo. Ever since, whenever I see him, I greet him in Spanish, and he responds in kind.
In a world filled with technology, we sometimes forget that the best way to connect is still the simplest. Academic prestige and scholarships attract young people from all over the world to Taiwan, driven by the cultural openness and inclusion of its universities. However, it is those small, everyday exchanges — a spontaneous greeting, a smile in the hallway or an attempt to understand each other — that remind us that, at the end of the day, the best degree we can take home from here is a good friendship.
Pablo Mendoza is a scholarship recipient from Guatemala under the Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative studying smart agriculture in Taiwan.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said yesterday that US President Donald Trump’s decision to block Russian sanctions only “rewards” Russian President Vladimir Putin and warned that Moscow was trying to deprive “millions” of Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.

The decision came despite Russia increasing strikes on Ukraine — especially its capital, Kyiv — in the fifth year of its offensive, which has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The Lindsey Graham Act — named after the deceased US senator who sponsored the bill — targeted Russia’s energy and defense sectors, as well as Putin and the so-called “shadow fleet” of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent Western sanctions.
Photo: Getty images via AFP
Zelenskiy said the decision came the same day as Russia attacked 15 critical power generation facilities across Ukraine in “one of the largest” attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” he said on social media. The Lindsey Graham Act, he said, was “supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” adding that the act “could have helped enormously — and still can!”
“A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” he said.
The Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to cause a “blackout” in Ukraine ahead of winter: “Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating.”
He called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow to “stop this.”
Last winter saw hundreds of thousands in Ukraine consistently without heat and electricity in freezing temperatures. A day after Trump waived the sanctions, causing Europe and Kyiv to worry which side of the war the White House is on, Ukraine said at least two people were killed in Russian airstrikes.
Officials said one person was killed in the southern city of Kherson in an attack that also wounded 22 people, including two children, and that another was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
The Kremlin and Putin have not yet reacted to Trump, but several Russian officials celebrated the move as a win.

Dmitriev said the act would have caused “serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets.”
Trump’s waiver comes after he struck a deal with Putin to ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
He announced the executive order on Friday, shortly after Putin appeared in military uniform and said that Moscow aims to capture the rest of east Ukraine.

Songshan airport important for defense, researcher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:56 UTC
01:47:56 KST

The primary value of Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) lies in its role in national defense, while its commercial benefits are an additional reason to keep it operating, Institute for National Defense and Security Research Defense Strategy and Resources Division director Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) said yesterday.
His comments came after Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeking re-election, on Oct. 9 proposed relocating the airport and redeveloping its site as an artificial intelligence hub featuring technology clusters, housing and public green space.
Songshan is a key takeoff and landing site for responding to crises in or around the capital, Su said, adding that it also serves as an alternative landing site and gives the military greater operational flexibility.
Photo: Lu Chun-wei, Taipei Times
The airport supports the Fokker 50 executive aircraft used by the president and other senior government officials. Aircraft carrying visiting US lawmakers, including US Senator Tammy Duckworth, have also landed there, he said.
These functions are part of the airport’s broader role in national defense and security, he added.
Su said arguments for relocating the airport based on the infrequent use of its runways by military aircraft overlook its wartime importance.
Military aircraft use Songshan airport less often in peacetime, because it is primarily designated for commercial aviation, he said.
Songshan is about 66km from the air force’s Hsinchu base. At a fighter jet’s cruising speed of about 900km per hour, or 15km a minute, the flight would take about four to five minutes, Su said.
The airport’s strategic value lies not simply in its location between Dazhi (大直) and Songshan (松山) districts, but in its role as a launch point for air operations over the capital and northern Taiwan, he said.
Su said the “Wan Chun Plan,” which was developed to protect the head of state, was only indirectly related to the debate over Songshan. The plan is intended to protect the president and other senior officials, and escort them to secure command centers to preserve the chain of command during wartime. Whether officials travel by aircraft is not central to the plan, he said.
Songshan’s economic contribution should also be considered, Su said, adding that its everyday benefits could be a more persuasive argument against relocation.
Relocating the airport is open to discussion, but airports allowing passengers to reach a capital’s downtown area within 20 minutes of landing can generate substantial economic benefits, he said.
About 5 million people use the airport annually, including about 3 million people on international routes, and it generates more than NT$60 billion (US$1.86 billion) in tourism benefits, Su added.

Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said on Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after US President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier on Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Photo: AP
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia’s appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president’s first term, which had largely been absent from his second.
In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House did not respond to a request for confirmation.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “’Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and that he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president said he would make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier on Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also would not say when her next press briefing might be.
Zacharia, a Pepperdine University law graduate, also faced criticism for describing herself as a lawyer when appearing as a commentator on conservative television outlets. Zacharia said the term was a proper one to use when she was offering legal analysis, and said she had worked as a lawyer in China.
That was part of the unusual amount of skepticism that Zacharia faced from those friendly to the administration, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who pressed the new White House spokeswoman on why she was not forthcoming about her professional background.
Hannity, known to be friendly with Trump, asked Zacharia after she confirmed she did not pass the bar exam in California, “Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine law school and then took a different career path and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?’”
“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney?” he asked.
Zacharia reiterated to Hannity that she was not acting as a lawyer nor offering legal advice. And she said on Friday during that Fox News interview that she was not asked about passing the bar before becoming press secretary. She and Trump have said she was hired to work in press and communications, not as an administration lawyer.
Before joining the White House, Zacharia had been working in communications for Trump Media, the company that oversees the president’s social media site, Truth Social. She also briefly worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the second Trump administration.
