China’s panda diplomacy is losing its charm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:51 UTC
01:47:51 KST

During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later. This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as a tool of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.
Perhaps the true message of this “panda diplomacy” lies in the manipulation and exploitation it embodies. While China claims the familiar black-and-white bear as its mascot, one of the species’ primary natural habitats is Wolong, which sits on the steep edge of the Tibetan Plateau. Within a horizontal distance of about 30 miles (48.2km), elevations range from alpine peaks exceeding 17,000 feet (5,181m) to below 1,600 feet (487m), creating a moist, temperate microclimate that sustains the high-altitude bamboo forests where pandas thrive.
Historically part of the Tibetan region of Kham, Wolong is under Sichuan provincial jurisdiction, in Aba Tibetan-Qiang Autonomous Prefecture — and China is all too eager to subsume everything that makes it culturally unique. Since China’s annexation of resource-rich Tibet in 1951, the government has sought to systematically erase Tibetan culture and identity, not least by incorporating the region’s distinctive geography, wildlife and natural resources into mainline Chinese national identity. China’s appropriation of others extends even to cherry-tree cultivation, which it has said began not in Japan or Korea, but in “China’s Himalayan highlands” — that is, Tibet.
Illustration: Tania Chou
The Tibetan Plateau is home to the endangered red panda, a housecat-sized mammal with a long, bushy tail, in addition to giant pandas, which are classified as a vulnerable species. There are fewer than 2,000 giant pandas left in the wild, and China claims ownership of almost all of them. This brings us to a second dubious element of China’s panda diplomacy: it is based on a lucrative “rent-a-panda-pair” program.
While China reaps the soft-power benefits of keeping its endearing mascot in foreign zoos, it charges those zoos high prices: up to US$1.1 million per year for the right to display and breed a pair of pandas. China retains ownership not only of the leased adults, but also of any offspring they produce. The leasing zoo must pay a one-time fee of approximately US$600,000 for each cub that is born during its lease. Facilities also often pay up to US$2 million in additional sponsorship and research commitments.
The fees add up. Between 1994 and 2023, China made almost US$300 million from its panda-rental program. Small wonder the Guinness World Records lists the giant panda as the “most expensive species in captivity.”
The money is just the start. The increasingly one-sided contracts that the state-run China Wildlife Conservation Association signs with zoos allow China to terminate an agreement unilaterally and prematurely recall pandas for a wide variety of reasons, such as the “unauthorized release of relevant information” to the public. China prohibits zoos from using terms such as “lease,” “rental,” “loan,” or “contract,” apparently to obscure the transactional nature of the arrangement.
China uses panda loans to send political messages. China gave a pair of pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972, following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing. In 2010, however, it accelerated the recall of two US-born panda cubs after the White House announced that then-President Barack Obama would not cancel a meeting with the Dalai Lama. In 2023, the three remaining pandas at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo were returned to China, the end of a tradition that had lasted more than a half-century.
And it is not just the US. This year, Japan returned its last two giant pandas to China, leaving it without any for the first time since normalizing relations with China in 1972. By contrast, when China sent a pair of pandas to Qatar before the 2022 World Cup, officials hailed the move as a reflection of the countries’ “depth of relations.”
However, the power of China’s panda diplomacy seems to be waning. While the general public might still find pandas appealing, visits to panda-hosting zoos tend to plateau after the novelty wears off, and conservationists stridently criticize the commercial and diplomatic use of a vulnerable species.
Most importantly for China, political analysts and lawmakers increasingly view panda loans as more of a charming distraction than a meaningful barometer of bilateral relations. This helps to explain why Xi’s “gift” to Zoo Atlanta attracted little US media coverage. As international panda-leasing programs dwindled from 21 countries in 2019 to just 16 today, even Chinese state media are asking whether panda diplomacy has “lost its sparkle.”
Giant pandas can appear cuddly and docile, but they are bears: they have long, sharp claws and a highly developed jaw structure, which delivers a bite force of almost 1,300 Newtons, almost as strong as that of lions. While captive-bred pandas introduced into the wild tend to die because they lack critical survival skills, wild pandas can be aggressive and dangerous. In this sense, perhaps pandas really are an accurate symbol of China: even when it appears harmless, it cannot conceal its teeth.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research and fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin, is the author of Water, Peace, and War:
Confronting the Global Water Crisis.
Taiwan might just give up. That’s the argument Simon Shuster made in The Atlantic’s October issue. The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

In attempting to stir up fear with talk of community centers, drugs and needles, Chiang’s comment section exploded. Rather embarrassingly, many commenters made a point

The Chinese vessels, numbered 3301 and 3303, entered the restricted waters at 3:34pm, the CGA’s Dongsha-Nansha Branch said in a statement issued on Friday night. The confrontation was still ongoing at the time the statement was released.
The Cijin patrol ship and patrol boat PP-10032 flanked one Chinese ship, broadcasting warnings in Chinese and English, and ordering it to leave.
Photo courtesy of the CGA
The CGA’s Dongsha command first detected the ships southwest of the atoll at about 2pm. Based on their courses and speeds, officials assessed that they might enter the restricted waters and directed the two Taiwanese vessels to respond.
The branch said the CGA had conducted 11 operations this year to expel Chinese coast guard ships from waters around Dongsha, involving 14 vessel encounters.
The branch cited Friday’s incident as Beijing’s use of purported law enforcement activities to expand its authority and create the appearance of jurisdiction over the area.
Taiwan has sovereignty over Dongsha and its surrounding waters, the branch said, pledging to take all necessary measures to defend Taiwan’s national sovereignty and maritime security.

A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.
The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.
A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
Photo: Reuters
Antonio Otanez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” However, he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
The Robinson brothers and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San Jose, about 80km from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.
Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.
Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15m deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.
The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested Garcia, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.
State authorities said Garcia had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.
Garcia’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N,” were also arrested in the case.
Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
State prosecutor Maria Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.
“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she said.

The official English name for Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign is “the Taipei Current.” It comes from the Chinese term yangliu (洋流), a direct translation of which would be “Ocean Wave,” using the last character of Shen’s name, yang (洋, “ocean”). The Chinese term is a reference to the 2018 campaign for Kaohsiung mayor that swept a hitherto marginal player within the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), who is now legislative speaker, whose successful campaign then was termed the “Han Wave” (韓流).
Shen’s usage of the Chinese term is intentional. He is the underdog in the Taipei mayoral race, taking on the incumbent, Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT. Historically, the DPP has not fared well in the nation’s capital. Just as Han secured an unexpected victory for the KMT in a DPP stronghold in 2018, Shen hopes to ride the “Ocean Wave” to victory on Nov. 28.
Two TVBS polls five months apart show Shen cutting Chiang’s lead from 28 percentage points in May to only 8 percentage points this month. Another poll, commissioned by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association and released on Tuesday last week, showed DPP Legislator Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the party’s candidate for New Taipei City mayor, having a 13.1 percentage point lead over her KMT rival, Lee Shu-chuan (李四川).
The loss of Taipei and New Taipei City would be catastrophic for the KMT. There are indications that some KMT figures have already started to think about the implications for their individual political prospects. It would certainly make sense of Han’s combative Double Ten National Day address last weekend, which last Sunday’s editorial (“Two different National Day speeches,” Oct. 11, page 8) called “a rant against the government” that was “strangely out of place for the context.”
In one interpretation, Han was positioning himself within shifting internal party dynamics, mending fences following his support — much-maligned within the party — of the government’s national defense proposals and his “dark forces” outburst against KMT legislative caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) in August.
The hubris of the Han Wave made Han think he could pursue the presidency in 2020, before he had even served half a term as Kaohsiung mayor. Had he completed his full term, gained the experience in governing and established himself, he might have been prepared for running in 2024. Instead, he was defeated by a landslide in 2020, recalled months later and cast into the political wilderness, until being offered the speakership in 2024. This time he will have more experience and a higher political profile.
There are four main KMT figures who might seek the party’s presidential nomination in 2028: KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文), Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), Chiang and Han.
According to an opinion poll released in mid-August by the online media outlet Z.Media (震傳媒), 20.4 percent of respondents said Chiang was their preferred KMT candidate for the 2028 presidential race, compared with 18.9 percent for Han, 16 percent for Lu and 3 percent for Cheng.
Cheng is not a forerunner for 2028, and if the KMT performs poorly in next month’s local elections, she would almost certainly face calls to resign, even more so if the party loses control of its traditional strongholds of the capital and New Taipei City under her watch.
Defeat next month would free Chiang up for a 2028 presidential run. While the Z.Media poll put him in front, his failure to secure a second term would mean losing control of the capital to the DPP, and Han would benefit from the damage that would cause to Chiang’s prospects. Lu is notoriously reticent about revealing her hand.
At the same time, the party’s loss of Taipei and New Taipei City would elevate the importance of Taichung and Taoyuan: If his colleague Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) is elected Taichung mayor, with Taoyuan Mayor Simon Chang (張善政) — Han’s running mate in 2020 — in place, Han would potentially have two influential allies to support him.
If he maneuvers himself into the right position, Han could even emerge from a potentially catastrophic result for the KMT next month into a relatively strong position for 2028.
In this light, last week’s National Day address could even be seen as laying the groundwork for riding a new Han Wave, with the benefit of having learned the lessons of the previous one.

What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

Soccer referee in Uruguay game tests electronic cards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:45 UTC
01:47:45 KST

A referee raised a phone-sized electronic device to caution a player during a Uruguayan cup match this week, replacing the familiar flash of a yellow card with a digital screen in a trial aimed at modernizing one of soccer’s oldest rituals.
Match official Eduardo Varela used the device during Nacional’s Copa Uruguay match against Rentistas on Thursday, testing a system designed to simplify referees’ administrative work by recording disciplinary decisions digitally.
“We are looking to bring technology to the only thing in football that is still analogue,” said Mauro Sacco, director of REFe, the company behind the project, in an interview with Uruguayan radio El Espectador Deportes on Friday.
The idea emerged more than three years ago when Sacco and fellow director Diego de la Pena watched a match in rainy conditions and considered how referees recorded cautions by hand before transferring the information to digital systems.
The new device logs match incidents with timestamps, with developers aiming to streamline the submission of official records to the Uruguayan Football Association’s COMET platform.
For Varela, the new tool was comfortable to use and its software responded quickly, although he acknowledged that it lacked the drama of the traditional gesture.
“You lose a little of the magic of the quick card, but I think it is something that will help us a lot, especially with the administrative side,” he said.
The first real-world tests have also exposed a problem: visibility. An earlier trial was abandoned because sunlight made the screen difficult to see, while spectators and television viewers struggled to distinguish some decisions during Thursday’s match.
“It’s a project with room for improvement. It looked much better live than it did on TV. The challenge we face now is to improve it for the whole audience,” De la Pena said. “The yellow card has to be yellow, the red card has to be red, and it has to be visible to people at the ground and on television.”
The developers are exploring changes, including LEDs around the device, to make the colors clearer to spectators.
Sacco said the brand had been registered, and the hardware and software patented, with the developers based in China.
The trial has drawn mixed reactions online.
“We have seen all kinds of comments, positive and negative. We have even laughed at the memes,” he said.
“The important thing is that people are talking about it. Any innovation takes time,” he added.
REFe hopes to refine the technology and eventually see it adopted by South American governing body CONMEBOL and world soccer’s FIFA.

Chinese cars a potential Trojan horse for Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:44 UTC
01:47:44 KST

Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles.
During a security exercise at Oslo airport on Sept. 14 to 18, waiting soldiers tapping on their vehicle’s screen discovered videos recorded by the onboard cameras, the Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) newspaper revealed.
The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities.
Photo: Reuters
In its report three weeks after the exercise, DN said the recordings came from rental vehicles — at least two of them Deepal-brand cars, made by Chinese state-controlled automaker Changan. They were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by the Chinese auto group Geely.
“Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Lieutenant Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen, Norwegian Home Guard spokesperson, said.
It was not known if the recordings were shared with a third party, notably in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility.
The case highlights a paradox: While Europe’s armies are bolstering their protection against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information. Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued to use the vehicles until the end of the exercise due to a lack of alternatives and the soldiers deleted the videos, DN reported. Judging that the impact of a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security gain, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, with possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors regardless of their origin. Hertz Norge stressed that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations.
“Our customers’ data is safe with us,” Hertz Norge marketing and communications director Hallvard Nerbovik said. “No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the onboard videos might have been transferred.
Changan group did not respond to AFP’s questions.
Last year, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilize its electric buses with their “over-the-air” update system.
Norway could use the buses one day to evacuate the population in the event of an emergency.
Ruter has since introduced mechanisms enabling it to monitor and delay incoming signals in order to control updates, it said.
Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses. Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information.
In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, notably in Afghanistan and Syria. In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board using the app. The Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) said modern vehicles are “rolling computers that collect information.”
“We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” NSM official Andreas Skjold-Lorange said.
The organization, which is responsible for minimizing strategic risks, including digital, said that beyond the data collected, Norway should be wary of excessive dependence on a single country.
Especially if that country does not cooperate with Norway on security matters.
“If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange said.

Sunak drew from a metaphor by former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀): A big fish will eat a smaller fish, and the smaller fish will eat the shrimp. Group calls for more vehicle safety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:44 UTC
01:47:44 KST

From 2019 to 2023, Taiwan recorded between 9,508 and 10,943 collisions involving large vehicles annually, resulting in 366 to 405 deaths per year, the Consumers’ Foundation said yesterday, calling for stricter safety requirements.
About 2,000 of these motor vehicle collisions each year are associated with vehicles turning due to blind spots and off-tracking, causing more than 2,000 casualties annually, the foundation said.
The foundation’s call followed an incident in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山) in which an elderly woman, surnamed Hsu (徐), died after being hit and run over by a bus on Jingzhong Street shortly after alighting.
Photo: Taipei Times
A preliminary police investigation attributed the crash to blind spots that prevented the driver, surnamed Chou (周), from seeing the woman.
The foundation pointed to other fatal motor vehicle collisions, including that of New Taipei City Councilor Chou Sheng-kao’s (周勝考) ex-wife who was hit and killed by a turning bus while using a crosswalk in New Taipei City’s Banciao District (板橋) on June 24.
On July 19 last year, Chou Chia-cheng (周佳正), a surgeon from Taoyuan General Hospital, was fatally struck by a bus while crossing a road in Taipei, the foundation said.
The government has continued to promote the installation of advanced visibility assistance systems for large vehicles in the past few years, with technologies such as side-view cameras, radar alerts and 360-degree surround-view systems being introduced, it said.
However, the key issue is not simply whether safety equipment has been installed, but whether the minimum safety requirements under the regulations are sufficient, it said.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications launched a research and development program in 2021 to promote active warning and assistance systems for large vehicles, it said.
The systems, which integrate surround-view displays, blind-spot monitoring, forward-collision warnings and lane-departure alerts, have been installed on 800 large vehicles, including 231 trucks and 569 passenger buses, it said.
The foundation urged authorities to review the rule allowing operators to choose just one of three safety devices.
High-risk large vehicles, particularly buses that carry large numbers of passengers every day, should be required to install composite safety systems, which combine video monitoring with active detection and warning technology, it said.
The government should provide subsidies to help operators upgrade equipment that was installed before any regulatory amendments but falls short of improved safety standards or the new requirements, it said.
The subsidies and installation period should be subject to a clear deadline, such as six months or one year, after which no further subsidies would be provided and enforcement under the revised regulations would begin, it said.
The next stage of large-vehicle safety regulations should go beyond checking whether equipment has been installed and instead assess whether it can effectively detect hazards, issue warnings proactively and reduce collisions, it said.
Authorities should ensure that drivers use the systems properly and do not switch off safety assistance functions, it added.

[ LETTER ]
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:42 UTC
01:47:42 KST

Abolishing entrance exams
As a university student preparing to take graduate entrance exams, it is difficult not to feel uneasy in the face of graduate schools changing their admission procedures one after another. Many departments are doing away with written exams entirely, instead evaluating only application materials and oral examinations for their selection process. For students who have already invested a significant amount of time in exam preparation, this is a major and unforeseen shift in their road to postgraduate studies.
National Cheng Kung University’s Department of Material Science and Engineering has announced that it would only review standard application documents for next year’s fall semester intake of graduate students. Likewise, the National Tsing Hua University Department of Computer Science’s Institute of Information Systems and Applications and Institute of Information Security have decided to drop written exams; applicants are instead screened first by application reviews, followed by an oral examination. Schools might feel that they can better assess a student’s research potential and learning record with thorough applications, but for students, graduate exams have long existed as a focus for their studies. Some might not have exceptional undergraduate records or a wealth of specialized experience, but are willing to put in the time and work to prepare well for the next step. For them, graduate exams are a way of demonstrating their abilities and securing admission to their chosen school.
However, many departments that have not done away with written exams already have restricted admission quotas, reducing options further. Academic records, letters of recommendation and evidence of research experience that an application looks at time to amass. Students who have only recently chosen their direction, lack research experience, or are wishing to start fresh in their studies would struggle to meet these requirements in a short period of time, no matter how hard they work.
I by no means oppose application-based reviews, nor do I believe that written exams are always fairer. However, admission reforms must consider not only how schools select talent, but how this affects the opportunities afforded to students of different backgrounds. At the very least, ample warning should be provided and new assessment criteria should be clearly explained whenever admission procedures are altered, allowing students enough lead time to prepare.
By all means, reform the postgraduate system and diversify its selection methods, but do not pull the rug out from under the students who have been working hard to seize their next opportunity. Should there not be a route for students without flawless records to develop and shape their own futures?
Su Yu-ching
Tainan

‘Sunflower Queen’ indicted on drug trafficking charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:42 UTC
01:47:42 KST

The New Taipei City Prosecutors’ Office earlier this month indicted former Sunflower movement protester Johanne Liou (劉喬安) on suspicion of smuggling 590g of cocaine into Taiwan by air in 2021.
Liou entered the public eye during the 2014 Sunflower movement protest after her looks caught the attention of the media, which dubbed her the “Sunflower Queen.”
She quickly fell from favor following allegations that she had introduced Taiwanese women to a ring that enlisted females for prostitution in the US in 2015.
Photo: CNA
She fled Taiwan after becoming a suspect in separate investigations, including embezzlement, fraud and drug-related cases, as well as being charged with brokering Taiwanese women to serve as prostitutes in the US.
She returned to Taiwan and was arrested upon arrival in June after being repatriated from the US for overstaying her visa amid US President Donald Trump’s anti-immigrant push.
Prosecutors said she had joined a drug-trafficking group in the US led by Wei Yip Lou, who was linked to the Hong Kong-based 14K triad.
The cocaine, worth millions of New Taiwan dollars, was allegedly shipped to Taiwan as part of the operation, investigators said.
Wei allegedly supplied the drugs, while a man surnamed Lin (林) was responsible for mailing the drugs and another man surnamed Tzou (鄒) collected payments from buyers, they said.
After joining the group in 2021, Liou was allegedly responsible for finding buyers in Taiwan, prosecutors said, accusing her of contacting an air hostess surnamed Hsieh (謝) to discuss smuggling the drugs into Taiwan.
Hsieh then allegedly recruited a man surnamed Chang (張) to receive the shipment, while a man surnamed Yang (楊) handled customs clearance, they said.
In July 2021, Liou and the others allegedly hid the cocaine inside candles and placed them in a package with clothing, chocolate and metal trays to disguise the shipment, prosecutors said.
An unwitting courier company was hired to deliver the package to Taiwan, they added.
Liou allegedly used Telegram to communicate with Hsieh and the other suspects about how to retrieve the cocaine by melting the candles, they said.
When the package arrived in Taiwan in October 2021, customs officials suspected it contained drugs and opened it. They referred the case to prosecutors, prosecutors said.
Investigators linked the shipment to Hsieh, Chang and Yang, and Liou was detained for questioning after arriving back in Taiwan on June 4.
A source said Liou initially denied involvement, but later admitted transporting the drugs after meeting repeatedly with her lawyer at the detention center.
She wrote a letter expressing remorse, the source said.
Prosecutors indicted Liou on charges of transporting a Category 1 drug, smuggling controlled goods and participating in a criminal organization, and asked the court to impose a heavy penalty for transporting the Category 1 drug.
According to the Judicial Yuan’s sentencing information system, the average sentence for people convicted of transporting a Category 1 drug who qualify for sentence reductions under the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act (毒品危害防制條例) and admit their crimes during trial is 15 years.
The accomplices in Taiwan have all been convicted, with Hsieh sentenced to seven years after identifying her supplier, Yang receiving nine years after turning himself in, and Chang sentenced to eight years.
Prosecutors said they would ask the court to reduce Liou’s sentence if she pleads guilty in her trial.

Taiwan in Time:How cold, dry winds powered Hsinchu’s rice noodle industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:41 UTC
01:47:41 KST

Oct. 19 to Oct 25
For many in Hsinchu, the cold, dry October winds bring uncomfortable weather. But in the past, rice noodle makers waited all year for these winds. Laid out on bamboo racks by the Keya River (客雅溪), freshly made noodles dried in the wind without compromising their quality or texture.
The ideal conditions, it was once said, were 70 percent wind and 30 percent sun.
Photo: CNA
Most producers were concentrated in the Nanshih (南勢) area, which became known as Mifenliao (米粉寮, literally “rice noodle shed”). The work in the early days was entirely manual and physically grueling, often starting at 2am and lasting until 4pm. Women were reluctant to marry into rice noodle-making families, and some who did eventually ran away. Yet there were those who made a fortune in the trade.
While Hsinchu’s rice noodles were already renowned during the Japanese era, the industry surged after World War II as fierce local competition led vendors to try selling their goods in other parts of Taiwan, where they proved unexpectedly popular.
To meet rising demand, manufacturers improved their machinery, rapidly boosting production. A machine-drying method introduced in the 1970s replaced traditional wind-drying, allowing the industry to later expand overseas to the US, Japan, Europe and Southeast Asia. The innovative machines also attracted interest from foreign noodle manufacturers.
Photo: Chen Wei-jen, Taipei Times
Larger factories became so efficient that smaller operations struggled to compete and were forced to shut down. It also became increasingly difficult to hire workers. As manufacturers increasingly added corn flour to cut costs, the traditional industry began to decline in the 1980s. A few producers, however, still insist on making rice noodles entirely from rice and drying them in the wind.
WAITING FOR THE WIND
Hsinchu’s funnel-shaped plain and its location in the rain shadow of the Xueshan Range bring strong, dry northeast monsoon winds, creating ideal conditions for quickly drying rice noodles. If the wind is too warm or the sun too strong, the resulting heat and moisture can cause the noodles to deteriorate, forming a thick film on the surface or making them brittle and unpleasant in texture, according to The History of Hsinchu’s Rice Noodle Industry (新竹米粉產業史).
During winter, makers could even dry noodles at night when orders piled up. They often kept watch over the noodles, using bamboo baskets to block some of the wind and sleeping in cloth sacks to keep warm.
Settlers from Huian (惠安) in China’s Fujian Province were already familiar with rice noodle-making techniques when they arrived in Hsinchu during the Qing Dynasty. Rice noodles were usually served at banquets and festivities, as they took less time to cook and were easier to transport than rice.
The process was arduous from start to finish and required specific varieties of long-grain Zailai rice (在來米), as the more commonly eaten Penglai rice was too sticky. Entire families took part, from washing and grinding the grains to mixing the flour into dough, cooking it, and then slicing and separating it into strips. Producers typically carried the noodles to the river for drying in large bamboo baskets balanced on their heads, walking barefoot on the rocky banks.
Photo courtesy of Hsinchu City Government
A producer recalled in The History of Hsinchu’s Rice Noodle Industry that they rarely got to eat the noodles themselves, especially when prices were high. There was little time for socializing, and some left the house only to recruit workers.
EVOLVING INDUSTRY
The noodles sold then differed from those sold today: they were thicker and boiled during production. In the 1910s, Kuo Shu (郭樹) traveled to Huian to learn a method that steamed the noodles instead, saving water and time. The thinner, springier noodles could be eaten fresh or dried in the wind for preservation and transport. They did not require such strong winds and soon became the area’s signature product.
During the 1940s, producers began using machines to reduce manual labor, but the work was still intensive. Many tried to save up and buy land so they could rent it to farmers and eventually switch to another profession.
With the economy in tatters after World War II, many Nanshih locals returned home to make or sell rice noodles, ushering in an era of many changes.
Kuo Chih (郭池) pioneered a system that allowed other rice noodle makers to use the machinery at his rice mill for certain stages of the process, helping mechanization spread throughout the industry.
Tseng Ching-fu (曾景福), who had trained and worked as a machinist, returned to the family business but struggled to find workers. In 1957, he cofounded a factory specializing in rice noodle-making machines. He developed a belt-and-gear system that could be powered by a single three-horsepower motor and became the main supplier of machinery to Nanshih producers.
Tseng Chi-fu (曾吉甫) got his start carrying 70 to 80kg of rice noodles, duck eggs and straw shoes on his back to nearby communities twice a day. After World War II, Tseng and his son began marketing the noodles in Keelung and Taipei, to surprising success. They acquired 20 small producers and expanded sales across Taiwan, helping bring Hsinchu rice noodles to national prominence. They entered the international market in the 1970s.
FADING TRADITIONS
The industry reached its peak in the 1960s, with more than 100 factories in Nanshih and the surrounding area. However, competition between producers led to rapid improvements in machinery, greatly increasing output over the following decades. By the 1970s, traditional family operations could no longer compete.
Rising rice prices in the 1970s also prompted some manufacturers to mix cheaper corn flour into the rice noodles. At first, they added only a little, but the proportion kept increasing, with some “rice noodles” made entirely from corn.
By the 1980s, Lin Yung-chih (林永志) had spent more than a decade tinkering with the machinery, testing his designs at his uncle’s Kuo Wei’s (郭煒) factory before placing them on the market. He eventually developed an integrated production system that streamlined the entire process.
This gave larger factories a further advantage, forcing many small and medium-sized producers to shut down, reshaping Nanshih’s once-thriving rice noodle trade.

Taipower now has to carry out the work in the plan and its own inspections on ageing, radiation and seismic resistance, then report back to the commission for review and on-site checks. Modular animal shelters in use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:41 UTC
01:47:41 KST

Modular animal shelters would be deployed on state-owned land to help accommodate free-roaming dogs, the Ministry of Agriculture said yesterday, adding that the first site would be set up in Taoyuan.
The ministry yesterday held an event at the National Taiwan Arts Education Center in Taipei to showcase its efforts to promote animal welfare education, featuring the stage play The Wandering Diary of Boss Black Cat and Dog A-Chi (黑貓老大與阿奇的流浪日記).
The stage play has undertaken 15 family theater tours and 82 campus tours nationwide since it was launched last year, bringing an audience of 35,000 people over the past two years, the ministry said.
Photo: CNA
It received an audience approval rating of 98 percent and won the London Design Awards last year, it added.
Animal Welfare Department Deputy Director Chen Chung-hsing (陳中興) said the ministry is planning to set up easy-to-build, mobile animal shelters to reduce the number of free-roaming dogs, as many animal shelters are nearly full.
Mobile shelters are simple building modules that can be easily set up and taken down, he said.
They would be set up on national land governed by the ministry without requiring land grading and building construction, Chen said, which would mitigate damage to the land.
The modular shelters could accommodate local free-roaming dogs for up to two years, Chen said, and would add capacity for permanent full-up shelters
The first modular shelters would be set up in Taoyuan’s Sinwu District (新屋), where 660m2 of national woodland would be used to create about 80m2 of accommodation space, Chen said.
The ministry has been surveying the number of free-roaming dogs in Taiwan every two years since 2018, he said.
The figure has decreased from 159,000 dogs in 2021 to 141,000 dogs in 2024, Chen said.
Animal welfare education is part of the 12-Year Basic Education Curriculum Guidelines in accordance with the Animal Protection Act (動物保護法), he said.
The ministry collaborated with Ifkids Theatre (如果兒童劇團) to develop the stage play to introduce the concept of animal welfare protection into young students’ daily life, Chen said.
The attitudes of humans toward animals could determine the animals’ future, he said.

This Chinese export boom really has legs – and wings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:40 UTC
01:47:40 KST

In an office reeking of cigarettes, Dang Yangyang (黨洋洋) slouches on a black leather sofa in exhaustion. The general manager at Wintop Food (山東春藤食品有限公司) has spent the past few days chaperoning clients from Ghana, Iraq, Jordan, Russia and Senegal. They all want the same thing: Chinese chicken.
Wintop processes 60 million chickens annually, selling breasts, nuggets, meatballs and dumplings to more than 20 countries. Exports accounted for half of its profits last year and are underwriting 33 acres of expansion.
“International clients used to distrust the quality,” Dang said during a tour of his facilities in August. “But when the meat is US$1,000 cheaper per ton than Brazilian and Thai competitors, they have to either buy from China or lose out.”
The company is part of a wave of Chinese protein producers overcoming the country’s checkered food-safety record and leveraging additional capacity to seize space on global supermarket shelves. Changing diets at home and Beijing’s emphasis on food security have pushed companies to invest in technology and expansion. Now, they produce more than China can consume and are offloading excess production abroad.
The surge in cheap Chinese protein is drawing scrutiny from Western producers and regulators, signaling fresh trade friction. The pattern echoes Beijing’s strategy in steel, solar panels and electric vehicles — flooding markets with low-priced products that undercut global rivals.
In July, the European Commission launched an anti-dumping probe into Peking duck imports after local producers alleged Chinese subsidies created unfair competition. Last month, the commission imposed anti-dumping duties of between 41 percent and 67 percent on Chinese pea protein. Chicken has so far avoided the same action, although European authorities are monitoring the market, a commission spokesperson said in an interview.
Agriculture and food are among the few categories where China still runs a trade deficit. At just more than US$100 billion last year, the gap is massive but shrinking.
China, already the world’s largest source of seafood exports, last year became a net exporter of chicken. Overall, China exported US$2.6 billion worth of chicken products last year, almost double 2020 levels, customs data show. Dairy exports are on track to hit US$600 million this year, doubling in three years.
For global consumers, the trend means cheaper protein. For foreign producers from Europe to Thailand and Brazil, it means new competitors.
China’s shift from buyer to emerging exporter is having a “disruptive” effect on the global meat market, said Michael Boddington, a Beijing-based agribusiness consultant.
In Asia, he said, shipments traditionally flowed in from Europe and the Americas. Now, there is a cheaper alternative — and producers globally are scrambling to compete.
China’s agriculture and commerce ministries did not respond to Reuters questions about the country’s burgeoning protein exports.
URBANITES SHUN PORK
For decades, protein in China meant pork. Pigs fed the workers who built the cities and staffed the factories that powered the country’s economic boom. China became home to half the world’s hogs, whose appetite for grain, especially soybeans, redrew trade flows from the US Midwest to Brazil.
The country’s appetite for pork provided livelihoods for small farmers such as Huang Weiying, who started raising pigs in her village in Hebei province 20 years ago, owning more than 500 at a peak.
That era is over. When reporters visited Huang in August, she was tossing slop to her last 10 hogs in a cobweb-covered barn. About US$75,000 in debt, she planned to slaughter them by autumn.
“I have been raising pigs for over two decades, but it has never been as hard as the last two years,” Huang, 57, said. “Pig prices are so low. People in the cities just stopped eating pork.”
The fatty pork cuts common in traditional Chinese cuisine have fallen out of favor with health-conscious urbanites. Per-capita pork consumption has fallen 13 percent since peaking in 2023, according to official data and state media. Chicken intake rose more than 50 percent per capita in the decade through 2024.
Yet production kept expanding across China’s meat and dairy sectors. Officials encouraged massive buildout with subsidies targeted at large corporate producers to boost food security and rebuild herds after the 2018 African swine fever outbreak and the COVID-19 pandemic. Subsidies accounted for about 13 percent of Chinese agricultural producers’ gross farm receipts between 2022 and 2024, according to the OECD — almost triple the level in the early 2000s.
Today, subsidized farms are contributing to overcapacity. Production has hit new highs despite an economic slowdown, tepid domestic demand and a shrinking population, government data show. Last year, China produced a record 59 million tonnes of pork; poultry output rose 7 percent. The dairy sector surpassed official targets for 2025 production two years early.
Pork prices are hardest hit because domestic demand is weakest, but prices have also fallen for poultry and dairy.
MOVING OVERSEAS
For the large producers who increasingly predominate, the way out is exports.
“Every Chinese livestock company is planning to expand overseas. If you want to grow, you must go abroad,” said Zhang Yuan (張源), head of baby formula marketing at dairy giant Yili (伊利集團), which plans to start selling formula in Southeast Asia as soon as next year.
It is a symbolic step for Asia’s largest dairy company, which had milk products pulled in a 2008 government crackdown after melamine contamination sickened thousands of babies. The scandal turned consumers away from domestic milk for more than a decade. However, Yili baby milk powder is now the top-selling brand in China.
Yili’s competitor, Feihe, launched its AceKid infant formula in Indonesia in April to compete with Nestle and Mead Johnson, after bringing the product to the Philippines a year earlier. Feihe did not respond to requests for comment.
Poultry producers are walking a similar path. At Wintop, in Shandong province, manager Dang has increased the number of chickens in each shed from 20,000 to 120,000 in a decade. The birds weigh 2.5kg on average – compared with 2.2kg for broilers from Brazil, according to S&P Global. They are slaughtered in under 42 days instead of 45, catching up to the 35-day US standard.
The local Tengzhou (滕州市) government is subsidizing the wage bill for Wintop’s more than 2,000 workers, the company said without offering specifics. Tengzhou authorities did not respond to a request for comment.
Rival processors such as Sunner are relying on higher-value processed products such as marinated chicken and ready meals to drive growth. Its overseas sales rose 42 percent to US$135 million last year.
Sunner said it is expanding the global presence of its breeds by working with countries including Uzbekistan to develop local capacity. The company developed China’s first domestically bred white-feather broiler and has begun selling it in Africa and Central Asia.
TOUGH COMPETITOR
As Chinese producers go abroad, they are grabbing market share from established players. Chinese milk powder competes with products from New Zealand and Europe in countries including Nigeria and Bangladesh, and is displacing Indian and Iranian producers in the Middle East, according to Yifan Li (李一凡), dairy analyst at commodity broker StoneX.
China has doubled its share of the EU processed-poultry market to 10 percent since 2022, and tripled its share in the UK to more than 14 percent, according to data from Gira, a food consultancy. That growth is challenging producers such as Germany. China’s share of the Japanese market is edging higher while the leader, Thailand, is slipping.
“It’s very worrying,” said Kukrit Arepagorn, manager at the Thai Broiler Processing Exporters Association, an industry body. “Customers increasingly use cheap Chinese chicken prices as a reference point for negotiation.”
Ezequiel Pires, chairman of Lisbon-based international meat trader Branexx, said his company began buying Chinese poultry in March after African customers sought cheaper alternatives to Brazilian imports. Chinese breast meat and leg quarters are 10 percent to 20 percent cheaper than Brazilian products, Pires said.
China has not fully shaken some of the negative associations arising from persistent food-safety scandals, analysts say. For its exporters, the challenge is to build “lasting confidence in the safety, traceability and consistency of their products,” said Gordon Butland, director at Bangkok-based G&S Agriconsultants.
In the EU, imported food must meet the same health and safety standards as local produce, the European Commission said. The bloc plans to strengthen EU-origin labeling, starting with poultry products next year.
Some clients prefer Thai poultry for its consistent taste and quality, said Rupert Claxton, meat and livestock director at Gira.
Still, for many customers, China’s lower price point is key.
“We’re exporting to whatever countries we can,” Wintop’s Dang said. “If you have a significant price advantage, many customers actively seek you out.”

Mortgage numbers for seniors surge to historic peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:37 UTC
01:47:37 KST

The number of mortgage borrowers aged 65 or older in Taiwan exceeded 61,600 at the end of last year, the most since records began in 2009, according to the latest available sample data.
As of December last year, the Joint Credit Information Center’s mortgage dataset contained nearly 1.51 million outstanding mortgage cases, of which more than 61,600 involved borrowers aged 65 or older, accounting for about 4.08 percent of the total.
The figure was up from nearly 54,700 a year earlier, an increase of 6,900, or more than 12 percent.
Photo: CNA
The number of mortgage cases involving borrowers aged 65 or older has more than tripled over the past decade, rising from about 19,500 in December 2016.
New mortgage cases involving borrowers aged 65 or older also remained relatively high. In the second quarter of each year from 2017 to this year, the number ranged from a low of 477 in 2017 to a high of 1,950 in 2022. The second-highest figure was 939 in 2024, while the latest data showed 547 new cases in the second quarter of this year.
Sinyi Realty’s (信義房屋) real estate research office project manager Tseng Ching-te (曾敬德) said that the number of elderly mortgage borrowers was substantial.
Some might need loans to access funds or purchase a different home, while it was unclear whether the trend was related to reverse mortgages, he said.
Banks’ willingness to lend to older borrowers also suggests confidence in their ability to manage lending risks, Tseng said, adding that the trend was unlikely to cause problems.
Colliers landlord representation services department director Huang Shu-wei (黃舒衛) said that banks generally consider a borrower’s age and the mortgage term when assessing loan applications.
Many use a combined borrower age and loan term of 75 to 80 years as a reference for risk management, although the actual repayment period depends on the bank’s lending policies and the borrower’s income and ability to repay, he said.
Taiwan’s emergence as a super-aged society, along with later retirement ages, the growing number of elderly people returning to work and increasingly diverse income sources, are challenging traditional methods of assessing mortgage repayment capacity, Huang said.
For wealthy borrowers, loans are increasingly serving purposes beyond home purchases, extending to broader asset allocation and wealth succession planning, Huang said.
However, outstanding debts can be deducted from an estate’s taxable value only if they meet tax-law requirements and are supported by adequate documentation. Borrowing money does not automatically reduce estate tax liabilities. Tax authorities are particularly likely to scrutinize the reasons for a loan, the movement of funds and their actual use when borrowing occurs late in life or during serious illness, Huang said.
Beyond reverse mortgages and trusts, the substantial property and financial assets accumulated by Taiwan’s post-World War II baby boom generation are gradually entering the wealth-transfer stage, Huang said.
How the financial sector redesigns lending, asset revitalization and wealth transfer tools would become a key challenge in the next phase, he added.

Sao Tome’s niche vanilla finds far-away fans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:36 UTC
01:47:36 KST

The plump, bright-green vanilla pods growing in tiny Sao Tome’s vast leafy plantations might end up in some of Europe’s finest dining.
Although better known for its cocoa, the central African island off the Gulf of Guinea has revived its cultivation of vanilla, the world’s second-most expensive spice, after saffron.
While his mother used to grow cocoa, Ifrasio de Barros Rompao has invested in the green pods that will turn yellowish on the thick, flat leaf vines once harvest arrives.
Photo: AFP
Spurred on by the promise of more profits, the farmer recently ventured into growing vanilla.
“Vanilla, in terms of money, for me, is essential,” De Barros Rompao said on his sloping forest plot in the heart of the island. “I have a big family at home and with this crop I manage to provide for our needs.”
Once nicknamed the “Chocolate Islands,” the Portuguese-speaking archipelago was the world’s leading cocoa producer at the beginning of the 20th century.
The Vanilla planifolia orchid is believed to have been introduced in 1880 as an offering by French colony Gabon to the Portuguese governor at the time.
Its cultivation never took off, neglected in favor of intensive production of sugarcane and later cacao and coffee.
However, the volatility of global cocoa prices and the aging of the island’s plantations have left Sao Tome scrambling to diversify its economy.
Hopes are pinned on its niche vanilla cultivation.
Only saffron commands higher prices than vanilla, which “adds an extra income for farmers,” said Juliette Dohar, cofounder of L’Atelier Vanilha.
The project was set up seven years ago and focuses on supporting the development of high-quality vanilla production in Sao Tome.
With cocoa, producers can expect to earn small amounts spread across the year.
Vanilla brings in “much larger sums once or twice a year,” Dohar said.
Her organization buys the spice from about 50 farmers to process locally before exporting it to European markets.
Producing the sweet-smelling spice is a lengthy process.
Vanilla can take up to three or four years to develop its first flowers.
At their facilities in Pema Pema on the outskirts of Sao Tome’s capital, the plant, once harvested, undergoes a long, artisanal preparation process.
First, the green vanilla is dried in the gardens in the sun.
“We’re in a very humid environment, so we need to remove part of the moisture from the pod fairly quickly,” said Francesco Mai, the other founder of L’Atelier Vanilha.
Afterward comes several months of drying indoors, massaging the pods, scalding, fermentation and curing.
The vanilla then turns from green to dark brown and develops its characteristic aroma.
“At full production, we’re at around 300 kilos. These are very small volumes, but the goal is to achieve high quality and target a premium market of fine grocery shops and Michelin-starred restaurants in France, Switzerland and Belgium,” Dohar said.
Madagascar and Indonesia dominate the global market, accounting for more than 80 percent of production with about 3,000 tonnes between them.
On the island of Sao Tome, where the mild, warm climate favors the growth of vanilla vines, cultivating the tropical orchid — which involves a demanding process of manual pollination — remains a largely underdeveloped sector.
However, more than 5,000km away, the vanilla of the “Chocolate Islands” is appreciated for its aromatic qualities.
“There are notes of cocoa nibs in the base notes,” said Mathilde Roellinger, managing director of Epices Roellinger, a Michelin-starred spice house in France.
“There’s a real floral elegance with violet notes,” Roellinger said from the family restaurant in Cancale Bay.
“Then at the heart of the vanilla you almost get hints of small red berries. It’s extremely rich in the diversity of its aromatic profile,” she added, breaking off to inhale the scent of a newly arrived pod from the island.
Its flavors give a tiny taste of the far-away archipelago of 210,000 people, which gained independence in 1975.
“For me, every spice carries the landscape it comes from,” Roellinger said. “And Sao Tome is a paradise island. There is a bit of that mystery and beauty in the vanilla bean.”

Official warns of China poll risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:36 UTC
01:47:36 KST

Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday warned of possible Chinese interference in next month’s local elections.
Shen made the remarks at the annual meeting of the Taipei-based Chinese Association of Political Science and an international conference titled “Rethinking Democracy: Continuity and Change in the Values and Practice of Modern Democracy.”
This year marks the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election. In 1996, despite missile threats from China, Taiwanese voters bravely went to the polls, marking a historic milestone in their ability to determine their own future through the ballot box, Shen said.
Photo: Reuters
Over the past 30 years, Taiwan has held eight direct presidential elections and experienced three changes of ruling party, consolidating its democratic system while becoming a key partner in the global artificial intelligence and semiconductor supply chains, he said.
Shen stressed that the fundamental difference between Taiwan and China lies in their political systems: democracy versus authoritarianism.
Beijing has long sought to impose its “one country, two systems” framework on Taiwan and uses “united front” tactics to infiltrate the nation and spread political propaganda, with the goal of eliminating the Republic of China (ROC) and annexing Taiwan, he said.
However, Taiwan’s mainstream public opinion has firmly rejected “one country, two systems,” Shen said. Nearly 80 percent of the public supports maintaining the cross-strait “status quo” in which the ROC and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other, a reality that must be acknowledged in any discussion of cross-strait relations, he said.
The challenges facing democracies today extend beyond conventional military threats to include authoritarian powers such as China and Russia using “gray zone” tactics, information manipulation and infiltration to divide democratic societies and undermine public trust and unity, he said.
With local elections to be held this year, Beijing might continue to interfere in Taiwan’s democratic processes to influence voters’ independent judgement, he said.
In response, Taiwan must continue to bolster its democratic safeguards and societal resilience to ensure that its democratic system remains free from external interference and that people can exercise their democratic rights in a free and secure environment, Shen said.

North Korea says tested AI-assisted torpedo system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:30 UTC
01:47:30 KST

North Korea has tested a “new-type” precision-guided torpedo system that uses artificial intelligence (AI) for target detection and guidance, state media reported yesterday, as the nuclear-armed country steps up weapons testing.
The announcement came days after Pyongyang said it had test-fired two types of cruise missiles from a submarine after weeks of friction with Seoul over a landmine explosion along their border.
Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile and weapons technology with support from Russia received in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine.
Photo: Reuters
The underwater test-fire of the “super-speed” Zam-2.0 torpedo system took place on Thursday “to confirm the successful technical updating” of the weapon, the Korean Central News Agency said.
“AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the new-type super-speed precisely guided torpedo,” KCNA said.
The test proved “the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion device,” it said, adding that it had completed “more than 180 rounds of different tests over the past five years.”
Earlier this month, North Korea announced the AI-assisted launch of an intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Pyongyang said at the time there was “no way to avoid” the hypersonic missile, which was “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude.”
Torpedoes are designed to strike enemy targets underwater at high speed, but the stated introduction of AI could also allow North Korea to carry out evasive maneuvers and make autonomous decisions to confuse an adversary, analysts say.
“South Korea and the United States deploy decoy targets to divert torpedoes, but AI could potentially help distinguish real targets from decoys,” Kyungnam University professor Lim Eul-chul said.
“From torpedoes to submarine-launched weapons, Pyongyang is pouring resources into demonstrating that US strategic assets can be rendered ineffective.”
In September, Pyongyang’s leader Kim Jong Un emphasized the need to raise “the level of artificial intelligence” in the country’s weapons systems.
Yesterday’s announcement came as the two Koreas appear to be intensifying an arms race over hypersonic missiles.
Hypersonic missiles travel at more than five times the speed of sound and can maneuver mid-flight, making them significantly harder to track and intercept.
Days after North Korea announced it had tested its AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile, Seoul test-fired its own weapon — a hypersonic glide vehicle it called a “key strategic asset capable of changing the course of the battlefield.”
North Korea this week cast doubt on Seoul’s test, saying it might have “failed to achieve hypersonic flight,” a claim South Korea rejected a day later. The latest weapons tests come amid growing speculation over a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as world leaders prepare to gather for next month’s APEC summit in China.

Taipei airport a medical evacuation hub: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:27 UTC
01:47:27 KST

There are about 300 medical evacuation cases from outlying islands each year, so if Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal of removing Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) proceeds, people in Kinmen County would be most heavily affected, a Ministry of Health and Welfare official said yesterday.
MAYOR’S PLAN
Chiang, who is seeking re-election, earlier this month proposed a plan to replace Songshan airport with an artificial intelligence (AI) park, which drew concerns that medical evacuations for people from outlying islands would become difficult.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Department of Nursing and Health Care Deputy Director-General Chen Ching-mei (陳青梅) said that the craft used for medical evacuations from the outlying counties of Kinmen, Lienchiang and Penghu vary.
In Kinmen, fixed-wing aircraft are used for medical evacuations, whereas Penghu and Lienchiang mainly rely on helicopters, she said.
Most of the evacuations are people with cardiovascular diseases or severe acute illnesses, she added.
People from outlying islands who need to receive emergency medical care are usually flown to Songshan airport, Chen said.
ALTERNATIVES
Separately yesterday, Chiang’s campaign spokesman Chen Po-hsiung (陳柏翰) defended the mayor’s proposal, including his remarks that high-speed rail is one of the transportation options that people evacuated from outlying islands can use to transfer to hospitals after arriving in Taiwan proper by plane.
High-speed rail is by no means intended to replace emergency medical air evacuation, Chen said.
Chiang has outlined a clear plan for medical evacuation following the proposed removal of the airport, which includes preserving operational space for helicopters, he added.

====================================================================================================

DR Congo city devoured by race for key minerals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:21 UTC
01:47:21 KST

From his yard, Chibang Kasump sees the comings and goings of the miners who dig for copper and cobalt, day and night, deep below his small, brick home in the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo).
The 47-year-old has lived for more than a decade in the Musonoi area of Kolwezi, the country’s mining capital, which sits atop coveted deposits at the center of a global race for critical minerals.
“I bought this house because it was quiet, close to the city center and near the lake,” he told reporters. “I didn’t know there were minerals beneath my feet. Now I live with a well in my yard.”
Photo: AFP
The vast central African nation produces about 70 percent of global cobalt output — key for making electric batteries and in defense technology — and holds some of the world’s richest deposits of copper, a metal in growing demand as countries expand electrical networks to harness renewable energies.
Mining companies and foreign investors have stepped up their expansion efforts, explorations and asset acquisitions. The next few years are expected to bring exponential growth in demand for critical metals that are indispensable to global industry.
China has been investing in the DR Congo for two decades.
The US signed a strategic partnership deal with the Congolese government in December last year, hoping to shore up supplies for its high-tech industry.
Kasump’s plot lies within Tondo Mining Co’s concession.
The Congolese firm holds the operating license for the site, which is next to the vast copper and cobalt deposit of Commus, a company controlled by Longyan, China-based Zijin Mining Group (紫金礦業集團).
Ahead of an industrial mining operation being set up, artisanal miners, known as diggers, have moved into the area — right up to Kasump’s yard.
The boundary between urban space and mining land is fading in Kolwezi, in the heart of the African copper belt.
Open-pit mines are gradually eating away at neighborhoods, while concessions are piling up on top of one another.
In Musonoi, the houses have numbers spray-painted on them.
“All the houses are identified for relocation,” said Kazadi Roger, a local administrative official. “The mining company is going to provide compensation, but people still don’t know when they’ll be leaving.”
Under Congolese mining law, a land title does not confer any rights over the minerals present in the subsoil, but a mining title also does not cancel out the rights of the occupants of a plot, who must be compensated in the event of expropriation.
Kasump initially refused, but said “with the pollution, the explosions linked to the extraction, I ended up saying yes.”
He does not know how much he will receive or where he will move to, though.
Behind him, dumper trucks rolled by, nonstop, along the road carved out by the neighboring Chinese industrial mine.
The dust settles on the rooftops and rainwater seeps into houses that have cracked as a result of the mining.
Under a white tarpaulin adjoining his house, a yawning chasm appeared in the ground into which a young digger disappeared.
A pump hummed softly, sending oxygen to those who had descended into the darkness.
At a depth of about 100m, some 30 men hacked away at the rock with pickaxes, filling sacks.
Using a rope, a human chain carried the ore — mostly copper — to the surface.
“We follow the vein,” one of the diggers said. “When we see the grade is good, we stop.”
The timber lining the walls acts as a support, but even the slightest collapse can prove fatal.
Some diggers earn about US$500 a month, others much less, depending on how much ore they have recovered and its quality.
All the artisanal stakeholders interviewed complained that the artisanal mining zones, which are provided for by law, were insufficient.
“Everywhere, concessions have already been granted,” said Sylvestre Petit-Petit, the artisanal miners’ local representative. “The state has not given enough space to the diggers.”
As a result, they work in private concessions, often without authorization.
Some break into large industrial mines, risking their lives.
“Over there, they’re shooting at us,” one of them said, adding that he had lost “several friends” that way.
The extracted ore is washed, sold to traders who are often Chinese, and then undergoes initial processing before being exported.
“The mines advance; the city retreats,” said Aaron Niumbi, a young resident of another Kolwezi neighborhood.
He, too, faces having to move out due to the expansion plans of Commus.

In the morning of that day, the KMT’s Taichung mayoral candidate, Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣), entered the venue accompanied by Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) and New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜).
That afternoon, the party’s New Taipei City mayoral candidate, Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), arrived, accompanied by Hou and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), while Han welcomed Lee onstage. The candidates’ entrance was the climax at both rallies.
When Cheng took the stage, not only did the mayoral candidates disappear, but the pan-blue camp heavyweights also kept their distance. Cheng has come to be perceived as politically toxic.
Originally, the nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28 were seen as a midterm referendum for President William Lai (賴清德), but they have become a defense battle for Cheng.
The one who took the first shot was KMT Legislator Hsieh Yi-fong (謝衣?) from Changhua County, who led the polls for leadership of the party. After being eliminated by Cheng, Hsieh bluntly said five months ago that lawyer Wei Ping-cheng (魏平政) — who was appointed by the KMT headquarters as its Changhua County commissioner candidate — has little chance to win as she asked Cheng to take full responsibility and resign if she could not hold Changhua County.
Indeed, Wei’s campaign has been sluggish all the way. Former Changhua County commissioner Cho Po-yuan (卓伯源) took the next shot, saying that the Changhua County commissioner election has entered its final stretch, and if the party performs badly, Cheng should step down to take responsibility.
Finally, there was former Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) chairman Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), who commented at a rally that Cheng might need to step down should the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) win in New Taipei City. While the KMT’s overall campaign is flashing warning signs, similar negative feedback would only increase.
Japanese academic Yoshiyuki Ogasawara, who has long studied Taiwan’s elections, boldly predicted that even if the KMT really suffers at the polls, Cheng is unlikely to step down. The biggest key lies in Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平), because the Chinese Communist Party is betting on her and is unlikely to agree to her resignation.
The defense battle of Cheng’s party leadership is ultimately a struggle between the Taiwanese public opinion and the will of Beijing.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a final appeal to voters considering a path toward independence in his home province of Alberta on Friday, warning that a referendum is a dangerous gamble at a time of growing threats to Canada’s sovereignty.
With US President Donald Trump waging a trade war and threatening to make Canada the 51st state, Carney said that the referendum comes at the “worst possible time” and urged Albertans not to take the outcome for granted.
“This is not a game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” Carney told a pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, where he grew up.
Photo: AFP
Monday’s vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, home to most of Canada’s proven oil reserves — the fourth largest in the world — would decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation.
Carney’s closing appeal came after two days of campaigning against separation in the province. Earlier on Friday, the liberal prime minister joined Alberta’s conservative premier Danielle Smith in a show of unity against independence.
Smith praised Carney for improving relations with a province that frequently clashed with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, over his carbon tax and other energy policies.
“I think what we can agree on is that we have had some real change in the last 18 months,” Smith said alongside Carney in Red Deer, Alberta.
At Thursday’s Calgary rally and Friday’s Edmonton rally, the crowd erupted in its loudest applause when Carney spoke about reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the US.
Carney acknowledged Alberta’s longstanding resentment of federal energy policies.
“Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” he said.
However, he also emphasized his deep ties to the province.
“Alberta is my home. I grew up here. This city, this province, this country have given me everything: my family, my education, my values,” he said.
Outside the Edmonton rally venue on Friday, Alberta independence supporters waved flags and held a sign reading: “say no to Carney’s new world order.”
Smith called the referendum despite opposing independence herself. She recently cited a poll showing 22 percent of Albertans support separation, a figure she said was still too high.
Smith also faces pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party. Former Premier Jason Kenney said the independence movement gained influence within the party as activists angry over COVID-19 restrictions, some influenced by conspiracy theories, embraced separatism.
However, some Albertans who want to remain in Canada are angry with Smith for calling the vote.
“I think it’s a travesty really to be putting our province and our country through this when such a small portion of people are rabble rousing and saying they want to separate from Canada,” said Deb Lee, a retired Calgary resident who voted in advance to remain in Canada.
Smith said Carney had substantially addressed seven of nine federal laws Alberta opposed. She also cited cooperation on a proposed oil pipeline.
Independence advocate Tanya Clemens dismissed the agreements between Carney and Smith as “basically pinky promises” that came with too many conditions.

TYPHOON WATCH
Champi closes to east
Typhoon Champi could continue to strengthen and approach waters off eastern Taiwan by Thursday, with some forecast models suggesting it could move west and cross the nation, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday. As of 2pm yesterday, Champi was 2,980km east-southeast of Oluanpi (鵝鑾鼻), Taiwan’s southernmost tip, and moving west at 22kph. It had maximum sustained winds of 162kph and a storm radius of 180km, CWA data showed. CWA forecaster Chang Cheng-chuan (張承傳) said Champi could intensify as it moves west before turning west-northwest toward Taiwan. The storm is expected to reach waters off eastern Taiwan on Thursday, after which it might turn north, he said. Other forecasts suggest that if a Pacific high-pressure system remains strong, Champi could take a more westward track and possibly cross Taiwan, he said.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
PUBLIC HEALTH
Vaccination rates soar
More than 3 million flu vaccines and almost 1 million COVID-19 vaccines have been administered under a publicly funded program launched two weeks ago, significantly from a year earlier, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday. From Oct. 1 to Friday, 3,151,137 people in the 11 groups eligible for the first phase of the publicly funded program received flu vaccines, while 988,347 received COVID-19 vaccines, it said. The figures were 15.8 percent and 39.7 percent higher than same period last year, CDC data showed. The second phase begins on Nov. 2 and covers people aged 50 to 64 without high-risk chronic illnesses.
Coast Guard
Turtle touching probed
Two foreign visitors are being investigated for allegedly touching a green sea turtle on Siaoliouciou (小琉球) off Pingtung County, a violation of the Wildlife Conservation Act (野生動物保育法), the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said yesterday. The CGA’s Southern Branch said it received a report on Thursday that two people had touched a protected sea turtle at Vase Rock Beach. Coast guard officers located the suspects and detained them for questioning, the branch said. Coast guard officers returned the suspects, both US citizens, by patrol boat to Taiwan proper for investigation, it said. Green sea turtles are protected wildlife under the act, the branch said. Anyone who disturbs, abuses, hunts, or kills protected wildlife faces up to one year in prison or a fine of up to NT$300,000. If the act results in the animal’s death, the penalty increases to up to two years in prison or a fine of up to NT$500,000.
