Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:51:12 UTC
21:51:12 KST

Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
TEHRAN - On 17 October, archaeologists and cultural institutions worldwide mark International Archaeology Day, highlighting archaeology’s contribution to our understanding of the human past. The occasion also invites reflection on the broader role of archaeology in reconstructing human history, investigating changing relationships between people and their environments, and communicating scientific knowledge to the public through museums and other cultural institutions.
In Iran, this day offers a valuable occasion to recognize a heritage that extends far beyond monumental architecture and written records. Long before the emergence of urban centers, human groups inhabited the Iranian Plateau and its mountain ranges, developed stone-tool technologies and other early technologies, adapted to changing climatic conditions, and exploited a wide range of environments. The Paleolithic represents the longest period of this history, and it places Iran at the center of important debates concerning human evolution, hominin dispersals across Eurasia, and adaptation during the Pleistocene.
Situated between Southwest Asia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent, Iran encompasses a remarkable diversity of landscapes and ecological settings. These environments formed part of the geographical context in which prehistoric populations moved, settled, and adapted to changing conditions. Iran should therefore be understood not just as a corridor between better-known prehistoric regions, but as a distinct archaeological landscape with real potential to contribute to future research on the early human occupation, Neanderthal behavior, and the dispersal of Homo sapiens.
The earliest chapters of Iran’s Paleolithic record are documented primarily through stone-tool assemblages recovered from open-air sites and sedimentary contexts. Sites such as Kashafrud in northeastern Iran and Dehtal, north of the Persian Gulf, have contributed to discussions of Lower Paleolithic occupation. Nevertheless, questions concerning chronology, stratigraphic integrity, and the relationship between artifacts and their depositional contexts remain important. Addressing these issues requires carefully designed field investigations, critical reassessment of existing collections, and reliable dating wherever suitable materials and archaeological contexts are available. Darband Rashi Cave is a key example, where modern dating methods and lithics associated with faunal remains in stratigraphic context help advance understanding of Iran’s Lower Paleolithic.
The Zagros Mountains are particularly important for understanding the Middle and Upper Paleolithic in Iran. Caves, rockshelters, and highland valleys preserve archaeological sequences that provide evidence of Neanderthal technology, subsistence strategies, and responses to environmental change. These records are also essential for investigating the arrival and subsequent expansion of modern humans, as well as the cultural and demographic processes associated with the Middle-to-Upper Paleolithic transition. Together, they offer a valuable basis for examining how human populations occupied and adapted to the varied environments of the Iranian highlands.
Over recent decades, Iranian archaeologists have advanced Paleolithic research through independent projects as well as, in some cases, collaboration with international colleagues. Their work has expanded field investigations, strengthened analytical capabilities, and brought Iran’s prehistoric record to greater attention within the international archaeological community.
The contributions of Iranian women archaeologists have been particularly significant, advancing scientific knowledge, broadening research perspectives, and strengthening the foundations of the discipline. Dr Marjan Mashkour has made major contributions to zooarchaeological research, deepening our understanding of past subsistence strategies, human–animal relationships, and interactions between human populations and their environments. Through her teaching and mentorship, she has also trained and helped shape a new generation of Iranian zooarchaeologists, many of whom are now conducting research at institutions across Iran, contributing to the development of the field nationally. Her work illustrates how specialist research can enrich museum collections and exhibitions, helping visitors understand how animal remains recovered from archaeological sites provide evidence of past diets, economies, and relationships between people and animals. Dr Sonia Shidrang has also made important contributions to Paleolithic research and to the international recognition of Iran’s prehistoric heritage, notably through her involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley, which were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025. Beyond research and heritage management, her commitment to teaching and organizing workshops at Shahid Beheshti University and other institutions has helped transmit specialized knowledge and practical skills to a new generation of archaeology students. Their work illustrates how Iranian women archaeologists contribute not only to scientific research and international collaboration, but also to the development of national research capacity and the future of the discipline.
Field archaeology matters just as much for heritage management, particularly when development projects threaten archaeological sites and landscapes. The Darian Dam Archaeological Salvage Programme in the Sirwan Valley, conducted in 2015–2016, demonstrated the importance of archaeological investigation in a landscape undergoing substantial transformation. Although salvage archaeology cannot replace the preservation of sites in situ, it can document threatened remains and recover information that would otherwise be lost. The project also underscores why prehistoric landscapes, even when they lack monumental structures or visible architectural remains, must be recognized as integral components of Iran’s cultural heritage.
The Khorramabad Valley occupies an exceptional place within this broader archaeological landscape. Its caves, including Kunji, Yafteh, and Ghamari, preserve important evidence for reconstructing Paleolithic lifeways and investigating the long-term human occupation of the Zagros. In 2025, the inscription of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley on the UNESCO World Heritage List marked a major achievement for Iranian archaeology. As a member of the nomination team, I witnessed firsthand the importance of a rigorous scientific foundation in securing international recognition for archaeological heritage. This inscription provides an important opportunity to advance archaeological research, strengthen site management and conservation, and communicate the valley’s significance to local communities and international audiences.
My work in Gilan Province similarly brought prehistoric research into dialogue with broader questions of cultural heritage through my involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Cultural Landscape of Masouleh. This experience highlighted the value of examining cultural landscapes across different timescales, taking into account the environmental and historical processes that have shaped them. Archaeological research can extend this perspective beyond standing architecture and documented history to explore the deeper relationships between people and their environments.
Museums play an essential role in connecting archaeological research with public understanding. In 2001, I led the establishment of the Paleolithic Gallery at the National Museum of Iran to present archaeological evidence in a form accessible to a wider audience. Stone tools may appear simple at first glance, but their technological characteristics, raw materials, and archaeological contexts can reveal important aspects of past human behavior when interpreted carefully. The challenge for museums is to communicate these findings clearly while preserving the scientific context essential to their interpretation.
The establishment of the Zagros Paleolithic Museum in Kermanshah extended this work into the region whose archaeological record constitutes a major part of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Regional museums are particularly valuable because they connect archaeological discoveries with the landscapes and communities from which the evidence originates. More recently, Paleolithic displays developed at the Archaeological Museum of Lorestan in 2024 have further strengthened the presentation of western Iran’s prehistoric heritage within its regional context. Together, national and regional institutions can help audiences appreciate the diversity of Iran’s archaeological record and its contribution to our understanding of the human past.
Museums also play a central role in the responsible management of archaeological collections. An artifact’s scientific value depends not only on its physical characteristics, but also on its provenance, stratigraphic position, and association with other evidence. When these relationships are lost, important opportunities for interpretation and future research are diminished or disappear altogether. Documentation, conservation, and responsible curation must therefore remain integral to archaeological practice.
International Archaeology Day provides a moment to recognize the scientific and public value of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Advancing research requires sustained fieldwork, renewed investigation of existing collections, interdisciplinary collaboration, and stronger connections between research institutions and the public. Such efforts can integrate Iran’s archaeological record more fully into international scholarly debates while ensuring that future generations of researchers have the evidence, expertise, and institutional resources needed to investigate it.
As head of the Paleolithic Department at the National Museum of Iran, my experience in field research, museum development, and UNESCO nominations has reinforced the importance of connecting scientific investigation with public interpretation and long-term heritage management. Archaeology achieves its greatest value when discoveries contribute not only to scholarly understanding but also to a broader appreciation of humanity’s shared past. Iran’s Paleolithic record offers an exceptional foundation for advancing that understanding, connecting the history of human adaptation across deep time with the responsibilities of scientific research and cultural stewardship today.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, appeared to question the reports of the attack on the Europeans, saying on X that they are “alleged” and require “compelling evidence”, despite acknowledging that published footage of the incident exists.

In the village of Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, she said settlers under army protection fired live ammunition at farmers in the al-Hariq area to prevent them from completing the harvest, forcing them off their land.
Settlers also smashed the vehicle of international activist Jonathan Budlak in the village and threw stones at a farmer’s vehicle.
In the village of Burqa near Ramallah, Israeli forces and settlers prevented farmers from picking olives, Odeh said, adding that settlers attacked farmers in the Wadi al-Sha’er area, southeast of Salfit.

“There have been 300 documented attacks since the beginning of October, and that has had a devastating impact on a very important season for Palestinian farmers,” she said, adding that danger comes from soldiers and settlers alike, as military forces routinely intervene to protect settlers and attack Palestinians defending their land.
Prominent rabbi justifies attacks
The attacks follow a religious edict issued by Dov Lior, a prominent rabbi for Israel’s National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and a leading authority among the Hilltop Youth, a religious Zionist group devoted to seizing Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank.
In the edict, Lior stated that harvesting olives in the “Holy Land” is entirely permitted for Jews and carries an added virtue, given security dangers.
He wrote that Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Israeli communities to publicly display ownership of the land and fulfil God’s commandment of conquering it. He claimed the land belongs to the Jewish people, and Palestinians did not buy or rent it.

Iran proposes joint tourism packages, measurable targets to boost Chinese arrivals
TEHRAN – Iran has proposed five practical measures to increase Chinese tourist arrivals, including joint travel packages, familiarization tours and direct cooperation between travel agencies, as it seeks to turn longstanding cultural ties with China into tangible tourism business.
The proposals were outlined in a message from Iran’s Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri, read at a specialized meeting on strengthening Iran-China tourism cooperation in Beijing on Friday.
Salehi-Amiri said that Iran eyes China to be become one of its most important tourism partners, stressing that the success of bilateral cooperation would depend on moving beyond discussions to concrete agreements and actual tourist exchanges.
The meeting, hosted by Iran’s embassy in Beijing, brought together officials and representatives of tourism companies from both countries to discuss barriers to bilateral travel, develop joint tourism products and expand cooperation between tour operators.
Marking the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Iran and China, Salehi-Amiri described the occasion as an opportunity to advance cooperation from dialogue to implementation.
He proposed establishing a joint working group of Iranian and Chinese travel agencies and tour operators, developing at least three travel packages specifically tailored to the Chinese market, and organizing familiarization tours in Iran for Chinese travel agency executives and journalists.
The other proposals focused on providing services suited to Chinese visitors, including Chinese-speaking guides and easier payment arrangements, as well as setting measurable targets and clear timelines for tourist exchanges.
“The outcome of this meeting should not be limited to discussions and exchanging business cards,” Salehi-Amiri said in his message. He called for an action plan, travel packages, contracts and the actual dispatch of tourists.
Referring to the historic Silk Road, which connected the two countries through trade and cultural exchange, he said tourism could give the ancient route renewed life.
“The Silk Road was once kept alive by caravans, and today it will be kept alive by the movement of tourists,” he said.
Iranian Ambassador to China Abdolreza Rahmani Fazli also emphasized the need to remove obstacles, reorganize cooperation mechanisms and increase China’s share of Iran’s tourism market.
He described the Silk Road as more than a commercial route, saying it had historically facilitated exchanges in culture, art, music and traditions. Modern technology, he added, offered new opportunities to strengthen people-to-people ties.
Rahmani Fazli also highlighted China’s potential role in Iran’s postwar reconstruction, following the recent war against the country, and said both nations sought peace and security in West Asia.
Chinese tourism representatives described Iran as a destination with considerable cultural appeal and economic potential, expressing interest in expanding travel between the countries. They also identified several obstacles, including the absence of an Iranian tourism promotion office in Beijing, flight disruptions following the war and limited opportunities for familiarization tours.
Their recommendations included establishing an Iranian tourism representation office in Beijing, organizing promotional events for Chinese media and travel bloggers, arranging familiarization trips, developing tailored travel packages and ensuring more stable air connections.
Participants also suggested using shared cultural interests, including tea culture, to promote tourism cooperation.
During the meeting, Roozbeh Kardooni, an adviser to the minister and director general of the ministry’s ministerial office, said Iran could host a group of Chinese tourism industry representatives in the near future. Such a visit could help Chinese tour operators assess Iran’s attractions firsthand and explore opportunities to develop joint travel products.

Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:44:22 UTC
21:44:22 KST

Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- University of Edinburgh
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.
- Share:
Brain cells that normally help protect the brain may play an unexpected role in cognitive decline as we grow older. Scientists have discovered that cells responsible for maintaining the protective coating around nerve fibers can become dysfunctional with age, potentially contributing to the gradual loss of memory and thinking abilities.
The research, published in Nature Medicine, challenges the long-held belief that these cells are always beneficial. By examining human brain tissue and conducting experiments in mice, researchers found evidence that problems with these normally supportive cells can damage nerve fibers and interfere with cognitive function.
The discovery also points to a possible new approach for protecting the aging brain. Drugs that act on the biological pathway involved are already being used to treat other neurological conditions, raising hopes that existing treatments could eventually be adapted to combat age-related cognitive decline.
Scientists Discover Changes in the Aging Brain
The study was led by researchers from the University of Edinburgh and the UK Dementia Research Institute, who investigated how changes in the brain relate to declining cognitive abilities later in life.
Their research focused on the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, a group of people whose cognitive abilities have been tracked from childhood into old age. This unusually extensive record allowed scientists to investigate how thinking and memory changed over decades.
Between ages 70 and 82, participants underwent assessments measuring memory, the speed at which they processed information, and their ability to understand spatial relationships.
Of the 1,091 people enrolled in the cohort, 866 completed additional cognitive testing after age 70. Nearly everyone experienced at least some decline, but the rate varied considerably. These differences gave researchers an opportunity to investigate what might distinguish brains experiencing faster deterioration from those aging more gradually.
When scientists examined brain tissue collected after death from a subset of participants, they discovered a striking pattern. Individuals who had experienced greater cognitive decline tended to have fewer large nerve fibers, along with an abnormal buildup of unhealthy myelin.
Myelin is the protective coating that surrounds nerve fibers, helping electrical signals travel efficiently through the brain. Although this insulation is essential for normal brain function, the findings suggest that excessive or abnormal myelin may become part of the problem.
The changes were especially pronounced around the large nerve fibers that remained. Importantly, these abnormalities were associated with how quickly cognitive abilities declined, rather than how well someone performed on cognitive tests at a particular age.
A Protective Brain Cell May Have a Hidden Weakness
To understand what might be causing these changes, the researchers turned their attention to oligodendrocytes, specialized brain cells responsible for producing and maintaining myelin.
Oligodendrocytes have traditionally been regarded as beneficial because they help keep nerve fibers insulated and functioning properly. However, the new findings suggest that these cells can become dysfunctional during aging and may contribute to the very problems they normally help prevent.
The researchers discovered that people with more severe cognitive decline had lower levels of a protein called NRF2 inside their oligodendrocytes.
NRF2 plays an important protective role in cells by regulating hundreds of genes involved in defending against damage and maintaining normal cellular function. When its activity decreases, cells may become less capable of protecting themselves and performing their usual jobs.
To investigate whether this protein was directly involved in the brain changes, the team conducted experiments in mice.
When researchers specifically reduced NRF2 in oligodendrocytes, the animals developed excessive myelin and lost large nerve fibers, closely resembling the abnormalities observed in human brain tissue. The mice also showed reduced improvements in cognitive performance as they aged.
These experiments provided evidence that declining NRF2 activity can directly disrupt oligodendrocyte function, potentially triggering changes in myelin and nerve fibers that contribute to cognitive decline.
Existing Drugs Could Offer a New Treatment Strategy
The findings may have important implications for developing treatments that help preserve cognitive abilities in older adults.
One particularly promising aspect is that the NRF2 pathway is already a target of medications used for other conditions, including a drug prescribed to treat multiple sclerosis (MS).
Previous studies have found that increasing NRF2 activity can improve cognitive function in people with MS. That raises the possibility that medications acting on the same pathway might eventually be repurposed to address oligodendrocyte dysfunction and age-related cognitive decline.
Although further research is needed to determine whether such treatments would benefit older adults experiencing cognitive decline, the discovery identifies a potentially valuable therapeutic target.
Veronique Miron, MRC Senior Non-Clinical Fellow and UK Dementia Research Institute Group Leader at the University of Edinburgh and St. Michael's Hospital, part of Unity Health Toronto, said:
"As the prevalence of cognitive decline is rising with an aging population and no current treatments exist, we are excited about this work as it points to a potential strategy for new therapeutic strategies to preserve cognitive ability in aging."
A New Understanding of Cognitive Decline
Beyond its potential medical applications, the research changes how scientists understand the role of oligodendrocytes in the aging brain.
Rather than simply providing support for healthy nerve function throughout life, these cells appear capable of becoming dysfunctional and contributing to cognitive problems.
Georgina Craig, the study's first author and a Postdoctoral Fellow at St Michael's Hospital in Toronto and the UK Dementia Research Institute, said:
"This study has fundamentally shifted how we think about these brain cells in aging. We have always considered oligodendrocytes as purely beneficial, yet here we surprisingly find that they can become dysfunctional and contribute to cognitive impairment in aging."
The findings suggest that maintaining healthy oligodendrocyte function could become an important strategy for protecting memory and thinking abilities as people grow older.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study was funded by the UKRI Medical Research Council (MRC) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR). The research also involved scientists from the University of Edinburgh's Lothian Birth Cohort studies and Northwestern University.

- Georgina A. Craig, Emeric Merour, Luise A. Seeker, Annette J. Haughian, Keon Arbabi, Jamie Rose, Alana Hoffmann, Jessica Thapar, Andrea Corsinotti, Stephen Mitchell, Janie Corley, Susan D. The incident came as former members of the Yellow Vest movement joined high school students, university students, farmers, climate activists and trade unionists in protests over living costs, public services and education.
French authorities expected up to 170,000 people to take part nationwide, with around 500 actions and more than 90 demonstrations planned, according to sources close to the Interior Ministry.

Police also reported 21 arrests after around 100 people targeted broadcaster CNews’ headquarters in Paris, blocking access to a car park, throwing projectiles and smashing windows.
Demonstrations were prohibited around several key locations in the capital, including the Élysée Palace, the prime minister’s office and the Champs-Élysées.
Yellow Vests return as discontent widens
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018, initially protesting fuel taxes and the rising cost of living before developing into a broader challenge to government policies and economic inequality.

In Lille, around 20 demonstrators, including Yellow Vest protesters, gathered outside the Hauts-de-France Regional Council behind a banner declaring that their struggle was continuing.
In Paris, authorities anticipated between 30,000 and 60,000 protesters. The main march was scheduled to leave Place de la République at 2 pm local time and proceed towards Place de Clichy.
Macron urges calm as tensions rise
President Emmanuel Macron called on Friday for calm and respect for people and property during the demonstrations.
The nationwide protests followed weeks of student-led actions and brought together a wider coalition of groups expressing concerns about living costs, public spending and social conditions.
The scale of the planned mobilisation and incidents reported in several cities placed renewed focus on the government’s response to public discontent, while authorities sought to maintain order and prevent further disruption.

Persian Gulf Internet, AI Infrastructures within Iran’s reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:29:27 UTC
21:29:27 KST

The threat of expanding the scope of a potential conflict between Iran and the United States to include the region’s digital infrastructure introduces new dimensions to the security equations in the Persian Gulf.
These infrastructures, which may appear unrelated to the military sphere, actually underpin significant portions of the economies, commerce, communications, and technological activities of nations in the region. Submarine internet cables, data centers, and facilities associated with artificial intelligence have now become strategic assets for these countries; assets whose damage could trigger consequences extending well beyond national borders.
In an interview with Press TV, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) Mohsen Rezaei discussed the possibility that regional communication and technology infrastructure could be targeted in the event of a renewed conflict with the United States. These remarks, viewed alongside the extensive investments made by the Persian Gulf Arab states in the digital economy and artificial intelligence, draw attention to the vulnerability of infrastructure that relies on high-speed connectivity, a stable and sustainable power supply, and expansive data transmission networks to function.
Submarine Cables: The Hidden Arteries of the Internet
A significant portion of international internet communications takes place via submarine fiber-optic cables. These cables are laid on the seabed and ocean floors, transmitting data over long distances using light pulses. Messaging, video calls, data exchange between companies, cloud services, and many international financial transactions all rely, directly or indirectly, on the capacity of these networks.
The significance of this infrastructure lies in the fact that a large portion of global digital communication relies on pathways that often remain hidden from users. Contrary to popular belief, the Internet is not merely a collection of wireless or satellite networks; the major portion of the global data transmission depends on terrestrial networks and fiber-optic cables. Submarine cables, in particular, play a fundamental role in intercontinental connectivity due to their high capacity and ability to transmit massive volumes of data.
The Persian Gulf and its associated communication routes are also part of this extensive network. The region’s geographical position, linking Asia, Europe, and other global economic hubs—lends particular significance to its data transmission routes. In the meantime, the Strait of Hormuz is crucial to security and economic calculations, given its strategic role in maritime transport and its proximity to regional infrastructure. However, the precise routing of cables and the degree of dependency vary from country to country. Therefore, it should not be assumed that all communication networks in the region rely on a single, unified path.
What are the consequences of damage to the cables?
Damage to a submarine cable does not necessarily mean a complete loss of internet access within a country or globally. Communication networks typically consist of multiple paths; if alternative capacity is available, some traffic can be rerouted. However, such rerouting often comes at a cost. If multiple paths are damaged simultaneously, or if the capacity of alternative routes is insufficient, there is an increased likelihood of slower speeds, higher latency, and disruptions to certain services.
The consequences depend on the location of the damage, the number of affected cables, the volume of traffic, and the capacity of alternative networks. Telecommunications companies, internet service providers (ISPs), financial institutions, and businesses that rely on the rapid exchange of information may face increased costs or a decline in service quality. Given that digital communications play a vital role in economic activities, such a disruption can escalate from a mere technical issue into a source of economic loss.
Repairing submarine cables is neither a quick nor a simple process. Locating the damage, deploying specialized vessels, and carrying out repairs depend on various technical and environmental conditions. Consequently, in the event of extensive damage or damage occurring simultaneously across multiple routes, restoring the network to its normal state can be time-consuming. The very characteristic has made the protection of such infrastructure a critical issue for communications security.
Data Centers and Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Critical Point for the Digital Economy
The significance of potential threats becomes even greater when data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure are taken into account. In recent years, the Persian Gulf Arab states, most notably Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, have made extensive investments in the development of their digital economies, cloud services, and artificial intelligence. These investments are aimed at diversifying their economies, reducing reliance on traditional energy revenues, and transforming the region into a global technology hub.
Data centers serve as hubs for storing and processing vast amounts of information, supporting services ranging from website and financial system hosting to complex artificial intelligence computations. The stable operation of these centers relies on several fundamental factors: reliable power, cooling systems, high-speed connectivity, and specialized equipment. A serious disruption in any of these areas can impair a data center's performance or, in extreme cases, bring its operations to a complete halt.
With regards to the artificial intelligence, the issue extends beyond the mere existence of powerful computers. Training and running advanced models require substantial computing power, as well as energy and data transmission infrastructure. Furthermore, the connectivity between data centers, cloud networks, and users constitutes an integral part of the service delivery chain. Consequently, any disruption to communication infrastructure or energy supply can drive up operational costs for technology companies and lead to delays in their development plans.
Of course, any disruption to internet cables should not be interpreted as a cessation of operations for artificial intelligence centers. Data centers may utilize diverse communication routes, redundant systems, and emergency power sources. The vulnerability of any given facility depends on its technical design, geographical distribution, level of protection, and capacity to shift processing workloads to other locations. Nevertheless, the interdependence of these infrastructures demonstrates that digital security is no longer merely a technical matter; rather, it is inextricably linked to the economic resilience and national security of nations.
Regional Consequences of a Costly Scenario
Should the conflict extend to digital infrastructure, its potential impact could spread to sectors such as financial services, e-commerce, transportation, corporate communications, and public services. Companies that rely on cloud computing or cross-border communications may face operational disruptions and increased costs. This situation is of particular significance for countries striving to attract foreign investment and enhance their standing within the digital economy.
Ultimately, concerns regarding the potential targeting of the region’s communication and technology infrastructure underscore that rivalry and tension in the Persian Gulf extend well beyond military capabilities or energy exports. Subsea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence infrastructure have emerged as strategic regional assets, and any security crisis could jeopardize their functionality. For nations investing billions of dollars in their digital future, the critical question is whether this technological expansion is accompanied by a commensurate strategy for infrastructure protection, the establishment of redundant pathways, and the enhancement of resilience against crises.

Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar

Hardline Israeli rabbi ruling on stolen Palestinian olives prompts uproar
A hardline religious ruling justifying the theft of Palestinian olive harvests escalates violence and political tensions before Israeli elections.
Prominent Israeli Rabbi Dov Lior issued a Jewish religious ruling on Friday permitting settlers to steal olives from Palestinian orchards in the occupied West Bank.
Lior’s ruling claims that Palestinian landowners who could not access their olives during the harvest season due to Israeli restrictions have been sufficiently compensated in the years they had access to the fruit. According to the ruling, Jews are permitted to pick these olives to claim ownership of the Palestinian land.
Lior, born in Poland in 1933, went as far as classifying the theft of olives from Palestinian farms as an “additional virtue”, as settler pogroms and Israeli occupation continue in the West Bank.
He added that settlers should “conquer the land” far from Jewish communities in order to publicly “demonstrate our ownership” and follow biblical commandment.
“The Jewish people have never given up on the Land of Israel, as we express in our prayers every single day,” the ruling continues. “The Arabs never purchased the land from the Jewish people or from any individual Jew, and therefore it is stolen land in their hands… They never bought it in any way and it remained under the ownership of the Jewish people.”
Harvest violence
The ruling coincides with another wave of settler pogroms against Palestinian farmers during the olive harvest season. On Friday. at least 19 people were injured in 34 attacks by the Israeli military and settlers on Palestinians harvesting their crops across the West Bank.
An American photojournalist working for The Washington Post was assaulted by settlers while covering the daily violence, and five vehicles were torched.
Many Palestinian farmers have been unable to access their crops due to Israeli restrictions and the dangers from the settlers.
While settler pogroms are not exceptional, they come weeks before Israeli elections, with a push by far-right parties to gain the support of settlers and their supporters. But not all Jewish religious leaders backed the call to steal Palestinian olives.
Religious backlash
Rabbis from the religious council of the Gush Etzion settlements published a letter calling the illegal harvesting of Palestinian crops theft, blasphemy, and a moral defect.
Tzohar, an organisation of 800 orthodox rabbis, said in a statement that only the state has the authority to confiscate property. As long as the state recognises Arab ownership of the olives, they belong to them, it added.
Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, told Al Jazeera that there could be political reasons behind the religious groups’ rejection of Rabbi Dov Lior’s comments.
“The position of the other rabbis who rejected this call might be a move driven by political motive and pressure from entities within the government to give the impression that these are anomalous voices that do not represent the general opinion of the settlers.
“The Israeli government is trying to portray that those who carry out these riots are a limited-number group that does not represent public opinion in the settlements, and that the settlers are peaceful, good, and law-abiding, and that the issue is confined to the ‘Hilltop Youth‘ boys who commit these crimes,” he explained.
Rabbi Dov Lior holds immense influence among hardline settler groups, such as the Hilltop Youth, who fiercely back his hardline religious decrees that oppose any territorial compromise with Palestinians.
He is also a prominent figure within Israel’s Religious Zionist movement and serves as the spiritual guide for the far-right Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
“Ben-Gvir relies on the religious rulings of Rabbi Dov Lior, which rely on biblical texts and the Book of Deuteronomy,” Abu Amer noted. He claimed that Rabbi Lior adopts the most extreme interpretations in the Jewish religion.
“There is an important matter, which is that Ben-Gvir competes via the TikTok platform, propaganda, and populist rhetoric, and this is a rhetoric that serves him and brings him votes, given the environment and general atmosphere in Israel after the events of October 7, as there is a ‘market for extremism’ in the Israeli society,” Abu Amer added.
Knesset member Gilad Kariv of the left-wing Democrats Party criticised Lior, accusing him and his followers of dragging Israel into a flood of moral vice.
“Whoever stands on the sidelines in this issue joins the camp of Rabbi Dov Lior and his criminals,” Kariv said.

NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:26:49 UTC
21:26:49 KST

NASA’s Webb reveals the wild weather of a mysterious world 20 light-years away
- Date:
- October 17, 2026
- Source:
- Trinity College Dublin
- Summary:
- NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed that a turbulent world 20 light-years away has a surprisingly orderly weather system, with three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature changes and shifting clouds. The breakthrough gives scientists a powerful new tool for uncovering weather patterns on distant worlds and understanding the conditions that shape their atmospheres.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a powerful new way to decode the weather on distant worlds, revealing surprisingly organized patterns hidden within the turbulent atmosphere of a mysterious object 20 light-years from Earth.
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin used observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to investigate SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf previously associated with phenomena resembling the northern lights. They found that its complex weather is largely governed by just two factors: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.
The discovery offers a new way to understand the atmospheric conditions of distant worlds and could help astronomers investigate planets far beyond our Solar System.
How NASA's Webb Telescope Decoded Alien Weather
To investigate SIMP 0136, the researchers analyzed observations collected by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) using a mathematical technique called Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
This technique helps scientists make sense of large, complicated datasets by identifying the strongest patterns within them. In this case, the team examined how the brown dwarf's light changed as it rotated, looking for subtle variations that could reveal what was happening in its atmosphere.
Rather than beginning with detailed assumptions about how the atmosphere should behave, the researchers allowed the observations to reveal the most important processes. The method also helped separate genuine atmospheric changes from minor fluctuations and random noise in the measurements.
Webb's exceptionally sensitive instruments made this possible by detecting extremely small changes in the object's brightness as different parts of its atmosphere rotated into view.
Scientists Discover Hidden Order in Chaotic Alien Weather
The results revealed something unexpected. Although SIMP 0136 appears to have a highly complicated atmosphere, nearly all of its observed atmospheric variability could be explained by just two dominant components, consistent with temperature fluctuations and changes in the vertical arrangement of clouds.
Even more remarkably, the researchers identified three recurring weather states that appear and disappear from view as the brown dwarf rotates.
Together, these states create a shifting atmospheric patchwork. Some regions are hotter and have thinner clouds, while others are cooler and contain thicker cloud layers that extend farther vertically through the atmosphere.
Instead of constantly changing in an unpredictable way, these weather patterns appear to follow an underlying structure.
The findings, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics, suggest that the seemingly chaotic atmosphere of SIMP 0136 is actually governed by a remarkably consistent set of processes.
Brown dwarfs occupy an unusual place between planets and stars. SIMP 0136 is larger and hotter than a typical gas giant planet, but it lacks the mass needed to shine like a star. Its atmosphere contains enormous cloud systems that evolve rapidly, making its weather more comparable to an extreme version of Jupiter's than anything experienced on Earth.
These immense weather systems can span planetary scales, continually changing the appearance of the distant world.
"We also discovered that these drivers of the weather patterns on SIMP-0136 persist over time, even as the detailed appearance of the atmosphere evolves over more than a dozen rotations," said first author Merle Schrader, a PhD candidate in Trinity's School of Physics.
"In relative terms, SIMP 0136 is one of the easier brown dwarfs for us to capture high-quality data from. These data have been studied before by established methods, allowing us to compare some of the results from this new technique to what we already know about this object. The technique has also helped us develop a better understanding of what drives the weather on this faraway world and how these weather patterns interact and co-exist, but perhaps even more importantly, it shows how this approach can be further refined and applied to other, less well-known brown dwarfs in different parts of space."
A Remarkable Connection Across 20 Light Years
For Schrader, the research also revealed an extraordinary personal connection to the distant object.
SIMP 0136 is located approximately 20 light years from Earth, meaning its light takes about two decades to reach us. The light captured by Webb in 2023, which provided the observations used in the study, had actually left the brown dwarf during the year Schrader was born.
"Light travels at around 300,000 km/s but, even at that speed, it took two decades to reach us, peering through the JWST lenses," she said.
"When you consider light takes just over a second to reach the Moon after leaving Earth, that gives a sense of how far away SIMP 0136 is, and how incredible astrophysical progress has been. I think it's amazing that we have been able to discern the intimate weather patterns of a distant world and map their interactions from our cozy little corner of the universe, when all we observe directly of these objects is a single pixel spread across the light spectrum."
The achievement highlights how much information astronomers can extract from seemingly tiny amounts of light. Even though SIMP 0136 appears as little more than a single point in telescope observations, changes in its brightness at different wavelengths can reveal detailed information about its atmosphere.
What This Discovery Means for Distant Planets
The new technique could have implications far beyond SIMP 0136.
Brown dwarfs are particularly valuable for investigating the atmospheres of giant exoplanets, which are planets orbiting stars outside our Solar System. Because brown dwarfs can often be observed directly, they give scientists an opportunity to study atmospheric processes that are much harder to investigate on most exoplanets.
By examining these objects, researchers can test how clouds form, how heat moves through an atmosphere, and how atmospheric circulation behaves under extreme conditions.
The technique developed by the Trinity team could make those investigations considerably more efficient. By quickly identifying the processes responsible for most of the observed atmospheric changes, astronomers can better determine which features deserve closer examination using more complicated computer models.
Professor Johanna Vos, Associate Professor in Trinity School of Physics, explained the potential significance of the findings.
"Our findings will transform how astronomers analyze future JWST observations. Since our approach rapidly identifies the dominant components of the atmosphere it offers an efficient first step before we begin computationally intensive modeling.
"Applying this technique to a wide range of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets will help us better understand the diverse weather systems that shape worlds far beyond our Solar System."
Ultimately, understanding weather on distant worlds is about more than identifying clouds and temperature changes. Atmospheric behavior can provide important clues about a planet's chemical composition, physical conditions, and overall environment.
Those insights are also relevant to one of astronomy's biggest questions: which planets beyond our Solar System might have conditions capable of supporting life?
By revealing how complex alien atmospheres can be understood from faint changes in light, this new approach could help scientists take another step toward answering that question.

Gonzales, Allison M. McCarthy, Caroline V. Morley, Barry O’Donovan, Cian O’Toole, Genaro Suárez, Xianyu Tan, Channon Visscher, Niall Whiteford, Yifan Zhou. PHNOM PENH, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- An archaeological team has completed 80 percent of the restoration of Angkor Thom's centuries-old laterite wall within the UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park in Cambodia's Siem Reap province, an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release said on Saturday.
The project, which began in April, focuses on the southwest section of the ancient wall near the prominent Tonle Om Gate.
Mao Sokny, a technical officer with the ANA's Department of Conservation of Monuments and Preventive Archaeology, said the reinforcement of the wall and its internal staircase is progressing smoothly.
"The reinforcement of the 15-meter-long wall is now finished," he said. "The team is currently backfilling the surrounding area with soil and applying mortar between the stones to secure its long-term structural stability."
Additionally, a 23-step internal staircase has been reassembled and reconnected to the wall, he added.
Built in the late 12th century by King Jayavarman VII, Angkor Thom was the grand capital of the ancient Khmer Empire, according to the ANA.
Its enclosure wall extends about 3 kilometers on each side, stands approximately 8 meters high, and is surrounded by a moat. The ancient city is accessed through five monumental gates. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: How Chinese TCM training hones Indonesian medical skills
China

2026-10-17

21:25:25 KST

Chen Zhigeng, director of the medical department at Wenzhi Traditional Chinese Medicine, demonstrates a technique during a training session at RSPPN Soedirman in Jakarta, Indonesia, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Veri Sanovri)
by Zhang Yisheng, Nurul Fitri Ramadhani
JAKARTA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- For three grueling months, even simple movements brought pain to Dr. Hetty Helen's hand. As a physician at Indonesia's Rumah Sakit Pusat Pertahanan Negara (RSPPN) Soedirman, her relief finally came from an unexpected source: the hands of a Chinese traditional medicine practitioner.
"The hand feels lighter and better," Helen said, visibly relieved. Having tried acupuncture before, she noted the technique used by the Chinese medical team was noticeably more precise, targeting the exact source of her pain.
Helen's experience underscores the unique value of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) and the vital role of medical exchanges in enhancing Indonesia's healthcare capabilities.
Under the "Belt and Road Acupuncture Station" initiative launched at RSPPN Soedirman, Chinese specialists worked shoulder-to-shoulder with Indonesian medical staff from Oct. 13 to 15. The program featured clinical training, free community consultations, and practical workshops on cutting-edge, AI-assisted TCM diagnostics.
Organized by the Shenzhen Shouzheng Innovative TCM Development Foundation, the training went beyond theory, guiding participants through needle safety, emergency protocols, and precise acupoint location. Doctors and students rolled up their sleeves to practice targeted techniques for shoulder and knee conditions, as well as specialized scalp and abdominal acupuncture.
For the Indonesian medical trainees, the program bridged the gap between textbooks and clinical reality, giving them rare, hands-on confidence under expert mentorship.
Natalia Santoso, a student of acupuncture and herbal medicine in Jakarta, felt a lightbulb moment during the workshops. She said learning directly from Chinese masters helped deconstruct techniques that had long puzzled her.
"Learning TCM, which we thought was difficult, turns out not to be so difficult once you understand the key points or acupuncture points," she said.
Santoso added that hearing the concepts explained straight from native Mandarin speakers gave her a far richer insight than reading translated Indonesian textbooks.
Beyond traditional techniques, the program introduced participants to AI-powered TCM diagnostic tools, offering them a firsthand look at the future of digital healthcare.
Hetty Helen Yanti, head of the hospital's TCM department, noted that such cross-border collaborations allow local doctors to refine their skill sets, particularly in mastering high-precision acupoint targeting.
Hafna Rosita of Indonesia's Traditional Health Council viewed the exchange as a dual opportunity: upgrading local practitioner skills while fueling the development of Indonesia's homegrown traditional medicine.
"TCM has advanced considerably, with extensive documentation, analysis and research," Rosita said, pointing out that Indonesia's traditional medicine similarly holds vast untapped potential.
The two systems could complement each other, for instance, by integrating precision acupuncture techniques with rich Indonesian herbal remedies, Rosita said.
Dr. David Song, a physician at the hospital's Traditional Indonesian and Chinese Medicine (TICM) division, emphasized that the initiative ultimately aims to fuse local Indonesian remedies with time-tested Chinese practices.
Through the TICM division at RSPPN Soedirman, "we are seeking to integrate Indonesia's local herbal remedies, known as jamu, with thousands of years of TCM wisdom to better serve our community's healthcare needs," Song said.
Looking ahead, Song said he believes partnership with Chinese institutions will drive deeper exchanges in medical technology, research, and clinical training.
Chen Zhigeng, director of the medical department at Wenzhi Traditional Chinese Medicine, a TCM-focused AI digital healthcare company, said the program's outcomes far exceeded expectations, voicing strong hopes for sustained partnership.
The event serves as a bridge for both medical and cultural exchange, enabling the Chinese side and its Indonesian counterpart to learn from one another and deepen long-term cooperation in traditional healthcare, he said. ■

TOKYO, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Japan and the United States will conduct large-scale joint military exercises at multiple locations across Japan from Oct. 19 to 29, involving nearly 60,000 personnel and drawing widespread concern and opposition in Japan, Kyodo News reported Saturday.
The drills, dubbed "Keen Sword 27," will involve comprehensive training by ground, maritime and air forces. The Japan Self-Defense Forces and the U.S. military will deploy about 45,000 and 12,000 personnel, respectively. Australia, Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand and the Philippines will also participate, with the latter five countries taking part for the first time, the report said.
Notably, the Type-25 surface-to-ship missile system, deployed in Kumamoto Prefecture in March despite local opposition, will take part in the exercises. The system will be moved to the Ohnobaru training area from its base in Kumamoto. The missile has a range of about 1,000 km, extending well beyond Japan's territory.
The U.S. military will also deploy advanced military equipment, including the Naval and Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System and the Marine Air Defense Integrated System, to Yonaguni Island in Okinawa Prefecture for the first time, according to the report.
The two militaries will conduct drills to counter ballistic missiles and military aircraft in waters off Hokkaido and northeastern Japan. Other exercises across the country will include parachute drops, amphibious vehicle landings, and casualty care and evacuation. Training will also cover support for ground, maritime and air operations in space and cyberspace.
The exercises have triggered widespread concern and opposition across Japan. Japanese media have reported protests in Okinawa, Nagasaki and Oita prefectures since the beginning of October, with demonstrators calling for the cancellation of the drills and an end to military training at civilian facilities.
Civic groups have warned that the joint exercises will only heighten regional tensions and put local residents at risk. ■

Kenya steps up Ebola containment as cases reach three
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:24:39 CST
21:24:39 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Kenya has intensified contact tracing, quarantine measures, screening at airports and border crossings, and infection prevention efforts as the number of Ebola cases in the country rises to three.
On Friday, Kenya confirmed its third case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease.
Patrick Amoth, director-general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health, said the patient, a 65-year-old woman, was a close relative of the first and second cases.
She had been in quarantine since Oct. 6 and had developed a fever, sore throat and malaise.
"Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease," Amoth said.
To prevent further spread of the disease, Amoth said Kenya had significantly scaled up its surveillance operations, successfully tracing and quarantining 127 of the 130 identified contacts.
"Of the 130 listed contacts, 127 (97.7 percent) have been traced and placed in quarantine, exceeding the global benchmark of 85 percent required to break the chain of transmission, while active efforts continue to locate and quarantine the remaining three," he said.
Amoth said the overall risk in the country remained low, as there was no evidence of community transmission. Contacts in quarantine were being closely monitored to ensure that any new cases could be detected and treated promptly.
On Oct. 12, Kenya declared Ebola a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act, with the government introducing new regulations governing disease surveillance, screening, isolation, quarantine and the management of suspected infections.
Under the regulations, public health screening must be conducted at major points of entry, suspected cases must undergo medical assessment, and patients must be isolated and referred for treatment. Individuals who may have been exposed to the virus must also be monitored and quarantined.
The regulations also require the designation of health facilities responsible for managing Ebola cases and the establishment of procedures for inspecting and decontaminating premises where infections may have occurred.
Kenya notified the World Health Organization (WHO) after reporting its first Ebola case, in accordance with the International Health Regulations (2005).
"The two new cases have been detected early because they were already in quarantine and were being checked every day," said Neema Kimambo, WHO representative to Kenya, on Friday.
She commended the Ministry of Health, the Kenya National Public Health Institute, and national and county health teams for their swift response.
"We thank the health workers, response teams and families in quarantine for their commitment," she added.
Kenya is the fourth country in the world to confirm Ebola virus disease in the current context, following the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda and France.
Most Ebola cases in Kenya and Uganda were imported from the DRC, while the case in France was travel-related and reported in June.
According to WHO, the early symptoms of Bundibugyo Ebola can resemble those of malaria and other common illnesses. They include fever, fatigue, muscle or joint pain, headache and sore throat.
There is currently no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for Bundibugyo Ebola, although clinical trials are underway in the DRC, according to WHO.
Kenya's borders remain open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings. ■

Protests sweep France as riots erupt in Marseille, police fire tear gas in Paris | Live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:22:22 UTC
21:22:22 KST

France is bracing for mass demonstrations Saturday as several protest movements join forces against the high cost of living, deteriorating public services and rising fuel prices. Tens of thousands of people are expected to take to the streets in demonstrations bringing together members of the Yellow Vests movement and student protesters, among others.
The student protest movement in France began Sept. 17 and has gained momentum in recent weeks, with students at hundreds of schools, particularly in impoverished, working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, blocking school entrances, taking over roads, setting trash cans on fire and attacking police officers and passersby. The students say they are protesting neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. The demonstrations erupted as the French government seeks to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to reduce the deficit.
In central Paris, large numbers of police officers gathered, particularly near the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe. Police also fired tear gas canisters at demonstrators in Place de la République. Some protesters wore masks and black clothing and launched fireworks.
But the more dramatic scenes, even before the demonstrations officially began, came from Marseille. In the southern city, protesters were filmed smashing windows at a local police station and spray-painting graffiti, including on police flags. Fires were set in the streets, with mannequins apparently looted from stores thrown into the flames.
Dozens of protesters also briefly stormed City Hall, shouting, "This is the revolution — we're storming the Bastille!" Police removed the demonstrators from the building and deployed officers at the entrance to prevent them from returning. Officers in the streets of Marseille also used tear gas, while some images showed arrests taking place.
By midday, French authorities had recorded approximately 140 protest actions involving tens of thousands of people. A total of 166 people had been arrested across France, including dozens in Paris. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he feared that "far-left elements" could inflame the demonstrations and turn them violent during the afternoon.
In a post on X, Paris police said, "We will not back down in the face of rioters and those who come to attack law enforcement officers," accusing "hostile individuals" of carrying out attacks against police.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," a 19-year-old protester who identified herself as Lola told Reuters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Thursday that authorities were concerned about possible riots during the protests. President Emmanuel Macron, for his part, called for "calm" ahead of Saturday's demonstrations but stressed that he believed in the right to protest. He urged demonstrators to respect people and property.
Opponents of the protests accused the France Unbowed party, led by radical left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel politician, of inciting violence and fueling the unrest. They also emphasized the involvement of immigrants and their descendants in the street violence. The party categorically denied the allegations.
Palestinian keffiyehs and flags were seen at many of the demonstrations. About a week and a half ago, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on the issue in a social media post, alleging that the protests were not really about conditions in schools but rather reflected immigration spiraling out of control and an attempt by Islam to take over France.
Police could resume use of stun grenades
Last week, France announced it was suspending the use of stun grenades following an incident in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand. Police said they had faced more than 200 students throwing stones and launching fireworks, and that the boy had picked up a grenade that exploded in his hand. Students, however, claimed he was struck directly after a police officer fired the grenade at him.
In another incident last week, a 14-year-old boy named Eden was struck in the face by a tear gas canister near Paris. According to his lawyer, he lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw.
On Friday evening, however, Interior Minister Nuñez announced that the use of stun grenades could resume.
"If there are clashes, all types of equipment may be used," he said in a television interview Friday.
The wave of unrest in France has erupted just six months before the presidential election, against an already tense social and political backdrop, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls and fuel prices soaring.
Current polls suggest that Le Pen will not win outright in the first round and that she will face radical left-wing leader Mélenchon in the decisive runoff — and defeat him.
Either way, such a showdown would signal that France is abandoning the political center and finding itself forced to choose between two parties widely regarded as extreme.

Israeli rabbi rules settlers can steal Palestinian olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:20:13 UTC
21:20:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli rabbi issues ruling permitting settlers to steal Palestinian olive harvests
A prominent Israeli rabbi on Friday issued a religious ruling that would allow Israeli Jews to steal olives from Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank, with several Israeli media outlets affiliated with the religious Zionist movement, including Channel 7, publishing the religious edict.
The ruling, issued by prominent religious Zionist rabbi Dov Lior, said that the olives belong to the Jewish people, and that taking the crops represents the implementation of what he described as the "commandment to occupy the land".
The ruling, titled “In response to numerous enquiries regarding olive harvesting in the groves throughout Judea, Samaria and Binyamin” — biblical names used by Israelis to refer to areas of the occupied West Bank — states that “the people of Israel have never relinquished the Land of Israel, as we express in our daily prayers".
This comes amid escalating Israeli settler violence and terrorism targeting Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank, with mobs stealing tractors, setting alight olive trees, and damaging cars.
Lior further claims that "the Arabs never purchased the land from the people of Israel or from any Jew, and therefore it is usurped in their hands".According to his assertion, Palestinians “did not acquire ownership of it by any means, and it has remained the property of the people of Israel".
The rabbi further states that if Palestinian farmers cannot reach their crops for security reasons, it can be assumed that they have abandoned the crops.
“If they planted trees that bear fruit, such as olives, the principle of despairing of recovering them applies to them. Therefore, if they are unable to harvest them for security reasons, it should be assumed that they have given up on them — and all the more so that they have given up on olives that have already been picked," the rabbi said.
He adds that even if the owners of the trees were entitled to compensation for cultivating them, they had already received sufficient produce from them over previous years. He maintains that the land and its fruits should ultimately return to what he describes as the ownership of the Jewish people.
Lior goes so far as to declare that settlers harvesting olives from Palestinian land is “entirely permissible". He adds that this act contains an “additional virtue”, given the security risks supposedly posed by Palestinians approaching settlements and settlement outposts.
His position is not limited to olive harvesting on land adjacent to settlements. He extends the ruling to groves farther away, stating: “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements, in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land, and thereby fulfil the commandment to conquer the land.”
Dov Lior is one of the most prominent rabbis associated with Israel’s religious-nationalist movement. He previously served as the chief rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement near Hebron. Lior is known for his hard-line religious and political positions towards Palestinians and his support for expanding settlements in the West Bank. He wields influence among settlers and religious movements associated with the settlement movement.
Israeli media reported that Lior’s ruling came in response to a religious ruling issued last Tuesday by seven rabbis from settlements in the Gush Etzion bloc, south of Bethlehem. Those rabbis prohibited settlers from stealing olives from Palestinian land, even when Israeli forces prevent the owners from accessing their property for security reasons.
The rabbis, including Ze’ev Whitman, Uri Lifshitz, Avi Bliedstein and Moshe Shifter, argued that preventing Palestinians from reaching their groves does not mean they have relinquished ownership of the harvest. They stressed that seizing the olives constitutes "theft forbidden by religious law and a desecration of God’s name".
The seven rabbis based their position on provisions of Jewish religious law prohibiting the theft of property belonging to non-Jews. They emphasised that even if the landowners were assumed to have abandoned their fruit, this would not make it permissible for others to take it.
The Tzohar movement, which includes prominent rabbis, also joined the opponents of Lior’s ruling on Friday. It stated that “theft is forbidden from any person, whether Jewish or non-Jewish”, and that individuals do not have the authority to confiscate property.
The circulation of the ruling comes amid escalating attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian farmers during the current olive harvest season. These attacks have included beatings, gunfire, the theft of crops, the burning of trees and vehicles, and preventing farmers from accessing their land.
Several areas of the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate witnessed widespread settler attacks on olive pickers on Friday. The attacks targeted the villages of Abu Falah, Turmus Ayya, Burqa and Deir Jarir, causing injuries among Palestinians and resulting in olive trees and vehicles being set on fire.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are considered illegal under international law.

Trump feud with Zelenskyy raises fears over Ukraine aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:20:00 UTC
21:20:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump’s growing dispute with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is raising concerns that Kyiv could lose critical American military and intelligence support as Russia continues its war, with Washington’s efforts to curb fuel prices adding to tensions between the allies.
From threats to restrict intelligence sharing to a potential deal to import Russian diesel, a series of developments has exposed the fragility of the relationship between Kyiv and its most important ally.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelenskyy over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he partly blames for rising energy costs.
The U.S. president has pushed Ukraine to stop targeting Russian energy infrastructure, but Zelenskyy has rejected the demand, arguing that Kyiv cannot halt its attacks while Moscow continues striking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The dispute intensified after disruptions to U.S.-controlled satellite internet services raised concerns about Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian missile and drone attacks, particularly as it prepares for another winter of assaults on its energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy has responded to Trump with unusually direct public criticism, accusing Washington of increasingly favoring Moscow.
His remarks have fueled fears that the deteriorating relationship could lead to further restrictions on U.S. weapons deliveries, a suspension of battlefield intelligence sharing or additional economic agreements that benefit Russia.
Despite the public confrontation, Kyiv wants to maintain contact with Trump's envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president's son-in-law, two Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Ukraine is also seeking to preserve its diplomatic relationship with Washington.
Denys Sienik, charge d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said Friday that Kyiv appreciated Trump's efforts to end the war and remained willing to engage in negotiations with Russia.
Trump, meanwhile, said he would continue dealing with both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"I want that war to end," Trump told reporters Friday.
Daniel Fried, a former senior State Department official responsible for European affairs from 2005 to 2009, said it remained unclear whether Washington was making a lasting shift away from Ukraine.
He warned, however, that the fallout was undermining prospects for ending the war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"It's not only a missed opportunity, it causes genuine suffering in Ukraine and encourages Putin to continue the war, so it's not cost-free," said Fried, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based think tank.
Trump's relationship with Zelenskyy has been strained for much of his presidency. In February 2025, Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly reprimanded the Ukrainian leader during a contentious meeting in the Oval Office.
Since returning to the White House, Trump has paused or slowed military assistance to Ukraine at various points, while allowing European allies to purchase American weapons for Kyiv.
Relations had shown signs of stabilizing before Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities became a fresh source of friction this year.
Rising fuel prices have added urgency to the dispute for Trump, whose Republican Party faces a difficult battle to retain its majorities in Congress in November's midterm elections. High gasoline and diesel costs remain a political liability for the administration, analysts say.
But experts attribute much of the increase in energy prices to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, which prompted Iranian attacks on energy infrastructure and largely shut the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Frustrated with Zelenskyy, Trump turned to Moscow in an effort to increase fuel supplies and contain prices, according to a person familiar with the internal discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Trump said Oct. 9 that he had reached an agreement with Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel.
The move raised concerns that Washington could ease economic pressure on Moscow while demanding concessions from Ukraine, potentially giving the Kremlin additional revenue to sustain its war effort.
For Kyiv, the consequences of a breakdown in relations with Washington could be immediate.
Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Ukraine had received no advance warning from Western partners before a deadly Russian attack on the capital, underscoring concerns about the reliability of intelligence support.
American intelligence has been central to Ukraine's ability to detect incoming Russian missiles and drones, assess battlefield developments and plan military operations. A reduction in that assistance could leave Ukrainian forces less prepared to counter attacks, particularly against power plants and other critical infrastructure.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy system during previous winters, seeking to disrupt electricity and heating supplies as temperatures fall.
Trump has said Washington continues to share intelligence with Kyiv. Zelenskyy, however, told NPR that U.S. officials had warned Ukrainian commanders that intelligence support could be reduced or cut off.
Concerns deepened after Ukraine's Starshield service, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system, was disrupted. Two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter said the disruption followed an order originating from the White House, Reuters reported Thursday.
The service has since been partially restored, but the episode highlighted Ukraine's dependence on technology controlled by American companies and potentially affected by decisions made by the Trump administration.
Satellite communications are crucial to Ukrainian military coordination, particularly on the front lines. Any prolonged interruption could complicate communications between units and undermine operational effectiveness.
That dependence also gives Trump leverage as he presses Kyiv to pursue negotiations with Moscow.
Trump's approach could face resistance from Republicans in Congress who remain supportive of Ukraine and oppose pressuring Kyiv into a settlement that favors Russia.
Some lawmakers have argued that Washington should maintain support for Ukraine rather than allow Moscow to benefit from a weakening of Western assistance.
Zelenskyy's increasingly forceful responses to Trump carry risks, particularly given Washington's influence over Ukraine's military capabilities. But he may be betting that the balance of power in Congress could shift after the November midterm elections, making it more difficult for Trump to ease sanctions on Russia or further reduce assistance to Kyiv.
That is the assessment of Brett Bruen, a former foreign policy adviser in the Obama administration who heads the Global Situation Room consultancy.
Bruen said Zelenskyy understood the risks of confronting Trump but appeared less intimidated by the president's threats than during earlier clashes.
"Zelenskyy knows who he's dealing with," he said. "Trump's threats don't have the same kind of effect as they did when JD Vance tried to shame him in the Oval Office."
