Typhoon Champi could bring heavy rain to Taiwan later this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:19:33 UTC
21:19:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A sea warning for Typhoon Champi could be issued as early as Wednesday night, with a land warning possible Thursday, according to the Central Weather Administration.
The typhoon could have its greatest impact on Taiwan on Friday and Saturday, bringing heavy to torrential rain to central and northern Taiwan. Forecast models differ on its path, however, and the storm requires continued monitoring, per CNA.
CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng (劉沛滕) said Champi, the year’s 29th typhoon, was about 2,470 km southeast of Eluanbi on Sunday afternoon, moving west-northwest at 20 km per hour. Maximum sustained winds near its center reached 53 meters per second, with a 200 km radius for winds of at least 7 on the Beaufort scale.
Liu said the storm could approach eastern Taiwan as a strong typhoon, although some forecast models suggest it could make landfall in Hualien or Taitung. Its eventual path will depend partly on changes in the Pacific high-pressure system.
Some models indicate it could turn north before reaching Taiwan, while others suggest it could move farther south through the Bashi Channel.
Liu said the weather would remain relatively stable early in the week, with mostly cloudy to sunny skies and highs of 33–34 C in western Taiwan. As the northeast monsoon strengthens midweek, temperatures in northern and northeastern Taiwan are expected to fall, with scattered showers in some areas.
The typhoon’s outer circulation could bring heavier rain to central and northern Taiwan from Friday. Its subsequent movement and intensity remain uncertain, the CWA said.

====================================================================================================

Forty years on from the tragic killing of Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, activists call for renewed fight against the far right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

“For my brother Ahmed, British values meant standing up for others. It was doing right. It was supporting and looking after the underdog, whoever that may be, regardless of their colour or background,” Selina Ullah says, of the brother she lost to a senseless act of violence 40 years ago.
Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, a British Bengali schoolboy, was 13 when he was murdered in a racist attack in the playground of Burnage high school, in south Manchester, in 1986, after defending young pupils from bullying.
Ahmed’s murder – by a 13-year-old white British pupil who was sentenced to the youth equivalent of life, was a landmark moment. The Macdonald inquiry into the racism and racial violence in Manchester schools that surrounded Ahmed’s death sparked a national debate about antiracism in education.
Forty years on, Ahmed’s memory is at the heart of the Ahmed Iqbal Ullah RACE Centre (AIU), which houses archives on Black figures in Manchester, community history on events such as Manchester carnival, and pan-African activism in the city and beyond.
The 1970s concept of “political Blackness” – the idea of a strategic multiracial alliance across groups affected by racism – fell out of favour in the 1990s, as it became seen as an inadequate reflection of differing experiences.
But the story of AIU speaks to the power of solidarity across communities. Since it was founded in 1987 in Ahmed’s memory by Lou Kushnick, a Jewish-American professor at theUniversity of Manchester – with teacher Jackie Ould as its education co-ordinator – it has provided archivists, teachers and campaigners with the inspiration and resources to document under-recorded Black, antiracist and migration histories, fight social injustice and push for greater representation in education.
A memorial event, The Legacy of Ahmed: 40 years on, was held last month. It was attended by Ahmed’s family, AIU’s head, Maya Sharma, justice campaigners from 1986, including lawyer Robert Lizar, and a new generation of antiracism activists.
At the event it was argued that “political Blackness” – the framework in which AIU was founded – had a new relevance in the face of a resurgent far right.
Zara Manoehoetoe, a youth worker with Manchester antiracism organisation Kids of Colour, said: “Politically black is the note that we have to ground ourselves in, because anti-blackness manifests for all of us.
“We are working with young people from across Greater Manchester … The international context lives in their DNA, it lives in their homes, it lives at the kitchen table, it lives in the food that their mothers and their nanas are putting on their plates.”
The writer and film-maker Tariq Mehmood was a speaker on the panel alongside Manoehoetoe.
In 1986 Mehmood joined the justice campaign, spearheaded by Selina Ullah, which preceded the Macdonald inquiry.
Mehmood urged activists today to move offline and into grassroots organising across communities, amid a “continuing struggle” against racism in the UK and genocide in Gaza.
He added: “We were not victims [in the 1980s]. We educated ourselves. We organised youth movements. We organised workers’ organisations. That’s Indians, that’s Pakistanis, that’s Bangladeshis, that’s Africans, a whole plethora of anti-imperialist organisations … and in that context, we were Black.”
Prof Gus John, who served on the panel for the Macdonald inquiry and co-authored the book of the report, Murder in the Playground, was among speakers at the memorial event.
John said of the inquiry and the book: “What we were saying was it was important that schools have a responsibility to teach children and enable them to understand racism, how it operates in society and how they could be implicated in perpetuating it.
“Kenneth Baker [then education secretary] refused to accept the report, refused to raise the matter in parliament, and refused to put this book in the House of Commons library. Roll on 40 years … and every day, we hear more and more stories of racist incidents.”
Nika Muthra-Shah, the director of educational innovation at the Rekindle Collective, the Black-led supplementary schools programme, spoke of how young people are “feeling a lot of anger and a lot of fear about the rise of the far right”, and how the collective was countering it through youth empowerment, education in critical thinking and encouraging dialogue.
The memories of speakers who were at school with Ahmed highlighted how racism – and the fight against it – shape young lives.
From the audience at the memorial event Naeem, who was in the playground the day Ahmed was stabbed, said: “Ahmed was a very good friend. I was sometimes jealous of him because he used to wear the best clobber – Adidas tracksuits, like Run DMC!
“[When Ahmed was killed] we didn’t get any help or support from nobody, and we just got on with our life. After then, my life just deteriorated, I wasn’t bothered with school, I was fighting, I was suspended, I became racially abusive towards people. I turned my life around, [but] it’s always in my heart.”
Pervez Iqbal, who was a year older than Ahmed at Burnage High and part of the original justice campaign, was inspired by the tragedy to pursue a career in education.
He said: “We grew up very quickly when in reality we were still children who needed some guidance. Those experiences eventually gave me the determination to do something positive in my life. I studied, became a teacher and eventually I returned back to Burnage where I worked for 23 years.
“Schools and communities can change, education can change attitudes, and people working together can create something better for the next generation. My message for today is simple. Never forget Ahmed [or] our responsibility to educate, guide, and protect people.”
In October, Home Office figures revealed racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK. Police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132.

Hurricane threatens to bring flooding, mudslides to Mexico's Pacific Coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

Hurricane Trudy may bring "life-threatening" flooding, mudslides to Mexico's Pacific coast
Hurricane Trudy brought heavy rain and powerful winds to parts of Mexico's Pacific coast on Sunday, impacting sections of the country's western and southwestern states that were already targeted by Hurricane Simon last week. 
The National Hurricane Center, which is based in Miami, warned that hurricane and tropical storm conditions could materialize in areas under weather alerts Sunday morning and afternoon. The center also urged people in coastal regions of Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco to prepare for potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides as a result of the impending rain.
A hurricane warning remained in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. As of the hurricane center's latest update, issued in the early hours of Sunday, Trudy had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. The storm had strengthened into a major Category 3 hurricane as it tracked toward Mexico late last week, but it has since weakened.
On Sunday, Trudy was about 135 miles west-southwest of Manzanillo and moving northwest at 10 mph.
Trudy's center was expected to remain near the Mexican coast through Sunday evening before moving south of the Baja California Peninsula. A tropical storm warning remained in effect for Las Islas Marias. A warning for the coast east of Punta San Telmo to Lazaro Cardenas was discontinued.
The Mexican Navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.
Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.
Trudy was expected to bring 4 to 8 inches of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of around 12 inches along and near the coast in Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco. The hurricane center said areas with steep terrain were particularly vulnerable to serious flooding and mudslides.
Other Pacific storms
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Typhoon Champi was passing Guam as a massive super typhoon, with fierce winds strong enough to be classified as Category 4. It was getting farther away from the island on Sunday after traveling near Guam's southern tip, with sustained winds of 150 mph.
As of Sunday afternoon, local time, Champi was 200 miles west of Guam and moving westward at 14 mph, according to the National Weather Service.
The storm could strengthen into a Category 5 super typhoon early Monday local time. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while the tropical storm warning and typhoon watch for Tinian and Saipan were canceled.
The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday.
On Saturday, President Trump approved an emergency declaration for Guam authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate all federal disaster relief efforts. FEMA announced that federal disaster assistance was available for the territory of Guam to supplement local response efforts following Typhoon Champi.
Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from FEMA.
The territories are still recovering from super typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

The European Union has pledged €20 million ($23 million) in defense assistance to Nigeria’s armed forces to strengthen security cooperation and support efforts to tackle persistent insecurity across the country.

On regional security, Musa identified the shrinking Lake Chad Basin, which supports more than 50 million people, as a source of potential instability.
He said preventing terrorists from using islands in Lake Chad as operational bases remained a key priority for the Multinational Joint Task Force, which coordinates regional efforts against insurgency.
Musa also stressed that Nigeria’s disarmament, demobilization and reintegration program should prioritize victims of conflict, including military personnel affected by the insurgency.
Nigeria has battled a long-running insurgency in the northeast, alongside banditry, kidnappings and other forms of violence in different parts of the country.

On Feb. 1, 2023, the Russian government claimed that NATO’s entire network of satellites was working to support Ukraine’s war effort. In July 2025 the Kremlin complained to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Radio Regulations Board (RRB) that European nations were using navigation and broadcast satellites for both civil and military purposes to support Ukraine, warning that as a result these were considered to be legitimate targets for Russian countermeasures.
Axios said experts had identified in May this year several instances of Russian satellites “executing a series of concerning maneuvers” around the Finnish craft, which the US military repeatedly warned that Russia was developing anti-satellite weapons.
They suggested that Moscow would seek to disrupt the satellite’s ability to provide high-quality imagery of Russian sites during the war in Ukraine – which could include aggressive space-based actions.

Swiss court denies James Bond fan a silencer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:27:03 UTC
17:27:03 KST

Swiss court denies James Bond fan a silencer
A James Bond fan and gun collector from the canton of Solothurn has been refused a silencer. His love of the films was not deemed sufficient grounds for an exemption.
The man wanted to fit his Walther PPK pistol – familiar from the James Bond films – with a suitable silencer, as the Solothurn Administrative Court noted in a recently published judgement. In support of his application, the gun owner stated that he was a great fan of the famous spy films.
He already owned a gun of the same design as that used by the famous British spy. He now wished to purchase the appropriate accessory, as James Bond also fires with a silencer on the big screen, after all.
No recognised collection
The cantonal firearms office and the relevant department rejected the application. The film fan challenged this decision in court, citing his alleged hobby as a collector. He argued that, amongst other things, he collected film props and required the accessory to complement his hobby. He also argued subsequently that he needed the silencer for specific shooting training sessions.
More
James Bond: half-Swiss, totally profitable
However, the Solothurn judges did not accept this line of argument. Simply because someone accumulates numerous weapons does not make them a recognised collector within the meaning of the law. This requires a clear historical, technical or cultural purpose. A purely subjective enthusiasm for a cinema character is definitely not sufficient for this.
Safety comes before a love of films
Under Swiss firearms legislation, silencers are generally considered prohibited accessories. They reduce the noise of a gunshot and could thus make the work of law enforcement agencies in investigating crimes significantly more difficult. Exceptions are therefore handled extremely restrictively.
The court concluded that the public interest in safety outweighs the man’s private desire to own a weapon exactly as it appears in the film. The James Bond fan must now not only forgo his accessory but also pay court costs of CHF800 ($968). It is possible to appeal the ruling to the Federal Supreme Court.

====================================================================================================

Russian satellite shadows radar sat used by Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:23:25 UTC
17:23:25 KST

- Russia’s Kosmos 2612 maneuvered on Oct. 16 and is holding position within about 5 km of commercial radar satellite ICEYE-X36, tracking data shows.
- Tracker Jonathan McDowell said it may be the first LEO rendezvous of two active satellites without one owner’s approval.
A Russian military satellite has maneuvered to within about 5 km (3 miles) of a commercial radar imaging satellite owned by ICEYE and appears to be holding position there, in what independent tracker Jonathan McDowell said may be the first rendezvous in low Earth orbit between two active satellites without the consent of one of the owners.
McDowell, an astrophysicist who tracks spacecraft using public orbital data, wrote on X that new tracking data showed Kosmos 2612 made a maneuver on Oct. 16 and was now station-keeping close to ICEYE-X36. He cautioned that he was still waiting for more tracking data to confirm it.
“New TLEs show that K2612 made a manuever on Oct 16 and is now stationkeeping within 5 km or less of ICEYE X36. To my knowledge this is the first LEO rendezvous of two active satellites where the owner of one of the sats did not give approval,” McDowell wrote.
He said the move looked like an unprecedented step by Russia if confirmed, but added that he did not think it quite violated the Outer Space Treaty, noting that he is not a lawyer.
Space tracking company LeoLabs told Axios that the Russian satellite’s movement appeared to be a deliberate approach and that, as of Oct. 17, Kosmos 2612 was roughly three miles from ICEYE-X36. ICEYE declined to comment, and the satellite is tied to the company’s U.S. arm, ICEYE US.
ICEYE, a Finnish-founded company, operates a fleet of small synthetic aperture radar satellites, which can image the ground at night and through clouds. Ukraine has used ICEYE imagery since 2022, including from a satellite bought with crowdfunded donations, and a Ukrainian official told Axios that the military works with the company but could not say whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports Ukraine.
Kosmos 2612 is one of six Russian military satellites launched on a Soyuz-2.1b rocket from the Plesetsk cosmodrome in April 2026, a launch The Defence Blog reported at the time. In May, five of those satellites carried out fuel-hungry maneuvers to shift their orbits into the same plane as ICEYE-X36, and one passed within about 2.5 km of it on May 26, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies. ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski later told Reuters the company had moved its satellite in response.
Trackers then watched Kosmos 2612 set up a closer approach. Around Oct. 12, analysts saw it make a single burn that put it back at nearly the same altitude, inclination and orbital plane as ICEYE-X36, trailing the commercial satellite by roughly 475 km (295 miles) and slowly catching up, before the Oct. 16 maneuver brought it alongside.
Russia has a history of parking its satellites near other countries’ spacecraft. In 2020, Kosmos 2542 and its subsatellite Kosmos 2543 trailed a U.S. government reconnaissance satellite, prompting public complaints from U.S. Space Command, and Russia has tested a projectile fired from one of its own satellites. Analysts say a satellite this close could photograph, monitor or potentially interfere with its target, though the purpose of Kosmos 2612 is not publicly known.

Türkiye’s carpet industry generated $2.017 billion in export revenue from shipments totaling 391.984 million square meters to 186 countries and free zones in the first nine months of 2026, according to data compiled from the Turkish Exporters Assembly (TİM).
Machine-made carpets accounted for the largest share of exports, bringing in $1.56 billion during the period. They were followed by tufted carpets with $352 million, handmade carpets with $92.2 million and kilims with $10.1 million.

The United States remained the largest single export destination, with sales rising 16.6 percent year-on-year to $448 million. It was followed by Saudi Arabia, where exports rose 9.4 percent to $181.3 million and the United Kingdom, where exports increased 23.4 percent to $114.2 million.
İskender Kaplan, chair of the carpet sector board of TİM, said exports had remained at last year’s levels despite global challenges.
Kaplan said raw materials, commodities and logistics issues had weighed on export performance and kept the industry from meeting its growth targets. He noted that conflicts affecting the Strait of Hormuz region and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine war had limited export growth.
He added that the sector had initially targeted $3.5 billion in exports for 2026 but later revised that goal downward because of logistical disruptions and rising transportation costs.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Indian-controlled Kashmir's traditional musical instrument makers strive to keep vanishing craft alive
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
20:06:13 CST
21:06:13 KST

by Peerzada Arshad Hamid
NEW DELHI, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Inside the courtyard workshop of his two-story home, Mushtaq Ahmad Dar examines each chisel with meticulous attention. Holding one in his left hand, he runs his right index finger along the bevel, then reaches into a water-filled jug for a soaking whetstone. He hones the blade until a faint smile crosses his face, then braces another dull chisel and rubs it steadily across the stone.
"My father says that it is always the tools that work wonders," said Dar, a traditional Kashmiri musical instrument maker.
At 10 a.m., his apprentice places a half-done Kashmiri rabab, an ancient, plectrum-plucked stringed instrument carved from a single piece of mulberry wood, before him. Dar drives a sharpened chisel into the wood, hammering its butt with his adze as shavings curl away, gradually shaping the rabab's deep, concave bowl.
Dar tells Xinhua that he learned the craft as a boy from his father, continuing a tradition dating back to his grandfather, a locally renowned singer.
"Not only am I, but my three brothers are also well-versed in the craft," Dar said. "We live in a joint family, and I am hopeful our children too will carry forward this legacy."
Among his brothers, Dar has perfected the skill and now often discusses the instruments' intricacies with clients on behalf of his father, who, because of his advanced age, can no longer devote himself fully to the trade.
At Dar's workshop in Budgam district, a 25-minute drive northwest of Srinagar city, the summer capital of Indian-controlled Kashmir, traditional string instruments, including the rabab, santoor, sarangi, Kashmiri sitar, and Sikh rabab, are being made.
Dar spends months crafting a single instrument, carefully selecting mulberry and walnut wood and prioritizing quality over speed. His instruments are in demand across India.
"For most of the instruments, we use mulberry wood, but for santoor, we use walnut wood," he said. "I am lucky enough that I have a good clientele. This craft has given us everything we have today. People place orders at my workshop in advance for the instruments of their choice."
"The music runs in our blood, as our forefathers have been associated with it for generations," he said. "I know how to play every instrument that I make. These objects communicate with me."
Dar is seen as one of the torchbearers of a craft many feared would die with the Indian-controlled Kashmir's last santoor maker, 85-year-old Ghulam Mohamed Zaz of Srinagar.
Surrounded by the vibrant walls of his room, Zaz ran his frail fingers across the sharp edges of a newly fashioned, trapezoidal box of walnut wood. He checked its precision with a scale, his movements slow and deliberate.
"A craft doesn't simply die -- it endures," he said. "What kills a craft is the flood of fakes and inferior copies replacing the authentic work. I hold the line for this art today, but I do not know who will carry it into tomorrow."
He is the last of the eighth generation in his family to carve the classical instrument and claims that all the acclaimed artists of the region played on the santoors made by them.
The word santoor in Persian means "a hundred strings." The traditional Kashmiri santoor typically has 100 strings. Worldwide, santoor varieties differ mostly in their string count.
In his uptown Srinagar office, Nazir Ganaie, the founder of Kashmir Rabab Academy, an institute that works to preserve the region's musical heritage, is busy putting the final touches on an upcoming concert schedule. The event offers a rare chance to hear a performance played entirely on traditional Kashmiri instruments.
Driven by a passion to protect these indigenous folk traditions, Ganaie built this platform to bring local artists together and showcase their talents.
"For me, the rabab is not merely a musical instrument. It is an emotion deeply etched into our collective soul. The moment I strike its strings, I am transported to the mountains and valleys of Kashmir, where every note carries a story, a memory and a sense of belonging," Ganaie said.
His love for playing the Kashmiri rabab took him to Dar some years back to place an order in bulk for Kashmiri handmade rababs.
Ganaie often visits Indian-controlled Kashmir's master instrument makers to chronicle their personal histories and the resilient spirit driving them to preserve their craft.
"Today Kashmiri rabab, santoor, and sarangi stand distinct from their global counterparts," said Muzaffar Ahmad Bhat, a Srinagar-based musicologist. "They are now deeply woven into the region's folklore, defining the vibrant rhythm of folk songs and the spiritual depth of classical Sufiana Mausiqi, a centuries-old classical choral ensemble music. Far more than mere tools for performance, these instruments have become inseparable fragments of Kashmiri society, culture, and identity."
The traditional craftsmanship required to make these instruments is rapidly vanishing. At the heart of this decline is the loss of aging master craftsmen, with few apprentices stepping up to fill the void.
"Low financial returns and shrinking demand make it difficult for remaining artisans to earn a living. Ultimately, the shift toward electronic music and cheap, machine-made instruments has severely threatened a legacy that once thrived on human hands," he said.
Ganaie, however, feels the internet and social media have opened up avenues for the musicians as well as makers of the musical instruments to keep the art thriving and prevent it from vanishing into the thin air.
"It is heartening to see rabab and santoor makers and other traditional instrument artisans finding renewed hope as online orders and social media open up new markets for their craft. The growing visibility of these instruments in major productions of Bollywood and music platforms has also helped introduce the region's rich musical heritage to wider national and international audiences," he said.
Meanwhile, a young musical instrument maker Altaf Ahmad Sheikh is hard at work in another Srinagar neighborhood. His hands steady, engraving delicate floral and foliage designs that weave gracefully between the bird motifs on a sarangi. The design has transformed a plain wooden instrument into an ornate work of art.
He has spent months crafting this sarangi, an instrument that represents not just his devotion to the craft, but his very livelihood.
Sheikh, a school dropout, learned the craft from his father, a renowned sarangi maker.
"I am striving hard to keep the craft alive," Sheikh said as his young son sat in front of him, perhaps trying to imbibe the skill. ■

Araghchi emphasized that Iran will not bow to threats and is prepared to defend itself, while remaining ready to pursue diplomacy.
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts.

Montenegrin president meets Chinese FM

CETINJE, Montenegro, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Montenegrin President Jakov Milatovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Cetinje, a city near Montenegro's capital, Podgorica, on Saturday, expressing Montenegro's willingness to deepen friendly relations and practical cooperation with China.
Milatovic asked Wang to convey his sincere greetings to Chinese President Xi Jinping, and welcomed the first-ever visit by a Chinese foreign minister to Montenegro.
Noting that this year marks the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Montenegro and China, Milatovic said the visit holds important symbolic significance.
Recalling his experience studying in China, Milatovic said he had gained a deeper understanding of China's economic and social development and the lives of its people, as well as the importance of cooperation with China.
Noting that European Union (EU) accession is currently a priority on Montenegro's foreign policy agenda, Milatovic said the country also attaches great importance to relations with China, with Montenegro firmly adhering to the one-China principle and remaining committed to friendly and mutually beneficial cooperation with China.
Over the past two decades, Montenegro-China relations have made significant progress across various fields, with infrastructure, economic and trade, and tourism emerging as three key areas, he said.
Earlier this year, Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic and Chinese Premier Li Qiang reached important consensus on further deepening cooperation during their meeting in China, Milatovic said, adding that Montenegro looks forward to maintaining political dialogue and deepening practical cooperation with China based on mutual respect, so as to bring greater benefits to the two peoples.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, conveyed Xi's cordial greetings to Milatovic, saying that despite the geographical distance, China and Montenegro have always respected each other and treated each other as equals, setting an example of friendly exchanges between countries of different sizes.
Wang said China appreciates Milatovic's rational and objective understanding of China and his active efforts to promote bilateral relations.
He said China has consistently maintained that all countries, big or small, are equal, and has always followed the path of partnership over alliance and dialogue over confrontation.
China appreciates Montenegro's firm adherence to the one-China principle, respects the path and governance model chosen by the Montenegrin people, and stands ready to be a reliable and trustworthy partner of Montenegro, he added.
Wang said China has engaged in practical cooperation with Montenegro in good faith, delivering tangible results. Describing Montenegro's north-south expressway as a landmark project of historic significance, he called on both sides to ensure the high-quality completion of its second phase.
Montenegro enjoys unique tourism resources and has a historical tradition of anti-fascism, Wang said, adding that China is helping restore the Tara River Bridge, which was featured in the famous Yugoslav film "The Bridge," and that more Chinese tourists are expected to visit Montenegro.
Wang said the two sides should take the 20th anniversary of diplomatic relations this year as an opportunity to review successful cooperation, jointly discuss ways to elevate bilateral relations to a higher level, explore new areas of cooperation, and build an even brighter next 20 years.
On China-EU relations, Wang said China and the EU are comprehensive strategic partners and their relations have remained generally sound and stable.
China has always maintained that China and the EU are partners, not rivals, he said, noting that differences over economic and trade issues, which have emerged amid increasingly closer cooperation, can be resolved through dialogue and should not affect the overall development of China-EU relations.
Wang said China understands Montenegro's efforts to join the EU and its choice to pursue European integration, noting that the process is fully compatible with deeper cooperation with China.
China believes Montenegro will become another good friend of China within the EU after its accession, and hopes Montenegro will play a unique and important role in promoting regional peace and stability and advancing China-EU relations, Wang said.
The two sides also exchanged views on international and regional issues of mutual concern, including the Ukraine crisis.
Before the meeting, Milatovic and Wang jointly visited a photo exhibition marking the 20th anniversary of China-Montenegro diplomatic relations.
During his visit, Wang also met with Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic and held talks with Montenegrin Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ervin Ibrahimovic. ■

Simulated diplomacy and economic pressure

Both Zelensky and Sybiha have warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets injects direct hard currency into the Russian state budget during active military operations, validating the Kremlin’s calculation that its war effort is yielding economic dividends rather than consequences.

11:55:21 UTC
20:55:21 KST

Russia has kept striking Ukraine’s energy sector throughout the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 18 October. From overnight into Sunday, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit substations, homes, and industrial sites from Odesa to Volyn. They killed civilians and left tens of thousands of families without power.
Russia fights along the front line while hitting cities and the grid behind it with drones, missiles, and glide bombs. Ukraine says Moscow plans up to 1,000 such munitions against 60 key infrastructure sites this winter, and jet-powered drones partly free it to concentrate missiles on fewer targets, the Institute for the Study of War assessed. With Graham Act penalties on hold and US sanctions on Russian diesel suspended, Russia faces no new US cost for its strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Protecting and restoring the grid falls to Ukraine’s air defenses and repair crews.
Russia hit energy sites 76 times in a week
Zelenskyy counted 76 deliberate Russian strikes on energy and oil-and-gas facilities since Trump’s announcement. Overnight, Russia hit substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa oblasts, he said. In the past week, Russia fired almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, mainly to cause a blackout. His message was aimed at Washington.
“America must see that Russia is not taking steps in return for the lifting of sanctions or deals. On the contrary, they take every signal that they can make money as proof that their bet on war is working and they can keep fighting,” Zelenskyy wrote.
22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
Overnight, Russia launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile and 180 Shahed-type drones, 26 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 152 drones, but strikes hit 20 locations.
Power cuts from Odesa to Ternopil
Strikes left about 24,000 consumers in Odesa Oblast without power, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. In Vinnytsia Oblast, the attack damaged critical infrastructure and forced emergency outages, oblast head Natalia Zabolotna wrote. Drones hit three energy facilities in Ternopil Oblast, one of them for the second time, and cut power to some consumers, oblast head Taras Pastukh said.
Civilians killed and injured
A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed a 27-year-old woman and injured two others, including a 16-year-old, the State Emergency Service reported. In Poltava, an evening attack killed one person, injured four, and damaged 10 detached houses, city council secretary Kateryna Yamshchykova said.
Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel
A drone hit a high-rise in Odesa and set its roof on fire. A 13-year-old girl was hurt, city military administration head Serhii Lysak said, and Kiper put the number of injured at two.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and artillery injured three people, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven civilians on Saturday, six of them in Sloviansk, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Fires in the west, alerts across the border
A morning drone strike set warehouse and production buildings ablaze at an enterprise in Manevychi, Volyn Oblast, oblast head Roman Romaniuk said. With heavy smoke blowing toward the town, Romaniuk urged residents to stay indoors, shut windows and doors, and switch off ventilation. A repeat strike set an enterprise in the district on fire again, the State Emergency Service said, adding that air tests found no dangerous concentrations outside the site. In Lviv Oblast, drone debris damaged a logistics warehouse and two houses, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
Polish military aircraft operated in Poland’s airspace twice during the attack, as the Government Security Centre warned residents of Lublin Voivodeship and later alerted Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In Lithuania, NATO jets failed to identify an object that apparently entered from Poland, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
A ceasefire Moscow never confirmed
Trump announced the energy ceasefire on 11 October, news that surprised Zelenskyy. A White House official said Russia was still weighing it. Hours later, Russia hit a Kharkiv power plant, and on 14 October it fired 39 ballistic missiles at the grid. Then Trump waived Graham Act penalties on buyers of Russian oil, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration wants 60 days to weigh the economic effects.

Midterm melee: Americans in the Netherlands gear up to vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:55:18 UTC
20:55:18 KST

Midterm melee: Americans in the Netherlands gear up to vote
Brandon Hartley
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Americans living abroad can often feel like they’re stuck on the political sidelines of their native land. With one of the most contentious midterm elections in US history coming up next month, we spoke with the Netherlands’ American community about how they’re getting involved in the race and the challenges they face.
For the past two years, Donald Trump has dominated headlines around the world. It seems like there’s little the divisive president and his administration haven’t disrupted within and well beyond US borders.
There’s no denying that much is riding on the country’s midterms on November 3 and that the result will have a defining impact on the course of global politics over the next few years.
As with prior elections, Americans living in the Netherlands may feel there’s little they can do besides mail in their absentee ballots – and even that is an often complicated process that many fail to complete.
Each state sets its own deadlines and decides whether ballots can go back by email, fax or post. A ballot posted from the Netherlands also has to cross the Atlantic in time to be counted.
Some don’t bother at all, and some feel they shouldn’t. “One of the reasons why many in the Netherlands don’t vote is because they’ve been here for a very long time,” said Tre’ Shawn Griffin-Noordermeer, vice chair of the Netherlands chapter of Democrats Abroad. “They feel like they shouldn’t be voting because they’ve lived outside the US for so long.”
In fact, federal law lets US citizens abroad keep voting in federal elections in the state where they last lived, however long they have been away.
To help get that message out, various groups here have been volunteering and hosting events in the days leading up to the midterms.
Reaching out to voters
Members of campaign group Democrats Abroad in the Netherlands have spent recent weeks running an email campaign and arranging “Vote From Abroad” gatherings on Zoom.
They’ve also been hosting lunches and other events in cities around the country to discuss the midterms along with putting up fliers and getting the word out on social media and via phone banking.
“We’ve got hundreds of volunteers here in the Netherlands who have been helping with this,” Griffin-Noordermeer told Dutch News. “A few weekends ago, we called over 13,000 people.”
Originally founded in 1964, Democrats Abroad serves as the Democratic party’s official organisation for American citizens living overseas. One of its primary tasks is encouraging its members and other voters, who are spread across 197 countries, to cast their ballots.
And that’s more difficult than it might seem.
Counting the voters
Nobody knows exactly how many Americans in the Netherlands can vote. The US does not require citizens to register with the government when they move abroad, and some states drop overseas voters from their rolls when they stop responding to election mail. That leaves neither the State Department nor voter lists with a reliable count.
The national statistics office CBS puts the number of US nationals living in the Netherlands at just over 27,000 in 2026 – though not all are old enough to vote, and Dutch-Americans with both passports are counted as Dutch, so aren’t included.
Worldwide, about 2.2 million Americans of voting age live abroad, according to the Federal Voting Assistance Program (FVAP), the US defence department office that helps military and overseas citizens vote. FVAP estimates only about 11% of them voted in the 2024 presidential election. Even fewer typically take part in midterms.
FVAP says 14.8% of eligible voters in Europe voted in 2024.
Preparing for the worst
Despite Trump’s low approval ratings, the path to a “blue wave” for the Democrats won’t necessarily be an easy one.
His administration also continues to meddle with the midterms. In August, the Pentagon, which runs FVAP, made last-minute changes to the Federal Post Card Application (the form overseas voters use to register and request ballots), removing the checkbox for US citizens who were born abroad and have never lived in the US. The Democratic National Committee has gone to court over the change.
That followed a March 2025 executive order in which Trump sought to add proof-of-citizenship requirements to the same form, parts of which federal courts have blocked. The order also aimed to stop states counting mail ballots that arrive after Election Day.
In June, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that states can keep counting ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrive later. That matters for voters whose ballots travel by international post.
Hayley Hughes, the co-founder of the Netherlands chapter of Indivisible, admitted she’s worried about how things might go.
She has already had discussions with the leads of other chapters about what to do if the administration interferes with ballot counts or sends government agents to polling stations.
Trump has said Republicans should “take over the voting” in at least 15 places, and his former adviser Steve Bannon has welcomed the idea of immigration agents at the polls.
“We’re already thinking we might have to mobilise,” Hughes told Dutch News.
“We’re looking at a protest here that week, if needed. In the US, there could be a mass mobilisation of peaceful protests and a general strike where people don’t go to work or school. We all hope that won’t be needed.”
The week of the midterms
Several midterm events are scheduled for the week of the elections. The Atlantische Commissie in The Hague is hosting an “American midterm election breakfast” on 4 November.
In Amsterdam, the commission is also helping with the John Adams Institute’s “Midterm Madness” event on November 6. It’s set to serve as an afterparty with a ‘festival-style experience’ featuring live music along with discussions and lectures about the results featuring Mark Leibovich, a staff writer at The Atlantic, and others.
Comedian Greg Shapiro is once again teaming up with Pep Rosenfeld for an Election Night Party at Boom Chicago. They’ve hosted these events since the ‘00s and are once again prepared to stay up late. The comedy club has vowed to remain open past 4:00 “if things get crazy.”
“How late, well, we’ll wait and see,” Shapiro told Dutch News. “I’ve got performances the next day. At some point I’ll have to get some sleep.”
Shapiro will be taking a break from his ongoing ‘KING ME: 250 Years of Donald Trump’ comedy tour for the Boom Chicago gathering. He’s worried about how much rewriting he’ll have to do for subsequent performances after the midterms.
“There’s no telling what could happen,” he said. “It could become January 6th on a national scale.”
If you’re an American living overseas and haven’t voted yet, there could still be time based on where you’re registered. Visit votefromabroad.org for further assistance.

There is increased discussion about how Israel might help Saudi Arabia against the Iranian-backed Houthis. If there is help, how might it take shape, and what might be most effective?
This also comes in the context of questions about whether Saudi Arabia will join the Abraham Accords. Questions about this have persisted since the Accords began in 2020. However, Riyadh has taken a wait-and-see approach, preferring that Israel make positive moves on the Palestinian issue.
US President Donald Trump has said that Saudi Arabia may be accepting help from Israel. Asked about whether he thought Saudi Arabia might normalize ties with Israel, he said, “I do, I think they will. Israel’s been very helpful to Saudi Arabia.” The comments come days after Saudi Arabia appeared to downplay whether Israel would support them.
This comes in the context of the Houthis increasing attacks on Saudi Arabia. The US has not joined the fighting but may be supporting the Saudis in various ways, such as via intelligence. The US has so far chosen not to join strikes on the Houthis. The Trump administration carried out strikes on the Houthis in March and April 2025. The administration eventually concluded that it was better to do a deal with the Houthis than continue strikes.

Pope Leo says he will "gradually resume my activities" after cancer surgery
Pope Leo XIV thanked thousands of faithful in St. Peter's Square on Sunday for their prayers while he was hospitalized for an operation to remove a malignant tumor, and said he plans to gradually return to his usual duties.
The crowd erupted in cheers when the pontiff showed himself in the window overlooking the square, where a week ago on the same occasion of the traditional Angelus blessing he revealed that a nodule had been located on his lung, and that it would be surgically removed.
''Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers," Leo said, his voice sounding strong four days after the lower lobe of his right lung was removed.
"This experience has made me feel particularly close to all those who are living with illness or infirmity," the pope said.
He told the crowd that he had ''truly felt your support,'' and expressed ''particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and all the staff at Gemelli Hospital," where he was treated.
The pope paused for a moment and waved to the crowd before retreating into his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.
A delegation from Africa in Rome for a congress danced and ululated after the pope's blessing.
''He was always in our prayers when he was sick, and we are happy to see him today,″ said Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of Congo. ″This is an expression of our joy.″
The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
He told a reporter in English that he was doing ''much better'' as he drove away from Rome's Gemelli Hospital to return to the Vatican, after a shorter hospital stay than had initially been anticipated. He was discharged Saturday after the four-day stay. No information about his prognosis has been publicly shared.
"I don't believe it, because he was just operated on the other day," said Cosimo Mastrocinque, a retired factory worker visiting the Vatican from the southern region of Puglia. "It is a miracle that he recovered already."
American tourists were especially eager to pray alongside the first pope born in the United States. Marla Marsala of Michigan was supposed to attend a Mass with the pope last week that was canceled due to his hospitalization.
''I am just happy that we are praying with him today instead of for him, like we were before,'' Marsala said. "It was a tough week for all of the people who love him, which are many. He seems like a very strong soul. So I think he will pull through and fight it, and succeed and keep doing the wonderful work he is doing.''
Claire Holland from Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt "very blessed" to be present for the pope's return to his flock.
"I'm so happy that he has recovered so quickly. I think there have been millions and millions of prayers. And he is a strong, determined man, and I am so happy that he is feeling well enough to do this," Holland said.
Leo's next major engagement is an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News on Saturday that "there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place."
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.

The initiative has encountered firm opposition across European capitals, particularly in Germany, where officials warn that reviving reliance on Russian hydrocarbons undermines continental energy security.
American negotiators argue that restoring Russian pipeline flows to Europe would provide the Kremlin with a commercial incentive to halt military operations, while generating valuable transit revenues for Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction. German pushback and Berlin security warnings
The prospect of restoring Russian pipeline supplies has provoked decisive resistance in Berlin, formerly the largest purchaser of Russian natural gas in Europe prior to the February 2022 full-scale invasion.

German officials emphasized that Russian gas remains Russian regardless of whether transactions are structured through intermediary traders or third-party brokers.
Former German Economy Minister Robert Habeck warned against repeating past strategic mistakes, emphasizing that Germany has fundamentally adapted its energy architecture away from Moscow.
“Europe, and especially Germany, must never again become dependent on Russian gas. We saw how unreliable Russia was,” Habeck stated.
The diplomatic friction unfolds against intense domestic political debate within Germany. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has polled near 30 percent in recent nationwide surveys, has campaigned heavily on restoring direct imports of cheap Russian gas to curb consumer inflation and lower industrial electricity tariffs.
German and European officials maintain that restoring energy flows to the Kremlin would undermine European sanctions packages and generate billions of dollars in hard currency that underwrite Moscow’s defense industry, complicating ongoing transatlantic negotiations over post-war security frameworks.

Janno Jakobson: Speaking Estonian not the same as teaching Estonian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:21:00 UTC
20:21:00 KST

Janno Jakobson: Speaking Estonian not the same as teaching Estonian
Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background, but teachers can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide, writes Janno Jakobson.
The transition to Estonian-language education is one of the most significant changes in Estonia's education system. No one questions its necessity anymore, but are we, as adults, prepared to make enough of an effort to ensure its success? We are demanding increasingly better Estonian-language skills from students learning Estonian as a second language, but are we also creating the conditions they need to achieve this?
In discussions with colleagues from different schools, one point keeps coming up: The problem is not always a lack of skills among teachers, but rather how existing knowledge and skills are applied in everyday teaching.
Imagine a student who spends an entire school day in Estonian-language classes. The teacher speaks Estonian, the textbooks are in Estonian and the student completes exercises in a workbook. By the end of the day, however, the student has spoken only a handful of sentences in Estonian. Does such a school day do enough to support the student's language development?
To acquire a language, students must have opportunities to speak, ask questions, describe, explain their reasoning and make mistakes. Teaching subjects in Estonian requires teachers to set language-learning objectives alongside subject-specific goals and create opportunities to achieve them. Many teachers already have the methodological knowledge needed to do this. Yet when explaining more complex concepts, it may seem easier to switch to Russian. Students understand the material more quickly and the lesson can move forward.
But what happens when a teacher explains an entire topic in the students' native language, while the quiz or test must be completed in Estonian? Can we expect students to achieve a passing grade if they have not been taught the relevant Estonian vocabulary or given opportunities to use it?
In such cases, students may understand the subject matter perfectly well but struggle to understand the questions or formulate their answers. A poor result may therefore indicate a mismatch between the language of instruction and the language of assessment.
Are we grading knowledge of language proficiency?
Recent fourth-grade national assessments highlighted a contradiction in our education system. While the assessment of Estonian as a second language takes students' expected language proficiency into account, the same students faced significantly more complex vocabulary, lengthy texts and multipart questions in the natural science assessment.
Commenting on the linguistic complexity of the assessments, the Education and Youth Board (Harno) explained that the tasks are aligned with the curriculum and use the same terminology. If students' Estonian-language skills are insufficient, the agency recommends choosing the Russian-language assessment.
However, the Harno representative fails to consider that the students who took the natural science assessment have been studying subjects, including natural science, in Estonian for three years and may not even be familiar with the relevant terminology in Russian. I must admit that such a response is frustrating for teachers. Is recommending a Russian-language assessment really the solution to the challenges of transitioning to Estonian-language education?
Of course, students must also acquire subject-specific terminology in Estonian, but fair assessment means giving them an opportunity to demonstrate their actual knowledge and skills. That is precisely why, rather than simply recommending a switch of languages, we should also seek ways to make assessments in Estonian linguistically accessible to students.
Students cannot be responsible for adults' choices
A range of support measures have been established to facilitate the transition to Estonian-language education. Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) methodology centers operate at educational institutions, the Institute of the Estonian Language provides support through initiatives including the "Keelesamm" program and teachers in Tallinn can turn to the Tallinn Teachers' House and its methodology and competence center, MEKK. Teachers can attend training courses, receive guidance, explore teaching materials and learn from their colleagues' experiences. However, no trainer or methodology center can put what teachers have learned into practice in the classroom for them.
School leadership also has an important role to play. Schools must have a shared understanding of what Estonian-language education means and what principles should guide it. It is not enough for some teachers to consciously create an Estonian-language learning environment if others consistently switch to Russian during their lessons. Nor can the state's responsibility be limited to setting requirements. We need meaningful oversight that assesses whether Estonian-language education is actually working in practice.
Discussions about the transition to Estonian-language education often focus on students' lack of motivation, the language environment at home and parents' attitudes. These factors affect learning, but they cannot justify prejudging students' abilities.
Students do not choose their parents, the language spoken at home or their socioeconomic background. Teachers, however, can choose how they support students and what learning opportunities they provide. Students learning Estonian as a second language do not need lower expectations. They need high-quality teaching, consistent language support and teachers who believe in their abilities.
The transition to Estonian-language education is not simply about changing the language of instruction. Its goal must be to equip students with sufficient Estonian-language proficiency to continue their education, pursue their chosen field of study and compete on an equal footing with others in the future.
Achieving this requires effort from everyone involved. Students have a duty to learn, teachers have a responsibility to teach with clear intent, school leaders must establish shared principles and the state must ensure realistic expectations and meaningful oversight.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Albanian PM says mass protests a threat to EU membership, not government
TIRANA, Oct 18 - Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Sunday rejected calls to step down from growing street protests, and said they were a threat not to his government but to Albania's progress toward joining the European Union.
Student-led demonstrations, fuelled by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, have engulfed central Tirana and spread to other cities in the past week.
Demonstrators demanding Rama's resignation have set fire to government buildings as well as banks and pulled up paving stones to throw at police, who have responded with tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets.
The unrest, which followed months of largely peaceful protests in the summer against a luxury coastal development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, pose the biggest challenge yet to Rama, who has governed since 2013 and last year won a fourth term in office.
"I am not being challenged, the government is not being challenged, a government majority or a winning party in the elections is not being challenged but a path is being challenged, a mission is being challenged," Rama said in a live address on Facebook.
“Albanians need to think very clearly: Do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
As Rama spoke, excavators were digging up and removing the paving outside his office in central Tirana as a new round of protests was expected.
Corruption scandals have tarnished Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.
However, Rama has said his government is tackling corruption as never before. Along with Montenegro, Albania is currently leading the posse of Balkan countries seeking to join the EU, and is aiming for entry by 2030.
Rama blamed unspecified foreign interests for the protests and for what he said was an attempted drone attack at his office this week.
"God knows what the consequences will be. There are no young people, no students, and no minors who would even think of implementing this plan. This is a foreign hand," he said.

Red flag warnings have also prompted utility provider Southern California Edison to implement public safety power shutoffs, leaving more than 90,000 residents in Los Angeles and Ventura counties without electricity.
A heat advisory remains in effect across parts of Southern California through Saturday evening as firefighters race to contain the multiple blazes threatening communities across the region.

New incident at Leipzig Airport: Fence rammed near Russian cargo aircraft
Kyiv • UNN
An unknown vehicle damaged the fence at Leipzig/Halle Airport near Russian An-124s. The camera was switched off, and the police did not find the vehicle.
In Germany, unknown individuals rammed through the fence of Leipzig Airport near Russian cargo aircraft. The surveillance camera did not record the damage to the Leipzig Airport fence—it was switched off, reports UNN, citing Bild.
Details
As BILD has learned, at Leipzig/Halle Airport, unknown individuals, apparently in a vehicle, broke through the fence near the parking area for Russian An-124 cargo aircraft. The damage was discovered the previous evening at around 11:00 p.m. After the incident, the northern runway was closed and flights were redirected to the southern one.
Federal and state police officers arrived at the scene. The airport grounds were searched, but neither the vehicle nor any outsiders could be found.
According to police spokesperson Theresa Leverenz, the theory that a vehicle rammed the fence is considered the most likely. Three Russian An-124s have been at the airport since 2022 and cannot take off because of European Union sanctions.
In addition
At Leipzig/Halle Airport, the camera installed near the site where the fence was damaged did not record what happened because it was switched off. Late in the evening of October 17, an unidentified vehicle apparently rammed the airport fence; however, according to BILD, police have still found neither the vehicle nor any outsiders.
Airport representatives explained that the 360-degree camera installed in this area is intended not for continuous security surveillance, but to monitor aircraft movements. It is switched on manually only when necessary.
According to the administration, the airport complies with all aviation security requirements, but providing round-the-clock video surveillance along the entire 40-kilometre perimeter is difficult. At the same time, three Russian An-124 cargo aircraft are parked approximately 1.7 kilometres from the scene; they have been prohibited from taking off since 2022 because of EU sanctions.
Context
This is not the first incident at Leipzig Airport. At the beginning of August, a drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. German authorities blamed Russia for the alleged attempted attack and warned of the threat of further hybrid attacks on critical infrastructure. Moscow rejected the accusations.

JPMorgan Chase Bank subsidiary discriminated against conservative customers, US investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:55:29 UTC
19:55:29 KST

A JPMorgan Chase Bank subsidiary was found to have discriminated against political conservatives, according to a statement by the US Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) on Wednesday, alongside the release of its supervisory review of nine US banks following accusations that they were "debanking" customers for political or religious reasons.
Debanking refers to the limiting or refusal of services to a bank customer, such as closing accounts or refusing loans. While not inherently illegal, debanking becomes controversial when a bank's decisions are based on factors such as politics or religion rather than on an individual's financial or compliance risks.
Although not a judicial ruling, the review, conducted under US President Donald Trump's August 2025 executive order, "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans," aimed to identify and document specific instances the Trump administration would view as violations of the order.
The review examined nearly 100,000 complaints between 2020 and 2025 and over 50,000 documents; additionally, it targeted Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, US Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank, which, together with JPMorgan Chase, make up the nine largest banks under OCC supervision.
The findings showed multiple discriminatory practices at several banks, with JPMorgan Chase subsidiary WePay Inc. having closed accounts associated with pro-Trump merchandise, such as MAGA hats, which were categorized by the bank as hateful and intolerant.
In a September 2021 case, WePay closed a conservative customer's account after the subsidiary flagged items the customer was selling, including a Trump election-victory flag and a shirt describing former US President Joe Biden as illegitimate.
In an additional 2021 incident, the subsidiary initially halted payment processing for an event after the organizer's social media posts were found to include descriptions of Biden and former US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director Dr. Anthony Fauci as enemies, though the decision was eventually reversed.
Also in 2021, WePay closed a nonprofit's account after discovering its positions on LGBTQ issues, with bank employees describing the "right-wing religious conservative" organization as having "strong anti-LGBTQ rhetoric."
WePay shut down following findings, JPMorgan spokesperson says
A JPMorgan spokesperson responded to the findings, telling CBS News that the subsidiary has since been shut down as a result of the revelations.
WePay "did not meet our expectations," the spokesperson told CBS. "We identified it, corrected it, and the business no longer operates."
The spokesperson emphasized that the bank's policies "prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views."
JPMorgan Chase staff were further found to have altered records of customers who were rejected because of their political views, including a case where a senior employee directed the removal of the phrases "right-wing" and "very tasteless, gun-centric videos" from records after a customer was denied commercial services multiple times between 2021 and 2023.
"As more far-right competitor(s) step in to take this company’s extreme clients, it may become more mainstream and more appropriate for JPM (JPMorgan) to bank," one redacted passage read.
In a further case of political discrimination, PNC Bank declined to extend a line of credit to a media company, in part because bank employees' personal politics conflicted with the business owners' conservative views, with an employee having written that "it becomes really difficult to justify aligning ourselves with a company whose owners have built very public personas around opinions very contrary to PNC’s beliefs/values."
Capital One denies services to groups across political spectrum
On the other side of the political spectrum, Capital One was found to have rejected Democratic pro-abortion organizations from opening accounts, though it did the same to a pro-gun group, a position generally seen on the political right.
Regarding religion, Wells Fargo terminated payment services for a religious nonprofit organization despite no violation of its agreement with the bank, according to an intermediary's initial determination.
Financial discrimination was also found across several banks investigated by the OCC, with small businesses receiving more stringent treatment than their larger counterparts, including instances in which wealthier companies faced negative publicity or even criminal proceedings.
Environmental aspects were also heavily considered for lending, as loans for non-renewable energy businesses were found to face stringent restrictions in several cases.
“Today’s report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation’s largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses,” said Currency Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould. “Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. Fair access to financial services is not a mantra; it is a mandate."
"Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," he added. "Accordingly, the OCC will be assessing further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework applicable to the largest banks to reduce the likelihood of these harmful practices recurring in the future.”
CBS reached out to other banks cited in the report beyond JPMorgan Chase, but they declined to comment, instead referring the news agency to a statement from a banking trade group.
"The banking industry supports fair access to banking services and has been working to ensure that government regulations and policies enable banks to serve law-abiding customers," said the Bank Policy Institute. "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk rather than reputational risk."

The language of extermination: NAZA, Artificial Intelligence and Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:51:04 UTC
19:51:04 KST

The 80-minute documentary NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, is chastening. It examines the conduct of the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) during its ferocious, unremitting war in Gaza, drawing upon the interviews of 24 anonymised military and intelligence personnel. The interviews were filmed on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with profiles and voices appropriately altered. The name of the documentary draws on a Hebrew acronym for nezek agavi or collateral damage, an obscene term used when counting the estimated number of civilians who will perish in a military strike. Last month, the film won the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, receiving a standing ovation lasting 25 minutes.
The interviewees focus on the terrifyingly relevant role played by Artificial Intelligence (AI) targeting systems used in guiding the bombing campaign launched in response to the Hamas-led attacks of 7th October 2023. In Abraham’s words, “the Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing is systemic: not by accident, but by design, actions of murder and policies that are based on the total dehumanisation of Palestinians.”
One of the interviewed subjects speaks of the goal being “quantity, not quality.” Another notes the conscious decision to target Hamas members, some even in the lower echelons, when they would be at home even if it meant killing family members and neighbours.
In one recalled instance, the phone of a 12-year-old girl was hacked to learn when her father would arrive home. The subsequent strike killed her. The cold logic is revealed in the rhetorical question posed by one of the interviewees: “When people talk about ‘flattening Gaza,’ what do you mean if not executing people?’
Despite being placed in a “too hot to handle” category by prominent indie studios, the self-distributed documentary managed to pass the US$500,000 mark in the United States after two weeks of release. Eight days after premiering at New York’s IFC Center, it went on to earn US$125,000. A further 85 theatres across 30 cities across North America then showed the film. Michelle Goldberg, writing in The New York Times, was impressed by the drawing power of the production when attending Walter Reade Theater for a screening. The venue, seating 268, was at capacity. “This is, in my experience, very unusual for documentaries of any sort, even those that, like ‘NAZA,’ win the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival.”
Militaries specialise in euphemised killing. A dedicated process of terminology and assessment sanitises and exsanguinates: death and murder become justifiable, necessary measures against an enemy bloated with wickedness and venality. In that process, mock tributes are paid to the canon of international law, notably international humanitarian law and doctrines of targeting. The more honest generals do us a favour by boasting about high casualty figures and mass mortality: they are not hiding matters and lurking behind worn ceremonies and the emperor’s non-existent clothes. Take the remarks of a former head of Israeli military intelligence made in a leaked audio: “For every one person [killed] on Oct. 7, 50 Palestinians must die.” Those militaries with a heavily staffed legal department supposedly providing guidance in striking a target, largely to reassure the squeamish that they are not implicated in acts of murder, are always suspect. In that regard, the IDF provides a model example, always claiming to do things differently from other powers in the region, yet resorting to the selective language of exculpation.
The reception of the film in Israel has been markedly hysterical. This was to be expected: the film unmasks and discomfits. It demolishes shibboleths. The IDF chief of staff Eyal Zamir vowed to use “every tool at our disposal” against the production. The Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar thought the film treasonous.
Abraham and Szor were “willing to harm their homeland in order just to get applause from antisemites around the world”. The irate minister was keen to “act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” he thundered in a social media post. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also called upon the passing of legislation stripping the duo of their citizenship, a curious point given the existing provisions of Israel’s Citizenship Law. (Making German Jews stateless was a specialty of the Third Reich: that the Jewish state would consider this to its citizens is a distinct, bitter irony, yet sadly permissible in light of the Israeli Supreme Court ruling in 2022 validating revocation for acts done in “breach of loyalty to the State of Israel”.)
Activists and members of the far-right party Jewish Power (Otzma Yehudit) led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir protested outside the parents of Szor’s house, with a speaker calling for both directors to be executed and the homes of their families to be demolished (collective punishment remains a great inspiration for tribal sentiment).
The IDF has marshalled its own response in a document accusing the filmmakers of presenting “a distorted, misleading and disingenuous picture of the IDF’s target planning and striking process.” The narrative of the documentary drew upon “substantial factual errors stemming from manipulative misrepresentations of reality.” Worth noting here is the lower register of critique that does not entirely repudiate the targeting practices of the IDF, dressed up in the apologetics of collateral damage. Concessions and confessions are always evident from those in and of power who resort to such dismissive language as “misrepresentative” and “disingenuous”.
Be that as it may, the agitated response is illuminating. The Lavender database, to take one objection, was apparently not one of targets, merely “a database that assists intelligence analysts.” This represents a distinction without a difference. The faith placed by militaries in the divinities of technology are hard to shake; there is nothing here to say that such analysts do not treat these data sets as unimpeachable. AI and religious deities serve to do the imagination for others; they discourage independent thinking and verification. Why bother when you have someone, or something else, doing it for you?
The response remains weak in claiming that the IDF believes itself “bound by and committed to international humanitarian law, its operational procedures are designed to implement those legal obligations, and it operates dedicated units and mechanisms to mitigate civilian harm.” The staggering death toll in Gaza, always sneered and jeered at by the Israeli authorities and their defenders, would suggest otherwise.
NAZA serves to, as the Israeli American historian Omer Bartov points out, address a “state of denial” by “actually speaking about the issue of what happened in Gaza rather than refusing to speak about it.”

It’s dealmaking time: despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late Saturday to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm election campaign.
