Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part on Monday in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries.
“This is an important relationship,” Rubio said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Friday that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill toward the “deepening partnership across Central Asia,” especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but only boasts a population of about 80 million people.
White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine -- with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia -- has repeatedly emphasized the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the secretary of state’s second official visit to India this year, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
Last February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fueled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by the Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani.

Zelenskyy Says Starlink Restrictions Apply Only in Ukraine While SpaceX Ignores Kyiv’s Inquiries

Zelenskyy Says Starlink Restrictions Apply Only in Ukraine While SpaceX Ignores Kyiv’s Inquiries
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of deliberately restricting Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, saying tests conducted in European Union countries showed that the same limitations did not apply outside Ukrainian territory. He also said the company had stopped responding to inquiries from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking to journalists in a group chat on October 17, Zelenskyy described the restrictions as a planned operation after Ukrainian officials tested Starlink terminals in moving vehicles across EU countries.
The President said Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine remain subject to a speed limit of approximately 161 kilometers per hour (100 mph). The restriction prevents Ukrainian forces from using certain drone interceptors against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, forcing them to rely on other air defense systems.
To determine whether the disruption resulted from technical problems or restrictions specifically targeting Ukraine, Ukrainian officials sent several vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into EU territory.
During the tests, the vehicles traveled at speeds exceeding 180 kilometers per hour (112 mph) where permitted, while their Starlink connections continued operating normally.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had documented the tests and collected evidence demonstrating that the restrictions applied inside Ukraine but not in EU countries.
He characterized the findings as evidence of a planned operation, although he did not publicly identify who had ordered the restrictions. The President also said Ukrainian military officials and diplomats were continuing efforts to contact SpaceX but had received no response through Defense Ministry channels.
According to Zelenskyy, explanations provided through other channels attributed the disruptions to technical problems. However, he questioned why those problems appeared to affect Ukraine specifically.
The accusations follow reports that SpaceX introduced new restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink, on October 14, without prior notification to Ukraine. The changes reportedly disrupted Ukrainian drone interception, strike operations, and frontline logistics.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk subsequently stated that Starshield was controlled by the US government, while the White House denied involvement and attributed the disruption to technical problems.
On October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported that Starshield connectivity during movement had resumed but said it was still investigating the restrictions.

Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:48:18 UTC
19:48:18 KST

Jordan-Israel border becomes new hotspot for sophisticated drug trade
Smugglers in the Negev desert are increasingly using drones and helium balloons to transport narcotics across the border into Jordanian territory.
Amman, Jordan – Jordanians fear the country’s border with Israel is turning into a major drug-smuggling route amid a surge in high-tech operations by gangs using drones and helium-filled balloons.
Organised networks active in southern Israel’s Negev Desert have links to groups in Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, operating along one of the most heavily surveilled borders in the world, with Jordanian authorities increasingly concerned about the implications this could have for the kingdom.
This escalation coincides with changes in the regional drug trade, particularly after the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in late 2024.
Elements in his regime were linked to the manufacturing and distribution of Captagon, an illegal amphetamine stimulant.
Syria became a hub for the distribution of Captagon to the Gulf, with Jordan a transit point and market for the drug. The Royal Jordanian Air Force carried out periodic strikes on drug manufacturing and smuggling points inside Syria, highlighting the huge security concerns Jordan had about the trade.
Since the collapse of the Assad government and the establishment of a new authority that views the Captagon trade as a national security issue, there has been a decrease in the drug trade from Syria into Jordan.
Although Druze militias in the Syrian province of Suwayda allegedly linked to Israel have been accused of continuing the drug trade, Jordanian security forces are increasingly focused on the Jordan-Israel border.
The use of quadcopter drones and balloons is reportedly among the new tactics used by gangs in Israel to smuggle hashish, crystal meth, and amphetamines into Jordan.
Jordanian security forces are said to be increasingly unhappy with the scale of the drug smuggling operations and have accused the Israeli army of not taking the issue seriously.
Initial data from Jordanian forces recorded 17 interception operations linked to drones during the first half of 2026 in Jordan’s southwestern border area with Israel.
They also recorded 231 smuggling and infiltration attempts and downed 56 drones across various borders during the same period.
Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told Al Jazeera that Jordanian forces were continuing efforts to prevent drugs from being smuggled into the kingdom. But they are evidently facing more complex activities by drug dealers.
“There is an increase in drug smuggling operations from Israel to Jordan using drones,” he said. “The number of seized drug cases during the current year reached 15,342 cases. Trafficking cases constituted about 28 percent of them, compared with 72 percent for usage cases.”
Israeli media reports indicate that gangs active in the Negev Desert are behind some of the smuggling operations into Jordan, where drugs can fetch higher profits.
There are estimates that 1kg of hashish can sell for approximately 7,500 pounds sterling (almost $10,000), according to the British newspaper The Telegraph, which recently uncovered the drug smugglers’ latest operations. Israeli security services believe that the price of hashish in Jordan is about 15 times higher than in Israel.
Due to widespread disenfranchisement and poverty, elements within Palestinian communities in Israel have been linked to the drug trade, according to reports. Multiple sources have accused Israel of allowing Palestinian towns and cities to become hotbeds of crime to create divisions and prevent calls for greater rights.
Ammar al-Qudah, a member of the Jordanian Senate and retired major-general in the Public Security Directorate, claimed that organised gangs in the Negev had obtained more than 1,000 drones that were originally used for agricultural and security purposes.
“The smuggling networks are linked to other gangs in Jordan, Sinai and the Negev, and rely on a route starting from Sinai, passing through the Negev, and reaching Wadi Araba, in addition to other routes including the Lebanese border with Israel and the Galilee region towards Syria,” he told Al Jazeera.
They are also using a range of sophisticated technology to bypass security on both sides of the border. This includes the use of helium-filled balloons equipped with GPS devices, drones capable of carrying about 50kg of narcotics, including black hashish and crystal meth, al-Qudah said.
He warned that a portion of the black hashish and crystal meth being smuggled into the kingdom is being sold domestically, with the rest going to other markets in the region.
With such high-tech operations, there are accusations that members of Israeli forces know about drug gang activities, based on past experiences in Egypt.
One West Point report said current and former trackers in the Israeli military in the Negev are being recruited by traffickers to provide intelligence to facilitate their operations in Egypt. In 2012, a number of Israeli service personnel were arrested on suspicion of collaborating with drug smugglers across the Egyptian border.
While there is no proof that the same situation is being repeated in Jordan, many have questioned how drones and balloons carrying drugs could cross a heavily surveilled and guarded Israeli border into Jordan.
Jordan’s counternarcotics department, in cooperation with the armed forces, has tracked such cases and made arrests.
Retired Brigadier-General Daifallah al-Daboubi, a strategic and military expert, said Jordan is witnessing a “reverse drug migration”, starting from the Sinai Peninsula, passing through the Negev region, and reaching the kingdom.
“Groups active in Beersheba and the Negev possess great financial capabilities and use advanced smuggling methods, most notably drones,” he said.
The Israeli army’s preoccupation with wars in Gaza, Lebanon and the occupied Golan Heights has provided smugglers with room to manoeuvre on the Jordan border, he added. But he ruled out the direct involvement of the Israeli political or military leadership in any drug smuggling.
Steps taken by Israel to boost security on its eastern border include the establishment of the 96th Division, which began operating in the Jordan Valley in 2025, and the construction of a controversial security barrier with Jordan.
But none of these measures appears to be designed to prevent drugs from leaving Israel; instead, they appear to be designed to prevent weapons and other illicit merchandise from entering the country from Jordan.

Ukrainian Officials Slam Trump's Waiver Of Russia Sanctions As Rubio Defends Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:36:13 UTC
19:36:13 KST

Ukrainian officials sharply criticized US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sweeping planned sanctions against Russia, saying that it "sends the wrong message to the aggressor" and "helps only the Russians."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration needed up to 60 days to assess the potential economic impact of the sanctions and tariffs, while the White House argued that imposing them immediately could hinder efforts to negotiate a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine.
"If Russians are cheering yesterday's decisions in the US, it is certainly not about effective pressure to end the war," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha wrote on X on October 17. "Indecisiveness sends the wrong signal to the aggressor. It only prolongs the war."
He added that "Lindsey Graham understood this well," referring to the late senator of South Carolina for whom the sanctions legislation, known as the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- was named. Graham, who died on July 11, was a prominent congressional supporter of Ukraine.
The bill passed Congress with overwhelming bipartisan support and was signed into law by Trump in September. But in an executive order signed late on October 16, Trump said withholding the measures was in the national interest of the United States. The order came just two days before the sanctions package was due to take effect on October 18.
The move prompted sharp criticism from Ukraine advocates and lawmakers from both parties who say the move undermines efforts to force Moscow to negotiate.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said removing the sanctions "definitely helps only the Russians."
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskiy wrote on X on October 17.
The law was designed to give the administration additional leverage over Russian President Vladimir Putin by authorizing tariffs of up to 100 percent on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and providing for sanctions targeting Russian officials, financial institutions, and the country's so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing restrictions.
Rubio defended the White House's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia on October 17, saying Washington needed time to assess the economic consequences of additional penalties as conflicts across several regions strain global energy supplies.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a series of diplomatic and trade talks in Central Asia, Rubio defended the administration's efforts to balance pressure on Moscow against economic concerns.
The waiver followed a diesel deal Trump announced with Russia on October 9 that prompted criticism that Washington was prioritizing domestic fuel prices over efforts to constrain the Kremlin's war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy called the waiver was an unfortunate decision to backtrack on the sanctions at a time when "pressure is needed."
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine -- right before winter," he said. "Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin -- all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."
A senior envoy to Russian President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, praised the waiver as "a truly historic moment."
Kirill Dmitriev, who heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, wrote on X late on October 16 that "economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interest of both nations."
Energy Costs Complicate Russia Sanctions
Rubio said the administration needed 60 days to assess the effects of sanctions and tariffs, including their potential impact on countries such as India, which continues to rely substantially on Russian energy despite efforts to diversify its supplies.
He pointed to disruptions involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement, and the war between Russia and Ukraine as factors putting pressure on global energy markets.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," Rubio said.
The United States was paying higher prices than it wanted, he said, while some other countries were approaching a crisis over energy costs and availability.
Rubio also defended the administration's diesel deal with Russia -- which Zelenskyy called "a gift" to Putin -- arguing the fuel would have reached international markets regardless of whether the United States purchased it. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," he said.
Energy analysts have questioned whether the deal would significantly lower prices for American consumers, while warning that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with substantial economic benefits.
The waiver blocks additional sanctions and tariffs approved by Congress to discourage major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, although existing sanctions remain in place.
The decision drew sharp criticism from both parties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible," while Senator John Cornyn said the late senator Graham "would be appalled." Democratic lawmakers also accused Trump of helping Russia finance its war.

Cypriot leaders attend bicommunal festival amid renewed push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:35:00 UTC
19:35:00 KST

Turkish Cypriot President Erhürman (C) and Greek Cypriot leader Christodoulides (L) sit together at the festival.
The leaders of ethnically-divided Cyprus attended an annual bicommunal festival in the village of Pyla late on Oct. 17, marking a symbolic step as diplomatic efforts to resolve the island’s long-standing issues are ongoing.
Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman attended the event wearing a neck brace due to a recurrence of a cervical disc herniation but made no public remarks.
Seated alongside Greek Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides, Erhürman also joined in the folk dancing at the festival.
The event, aimed at fostering cultural ties and dialogue between Turkish Cypriots and Greek Cypriots, was also attended by Turkish Cyprus’ Republican Turkish Party (CTP) and the Greek Cypriot left-wing party AKEL.
Pyla, known as Pile among Turkish Cypriots, is one of the few villages in the U.N.-controlled buffer zone that continues to host both Turkish Cypriot and Greek Cypriot communities. The peace festival returned this year after a six-year hiatus.
“We are conveying a message of peaceful coexistence and underscoring the need to reunify our homeland once and for all,” Christodoulides said.
He added that, as he had recently told the Turkish Cypriot press, the island would undoubtedly be reunified if the decision rested solely with the two communities.
The Greek Cypriot leader also appeared to take an indirect swipe at the other side over the failure to reach agreement on a U.N. proposal concerning the opening of additional crossing points. He said U.N. envoy Maria Angela Holguin knew which side had immediately accepted the proposal and which had rejected it, without explicitly identifying either party.
Asked whether joint appearances with Erhürman at festivals and other events could become a regular feature, Christodoulides said he supported making such engagements routine, adding that this was precisely why he had attended the festival.
According to the media, Erhürman chose not to respond to Christodoulides’ remarks in order to preserve the positive atmosphere of the event.
Beyond their appearance at the festival, the two leaders are expected to attend upcoming meetings of the bicommunal technical committees on cultural heritage and youth, as well as the steering committee of the civil society consultative body. The two previously agreed to meet once a week.
Speaking to reporters on the second day of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 16, Christodoulides said the Cyprus issue would be discussed at a high-level meeting between the European Union and Türkiye scheduled to take place by the end of October.
Erhürman and Christodoulides are both expected to attend the U.N. Climate Change Conference (COP31), which will be held in Turkish city of Antalya in November.
In a statement issued on Oct. 14, Erhürman announced that he had received an invitation to the summit from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and would be in Antalya on the scheduled dates. Christodoulides confirmed his attendance in a statement a day earlier.
Erhürman said he had learned through the media that Christodoulides would also attend the summit, adding: “As we have always said, diplomacy and dialogue are always good.”
It remains unclear whether the two leaders will meet on the sidelines of COP31.

A “massive” Ukrainian drone attack on St Petersburg in Russia has killed at least one person and injured five others, the city’s governor said on Sunday.

Moscow’s defence ministry said 1,015 Ukrainian drones were neutralised overnight.
Russian strikes kill two
In Ukraine, Russian forces struck residential buildings overnight, killing two people and injuring 12, including two children, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Sunday.
“This morning, there was a strike on an agricultural enterprise in Volyn. All necessary services are working at the site,” he said.
“In total, over this past week, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic.”
The attacks came after Zelenskyy said this week that Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries, insisting he was standing up for his war-torn country, as support from the United States declined.
Zelenskyy told the British newspaper the Financial Times this week that Kyiv was “done” with an “energy ceasefire” unilaterally declared by United States President Donald Trump and would resume strikes on Russia in retaliation for a wave of attacks.
‘Energy ceasefire’ falters
Trump announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine last week, but Zelenskyy said Moscow continued to violate the deal.
“Since the American President announced the energy ceasefire a week ago, Russia has deliberately attacked Ukraine’s energy and oil and gas sectors 76 times,” he wrote in his X post on Sunday.
“Last night alone, there were strikes on substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions,” he wrote, adding that tens of thousands of families remained without power as energy workers and repair crews worked round the clock to restore supplies.
Zelenskyy also said that the main targets of Moscow’s recent strikes were energy facilities, as the Russians were trying to “cause a blackout”.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said.
Trump is also facing criticism in both Europe and the US after he signed an executive order on Friday to waive sanctions and tariffs targeting Moscow’s energy revenues.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that Trump’s waiver would be a pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.
“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.
Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US.
“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”

Swiss cantons weigh lower social assistance for Ukrainian refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:17:21 UTC
19:17:21 KST

Swiss cantons weigh lower social assistance for Ukrainian refugees
Next year, 46,000 Ukrainian refugees in Switzerland will be eligible to receive social assistance for the first time. The federal government now wants to allow the cantons to decide for themselves on the level of these payments. Local authorities consider the change to be fair, while aid organisations warn of the social consequences.
If Asylum Ordinance 2 were not amended, people with protection status S – a special temporary protection status in Switzerland designed for people fleeing war – primarily Ukrainian refugees – would receive the same social assistance as Swiss nationals. This would mean a higher rate than the current social assistance for asylum seekers, explained Mathias Reynard, President of the Conference of Cantonal Social Directors (SODK), in response to a query from the Keystone-SDA news agency.
This would entail a significant increase in costs for the cantons, not least because, as part of Relief Package 27, the federal government’s lump-sum payment to the cantons for people with S status has been abolished where such status is linked to a residence permit valid for five years or more, the canton Valais member of the cantonal government went on to write.
The cantons had called on the federal government to allow them to determine the level of contributions themselves. This request had been incorporated into the consultation draft, Reynard stated. This would enable the cantons to pay lower contributions to those affected in future, right down to the level of asylum social assistance.
The municipalities welcomed the amendment to the Asylum Ordinance, but also want a say in the matter. After all, they would bear the main financial burden, according to the Swiss Association of Municipalities.
Those who pay less will make up the shortfall
The Social Democratic party, the Greens and aid organisations such as Caritas, Heks and Swiss Refugee Aid (SFH) fear that the cut in social assistance will lead to poverty and legal inequality. Ultimately, they also reject the draft because it hinders integration and social participation.
+ Switzerland extends Ukraine S status until March 2028
They warned that the proposed amendment to the ordinance also carries the risk of legal action. Depending on the ruling, the cantons might have to make back payments for the full amount of social assistance. The Radical Liberal party also pointed out to the federal government that the compatibility with the Refugee Convention is currently unclear.
The party called for the legal situation to be reviewed and for the amendment to the ordinance to be adopted this autumn, so that the cantons would have sufficient time to amend their social assistance laws by March 1, 2027.
The right-wing Swiss People’s Party concerns are quite different. The party welcomes the fact that persons in need of protection with S status will no longer be entitled to the same level of social assistance as Swiss nationals.
However, they argue that there is still considerable untapped potential for savings in the asylum sector. The party is therefore calling for the bill to be tightened up.

World Insights: Leaders' summit puts security, regional cooperation, finance at heart of upcoming COP17
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
18:16:32 CST
19:16:32 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Global efforts to halt biodiversity loss face a common test: whether conservation commitments can withstand the pressures of poverty, conflict and competing economic priorities.
At Friday's Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, those pressures brought the challenge of implementation into focus ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled to begin Monday in the Armenian capital.
The discussions underscored how closely biodiversity protection is tied to security and development, how much shared ecosystems depend on cross-border cooperation, and how implementation hinges on accessible finance and broad participation.
NATURE AS A SECURITY CONCERN
Speakers at the summit underscored how environmental pressures can compound security risks.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian warned that pollution spreads beyond national borders, while Lebanese Environment Minister Tamara El-Zein cited World Bank estimates putting environmental damage from the Israel-Hezbollah conflict in 2023-2024 at more than 500 million U.S. dollars.
The security argument also extended to economic resilience. Britain's representative described nature as critical infrastructure supporting prosperity, security and resilience. European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera said 55 percent of global GDP was highly dependent on nature.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres linked biodiversity loss to conflict, climate disruption, food insecurity and disease, arguing that these crises could not be addressed separately.
With nature protection increasingly seen as essential to peace and security, Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu called for win-win cooperation and multi-stakeholder governance to strengthen biodiversity conservation and resilience for sustainable development.
GLOBAL GOALS, REGIONAL REALITIES
The summit's regional examples exposed another challenge: ecosystems cross borders, while policies and funding are largely organized nationally.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the Caspian seal population had fallen from 1 million to 270,000 over the past century, invoking the ecological disaster of the Aral Sea and urging action to prevent a similar fate for the Caspian. He reiterated Kazakhstan's proposal to establish an international water organization within the UN system, suggesting it could become a joint Central Asian initiative open to other countries.
The pressures extend beyond the Caspian. Tajik President Emomali Rahmon said his country had lost more than 1,300 glaciers in recent decades. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said only around 30 of the 101 rivers that historically flowed into Lake Issyk-Kul now flowed year-round.
Such changes threaten water supplies, ecosystems and livelihoods simultaneously, underscoring the need for cooperation on shared waters and habitats. Proposals included a regional center to combat desertification in Central Asia and an Armenian initiative for a Yerevan platform on biodiversity, mountain and freshwater ecosystems.
Yet regional cooperation must also deliver effective protection on the ground. International Union for Conservation of Nature President Razan Al Mubarak cautioned that simply meeting the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework's target of conserving at least 30 percent of terrestrial and inland water areas, and marine and coastal areas by 2030 would not guarantee lasting conservation outcomes. Protected areas also need effective management, equitable governance, ecological representation and connectivity.
Huang, the Chinese environment minister, called for advancing national biodiversity strategies and action plans and translating global targets into national policies and practical measures.
FINANCING DELIVERY
Even well-designed plans face a financial obstacle: money continues to flow overwhelmingly toward activities that damage nature.
Guterres said that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, 30 dollars were spent destroying it, with nature-negative financial flows reaching 7.3 trillion dollars in 2023. The challenge is therefore both to increase conservation funding and redirect investment and incentives that undermine it.
Speakers outlined several funding commitments. Ribera, of the European Commission, said the European Union was on track to double its international biodiversity finance to 7 billion euros (7.86 billion dollars) over 2021-2027. Britain said it would allocate around 6 billion pounds (7.98 billion dollars) in international climate finance over the next three financial years, with roughly a quarter expected to support nature.
For developing countries, however, the test is whether such commitments translate into predictable and accessible support. Indonesian Environment Minister Mohd Jumhur Hidayat stressed that other funding sources should complement, rather than replace, international public finance. Zimbabwean Environment Minister Evelyn Ndlovu highlighted the priority of delivering at least 30 billion dollars annually in international biodiversity finance by 2030.
Beyond funding, Huang said, technological and capacity-building support was also needed, pointing to China's contribution of 1.5 billion yuan (about 224 million dollars) to establish the Kunming Biodiversity Fund.
The summit's closing Yerevan Declaration called for political commitments to translate into measurable action and lasting results. As COP17 opens on Oct. 19, the challenge will be to turn that resolve into decisions that give countries the resources and support to deliver on their biodiversity promises. ■

People watch the burning oil terminal following an air attack in Saint Petersburg on October 18, 2026, amid the ongoing Russian-Ukrainian conflict. (AFP Photo)
A Ukrainian drone attack overnight killed one person, wounded five others and set two oil refineries ablaze in the Russian city of Saint Petersburg, its governor said on Oct. 18.
“One person was killed and five others hurt and hospitalized following a massive attack carried out by Ukrainian Nazi military drones,” Alexandre Beglov said.

Warrior disposal dates withheld on security grounds

Unknown Publisher

11:15:37 BST
19:15:37 KST

The Ministry of Defence has refused to say when each of the seventy-eight Warrior infantry fighting vehicles removed from the fleet in the past year was disposed of, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the dates on which each vehicle was disposed of, following an answer of 7 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The answer to Question 23452 explained that the seventy-eight Warrior Infantry Fighting Vehicles removed from the reported fleet between 2025 and 2026 have been disposed of in accordance with Defence disposal policy. It would be inappropriate for me to provide exact disposal details, such as dates or variants as to do so could, or would be likely to, prejudice the capability of our Armed Forces.”
The number leaving the fleet has been confirmed, but not when they went or which variants they were, so the rate at which Warrior is being drawn down cannot be read from the published record.
The FV510 Warrior entered service in 1988 as the British Army tracked infantry fighting vehicle, carrying a section of dismounted infantry behind a two man turret armed with the 30mm RARDEN cannon.
A programme to rebuild the fleet around a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon, the Warrior Capability Sustainment Programme, was cancelled in March 2021 after more than a decade of development and around £430 million of spending, and the vehicle has been running down since.

Stampede at Hindu festival in India kills 19

19:09:09 KST

Purses and other belongings left behind by devotees lie on the floor of a worship venue for the Hindu festival of Durga Puja following a stampede, in Kolkata, India, Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026. (AP Photo)
A stampede during a major Hindu festival in eastern India’s West Bengal state has left at least 19 people dead, officials said on Oct. 18.
The stampede in the state capital of Kolkata happened on Oct. 17 night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga. According to police, some worshippers fell on the road, triggering the stampede.
Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment. He announced an investigation by a Special Investigation Team to be headed by a judge of the state’s High Court.
Police detained some pavilion organizers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Around 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions, known locally as pandals, have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Crowd crushes are relatively common in India during religious festivals, as large crowds, sometimes in the millions, gather in confined areas with few safety or crowd control measures. In January of 2025, at least 30 people were killed as tens of thousands of Hindus rushed to bathe in a sacred river during the Maha Kumbh festival, the world’s largest religious gathering.

Turkish police have arrested two foreign nationals in Istanbul after discovering 213 kilograms of synthetic drugs in a caravan allegedly used as a mobile laboratory, in an operation reminiscent of the U.S. television series “Breaking Bad.”
Police began monitoring the suspects after noticing two men carrying bags from a foreign-registered caravan parked on a street in the Şişli district. Officers discovered three concealed compartments beneath the vehicle containing liquid synthetic drugs and continued their investigation.
After around 15 days of surveillance, police determined that the suspects had rented a house two streets away from where the caravan was parked. Police raided the identified locations, arresting both suspects. Searches uncovered a total of 213 kilograms of synthetic drugs, including 162 kilograms in liquid form and 51 kilograms in solid and crystal forms. Authorities also seized materials allegedly used in drug production at the caravan and the house.
The suspects were referred to a court after police questioning and remanded in custody.
The operation recalled “Breaking Bad,” the American crime drama that aired from 2008 to 2013. The five-season series follows Walter White, played by Bryan Cranston, and Jesse Pinkman, played by Aaron Paul, as they manufacture and distribute methamphetamine. In the show, the two use a caravan as a mobile laboratory to conceal their activities and evade law enforcement.

PARIS – France woke on Oct 18 to the wreckage of one of its most violent days of unrest in years after protests over high prices and public services left one demonstrator dead, hundreds of police injured and nearly 1,800 people arrested.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted into riots on Oct 17, with a town hall torched, shops ransacked, and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.
One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris, where police made a record 855 arrests.
Across France, more than 500 officers were injured, the interior minister said.
“It’s like a war zone here,” said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, which suffered major damage on Oct 17.
More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.
President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8pm local time on Oct 18 (2am Singapore time on Oct 19), his office said.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.

He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the million euros needed to repair the city hall.
The unrest has increased pressure on Macron and his government, with a presidential election due in 2027.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be “intimidated” by violence and blamed the unrest on the “ultra-left” and criminals.
Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Oct 18 for business owners who suffered losses.
“Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos,” Lescure said in a statement.

French retailer Carrefour’s Chief Executive Alexandre Bompard told BFMTV that 50 of the company’s shops had been damaged including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the dozens of millions of euros.
The protests began in September over school conditions and teacher shortages in working-class suburbs, before broadening into a movement against inequality, public spending cuts and the rising cost of living. REUTERS

Damage to the perimeter fence was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Saturday night shortly before 11 pm (2100GMT).
Police said it is “highly likely” that a car drove into the airport grounds, in an area close to some Russian Antonov cargo planes that were parked there, according to the German daily BILD.
Numerous emergency responders searched the airport. Police spokeswoman Leverenz said, “It is highly likely that a vehicle drove through the fence. However, during the search of the grounds that night, neither a vehicle nor any unauthorized persons were found on the premises.”

The breached fence near the Russian Antonovs was secured and cordoned off. The three An-124 cargo planes have been stationed in Leipzig/Halle since 2022. They are no longer allowed to take off because of EU sanctions against Russia.
Second incident at Leipzig Airport in three months
This is the second security-related incident to take place at Leipzig Airport in three months. In early August, a drone rigged with explosives was discovered on the grounds of the airport next to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes.
The German government blamed Russia for the attempted attack. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt stated that the investigation confirmed Russian responsibility. The federal government subsequently warned of a further escalation in Russian hybrid attacks on critical infrastructure in Germany. Moscow rejected the allegations.

Iran said Sunday it may not endorse a resolution on Yemen being discussed at a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad unless what Tehran considers “fairness and balance” is reflected in the text.
Speaking on the sidelines of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said “serious discussions” had taken place on Yemen, according to the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
“Saudi Arabia had its views, and we and other countries also expressed our views,” Araghchi said, adding that the proposed resolution had not yet been finalized.
“We hope that fairness and balance will be observed in this resolution and the final statement. Naturally, if this does not happen, the Islamic Republic of Iran cannot join this resolution,” he said.
Araghchi said a significant bloc of OIC members holds positions close to Saudi Arabia, adding that Tehran had conducted extensive consultations with other member states and that his speech at the meeting had emphasized a solution to the Yemen issue.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government.
The conflict has recently spilled into Saudi Arabia, with Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom, including its oil infrastructure, following the group’s declaration of a maritime blockade in July.
Turning to relations with the US, Araghchi said Iran’s conditions had been presented to Washington as part of what he described as a “7-day plan,” and that the US had submitted its views, to which Tehran was still preparing a response.
“From our point of view, the 7-day plan is on the table,” he said.
“If there is sincerity on the American side — which there is not — the path is clear. If they fulfill those conditions, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will begin on the seventh day,” he added, referring to the Strait of Hormuz.
The remarks came during the 52nd session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad, where Iraq assumed the rotating presidency of the council from Türkiye.
The meeting brings together foreign ministers and representatives of the 57-member organization to discuss regional and international issues, including developments in Yemen and Palestine.
Araghchi also said Iran attaches particular importance to neighboring Iraq and expressed hope that Baghdad’s presidency, along with the appointment of a new OIC secretary-general, would give the organization “new momentum.”
He said Tehran expects the OIC to play a constructive role in resolving disputes among Muslim countries.

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:22:44 UTC
18:22:44 KST

Food or medicine? The impossible choices facing Sudan’s chronically ill
Sudanese are facing growing costs of medicine caused by the country’s civil war.
Hasanat al-Rashid, 48, has lived with diabetes for 15 years, and the three-and-a-half-year civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group has worsened her situation. Finding the treatment she needs has become a daily struggle.
When the war broke out in April 2023, she was forced to flee south from her home in Haj Yousif in Khartoum North to Umm Daw Ban in Khartoum State.
During her displacement, she went for days without medication and was forced to eat foods unsuitable for her condition, such as asida, a traditional Sudanese porridge.
She underwent operations on her foot twice when she developed complications of diabetes, including a severe infection.
She moved between hospitals in Gezira State south of Khartoum, seeking treatment in Rufaa, Wad Madani and Al-Hasahisa. When fighting spread to these areas in December 2023, she fled again, arriving in Port Sudan, a city on the Red Sea that was less affected by the war.
Her condition has worsened to the point that she now has to use insulin every day and with this comes added costs, something that forces diabetes sufferers in Sudan to choose between medicine and other essentials, such as food.
“The doses vary depending on whether my blood sugar is high or low,” she told Al Jazeera.
The war has pushed income levels in Sudan back to those last seen in the 1990s, according to the United Nations Development Programme. This means Hasanat and other diabetes sufferers are struggling to afford the medicine they need to treat the condition.
Hasanat’s doctor recommended she use an insulin pen, a device used to inject insulin under the skin. She would need one or two of the devices a month, but the cost at 70,000 Sudanese pounds ($8) is more than she can afford up front, so she opts for a vial of insulin.
This is cheaper at 17,000 Sudanese pounds ($1.80), but there is the additional cost of buying ice every day to keep the insulin cool. She spends 180,000 pounds ($20) a month on ice to preserve the medicine. But she is able to spread these costs out through the month, making the vials her only viable option even if the overall costs are higher than an insulin pen.
“It may last a month or less, but the challenge is that I don’t have a refrigerator, so I struggle to store the insulin properly,” she said.
She also needs painkillers and vitamins on a regular basis to manage complications caused by the diabetes.
The rising cost of treatment
Fatima Adam, 75, is among the patients at Port Sudan Hospital struggling to afford the medicines she needs to manage her hypertension and a thyroid condition.
She was admitted to the hospital with complications caused by high blood pressure, which has started to impact her heart. Too unwell to speak to Al Jazeera herself, her daughter, Aisha, described how the rising cost of treatment has affected her whole family.
Before the war, Fatima received medicine through the National Health Insurance Fund. She paid a quarter of the cost while the fund covered the rest. But when the war started and the economy collapsed, the medicines she needed were no longer covered by the scheme.
“My mother takes six different medicines because hypertension has affected her heart in addition to her thyroid medication. The war has made things harder because the prices of these medicines have gone up,” Aisha told Al Jazeera.
The responsibility for paying for Fatima’s treatment and supporting her and her daughter falls on her son, who works as a casual worker. With no fixed income, he goes to the market every day in search of work but sometimes returns home empty without any luck.
“Sometimes, when my brother finds work, we buy enough medicine to last a month. Other times, we have to buy smaller quantities and take the medicines intermittently,” Aisha said.
She bought a month’s supply of her mother’s medication a few days ago for 160,000 Sudanese pounds ($17.80), a substantial expense for a family whose income depends on day labour but essential to treating Fatima’s condition.
War damage
The war has caused an estimated $500m in losses to medicine stocks, infrastructure and transport fleets, dealing a major blow to Sudan’s pharmaceutical supply system, the National Medical Supplies Fund told Al Jazeera.
The National Medicines and Poisons Board estimated that only eight of the 30 pharmaceutical factories in Khartoum that shut down during the conflict have resumed operations despite the security situation in the capital recently improving.
This has increased Sudan’s reliance on imported medicines, but the subsequent depreciation of the Sudanese pound has driven up the costs of pharmaceutical procurement and production.
Hossam al-Naeem, who works as a pharmacist in Port Sudan, said customers with diabetes and hypertension require regular painkillers and vitamins to help their overall condition.
“I feel deeply saddened when I see the expressions on some patients’ faces as they ask about the prices of medicines and discover how much they have increased because of the depreciation of the Sudanese pound,” Hossam told Al Jazeera.
The currency’s collapse has created added challenges for pharmacists. Before the war, a dollar traded for roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Now black-market currency traders are quoting rates of 9,300 pounds to the dollar, meaning higher costs for most goods in Sudan.
Sometimes Hossam incurs losses himself when he finds that the prices of drugs have risen sharply, and keeping essential medicines stocked is becoming difficult.
“I used to sell a strip of cold and flu tablets for 6,000 Sudanese pounds [70 cents]. But when I went to buy new stock, I found that the supplier’s price was also 6,000 pounds per strip. That means I made no profit, not even enough to cover the pharmacy’s operating costs,” he said.
The struggle to afford heart medication
Huda Mahmoud, 58, lives in el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state in south-central Sudan, where drone attacks and other violence remain a problem while the military is making advances towards the city.
Huda has lived with heart problems for more than 12 years and described the impacts of the war as being physical, financial and emotional.
“I take five different medicines. There was a time when they weren’t available, and I suffered a lot. Sometimes, I had to ask people in Wad Madani, Sennar or Port Sudan to send them to me,” she told Al Jazeera. “The medicines were extremely expensive, costing me 300,000 Sudanese pounds [$33.30] a month.”
Taking medication has become a carefully managed routine with each pill tied to a specific time of day.
“I’ve become tied to my pills: this one before eating, that one afterwards. If I forget one, my heart starts beating very fast,” she added.
In March, Huda was forced to travel from el-Obeid to Omdurman. Following her strict treatment regimen has become increasingly difficult during repeated periods of upheaval.
She has now returned home to el-Obeid, where her regular medicine is priced at 151,000 Sudanese pounds ($16.80) a month, something she can barely afford.
Her greatest fear is running out of medicine or being unable to afford her next supply, which would put her at risk of a blood clot.
“I’m afraid of becoming incapacitated. I used to be responsible for the whole household, but now I need help. I feel like I’ve become a burden on my family,” she said.

Houthis release video of Saudi AH-6i helicopter being hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:22:20 UTC
18:22:20 KST

- The Saudi-led coalition said a National Guard AH-6i helicopter crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing both crew members.
- Houthi footage appears to show the helicopter being hit by a 358-family loitering munition, which the group calls Saqr.
Footage released by Yemen’s Houthis appears to show a Saudi National Guard AH-6i helicopter being struck by a loitering munition over Saudi Arabia’s Najran province, after the Saudi-led coalition said the aircraft crashed because of a technical malfunction, killing its two crew members.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said on Oct. 18 that the AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter, which belonged to Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of National Guard, crashed and was destroyed inside Saudi territory in the Najran area, near the border with Yemen. Both officers on board were killed. The coalition did not identify them or give further details.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree had said a day earlier that the group shot down a Saudi helicopter, which he described as an Apache, near Najran while it was attacking Houthi positions along the border. Al-Maliki responded on social media with a photo of a row of Apache helicopters, writing that the Houthis claimed to have shot one down but that it would enter the battlefield soon.
The video the Houthis later published appears to show a small helicopter consistent with the AH-6i being hit in flight. The weapon in the footage appears to be an Iranian-designed loitering munition from the 358 family, which the Houthis field under the name Saqr.
The 358 is a small, jet-powered surface-to-air loitering munition. Launched from a rail, it can circle over an area, search for low, slow targets such as helicopters and drones, and detonate near them. Iranian-made 358 components have been found in weapons shipments to the Houthis intercepted at sea, and the group has used the munition against drones over Yemen.
The AH-6i is a light attack and reconnaissance helicopter built by Boeing and based on the MH-6 Little Bird used by U.S. special operations forces. It carries a crew of two and can be armed with machine guns, rockets and guided missiles. The Saudi Arabian National Guard ordered about two dozen of the helicopters from the United States in the mid-2010s and uses them for reconnaissance and close air support.
Najran has come under repeated Houthi drone and missile attacks in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated. A week before the crash, Houthi strikes killed 13 people at Riyadh’s international airport, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:19:00 UTC
18:19:00 KST

Vietnam signs free trade deal with four European countries
October 18, 2026
Vietnam and four European countries signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on Sunday.
The deal was announced by the governments of Vietnam and Norway.
Vietnam's Trade Ministry said it signed the deal with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), which is made up Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
The four European countries are not part of the European Union (EU).
The official talks between Vietnam and the EFTA began in 2012. The talks were interrupted in 2018 and only resumed last year.
How does the deal benefit Vietnam?
The agreement between Vietnam, which is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) waives or reduces customs duties, including on imports of industrial, fish and agricultural products.
Under the deal, around half of Norway's exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free, with more than 98% to be tariff-free within seven years, the Norwegian government said in a statement.
According to the signing parties, the deal covers trade in goods and services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development, among other areas, both parties say.
Last year, the trade value between the EFTA and Vietnam stood at €4.8 billion ($5.4 billion), according to the association.
Vietnam said the agreement showed the parties' resolve to "reinforce the rules-based trading system amid continued volatility in the global economy," according to a government statement.
It was also expected to help Vietnam "diversify its import and export markets" and "integrate more deeply into global value chains," the government said.

How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:18:40 UTC
18:18:40 KST

There is no single interval for every part. Brake pads may be replaced according to wear, while timing belts usually follow a specific mileage or time interval.
Owners searching for kia spare parts sharjah, hyundai spare parts sharjah, or infiniti spare parts sharjah should match parts with the exact model, engine specification, and manufacturer requirements. Al-Miyar offers replacement parts matched to different vehicle specifications.
How Often Do Car Parts Need to Be Replaced?
Every component experiences different stress. Some parts wear through friction, while others deteriorate because of heat, vibration, contamination, or age. As a result, car parts replacement intervals vary significantly.
Driving conditions also affect car parts replacement schedule. Heavy traffic, short trips, dusty roads, extreme temperatures, towing, and heavy loads can increase wear.
A practical plan should consider:
· Mileage and vehicle age
· Manufacturer recommendations
· Driving and road conditions
· Climate
· Visible wear or damage
· Changes in performance
· Maintenance history
This provides a more realistic way to determine how often to replace car parts.
Which Car Parts Usually Need More Attention?
Some components need regular inspection because they experience continuous wear or affect vehicle control. Understanding when to replace car parts is particularly important for brakes and tires.
Brake Pads and Brake Rotors
Brake components directly affect stopping performance. Brake pads become thinner through friction, but their service life varies with driving habits, traffic, vehicle weight, road conditions, and brake-system design.
Warning signs include:
· Squealing or grinding
· Vibration during braking
· Changes in pedal feel
· Longer stopping distances
· Reduced pad material
Brake rotors may also require replacement when excessively worn, damaged, or below the manufacturer's specified thickness. Inspection is more useful than relying only on mileage.
 
Tires
 
Tire replacement cannot be determined by mileage alone. Tread depth, uneven wear, cracks, age, damage, and handling changes can indicate that a tire needs attention.
 
Incorrect pressure and poor wheel alignment can accelerate uneven wear. Regular inspection helps maintain traction and handling.
 
Engine Oil and Filters
 
Engine oil becomes contaminated and may lose protective properties. Oil-change intervals depend on the vehicle, engine, oil specification, driving conditions, and manufacturer recommendations.
 
Oil filters are commonly replaced during an oil service. Al-Miyar offers parts for different vehicle models.
 
Parts With Longer but More Important Replacement Intervals
 
Some components remain in service longer, but their specified intervals are important.
 
Timing Belts
A timing belt synchronizes important engine components and may fail without an obvious warning. Replacement is generally based on the manufacturer's mileage or time interval.
 
On some engines, failure can cause significant engine damage. The car parts replacement schedule should account for both mileage and age when specified.
 
Batteries
 
A battery gradually loses its ability to hold a charge. Climate, driving patterns, electrical demand, battery type, and vehicle usage affect its useful life.
 
Slow cranking, dimming electrical systems, or starting difficulties may indicate that testing is needed. Unlike a timing belt, a battery does not have one universal replacement point.
 
Spark Plugs
 
Spark plugs are essential to petrol-engine combustion, but service intervals vary by engine and plug type.
 
Worn plugs can contribute to rough running, difficult starting, reduced fuel efficiency, or misfires. The vehicle-specific maintenance schedule is more reliable than a generic mileage figure.
How Driving Conditions Change Replacement Timing
 
Two vehicles with identical mileage can have different maintenance requirements. A vehicle driven on open roads may experience different wear from one driven the same distance in congested traffic.
 
Severe conditions include:
 
1.     Frequent short journeys
 
2.     Heavy stop-and-go traffic
 
3.     Extreme temperatures
 
4.     Dusty or poorly surfaced roads
 
5.     Heavy towing or loads
 
6.     Long periods of inactivity
 
Therefore, how often to replace car parts should be considered alongside actual vehicle use. Urban braking can increase brake wear, while dusty roads may require more frequent air-filter inspections.
 
A Practical Replacement Schedule
 
There is no universal schedule, but this framework identifies key items to monitor.
This table is a general framework, not a substitute for the maintenance schedule for a specific vehicle.
 
When Should You Replace a Part Before It Fails?
 
Waiting for complete failure is not always appropriate, particularly for braking, steering, suspension, tires, and engine timing components.
 
The useful question is whether the part still operates within its required limits. Replacing a brake pad at its specified wear limit is different from waiting until all friction material disappears.
 
Similarly, replacing a timing belt at its scheduled interval is different from waiting for failure. Understanding how often should car parts be replaced can help address wear before it becomes a larger mechanical problem.
 
The Maintenance Schedule Is a Starting Point, Not the Whole Story
 
A manufacturer's schedule provides a baseline for a specific vehicle and powertrain, but actual component condition also matters.
 
Drivers should notice unusual sounds, vibrations, warning lights, fluid leaks, braking changes, starting difficulties, or handling changes. Regular inspections can identify developing problems before they result in expensive repairs.
 
A vehicle-specific maintenance plan is the clearest reference for "how often do car parts need to be replaced", while inspections help account for actual wear and changing driving conditions.
 
Maintenance records are also useful for tracking time- and mileage-based services. For owners asking how often do car parts need to be replaced, the most reliable approach combines manufacturer recommendations, mileage and age, and the actual condition of each component.
 
Not sure whether a part is due for replacement or simply needs inspection? Start with the vehicle's maintenance schedule, then have the component's actual condition checked before deciding to replace it.
 
Conclusion
 
There is no universal answer to how often do car parts need to be replaced because components have different service requirements. Brake pads and tires depend heavily on wear and driving conditions, while timing belts and spark plugs generally follow vehicle-specific intervals.
 
The practical approach is to combine the manufacturer's schedule with regular inspections and attention to warning signs. This helps owners address worn components before complete failure.

Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
09:16:54 UTC
18:16:54 KST

Fighting intensifies across Yemen as humanitarian crisis deepens
Clashes between Yemeni forces and Houthis cause casualties on both sides as aid agencies warn of a deepening human crisis.
Fighting between government forces and Houthi fighters has intensified across multiple fronts in Yemen amid a spiralling humanitarian crisis.
Eight soldiers loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government were killed during heavy clashes on the al-Maqatirah front in Lahij governorate, the government-affiliated Tur al-Bahah military axis said in a statement on Saturday.
In Taiz governorate, government troops said they killed 12 Houthi fighters in al-Aqroud, following days of fighting on the outskirts of Taiz city, where Saudi Arabia-backed government forces reported repelling Houthi advances and inflicting heavy losses on the group.
Elsewhere in Taiz, government forces said they broke a Houthi attack on the al-Shaqab front, while government-aligned Homeland Shield Forces reported destroying a Houthi supply vehicle with a drone in al-Wazziyah. The Southern Giants Brigades also said they targeted Houthi positions with precision strikes in al-Madaribah, near the Lahij border.
Meanwhile, government troops and allied Popular Resistance fighters pressed ahead with their offensive in al-Jawf and Marib.
Military officials reported using artillery barrages and drone strikes against Houthi military positions, barracks and troop assemblies in al-Jawf, while coalition aircraft bombed Houthi command hubs and supply depots.
Government artillery and missile units also targeted Houthi lines in Marib.
Yemen’s war has escalated sharply since the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized strategic territory from forces loyal to the country’s internationally recognised government along the Red Sea coast last month.
Government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, responded to the losses with a counteroffensive, and then launched the “Dawn of Yemen” operation, which aims to recapture Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, seized by the Iran-aligned group in 2014.
Saudi helicopter crashes
On the aerial front, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed that the group’s air defence forces brought down a Saudi reconnaissance drone over the governorate of Hajjah. He identified the aircraft as a Turkish-manufactured Lentatek Karayel drone, saying it was the fourth of its kind downed since the latest escalation began.
The Houthis also claimed they shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter in the kingdom’s border province of Najran.
Saudi-led coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki said an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter had crashed in Najran due to a technical malfunction, killing two crew members.
Houthi media also reported 10 Saudi air strikes targeting sites in Saada governorate.
Off the coast of al-Mukalla, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency reported that at least seven armed men on board a skiff attacked a liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker. They fired two shots at the tanker before the vessel’s onboard security detail returned two warning shots, forcing the attackers to change course and disengage.
Worsening humanitarian crisis
Meanwhile, the human cost of the conflict continues to rise, with humanitarian agencies warning of worsening conditions for civilians.
According to the International Organization for Migration, more than 233,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in Yemen, including about 121,000 in Taiz governorate alone.
The World Health Organization has also warned that Taiz city has become functionally isolated, with its 12 hospitals holding fuel for only four days, no surgical supplies, and facing critical shortages of oxygen and medicine amid a growing cholera outbreak.
The displacement crisis has spread to East Africa, with the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) confirming that more than 4,000 refugees have reached the region — 3,800 in Djibouti and roughly 200 in Somalia. The UNHCR also reported that health workers are treating a cholera outbreak at Djibouti’s Markazi camp, where 31 cases and one death have been recorded.

Why Starlink is so important for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:58:00 UTC
17:58:00 KST

How reliant is Ukraine on Starlink systems?
October 18, 2026
Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.
According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.
The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.
However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.
This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.
This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean
According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).
Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet
However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.
This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.
The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.
This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.
The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

Gaza buries remains of 75 Palestinians recovered from rubble of homes destroyed by Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:57:56 UTC
17:57:56 KST

Ramzi Mahmud and Sahin Demir
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Hundreds of Palestinians on Sunday attended the funeral of 75 people, including women and children, whose remains were recently recovered from beneath the rubble of homes destroyed by Israeli forces in Gaza City during the early months of Israel’s genocidal war.
The funeral procession began outside the Daraj Sports Club before the remains were buried at Sheikh Radwan Cemetery in Gaza City.
The remains, wrapped in Palestinian flags, had been laid out at the site Saturday evening to allow relatives to bid farewell.
Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media for Gaza’s Civil Defense, told Anadolu that the remains had been recovered over recent weeks from several destroyed homes in the Daraj neighborhood in northeastern Gaza City.
He said the buildings were bombed while residents were inside during the early months of the war and that the victims belonged to around 20 Palestinian families, including people who had been displaced to the homes.
Majdalawi said efforts to recover bodies from beneath the rubble continue to face severe difficulties due to a lack of equipment and heavy machinery.
The recovery operations are part of the second phase of the Civil Defense’s project to retrieve the bodies of Palestinians trapped under rubble, launched on July 19.
Civil Defense spokesman Mahmoud Basal said at the time that the phase would involve searching 147 destroyed homes across Gaza City and the northern and central parts of the enclave, where an estimated 1,072 bodies were believed to be trapped.
The first phase, launched in November 2025, recovered 333 bodies and remains out of 559 people believed to be buried beneath 54 destroyed homes and buildings. Limited resources prevented teams from reaching around 226 others.
Basal told Anadolu on Oct. 7 that more than 8,000 missing Palestinians were still believed to be under the rubble and warned that recovering them with currently available resources could take around eight years.
Under the first phase of a ceasefire agreement in effect in Gaza since Oct. 10, 2025, Israel was expected to allow heavy equipment and machinery into the enclave, but Palestinian authorities and factions have accused it of failing to meet that and other commitments.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, while around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed.
