Clashes, blazes and wide-scale looting in France during protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:57:45 UTC
17:57:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Clashes, blazes and wide-scale looting grip France on day of protests
Clashes between police and protesters, massive looting and multiple blazes gripped France on Saturday, as nationwide marches against soaring inflation degenerated into street violence of "extreme intensity".
The widespread unrest follows weeks of student protests and deepens political uncertainty as the country readies for elections in six months' time to replace President Emmanuel Macron.
Whole streets in Paris "have been devastated", the city's mayor, Emmanuel Gregoire, said as groups of masked young men torched parked cars and ransacked many shops.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who earlier slammed the "violence of extreme intensity", said late Saturday that 1,200 people had been arrested and 150 police officers hurt.
The violence began on the sidelines of marches in the capital and other cities over the cost of living that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union, which took part, said 800,000 people participated.
Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks. A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.
Looting in many cities
During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.
Scores of shops, supermarkets, pharmacies, luxury boutiques, clothing retailers, opticians, cosmetic vendors and consumer electronics stores were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg.
AFP reporters in Paris saw groups of half a dozen young men often attacking the shops in an organised way: wearing masks and gloves, they first disconnected security cameras before smashing windows to get in.
The looting added to a day of destruction and vandalism, with town halls in several cities targeted.
The one in Limoges, more than 140 years old, was largely destroyed by a blaze set by masked protesters who broke in, according to the region's top official. Protesters also broke into and vandalised two other buildings in Marseille and Lille.
A police compound in Bordeaux was also vandalised, while in Lyon protesters set ablaze a tourist office.
Macron vowed on X that "those who carried out vandalism, attacked administrative offices or businesses, or carried out looting, even in our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished".
Opposition politicians vying to replace Macron in the April and May presidential elections seized on the chaos.
Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen condemned "the rioters" and claimed that the party of her far-left rival for the presidency, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, had "legitimised the violence".
She said on X that, if she came to power, she would protect the French "from the violence of the extreme left".
Mélenchon, who had prominently supported the demonstrations and the student protests that preceded them, urged demonstrators to avoid looting, describing it as "contrary to our methods".
A 'revolution'
France's Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against Macron's government over planned fuel tax hikes, had called for Saturday's "yellow and youth" demonstrations.
The main grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East, which has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
But there were other issues too.
In Paris, tens of thousands marched across the east and north of the city in one major march, some shouting "Everyone hates the police" and "Macron, resign".
High school student Kamil Alahyan, 18, said he was protesting "for so many reasons, the elections coming up in 2027, politicians who lie, the ultra-rich who've been taking more and more wealth over the past 10 years".
Several protesters sought to draw parallels with the French Revolution of 1789.
"It's the Revolution, we're taking the Bastille!" some shouted in Marseille during the forced entry of the mayor's offices.
In the western city of La Rochelle, marchers streamed behind a placard reading: "Revolution or death."
In the southern city of Montpellier, marchers unfurled a giant blue sign reading "The people will win" above a central square.
"The government is trembling and it's right to tremble because when the French people are angry, they never let up," Ryad Rani, the head of the LSU high school student representative body, told journalists in Paris.

Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, killing 3 and injuring 21
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:56:01 UTC
17:56:01 KST

Kanyshai Butun
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Russia and Ukraine exchanged overnight strikes Sunday, killing three people and injuring 21 others, officials on both sides said.
Ukrainian drones targeted oil facilities and an Ozon logistics center in St. Petersburg, as well as Russian social media company VK’s data center in the Leningrad region.
In St. Petersburg, one person was killed and five others were injured, Gov. Alexander Beglov said on Telegram. The city’s oil terminal, Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses caught fire during a “massive” drone attack.
Beglov said 12 apartment buildings and two private homes were damaged, and emergency crews continued to battle the fires.
An Ozon logistics facility was also hit, sparking a fire and prompting staff to evacuate. No injuries were reported at the site, the company said.
Meanwhile, Leningrad Region Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said four people were hospitalized. Drone debris fell on an apartment building in Gatchina, while 55 parked vehicles were damaged in Novosyolye, he said.
An emergency power outage affected 50 apartment buildings, leaving about 20,000 people without electricity, he added.
Russian social media company VKontakte said its data center in the Leningrad region was also targeted but that its services remained available.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian territory, Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014, and the Black Sea.
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 512 drones headed toward the Moscow region overnight, most of which were destroyed by air defenses at a distance from the capital.
Attacks on Ukraine
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, two people were killed and 12 others injured in Russian overnight strikes on residential buildings across the country, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In a post on US social media company X, Zelenskyy accused Moscow of “deliberately” attacking Ukraine’s energy, oil, and gas sectors 76 times since US President Donald Trump announced an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow last week.
He said Moscow targeted substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions overnight, leaving “tens of thousands” of families without power.
Zelenskyy added that Russia had attacked Ukraine with nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, over the past week, stressing that energy facilities were the main targets.
“And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces launched overnight strikes on Ukrainian logistics centers, ports, and vessels allegedly used to support Ukraine’s armed forces.
The ministry said a logistics center operated by Ukrainian postal company Nova Poshta in Rivne was hit. It alleged the facility stored and distributed dual-use goods, including components for long- and medium-range drones.
It added that a cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods was hit at sea about 30 kilometers (19 miles) east of the port of Odesa.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 152 Russian drones during the overnight attack.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

Nighttime museum visits exceed 1.3 million

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:54:38 UTC
17:54:38 KST

The number of visitors to museums and archaeological sites in Türkiye under the nighttime museum program reached 1,326,590, a 32 percent increase compared with the same period last year, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has announced.
The program allows visitors to explore the country’s historical and cultural heritage after sunset, offering a different perspective on museums and archaeological sites.
Announcing the figures on social media, Ersoy said the program had attracted growing interest, adding that the ministry would continue working to bring cultural heritage to wider audiences and transform museums and archaeological sites into living spaces.
“We are delighted to bring the unique beauty of our history and cultural heritage together with visitors in the enchanting atmosphere of the night,” Ersoy said.
The total number of visitors rose from 1,008,080 last year to 1,326,590 this year, according to the minister.
Ephesus Archaeological Site in İzmir ranked first, welcoming 501,811 visitors, up 36 percent from 368,731 last year.
Istanbul’s iconic Galata Tower came second with 277,557 visitors, an increase of 35 percent from 205,344 a year earlier.
Hierapolis Archaeological Site in Denizli, also known as Pamukkale, ranked third with 190,910 visitors.
The Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology in Muğla followed with 62,071 visitors, ahead of Didim Archaeological Site in Aydın with 60,884 and Marmaris Museum in Muğla with 50,053.
Several other museums and archaeological sites also recorded substantial growth.
Visitor numbers at the Istanbul Archaeology Museums rose from 8,789 to 24,850, an increase of 183 percent.
At Didim Archaeological Site, the figure climbed from 27,846 to 60,884, representing a 119 percent increase.
Patara Archaeological Site in Antalya welcomed 28,021 visitors, up 98 percent from 14,141 last year.
At the Terrace Houses of Ephesus in İzmir, visitor numbers increased by 82 percent, from 10,718 to 19,541.
HH Nighttime visits extended at selected sites
The 2026 nighttime museum program ran from June 1 to Oct. 1 at 22 locations affiliated with the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums, comprising 11 museums and 11 archaeological sites.
Following public demand, the program was extended until Oct. 15 at Ephesus and Side, while nighttime visits at Göreme Archaeological Site in Nevşehir will continue until Oct. 31.
The program at Galata Tower in Istanbul will operate throughout the year.
The ministry aims to expand access to the country’s cultural heritage by extending visiting hours at museums and archaeological sites.

Ukraine Repels Russia’s Largest Motorcycle Assault of 2026 Near Pokrovsk, Video
Ukrainian forces repelled what they described as the largest Russian motorcycle assault of 2026 in their area of responsibility near Pokrovsk, killing 43 Russian soldiers, wounding 12 others, and destroying nine motorcycles and a passenger vehicle.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 155th Separate Mechanized Brigade on October 17, the Russian troops attempted to exploit weather conditions to advance toward Ukrainian positions on motorcycles. The attack was stopped by the brigade in coordination with neighboring Ukrainian units.
The brigade reported that Russian forces suffered 55 casualties during the engagement, including 43 killed and 12 wounded. Ukrainian troops also destroyed nine motorcycles and one civilian-type passenger vehicle used during the assault.
Following the failed attack, surviving Russian soldiers attempted to take cover in nearby shelters and defensive positions. Ukrainian forces subsequently struck 36 locations where Russian troops had reportedly sought refuge.
Russian units also deployed several types of drones to support the ground assault. Ukrainian defenders reported destroying 19 FPV drones, two FPV drones positioned to wait for targets, and five Russian Molniya strike drones.
Footage published by the 155th Brigade shows Ukrainian drones targeting Russian personnel and motorcycles during the engagement. The video documents several strikes against Russian assault units, although the full casualty figures could not be independently verified.
The brigade described the engagement as the largest motorcycle assault it had encountered since the beginning of 2026 within its assigned sector of the front.
Motorcycles have become one of the vehicles used by Russian assault units attempting to cross exposed terrain and approach Ukrainian defensive positions. Their mobility allows troops to move quickly across certain sections of the battlefield, although riders remain vulnerable to drone surveillance and precision strikes.
Earlier, Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps reported killing more than 250 Russian troops at a single location during Operation Vivaldi. Ukrainian commanders said they exploited a narrow, 100-meter-wide area to repeatedly target Russian infantry reinforcements, disrupting troop movements and preventing Russian forces from establishing defensive positions.

British startup develos modular ground drone for front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:04:50 UTC
17:04:50 KST

- UK-based Stratonex Defence Technologies unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept for ISR, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
- The company says VARAN can navigate without GPS, uses passive 3D sensing and is designed for low visual, thermal and acoustic signatures.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies has unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept designed to accompany and support forward units on the battlefield, with swappable mission equipment and the ability to navigate without satellite positioning.
The company introduced the vehicle on social media and on its website, describing VARAN as a payload-agnostic platform that can be configured for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
Stratonex says VARAN uses autonomous navigation and passive 3D sensing to move across rough terrain, including in areas where GPS and other satellite navigation signals are jammed or unavailable. Passive sensing means the vehicle builds a picture of its surroundings without emitting signals such as radar or lidar pulses that an enemy could detect, and the company says the platform is designed to keep a low visual, thermal and acoustic signature.
The vehicle is built on an open systems architecture, which Stratonex says allows mission-specific payloads and future technologies to be integrated as requirements change. The company pitches VARAN as a way for troops to move farther and carry more in expeditionary operations, from reconnaissance support to counter-drone and rapid deployment tasks.
Stratonex framed the platform around configuration and integration, asking what capabilities potential users would want added to an unmanned ground vehicle.
Stratonex is a UK-based company co-founded by Ben Everitt, a former Conservative member of Parliament for Milton Keynes North, and describes itself as a developer of autonomous systems and mission software focused on sovereign capability for Britain and its allies. In July 2026, Nasdaq-listed VisionWave Holdings appointed Stratonex as its commercialization and integration partner for the UK and Europe under a non-exclusive distributor agreement covering VisionWave’s autonomous systems, sensing and counter-drone technologies.
Uncrewed ground vehicles have become a growing focus for European armies after their wide use in the war in Ukraine, where both sides rely on them to haul supplies, evacuate wounded troops and carry weapons along front lines exposed to constant drone surveillance. Britain’s Ministry of Defence has also been funding and trialing uncrewed ground platforms for logistics and combat support roles.
Stratonex presents VARAN as a concept platform, and the company is inviting feedback from potential users on which capabilities to integrate as development continues.

The American creative who devoted his career to an imaginary Swiss art school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

The American creative who devoted his career to an imaginary Swiss art school
Dan Levenson is an artist based in Los Angeles. He has invented a Swiss art academy that never existed, complete with a curriculum, furniture and tens of thousands of students. What drives him?
“It really appeals to me to make art in a language that is foreign to me,” Dan Levenson says. He works as an artist in Los Angeles, as far as one gets from Switzerland in terms of time zones. Yet for many years, his work has revolved around the Staatliche Kunstakademie Zürich (SKZ), or Zurich State Academy of Art. But the SKZ never existed. Levenson invented it. He has never made a secret of that.
In his exhibitions, he shows exercises exploring colour scales and paintings built around basic geometric forms. Many of the works appear heavily aged. His performances recreate classes from the art school, and he sometimes exhibits painting aprons that look as though they have been used for years.
The artists whose names appear beneath the paintings – Hanneli Frick, Ramona Gutknecht and Christoph Randegger – never existed. In 2004, a computer programme generated their names from surnames in Zurich’s telephone directory and common Swiss first names. Levenson compiled 135,000 of these names into a book and published it. Ever since, he has drawn on this pool of names for his painting titles, in random order. No name is ever repeated.
Some of the furniture bears traces of genuine studio work. Other objects and paintings are subjected to processes that accelerate their deterioration: Levenson sands them down, soaks them in water and sometimes leaves them exposed to the elements for years. What remains are hairline cracks, scuff marks and stains – as if the objects had spent half a century in storage.
The SKZ is the centre of an entire parallel universe that Levenson has created over the past few years. Its fictional graduates sell their work through the “Little Switzerland” gallery, supposedly founded in the mid-1990s, according to Levenson’s account, by an idealistic group of newly graduated SKZ students.
They ship their art in sturdy wooden crates made by the fictional company Tsüri Logistik. While waiting for their paint to dry, they smoke the fabricated “Letzte” brand of tobacco or hang out at the equally fictitious “Rösti-Wirt” restaurant.
Why Zurich?
Levenson spent a long time thinking about where his fictional art academy should be based. New York was not an option: he was living there himself in the early 2000s, and it would have made the project too autobiographical. “With Berlin and Paris, the associations were too strong for me,” he says. He settled on Zurich.
Language was one factor. Swiss German, which Levenson neither speaks nor understands, crops up repeatedly in his work. His Social History of the SKZExternal link, for example, features fictional first-hand accounts by female students written entirely in Swiss German. For the recordings, he hired professional dialect speakers and translators.
“Even speakers of standard German often don’t understand this language, and I like that it doesn’t have a standardised orthography,” Levenson says. Just as he situated his project geographically at a distance from himself, he put it in a language foreign to him. “It’s twice removed from me,” he says.
Another factor in choosing Zurich was Switzerland’s reputation for being “somewhat harmless”. At the same time, the country plays a surprisingly significant role in the art world and is closely associated with the history of the 20th-century avant-garde.
In Zuefallsoperatione (Chance Operations), an art game for children in which shapes can be rearranged endlessly in different combinations, Levenson makes a clear reference to the chance-based games of the Dadaists, who repeatedly recombined words and forms through collage. The Dadaists came together in Zurich in 1916.
Modernism as a haunted house
The formal exercises Levenson paints under the names of fictitious Swiss artists are rendered in the style of classical modernism from the first half of the 20th century. In this tradition, good form was not merely a question of beauty; it was also bound up with the hope of creating a better world.
Yet the modernism that Levenson repeatedly revisits through formal exercises also resembles a haunted house. “Since the 1960s or 1970s, fine art education has moved away from this idea of fundamentals, of formalism, of composition, of colour theory,” Levenson says. “But the older generation remained a kind of antagonist, and that kind of painting and modernism and tradition haunted my generation of artists.”
Many of his exhibition pieces, with their dusty, museum-like appearance, seem like relics of a fallen regime. Levenson’s early works that explored Switzerland were interested in the aesthetics of bureaucracy: files and collective standards such as the A4 paper format, which is uncommon in American usage.
Given the strong connection to Zurich, it is tempting to see the strict geometries of his paintings as an echo of the Zurich Concretists. This movement, whose artists included Max Bill, set out to shape the entire environment for the better, “from the spoon to the city”. They later achieved international success, particularly with their meticulous typography and sophisticated corporate designs for major companies.
In the 1960s, modernism’s enthusiasm for form came under fierce attack, as young artists mocked it. Despite what his paintings might suggest, if nostalgia surfaces in Levenson’s work, it is directed less at early modernism than at the creative force of the 1960s.
He sees himself as part of the tradition of artistic institutional critique practised by Marcel Broodthaers. In 1968, the Belgian artist appointed himself director of his own Musée d’Art Moderne, Département des Aigles (Museum of Modern Art, Department of Eagles). He opened its first department in his Brussels apartment.
“As an 80s kid, with parents who lived through the 1960s, they were always talking about this magical but also disorienting time that happened just before I was born. I think I grew up with the feeling that I had somehow been born post-festum, after the party,” Levenson says.
While studying at the Royal College of Art in London in the 1990s, he was “constantly angry”. After the Cold War, art schools, too, began orienting themselves more towards the market. But Levenson had no desire to paint portraits for patrons, and he also struggled with the demand to specialise. He wanted to move between styles and work across painting, installation and performance.
“There’s something about being an art student that is more pure or authentic than being a professional artist. Art school should be years where you’re protected from the market. It should really just be about creativity, growth, exploration and community,” Levenson says.
That is why his fictional Swiss artists have no biographies. He used to invent them, he says, but found the exercise unsatisfying: “I really downplay their individuality. The important thing is that they are working together to try to solve a problem.”His imagined Switzerland also embodies this idea: it is an “idealised image of a true community, where people are bound together by a language, by a programme of research and by creative exploration.”
For Levenson, the SKZ is also a kind of second youth: “The point of my work is to send myself back to school.”

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

After a year in turmoil, the Louvre faces uncertain future
PARIS – The Louvre is gradually plugging the security gaps exposed by the spectacular burglary of Oct 19, 2025, but its reputation has taken a battering and its creaking infrastructure is a growing source of concern.
The beloved Parisian museum, one of the most visited in the world, has spent a year as the subject of police investigations, government reports and parliamentary inquiries following the theft of eight crown jewels in broad daylight a year ago.
The heist exposed a string of failures, from old or non-existent CCTV cameras and a chronic shortage of equipment to the lack of a modern security control room and a security director.
“We still feel the trauma of the burglary,” Valerie Baud, a workers’ representative from the CFDT trade union, told AFP.
Parliament has heard how, in the run-up to the burglary, the institution had spent just €3 million (S$4.3 million) out of €83 million earmarked for a security masterplan because of administrative delays, management decisions and red tape.
The museum had “prioritised projects that were visible and attractive”, the French Court of Auditors found in one of many damning judgements.
That report and others, compounded by a staff strike and a spate of other incidents – including a water leak and a major ticket-fraud scandal – hastened the downfall of Louvre president Laurence des Cars, who resigned in February.
“The Louvre needs a change in security culture, which has yet to happen and will take several years,” said Laurent Lafon, who is monitoring the museum as chairman of the Senate’s culture committee.
“The Louvre’s leaders must embrace the idea that security is a priority, which wasn’t the case,” he told AFP.
‘Rapid progress’
New museum chief Christophe Leribault, who replaced des Cars in February, argues that change is taking place.
“The security masterplan is making rapid progress,” he told AFP in a written statement, while stressing the “complexity” of carrying out the work while keeping the museum open to the public.
The museum has pledged to invest around €20 million a year until 2032 and, since July, has a new dedicated security director.
Short-term worries about security are also giving way to longer-term questions about how to finance a palace-wide modernisation programme.
Every year, nearly nine million visitors walk the Louvre’s galleries, many unaware of the decrepit state of some of the rooms, the ageing plumbing and wiring, as well as poor ventilation in summer and non-existent heating in winter.
Leribault issued his most alarming warning yet earlier this week, telling Le Figaro newspaper “that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated, and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public”.
Money worries
French President Emmanuel Macron unveiled his vision – called “Louvre – Nouvelle Renaissance” – in January 2025 which included a new entrance and gallery for the Mona Lisa among other changes.
It came with an eye-watering proposed price tag of a billion euros – which now looks unrealistic for a country facing a severe budget crunch.
Unions accused him and Louvre management of prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.
“We can step up security without going through with this project, which does not address the priorities and states as its goal an unsustainable increase in visitor numbers,” said Christian Galani, a representative of the hard-left CGT union.
Leribault remains committed to it, however.
Part of his task as Louvre head is finding new private sources of income from donors who will be invited to sponsor work – and earn public recognition and perhaps naming rights in return.
Other sources of income could come from further ticket price hikes.
The target is €360 million.
“It’s a huge challenge, and I don’t know whether I’ll succeed,” he said in June. AFP

NEW DELHI: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh will visit Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 19 and 20 to represent India at the 25th meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) Council of Heads of Government.According to news agency ANI, citing the Ministry of Defence, the meeting will focus on strengthening multilateral cooperation among SCO member states in trade, economy, investment, connectivity, innovation and cultural-humanitarian exchanges. The participating countries are also expected to review ongoing cooperation initiatives and consider decisions related to the organisation’s financial and institutional functioning.The agenda is expected to cover trade and investment cooperation, transport and logistics, industrial cooperation, the creative and digital economy, innovation and financial interaction, according to Interfax, which cited the Russian trade mission in Tajikistan. Social and cultural-humanitarian cooperation is also expected to feature in the discussions.India has highlighted the need to expand intra-SCO trade, lower trade costs, strengthen supply chains and improve connectivity.
At a meeting of SCO ministers responsible for foreign economic and trade activities in Dushanbe in September, India called for simplified customs procedures, paperless trade, electronic document exchange and stronger multimodal connectivity, according to the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.India also highlighted opportunities for cooperation in agriculture, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing, electronics, energy security, renewable energy and green hydrogen. It called for greater use of digital and cross-border payments and improved access to trade finance for micro, small and medium enterprises and start-ups.The October meeting will provide India an opportunity to exchange views with other SCO member states on advancing practical and mutually beneficial cooperation. India remains actively engaged in SCO mechanisms and contributes to regional cooperation through initiatives in start-ups and innovation, digital public infrastructure and people-to-people exchanges, the Ministry of Defence said.
The Council of Heads of Government adopts the SCO’s budget and addresses key issues related to cooperation within the organisation, particularly in the economic sphere. The body meets annually and is distinct from the Council of Heads of State, which serves as the organisation’s highest decision-making forum.The previous meeting of the Council of Heads of Government was held in Moscow on November 18, 2025, where India was represented by external affairs minister S Jaishankar, according to ANI.

Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:59 UTC
16:32:59 KST

Why Iran-US negotiations keep failing
Relations between the two countries are dominated by policy complexes shaped by a history of hostility.
Since the start of the war, there have been several negotiation initiatives between the United States and Iran. Only one – the memorandum of understanding signed in Islamabad on June 18 – was concluded, but it collapsed within days.
While prevailing analyses tend to explain this failure through the details of the provisions, this article proceeds from a different premise: that the diplomatic stalemate between the two sides is shaped by a syndrome that has governed US-Iranian relations for years.
In international relations, psychological syndromes can arise as a result of deep crises that leave their mark on political consciousness and memory, potentially obstructing efforts at rapprochement and negotiation between countries.
In the case of Iran and the US, the syndrome is comprised of two complexes: the complex Washington developed as a result of the 1979 siege of the US embassy in Tehran and the complex Tehran developed as a result of historical US hostility and its withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018.
The roots of the rupture between the two countries go as far back as August 1953 when US and British intelligence agencies helped overthrow the nationalist government of Mohammad Mosaddegh after it nationalised the oil industry in 1951. Since then, a perception has become entrenched in Iranian consciousness: that Washington does not accept an independent government in Tehran and it is prepared to sabotage it if it goes against its interests.
From this perspective, Washington’s decision to host Shah Reza Pahlavi, who had just been overthrown by his people, for medical treatment in October 1979 was read in revolutionary Tehran as a prelude to a second coup.
Iranian students stormed the US embassy on November 4 that year and held 52 Americans for 444 days. Diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed and have not been restored to this day.
While the incident is portrayed in the Iranian narrative as a defence of the revolution, in American consciousness, it established the image of Iran as a state that does not respect international norms, whose word cannot be relied upon and whose behaviour should not be rewarded.
That is the embassy siege complex. It is not about the incident itself so much as the informal rule it produced in US decision-making: that Iran must concede first and its concession must be verified before it receives anything in return.
The Iranian complex was shaped by this history as well, but it reached its peak in May 2018 when US President Donald Trump withdrew from the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) despite the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA’s) confirmation that Tehran was complying with it.
Just two weeks later, US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced 12 demands for a new deal, only four of which were related to the nuclear file. Seven of them were related to Iran’s regional behaviour in Lebanon, Palestine, Iraq, Yemen, Syria, Afghanistan and the Gulf. In other words, Washington did not merely revoke an existing agreement; it also raised the ceiling of its conditions for any future agreement.
The knot then deepened in June 2025 when the US took part in the Twelve-Day War and struck the nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at a time when a new round of indirect negotiations was scheduled in Muscat. It then reached its furthest point with Washington’s participation alongside Israel in the current war.
Accordingly, a conviction became entrenched in the Iranian consciousness that an American signature guarantees nothing, that any agreement can be overturned with a change of administration and indeed that negotiation itself may be a cover for war rather than an alternative to it.
The informal rule this has produced in Iranian decision-making is that there will be no step taken before binding guarantees and no concession before pressure is lifted.
Thus, the two complexes stand at opposite ends: The first requires Iranian action before an American quid pro quo while the second requires an American guarantee before Iranian action.
A reading of the recent negotiation initiatives shows that every US initiative bears the imprint of the embassy siege complex. The 15-point plan put forward in March demanded the dismantling of the Natanz, Isfahan and Fordow facilities; an end to uranium enrichment; the suspension of Iran’s missile programme; and the abandonment of its allies in exchange for promises to lift sanctions later.
The May draft by White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner linked the release of Iran’s frozen funds to the suspension of enrichment first. The American response in September also stipulated the freezing of enrichment and the entry of inspectors throughout the negotiation period.
What remains constant in the American initiatives is that Iranian action precedes the quid pro quo and verification precedes trust.
The imprint of the JCPOA withdrawal complex in the Iranian initiatives is also a constant. The five-point response in late March demanded guarantees that war would not be repeated. The 10 points put forward in April demanded a binding UN Security Council resolution shielding any agreement from being overturned. And the 14 points in May demanded a nonaggression pledge that includes Israel.
Meanwhile, the seven-day plan proposed by Tehran last month stipulated the lifting of sanctions and the US naval blockade on Iran before the opening of the Strait of Hormuz on the sixth day and the start of nuclear negotiations on the seventh. What remains constant in the Iranian initiatives is that guarantees precede action and the lifting of pressure precedes Iranian concessions.
All these initiatives were dialogue between two complexes with each side drafting its text to protect itself from a repetition of its historical experience with the other, rather than to meet the other halfway. This may explain why the gap in substance has narrowed, but the gap in trust has not.
The Islamabad memorandum represents the exception that proves the rule as it was the closest moment to a settlement because it was formulated to reassure both sides over their core concerns. To reassure Washington, it stipulated the dilution of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium and made the lifting of sanctions and unfreezing of funds conditional on Iranian implementation.
To reassure Tehran, it provided for an end to hostilities, respect for mutual sovereignty, a mechanism to monitor implementation and UN Security Council approval of the final agreement. Ballistic missiles were also entirely absent from the text.
But this agreement did not hold. Tehran suspended its participation in the Geneva round of talks because of the absence of a ceasefire in Lebanon, which had been a consistent demand in every Iranian initiative since March. In the Iranian reading, Washington’s inability to rein in Israel confirmed that an American signature was not enough. The JCPOA withdrawal complex immediately kicked in, and the two sides returned to square one.
By late September, the dispute appeared to have shifted definitively from substance to sequencing. Informed sources indicated that it now revolves around the order of steps rather than their content and the stated goal has become a return to an enhanced version of the June memorandum.
Here the two complexes appear in their clearest form: Washington wants the Strait of Hormuz opened and enrichment frozen first because it does not trust Iran while Tehran wants the naval blockade lifted first because it does not trust the US.
A comparison between Pompeo’s 2018 conditions and the June 2026 memorandum shows that US demands have retreated from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear file and the Strait of Hormuz while Iranian demands have shifted from compensation to be paid by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties.
In other words, the substantive gap between the two sides has narrowed considerably – something that would have been unimaginable eight years ago.
However, the two complexes have not diminished; indeed, they may have deepened because of the war. Each complex feeds the other until together they have become a single syndrome, and diplomatic deadlock has turned from a passing condition into a stable structure.
Accordingly, any new formula for sequencing the steps, however precise, will remain unable to break this deadlock unless it addresses both complexes at once – something that requires a third party capable of guaranteeing both the action and the reciprocal action simultaneously.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

CURE Art Gallery opens in Bursa with works by Oran, Yalçındağ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:32:18 UTC
16:32:18 KST

AA Photo
CURE Art Gallery opened in the northwestern province of Bursa’s Balat district on Oct. 15 with an inaugural exhibition featuring recent works and previously unseen pieces by Turkish artists Ahmet Oran and Ekrem Yalçındağ.
Running through Nov. 12, the exhibition brings together two distinct approaches to contemporary painting, exploring color, texture, repetition and abstraction.
Oran builds layered surfaces by applying paint in different colors onto canvas and selectively scraping away sections with spatulas and scrapers. The technique reveals underlying layers, creating lines and bands of color across the surface.
Yalçındağ incorporates recurring botanical motifs and circular compositions into his paintings. His dense application of paint through small brushstrokes creates a raised, textured surface. Both artists have exhibited in Türkiye and abroad.
The gallery’s founders said the initiative establishes a dedicated space in Bursa where audiences can regularly engage with contemporary art and interact directly with artists.
Beyond its exhibition program, CURE Art Gallery plans to develop long-term relationships with artists, collectors, art writers and other professionals in the art world.
The opening exhibition was held with the participation of Oran and Yalçındağ, in collaboration with Lexus Nilüfer. The works remain on display at the gallery until Nov. 12.

Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Israel’s ties with Europe are fraying. Can its election change that?
European condemnation of Netanyahu is mounting, but analysts say Israel’s election offers little prospect of a material change for Palestinians.
While marking Israel’s 75th anniversary, Ursula von der Leyen offered solidarity.
“Europe and Israel are bound to be friends and allies,” the European Commission president said on April 23, 2023.
That friendship reached beyond diplomacy. Israel played international football in Europe, competed in Eurovision and shared intelligence with European governments. Its weapons industry was woven into European production lines.
Those ties still exist, but have since become battlegrounds after Israel’s systematic destruction of Gaza, which has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians.
European countries have withdrawn from Eurovision over Israel’s participation. European footballers have refused to play the Israeli team. Some declarations of friendship have been recast as condemnation.
Ireland and Spain have long led criticism of Israel’s oppression of Palestinians.
At the recent UN General Assembly, Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin said Israel’s actions in Gaza “will shame the world”, while Spain’s Pedro Sanchez spoke of “condemning unequivocally the genocide that Netanyahu continues to perpetrate in Gaza”.
Recently, in a sign of how much has changed in three years, Britain, whose Balfour Declaration helped lay the foundations for Israel’s creation, imposed a ban on goods from illegal settlements, while its foreign secretary accused Israeli settlers of ethnic cleansing.
On Saturday, a group of settlers attacked European diplomats and officials from Belgium, France and Poland who were visiting Palestinian olive harvesters near the village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank. The assault, which came a day after settlers attacked a United States journalist north of Ramallah, drew widespread international condemnation.
Scarred relations between Europe and Israel may never fully repair, experts said as Israel heads to an election on October 27 that is too close to call.
Will the result affect Europe-Israel ties?
Yossi Mekelberg, a Middle East analyst at Chatham House, said if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returns with the far right, “certain things will become irreversible. The damage caused by this government is deep”.
Nicola Perugini, a senior lecturer in international relations at the University of Edinburgh, warned that the re-election of the leader, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC), would see Gaza’s population continue to struggle under “unliveable” conditions.
A Netanyahu coalition with more liberal parties might slow settlement expansion. But having a premier wanted by the ICC at the helm would likely lead to a continued deterioration of the Israel-Europe relationship. Replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a break with the policies driving European criticism, experts said.
For instance, Gadi Eisenkot, former military chief and leader of the centrist Yashar party, viewed as Netanyahu’s main challenger, has opposed Palestinian statehood.
An annual public opinion survey by Israel’s Mitvim Institute last year showed that 67 percent of Israelis regarded the EU more as an adversary, compared with 14 percent who saw it as a friend.
Mekelberg sees potential for a different relationship under a more liberal government.
“The conversation with Europe would be more reasonable and rational,” he said, but warned that the picture would not change overnight.
More humanitarian aid could be delivered to Palestinians and the rate of settlement expansion could slow, analysts said. The E1 settlement plan could be abandoned.
But Julie M Norman, an associate fellow at Chatham House, said that may not be enough for European governments to make amends.
Rather, Europe would look for concrete moves towards Palestinian statehood and ending the occupation.
“But so far, we’re not seeing that under the current government and probably not under the next,” she said.
‘Ruling elite in several countries trying to align with the public’
At the beginning of Israel’s war on Gaza, Western leaders supported Israel’s campaign.
But sustained pressure from groups demanding action to stop the onslaught in Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank – from civil rights organisations, international courts, trade unions and professional bodies to millions of protesters across the world – forced governments to act, analysts said.
“Now the ruling elite in several countries is trying to align itself with the public,” Neve Gordon, an Israeli professor of human rights law at Queen Mary University in London, told Al Jazeera, adding that the pro-Palestine movement had changed the “common sense” position of governments.
Pew Research Center polling in the UK found that the proportion viewing Israel unfavourably rose from 61 to 69 percent between spring 2025 and spring this year, from 66 to 75 percent in Italy and from 64 to 73 percent in Germany, one of its strongest allies.
Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist, linked that pressure to recognition of Palestinian statehood, moves towards suspending the EU-Israel association agreement and bans on settlement imports.
“If anything has had any impact on European policy towards Israel, it is precisely the wave of protests over the last few years,” she said.
Norman at Chatham House said European states have shifted from targeted measures, such as sanctioning far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, towards “broader structures, in terms of scrutiny of the Israeli state itself”.
But support for Israel persists in parts of Europe, noted Oxford University professor Janina Dill.
Two successive German governments have been “utterly unwilling to act on justified public criticism of Germany’s diplomatic and material support for Israel”, she said.
With support generally on the decline, Israel has cultivated ties with Europe’s far right, finding common ground in nationalism and hostility towards Islam, despite historic and current ties to anti-Semitism.
Menachem Klein, a senior lecturer at Bar-Ilan University, told Al Jazeera, that the current government has caused “huge damage to relations with friends and allies” – and scars will take time to heal.
Mekelberg added that improving relations requires concrete steps towards a peace process and a different future for Palestinians. Even then, the damage will endure.
Israel’s isolation
The election debate in Israel has focused on security, rather than the morality of the continued killing of Palestinians or the country’s international standing.
Israel’s wars abroad appear to have widespread domestic support.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey in April found that 92 percent of Jewish Israelis highly rated the military’s management of the Iran war. Eighty percent supported continuing the fighting against Hezbollah, even at the cost of friction with Washington. In September, Jewish People Policy Institute polling found that 72 percent of Jewish Israelis would not accept withdrawal to Gaza’s border without retaining an Israeli security perimeter inside the territory.
Israel’s diplomatic isolation might therefore seem an obvious election issue. Instead, “it is barely discussed”, Yaakov Katz, cofounder of the Middle East American Dialogue Forum, wrote in an article for Chatham House.
Rather, the main talking points are the degradation of Hamas and the weakening of Hezbollah and Iran, while the opposition promises to lower living costs, investigate the failures surrounding October 7 and draft members of the ultra-Orthodox community into the military.
“It is not that Israelis are unaware of the campus protests, the arms embargoes, growing European sanctions and recognition of a Palestinian state, and the International Criminal Court arrest warrants,” Katz wrote. “The 7 October attack has shaped public opinion in Israel to such an extent that when a foreign government criticises Israel … Israelis see only two viewpoints: that the criticism is either antiSemitic or it is ignorant.”

Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

16:03:00 KST

Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections
October 18, 2026
The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.
The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.
The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.
What happened in the Czech Senate elections?
Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.
The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.
Babis called the result "catastrophic."
"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.
That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.
His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.
Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

‘Keep away from the doctor’: a visit to an influencer’s wellness event, where the advice could kill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
07:00:54 UTC
16:00:54 KST

A roar of laughter erupts from a crowd inside a large conference room at the De Vere Cranage Estate hotel. The joke? The idea that visiting the doctor could help treat a serious illness.
On stage the controversial Australian proponent of natural remedies Barbara O’Neill is taking part in a question-and-answer session during a five-day wellness conference, where science mixes uncomfortably with Bible verse and potentially deadly pseudo-scientific practices.
She is advising people attending at the event in Cheshire on a variety of medical ailments, and dismisses the use of antibiotics, vaccines or scientifically proven cancer treatment.
Tickets for the residential retreat can cost up to £1,300. An undercover reporter for the Guardian attended for one day, observing four sessions covering topics including the immune system and one titled Barbara Under Attack.
The audience’s rapturous laughter is prompted by a woman asking O’Neill if there is anything that could help her lupus, which she says has not responded well to the doctor’s treatments. “Yes, keep away from the doctor,” quips O’Neill.
O’Neill tells the audience that she is “just a little lady”, but she is an incredibly influential one, with 3.6 million Instagram followers and 1.7 million on Facebook. Many of her videos rack up millions of views.
Having initially found success promoting alternative treatments in Australia, in 2019 O’Neill was banned from providing any health services in her home country, where authorities found she was responsible for “misleading vulnerable people”. They said she “made dangerous claims not supported by evidence and posed a risk to public safety”.
She has since taken her unregulated services overseas, most recently with a string of appearances in the UK and Ireland which prompted concern from experts in both countries. A number of prominent doctors and scientists have told the Guardian her advice is “dangerous”, with some warning it could kill.
O’Neill appears regal sitting on stage in an armchair offering audience members softly spoken advice on endometriosis, varicose veins and constipation.
The 73-year-old is dressed in a long skirt with a woollen wrap, which she later switches for a soft cardigan, creating a look that sits somewhere between Queen Elizabeth II at Balmoral and Claudia Winkleman in The Traitors. The Highlands-inspired attire is a nod to her Scottish heritage, which the Australian mentions on multiple occasions.
She carries an air of authority to her devoted followers, many of whom seem confident that her doctrine could improve their health.
Much of her core teaching aligns with established scientific health advice: few doctors would dispute that a balanced diet, regular exercise, hydration and plenty of sleep are important factors for good health, while it is advisable to avoid alcohol, caffeine and smoking.
During some of the lectures, O’Neill draws diagrams on a whiteboard while issuing long scientific-sounding explanations.
She talks about the glycocalyx lining of the endothelium cells, which provides anticoagulant effects and releases nitric oxide, a vasodilator.
But she also makes some highly unscientific and potentially deadly recommendations.
During the Q&A session, a woman says that while she recently underwent tests, doctors found a stomach tumour, which she says two specialists have advised her to have surgically removed.
“Sometimes scans are not right,” replies O’Neill, who advises the woman to treat the tumour with a castor oil compress – kitchen roll soaked with high viscosity oil from the castor plant – on the outside of the body.
That day O’Neill recommends the same remedy for nasal polyps, endometriosis, carpal tunnel syndrome and bile duct stones. Medical experts told the Guardian there was no evidence castor oil compresses did anything to improve any of those conditions.
She suggests using castor oil with a pinch of cayenne pepper in the eye to an audience member with glaucoma and high blood pressure.
Prof Gus Gazzard, a leading glaucoma expert, says: “There is absolutely no evidence to support these claims, and unfortunately, there’s the possibility that they might indeed cause harm.”
The questions continue, read out by her husband, Michael, who gives some of his own lectures during the retreat. The pair stumble over long names of medical conditions, while the audience laughs along.
O’Neill advises a pregnant woman against taking folic acid, which randomised controlled trials have shown can protect against neural tube deficits in babies. To someone else, she claims antibiotics are “the worst thing to give” for infections.
To a woman who says she does not have a functioning thyroid, she recommends slowly stopping her dose of thyroxine, which is prescribed for thyroid dysfunction, to “see what the body does”.
Medical experts say this would lead to fatigue, hair loss, weight gain, a slow heart rate and low mood. Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, says: “Someone without a functioning thyroid cannot make thyroid hormone, so stopping thyroxine to ‘see what the body does’ really makes no sense and risks serious, potentially life-threatening illness.”
A woman who says she has diabetes tells O’Neill she is hoping to come off metformin, a drug used to lower blood sugar levels. Metformin is typically used to treat type 2 diabetes, which can respond to a change in diet, while type 1 requires daily insulin injections. Both types require blood glucose monitoring. O’Neill advises her to stop testing her blood sugar because it would “balance right out with the change in diet”.
This advice is “very dangerous”, according to Gill Livingston, a professor of psychiatry of older people at UCL. “Untreated diabetes means the body is bathed in bloodstream high sugar and increases the risk of multiple physical illnesses, such as loss of eyesight, loss of peripheral sensation, dementia and sometimes death.”
Refusing medical tests is a regular theme in O’Neill’s teachings across her publications, her social media and her public appearances. “It’s amazing how many tests are creating illnesses,” she says at the Cheshire event.
At another point, not long after encouraging a follower to ignore her oncologist’s recommendation to take a drug, and without any clarification about the type of cancer the woman was being treated for, she says: “They give you a label and then they give you a drug.”
Interspersed throughout the day are claims that people have recovered from illnesses after taking her advice. She cites a man who had suffered a stroke, and had “no adverse effects at all” when he stopped taking medication prescribed by his doctor, including statins and blood thinners, on one of her retreats.
“It’s outrageous what medicine will do. We have to start saying ‘no, thank you’,” she says. “It doesn’t matter what they say to you, what fear they put into you, say no.
“The body, it’s got an inbuilt ability to heal itself.”
Prof Liam Smeeth, director of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, calls her claims “extraordinary”. He says: “Most disturbingly, many of these – if followed – will cause substantial harm, and this could include death.”
It is clear some of her followers have a lot of trust in her. Speaking to the Guardian’s undercover reporter at the end of the day, one audience member says O’Neill’s answer to her question was “very helpful” and she now has the confidence to go against specialists’ advice for surgery for a health condition.
In other conversations during breaks, some people attending say they have lost trust in western medicine after side-effects or failed treatments.
One woman in her 60s explains that she and her family refused masks and vaccines during the Covid crisis, had gatherings and “actually washed my hands less than normal”. She says her husband went into hospital in early 2020 with pneumonia and died two days later. She blames the medics for his death.
“You know they’re satanists, don’t you?” she says, of the government and those who run major global institutions. “The elite are all flesh-eating paedophiles.”
Some at the conference wear amulets they claim protect against 5G signals and a stall selling them proves popular. There is no evidence that 5G signals cause harm and yet O’Neill advises those working at a computer to invest in a device to protect against damage she says is caused by electronic devices and “balance the body after exposure to an electromagnetic field [EMF]”.
Dr David Robert Grimes, an expert in biostatistics at Trinity College Dublin, says fear of modernity is a common pseudoscience trope.
“The canard that EMFs are ‘damaging’ us is a tired one that exploits our ignorance of technical terms to instil fear,” he says. “There is no device that ‘balances’ you after exposure, because the central conceit is nonsense. We live in a world with light, heat, radio waves, and the sun, so EMFs are all around us. The idea of balancing is really meaningless.”
He adds: “The evidence is clear that patients seduced by the false allure of complementary medicine fare objectively worse than those that stick to conventional treatments. These patients are typically convinced by dubious healers to delay or reject life-saving treatments until it’s too late, with often tragic consequences.”
Before O’Neill’s most recent tour, senior doctors and medical experts, including Grimes, wrote to some of the venues hosting her conferences urging them to reconsider holding events that would “spread dangerous health fictions to a susceptible audience”.
O’Neill’s husband, Michael, co-runs her company and is the engine behind her tours. In an afternoon session titled Barbara Under Attack, he describes her “persecution” by authorities, the scientific community and the media . “There is a war against us,” he tells the audience.
After an approach from the Guardian to O’Neill for comment on her claims at the conference, a video of the couple appears on her Instagram and Facebook pages warning their followers of “disgusting” reporting. Michael reads out the statement issued to the Guardian.
“The complaints against Barbara are purely speculative, based on an ideology that the only legitimate way to health is through the medical profession,” he says.
Michael claims the couple have not received complaints about O’Neill’s work and highlights statistics about medical mistakes in the NHS.
He adds: “The campaign against Barbara by the media, and academics is a modern-day witch-hunt that has no substance in facts, but purely an ideology that supports the most corrupt organisation in the world; the pharmaceutical industry.”
The pair have vowed to continue holding events. O’Neill says she is driven by God, who she believes spoke directly to her.
“It would be wrong of me to stop.”

No arrests after West Bank settler attack; police accuse European diplomats of not cooperating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:31:27 UTC
15:31:27 KST

No suspects have been arrested in the attacks on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the West Bank over the weekend, and Israeli police officials are now accusing European diplomatic missions of failing to cooperate with the investigation into Saturday's assault near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, northeast of Ramallah.
According to police sources, investigators have sought detailed witness statements and photographic evidence from the European diplomats who were attacked by Jewish rioters while attending an olive harvest. However, the officials claim that the diplomatic missions involved have so far failed to cooperate with those requests.
Police said investigators from the West Bank District had contacted Israel's Foreign Ministry to approach the diplomatic missions and arrange the collection of evidence. As of Saturday evening, according to the sources, the missions had not provided the requested cooperation.
Investigators are seeking detailed testimony, video and photographic material, access to the vehicles involved in the attack and permission to collect forensic evidence. Police officials said the requests were intended to help identify the attackers, arrest them and ensure that everyone involved is brought to justice.
The investigation is continuing, but no arrests have been made in connection with either Saturday's attack on European diplomats in Taybeh or Friday's assault on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post, in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Police said their investigators and the Shin Bet domestic security agency were continuing efforts to identify those responsible for the attack on Levine, who underwent surgery on her hand Saturday.
Her daughter, Ashley Milner, said one of the fingers on her mother's left hand had been cut so deeply that the bone and tendon were exposed. Levine also suffered a broken rib, fractures in several vertebrae and cuts across her body.
According to police sources, West Bank District commander Maj. Gen. Moshe Pinchi is personally overseeing the investigations into the weekend's violence. He has assigned both cases to the district's central investigative unit, which is working alongside the Shin Bet.
Additional investigators have been assigned to the cases, and Pinchi has emphasized the importance of intelligence sharing and investigative cooperation between police and the Shin Bet to identify the attackers and bring them to justice.
Saturday's assault on the European diplomatic delegation took place during an olive harvest in Taybeh, the last entirely Christian Palestinian village in the West Bank. The delegation included representatives from France, Belgium and Poland, as well as French Mayor Bernard Baudoux of Aulnoye-Aymeries, whose municipality has a sister-city relationship with Taybeh.
"They were attacked by seven adult men, ages 20 and older, who apparently did not come from a nearby outpost but from farther away, meaning they had been specifically summoned," one of the diplomats present at the scene told ynet. "They kicked the French mayor, and he was injured."
A European diplomat traveling in one of the vehicles described how the delegation was forced to flee when masked settlers approached carrying sticks and metal crowbars.
"The residents of Taybeh invited diplomats and peace activists to the olive harvest to protect them. At one point, we heard that settlers were approaching, so we immediately got into the car and started driving. Then I saw masked settlers carrying sticks and metal crowbars running toward us. It was clear they had no good intentions. It was frightening. They hadn't come to pick olives," the diplomat said.
"They kicked the French mayor, and after beating him, they shouted 'Viva la France.' They had recognized the French flag," he continued. "They also attacked the Belgian vehicle. When you see something like that, you say to yourself, 'My God, how can something like this happen?'"
The diplomat said the delegation had arrived with security personnel and found it particularly troubling that the violence occurred in an area under Israeli control.
"We knew settler violence was serious, but when you witness it firsthand, you understand just how terrible it is, especially for the residents who depend on the olive harvest for their livelihoods," he said.
Although the reported assault on Baudoux was not captured on camera, footage subsequently showed him on the ground, while photographs documented a shattered window in a vehicle belonging to the Belgian Consulate.
The attacks have provoked an international outcry and exposed conflicting responses among senior Israeli officials. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, the IDF and Israeli police condemned the violence, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office issued an English-language statement questioning whether the available evidence established the full sequence of events and the identity of those responsible.
The Prime Minister's Office also noted that the delegation had entered a sensitive area without prior coordination with the IDF and raised concerns about what it described as a coordinated campaign to discredit Israel and Jewish residents of the West Bank during the olive harvest.
Members of the European delegation rejected the suggestion that they should have coordinated the visit with the military.
"That is a misleading claim," delegation members said. "Taybeh is in Area B, and visits there do not require coordination. Diplomats visit frequently, and the military has never escorted them or required prior coordination."
One of the diplomats also criticized Netanyahu's response, saying the prime minister had failed to acknowledge the significance of the attack on a delegation visiting a Christian community.
"The mayor's political background is irrelevant to the question of who attacked him. Netanyahu's statement completely ignores the fact that this is a Christian village and that the delegation came from Catholic countries that consider themselves committed to protecting Christians in the West Bank. In Europe, Netanyahu's statement is seen as shocking," the diplomat said.
The incident has also prompted warnings of diplomatic consequences for Israel. Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said his country would continue pushing for European Union sanctions against those responsible for settler violence and those supporting it.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot demanded that Israeli authorities arrest and prosecute those responsible for the attack and take urgent steps to protect civilians from further violence. Poland's Foreign Ministry also condemned the incident.
The assault on Levine the previous day drew sharp criticism from Washington. U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee described the attack on the unarmed photographer as a despicable act of violence and called for a full investigation, arrests and prosecutions.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also expressed concern over the incidents and called on Israel to take stronger action against settler violence.
"We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing. We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio told reporters.
The violence has renewed attention on the situation in Taybeh, where residents have reported repeated attacks on homes, vehicles and agricultural land. The village, which holds particular religious significance for Christians, has seen families leave amid growing fears over their safety.
In July 2025, following an attack in which rioters set fire to a cemetery and desecrated a church, Huckabee visited Taybeh and described the incident as an act of terrorism.
Despite the repeated condemnations from Israeli and foreign officials, no suspects had been arrested in either of the two latest attacks as of Sunday morning. Police say they are continuing their efforts to identify those involved and bring them to justice.

Months-long Indonesia wildfires spew toxic haze across Southeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:30:35 UTC
15:30:35 KST

Months-long Indonesia wildfires spew toxic haze across Southeast Asia
Parts of southern Southeast Asia have been put under the highest-level haze alert as wildfires that have swept Indonesia for months continue to belch toxic smoke across the region. The seasonal wildfires are worse this year due to the drought conditions caused by a severe "super-El Nino" effect.
Fires in Indonesia that have sent toxic smoke sweeping across Southeast Asia have triggered the highest-level alert by the regional bloc's meteorological monitor.
The months-long pollution spell has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
The haze is made up of fumes the forest and peatland fires that have ravaged parts of Indonesia, most notably on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra.
These areas are covered in dense forests and vast stretches of peatland that are especially prone to fire during the dry season, which usually runs from April to October.
The region is also currently under the influence of severe "super-El Nino" weather conditions, which brought additional heat and dryness and caused wildfires to spread more quickly.
While the extent of the damage remains unknown, environmental group Auriga reported that more than 637,000 hectares were burned from January to August this year, nine times the area of Singapore.
Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas put the figure even higher at nearly 900,000 hectares.
'High risk'
"This thing needs to stop," Zul Hafiz, a 39-year-old teacher cycling from the Malaysian city of Shah Alam to the capital, told AFP on Saturday, calling on the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to take action.
The 11-country organisation's ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre (ASMC) said in a notice on its website on Friday that it had activated "Alert Level 3 for the Southern ASEAN region" – the highest rung of a four-tiered alert system.
The alert level is triggered when there is a "high risk of severe transboundary haze in the region" and is reserved for widespread moderate to dense smoke haze, observed over two or more consecutive days.
The ASMC has already issued two Level 3 alerts this year, according to its website.
Singapore ranked second on IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities behind Baghdad on Saturday, with Kuala Lumpur third. All readings showed "very hazardous" levels."
'Irresponsible behaviour'
Indonesia said Saturday it had been using dry ice at one of South Sumatra province's main airports in an attempt to disperse the haze.
The country's national disaster mitigation agency said that 2.4 tonnes of dry ice were dispersed by plane.
"The smoke not only reduces visibility and disrupts aircraft operations, but also affects residents' health," the agency warned.
The haze has disrupted life across Southeast Asia, sparking fresh calls for action from those affected.
"It's a bit unfair on Malaysia because of the irresponsible behaviour of our neighbouring country," Khairul Azhar, a 33-year-old bank officer told AFP in Kuala Lumpur.
"This is affecting our weekend routine – not just for us but many Malaysians," he said.
In Indonesia's Palangkaraya – part of the epicentre of the fires where thick haze turned the skies into apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange – residents said they were suffering from its effects on Saturday.
"The haze has a big impact on us, especially on health and the economy, with our income decreasing," said Marzuki, a 38-year-old mechanic who like many in Indonesia, goes by only one name.
"Right now the economy is already very difficult, and the haze just makes it worse," he told AFP, adding that this year's situation was worse than even previous major bouts of haze in 2015.
"Hopefully it rains soon, the fires go out, and the smoke disappears so that activities can return to normal and it's easier to earn a living again," he said.
'What else to do?'
Joko, 51, a construction worker, said he had no choice but to keep on working or he would lose out on income.
"The thick smoke, when inhaled, makes it hard to breathe and stings the eyes, but what else can you do? This is how we earn a living," Joko said, explaining he had no fixed income and relied on daily wage jobs.
In East Timor, unhealthy air pollution persisted on Saturday, including in the capital Dili, according to IQAir.
Authorities warned that the situation may worsen on Saturday and schools were closed.
Singapore said Friday it would issue warnings to seven companies in Indonesia it identified as responsible for the fires.
Philippines foreign department spokesman for ASEAN issues, Dominic Xavier Imperial, said Friday that the haze would be discussed at upcoming meetings ahead of a November ASEAN summit in Manila.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

The last lace mill – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

MYB Textiles Ltd is the last mill in the world weaving patterned Nottingham lace on traditional looms. Once there were 20 lace mills in the Irvine Valley towns of Newmilns and Darvel alone. The lace industry became the largest employer in the area for a time and flourished until the late 1970s when competition emerged from other European countries and Asia. Now the majority of their trade comes from the film, theatre, TV and entertainment industry
Margo Graham, the design director in the mill’s finishing department where the finished lace is inspected, inspects black lace in a pattern called Jane. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
The Lace Darner, on a gable wall on Castle Street. A tribute to the skilled hand-darners who inspected and repaired lace, based on a photograph of long-serving MYB Textiles employee Janey Gray. Created by local artists Frank and Mandy Carty of Artisan ArtworksPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
MYB Textiles Ltd is the last mill in the world now weaving patterned Nottingham lace on traditional looms. Once there were 20 lace mills in the Irvine Valley towns of Newmilns and Darvel alone, employing about 2,000 peoplePhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
The looms, mostly over a century in age, date from 1913. One loom requires 10,000 spools of thread to supply its warp as it weavesPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
MYB now employs 42 people and has fought to survive in recent years. They are quietly famed for their Scottish Leno gauze weave (later known as Madras) and Nottingham lace. The former came to be called Madras because Scotland exported so much of it to India and to British colonies, because mosquitos could not get through the fine nettingPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Handloom weaving was brought to the Irvine Valley by Flemish refugees who settled in the area at the end of the 16th century. This was followed by the invention of the power loom in 1877Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Darning to replace broken or missing threads in the mill’s finishing department, where the finished lace is inspected and missing portions left in the fabric before the loom was stopped are painstakingly repairedPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Due to the antiquity of the looms, Thursday is set aside as a day for repairs and maintenance. The weavers stop the loom when a thread breaks and quickly remedy the problemPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Stocks of fine lace in the storeroom. Despite challenges, MYB Textiles has maintained high-profile collaborations with designers, institutions, performers and artists. Projects in the past have involved translating metalwork to lace, recreating archive museum textiles and collaborations with design studios such as Timorous Beasties and Eley KishimotoPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
This machine fills the brass-centred bobbins with its 400 yards of thread. One loom requires 10,000 spools of thread to supply its warp as it weavesPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Working with the V&A Design Museum in Dundee, MYB Textiles featured in the Design in Motion exhibition in 2015. They supplied material for curtains in Spielberg’s film Lincoln, and their lace has been used on the sets of Martin Scorsese’s Boardwalk Empire. Lincoln’s 12 Oscar nominations in 2013 included one for best production design, which it wonPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
A mill worker selects a pattern from a library of thousands of massive, finely punched cards. Hundreds of these lengthy, perforated cards – forerunners of computer programs – hang inside the entrance like an ancient library. There are 50,000 samples and 20,000 designs in the mill’s archivePhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
Sherry Campbell, Scottish Madras designer in the finishing department. The pattern on the left is St Andrews; the one on the right is Paradiso. While they have recently sold fabric to historic houses and high-end hotels, and some to the fashion industry, the majority of MYB’s trade now comes from the film, theatre, TV and entertainment industry. Sheets of lace are used as backdrops, and scrims that can be painted with traditional patterned lace are much in demand for period drama. The company was badly affected by the US writers strike due to the effect this had on film and theatre productionPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian
