£3,500 and no work done: the offer to help that’s really a roofing scam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

The builder who calls at your door says they are doing some work in the area and has spotted a loose tile on your roof. They offer to fix it for a good price that you agree to.
But when they go up on their ladder to inspect the problem, they see another problem. Rain has been splashing out of the gutters and the wood around them is getting damaged. The only solution, the builder says, is to have rigid PVC trays installed to divert the water.
More rain is forecast and you are worried about what damage could be done so you pay the builder via bank transfer to get the job done there and then. They are gone within an hour, having apparently completed the work.
But nothing was done because there was no problem with your guttering. Instead you were one of a growing number of people who have been targeted by criminals posing as roofers, only to make off with payment after doing unnecessary or no work.
The charity Citizens Advice says suspected roofing frauds were the top scam it heard from consumers about in the last year. It received more than 2,200 complaints of suspected roofing scams in the year to August in England and Wales, about 10% more than the previous year.
“The vast majority of cases is … somebody just knocking on your door saying that they’ve noticed that there’s something wrong with your roof and they’re in a position to help you,” says Ruwani Purcell, the director of external affairs at Citizens Advice.
“The difficulty is [that] your roof is out of sight and out of reach. You can’t fully see what’s going on.”
Purcell says the fraudsters use really persuasive tactics to offer you confidence and reassurance that they know what they’re talking about. “And you might not be familiar with [the] terms,” she says. “In the worst case scenarios, they’ve been quite intimidating to compel people to hand over money there and then.”
What it looks like
While more than three-quarters of the roofing scams reported to Citizens Advice start with someone knocking at the door, some criminals look online for potential victims.
In one case dealt with by Citizens Advice, a 65-year-old woman posted on an online platform that she needed someone to fix a dripping sound in her gutters. A builder phoned her to say that it would cost £250 but when he and another man came and examined her roof they said they had discovered more problems and the price quickly grew. At one point they showed her a bucket of cement and said it was crumbling from under the tiles.
The woman said the man and his accomplice said the work needed to be done immediately and once they claimed to have finished they wanted the payment straightaway.
“I was afraid, two men in front of me in the dark, demanding money and making it clear they weren’t moving,” the victim told Citizens Advice. “They knew I was alone, I didn’t feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500.”
She paid it using bank transfer. “The next day there was no trace that any work was done,” she said. “I felt stupid, and tried to contact them, but couldn’t get through.”
What to do
Be wary of anyone offering unsolicited work by cold calling and demanding confirmation of a job and payment there and then. No reputable builder will do that, says Purcell.
To check the roofer’s authenticity, ask for references and for all proposed work to be confirmed in writing. Treat it as a red flag if they refuse this or if they insist on being paid in cash.
To see if a trader is reputable, you can check your local council’s website as it often lists trusted traders. The government runs the TrustMark scheme which lists approved tradespeople.
Citizens Advice says that if a trader has done a poor job without reasonable care and skill, the victim is entitled to ask for the problem to be fixed or get a refund under the Consumer Rights Act 2015. Keep any paperwork and receipts, take photos and document what happened to make your case.

US goes on the offensive in Central Asia

AI generated
WASHINGTON – It is deal-making time: Despite the roiling geopolitical tensions embroiling Washington on several fronts, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio headed to Central and South Asia late on Oct 17 to boost commercial ties – and gain an edge over Russia and China.
With the US mired in its war with Iran, and the conflict in Ukraine showing no signs of abating, Rubio has stepped up his foreign travel with recent trips to Europe and Latin America, smack in the middle of the US midterm polls campaign.
He has largely ceded control of the contentious Iran, Ukraine and Gaza situations to US President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Rubio was instead leading a massive delegation of 200 business leaders to Uzbekistan, where he will take part in a ministerial meeting of five Central Asian countries on Oct 19.
“This is an important relationship,” he said shortly before his departure, calling the trip a strategic visit. “There’s countries you’d like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them.”
A senior State Department official told reporters on Oct 16 that Rubio was demonstrating Washington’s goodwill towards the “deepening partnership across Central Asia”, especially in the energy sector.
Central Asia is a resource-rich region as vast as the European Union but has a population of only about 80 million people.
“We’ve been planning this for several months, and it’s an incredible opportunity to bring the United States into a region of the world that is vitally important,” said a second senior US official, on condition of anonymity.
During his visit to the Uzbek city of Samarkand, an emblematic stop on the historic Silk Road, Rubio will participate in a C5+1 meeting with ministers from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
In November 2025, Trump welcomed the leaders of those countries to the White House.
The former Soviet republics remain linked to Moscow by energy pipelines, as well as security and migratory networks, but Russian influence has eroded since the start of the war in Ukraine – with China reaping the benefits.
Beijing is the main trade partner of all five Central Asian nations.
Chinese companies have signed a number of energy-related deals, seeking to buy natural gas in Turkmenistan, uranium in Kazakhstan and rare earths in Tajikistan.
The US also has made sourcing rare earths and improving its energy mix key parts of its foreign policy.
The US Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor – who also serves as the special envoy for Central and South Asia – has repeatedly emphasised the need for Washington to have better ties across the region.
Trade deal
After his visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio will head to India, with stops in Mumbai and Jamnagar in Gujarat state. Both are industrial hubs and major international port cities.
It will be the Secretary of State’s second official visit to India in 2026, after a May trip to New Delhi and Kolkata, signifying Washington’s push in the region.
“We’re very close” to a trade deal with India, the second senior US official said of negotiations that have dragged on for months.
In February, the two sides reached a provisional agreement aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian products.
But just a few days later, the US Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s tariffs, which fuelled uncertainty about when a bilateral trade deal could take effect.
Ever since, Washington and Delhi have been locked in negotiations.
Relations were rattled when Trump imposed 25% tariffs on Indian goods in retaliation for Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil, but those duties have since been lifted.
In Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio will offer the new US brand of so-called “commercial diplomacy” in his meetings with Indian business leaders.
He will notably raise plans by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries to finance a refinery in Texas. Reliance is led by billionaire Indian tycoon Anant Ambani. AFP

====================================================================================================

Leisure out of reach for one in eight people in the EU: Where is the problem biggest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:54:13 UTC
14:54:13 KST

From sport to cinema trips, regular leisure activities are out of reach for around 46 million people in the EU. Income helps explain the gap between countries, but it does not tell the whole story.
About 46 million people in the EU miss out on regular leisure activities because they cannot afford them, according to Eurostat. In Greece, more than one in four people face this barrier — the highest share in the bloc.
The figures reveal wide differences across Europe, even between countries with similar income levels.
Several studies link social and leisure participation to better mental well-being and fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety. Eurostat also highlights the role leisure and social interactions can play in improving quality of life.
So, where are costs most likely to prevent people from taking part, and how much does income explain the gap?
In 2025, the share of people who couldn't afford to participate regularly in a leisure activity ranged from 3.9% in Croatia to 27.3% in Greece, compared with an EU average of 12.1%, according to Eurostat.
Figures cover people aged 16 and over. With about 381 million people in this age group in 2025, this means around 46 million people in the EU faced this financial barrier.
This share was also above 15% in Romania (23.3%), Lithuania (17.9%), Latvia (16.2%), North Macedonia (15.9%) and Hungary (15.8%).
France and Spain are above the EU average
More than 13% of people in France (13.9%) and Spain (13.4%) also reported that cost prevented them from taking part regularly in leisure activities. Switzerland (13%) was also above the EU average.
Germany (11.7%) was just below the EU average. In Italy, regular leisure activities were out of reach for 10.7% of people because of the cost.
Czechia (4.1%), Luxembourg (5.4%), Norway (5.7%) and Slovakia (5.7%) were also close to Croatia (3.9%) at the lower end.
The share was also higher than in Croatia in the Nordic EU countries: Denmark (10.4%), Sweden (9.7%) and Finland (7.9%).
Elsewhere, it stood at 6.7% in the Netherlands, 8.7% in Turkey and Portugal, 9.2% in Ireland and 9.7% in Belgium.
Leisure activities are less affordable for women
Except for Malta, where the difference was slight at 0.1 percentage point, leisure activities were less affordable for women than men. In the EU, the share was 13% among women, compared with 11.1% among men.
The gender gap was particularly large in several countries: 5.1 percentage points (pp) in Lithuania, 4.7 pp in Romania, 3.9 pp in Denmark and 3.7 pp in France.
Is income linked to leisure affordability?
Analysis by Euronews Business covering 33 European countries shows that income plays a role, but it does not tell the whole story. There is a moderate link between median income and the share of people who miss out on regular leisure activities because of the cost. Income data come from Eurostat and show median equivalised income in purchasing power standards (PPS).
Income accounts for less than a fifth of the variation between countries. Czechia, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had almost identical median incomes, all between 17,097 and 17,190 PPS. Yet only 4.1% of people in Czechia couldn't afford to take part regularly in a leisure activity, compared with 10.7% in Estonia, 16.2% in Latvia and 17.9% in Lithuania.
The same pattern appeared among wealthier countries. France and Cyprus had virtually the same median income, at 23,792 and 23,782 PPS, respectively. But the share of people facing this financial barrier was more than twice as high in France (13.9%) as in Cyprus (6.3%).
Greece had the highest rate at 27.3%, with a median income of 13,612 PPS. Turkey (8.7%) and Serbia (9.9%) had lower incomes but much lower rates. Croatia, Czechia and Slovakia had some of the lowest rates despite incomes below the EU median of 22,638 PPS.
The role of inequality within countries
Across the EU, people below the poverty line were more than three times as likely to miss out on regular leisure activities as those above it, with 29% unable to afford them.
While inequality within countries may play a role, Euronews Business analysis finds only a weak link between income inequality and leisure affordability, which is not statistically significant.
The analysis uses Eurostat’s Gini coefficient, a measure of how unevenly income is distributed.
How people answer the survey may affect the results
How people answer the survey matters. A Eurostat working paper by Anne-Catherine Guio and colleagues found that “poor people may report that they do not want things, simply because they cannot afford them”. They found that leisure was the item most often not seen as a necessity.
What is a leisure activity?
According to Eurostat, leisure activities include sport, cinema and concerts, among others, and should take place outside the home. These activities involve spending money on entrance fees or travel, such as for swimming; on equipment, such as a bicycle; or on participation in organised activities, such as football club fees.

In pictures: Orangutans rescued from Indonesia blazes as species faces extinction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18

14:13:11 KST

Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in recent weeks from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia, conservation groups said.
The fires have triggered a months-long pollution spell that has closed schools, fuelled a surge in respiratory conditions both among humans and animals, and restricted outdoor activities in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor.
Pollution levels again ranged from unhealthy to very unhealthy across the region on Sunday, cloaking many areas across southern Southeast Asia in toxic haze.
Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir again ranked Singapore and Kuala Lumpur among the world's top five most polluted major cities as fires on Borneo and Sumatra islands, intensified by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, keep emitting smoke.
In Indonesia, groups are working to save wildlife from the fires, including orangutans.
On Saturday, the West Kalimantan conservation agency and Indonesian non-profit YIARI said a team evacuated 51 orangutans from locations in the province from August 6 to October 19.
And figures from Indonesia's forestry ministry suggested this week that the number rescued over recent months in Kalimantan could be as high as 96.
Officials could not be immediately reached to clarify the number.
The latest rescue came on Saturday, when three conservation agencies rescued a 20-year-old male orangutan in Hampangen village in Central Kalimantan, on Borneo island.
"The evacuation process was carried out with great caution," the agencies said.
"After the orangutan was sedated, the medical team immediately conducted a health examination before taking the animal to the... rehabilitation center," it said.
Indonesia's transport ministry also said around 2,400 flights across the country have been affected by the haze since mid-August.
"Haze reduces visibility around airports, which can lead to delays, disruptions, and even flight cancellations. Every operational decision is made with safety as the top priority," the ministry said.
All three orangutan species face a critical risk of extinction due to deforestation, wildfires, habitat loss and illegal hunting.

Israel's opposition will not defeat Netanyahu by focusing on October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:48 UTC
14:11:48 KST

The clock is ticking toward October 27, and tensions are running high. The central question is whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will manage to hold on to power, although most polls suggest that his chances are slim. Yet a closer look at the election campaigns of Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu reveals that each side has its own interpretation of why the 2026 election is critical to Israel’s future.
While Eisenkot and his fellow leaders of the center-left bloc, including Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan, have placed the October 7 failure and the question of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription at the center of their campaign, Netanyahu is seeking to highlight the achievements of the War of Redemption [the multifront conflict following Hamas’s 2023 attack] while downplaying his responsibility for the October 7 failure.
Alongside allegations that Netanyahu received two warnings of an impending attack, from the Emiratis and the Egyptians, the statements made by his former military secretary, Avi Gil, are regarded by the opposition as compelling evidence of Netanyahu’s failure.
Eisenkot’s camp has also continued to emphasize that Netanyahu’s inner circle is tainted by corruption and a lack of integrity. In addition to the alleged attempt to falsify the official record, Netanyahu presented a selective account of the State Comptroller’s Report on the October 7 failure.
The opposition’s claims are certainly open to debate, and a closer examination of Gil’s statements only reinforces the conclusion that the security establishment failed on that terrible night. Nevertheless, several questions arise when we analyze the arguments put forward by both sides.
Analyzing the arguments
First, although Netanyahu pursued a failed policy toward Hamas, motivated in part by a desire to avoid a confrontation that could derail efforts to normalize relations with Saudi Arabia, the fact remains that he received intelligence indicating an impending attack only after it had begun.
Unlike the hours preceding the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War, when then-prime minister Golda Meir was involved in the decision-making process and could have ordered a preemptive strike against Egypt, Netanyahu was not even given an opportunity to influence events that night.
Second, questions also arise regarding the claim that the alleged criminal attempt to change the time of a phone call in the official record, from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m., was intended to reinforce the bizarre conspiracy theory that a generals’ revolt had taken place. Netanyahu’s opponents argue that members of his inner circle sought to create the impression that the generals had deliberately failed to wake him.
An alternative explanation, however, is that the change was intended to demonstrate that Netanyahu had not been asleep while Hamas terrorists were infiltrating communities near the Gaza border. If Netanyahu’s associates had wanted to emphasize that the generals had kept him in the dark, it would have made more sense to leave the call time at 6:40 a.m., allowing them to argue that he had been informed only 11 minutes after the attack began.
Third, Netanyahu’s strained relationship with the security establishment’s leadership was shaped in part by his insistence, during the judicial reform debate, that the phenomenon of military refusal be confronted rather than tolerated. Critics argue that Netanyahu chose to disregard the security chiefs’ warnings about the implications of the proposed judicial legislation and the threat it posed to national security, as well as their less specific warnings of a possible war.
Others, however, argue that had the IDF responded to military refusal as it did during the Disengagement from Gaza, Yahya Sinwar and Mohammed Deif might have thought twice before launching their attack.
This raises another question: If the security establishment’s leaders had warned of an impending war, why was the IDF so unprepared on that fateful day and caught so completely off guard?
In conclusion, Netanyahu has effectively been campaigning continuously since the 2022 election, particularly in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, massacre. Yet focusing on the alleged falsification of official records and the conduct of Netanyahu’s inner circle is unlikely to be the key to defeating him in the 2026 election.
Israel’s political history repeatedly demonstrates that corruption is not necessarily a decisive issue for voters. Arye Deri, for example, led Shas to 17 seats in the 1999 election despite having been convicted of bribery. Ariel Sharon led Likud to 38 seats in the 2003 election despite the cloud of suspicion surrounding the Cyril Kern affair.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, has consistently secured more than 30 seats in elections held since he became a criminal defendant. Rather than dwelling on the past, the opposition would be better served by persuading the public that Israel has a better future beyond Netanyahu’s leadership. That is how elections are won!
The writer is a lecturer and research fellow at the University of South Wales in the United Kingdom. He is the author of Collapse: The Israeli Labor Party, 1992–2024.

Israel’s election puzzle: Why are so many voters still backing Netanyahu? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:25 UTC
14:11:25 KST

I thought that after living here for 32 years (this week marked our “aliyahversary”), I finally understood Israelis. But perusing the pre-election polls, I realize how little I know about my neighbors outside our insular Anglo bubble.
How is it that, three years after the Oct. 7, 2023 failure of the entire military and political establishment, the current coalition is, in some polls, tied with the opposition parties and, in Channel 14’s pro-government poll, scoring a resounding win? That is not what I hear from friends and acquaintances in the ’hood.
On October 8, it was widely predicted that the coalition would fall – imminently. Indeed, the depravity of the massacre spurred a kind of dark hope for the future among those of us opposed to the relentless proliferation of hate and divisiveness that has been Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s key strategy to stay in power.
Yet, not only did the coalition serve its full term, but the narrative has been so twisted that Netanyahu’s Likud party has regained much, if not all, of its support.
Adding to this turnaround, inexplicable in southern Jerusalem, the anniversary of Oct. 7 doesn’t seem to have moved the dial a bit. Voters made up their minds long ago. There’s little chance of committed Likud voters changing sides, even as new examples of corruption and disregard are disclosed daily.
How did we get to this place? The answer, sadly, at least from where I’m sitting, seems to be racism. You only have to look at the giant election billboards with the rhyme “Yamin or Palestine” (in Hebrew, “yamin” means “right”), or the horrifically insensitive AI ad with the opposition party Yashar’s leader Gadi Eisenkot running to greet his dead son in a field, only to bypass him to embrace Ra’am (United Arab List) head Mansour Abbas.
That message is outrageous on so many levels.
Equality at Hadassah-University Medical Center
I spent two months hospitalized at Hadassah-University Medical Center, in Ein Kerem this summer. The institution epitomizes equality in this country. Some of the best doctors and nurses who cared for me were Arab Israelis. Fifty percent of all pharmacists in Israel are from the Arab sector. I never felt I was getting anything but the right treatment from the entire staff, even as they were pricking my tired fingers to make sure my glucose wasn’t spiking.
Earlier this year, I went to hear Naftali Bennett, who leads the opposition B’Yachad (Together) party, speak at an English-language event at Jerusalem’s Begin Heritage Center. When asked if the opposition should include an Arab party like Ra’am in a coalition, as he had done previously during the short-lived “change government,” he danced around a direct answer.
He would consider any party that affirms the right of the Jewish people to a state of their own in Israel, he implied, among other criteria. Ra’am has done this – and gone one step further, by adding a Jewish Israeli, Yoav Segalovich, as the party’s number two, with the specific mandate to fight crime in the Arab sector, an issue about which there should be consensus.
Eisenkot, pressured by right-wing goading, has stated publicly that he would not include any Arab parties in a future coalition, but if it’s between bringing in Ra’am again or returning to elections, I wouldn’t believe everything that’s said on the campaign trail.
At this point, I’ll reveal who I’m voting for: Bennett. His won’t be the largest party among the opposition. But Bennett has put together a series of detailed working plans to fix what’s wrong with this country, covering everything from transportation to education to the military.
His list includes skilled technocrats who have run ministries in the past and can hit the ground running. I hope that, if Eisenkot gets enough seats and is able to form a coalition, he’ll put some of Bennett’s team in place as ministers.
And yet the opposition can’t seem to decide on a consistent strategy. Should it hammer away at government corruption and the threat of a renewed judicial coup? What Netanyahu knew, or didn’t know, on Oct. 7? Should establishing a state commission of inquiry be the main talking point? Or can it harness the overwhelming fury of the non-haredi population by doubling down on a proposed law to draft ultra-Orthodox yeshiva boys into an army that is tens of thousands of soldiers short.
Compare that to Netanyahu, whose anti-Arab messaging is unwavering.
One last indelicate thought: Why is Netanyahu still around? He’s 76 and presumably in ill health. He has a pacemaker and cancer (supposedly in remission, but he hid his treatments from the public, so why should we believe him?).
I’ve seen pictures of Netanyahu lately. He’s so thin. I know, I should give him the benefit of the doubt (he must be exercising more). But I know better than many that when you’re faced with grave health challenges, you can shed a lot of weight quickly.
If Netanyahu lost the election, would that prompt him to accept a plea bargain in his criminal trial and leave politics to avoid jail? If so, why couldn’t he have done that already?
I’m not planning to leave Israel, regardless of the outcome. But my children might. My doctors might. Our tax-paying techies and overburdened reservists might. According to a Channel 12 survey, 23% of Israelis have developed contingency plans to emigrate if the current coalition continues its drive toward totalitarianism.
I pray that, in arguably the most consequential elections in Israel’s history, there will be a surprise surge that will shake the public out of its status quo slumber, so we can begin to repair this country we all love so much.
Maybe then I’ll finally understand Israelis.
The writer’s book, TOTALED: The Billion-Dollar Crash of the Startup that Took on Big Auto, Big Oil and the World, was published earlier this year as an audiobook. It is available on Amazon and other online booksellers in print, eBook, and Audible formats. brianblum.com

Paris's cost of living protests spiral into France's worst violence, riots in decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
05:11:23 UTC
14:11:23 KST

Rioting erupted in cities across France on Saturday as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiraled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze; in Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city's tourist office.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the government would not be "intimidated" by violence, and blamed the unrest on the "ultra-left" and criminals just months before a presidential election next year.
"To those who clearly want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' before the presidential election, I say clearly: We will not let ourselves be intimidated. No one will impose their political agenda through violence," he wrote in a post on X/Twitter.
Some 1,200 people had been arrested during the protests, Lecornu added while visiting the sites in the evening.
Around 550,000 people had participated in the demonstrations across the country, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. The CGT union told Reuters it estimated the protesters at 800,000.
President Emmanuel Macron vowed to prosecute and punish people who had carried out the attacks.
"We will all stand united against the sowers of chaos, who only seek to undermine our institutions and prevent those who peacefully express their demands from doing so," he wrote in a post on X.
Protests rage across Europe amid rising living costs
Belgium, Portugal, and Italy also saw smaller-scale protests on Saturday as living costs rise in Europe, while protesters in Albania again rallied against perceived government corruption, job shortages, and poor education standards.
Protesters said most people had marched peacefully, and put much of the violence down to troublemakers who had set out to cause damage and clash with the police. Many held signs bearing slogans against the police, the president, and the wealthy.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
Most protests kicked off around midday, with some beginning before the official start of the demonstrations.
In some parts of Paris, police fired tear gas rounds as they retreated in the face of mostly young protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore hoodies, masks, and goggles to protect against tear gas.
Rioters tried to break into the Galeries Lafayette department store, smashed up banks, ransacked a Lacoste store as well as other boutiques, and looted an SFR mobile phone shop. Protesters had been setting objects ablaze all day, including numerous cars.
In protests partly inspired by those in France, several hundred mostly young people protested in Brussels, and some clashed with police. Belgian student groups have said they are protesting against rising education costs and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
In Albania, police fired what appeared to be rubber bullets at protesters during a fifth day of mass student demonstrations calling for Prime Minister Edi Rama to step down.
In Portugal, tens of thousands took to the streets of Lisbon following days of unrest to protest against housing and other living costs. Housing prices in Portugal have doubled since 2017, fueling one of the worst affordability crises in Europe.
In Italy, a march against high costs of living in Milan degenerated into disorder, with police clearing the central cathedral square with tear gas. Police in Bologna used water cannons to try to disperse crowds and made seven arrests after another protest turned violent, the ANSA news agency reported.
The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris' working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending, and living standards.
In Paris on Saturday, protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, recalling the Yellow Vest movement that marked Macron's previous term in office.
Saturday's protests eclipsed the size of the crowds at the peak of the Yellow Vest movement, though they were far lower than the levels seen at the protests in 2023 against Macron's pension overhaul.
Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, facing a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have not reassured investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in over two decades.
Police tactics criticized after demonstrators injured
Police tactics have drawn criticism following injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence.
Lecornu said more than 150 police officers had been injured in Saturday's protests, but did not say whether any protesters had been hurt.
Nunez confirmed reports that one person had his hand torn off in clashes with police on Saturday. French media reported he tried to pick up a stun grenade.
The UNSA police union posted a video on X showing crowds attacking police vans with clubs and bricks in multiple locations. The union warned the government police forces were at breaking point.
"Today again, in every corner of France, our colleagues are being used as punching bags. Pelted with stones, injured, trapped in real ambushes," the union said. "Let everyone take responsibility: this cannot go on indefinitely. The rope is stretched to its maximum."

SOPOT, Poland, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China and Europe should strengthen dialogue and mutual understanding to promote practical cooperation in a changing world, a Polish expert on China has said.
Bogdan Goralczyk, a professor at the Centre for Europe at the University of Warsaw, told Xinhua in a recent interview on the sidelines of the 15th European Forum for New Ideas that Europe needs to better understand China, which has become a major global economic and technological power.

Europeans visiting China will discover a country different from the one portrayed in some media, he added.
Goralczyk also noted growing interest in China among younger generations in Europe. He said young Europeans visiting China are witnessing its modern society and technological advances, which inspire them to learn Chinese.
He called for closer academic exchanges between China and the EU, including more Chinese participation in Erasmus+, an EU program supporting education, training and youth exchanges. ■

Tunisia’s economic crisis deepens as the promise of a better life fades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:14:42 UTC
13:14:42 KST

Tunisia’s economic crisis deepens as the promise of a better life fades
Joblessness, failing services and rising costs deepen hardship across the country.
Tunis, Tunisia – Like many Tunisian university graduates, Cherine Ghanmi believed a degree would offer her family a way out of poverty.
Growing up in the marginalised town of al-Mazzunah, in the central Sidi Bou Zid governorate, Ghanmi had walked 5km (3.1 miles) to the school her parents struggled to put her through. They hoped she would eventually find a job and support them financially, easing their burden after years of sacrifice.
But more than a decade after graduating in 2012, she remains unemployed. Instead of supporting her parents, she says, she continues to rely on them.
“We studied and graduated believing we had finally found a way out of poverty,” she said. “We thought that once we found jobs, we could make up for all that hardship, repay our parents for their sacrifices and make them happy.”
“Unfortunately, reality was a big shock for us,” she added. “Instead of helping them, we have burdened them even more.”
For Ghanmi and thousands of other unemployed university graduates, the struggle to find work has become a symbol of Tunisia’s wider economic crisis, marked by limited opportunities, mounting financial pressure and growing frustration with successive governments.
The ‘Dignity March’
On September 27, unemployed university graduates began a roughly 300km (186-mile) march from Menzel Bouzaiane in central Tunisia towards the capital, Tunis, to demand jobs and the implementation of legislation intended to provide a clear path to public-sector employment.
Known as the “Dignity March”, it began with 23 participants, according to organisers. More graduates joined along the route, with the coordinating committee later estimating that the number had grown to more than 120.
The journey was physically demanding. Participants paused at points because of exhaustion and injuries before continuing towards the capital.
On October 6, police blocked the group from moving forward in the town of Borj Cedria, south of Tunis. Participants said they were told they could travel individually, but not as a group. The marchers had hoped to reach the Tunis suburb of Carthage, where the presidential palace is located, to press their demands.
For Ghanmi, “the Dignity March was not just a march”, she said, describing it as an expression of the hardship and disappointment experienced by graduates who had spent years searching for work.
Many protesters say they have waited years for promises of public-sector recruitment to translate into real opportunities.
Their demands came amid broader discontent over Tunisia’s economic and political direction.
On October 17, thousands gathered in Tunis to protest against President Kais Saied’s government, deteriorating living conditions and restrictions on freedoms. The demonstration, led by the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), opposition groups and civil society organisations, was among the largest against Saied in years.
Participants voiced frustration over unemployment and the difficulties many households face in meeting their basic needs.
Saied, who has concentrated power since 2021, has presented his political project as a response to corruption and the failures of the established political class. Critics say the concentration of power has weakened democratic checks and balances while doing little to resolve the country’s economic problems.
Stalled promises
The unemployment figures reflect the scale of the challenge. According to Tunisia’s National Institute of Statistics (INS), the overall unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026. Among university graduates, it was 26.6 percent. The rate for women graduates was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent for men. Among those aged 15 to 24, unemployment reached 35.4 percent.
“Almost all the governments that succeeded one another after the [2011] revolution did not make the economic situation, development and the treatment of social issues real priorities,” Cherif Khraifi, spokesperson for the Tunisian Union of Higher Education Graduates, told Al Jazeera.
“Their biggest concern was ensuring they stayed in power.”
Attempts to address graduate unemployment have repeatedly raised expectations. The 2022 Law No. 38 intended to establish an employment pathway for long-term unemployed university graduates, but the law’s implementation stalled amid financial constraints.
Khraifi said measures intended to address the crisis have too often served as “tools for letting off steam” rather than resolving the problem.
The 2025 Law No. 18 provides for the exceptional recruitment of long-term unemployed university graduates into the public sector and civil service. It calls for a digital platform to register eligible applicants and sets out criteria for prioritising candidates. Recruitment is to take place in phases over no more than three years from the law’s publication.
The law was dated 22 December 2025 and published in Tunisia’s Official Gazette on 23 December 2025, when it entered into force. Article 6 provides for recruitment in phases over a period not exceeding three years from the date of publication.
The graduates taking part in the Dignity March have demanded a clear process for implementing the law, including practical arrangements and a timetable for recruitment. For people who have already spent years out of work, another promise offers little reassurance without concrete steps towards employment.
Ghanmi is also sceptical of Saied’s community-based companies programme, which aims to promote local development and employment through projects established by people in their communities.
“The authorities insist on promoting community companies as a solution for jobs and development, yet none of these companies managed to do that,” she said.
Public-sector recruitment alone cannot resolve a problem of this scale, Khraifi argued. Tunisia also needs investment and businesses capable of expanding and hiring. In disadvantaged regions, where employment is scarce and access to capital is limited, starting a business can be difficult.
For graduates such as Ghanmi, the central question is whether government policies will translate into actual jobs.
An economy struggling to create opportunities
Anis Ben Said, a tax adviser and university professor, said Tunisia’s “problem is not a lack of skills, but the economy’s inability to turn skills into production, investment and job opportunities”.
Weak investment has constrained the creation of businesses and jobs, he told Al Jazeera. Poor infrastructure and unreliable public services also make it harder for businesses to operate, particularly in regions already struggling to attract investment.
According to the INS, Tunisia’s economy grew by 2.7 percent in 2025 and by 2.4 percent in the first half of 2026. In September, the World Bank projected growth of 2.3 percent for the full year.
But economic growth does not necessarily create enough jobs for those who need them. For unemployed graduates, the figures offer little reassurance unless growth translates into accessible employment opportunities.
“The financial crisis explains part of the problem, but it does not justify all of it,” Ben Said said.
He pointed to shortcomings in investment and the management and maintenance of public infrastructure as barriers to economic activity.
“Infrastructure investment is not just a public expense, it is a productive economic investment,” he said
This summer, extreme heat coincided with electricity cuts and water shortages in several parts of Tunisia. Disruptions to these basic services affected businesses and added to public frustration.
The Reuters news agency reported that recurring power and water cuts were among the grievances raised at the October 17 demonstration.
For small businesses, interruptions to basic services can mean lost customers and income. Where jobs are already scarce, such disruptions make earning a living even harder.
In L’Aouina, a northern suburb of Tunis, 20-year-old barber Khalil said he was waiting for an opportunity to leave the country by boat.
“There’s nothing worth staying for in this country. Dying at sea would be a relief,” he said.
“I’m going to leave as soon as I can, and let them figure out the solutions on their own. Our generation has borne the brunt of all these crises, and nothing is left for us.”
Others struggle to keep their business afloat.
Khalil’s neighbour, a grocery shop owner who asked not to be named, said persistent problems with the water supply had become exhausting.
“I think the only solution is for someone to take over this shop. I cannot keep up with these crises any more,” he said.
For Ghanmi, the years without work have brought more than financial hardship.
“The wound on the body heals, but the wound in the mind and heart does not heal,” she said. “It really does not heal.”

Feature: As tigers return, technology protects wildlife and people who share their habitat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:13:49 CST
13:13:49 KST

CHANGCHUN/HARBIN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A tigress moved through the forest, followed by five cubs, their small bodies weaving through the undergrowth.
This rare scene was captured by an infrared camera in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park (NCTLNP) late last year. It was the first recorded footage in China of a wild Siberian tiger accompanied by an unusually large litter of five cubs, offering a glimpse into the recovery of these endangered big cats.
Transmitted to the park's monitoring center in real time, the footage became part of a growing body of data that helps conservation workers identify individual animals and track their movements without having to follow them deep into the forest.
Latest monitoring shows that three of the tigress's five cubs have already left their mother's side, while the other two are still with her.
Siberian tigers, also known as Amur tigers, along with Amur leopards, are flagship species for biodiversity conservation and important indicators of a healthy ecosystem. Following a pilot phase launched in 2017, the NCTLNP was officially established in 2021 as one of the first five national parks in China.
Leveraging new technology, this park has built an integrated monitoring system that combines satellite remote sensing, ground-based infrared cameras and aerial surveillance involving drones, covering most of its 14,100-square-kilometer area across Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces in China's northeast.
A major challenge in building such a system is network coverage. The park has established 95 wireless communication base stations and deployed around 30,000 cameras, according to Sun Pengyu, the person responsible for the forestry and grassland sector at Jishi Media, the main constructor of the system.
Wireless data transmission covers more than 80 percent of the park area, allowing footage to reach the park administration within roughly a minute of being captured, Sun said.
Empowered by artificial intelligence, the system can identify more than 30 wildlife species and make preliminary identifications of individual tigers and leopards based on their distinctive coat patterns, said Chen Xiaocai, head of the park administration's comprehensive office.
Researchers then cross-check the initial identifications against other biological features, including facial contours, to verify each animal's identity and build individual profiles for further research and conservation work, Chen added.
The park has also restored forest habitats and improved ecological connectivity. Along the China-Russia border, more than 290 sections of fencing in areas frequented by tigers and leopards have been removed, helping reopen cross-border routes for wildlife.
The latest monitoring data show that the number of wild Siberian tigers in the park has risen from 27 in 2017 to 72, while the wild Amur leopard population has grown from 42 to 115. Sightings of other wildlife, including deer and roe deer, offer further indications of an ecosystem supporting the return of its top predators.
For Li Gang, deputy head of Chaoyanggou forest farm in Dongning, Heilongjiang Province, the changes brought by technology are tangible.
Li has worked at the forest farm, also a core conservation area, since 2009. In the early years, maintaining infrared cameras meant trekking into the mountains to replace batteries and retrieve memory cards.
This process not only delayed access to information but also exposed staff to risks posed by rugged terrain and encounters with large predators.
"On one occasion, I walked 17 kilometers carrying about 200 batteries and spare cameras," he recalled.
Now, cameras equipped with wireless transmission can send images and video directly to a central platform. Satellite imagery helps workers assess habitat conditions across large areas, while drones can inspect remote terrain, check for suspected forest fires and investigate possible illegal activities.
Li has also seen changes in the wildlife around him. "Sika deer were scarce in the area when I began working here, but during a recent outing, I saw more than 100," Li said.
As tigers and leopards reclaim more territory, protecting them also means keeping people safe. In parts of the national park, villages and wildlife habitats overlap, making early warnings an important part of conservation.
Cameras near settlements can detect tigers, leopards, bears and wild boars entering designated risk areas. Alerts are then sent to patrol teams and nearby residents, giving people time to avoid potentially dangerous encounters.
In Dongning, information can also be shared via local chat groups, allowing rangers to warn residents when a tiger is spotted.
For Li and his colleagues, such technology does not replace fieldwork for rangers, but it helps make patrols more targeted, reducing unnecessary journeys into sensitive habitats.
"We want to give people and wildlife room to live without disturbing one another, for the benefit of both," Li said. ■

World Insights: LatAm journalists explore drivers of China's NEV industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:13:44 CST
13:13:44 KST

by Xinhua writers He Yixuan, Xi Yue, Zhao Yanchao
CHANGZHOU, China, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Cameras clicking and smartphones raised, a group of Latin American journalists moved through the production workshops of a Chinese new energy vehicle (NEV) maker in Changzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, capturing robots at work and vehicles taking shape on the assembly line.
For some, the scene offered a glimpse into the technology behind Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) they had already seen on the streets back home. Thousands of kilometers away, Chinese-made EVs are becoming part of everyday life in Latin America, while charging facilities and power transmission projects are opening up new avenues for green cooperation.
During the 2026 Belt and Road Journalists Forum, dozens of journalists from Latin American countries visited Changzhou, known as China's "capital of new energy," to explore the industrial strengths behind China's green development and discover opportunities for cooperation with Latin America.
FROM FACTORY FLOORS TO EVERYDAY MOBILITY
For Rody Olivera, president of the Uruguayan Press Association, the visit was more than a tour of a manufacturing facility. Having purchased a Chinese NEV in May, he was eager to see how it was made. Inside the welding workshop at Li Auto's manufacturing base in Changzhou, he said the visit had confirmed that he had "made the right decision."
"The factory is impressive in terms of its size and productivity. Electric vehicles offer many advantages, as they provide a quieter driving experience, numerous driver-assistance features and greater comfort," Olivera said.
In his view, China's progress in the sector stems from both policy support and industrial capabilities. "China is a pioneer in this technology," he said, attributing the country's achievements to its innovation capabilities and the development of a complete industrial chain.
At the exhibition hall of Segway-Ninebot, a renowned electric two-wheeler maker, Angel Sanchez, president of the Federation of Journalists of Peru, recognized the company's electric scooters, saying they could offer a convenient transportation option for young people and office workers in Peru.
"They have many advantages, including quick responsiveness, flexible center-of-gravity control and a portable design," Sanchez said, adding that China's development of new energy and other emerging technologies ultimately aims to improve people's lives.
Such products offer a glimpse into the broader industrial ecosystem that has taken shape in Changzhou. Its industrial chain spans five areas: energy generation, storage, transmission, consumption and distribution networks. In 2025, the scale of the city's new energy industry exceeded 1 trillion yuan (about 150 billion U.S. dollars).
CONNECTING INDUSTRIAL STRENGTHS WITH LOCAL NEEDS
The city's industrial strengths extend from NEVs and key components to charging infrastructure and power transmission equipment, creating opportunities for cooperation across different stages of the energy transition.
At the exhibition area of charging infrastructure operator Star Charge, Virgilio Arias, president of Mexico's Front Page Club, stopped in front of a photograph showing an electric-bus charging station in Mexico City.
"I've just learned that this Chinese company has provided charging facilities for three Bus Rapid Transit lines in Mexico City and Monterrey, supporting the operation of more than 150 electric buses," Arias said.
The example highlighted how Chinese technologies are being applied to local transportation systems in Latin America. As Mexico and other countries in the region accelerate their energy transitions, cooperation in charging infrastructure and electric mobility could help address practical needs while advancing shared sustainable development goals, Arias said.
Green cooperation also extends beyond transportation to the infrastructure needed to transmit clean energy over long distances.
For Samira de Castro, president of the National Federation of Journalists of Brazil, a visit to NR Electric brought an unexpected connection to a project she had covered years earlier.
In 2012, she wrote a report on Brazil's Belo Monte hydropower project. During her visit in Changzhou, she learned that the company's technology had been used in the project's second-phase ultra-high-voltage transmission system.
Now operational, the transmission project helps deliver hydropower from northern Brazil to distant consumption centers, including areas serving Rio de Janeiro. Castro said the advanced technology had made a significant contribution to Brazil's electricity supply and changed the lives of local residents.
TURNING SHARED GOALS INTO GREEN COOPERATION
"There is an ecosystem of companies here that are collaborating to advance clean energy. Renewable energy is the future, and it is happening right here, right now," said Geraldo Cantarino, a member of the Brazilian Press Association, during his first visit to China.
For Latin American countries with diverse energy resources and growing demand for cleaner development, cooperation with China could create further opportunities in equipment manufacturing, infrastructure construction and the application of new energy technologies.
For the journalists visiting Changzhou, the trip offered a closer look at the industrial capabilities underpinning China's new energy development and their potential relevance to Latin America. From EVs and smart mobility products to charging networks and power transmission systems, the examples they encountered demonstrated how green cooperation can take shape across an interconnected industrial chain.
As the visit drew to a close, the journalists took away more than photographs of production lines, electric scooters and power transmission equipment. They had also gained a firsthand understanding of how technologies developed in a Chinese industrial hub could connect with the green development ambitions of countries across Latin America.
For Castro, the next step was to share these observations with a wider audience.
"As a journalist, I hope to tell more people the stories of China-Latin America cooperation in the new energy sector, so that the world can see China's commitment to high-quality development, openness and cooperation," she said. ■

Chinese embassy condemns Japanese leaders' Yasukuni Shrine moves as affront to historical justice: spokesperson
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
12:13:42 CST
13:13:42 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Japan on Saturday strongly condemned Japan's latest negative moves concerning the war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, after Japanese leaders sent ritual offerings to the shrine and some cabinet members and lawmakers visited it.
Japan launched wars of aggression against other countries and regions during World War II and committed heinous crimes, the spokesperson said in response to media inquiries.
The so-called Yasukuni Shrine enshrines 14 Class-A war criminals directly responsible for the wars of aggression and is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism, the spokesperson said.
No matter what excuses Japanese officials make for paying homage to the shrine, they cannot conceal their true intentions of rehabilitating war criminals, covering up wartime crimes, distorting historical facts and paving the way for accelerating Japan's remilitarization, the spokesperson said.
Such erroneous acts desecrate historical justice, challenge the bottom line of human civilization and constitute a provocation to the postwar international order, drawing firm opposition from the international community, the spokesperson added.
Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, the spokesperson said that a correct understanding of and attitude toward history are essential for Japan's return to the international community after the war, constitute a political foundation for its relations with neighboring countries, and serve as a yardstick for assessing whether Japan honors its commitment to peaceful development.
China solemnly urges Japan to deeply reflect on its history of aggression, face up to its wartime crimes, exercise prudence in words and deeds on issues concerning the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely break with militarism, the spokesperson said, calling on the Japanese side to win the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete actions. ■

Exclusive: Documents Show How Israel Steered Qatari Payments to Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
04:01:09 UTC
13:01:09 KST

As Israeli voters prepare for elections on Oct. 27, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tried to defend and distance himself from one of his government’s most controversial policies: allowing Qatar to funnel nearly $2 billion into the Hamas-controlled Gaza Strip for more than a decade. Previously undisclosed documents obtained by TIME, including letters from senior Israeli security officials to Qatari leaders, reveal that Israel encouraged and played a direct role in a payment program that was more extensive than Netanyahu has publicly acknowledged.
Beginning in 2012, Netanyahu’s government helped to facilitate Qatari payments to Gaza that had begun after Hamas seized control in 2007. By 2018, Qatar had sent roughly $1.1 billion into the Strip, according to an analysis provided to Israeli ministers, the Israeli daily Haaretz reported, with the funding designated for humanitarian assistance, fuel, and government salaries. That year, after Israeli officials castigated Qatar for allegedly financing Hamas, the Qataris began demanding formal documentation of an arrangement the two governments had agreed was meant to provide relief to citizens of the beleaguered enclave.
The extent of Israel’s cooperation with the payments was reflected in a 2020 letter from Yossi Cohen, then director of the Mossad, Israel’s intelligence agency, to Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. “It is indeed a great opportunity to express our gratitude and appreciation for the humanitarian aid efforts that the State of Qatar has provided the last few years to the Gaza Strip,” Cohen wrote. “Undoubtedly, these humanitarian efforts have played a crucial role in improving the humanitarian situation within the Gaza Strip, and ensuring stability and safety in the region.”
The payment arrangement had the support of successive Israeli governments, the Palestinians, the Trump and Biden Administrations, the United Nations, and European powers, according to officials who served in both the Trump and Biden Administrations. The flow of money from Qatar into Gaza has taken on new significance since October 7, 2023, when Hamas terrorists stormed southern Israel, murdered some 1,200 people, and took 251 more hostage. The worst security failure in the country’s history raised troubling questions about whether the financial lifeline helped to sustain Hamas’s grip on power and, in turn, enabled it to carry out the assault.
Since then, Qatar has been frustrated by allegations leveled by Israeli political leaders that its payments to Gaza had helped finance the deadliest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust. “All of Qatar’s financial assistance in Gaza has been directed to Palestinian citizens through mechanisms coordinated with the Israeli authorities and international partners. Under previous aid mechanisms, all financial assistance, as well as goods such as food, medicine and fuel, passed through Israel before entering Gaza,” a spokesperson for Qatar’s International Media Office tells TIME. “Nothing was delivered directly by Qatar; we provided the aid, while delivery was carried out by the United Nations’ organizations in coordination with the Israeli authorities. If any funding reached Hamas, as alleged by individuals and groups with political agendas against Qatar, the responsibility lies with Israel, which oversaw the delivery and created the mechanism.”
Critics have long argued that Netanyahu sought to sustain Hamas rule in Gaza to keep the Palestinians divided between the Islamist terror group and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, foreclosing the prospect of a unified Palestinian leadership capable of negotiating a two-state solution. Netanyahu’s wager, according to these critics, was that the aid would give Hamas something to lose and would therefore help contain the group while Israel pursued normalization with the Arab world without resolving the Palestinian question. Instead, as Israel moved closer to a historic agreement with Saudi Arabia, Hamas launched an assault that upended the region, plunging it into war.
The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment for this story.
The documents now give Israelis a fuller accounting of a policy that preceded the catastrophe, as they prepare to render a verdict on the man who presided over both. “It was a policy failure on our part born of good intentions that multiple prime ministers kept going,” says one former Israeli defense official. “But Netanyahu was unquestionably at the center of it. He was the one who championed and accelerated the program, his government was in charge of the way it was run, and now we know as a society that we can never afford to make a mistake like that again.”
Ehud Olmert was still prime minister when Qatar began sending money to Gaza in 2007, after Hamas won control of the coastal enclave. At the outset, the Israeli government was not directly involved in the transfers. That changed under Netanyahu. By 2012, his government had approved a system that gave Israel a direct role in facilitating Qatari assistance: delivering food and medical supplies, determining which Palestinian families qualified for financial aid and disbursing the funds, and enabling Qatari financing to expand Gaza’s electricity supply, according to Israeli and Arab officials, as well as official documents obtained by TIME.
At first, the arrangement was informal. Qatar supplied the money with Israel’s approval, even as Israeli officials publicly criticized Doha for financing Hamas, according to sources familiar with the negotiations. The contradiction aggravated the Qataris, a senior official in the first Trump Administration tells TIME: Israeli officials would denounce the payments in public, then privately ask Doha to renew them.
Qatar, a gas-rich monarchy in the Persian Gulf, is accustomed to walking a fine line. It plays host to both the U.S. Central Command and to senior Hamas officials. The country set up a Hamas political office in Doha at the request of the U.S. in 2011. In contrast to other Gulf monarchies, especially Saudi Arabia, Qatar sees no threat in the Muslim Brotherhood, the political movement that spawned Hamas. After Oct. 7, Qatar's government emerged as the go-between in negotiations among Israel, Hamas and Washington, where Biden Administration officials privately praised the Qataris as honest brokers.
By 2018, Qatar sought written documentation of the Israeli government’s role in the aid agreement. It was subsequently formalized through a trilateral mechanism involving Qatar, Israel, and the United Nations, designed to administer the aid with international and Israeli oversight. On October 2, 2018, Israel and Qatar, together with the United Nations, signed an agreement to finance fuel deliveries into Gaza.
A spokesperson for the United Nations declined to comment for this story but referred TIME to statements the body’s special coordinator for Middle East peace, Tor Wennesland, made in 2021 acknowledging the arrangement. “These efforts are vital to improving the dire socioeconomic and humanitarian situation in Gaza,” he said at a UN Security Council briefing.
In August 2021, Qatar signed another agreement committing $40 million to a cash assistance program that would give nearly 100,000 Palestinian households $100 per month for four months. The arrangements were subsequently extended. American officials were brought into the discussions as well. According to a diplomat briefed on the process, who asked for anonymity to divulge details because they were not authorized to comment publicly, Qatar wanted Washington to understand precisely how the system worked, fearing that Israeli officials might later accuse Doha of financing Hamas without acknowledging Israel’s own role. “The Israelis kept insisting on doing it this way, so that they can control what goes in and out,” the official told TIME, rather than establish “something more regular and something which goes directly to the people.”
Under the system, according to U.S. and Israeli officials, Qatar paid for fuel and electricity purchased from Israel to increase the number of hours Gaza received power, a structure coordinated with Israeli security services. It transferred money through the United Nations for projects in the Strip. And it provided monthly $100 payments to some of Gaza’s poorest families. According to diplomats familiar with the system, Israel vetted the recipients and oversaw the distribution mechanism, with funds transferred through the World Food Programme and eligible families notified by text message before collecting their assistance at designated locations. “If the money ever got in the wrong hands, it was because of the Israelis,” the diplomat said, “because they were the ones overseeing the whole thing.”
Netanyahu’s government was so committed to the policy that when Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas cut payments to government workers in Gaza in 2018, Israeli security officials shuttled Qatari cash into the Strip in suitcases, U.S. and Israeli media reported at the time. Naftali Bennett, then Netanyahu’s education minister, publicly opposed the transfers, denouncing them as “protection money.” Netanyahu briefly suspended the payments in January 2019 amid renewed violence along the Gaza border, using the prospect of their resumption as leverage to pressure Hamas to stop firing rockets.
But while critics on the Israeli right railed against the deal, Netanyahu’s deputies worked behind the scenes to preserve it, according to correspondence obtained by TIME. In July 2019, according to one letter, Qatar notified the Netanyahu government that it was transferring $6 million to 20,000 beneficiaries in Gaza, with each receiving $300. It is unknown how many of those beneficiaries, chosen by Israel, were connected to Hamas or had family members who belonged to the group. Over the last two decades, Hamas has been deeply embedded in Gaza, operating not only as an armed militant organization but also as a political movement and governing authority, employing civil servants responsible for the territory’s public services and infrastructure.
In 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic swept through Gaza, R. L. Maoz, a member of Netanyahu’s National Security Council, urged Qatari officials to maintain the payments despite the Israeli government’s public criticism. “We reiterate the importance of continuing to transfer the Qatari humanitarian financial assistance through the existing mechanism,” Maoz wrote. “We ask that Qatar’s financial assistance not be transferred through mediators or countries other than the ambassador, Mohammed Al-Emadi,” he added, referring to the chairman of the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza. “We greatly appreciate your cooperation and open discourse to safeguard stability and security in the region and to bring our countries and peoples closer together.”
The program survived Netanyahu’s departure from power. His successor, Bennett, had been among its fiercest critics, raising the prospect that the arrangement might finally end. At that point, Qatar prepared to halt the program, a former Biden official tells TIME. Instead, after taking office in 2021, Bennett ended only the delivery of cash-filled suitcases, not the broader flow of Qatari assistance to Gaza, the Associated Press reported. According to people familiar with discussions about the policy, Bennett’s prior objections were a message intended for his domestic political constituency. “There’s no issue,” an Israeli representative told a Biden envoy, according to an official present. “We want to continue with it as is.”
To some of the officials involved, the compact contained a fundamental flaw: both the Israeli government and Hamas retained control over aid intended for ordinary Gazans. “Bibi and Hamas hold the tap, essentially,” one of the officials told me. Hamas could restrict the system to exert pressure internally, the official said, while Netanyahu could restrict it to pressure Hamas. “We knew this was not something that was beneficial for the long term. We need to have something that’s sustainable, that empowers the civilians.”
By 2023, with tensions mounting between Israel and Hamas, Qatari officials pressed for a different model, one that would deliver assistance to Gazans without making civilians dependent on either Hamas or the Israeli government. But Netanyahu’s government wanted the existing framework kept intact, according to multiple sources who spoke to TIME, including an Israeli official and an international diplomat.
Two weeks before October 7, Mossad director David Barnea traveled to Doha and asked Qatar to renew the funding, the New York Times reported in 2023. The Qatari officials agreed but warned Barnea that it would be the last renewal. With tensions rising between Israel’s far-right ministers and Hamas, the arrangement had run its course, Qatar believed. Barnea asked for two more months. The rationale, according to the officials familiar with the conversation, was that continuing assistance to Gaza’s civilians gave Hamas something to lose and therefore gave Israel a measure of leverage over the group. After two months, the parties could reassess Hamas’s behavior and devise a more durable mechanism for delivering aid.
They never got the chance. With the brutal Oct. 7 attack on southern Israel, the Qatari aid arrangement that successive Israeli governments had spent years helping to build, modify, and preserve was over.
Ever since, Netanyahu has faced accusations that he deliberately strengthened Hamas to keep the Palestinians divided—between Hamas in Gaza, and the secular Fatah party that under Abbas governs the West Bank—and forestall a peace agreement. Critics point to remarks Netanyahu allegedly made at a 2019 Likud Party meeting. “Anyone who wants to thwart the establishment of a Palestinian state has to support bolstering Hamas and transferring money to Hamas,” he said, according to a report in the Jerusalem Post. “This is part of our strategy—to isolate the Palestinians in Gaza.”
In a 2024 interview with TIME, Netanyahu denied making the statement, insisting that the payments were meant to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe. “The reason that successive governments agreed to that is that we wanted to make sure that Gaza has a functioning civilian administration to avoid humanitarian collapse,” he said. Without the money to maintain sewage systems, water supplies, and schools, he argued, the territory could have descended into chaos and disease. Netanyahu claims that Iran supplied Hamas with weapons through separate channels, including suspected smuggling routes across Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.
Netanyahu’s dealings with Qatar have also become a source of controversy in Israel. Netanyahu has been under intense scrutiny in recent weeks over the so-called Qatargate scandal, in which former and current aides to the Israeli premier allegedly received payments to conduct a public relations campaign to cast Qatar in a favorable light for more than a year after the Oct. 7 onslaught.
Now, as international diplomats contemplate Gaza’s reconstruction, they face a version of the same dilemma: how to provide essential assistance without strengthening Hamas or another militant organization. Trump Administration officials, led by envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are working with Qatar and other Arab governments on a framework that would restore basic services while eliminating Gaza’s dependence on Islamist armed factions. “We want to ensure that the civilians are reliant on themselves and not on anyone else,” an international diplomat tells TIME. “So it’s providing actual opportunities for civilians to make money and be sustainable.”
The question confronting Israel and its international partners is not simply whether money should flow into Gaza, but also who controls it—and whether the next arrangement will avoid the failures of the last.

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet wins Top 100 Australian Books countdown — as it happened

Tim Winton's Cloudstreet wins Top 100 Australian Books countdown — as it happened
Tim Winton’s 1991 classic, Cloudstreet, has placed first in ABC Radio National’s Top 100 Australian Books.
The West Australian author had four books feature in the top 100, with Breath (2008) coming in at 33, Dirt Music (2001) at 41 and Juice (2024) at 88.
Winton, in the Perth studio, said he was honoured and slightly "bewildered" by the news.
"It's something I wrote when I was in my 20s. I'm not ashamed to have written it, but I can't quite make out what the fuss is about. I don't go back and read it but I'm quite aware of the place it has in some people's hearts because they write to me about it still.
"It's a mystery, but it's a great mystery. Somehow stories touch people."
Rounding out the top five were The Book Thief by Markus Zusak, Boy Swallows Universe by Trent Dalton, Burial Rites by Hannah Kent and A Fortunate Life by AB Facey.

Hannah Kent: 'No-one's going to read that'
Kent was a 17-year-old exchange student in Iceland when she first encountered the story of Agnes Magnúsdóttir (something she recounts in her 2025 memoir Always Home, Always Homesick).
Speaking on air now with Claire Nichols, she reflects on that teenage obsession:
"I never thought I would write a book about it … but this story haunted me for many years and the process of writing it was also one that changed me as a person and as a writer."
She says when she told people she was writing a book about the last woman to be executed in Iceland, she was often met with scepticism.
"I remember someone once telling me: 'No-one's going to want to read that — it sounds so bleak and so sad.'"
Well, turns out they were very wrong! The book has come in at #4 in the Top 100 Australian Books and #6 in the Top 100 Books of the 21st Century in 2025.

LISBON – Protesters pitched dozens of tents in Lisbon on Oct 17, demanding action to stem housing and living costs in Portugal, mirroring demonstrations that have gripped neighbouring Spain for weeks.
Hundreds of protesters rallied at night in Rossio Square – in the bustling, tourist heart of the Portuguese capital – following a march that had drawn thousands of people nationwide.
The mostly young attendees vowed to stay overnight, with hundreds singing songs as they sat around the statue of King Pedro IV that dominates the square, according to AFP journalists.
“The Portuguese social class that pays taxes, that which keeps this country going, is under attack and is losing its rights, notably its right to housing,” said Elena Costa, a 46-year-old social assistant.
“So we are all here together to try to explain that we are suffocating,” she said.
Engineer Antonio Margado, 52, criticised the centre-right government for “a total liberalisation of rents; owners are protected more and more, while tenants who need a house are those who are protected less and less”.
Portuguese housing prices rose by 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the European Union average, according to official data.
The impact is especially harsh on young people and in Lisbon, which concentrates around one-quarter of Portugal’s more than 11 million inhabitants, including the capital’s greater metropolitan area.
Another protester, Isabel Guerreiro, told public broadcaster RTP: “As a self-employed professional, I obviously don’t have the means to pay Lisbon’s exorbitant rents – and I’m a daughter of Lisbon.”
The Oct 17 camp in Lisbon amplified a housing protest that began in the northern city of Porto, where dozens of tents were set up.
‘Matter of survival’
At the earlier protest in Lisbon called by the main CGTP union, demonstrators called for better public services, pensions and wages as well as measures to tackle soaring housing costs.
Marching to the roar of drums, they held placards with slogans, including “Their greed, our misery” and “the cost of living increases, the people can’t take it any more”.
“There are many problems. Wages, housing, the cost of living: it’s a matter of survival,” said Yolanda Silva, a 43-year-old civil servant.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said “we fully understand that people want answers” and to “express their outrage at what, in their view, may be omissions in public policies”.
But he warned political rivals against “importing into Portugal climates of instability and protest that, in fact, have no support in Portuguese society”, in a likely reference to violent protests that have rocked France.
The expanding Portuguese movement comes as Spain is gripped by housing protest camps and demonstrations now in their fourth week, which have culminated in the calling of an early general election for Nov 29. AFP
