Moon rocks offer clues to its two faces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:30:17 UTC
12:30:17 KST

Moon rocks offer clues to its two faces
Samples returned from the Moon’s far side suggest that uneven heating caused by Earth’s gravity helped shape its contrasting hemispheres billions of years ago, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing a study published in National Science Review.
A team led by Professor Hejiu Hui of Nanjing University examined rocks collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission, which returned the first samples from the lunar far side in 2024. Researchers compared their chemistry with material brought back by Apollo and Chang’e-5 missions.
The Moon’s Earth-facing side contains extensive dark volcanic plains, while its far side has a thicker crust dominated by ancient, heavily cratered highlands.
The analysis found that rocks originating from the mantle beneath both hemispheres had broadly similar chemical characteristics. Far-side crustal rocks, however, were richer in magnesium, while other samples contained less material enriched in potassium, rare earth elements and phosphorus.
The researchers propose that these differences developed as the Moon’s ancient ocean of molten rock cooled and solidified.
After the Moon became tidally locked, keeping the same hemisphere facing Earth, stronger tidal heating on the near side may have driven vast currents beneath the developing crust. These flows could have carried early magnesium-rich crust toward the far side, thickening it while concentrating remaining molten material on the near side.
“This systematic geochemical comparison … indicates that the mantle displays no clear compositional dichotomy,” the authors wrote.
The proposed mechanism offers an explanation for how similar underlying mantle materials produced such different lunar landscapes. However, the researchers acknowledge that the samples may not represent the entire far side and that their model is not the only possible explanation. Further geochemical evidence will be needed to test the findings.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that October’s skywatching highlights include Saturn at opposition, the Orionid meteor shower and the Moon appearing near the Pleiades star cluster.

JNF allocates NIS 33 million to rebuild border-adjacent northern towns 2-5 km from Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:24:59 UTC
12:24:59 KST

The Board of Directors of the Jewish National Fund (JNF) approved on Tuesday a NIS 33 million budget to support 22 communities along the northern border, 2 to 5 kilometers from the Lebanese border.
Under the decision, each community evacuated during the fighting that has not yet received JNF support will receive 1.5 million NIS for infrastructure rehabilitation and development.
Among the benefiting communities are Kibbutz Ma'ayan Baruch and Kibbutz Dan in the Upper Galilee Regional Council, Beit Hillel, and Ramot Naftali. The plan also includes the remaining communities in the Mevo'ot HaHermon Regional Council, Liman in Mateh Asher, Ibn Menachem, Elkosh, Goren, Manot, and Avdon in Ma'ale Yosef, as well as Kerem Ben Zimra and Alma in the Merom HaGalil Regional Council.
Unlike the government's uniform funding model, JNF adopted a graduated support model based on distance from the Lebanese border and the severity of damage to the communities. Under this framework, front-line communities, including Kibbutz Manara and Moshav Dovev, are eligible for NIS 2.5 to 3 million per community. The current phase approves support for communities 2 to 5 km from the border, while the next phase plans to fund approximately 1 million NIS for each community 5 to 9 km away.
The funds are earmarked for infrastructure development, upgrading and fortifying public buildings (such as kindergartens, community centers, and dining halls), and enhancing open public spaces. Residents and local leadership will decide on specific projects independently.
Communities to be visited, plan to begin soon
JNF professional teams are scheduled to visit the communities in the coming days to formulate the project list, aiming to begin execution within roughly a month and a half. This step joins additional JNF investments in northern cities and regional hubs, including Tiberias (allocated approximately NIS 35 million), Karmiel, Afula, and Beit She'an.
JNF Chairman Eyal Ostrinsky commented on the expanded support plan: "We decided that JNF's northern rehabilitation efforts will not stop at the 2-kilometer border line. Adjacent communities within up to 5 km also paid a heavy price during the war and continue to pay."
Ostrinsky added: "JNF stands with the women and men of the North, and I promise we will remain shoulder-to-shoulder with them. In our view, national responsibility means looking at the broad picture, not leaving communities behind, listening, and helping. JNF acts to make rehabilitation a reality on the ground."
The Moshavim Movement welcomed the decision. Amit Yifrach, the Movement's general secretary and chairman of the Israel Farmers Association, said JNF is a true partner to the moshavim and the entire rural sector. He said this cooperation will strengthen border-adjacent moshavim and rural settlements as a whole, emphasizing that the resilience of border communities is integral to the resilience of the State of Israel.

Israel launches NIS 25 million initiative to close high-tech gender gap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
03:24:01 UTC
12:24:01 KST

The Israel Innovation Authority and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry announced in mid-October that they will jointly invest NIS 25 million in training senior female high-tech executives, integrating women into the tech industry, helping women return to work after a long break, and reducing the gender wage gap in the high-tech sector.
This initiative is a response to persistent gender gaps in the high-tech industry, both in representation across technical and managerial positions and in salary levels.
The funding will support programs targeting five challenges identified by the IIA and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry: advancing women into senior high-tech management roles, integrating highly educated women into deep-tech industries, helping experienced women return to the sector, supporting career advancement after maternity leave, and promoting gender equality within high-tech companies.
This budget, which includes matching funds from private organizations, will be allocated to 15 programs designed to address the barriers facing women in high-tech in Israel.
Orgs identify significant wage and representation gaps in the high-tech sector
Women in high-tech earn an average of approximately NIS 23,000 per month compared with approximately NIS 33,000 among men, according to the IIA and the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry. This represents a gap of approximately NIS 10,200 per month, with men's salaries about 44% higher than women's. Significant gaps also exist within different occupational categories, including research and development, corporate staff, and management positions.
"The increase in life expectancy and changes in the labor market require us to prepare for a diverse, inclusive employment market adapted to all age groups," Labor and Social Affairs Ministry Director-General Robi Shemesh said. "Employment rates among both women and men begin to decline as early as age 50, and ageist perceptions, including internalized ageism, constitute a significant barrier to continued participation in quality employment.
"The new programs are part of this approach, which seeks to enable women to make use of their experience, skills, and professional abilities, reintegrate into the labor market, and advance to meaningful positions in knowledge-intensive industries," Shemesh added.

U.S. measles cases top 4,400 as Pennsylvania outbreak worsens
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
11:23:53 CST
12:23:53 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The United States reported 4,410 confirmed measles cases in 2026 as of Thursday, nearly double the 2,289 cases reported for all of 2025, putting the country on track for its highest annual total since 1991, according to the latest data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Of the confirmed cases, 4,392 were reported by 47 jurisdictions, while 18 cases were reported among international visitors to the United States, the CDC said.
Children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 accounted for the largest share of cases, with 1,856 infections, or 42 percent of the total.
A total of 451 patients, or about 10 percent of all confirmed cases, have been hospitalized. About 96 percent of cases were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown, according to CDC data.
Meanwhile, the outbreak in the U.S. state of Pennsylvania continues to grow. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Friday that 1,260 measles cases have been confirmed across 43 counties in the state so far this year, including 238 hospitalizations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths.
The state reported 38 new cases since Wednesday. It is also investigating a recently reported death in Franklin County, the department said.
The CDC plans to send one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help respond to the outbreak, NBC News reported Thursday, citing a CDC spokesperson. The scientist, an officer with the agency's Epidemic Intelligence Service (EIS), is expected to arrive later this week. EIS officers are often referred to as "disease detectives" because of their work investigating disease outbreaks.
"CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health," the CDC spokesperson was quoted as saying.
The CDC recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine as the best protection against measles.
The agency says that when more than 95 percent of people in a community are vaccinated, community immunity, also known as herd immunity, helps protect more people from the disease. ■

Interview: Confidence, resilience, courage: China's Asian Para Games flagbearers aim to inspire
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
10:34:09 CST
11:34:09 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- When para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan learned they had been chosen as flagbearers for China at the opening ceremony of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Nagoya on Sunday, they were thrilled but keenly aware of the responsibility that come with the honor.
"It feels like a big vote of confidence in me," Li said. "This time I'm not just representing myself, but the whole Chinese delegation. It's not just an honor, it's a responsibility."
Yan said he felt humbled by the appointment. "There are people on the delegation who have achieved more than I have," he said. "I still have room to improve."
Both athletes bring impressive resumes to Nagoya. Li won China's first-ever Paralympic taekwondo medal in Tokyo and went on to claim the country's first Paralympic taekwondo gold in Paris. She was named 2025 World Para Taekwondo Female Athlete of the Year, becoming the first Team China athlete to receive the honor.
Yan has established himself as a leading force in para powerlifting, winning gold at the World Cup, the Tokyo Paralympics, the World Championships, the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and the Paris Paralympics.
Serving as flagbearer, Yan said, brings both pressure and motivation; for Li, the role has given her a renewed sense of purpose.
"Before, when I stepped onto the mat, I was mostly focused on each round and each technique," she said. "But walking out as a flagbearer, I feel a mission. Beyond giving everything in competition, I want to show the confidence and positive spirit of athletes with disabilities."
Both athletes have ties to Beijing Sport University: Li is studying sports training there, and Yan is a recent graduate.
"I had a really fulfilling time at university," Yan said. "I didn't just learn from textbooks. I made a lot of friends, and group activities taught me how to work with others."
Those teamwork lessons could prove useful in Nagoya, where Yan will compete in the mixed-team powerlifting event, making its debut at the Asian Para Games.
"In the lead-up to the competition, I need to communicate more with my teammates and keep myself in top form for longer," he said.
He will also compete in an individual powerlifting event: "My goal is to show everything I've put into training and to remain calm. If I get a good result, that will be great."
"I want to show the self-confidence, independence, resilience and courage of athletes with disabilities," Yan added. "No matter who we face, we'll keep fighting and never give up. I hope people can see the power of perseverance and find the courage to chase their own dreams."
Li will compete in the women's K44-57kg para taekwondo category. "My goal is simply to fight every bout well and go all out for gold," she said. "I want to show that athletes with disabilities are not afraid of challenges, and that we, too, can compete on the big stage and enjoy it."
"I hope more people will see that sport has no boundaries," she added. "Whatever our physical condition, we can all gain confidence through sport. Through my own story, I want to encourage more people with disabilities to step out of their homes, take up exercise, and feel the power sport can bring." ■

Search continues for 11 missing after boat sank off Mexico’s Baja coast
Some of 16 survivors treated for suspected shark bites, US coastguard says.
The search continues for 11 people still missing after a boat capsized off Mexico’s Baja California coast on Friday, as multiple survivors have been treated for suspected shark bites, according to the US coastguard.
“Several of the individuals rescued were suffering from severe injuries consistent with shark bites, and the Coast Guard provided life-saving first aid while en route [to] San Diego,” the coastguard said in a statement on Saturday.
Sixteen Mexican nationals were rescued on Friday. Survivors told officials there were 27 people on board.
The coastguard and US Navy used multiple aircraft and boats, along with assistance from the Mexican Navy, to search the area for the remaining passengers. An additional helicopter will be deployed later on Saturday, according to the coastguard.
A Mayday call was transmitted from someone on the boat at about 1am on Friday, coastguard Lieutenant Santiago Tamburini said on the day.
A rescue helicopter reached the site about two hours later. It took about 90 minutes for the crew, which included a rescue swimmer, to pull the 16 people from the water, he added.
The boat went down about 225km (140 miles) west of Ensenada, Mexico, an area popular with fishing and leisure boats, but that is also frequented by smugglers.
Although the incident did not happen in US waters, coastguard official Charlie Valor said on Saturday they “were able to help, and that’s why we launched our assets”.
Fatal attempts to transport refugees and migrants from Mexico to the US have occurred in the past.
In May 2025, at least three people died when a boat flipped off the coast about 56km (35 miles) north of the US-Mexico border.
In 2023, eight people were killed in one of the deadliest maritime smuggling accidents off the US coast, when two boats approached a San Diego beach in heavy fog, and one capsized in the surf.

Keen for change, Israel’s Arab minority sees election as existential
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

Keen for change, Israel’s Arab minority sees election as existential
Majd al-Krum, Israel – After boycotting Israeli parliamentary elections his entire life, 55-year-old Said Kabat will head to the polls for the first time on Oct 27.
For him, the vote is existential – if a right-wing government is returned to power, he fears for the future of Israel’s Arab minority, to which he belongs.
The pharmacist from the Arab village of Majd al-Krum in northern Israel told AFP he used to boycott elections “all the time”.
“But now, I will go out and vote,” he said, concerned that a low turnout among the Arab population would embolden the far-right elements of the current ruling coalition.
Arab Israelis, also known as Palestinian citizens of Israel, account for about 21% of the country’s population.
They are descendants of Palestinians who remained within Israel’s borders after the state’s creation in 1948, and have long complained of discrimination compared with Israel’s Jewish majority.
The close-fought election is sparking calls for a mobilisation push among Israel’s Arab population, after their situation worsened under the outgoing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – one of the most right-wing in the country’s history.
Driven by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, settlement construction in the occupied West Bank has soared, and their attention is now turning to predominantly Arab areas inside Israel.
In September, land belonging to Kabat’s family in Majd al-Krum was the site of a confrontation between residents and Jewish Israelis who came to establish an outpost – a tactic used by West Bank settlers to take control of land.
Israeli police eventually removed the outpost, which had garnered the backing of Smotrich, who held a rally at the site and in August unveiled a plan to “Judaise” Israel’s predominantly Arab regions.
“In the light of the events, whether in Majd al-Krum or other villages, I urge every young person and everyone with a vote to cast it,” Kabat said.
‘Battle for existence’
Turnout among the Arab minority has traditionally been lower than that for Israel as a whole.
In the last election in November 2022, turnout among Arab and Druze voters was around 53%, while the country’s overall figure stood at around 70%.
In Majd al-Krum, activists like 31-year-old Dana Salameh were touring the village to explain the importance of voting.
“Everyone, even those boycotting and those unconvinced about voting, has begun to see the danger very close to them if this government remains in power,” Salameh said.
“They don’t want Arabs in this state at all... whether here or in Gaza or the West Bank,” she added.
On Oct 27, the Arab vote is expected to be split among four parties running on two lists.
The far-left Joint List brings together three parties, while Raam, or the United Arab List, is more open to negotiating with the right.
Raam became the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a 2021-2022 coalition, and it could again play a kingmaker role this year.
A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 projected that the two lists would garner 13 seats in the next Israeli Parliament. They currently have 10 between them.
For Salameh, the poll is evidence of a growing conviction among Israel’s Arab citizens that they are facing “a battle for existence”.
Surging crime levels within the community could also push people towards the ballot box.
Since the start of 2026, at least 175 Arab citizens have been killed in violent crime incidents, according to the Abraham Initiatives coexistence organisation.
The violence is predominantly driven by criminal gangs, with Arab Israelis accusing the police – under the ministerial responsibility of Ben-Gvir – of lax enforcement. “The state has completely withdrawn from the scene,” said criminologist Walid Haddad.
‘Change is in our hands’
In Majd al-Krum, home to about 17,000 people, campaign billboards for the Joint List have popped up bearing the slogan “The change is in our hands”.
Several homes in the village face the threat of demolition, reflecting the reality for Arab localities across the country.
The Israeli authorities say the houses were built without permits or on state-owned land, but Palestinians say permits are near impossible to obtain.
In the city of Tayibe in central Israel, around 40 members of the Abu Mtair family face the looming threat of displacement, waiting for a decision on demolition orders that have been temporarily frozen.
“I cannot imagine this right-wing government returning,” said Akram Abu Mtair, 47, urging the city’s residents to vote.
Farther south, in the Negev desert, Israeli bulldozers recently demolished around 80 structures housing about 400 people in the Bedouin village of Al-Dahiya.
For Adnan Abu Wadi, who was left homeless with his four children, the demolitions were nothing more than an election stunt.
“People will turn out to vote in large numbers. We will vote as Arabs to change the government and remove the extremists.” AFP

Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion

Fears grow in DRC as former President Joseph Kabila joins rebellion
Kabila’s move raises fresh questions about the war in eastern Congo and prospects for peace.
Goma, DR Congo – Hopes for peace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have suffered another setback after former President Joseph Kabila joined a new political-military coalition challenging President Felix Tshisekedi.
Announced in Goma on Monday evening, the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN), or Front for the Refoundation of the Nation, is led by Kabila and replaces the existing alliance between the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and the March 23 Movement (M23). The new coalition brings together figures and forces associated with the two movements, accuses Tshisekedi of tyranny and calls for resistance by all means, including force.
Goma, the main city in eastern Congo’s North Kivu province, has been under M23-AFC control since January last year. Kabila’s move brings a former head of state directly into the leadership of the rebellion.
The conflict has displaced millions and drawn in neighbouring countries. Its roots stretch back decades, shaped by regional rivalries, unresolved security concerns and competition for territory and mineral resources. The aftermath of Rwanda’s 1994 genocide helped fuel wars across the region, while tensions between Kinshasa and Kigali continue to shape the fighting.
M23 says it took up arms because the Congolese government failed to honour earlier commitments. The Congolese government and international actors have accused Rwanda of supporting the group, an allegation Kigali denies, citing security threats from armed groups operating in eastern Congo.
Whether Kabila’s leadership will reshape the rebellion or further complicate efforts to end the war remains unclear. In Goma, residents fear the latest realignment will push peace further out of reach.
Why do residents fear the war is far from over?
For Basa Juhudi, Kabila’s decision has revived fears that the conflict will drag on.
“As a resident of Goma, I believed the war might end in the very near future, hoping that the Congolese government would liberate us. And we are greatly surprised that even our former president has joined the fray,” he told Al Jazeera.
Juhudi said Kabila’s political experience makes his involvement particularly troubling.
“The fact that Joseph Kabila has joined the rebellion, bearing in mind that he is our former president and knows this country inside out, means the war is far from over. I am not happy about this frightening situation.”
He also fears for the country’s democratic future, recalling the peaceful transfer of power in 2019, when Tshisekedi succeeded Kabila.
“Today, I am very afraid. I don’t know if I will be lucky enough to experience a proper democracy in the DRC. I was delighted by the country’s very first peaceful transfer of power,” Juhudi said.
How does Kabila’s past shape his return to the conflict?
Kabila came to power in 2001 following the assassination of his father, Laurent-Desire Kabila. He was elected president in 2006 and re-elected in 2011.
His second constitutional term was due to end in 2016, but elections were delayed. Critics accused him of seeking to remain in power beyond the constitutionally permitted two terms. Protests against the delays were met with deadly violence before a political compromise paved the way for elections in December 2018.
Tshisekedi was declared the winner and took office in January 2019, marking the DRC’s first peaceful transfer of presidential power through elections. Kabila defended the election delays, arguing that the Congolese people had ultimately resolved their problems through dialogue.
His alignment with the FRN marks a new phase in his confrontation with Tshisekedi. The coalition presents itself as a political alternative to the government while maintaining an armed challenge to its authority. Whether Kabila can translate his political experience and networks into wider support remains uncertain.
Can dialogue still avert a wider confrontation?
Kabila’s move has drawn criticism from within the Congolese political establishment.
Vital Kamerhe, a former speaker of the National Assembly and leader of the Union for the Congolese Nation (UNC), urged the movement to abandon armed struggle.
“You cannot erase your own record by accusing your successor,” Kamerhe declared in a speech on Wednesday.
“I call on the leaders of this movement to abandon their plans and prioritise the path of dialogue. Whatever our frustrations, our differences or our ambitions, nothing, absolutely nothing, can justify us taking up weapons against our own country, at the risk of sacrificing our own Congolese lives,” he said.
His appeal highlights the central challenge facing peace efforts: political grievances remain unresolved, while renewed fighting threatens a population already battered by conflict.
What does Kabila’s move mean for peace initiatives?
The United States and Qatar have pursued separate diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the conflict.
In Doha, representatives of the Congolese government and AFC-M23 have discussed a ceasefire, the return of refugees, the release of detainees and measures to counter rhetoric that stigmatises ethnic minorities.
Washington has pursued an agreement between the DRC and Rwanda, including commitments relating to the neutralisation of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) and the withdrawal of Rwandan troops from Congolese territory.
The initiatives address different but connected dimensions of the crisis. Kabila’s emergence as leader of the FRN raises questions about who will represent the armed opposition and whether existing commitments will be respected.
However, the new coalition has said it intends to honour commitments made during the Doha negotiations.
In a communique released on Wednesday, Freddy Kaniki, one of the FRN’s leaders, said the signing of the coalition’s memorandum of association and its official launch marked the dissolution of the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), which the FRN succeeds by right.
The communique said the FRN would assume the AFC’s “rights, obligations and commitments, in particular those entered into as part of the Doha negotiations”.
The statement suggests that the coalition intends to maintain the commitments made by its predecessor. It remains to be seen, however, how this pledge will translate into progress towards a ceasefire and a lasting settlement.
For Josue Akuzwe Walayi, a Congolese human rights activist, the development threatens to undermine hopes raised by the negotiations.
“My greatest fear is for the future of the Doha and Washington peace initiatives; it is not just that they will be a diplomatic failure, but that they will become yet more agreements without any real peace for the Congolese people,” he tells Al Jazeera.
Walayi argues that agreements without effective accountability mechanisms risk becoming empty promises. Lasting peace, he says, requires parties to honour their commitments and violations to be documented, investigated and punished in accordance with the law.
“What would the Doha and Washington agreements be worth if, despite the negotiations, Congolese people continue to die, families remain forced into exile and communities live in fear? The danger would be to normalise the war whilst the people pay the price,” he warns.
Could Kabila’s return pose a broader challenge to Kinshasa?
Kabila’s return to the centre of the conflict comes amid his legal confrontation with the Congolese state. Last year, a Congolese military court sentenced him to death in his absence on charges, including treason and war crimes, linking him to the M23 rebellion. His relatives described the conviction as “unjust” and “politically motivated”.
Goma resident Willo Riziki says Kabila’s involvement should prompt the government to reassess the challenge it faces.
“The Congolese authorities must now take this war very seriously. If Kinshasa thought it was dealing with puppets, that is no longer the case. There are people all over the country who remain loyal to Kabila,” Riziki told Al Jazeera.
How far that loyalty extends, and whether it can translate into organised political or military support, remains uncertain.
There has been no official government reaction to the coalition’s announcement. Last week, after Kabila warned that the country was in peril and needed to be saved, government spokesman Patrick Muyaya said the former president had “nothing to offer but chaos”. In a post on X, Muyaya described Kabila as a “man of the past, nostalgic for anti-democratic methods”.
The confrontation between Kabila and Tshisekedi reflects a wider struggle over the country’s political future. But for civilians in the east, the immediate question is whether the latest realignment will bring more fighting and further delay a negotiated settlement.
“We don’t know if the war will end here,” said Juhudi.

‘They kicked the French mayor, shouted Viva la France’: Diplomat recounts West Bank settler attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
02:17:57 UTC
11:17:57 KST

Israel's diplomatic standing in Europe is at a historic low, and as if that were not enough, Saturday afternoon brought an attack on European diplomats by Jewish rioters. Once again, security forces failed to arrive at the scene in time, and the suspects fled without being arrested. "They were attacked by seven adult men, ages 20 and older, who apparently did not come from a nearby outpost but from farther away, meaning they had been specifically summoned," one of the diplomats present at the scene said. "They kicked the French mayor, and he was injured."
A European diplomat who was in one of the vehicles targeted in the attack described the terrifying moments to ynet. "The residents of Taybeh invited diplomats and peace activists to the olive harvest to protect them. At one point, we heard that settlers were approaching, so we immediately got into the car and started driving. Then I saw masked settlers carrying sticks and metal crowbars running toward us. It was clear they had no good intentions. It was frightening. They hadn't come to pick olives."
"They kicked the French mayor, and after beating him, they shouted 'Viva la France.' They had recognized the French flag," the diplomat continued. "They also attacked the Belgian vehicle. When you see something like that, you say to yourself, 'My God, how can something like this happen?' We came with security personnel, and it's absurd because this is an area under Israeli control. We knew settler violence was serious, but when you witness it firsthand, you understand just how terrible it is, especially for the residents who depend on the olive harvest for their livelihoods."
The mayor is Bernard Baudoux of Aulnoye-Aymeries, France, a member of the French Communist Party. The attack itself, which took place in the Christian village of Taybeh in the Binyamin region of the West Bank, was not captured on camera. However, Baudoux was subsequently filmed lying on the ground, and a vehicle belonging to the Belgian Consulate was photographed with a smashed window.
"This was professional-style violence, far more severe than anything we have seen in previous incidents," the diplomat said, emphasizing that all members of the delegation were "convinced" it was "an organized operation intended to send a message to Europeans, rather than to local residents."
The diplomat said members of the delegation were deeply angered by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's response to the incident. Netanyahu has so far refrained from explicitly addressing the attack, as have the leaders of other parties in his political camp. However, the Prime Minister's Office issued a statement in English casting doubt on the European account, even after Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and the IDF said "Israeli rioters" were responsible for the incident.
Beyond the fact that Israel is once again presenting conflicting messages to the international community, with its own officials contradicting one another, the diplomat said, "The mayor's political background is irrelevant to the question of who attacked him. Netanyahu's statement completely ignores the fact that this is a Christian village and that the delegation came from Catholic countries that consider themselves committed to protecting Christians in the West Bank. In Europe, Netanyahu's statement is seen as shocking."
'This was an attack with clubs'
Members of the European delegation also responded to claims made in Israel that the visit should have been coordinated with security forces so they could provide protection for participants.
"That is a misleading claim," delegation members said. "Taybeh is in Area B, and visits there do not require coordination. Diplomats visit frequently, and the military has never escorted them or required prior coordination."
The Prime Minister's Office, for its part, issued the following statement:
"The diplomatic delegation entered a sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination with the IDF, as officially confirmed by the military. Such coordination is essential to protecting visiting diplomats and preventing violence. The visit included Bernard Baudoux, a French Communist Party mayor who previously raised the Palestinian flag over his municipal building, prompting French authorities to order its removal.
"Published footage shows masked individuals confronting a diplomatic vehicle. Separate images show a smashed window and a person lying on the ground. These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility. Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible.
"These reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge."
The European delegation included representatives from Belgium, Poland and France, along with the French mayor, whose municipality has a sister-city relationship with Taybeh. They arrived a day after an attack on photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was moderately injured and underwent surgery in Israel.
"They came to the only remaining entirely Christian village in the West Bank to show solidarity during the olive harvest," the diplomat said. "An 'alleged attack' or a 'confrontation with a vehicle' does not describe what happened. This was an attack with clubs, and a French elected official was injured."
Unlike the leaders of parties in Netanyahu's political camp, Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party condemned the attack. "The violence displayed by a handful of extremists in Judea and Samaria against diplomats is serious and deserves unequivocal condemnation," the party said. "This violent minority does not represent the residents of Judea and Samaria. It tarnishes the reputation of the great Zionist settlement enterprise in Judea and Samaria and harms the settlements themselves. Anyone who supports the settlement enterprise must condemn this violent minority and take firm action against it."
In Israel, meanwhile, there are concerns that the growing frequency of violent incidents in the West Bank, coupled with the failure of police and the IDF to contain them, could lead to tougher sanctions against Israel, potentially extending beyond the settlements. Following the incident, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot said his country "will continue to push for European Union sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
On Saturday evening, hours after the incident, which occurred amid turmoil in France itself, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said, "The Israeli authorities must arrest those responsible for these despicable acts and bring them to justice. They must, with the utmost urgency, put an end to these criminal acts of violence and ensure the safety of civilian populations, as they are required to do under international law."
Poland's Foreign Ministry also expressed outrage over the attack, as did several other European countries whose representatives had not participated in the delegation.
Meanwhile, U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee addressed the attack on Levine, saying, "Heidi is US Citizen, clear ID as journalist. Details of who under investigation, but those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison. We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.  Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards. Dishonorable act of senseless violence."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also commented overnight on the attacks in the West Bank, calling on Israel to take strong action against settler violence.
"We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing. We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff," Rubio told reporters.
His remarks followed the release of footage showing the attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post. Levine was injured Friday during an assault by settlers on Palestinians. Rubio said the State Department had sought to establish the circumstances of the incident and that he expected to receive answers from the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. He made the remarks before departing for Uzbekistan.
The village that is disappearing
Taybeh is the last village in the West Bank whose entire population is Christian, without exception. In ynet's "No Man's Land" series, Rabbi Benny Lau noted that the Christian population between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea has been steadily declining and now accounts for less than 1% of the Palestinian population in the area. Signs of this exodus are visible in the village's empty homes. Since October 7, 15 families have left Taybeh and the country, relocating to places where substantial communities of Taybeh expatriates have already established themselves.
Father Jacques, one of the local church leaders, described to Lau how despair has been taking hold among residents. He spoke nostalgically about the years before the Second Intifada and the Oslo Accords, when, he recalled, he could get into his car and drive to Jaffa, while settlers would stop in the village to buy popsicles and ice cream for their children.
The settlement of Ofra lies west of Taybeh, and numerous settler farms have been established around the village in recent years. Christian tradition identifies Taybeh with the ancient town of Ephraim, where Jesus stayed with his disciples before traveling to Jerusalem. The village is therefore considered a holy site and is home to historic churches and Christian institutions.
Taybeh is also home to the brewery that has produced Taybeh Beer, the first Palestinian beer, since 1995. The village hosts an Oktoberfest-style beer festival that typically attracts Europeans visiting the region.
Since 2025, Taybeh has been subjected to several attacks by Jewish rioters, including incidents in which vehicles and homes were set on fire. Several Palestinians have also been killed by live gunfire.
In one incident in July 2025, rioters set fire to a cemetery and desecrated a church, prompting Huckabee to visit the village and describe the incident as an act of terrorism.
But even after that visit, settlers continued their attacks, setting Palestinian vehicles on fire and spray-painting graffiti that read, "You will regret this."

CALGARY – Multiple people were killed and injured after a “serious incident” caused a fire that tore through a Canadian military base in Alberta, officials said on Oct 17.
Defence Minister David McGuinty said at a brief press conference that the “very tragic events” at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright had led to a number of casualties.
“I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” he said, without providing details.
The minister said it was an ongoing emergency.
CFB Wainwright, located about 210km south-east of Edmonton, is one of the busiest army bases in Canada.
The Wainright RCMP detachment said it responded to the base at about 4pm local time.
Civilian first responders were on the scene along with military personnel, McGuinty said, describing it as an “active and delicate” situation.
“I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” he said.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be involved in investigating the incident, he added.
Hospitals in Edmonton activated a code orange, used for mass casualty events, as they expected a surge of patients with local hospitals overwhelmed, the Canadian Broadcasting Corp reported.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier on social media that “a serious incident creating a major fire” had occurred at the base.
The municipality of Wainwright said the fire “crossed the base fence earlier today and is being actively managed”.
High winds in the region caused the fire to spread.
Fire crews from several regions are working and an emergency response has been set up.
The town has a population of about 7,000 people.
Crews from neighbouring Saskatchewan were providing support, the province’s Premier Scott Moe said on social media.
Alberta, a province of five million people, is set to vote in a referendum on Oct 19 in which voters could choose to begin a process to separate from Canada.
Advance polls in the area were shut down due to the emergency, the provincial elections agency said.
Wainwright is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which prepares soldiers from across the country for “realistic” battlefield conditions. It has suffered casualties during exercises in the past. In 2020, a soldier died after sustaining a gunshot wound during training.
Incidents in 2017, 2014 and 2005 each killed one soldier and collectively injured at least seven in rollovers of light armoured vehicles. BLOOMBERG

Man fishing near a Florida lake killed by alligator

Man fishing near a Florida lake killed by alligator
Emmett Lindner
- A 71-year-old man, Steven Hamilton, was bitten and killed while fishing at Dr Bradford Memorial Park on Lake Apopka, Florida, on Oct 16.
- Police said the nearly 3.6m alligator was “removed as a danger to the public” after the attack. Fish and Wildlife is investigating.
- Officials said alligators are common in the area and Florida has more than 1 million alligators, but attacks on people are rare. They warned: “respect it, keep your distance”.
AI generated
FLORIDA – A man who was fishing on the shore of a Florida lake was bitten and killed by an alligator on Oct 16, according to US police and wildlife authorities.
Steven Hamilton, 71, was fishing at Dr Bradford Memorial Park on the south side of Lake Apopka, a spokesperson for the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said in a statement.
The alligator, which was nearly 3.6m long, was “dispatched”, Captain Michael Mason of the Winter Garden Police Department said during a news conference on Oct 16. Asked if it had been euthanised, he said only that it was “removed as a danger to the public”.
Police first responded to the lake area – a known alligator habitat in central Florida – at about 5pm on Oct 16, he said.
“Lake Apopka has tons of alligators in it,” he said, “so it’s not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town.”
The Fish and Wildlife commission, which is investigating alongside police, said emergency personnel declared Hamilton dead at the scene. An alligator trapper was then sent to find the reptile.
It was not immediately clear what injuries Hamilton sustained.
Lake Apopka, which is 24km to 32km north-west of Orlando, is Florida’s fourth-largest lake at roughly 12,130ha, according to the St Johns River Water Management District. In 2024, it had the 14th-largest alligator population among lakes in the state, with more than 4,600, The Palm Beach Post reported.
There are alligators in all 67 Florida counties, according to the Fish and Wildlife commission. It estimates that the state has a healthy and stable alligator population surpassing one million.
Though there is a robust number of the reptiles throughout Florida, attacks on people are rare. They are more common in or around water, as they are not well adapted to capturing prey on land. They can, however, lunge at prey within a few feet of a shoreline.
“Local wildlife, respect it, keep your distance,” Mason said on Oct 16. An alligator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like your Florida emblem. But it can be dangerous”. NYTIMES

China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
Unknown

01:30:06 UTC
10:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
China’s ‘golden week’ holidays come at a cost
A week of uninterrupted leave might look generous on paper, but it can conceal the working days shifted elsewhere to make it possible
4-MIN READ4-MIN
1
 Listen
Michael Han is assistant president and Shanghai general manager at Yuepu Technology Group. 
For iPhone users in China, the calendar has long presented a small but recurring problem. On a Sunday designated as a make-up workday, an alarm might remain silent. On a regular Friday converted into a day off, it might ring anyway.
Nearly 17 years after entering the Chinese market, Apple quietly updated its operating system in September to automatically recognise China’s official schedule of adjusted holidays and workdays. The fix is modest, but it points to a larger question: what happens when a society’s working week no longer matches the natural cadence of the days?
The issue transcends a foreign tech giant adapting to local rules. China’s holiday calendar is not a static record of dates but a dynamic mechanism for redistributing public time. By moving weekend leave to around national holidays, policymakers engineer longer continuous breaks at the expense of a predictable working week, effectively using time as an administrative lever.

Two killed, including 6-year-old, when truck drives through youth soccer game in US, police say
- A truck drove into a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, killing a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, police said.
- Ten others were hospitalised with injuries, but none are thought to be life threatening, and one more adult was treated for non-traumatic medical issues.
- Police said the 34-year-old driver is in custody and is cooperating, while officers are still trying to find out why the crash happened.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A truck drove into a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, leaving a six-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man dead, and 10 others hospitalised with traumatic injuries, the police said on Oct 17.
The injuries ranged from minor to severe, but none appear to be life threatening, Wichita police Captain Aaron Moses said at a news conference.
The two people killed were pronounced dead at the scene, he said.
Moses said a 34-year-old woman was driving the truck, which ended up in a field at the west end of the Stryker Sports Complex.
She has been cooperating with investigators, he said, but when asked whether she had been arrested, he said only that she was in custody.
“We know what happened, but now we’re working very hard to find out why it happened, and we’re not there yet,” Wichita police Chief Joe Sullivan said.
The injured include two aged five, two aged eight, a nine-year-old and five adults, the police said.
In addition to those 10 people, one adult was hospitalised for non-traumatic medical issues.
The driver had a child playing soccer at the complex, but not on the field where the incident took place, Moses said.
The truck involved had two juveniles as passengers, he said.
Emergency dispatchers started getting calls about the incident at 3.25pm local time, Moses said.
“Today is a heartbreaking day for Wichita,” Mayor Lily Wu said.
“Families came to Stryker Sports Complex to enjoy a Saturday afternoon, watching their children play soccer and no one could have imagined the tragedy that would unfold.” REUTERS

FSSAI cracks down on Priyagold biscuit maker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
01:23:39 UTC
10:23:39 KST

The FSSAI has taken legal action against three companies over serious violations of food safety standards
NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has stepped up enforcement against major food companies, sanctioning prosecution against Priyagold biscuit maker Surya Food & Agro Ltd, Dodla Dairy Ltd and Ueir Organic Foods Pvt Ltd, while issuing notices to Nestlé India and Hindustan Unilever (HUL) over alleged labelling violations and misleading product claims.Action against Surya Food & Agro followed a consumer complaint that led officials to find bran meant for cattle feed being used as a fibre source in Priyagold biscuits.The gunny bags containing the material for the biscuits were marked for cattle feed. Inspectors also flagged deficiencies in plant hygiene, pest control, raw material storage and segregation, personnel hygiene and premises maintenance. The company’s FSSAI licence was suspended following the inspection, and the competent authority has now sanctioned prosecution. Attempts to reach the company for comment were unsuccessful.
FSSAI has issued notices to Nestlé India over its Nescafé ready-to-drink range, including Cappuccino, Choco Mocha and Chilled Latte, manufactured by Schreiber Dynamix Dairies and Lotus Dairy Products. The regulator flagged discrepancies between the front-of-pack description “Flavoured Milk” and the back label, which classified the products as “Proprietary Food – 1.12 Dairy Based Drink”.
Online listings described them as “Coffee Flavoured Milk” and carried claims about the goodness of flavoured double-toned milk, which FSSAI said were inconsistent with the declared product category. The companies have been asked to explain why action should not be initiated under food safety laws.A separate notice to Nestlé concerned its Resource Renal vanilla flavour powder, intended for dietary management of people with conservatively treated chronic kidney disease. FSSAI said the product lacked the required prior approval and that the prescribed vegetarian or non-vegetarian symbol was missing from the label.In a statement the company said, “FSSAI has sent a communication to Nestlé India concerning the label declarations/classification of the Nescafe Ready To Drink products. This does not relate to product safety or product quality. Mentioned products are safe to consume and meet all applicable food safety requirements.
We will be submitting our response to the authorities and will be engaging with them as per due process established under law.” Hindustan Unilever was issued notices over claims on Horlicks Women’s Plus Chocolate Nutrition Drink, including “Nutrition for Strong Bones” and “Clinically Proven to Help Improve Bone Strength in 6 Months”.In a statement to the press, the company spokesperson said, “Hindustan Unilever Limited is committed to providing safe, high-quality products that comply with all applicable regulatory requirements. Horlicks Women’s Plus and Mother’s Plus has been developed based on established nutritional science and is manufactured in accordance with stringent quality and safety standards. All product communication is developed in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, and governance processes. We will share all the scientific and regulatory evidence with the authorities as per normal process of review.”

Saudi Arabia reports incoming fire as Egypt weighs sending help
RIYADH – Saudi Arabia said on Oct 17 that it had intercepted a fresh wave of incoming drones, as its ally Egypt weighed sending help in defending against repeated attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
Riyadh leads a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its war with the Houthis, and a military spokesman for the Iran-backed group said on Oct 17 that dozens of Saudi strikes over the past day had killed and wounded “numerous” people.
Since Yemen’s conflict flared back to life in July after a years-long hiatus, Saudi Arabia has faced sustained Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its oil installations, tankers and transit hubs, including one on Riyadh’s airport last week that killed 13 people.
A spokesman for the Saudi coalition said on Oct 17 that it had “intercepted and destroyed four drones over the past few hours in Riyadh, the Eastern Province and the South”.
The interceptions came as the President of Egypt, which is a member of the coalition, said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt was not looking to intervene in regional wars, but added that it was “inconceivable” for Cairo to stand by while the kingdom was “harmed or its security and stability threatened”.
“I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said. “We are speaking only about defence.”
Though Egypt is a member of the anti-Houthi coalition, its role has mostly concerned Red Sea maritime security rather than the fighting in Yemen. It and Saudi Arabia are historically close and have strategic economic ties.
Egypt’s Parliament will hold an emergency session on Oct 18 at Sisi’s request.
The repeated Houthi strikes have prompted foreign embassies to warn their citizens not to use Saudi airports or not to visit the country altogether.
The Saudi Education Ministry on Oct 17 announced the extension of remote learning measures for students in Riyadh and nearby Diriyah.
Residents of the Saudi capital received a mobile phone alert on Oct 18 warning of a “hostile aerial threat” and to stay away from windows and doors. It was lifted after a few minutes.
‘Political process’
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis’ recent escalation, a charge Tehran denies.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Oct 17 that Tehran supported a “comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve” the conflict on the Arabian Peninsula.
He repeated Iran’s offer to mediate between the two sides.
Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh had not responded to Iran’s overture. But Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba rejected Iran’s offer in a statement on X on Oct 17, saying “the Tehran regime is a party to the war against Yemenis, not a mediator”.
The Houthis are part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” against Israel and the US, but both they and Tehran insist the group acts independently.
Saudi Arabia has carried out daily air strikes on the Houthis in Yemen, where government forces are seeking to roll back gains the group made in a lightning offensive in September.
On Oct 17, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Riyadh had conducted 53 strikes on the Yemen capital Sanaa and six other provinces over the past 24 hours, with “numerous dead and wounded”.
A Houthi-affiliated news agency had earlier accused Saudi warplanes of targeting “civilian residences” in Dhamar and Taiz provinces, killing 12 people and wounding more than 30. It alleged that the strikes were carried out “using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally”. AFP

Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:30:00 UTC
08:30:00 KST

News analysis
Why a ‘killer switch’ to tackle Europe’s trade issues with China may not be so straightforward
- EU leaders backed new trade defence tools against China, including a possible “killer switch” to impose tariffs or quotas fast. The move follows a trade deficit of more than €360 billion and rising Chinese exports.
- The plan is still vague. There is no legal text, trigger or scope yet, and the European Commission is expected to propose ideas by the end of 2026. Many states may resist giving Brussels such wide powers.
- Support is growing in Brussels as chemicals, machinery and wind turbines face pressure from Chinese imports. The European Parliament called Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”, showing the hardening mood.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – European Union leaders ended their summit in the late hours of Oct 16 with no deal on the Union’s future budget, but with a new and surprisingly strong resolve to adopt new defence tools to tackle a ballooning trade deficit with China.
Heads of state and government of the EU’s 27 member-nations approved a trade deal concluded in Beijing earlier in October, under which China voluntarily agreed to cut by almost half its exports of electric vehicles to Europe.
But the member-states still deemed this Chinese concession insufficient in addressing bigger trade questions, and they authorised the European Commission, the EU’s executive, to create “without delay” a toolbox of new trade defence instruments. That included a so-called “killer switch” provision that will enable the Commission to impose quotas and tariffs on products at a moment’s notice.
The Commission is expected to come forward with such proposals by the end of 2026. There is, as yet, no legal text, no defined trigger, no agreed scope and no answer to the question of what a trade “cut-off” would mean in practice.
Still, should the Commission gain such “killer switch” powers, the entire structure of Europe’s trade with the world could be revolutionised. And a trade war with China will be almost inevitable.
China loomed large at the EU leaders’ summit, as the European bloc faces a trade deficit of more than €360 billion (S$519 billion) with Beijing in 2026, or about €1 billion each day. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has long warned the Chinese authorities that such deficits are “unsustainable”.
Yet the latest EU statistics indicate that Chinese exports to the Union expanded by a further 25% during the first eight months of 2026. Europe’s car industry is no longer the primary concern; the continent’s chemicals and industrial machinery are now the latest sectors acutely vulnerable to what is described as a Chinese export onslaught.
A decade ago, the EU registered a yearly deficit of €71 billion in industrial machinery trade with China but enjoyed a surplus of €6 billion in trade in chemicals. Today, the machinery deficit has grown to €206 billion, while a gaping trade deficit has developed in chemicals, to the tune of €24 billion a year.
At the latest summit in Brussels, the seat of the European Commission, Belgium, Denmark, France and Germany backed the Commission’s determination to move fast on seeking to protect these sectors. EU anti-dumping investigations into chemicals, pharmaceuticals and machinery are expected within weeks, and an investigation into Chinese-manufactured wind turbines is not far off either.
In a joint letter released on Oct 5, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued that the Commission should be granted powers to, in the authors’ phrase, “cut off access to the European single market if needed if another trading nation deliberately ignores calls for the restoration of fair trade conditions”.
The proposed weapon could be deployed not only if trade in a particular commodity suddenly balloons and no action is taken, but also if another country were to use other coercion instruments – such as a cut-off in supplies of critical raw materials – in an effort to avoid serious discussions about trade imbalances.
If that happened, “the EU must be able to inflict damage comparable to that being done to us”, a German government official explained soon after the Franco-German proposal was released.
Challenges of a ‘switch’
EU officials are refusing to identify any country to which such a provision may apply.
Still, it is a legal necessity dressed as diplomatic courtesy: A China-specific regulation would be indefensible at the World Trade Organization and awkward for many European nations still hoping to maintain friendly relations with Beijing.
Yet nobody is fooled. The entire discussion about this “killer switch” provision – from subsidies and non-tariff barriers to overcapacity and dumping – amounts to the EU’s longstanding gripes against Beijing.
Currently, the EU’s powers of dealing with trade problems are cumbersome.
The Commission must start an investigation into alleged fair-trade distortion. The findings must be substantiated. And any measure taken against a nation exporting to the EU must be approved by a majority of the Union’s member-states.
Until now, China had little problem in rendering such European measures irrelevant, either by launching its own trade distortion investigations into European products entering Chinese markets, or by dangling economic favours to a number of individual European nations, in return for their pledge to veto Commission measures against Chinese trade.
But if the “killer switch” proposal is adopted, that will transform the entire trade debate.
The Commission will be able to dispense with most of the elaborate investigation procedure. And incoming goods in a particular sector could be immediately subjected to tariffs or blocked altogether without first asking for the approval of the EU member-nations.
This is, to all intents and purposes, a revolution in the way Europe does business.
Beijing seems to have understood the significance of this proposal; this is assumed to be the main reason why China offered a highly unusual voluntary concession on future exports of electric vehicles. However, the trade debate in Europe was never principally about cars; it was a template for broader discussions on China’s trade volumes.
So, while Beijing thought that its concession on cars was a one-off gesture to silence the debate, the agreement to limit the volumes of Chinese EVs sold in Europe encouraged EU member-states to believe that it was precisely the discussion about the “killer switch” that forced China into giving way.
The question now is whether a consensus really exists over the adoption of such a measure, and how quickly it can be implemented.
While the EU’s biggest economies support the “killer switch” suggestion, many governments may yet baulk at the idea of granting the Commission wide powers; the idea that the Commission can make such critical decisions without prior authority from member-states is controversial. So, all that has been agreed at this stage is that the Commission will come back with its proposals.
Then, there is the question of how quickly such measures could become legally enforceable. The guess in Brussels is that, even if new powers are adopted, the Commission will not be able to use them until the second half of 2027 because the necessary legislation will take time to be enacted.
Still, the anti-China mood is growing in Brussels. The European Parliament approved on Oct 7 by 454 votes to 86 – with 110 abstentions – a resolution calling Chinese industrial policy “an existential threat to the EU”.

Trump's team proposes that Europe buy Russian gas, NYT reports
US President Donald Trump's administration has proposed that Europe resume buying Russian gas.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: The NYT notes that "a key element in the Trump administration's broad plan for securing peace in Ukraine is a proposal that would turn years of American energy policy upside-down".
Quote: "Europe, the US pitch goes, should resume buying more Russian gas – a move that would be an economic boon for Moscow and give it renewed influence in the region."
Details: The NYT sources familiar with the negotiations said Trump's peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff had raised the idea during talks with Ukrainian and European officials, including President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv last month.
Quote: "To help entice Russia to end the war in Ukraine, the Americans have argued, Ukraine should consider restarting pipelines that used to carry Russian natural gas to Europe."
Details: European officials involved in the negotiations reacted negatively to the proposal, which would undo years of efforts by the European Union, backed by Washington, to move away from Russian gas. However, Trump's representatives view Russian gas exports as a potential part of a peace settlement, citing "the revenues that would flow to Ukraine" and what they see as "the inevitable desire for cheaper energy by European voters".
Quote: "The disconnect underscores the unusual – and, critics say, fatally flawed – nature of Mr Trump's renewed diplomatic effort to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Rather than pressure President Vladimir V. Putin or try to strengthen Ukraine's war effort, the administration has spent significant time exploring economic incentives for Russia and raising them in talks with Europe and Ukraine." [N.B. Ukrainska Pravda does not recognise Putin as president – ed.]
Details: The NYT reports that US and Russian officials have been discussing potential business deals since last year, but the prospect of such deals appears to have had little impact on persuading Putin to abandon his core demands. Given how strongly European and Ukrainian leaders oppose a return to dependence on Russian gas, the proposal could further complicate the Trump administration's efforts to end the war.
The White House said in a statement that the war is "driving up energy prices across Europe and creating significant economic hardship in both Russia and Ukraine".
Quote from the White House: "The United States has been working closely with Ukraine and our European partners on a comprehensive peace proposal that includes economic incentives for both Russia and Ukraine as part of a final settlement. Our objective is not simply to end the fighting, but to create the conditions for lasting peace, economic recovery and greater stability across the region."
Background:
- Trump signed an executive order waiving certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the lifting of sanctions against Russia as a "sanctions blackout". However, he believes the legislation could still be used to put pressure on Russia.
- On 16 October, the European Council instructed the European Commission to prepare proposals to cover Ukraine's €70 billion budget shortfall for 2027.
Previously:
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through its Office of Foreign Assets Control, issued General Licence No. 135, authorising transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Trump, calling the agreement with Moscow on diesel fuel a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to revoke the licence immediately and fully implement the Graham Act.
- On 15 October, 22 Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
- Senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the Graham Act, sharply criticised Trump for refusing to take further steps to put pressure on Russia under the law.
- Kirill Dmitriev, Russian ruler Vladimir Putin's chief economic envoy, called Trump's decision not to impose restrictions on Russia under the Graham Act a "historic moment".

Palestinian factions conclude 2nd round of dialogue in Cairo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
06:16:57 CST
07:16:57 KST

GAZA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The Palestinian National Liberation Movement (Fatah) and the Islamic Resistance Movement (Hamas) announced on Saturday that the second round of Palestinian dialogue had ended in Cairo under Egyptian sponsorship, with both sides describing the talks as positive.
Monzer al-Hayek, Fatah spokesperson in the Gaza Strip and member of its Revolutionary Council, said in a press statement that the talks aimed to build common ground on political, national and organizational issues.
He said the discussions sought to promote Palestinian unity and protect the Palestinian national project, including the establishment of an independent Palestinian state based on the program and commitments of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).
Fatah's delegation, headed by Jibril Rajoub, secretary of its Central Committee, praised Egypt for hosting the talks and supporting Palestinian unity, according to the statement.
In a separate press statement, Hamas said its delegation, headed by its leader in the West Bank Zaher Jabarin, had concluded several days of national dialogue in Cairo.
The delegation held meetings to discuss ways to unite Palestinian positions and address national issues, the statement said.
Hamas said its delegation first met with Fatah representatives to discuss ways to ensure the dialogue's success.
It later held an expanded meeting with representatives of Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the reformist current within Fatah.
Participants stressed the need to resolve issues that had hindered previous rounds of dialogue, the statement said.
Hamas said comprehensive national dialogue was essential to addressing Palestinian issues and confronting Israeli occupation plans.
It called for a shared vision to rebuild and reform the PLO to ensure the participation of all Palestinian factions and political forces, as well as agreement on a common strategy and greater efforts to promote the Palestinian cause at the regional and international levels.
Hamas said the factions had agreed to continue dialogue until reaching common understandings, while praising Egypt's role in hosting the talks.
Cairo hosted the first round of consultations on Palestinian national dialogue earlier this month.
The Palestinians have been divided since mid-2007, when Hamas took control of the Gaza Strip, while the Palestinian Authority has exercised limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank. ■

Chinese Premier Li Qiang meets with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
TASHKENT, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Saturday that China stands ready to ensure the high-quality implementation of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project.
During his meeting with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev here, Li also said that China supports more capable Chinese enterprises in investing and doing business in Uzbekistan and hopes that the Uzbek side will continue to provide a favorable business environment for these enterprises.
In recent years, under the strategic guidance of President Xi Jinping and President Mirziyoyev, the building of a China-Uzbekistan community with a shared future has continued to achieve new results, Li said.
In the face of a complex and turbulent international landscape, China and Uzbekistan should strengthen solidarity and cooperation and remain firmly committed to moving forward together, he said.
China stands ready to strengthen strategic communication with Uzbekistan, continue to firmly support each other's core interests, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation to deliver greater benefits to the peoples of both countries, Li said.
China is ready to work with Uzbekistan to expand bilateral trade and optimize its structure, strengthen cooperation in areas such as energy, minerals, finance, and connectivity, and deepen cooperation in scientific and technological innovation in fields such as artificial intelligence, the green economy, and aerospace, so as to jointly seize future development opportunities, Li said.
Both sides should also promote people-to-people connectivity and facilitate the establishment of cultural centers in each other's countries as soon as possible, Li said.
China is ready to strengthen coordination of positions with Uzbekistan on major issues, enhance collaboration within multilateral frameworks such as the China-Central Asia mechanism and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), safeguard the common interests of both countries, and contribute to peace and development at both the regional and global levels, Li said.
For his part, Mirziyoyev congratulated the Communist Party of China on the 105th anniversary of its founding, saying that under the wise leadership of President Xi, China is forging ahead toward national rejuvenation.
Uzbekistan-China relations are currently enjoying a "golden age," he said, adding that his successful meeting with Xi on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek charted the course for advancing bilateral cooperation.
Uzbekistan firmly adheres to the one-China principle and firmly supports China in safeguarding its core interests, he said, noting that Uzbekistan will continue to work with China to combat the "three evil forces" of terrorism, separatism and extremism.
Uzbekistan welcomes more Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in the country and stands ready to work with China to accelerate the construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway and advance exchanges and cooperation across various fields, he said.
Uzbekistan supports the four global initiatives proposed by Xi and is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with China in multilateral affairs, promoting continued progress in the Uzbekistan-China all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era, he added. ■

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 18, 2026
Mass protests in France spiral into worst riots in years
Rioting erupted in cities across France on Oct 17 as demonstrations against rising living costs and declining public services spiralled out of control in some of the worst violence the country has witnessed for decades.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.
In Limoges, the city hall was set ablaze, as Marseille black-clad protesters broke into City Hall and defaced the building with anarchic graffiti and in Lyon protesters torched the city’s tourist office.
‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview
The captain of a flydubai flight whose co-pilot attacked him with an axe in an alleged bid to bring down the plane said one thought kept running through his head as the harrowing ordeal unfolded: “You can’t die like this.”
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar recounted the “traumatic” experience to Sky News Arabia in his first interview since the incident late in September in which he, passengers and other crew members were credited with averting disaster on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
With his head and one hand bandaged and glasses perched on his nose, Machchhar spoke from his hospital bed in the UAE.
Haaland brace extends Man City’s winning start in Premier League
Erling Haaland struck twice as Manchester City defiantly extended their blistering start to the Premier League season with a 3-2 win against Ipswich on Oct 17.
Phil Foden put City ahead in the first half at the Etihad Stadium before Daizen Maeda grabbed a shock equaliser for Ipswich.
Haaland netted before the interval and struck again after the break to take his tally for the season to 12.
It was City’s second win since the club were found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League financial regulations in September.
A reporter who saw Covid-19 coming has died
Helen Branswell, a leading reporter on infectious diseases who wrote with foresight, urgency and clarity about the emerging danger of the Covid-19 pandemic, ahead of the vast majority of journalists and even many medical experts, died on Oct 13 in Ottawa. She was 69.
Her death, at a hospital, was from complications of a recurrence of breast cancer, her sister Brenda Branswell said.
Branswell “saw the pandemic coming well before anyone was paying attention,” Ashish Jha, the White House Covid-19 response coordinator in 2022 and 2023, said on social media.
Alberta support for Canada rises ahead of separation referendum
Support for Alberta remaining in Canada gathered pace ahead of a referendum on whether the province should begin a legal process to separate from the country, according to a poll from Abacus Data.
The survey of 1,021 eligible voters, released on Oct 17, found 68% of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, up from 64% last month. Support for beginning a legal process that could ultimately lead to separation was unchanged at 24%, while the share of undecided voters or those planning not to vote in the Oct 7 to 13 poll fell to 8% from 12%.
Albertans will decide on Oct 19 whether to remain a Canadian province or to set the stage for a second, binding vote on secession. At stake is the future of Canada’s largest oil-producing province, which pumps more than 4 million barrels a day, most of it for export to the US.
