Prices of 137 cancer drugs to fall by up to 70% from November 9
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:02:18 UTC
07:02:18 KST

This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients
In good news for cancer patients, prices of 137 drugs are set to be reduced by up to 70% from Nov 9, with govt capping trade margins by 30%. Drug prices regulator National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) Saturday notified the 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs to address the issue of excessive trade margins, invoking Paragraph 19 of DPCO, 2013. Significantly, patented drugs are also included in the list.The trade margin rationalisation at 30% of MRP, excluding GST, corresponds to a mark-up of 42.9% on price to stockist/price to distributor (PTS/PTD), according to the minutes of the NPPA meeting accessed by TOI. Simply put, PTS/PTD is the first point of sale of the drug.
This follows a nudge by Supreme Court, flagging the huge gap between price to retailer and MRP of medicines billed to patients, in certain cases of 10 times.The MRPs of certain drugs — including pertuzumab + trastuzumab, atezolizumab, teclistamab, inotuzumab ozogamicin and daratumumab — are up to Rs 5 lakh per vial/pack.All manufacturers will be required to inform NPPA of their revised prices within seven days of publication of the gazette notification. Manufacturers will be req-uired to display the price lists on their website and widely disseminate them to all retailers and hospitals, with the latter also required to display the revised prices on their websites prominently.
The authority approved the calculation of the revised MRP based on PTS/PTD for March 2026 as the reference month.NPPA said patient assistance programme quantities may be excluded from the calculation of PTS/PTD and MRP for trade-margin capping only. These programmes, where drugs are supplied free of cost, are typically run by MNCs.As a substantial supply of anti-cancer drugs is directly made to hospitals and medical institutions, they shall be responsible for ensuring revised prices of such drugs from the date of implementation, NPPA said. State drug controllers will take necessary steps to ensure compliance by manufacturers, dealers including retailers, hospitals and medical institutions, it added.In a bid to tighten rules further, NPPA said uninterrupted availability of the covered formulations needed to be ensured. Any manufacturer intending to reduce monthly production levels would have to obtain permission.
Consumers can use the Pharma Sahi Daam app and NPPA website to check revised prices of drugs, an official release said.In 2019, the MRP of 526 brands of non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines was reduced by up to 90%, NPPA said. The present exercise extends this approach to a larger set of drugs, based on the list recommended by an expert committee under Directorate General of Health Services.

Mothers and fathers may pass along different kinds of sexism to their kids, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
22:00:34 UTC
07:00:34 KST

A new study published in Sex Roles suggests that 8-year-old children’s views about women tend to mirror their parents’ sexist attitudes. Fathers’ hostile sexism and mothers’ benevolent sexism were most consistently linked to their children’s views, hinting that mothers and fathers may play different roles in passing these beliefs along.
Psychologists often divide sexism into two distinct categories: hostile and benevolent. Hostile sexism involves openly negative feelings toward women, particularly those who are perceived as challenging male power. Benevolent sexism is more subtle, as it involves idealizing women who conform to traditional gender roles and believing that they are delicate and require men’s protection.
Research suggests that benevolent sexism, despite its polite surface, can reinforce an unequal division of household labor and limit women’s career ambitions. Parents appear to be one source of children’s ideas about gender: a 2002 meta-analysis found that parents with more traditional views about gender tended to have children with more traditional views.
Studies of whether parents pass on hostile and benevolent sexism specifically have mostly involved teenagers. A 2012 study, for example, found that mothers who endorsed more benevolent sexism tended to have teenage daughters who did too. Some theorists had argued that benevolent sexism only emerges in adolescence, but a 2020 study co-authored by Hammond, which introduced the stuffed-toy task used in the new research, found that children as young as 5 already agree with both hostile and benevolent ideas about women.
Parental sexism may also show up in everyday interactions: research covered by PsyPost in 2023, led by Overall, found that mothers and fathers higher in hostile sexism were less responsive toward their young children during family interactions.
To build on this line of inquiry, researchers Oksana S. Voznyuk, a PhD candidate at the University of Auckland, Nickola C. Overall, a professor at the University of Auckland, and Matt Hammond, an associate professor at Victoria University of Wellington, set out to test the direct intergenerational links between parents and children. They wanted to see if mothers’ and fathers’ specific sexist attitudes predict their children’s agreement with similar statements.
“In the big picture, we wanted to investigate why gender gaps persist worldwide, even as generations of women and men have been fighting for gender equality,” Voznyuk, Overall, and Hammond told PsyPost. “We thought that an overlooked process that may contribute to this slow progress toward gender equality could be the transmission of sexist beliefs intergenerationally – from parents to their children.”
The research team collected data from 175 family groups, each consisting of a mother, a father, and their 8-year-old child. The families lived in New Zealand and were part of a larger study that began when the children were 4 or 5. The children were fairly evenly split by gender, with 51 percent being girls and 49 percent being boys. Parents filled out standard questionnaires designed to measure their levels of hostile and benevolent sexism.
To assess the children’s attitudes, the researchers used a specially designed laboratory activity that young kids could easily understand. An experimenter introduced each child to a stuffed toy named Feppy, explaining that the toy was a visitor from far away. Feppy then made a series of statements about men and women.
Some of the toy’s statements reflected hostile sexism, such as saying that women get upset easily over jokes. Other statements reflected benevolent sexism, such as claiming that men need to protect women from danger. The children were asked to indicate whether Feppy was “sort of” or “really” right or wrong about each statement. On average, children rated Feppy’s hostile statements as sort of wrong and its benevolent statements as sort of right, and boys and girls gave similar answers.
When the researchers analyzed the responses, they found distinct patterns connecting the parents’ views to their children’s views. Because both parents’ attitudes were analyzed together, each link held even after accounting for the other parent’s views. Fathers who expressed higher levels of hostile sexism tended to have children who also agreed more strongly with hostile gender attitudes. This link was present regardless of whether the child was a boy or a girl.
A different pattern emerged for benevolent sexism. Mothers who endorsed benevolent sexist beliefs were more likely to have children who agreed with benevolent gender attitudes. Just like the link between fathers’ and children’s hostile views, this connection applied to both sons and daughters. Fathers’ benevolent sexism, by contrast, was not linked to their children’s benevolent attitudes.
The researchers also found that a mother’s hostile sexism was linked to her child’s views, but only for sons. The authors note the reason is unclear, but one possibility is that mothers higher in hostile sexism parent boys differently, for example by being more controlling with sons.
“The big takeaway from our findings is that children learn from the attitudes, behaviors, and everyday conversations they see at home, and the messages we send about expectations for women and men, or girls and boys, likely have a lasting impact,” the researchers noted. “This matters because those beliefs can shape everything from career opportunities to romantic relationships later in life.”
“One surprising outcome was that mothers and fathers may play unique roles in passing along sexist beliefs,” the researchers explained. “These differences may be about the roles that fathers and mothers play. Fathers who agree with hostile sexism believe that they should be the authority in the family, and they may use more controlling parenting behavior and express hostile sexism by behaving aggressively toward mothers. These behaviors can show children that men should have power and authority and therefore socialize children’s hostile gender beliefs.”
The authors suggest that mothers who endorse benevolent sexism might actively teach these values to their children, as these beliefs often appear socially acceptable or positive on the surface. “Mothers who agree with benevolent sexism may be more likely to hold traditional homemaker and caregiver roles,” the team added. “This may give them more opportunity to model and teach children ideas about protecting and valuing women who fit traditional expectations of what good girls and good women should be like.”
To ensure these links were not driven by other factors, the researchers adjusted their statistical models for the parents’ education levels, employment status, perceived socioeconomic status, and whether the mother or father was the primary caregiver. They also controlled for the children’s age and their “theory of mind,” which is the psychological term for a person’s ability to understand that other people have their own separate thoughts and feelings. Even with these adjustments, the connections between the parents’ and children’s sexist attitudes remained, and incidentally, parents’ hostile sexism was linked to lower theory-of-mind scores in children.
“The most important note is that this research is not about blaming parents, but about recognizing that we all play a role in transmitting and reinforcing gender beliefs,” the researchers emphasized. “Small changes may make an important difference. Many of us have internalized sexist attitudes to some extent, and often we don’t even know what they are, their impact, or how we display them. This research is a good reminder that the little things we say and do can shape how children think about women and men.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The links were modest: the correlation between fathers’ and children’s hostile attitudes, for example, was about 0.29, on a scale where 1 would mean a perfect match.
“As with most research about beliefs and attitudes, the effect size of parents’ sexist beliefs on children’s beliefs is relatively small,” the researchers pointed out. “Children are likely to have many experiences that contribute to their beliefs about women and men, but as children’s first and often most long-term role models, parents are likely to be particularly impactful influences in children’s development of sexist attitudes and an important intervention point.”
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot establish a direct cause and effect. There is also a possibility that children influence their parents’ views over time as they express their own ideas about gender. Additionally, the stuffed-toy task was developed with U.S. children, and one hostile item had to be dropped for poor fit with this New Zealand sample. All of the families were mother-father couples in New Zealand, so the patterns may differ in other family types and cultures.
Future research will need to explore these dynamics in single-parent households, families with LGBTQ+ parents, and across different cultural contexts.
“We believe two main directions are important for the next steps in this research,” the researchers said. “The first is to investigate whether children’s gender attitudes are related to negative outcomes for children’s wellbeing and their social, emotional and educational development.”
They suspect these attitudes could affect how children see themselves, how they do in school, and how they get along with peers. “The second is to investigate how parents are passing down their beliefs – are parents modeling traditional gender roles at home, treating sons and daughters differently, or shaping how children dress and behave in a way that communicates these gender beliefs?” they added.
The authors argue that because children’s early beliefs about gender may shape their later interests, schooling, and relationships, efforts to reduce gender stereotypes in childhood will likely need to engage parents as well as children.
The study, “Intergenerational Links Between Parents’ and Children’s Hostile and Benevolent Sexism,” was authored by Oksana S. Voznyuk, Nickola C. Overall, Matthew D. Hammond, Rachel S. T. Low, Annette M. E. Henderson, Valerie T. Chang, and Myfanwy Christensen.

Internet is fundamental right of all, even children: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
21:54:56 UTC
06:54:56 KST

It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.
NEW DELHI: Raising citizens’ right to access and use of internet to the level of fundamental right, Supreme Court has held that even children are entitled to that right and said it does not endorse imposing in the name of safety a blanket ban on children accessing internet. At the same time, it favoured restricting access to content that is inherently harmful to kids.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Chandran said that right to access and use of the internet is part of Article 21 (right to life and liberty) and Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression). The internet is “priceless” as it provides access to information and education to all in even remote areas, where it is often the only source of learning for many children. Noting that the SC had earlier refrained from expressing a definitive view on whether the right to access the internet is, by itself, a fundamental right, the bench said, “...we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.”
SC: Internet’s value priceless, efficacy of curbs not provedSC said, “Our children, irrespective of their age enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or freedom of speech worth expressing.”
The order was passed on a public interest litigationfiled by NGO ‘Just Rights for Children Alliance’, which highlights continued lapses by intermediaries in tackling child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) despite SC’s 2024 judgment in this regard.
Agreeing with its plea, SC said there has been “no progress worth the name” in the last two years.Acknowledging that there has been “a growing yet short-lived tendency across the globe in the recent past to limit the access of children below a certain age to the internet, more particularly to social media platforms,” SC said, “we too gave this our anxious consideration, and only thereafter, we decided consciously not to endorse the same”.It said the efficacy of such restrictive measures remains far from established in countries which have imposed them.“... Children do not cease to use the internet merely because the law prohibits them from doing so ... They move to other platforms and websites that are unregulated and even more unsafe,” SC said.“All that we are trying to say is that any blanket restriction on access to internet by children is nothing more than unproven measures of proven disproportionality. No jurisdiction has, so far, been able to demonstrate that children are any safer on account of such measures,” it said.It said some age-based restrictions and safeguards should exist for the safety of children online.

Hebrew University receives record $250 million donation from philanthropist John Paulson

American philanthropist and investor John Paulson announced a historic $250 million donation to the Hebrew University of Jerusalem at the university’s Board of Governors gala on Saturday evening, marking the largest gift in the institution’s history, the Calcalist reported.
The donation will fund the establishment of a new Faculty of Engineering, expand activities in medicine and biomedicine, and advance research and treatment related to trauma and post-traumatic stress.
In recognition of the gift, the university’s historic Mount Scopus campus will be renamed the Alina and John Paulson Campus, Mount Scopus, Jerusalem.
The contribution follows Paulson’s previous support for the university’s computer science and electrical engineering programs.
Paulson’s donation a 'profound expression of confidence in Israel’s human capital'
“This donation bolsters our ability to recruit world-class faculty, support outstanding students, equip laboratories with cutting-edge technology, and transform bold ideas into life-changing breakthroughs,” said Prof. Tamir Sheafer, president of the Hebrew University.
“This is far more than a historic act of philanthropy. It is a profound expression of confidence in Israel’s human capital.”
Paulson, founder of the hedge fund that bears his name, is known for his philanthropic support of higher education, including a gift of roughly $400 million to Harvard University about a decade ago, which remains the largest donation in the institution’s history.
“I made the choice to shift my philanthropy toward Jewish causes in general, and toward Israel in particular,” he told the Calcalist.
“Israel is currently facing numerous challenges. There is anti-Israel sentiment and a global rise in antisemitism. I decided it was crucial to demonstrate support for Israel, and a fantastic way to do so is by supporting Israel’s leading university.”

The Talmud teaches that whoever saves a single life is as one who saved an entire world. If that’s the case, SACH (Save a Child’s Heart) can be credited with saving some 9,000 worlds.
SACH is Israel’s leading practitioner of medical diplomacy.
Founded in 1995 by the late Dr. Ami Cohen and headquartered in the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital at the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, it provides free cardiac surgery for children with heart ailments regardless of their religion, ethnicity, or nationality. This includes children from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel, and youngsters from countries that are sworn enemies of Israel. To date, over 9,000 children from more than 75 countries have been brought to Israel for treatment. Each child is accompanied by a family member or nurse from the child’s home country.
In addition, medical personnel from third-world countries are brought to Israel to train in all aspects of cardiac surgery, so that children with heart problems can be treated closer to home. SACH teams frequently travel abroad to evaluate children with congenital and rheumatic heart diseases, and often perform urgent surgeries when the child’s condition is so serious that immediate treatment is required.
SACH volunteers and supporters met last Friday with President Isaac Herzog at his official residence to celebrate the 30th anniversary of SACH’s founding.
Along with the above were medical personnel, ambassadors and other diplomats from some of the African countries from which children have been brought to Israel for surgery, representatives of African hospitals whose pediatric cardiology teams were trained in Israel, representatives of international foundations which help fund SACH, and mothers with children who recently underwent successful surgeries and who will soon be returning home.
'We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds'
SACH Executive Director Simon Fisher described the children who came under SACH care over the years as “living miracles,” adding, “We are celebrating 30 years of saving worlds.”
Fisher emphasized that SACH had grown from a small group of dedicated professionals to global proportions.
In explaining this, Fisher said, “A child in need is part of our collective responsibility.
Herzog, who has long been familiar with SACH's work, said that the organization deserved a Nobel Peace Prize and pledged to do everything he could to bring that about.
He declared that he was honored to host a milestone anniversary of “a remarkable Israeli humanitarian organization of which we’re very proud.”
Herzog characterized SACH’s achievements as “the triumph of human kindness which connects a wide heart of human effort.”
But it is more than simply healing a diseased heart, he pointed out. “From Iraq to the Palestinian Authority, all have been welcomed with wide open arms - simply because they are children in need.”
Herzog saw the effects of this a year ago when he paid a state visit to Zambia, and met with adults who as children had been healed in Israel, and were leading fruitful and meaningful lives.
“Few things leave me prouder to be Israeli,” he said.
“This is the essence of doing good in the world. This is something the international community should bear in mind when they accuse us of something else.”
In closing Herzog implied that SACH received its inspiration from the Biblical Noah - “one man who braved the current and ultimately saved the world.”
SACH co-chair Robert Baruch noted that over the years, SACH has given thousands of children a second chance at life, and has not been deterred by the child’s place of birth. Children come to Israel as the hope of families who cannot find treatment at home, he said. “It’s a reminder of what can happen when people decide to act. The impact of SACH is far greater than its size.”
Mega philanthropist Sylvan Adams, who, together with a group of other philanthropic families living in Israel, established the Sylvan Adams Children’s Hospital within the Wolfson Medical Center in Holon, shared some of his own SACH experiences.
The first time he visited, more than a decade ago, he was on a tour, and SACH staff asked whether he would like to spend a few minutes watching open-heart surgery. He agreed and was so fascinated by what he saw that he sat for hours and instantly became a donor. The children’s hospital that bears his name came into being because there was no children’s hospital in Holon before then. Since its inception, he has visited many times.
On that first occasion, he saw the surgeon being assisted by a doctor from Tanzania. What amazed him was that the two were conversing in Hebrew.
One per cent of all children are born with heart defects
Adams was shocked to learn that one per cent of all children are born with heart defects, which makes SACH’s work all the more vital.
During his visits, he has witnessed children from Gaza arriving with their parents and sometimes accompanied by their physicians. They were always treated with dignity - even after October 7, he said.
\In relation to the attitude toward Gazan children being treated in the same friendly manner as children from anywhere else, Adams is certain that there are people in Gaza who do not bear hostility toward Israel.
Along the entrance to the main building in the presidential compound, there were tall round tables bearing enlarged photographs of children who came with hope and left healed. Alongside each photograph was a round vase filled with white tulips. When the petals of a tulip first open, they form the shape of a heart. The message, though subtle, was clear.

Two styles of meditation eased depressive symptoms in a four-week trial, possibly through different routes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
20:00:58 UTC
05:00:58 KST

A randomized controlled trial found that two different styles of meditation, one centered on focused attention and one on self-inquiry, reduced depressive symptoms over four weeks compared with a wait-list control group in adults without a depression diagnosis. Exploratory analyses suggested that the two practices may work through partially different psychological processes. The paper was published in Mindfulness.
Meditation has long been studied as a way to ease depression. However, an important question is why meditation works, and whether all forms of meditation work in the same way. Depression is often maintained by rigid negative beliefs about the self, habitual patterns of thinking, and a tendency to interpret experiences as threatening or personally damaging. Meditation may interrupt this cycle through cognitive decentering, which helps people observe thoughts and emotions without immediately treating them as facts or as reflections of who they are.
This shift may also contribute to a broader psychological state sometimes described as selflessness, in which the self is experienced as less rigid, less isolated, and less central to every experience. The idea has roots in Buddhist traditions, which regard attachment to a fixed and independent self as an important source of suffering.
Modern psychology has begun to translate this idea into measurable processes such as connectedness to other people and nature, along with the ability to adopt a more detached perspective on one’s own thoughts and feelings. However, meditation is not a single technique. Different practices may influence these processes in different ways.
Study authors Céline Stinus of the University of Navarra in Spain and Sophie Berjot of the University of Reims Champagne-Ardenne in France conducted a randomized controlled trial comparing the effects of two types of meditation on depressive symptoms and several related psychological characteristics. They expected the self-inquiry practice, which targets rigid beliefs about the self more directly, to produce larger benefits.
Focused-attention meditation involves sustaining attention on a chosen object, such as the breath, noticing when the mind wanders, and repeatedly returning attention to that object. Self-inquiry meditation is a practice in which people examine their thoughts, beliefs, and sense of self by asking questions about where these mental experiences come from and how they shape emotions and behavior. The self-inquiry program used in the study was secular and did not include Buddhist teachings.
The final sample included 147 adults recruited in France through social media, university campuses, and the researchers’ professional networks. People were not eligible if they were taking psychiatric medication, had previously been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, or were experienced meditators.
Participants were randomly assigned to focused-attention meditation, self-inquiry meditation, or a wait-list control group, with 49 people in each group in the final analysis. The average age was about 49 in the focused-attention group, 46 in the self-inquiry group, and 44 in the control group, and each group was mostly made up of women.
Participants in the meditation groups were not told which type of meditation they had been assigned to, while those in the control group were told they had been placed on a wait-list. Each meditation program lasted four weeks and included five 60-minute online group sessions, all led by the study’s first author, plus 20 minutes of individual practice a day, five days a week. The two meditation groups attended sessions and practiced at home at similar rates.
Participants completed assessments a week before the programs began and within seven days after they ended. The assessments included measures of depressive symptoms (the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), dysfunctional attitudes (the Dysfunctional Attitudes Scale), identity threat, or the perception that one’s sense of self is being undermined or devalued (the Threat Appraisal Subscale of the Cognitive Appraisal Scale), cognitive decentering (the Metacognitive Processes of Decentering Trait scale), connectedness to nature (the Connectedness to Nature Scale), and connectedness to humanity (the Connectedness to Humanity scale).
Both meditation programs led to greater reductions in depressive symptoms and identity threat than the wait-list condition, with moderate effect sizes, and both increased cognitive decentering. There were no reliable differences between the two meditation programs on these outcomes. Contrary to the researchers’ expectations, only the focused-attention group showed a reduction in dysfunctional attitudes relative to the wait-list group; the self-inquiry group did not.
The meditation programs did not differ reliably from the wait-list group in their overall effects on connectedness to humanity or nature. However, exploratory analyses found that only the self-inquiry group showed increases in both forms of connectedness from before to after the program.
Exploratory analyses of the processes behind these changes suggested that, in the focused-attention group, increases in cognitive decentering fully accounted for the reduction in depressive symptoms and partly accounted for the reduction in dysfunctional attitudes. In the self-inquiry group, increases in connectedness to humanity partly accounted for reductions in identity threat. Unexpectedly, increases in connectedness to nature in this group were linked to smaller reductions in identity threat, and none of the measured processes explained the self-inquiry group’s reduction in depressive symptoms. Because these analyses were run separately within each group, they do not allow a direct statistical comparison of the two practices’ mechanisms.
“Attentional and deconstructive meditation practices yield comparable benefits for depression-related outcomes but operate through partially distinct mechanisms. Cognitive decentering played a central mechanism in attentional meditation [the focused-attention meditation procedure] while deconstructive practice [the self-inquiry meditation procedure] showed exploratory associations with connectedness [to nature and to humanity], warranting cautious interpretation,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the mechanisms through which meditation practices might affect depressive symptoms. However, it should be noted that participants in the control group knew they were not receiving treatment, and all outcomes were based on self-reports, which leaves room for expectancy effects and self-report bias. Participants had not been diagnosed with depression or any other psychiatric condition, and their average depression scores were low and within the nonclinical range.
Both meditation programs were delivered by the same instructor, who was also the study’s first author, leaving open the possibility that instructor-related effects influenced the results. In addition, 20 participants dropped out of the wait-list group compared with four or five in each meditation group, the study was not preregistered, and there was no long-term follow-up. Participants were also mostly women who signed up for a meditation study and may have been especially receptive to it.
The paper, “Preventing Depression through Selflessness: Effects and Mechanisms of Attentional vs. Deconstructive Meditation in a Three–Arm Randomized Controlled Trial,” was authored by Céline Stinus and Sophie Berjot.

Pope's surgeon details operating on the "ideal patient" after lung cancer discovery "entirely by chance"
The surgeon who operated on Pope Leo XIV earlier this week detailed in an interview with Vatican News how the pope's cancer was discovered, moments before and after his surgical procedure and the importance of prevention.
The pope was discharged from the hospital Saturday — four days after his surgery — to a large crowd of well-wishers cheering for him.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, director of the thoracic surgery unit at the Agostino Gemelli University Hospital Foundation, spoke to the Vatican News in a lengthy interview and said the pope's lung cancer was discovered "entirely by chance."
"The Holy Father falls into the category of people who discover they have lung cancer entirely by chance — not because they are undergoing preventive screening, but because they undergo examinations for other reasons," Margaritora said.
Margaritora said the tumor was found at the base of the right lung, but if it had been "a little higher up, it certainly would not have been seen."
Unfortunately, the doctor said, in its early stages, cancers can show no symptoms — such as the lung cancer the pope was diagnosed with. That's why regular preventive checkups for other cancers are so important, he said.
"He had no respiratory symptoms and felt perfectly well," said Margaritora.
The 71-year-old pontiff revealed the news at the end of his Sunday noon blessing last week before thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.
Margaritora said the operation to remove a lung nodule was routine and went forward "without any complications." The pope was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common cancer, during the surgery.
The doctor said that for the four days the pope recovered at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, he was "an ideal patient."
"I am not saying that to flatter him. He truly did not cause the slightest problem for the team caring for him ... ," the doctor told Vatican News.
He said on the second day following the surgery, medical staff found the pope arranging the chairs in the hospital's makeshift chapel. Margaritora recounted that staff offered to move the chairs, "Holy Father, we can do that." And he replied, "It doesn't matter. I can do it, so I will."
The pope had already resumed some work activity on Thursday. By Friday, the pope had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone. Pictures of the American-born pope standing at an altar in green vestments, celebrating Mass at a small hospital chapel, were released by the Vatican.
He also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome. The pope is scheduled to travel Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

High oil prices are going to be an issue over the next few weeks if they continue to stay above $100 a barrel. That is a clear challenge for the United States and also potentially for Israel in terms of keeping a lid on a renewed conflict with Iran prior to the elections in both countries.
It is no secret that the looming elections have shifted dynamics, expectations, and assessments of whether the conflict could restart.
The high oil prices come amid a decline in stock prices on Wall Street, amid concerns about AI companies and energy prices. That could tend to be a kind of triple threat affecting the United States, and thus also affecting Israel.
That is because the United States has been working hard to keep diesel and oil prices from skyrocketing. There has been a lot of messaging that the Strait of Hormuz is open and that other energy sources exist, but the question is whether the global market will accept those assertions.
Recent videos showing ships sinking in the Strait of Hormuz and all sorts of containers floating away as ships are in distress are certainly not something that will boost global optimism regarding supply chains, and it always remains a question whether enough ships are transporting energy supplies.
What will the Houthis do?
It also leads to questions about what the Houthis might do. The Houthis could try to threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. They could also encourage other Iranian proxies, such as those in Iraq, to continue attacks on Saudi oil and gas energy infrastructure.
A mysterious explosion in Iraq on Saturday appears to have struck an Iranian proxy group there. All this could continue to disrupt global trade. For example, when attacks hit pipelines or transit points in Saudi Arabia, repairs can take weeks. That creates disruption, and all those disruptions add up to the feeling in the global market that there is too much uncertainty.
This kind of uncertainty will affect the US. It already appears to be affecting policy regarding the Ukraine-Russia war, and this is the kind of thing that can lead to escalation in the Middle East or miscalculations in which something happens again with Iran.
Meanwhile, Iran continues to be blockaded, but it also tends to feel a bit confident about its next steps. As a result, we see potential for escalation within the next week or two.
Iran also knows there are elections in Israel and the United States; therefore, Iran and its proxies may want to take advantage of this period.

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
19:48:54 UTC
04:48:54 KST

At least 19 killed in stampede at religious gathering in India
Incident took place at festival in Kolkata, in India’s West Bengal state, amid large crowds and rainfall, police say.
A “stampede” during a Hindu religious festival in eastern India has killed at least 19 people and injured 25 others, officials said.
The stampede in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state, happened on Saturday night when a crowd near a pavilion ran for cover as it began raining during Durga Puja, an annual Hindu festival celebrating the goddess Durga.
According to police, some worshippers fell on the road and were trampled.
West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, who visited Kolkata Medical College and Hospital where victims were taken, said 19 people had died and 25 were receiving treatment.
Among the dead was a seven-year-old girl, Adhikari told reporters.
He announced that a special investigation team to be headed by a judge of the state’s high court would look into the disaster.
Police detained some pavilion organisers, private security personnel and on-duty staff, and launched a probe into any crowd-control and safety lapses.
Police said the injured were taken to hospital from a Durga Puja pandal, a temporary pavilion housing idols of the goddess Durga at a festival which attracts thousands of devotees.
A police statement said the stampede happened in the evening due to “heavy crowds of pandal hoppers amid rainfall”.
A senior police official at the scene told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused “commotion” after it started raining and the “crowd waiting outside the pandal [pavilion] was pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.”
Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the incident as “saddening”.
“Condolences to the bereaved families. Wishing the injured a speedy recovery. The West Bengal Government is providing all possible help to the affected families,” Modi wrote on X.
Modi’s office announced compensation of 200,000 rupees ($2,106) for the next of kin of those who died and 50,000 rupees ($527) each for the injured.
Interior Minister Amit Shah said the “administration is ensuring that all possible medical facilities are being provided to the injured”.
About 3,500 Durga Puja pavilions have been set up across Kolkata for the festival. Following the stampede, authorities advised several of Kolkata’s most heavily attended venues to temporarily close to visitors.
Deadly crowd incidents happen frequently at Indian mass events, such as religious festivals, often due to poor management and safety lapses.
Last year, a stampede at India’s Kumbh Mela religious fair killed 30 people and injured several others. In Bengaluru, 11 fans were crushed to death during celebrations for the local cricket team’s first Indian Premier League title.
In southern Tamil Nadu state, 36 people were killed in a stampede at a campaign rally for a popular actor-turned-politician.
In 2024, 121 people were killed in northern Uttar Pradesh state during a Hindu religious gathering.

====================================================================================================

Is New Zealand holding back women's Test cricket?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:39:59 UTC
03:39:59 KST

For years fans and players have been crying out for more women's Test cricket.
Yet by the time Australia's women next don the whites at Headingley to kickstart the 2027 Ashes, 15 months will have passed since their last red-ball match.
Much of this comes down to the team's limited opposition. Just four of the top-ranked women's teams have cricket boards willing to commit to Tests.
Australia, England, India and South Africa have been pushing forward the past five years.
They've played 13 Tests since 2021, either as a standalone or part of a multi-format series, a significant improvement on the five years prior when two Tests were played worldwide.
Both of these fell in the 2017 and 2019 Ashes. The biennial contest has safeguarded tradition for England and Australia at a time when governing bodies have been hell-bent on growing the women's game through the shorter formats.
In fact, the Ashes points-based system used to determine the better side across three T20Is, three ODIs and a single Test, has widely been suggested by administrators and players as the best way to increase women's Tests overall. Enticing those on the fence to give it a go.
Tacking on a four-day Test match to a tour that already features six white-ball fixtures sounds like a no-brainer.
Unfortunately, two countries have knocked back that idea this year.
Australia missed out on a chance to face the West Indies in a Test for the first time in 50 years in March when their plans to play a multi-format series in the Caribbean fell through.
Then New Zealand declined to play a Test against Australia later in the year.
The three T20Is and three ODIs scheduled between the trans-Tasman rivals were originally supposed to run through February and March, but when the ICC's inaugural Champions Trophy shifted on the calendar, the tour had to be split.
Instead the three T20Is will now be played at North Sydney Oval, starting Sunday, while the ODIs will still be played at the end of the summer.
As close neighbours, the White Ferns would be ideal opponents for regular Test match cricket. Both in proximity and habit, the sides already meet most seasons for the Rose Bowl series.
Sadly, New Zealand Cricket doesn't share that view.
Despite being one of the first three nations to play women's Test cricket in the 1930s, it now refuses to play the longest version of the game.
Limited overs prioritised
The summer of 1934–35 saw the birth of women's Test cricket, when Australia and New Zealand hosted England on its first overseas tour.
Now, the White Ferns haven't played a Test since 2004.
After the governance of the men's and women's sides of the game were amalgamated, the frequency of Tests for the White Ferns gradually decreased and have now been non-existent for 22 years.
It also appears New Zealand Cricket is unwilling to budge on the matter, as per their previous statement in the media:
"The limited-overs formats have proven to be very effective in terms of attracting and retaining young players, which is a significant factor in the health of the women's game here.
"In time, this will provide a bigger base from which talented players will emerge to ultimately play for the White Ferns.
"Focusing on formats which include ICC global events, such as World Cups, is our preference for now."
ABC Sport requested a fresh response and more clarification but did not hear back.
That means retiring Kiwi legends Sophie Devine, Suzie Bates and Lea Tahuhu never got to experience red-ball cricket internationally.
At the end of the T20 World Cup the trio retired.
Various Australian players told ABC Sport it was an "atrocity" and a "real shame" that after 15 to 20 years of service the trio weren't offered the opportunity.
"Those girls are absolute icons and to think that they've never played a Test match and never will, knowing that they want to, that's tricky," Australia captain Sophie Molineux said.
"Hopefully one day we can play another Test against New Zealand, that would be really special."
"It's a tragedy that they won't get a baggy black cap," Beth Mooney said.
"I feel really sorry for them," Ellyse Perry added.
"They've had amazing, decorated international careers and never got to experience it."
Equal pay to blame
In 2022, New Zealand Cricket was heralded for a groundbreaking pay deal that granted men and women equal match fees.
From then on, when representing their country, both sets of athletes would be paid $NZ4,000 ($3,245) per ODI and $NZ2,500 per T20I.
Although this five-year agreement, due to expire next year, was a positive step in the recognition of female cricketers, it seems to have put the final nail in the coffin for Tests. Requiring a fee of $NZ10,250 per player, it pushed the dream further out of reach.
Especially in light of New Zealand Cricket's latest budget update, which predicted a $NZ7.3 million deficit for the past financial year.
New chief executive Geoff Allott started in the role in July and has indicated the organisation will need "to be prudent" as it looks to get back on track and "ensure long-term sustainability" of the game.
White Ferns head coach Ben Sawyer recently finished up a four-year tenure where he took the team to its maiden Women's T20 World Cup victory in 2024 and a bronze medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.
Speaking with ABC Sport, Sawyer highlighted the financial burden and the recent news that the England and Wales Cricket Board is considering footing the bill for its April Test match against the West Indies in order to ensure their 2027 multi-format series goes ahead.
"The reality is that it's a very expensive venture because of the equal match payments in New Zealand, and the cost is a huge part of it," Sawyer said.
"I'm assuming that's over $NZ150,000 in match payments and there are other priorities for them.
"Their domestic structure isn't full-time, and so it's my opinion that they think that money could be better used elsewhere."
Sawyer has previously held a range of coaching roles in women's cricket — as an Australian assistant, the head coach of the Sydney Sixers and the head coach of the Birmingham Phoenix.
He explained that New Zealand's top players are only contracted from October to March for eight hours per week. They train individually in the off-season and with teammates in-season at night after work.
When Sawyer first took on the White Ferns job, he recommended the national sporting body copy England's county system and gradually build their numbers the same way; starting with two to three professionals in each county, before eventually signing five to seven and then making the entire team full-time.
Since then, he hasn't seen any progress in this regard.
"I've always respected the vision that Cricket Australia have for five to 10 years down the track and the money they're willing to invest; that's what makes them the best in the world," he said.
If New Zealand Cricket was to change its mind and green-light a women's Test, Sawyer believes it'd be better to play someone with a lower ranking and a similar part-time domestic structure.
"They'd need a good lead in, and I wouldn't necessarily want to play Australia first.
"Maybe that's where two countries like New Zealand and Sri Lanka get together and say let's play one.
"I've got no doubt it'd be tough and hard the first time, but it's the only way to get better."
This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview

‘You can’t die like this’: flydubai pilot recalls attack in first interview
DUBAI – The captain of a flydubai flight whose co-pilot attacked him with an axe in an alleged bid to bring down the plane said one thought kept running through his head as the harrowing ordeal unfolded: “You can’t die like this.”
Indian pilot Smit Machchhar recounted the “traumatic” experience to Sky News Arabia in his first interview since the incident late in September in which he, passengers and other crew were credited with averting disaster on the Tel Aviv-bound flight.
With his head and one hand bandaged and glasses perched on his nose, Machchhar spoke from his hospital bed in the United Arab Emirates.
“My vision was restricted to a few inches,” said the pilot, describing the effect of being struck in the back of the head with an emergency axe by his co-pilot, who had positioned himself behind Machchhar’s seat.
Thinking that a part of the airplane’s ceiling had come loose, he then received several more blows and was wounded in the hand as he tried to shield himself.
Machchhar recalled struggling to open the cockpit door so another pilot who was travelling on board could get inside.
“So I was screaming his name, and I was trying because the switch that was very close to me to open the door, I was trying to just get help in,” he said.
“But I remember being able to open the door,” he went on, only for it to shut again.
“And at that point, I felt all the blood, you know, everything rushing down, my energy, everything, I was just, I was barely staying in consciousness.
“Soon after that, that was the time when I heard the engine sounds going down. And then immediately after that, I felt the aircraft going into a dive.”
According to findings released by the Emirati attorney-general, Machchhar’s 29-year-old Omani co-pilot had planned to use the plane to carry out a suicide attack on the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, inspired by the Sept 11, 2001 attacks in New York.
He claimed to have acted alone, something investigators are still working to verify.
The prosecutor found that the other pilot on board, having seen the cockpit door open and close “in an unusual manner”, entered the flight deck and with the help of another crew member and passengers, subdued the co-pilot and regained control of the aircraft.
The jet, which plunged violently during the fray, was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar said the way his colleague was able to intervene and safely land the plane was “commendable”.
“It’s something that I’ll keep with me till I die.” AFP

He is YouTube's spiciest music analyst but Rick Beato loves the backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Rick Beato on interviewing music icons, YouTube backlash and Australian tour
He has interviewed some of music's biggest names and his videos regularly attract millions of views on YouTube.
So, how did Rick Beato become one of the internet's biggest music personalities?
"I always tell people that my channel was just one video at a time," the 64-year-old says.
"I didn't have any grand strategy. I just made videos on things I was interested in."
That curiosity began in 2016, when Beato was just a proud dad showcasing his young son Dylan's perfect pitch. A clip challenging him to identify complex chords by ear swiftly went viral.
Today, his channel Everything Music has 5.8 million subscribers, sharing not only his hot takes on contemporary music and the perils of AI, but thoughtful dives into instrumental technique, technology and trends.
His popular What Makes This Song Great? segment dissects the production, songwriting and music theory of iconic records; everything from Nirvana and Fleetwood Mac to Adele.
Beato's passion and expertise has earned him the trust of huge talent. Sting and Flea have personally requested to be interviewed, adding to a star-studded CV that includes Billy Joel, Seal, Sheryl Crow, Josh Homme and super producer Rick Rubin.
His golden rule? "I never talk about myself. I always think … I'm here to talk about music and about them. That's my job."
Beato thoroughly enjoys it. You can see a "pinching himself" grin creep across his face as he basks in awe of a jazz great's improvisational skill or soaks up a rare showbiz anecdote.
A pandemic interview with Brian May was a turning point, helping him appreciate that rock stars are human beings, too.
"He was so nice! It was really disarming because he was like, 'Rick, I can't believe I'm talking to you. I've seen you in that same spot all the time.' And I was like, 'Same to you, Brian!'
"He made it easy to talk to these incredibly talented, gifted people after that," he continues.
"Even though a lot of them have written the most famous songs of all time … when it comes down to it, they're like you and I. Except, when they put their pants on, they make gold records, as Christopher Walken would say," he says, quoting a classic Saturday Night Live skit.
There are still plenty of names on Beato's bucket list:
"Paul McCartney, Angus Young, Jimmy Page, Keith Richards, Eddie Vedder, Dave Grohl," he says.
A few may be ticked off already, but "I never say it before it happens because I don't want to jinx it."
The Australian connection
Beato took his video content to the live stage a few years back. Facing an audience instead of a camera was "a little strange at first" but public speaking was "no big deal" thanks to his background as a college professor.
He's "super excited" for his first visit to Australia this month. His fans feel the same, selling out shows in Melbourne and Brisbane and prompting a venue upgrade in Sydney.
Beato's first major label gig was producing an Australian singer, the late, Perth-born American Idol contestant Michael Johns.
"He was one of my closest friends. I produced a band he was in before he got signed [The Rising], then we did demos and co-wrote a bunch of songs together," he explains.
Beato took Johns's death, in 2014 at age 35 from a blood clot, really hard. "Tragic," Beato reflects. "He was an incredibly talented guy. One of my favourite singers."
Becoming Beato
Born in Fairport, New York into a musical family, Beato played cello and double bass as a child before teaching himself guitar at age 13.
He earned degrees in classical music and a master's in jazz guitar in 1987. He would go on to lecture at several music institutions, including the prestigious Berklee College of Music and his alma mater, Ithica College.
In the 90s, he inked a songwriting deal and was a member of rock band Billionaire. He moved to Atlanta in 1995 and bought Black Dog Sound Studios, which he operates to this day.
Unafraid to voice his distaste on popular music or the financial fallout of streaming, Beato divides opinion. To some, he epitomises "old man yells at clouds" clickbait. For many, it's never just "this sucks", it's always "this sucks because …"
How does he cope with backlash?
"I think it's funny. I enjoy when people criticise my opinions," Beato says.
"As a matter of fact, I have friends that made videos critical of videos I've made, and I'll text them, 'I thought it was great.' I don't take it personally. I think it's really flattering."
And what do his three teenage children think of their dad being internet famous?
"They make fun of me all the time: 'Why did you do that rage-bait video?'"
Whenever strangers approach him for a selfie or chit-chat, his kids are there to deflate his ego. "And they're good at it."
Audience vs algorithm
It's clear the YouTuber has a thicker skin than most of the creatives he interviews.
"It's hard for a lot of artists that I talk to, they can't read any critiques of their music or get into the comments section. And I always tell them, 'Look, the comments are about the people that are writing them. They're not about you.'
"Don't take it to heart because it's literally a reflection on them, as is the algorithm on these platforms are a mirror for people. It just feeds back exactly who they are to them over and over.
"That's the problem with algorithms, because it only shows them things that they want to see.
Before his son's viral video, Beato was a producer, session player, label boss and educator who preferred to keep out of the spotlight.
He recognises the irony of finding success in putting his face to addressing an audience of millions.
"I couldn't have imagined it. I just wanted to give back and teach people things."
Rick Beato's Australian tour begins on October 29 at Sydney's Enmore Theatre, then heads to Melbourne's Thornbury Theatre on October 30 and Brisbane's Princess Theatre on October 31.

Cosmic Breath: Global calls to prayer answer rising Islamophobia in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
18:24:03 UTC
03:24:03 KST

Tucked away just a stone’s throw from the relentless hum of Oxford Street, a new sonic sanctuary has taken root in central London. Joe Namy, an American-born Lebanese artist and composer whose practice encompasses sound, its history, and its physical impact on the built environment, has brought his multi-channel sound installation, Cosmic Breath, to the UK capital, Anadolu reports.
The work is reimagined for Ibraaz’s Musalla, a space dedicated to spiritual practice as both lived experience and creative expression.
Composed of recordings of the adhan—the Islamic call to prayer—the installation brings together historical and contemporary calls from different geographies, amplified through horn speakers like those mounted on mosque minarets.
Played simultaneously, each speaker softly emits a different adhan recording, inviting the audience to lean in and listen closely. At prayer times, the volume increases, making the calls clearly audible throughout the room, creating a congregation of calls to prayer.
‘Interested in collective sound experiences’
The work forms part of Namy’s wider exploration of sound systems, community, and spirituality.
First commissioned for the Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah in 2023 by its artistic director and architect, Sumayya Vally, the installation explores collective auditory experiences and public sound landmarks.
“A lot of my work deals with the politics of sound, and deals with the spirituality of sound as well, how it affects us in different ways,” Namy explains. “So, I’m interested in sound system cultures (and) collective sound experiences as well, and how they impact our lives.”
Developed in close collaboration with Vally, who designed the installation’s spatial scenography, the artwork grew out of a poetic reflection on time and geography.
Namy was moved by the idea that “at any moment in time on Earth, there is an adhan happening somewhere on this planet, which I think is such a really powerful and beautiful gesture.”
Approaching the adhan through a sociological lens, Namy examines how an ancient oral tradition has transformed alongside modern technology, amplification, and recordings.
Bringing the piece from Saudi Arabia to London reshapes its meaning dramatically, particularly given the current social atmosphere in the UK.
READ: UK security adviser’s wife faces scrutiny over Palestine Action post
From Jeddah to London: A different political soundscape
“Showing it for the first time in Jeddah was a very different experience than showing it here in London, which … situates the work very differently than how it was situated there,” Namy underlined.
He pointed directly to the heightened hostility surrounding the current political landscape: “Especially now today in the current kind of political climate here in London… there’s just a more heightened kind of Islamophobia, xenophobia, prejudice… all these things that we’ve been experiencing and has been increasing.”
For Namy, installing the piece in the heart of London serves as a sanctuary and an antidote to that hostility.
“I feel like it’s a more powerful gesture to be able to show it here in the center of London, you know, just off of Oxford Street, and to be able to have this space for people to be able to come, relax,” he said.
He notes how rare it is in contemporary art spaces to engage with faith so openly: “I think, what I really enjoy is the fact that it’s thinking about the spirituality in relation to art, which you don’t always get a chance to explore, but also providing a kind of third space for people to explore more.”
A London memory born during lockdown
To ground the exhibition in its current environment, this iteration at Ibraaz features a local recording. “So, this recording is from London,” Namy notes.
“Actually, it was important to bring in something that was local as well, and so this was actually one of the first recordings of a public adhan in London that happened in Walthamstow during COVID. It was again a time (when) everyone was social distancing, and so it was a way for the community to be able to kind of — although they were distant — to feel closer together, so it was important to bring in a local element into the setting as well, so that we have some a more closer connection to where we are here in London.”
The recording captures the historic call performed by the Waltham Forest Islamic Association in 2020, offering a sonic expression of shared experience when physical gathering was impossible.
Adhans from Mecca to Singapore, Tbilisi to Khartoum
The audio selections in Cosmic Breath span more than a century and cross vast physical and acoustic terrains, revealing how each call carries a unique character shaped by local traditions, acoustic environments, and regional histories.
“The selections that we included within this installation each represent a certain aspect, or have a unique aspect for the adhan,” Namy says. “Part of it is thinking about spaces (where) you normally wouldn’t encounter the adhan, spaces in which recordings of the adhan are kind of historically significant as well.”
Among the archival highlights is what is considered the first recording of the adhan at the Haram Mosque in Mecca, dating back to the late 19th century. “I think this one is the first recording that was ever done of the adhan from the late 1800s in Mecca. You can kind of hear the grain of the recording. It’s not a really great recording, but it’s interesting to hear it in context of all the other ones,” Namy reflects.
From Asia, the piece gathers landmark history and geography.
“From the Philippines, (there is) an archival recording from the 1950s. It was one of the first recordings of the adhan in the Philippines,” Namy points out.
Contemporary and historical selections also feature the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem and Singapore’s Sultan Mosque, thought to be the first mosque to adopt loudspeakers in the 1930s.
READ: Protest outside Azerbaijan’s embassy in London against hijab ban in schools
“This one is from Singapore, and this was recorded at the first mosque that actually used speakers to amplify the call to prayer. The mosque is still there, and that was important,” he adds.
Other field recordings offer stark contrasts in style and setting—from the ornate to the stripped-back.
“This one is Georgia Tbilisi, and this one is probably the most flowery, I think. You really hear the improvisation and the embellishments and how the voice gets extended in the recitation,” Namy says.
In contrast, “one is from the Sahrawi refugee camp in Algeria, and it’s one of the only ones that’s not recorded, that’s not amplified,” Namy explains saying, “It’s somebody who is old school-style, kind of just reciting it without any speakers or anything like that, just their voice.”
The installation captures deeply intimate acts of faith as well as distinct colloquial traditions.
“I think this one is from Japan,” Namy shares, explaining that similar to the recording mentioned before, it was “somebody just kind of reciting it into the forest for themselves, basically, which I thought was a really beautiful gesture. So, it’s a very personal personal recording reflection.”
A call to prayer from Khartoum highlights regional identity: “This one is Khartoum. It’s recorded in Sudan, and again, you hear the colloquial differences and how the adhan is recited. It’s very different in the recitation. It’s very Sudani in its style, which I really love.”
Not every place could be captured on audio.
Namy recalls attempting to record the first mosque built in South America, located in Brazil. Because the building is reserved for special occasions, “you don’t hear the adhan there, so we recorded just kind of like the empty space from that room, just to have that kind of gesture,” though it ultimately remained unreleased alongside seaside field recordings from Egypt.
From South Africa, a protest becomes the seed of Cosmic Breath
The initial impulse for Cosmic Breath traces back to a pivotal moment of civic resistance in South Africa. During the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, rising social tension, Islamophobia, and xenophobia in Durban led to a local ban on publicly broadcasting the adhan.
In response, an act of interfaith solidarity emerged. “This protest was actually organized by a Hindu community member. He wasn’t Muslim, but he organized this protest in solidarity with the Muslim community there,” Namy recalls.
Sumayya Vally shared the link to the event with him, sparking the broader concept.
Restricted by social distancing rules, residents adapted: “How do you protest at a time when you can’t congregate and gather together? And so they asked everybody to bring their cars and made this huge parade. Everybody tuned their car stereo systems to one of the channels that was broadcasting the adhan.”
The resulting soundscape of hundreds of car speakers reverberating through the streets of Durban provided the foundation for the entire project. “This is the recording from that experience as well,” Namy reflects.
“And that was kind of the first recordings that really made me think about the piece… and bring everything together.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Saturday that U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to waive impending sanctions and tariffs on Russia would hand Moscow an economic reprieve and risk emboldening further Russian aggression.
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians."
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related U.S. sanctions and tariffs - including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas - that had been scheduled to start next week under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelenskyy said Trump's latest action emboldens Russian President Vladimir Putin and encourages more attacks by Russia.
"It only fuels their satisfaction and their desire to keep killing people," wrote Zelenskyy, who said Russia on Friday struck more than 15 Ukrainian power generation and transmission sites. "This certainly does not stop the war."
The Ukrainian leader accused Russia of planning to ramp up strikes in western Ukraine. "Is Russia preparing for this? I think so," Zelenskyy wrote.
Russia's investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Friday called the Trump waiver "a truly historic moment," posting on X that had the penalties taken effect, they could have effectively brought all economic cooperation between Russia and the US to a halt.
Weeks before U.S. midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked further raising oil prices as Americans face increased costs largely attributed to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.
The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the U.S. from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, however, had raised concerns about the Graham Act.
Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.
But the Graham Act also allows the president to waive sanctions by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest. Friday's executive order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determine that "further action is appropriate."
U.S. Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, said Trump was giving in to Putin.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement on Friday.
Graham, who died in July, strongly supported U.S. assistance to Ukraine. The passage of the bill named for him had provided hope that there would be continued bipartisan support for Kyiv, wrote Zelenskyy, who lamented the late senator's absence.
"It’s difficult without him, I’ll be honest," Zelenskyy posted on Saturday.
The Ukrainian leader predicted that the U.S. under Trump will continue sanctions relief for Russia beyond Friday's waiver and the diesel export agreement announced earlier this month.
"I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately," Zelenskyy wrote.

Alberta support for Canada rises ahead of separation referendum
CALGARY, Alberta – Support for Alberta remaining in Canada gathered pace ahead of a referendum on whether the province should begin a legal process to separate from the country, according to a poll from Abacus Data.
The survey of 1,021 eligible voters, released on Oct 17, found 68% of Albertans would vote to remain in Canada, up from 64% last month. Support for beginning a legal process that could ultimately lead to separation was unchanged at 24%, while the share of undecided voters or those planning not to vote in the Oct 7 to 13 poll fell to 8% from 12%.
Albertans will decide on Oct 19 whether to remain a Canadian province or to set the stage for a second, binding vote on secession. At stake is the future of Canada’s largest oil-producing province, which pumps more than 4 million barrels a day, most of it for export to the US.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to reject separation at a rally in Edmonton on Oct 16, warning that a vote against Canada would bring “years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities”. An increasingly divided world makes national unity more important, he said.
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, acknowledged longstanding grievances towards the federal government, saying frustrations over Ottawa’s treatment of the province’s resources and energy industry were “real”.
His government has made a number of policy moves to address tensions in the province of 5 million people, by easing restrictions on oil and gas development and promising to financially back a new oil pipeline, known as Pacific Link, capable of carrying 1 million barrels a day to the west coast for export to Asia.
Carney on Oct 16 cast the pipeline as part of the case for remaining in Canada, saying it would help reduce Alberta’s dependence on the US, open new export markets and generate more than 140,000 jobs.
“Canada is where we can build bigger, faster and better than we ever could alone,” he said. “Don’t let anyone tell you this is already decided. Turnout will determine the outcome.” BLOOMBERG

The same day, Rabbi Dov Lior, “spiritual guide” of Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party, ruled that settlers may take Palestinian olives, calling it an “additional virtue.”
Analysts see political pressure behind that, an effort to present the arsonists as a few Hilltop Youth rather than a movement. Israel is scheduled to vote on October 27, and Ben-Gvir is hunting settler ballots.
Washington’s response followed the usual script. The State Department condemned violence “by any party,” as if victim and attacker shared the blame. Senator Chris Van Hollen asked, “When will Trump and Rubio DO SOMETHING?” Representative Ro Khanna demanded an end to aid that funds settler activity. Meanwhile weapons keep flowing.
Levine is far from the first reporter hit. Sara Qudah of the Committee to Protect Journalists called the beating part of a “disturbing pattern.”
CPJ counts at least 247 journalists and media workers killed since October 2023, 241 of them by Israel, more than any government it has tracked since 1992. Shireen Abu Akleh, an American citizen, was killed in Jenin in 2022 while wearing a press vest. Nobody has answered for it.
Abu Falah’s mayor, Nazem Saleh Shuman, said settlers burned three cars there recently. “It’s become a hell for us,” he added. “We have nowhere else to go.”

Trump’s White House chaotically turns on itself as Republicans brace for defeat
TEHRAN — A press secretary hired on a Friday and gone the next. An ambassador’s ouster announced during her only briefing. Loyalists feuding over money while the chief of staff’s family draws scrutiny. With the November 3 midterms less than three weeks away, Donald Trump’s White House has stopped hiding its disorder.
Katie Zacharia, a Fox News commentator few in the building knew, got the job because Trump was angry that nobody defended him on television as Republican prospects sank. He offered it in an Oval Office talk Chief of Staff Susie Wiles missed. “Did anyone vet her?” one adviser asked. Officials told CNN no one had.
Her only briefing, on Tuesday, ran 14 minutes and took three questions, all from friendly outlets. Asked where she had passed the bar exam, she answered, “When I moved to China.”
She later admitted she failed the California bar in 2011, though her own X reposts and the White House announcement called her “an attorney.”
After Sean Hannity and “Fox & Friends” pressed her, Trump claims he told her, “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.” Hours later, it was leaked that she is gone.
Citing two anonymous sources, CNN reports that Wiles helped arrange the Hannity slot, one calling it a “sanctioned hit.”
Purges, feuds and a sidelined friend
The single piece of real news delivered during Zacharia’s brief time at the podium was that Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign from her post as ambassador to Greece.
Guilfoyle, a television commentator and the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., faced intense public scrutiny after reports revealed she sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to settle a personal credit card bill in exchange for granting political access.
Meanwhile, Trump spent Oval Office time on a vicious fight between Richard Grenell and Alina Mildon, who both owe their posts to him.
Paolo Zampolli, who says he introduced Trump to Melania, was pushed out at the State Department after a feud with Deputy Secretary Christopher Landau spilled into the press.
None of these moves look coordinated.
The chief of staff’s exposure
Wiles has her own problems. She worked on Netanyahu’s 2020 reelection campaign and helped isolate Trump to be fed “Mossad talking points,” according to American journalist Max Blumenthal.
Her daughter Katie is a partner at Continental Strategy, a lobbying firm reportedly paid $35,000 a month by Republika Srpska, the Serb-led Bosnian entity aligned with Milorad Dodik.
The firm claims she did not lobby U.S. officials for it and visited for another client. Still, photographs circulated just after Wiles allies James Blair and Chris LaCivita took paid consulting work there.
Trump reportedly called them “outside consultants” and threatened to “terminate them, immediately!” One person told Reuters that Wiles approved the trip without telling him.
Trump reportedly has said that Wiles will remain in her position. Reports say he has nonetheless sounded out allies about replacements. Stephen Miller, Bill Pulte and Lee Zeldin are all angling.
Pulte hauls poster boards of proposals onto golf courses and Air Force One, enough that Trump has complained about the clutter.
Corey Lewandowski, a Wiles rival, denies discussing Pulte with the president. One ally described the mood to Washington Post reporters as “the new Wild Wild West.”
Behind the panic
The panic has numbers behind it. Trump’s approval is the lowest of his presidency, dragged down by prices and dissatisfaction with the war on Iran. Aides reportedly expect to lose the House, call the Senate a coin flip, and admit Kansas and Texas are in play.
MAGA Inc. has spent about $200 million with little to show, and the Texas redistricting Trump pushed, one source told Reuters, “diced up the Trump voters too much.” Trump, who is not on the ballot, keeps telling rally crowds to pretend he is.
Washington keeps promising victory over Iran. It cannot yet keep a press office staffed for a week.

Araghchi made the remarks at the 52nd Session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in the Iraqi capital Baghdad, according to a statement by the Iranian Foreign Ministry.
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation," he said.
Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's commitment to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, noting the waterway was open before the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28.
He said Iran has conveyed a "concrete" seven-day plan to the United States through Qatar, under which, if the necessary conditions are met, the strait could be reopened within seven days.
"The choice now rests with the United States," the minister added.
Araghchi stressed that Iran will continue to defend its people, sovereignty and legitimate interests by any means, and that it has never attacked its neighbors, only the U.S. military bases and installations in those states. He stressed that each regional state's territory, airspace and infrastructure should be used only to serve regional security and never as a platform for attacks on a neighbor.
"No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others," Araghchi said. "We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers."
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program and the removal of sanctions. However, they failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal as tensions continued to escalate. ■

Protests in Albania escalate into violent clashes
China
Unknown Publisher
