A public facility damaged during protests is pictured in Tirana, Albania, Oct. 16, 2026. Protests in Albania continued on Saturday, which have escalated into violent clashes with police and left government buildings, banks, businesses and public facilities damaged in the capital Tirana. (Xinhua/Chen Gang)
TIRANA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Protests in Albania continued on Saturday, which have escalated into violent clashes with police and left government buildings, banks, businesses and public facilities damaged in the capital Tirana.
The latest wave of protests began on Oct. 13, when students gathered outside the Ministry of Education to demand better university conditions, lower education costs and improved youth employment prospects, according to local media.
Clashes broke out that afternoon, when some demonstrators threw stones and other objects at police and government buildings. Police responded with tear gas and water cannons to disperse the crowds. The situation remained tense into Friday evening, with large numbers of riot police deployed to disperse protesters.
Widespread damage was caused to public institutions, banks, businesses and public facilities in Tirana. The Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice and the central bank were among the institutions targeted.
Albanian police said on Friday that 56 people had been arrested in connection with the unrest, while another 97, including 16 minors, had been placed under criminal investigation.
The protests have spread to several cities across the country, further deepening political divisions between the government and the opposition over the unrest.
Prime Minister Edi Rama said he would not yield to violence and accused the opposition of seeking to exploit the protests to destabilize the country, according to Albanian media reports.
The latest protests have unfolded amid the broader "Flamingo" movement that began in late May. According to local media reports, the movement initially focused on opposition to a proposed tourism project in a protected coastal area in southern Albania linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
The movement later expanded to address concerns over corruption, the cost of living, health care and education.
UN agencies in Albania called on all sides on Friday to end the violence, ease tensions and resolve differences through dialogue. ■

Roundup: China's zero-tariff policy seen as catalyst for Ghanaian exports, industrial growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
01:39:14 CST
02:39:14 KST

by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- A section of Ghanaians who spoke to Xinhua have expressed eagerness to see an enabling environment for Ghanaian businesses to become globally competitive amid the Chinese government's zero-tariff trade offer to 53 African countries.
Pearl Naheema Hanson, Ghanaian female industrialist, said in an interview on the sidelines of the recently held Ghana-China Zero-Tariff Forum 2026 in Accra, the Ghanaian capital, that the zero-tariff policy is a wonderful opportunity, especially for exporters looking to enter the Chinese market.
Hanson, whose company, AA Food and Beverages Limited, produces handcrafted butterscotch-flavored liqueur, pointed out that the offer would allow many Ghanaians and African manufacturers and traders to produce at scale, meet required global standards, and master the rudiments of exporting, especially to China.
"It is a win-win situation, benefiting both Chinese and Ghanaian exporters. In the end, the numbers that we're talking about are huge. So, the capacity is a lot, and it's not something that one company alone can do," she said.
The industrialist added that there is a need for companies to team up and build synergies to take advantage of the zero-tariff offer since the demand in China is so large that small exporters and manufacturers might not be able to meet the high demands if they operate individually.
"You need to get a group of like-minded people who realize the opportunities in the zero-tariff offer; then they can take advantage of all that it offers," Hanson stressed.
But for that to succeed, she said the government needs to create the enabling environment for Ghanaian businesses to become competitive in the global marketplace, particularly by taking steps to reduce the cost of doing business and ensure that Ghanaian businesses produce at competitive prices with global standards.
"We need some incentives, tax rebates here and there, so that we're actually able to offer competitive pricing," Hanson stated. "The cost of production in Ghana is very high, which results in our overall product costs being expensive."
Jabir Mohammed, Senior Lecturer at the University of Ghana Business School, noted that although the zero-tariff policy is an agreement between the Chinese government and the various African governments, the direct operators are private sector players, and the government must ensure that these private sector players are well-educated about the requirements for accessing the Chinese market.
"Let's move into action: The Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry, and other relevant agencies must come together to ensure that we work in a network to take advantage of the policy," Mohammed urged.
He called on the state agencies to carry out a study of the Chinese market, identifying the standards, the competition, the products, and non-tariff barriers that Ghanaian exporters have to deal with, and compile these into easy-to-understand manuals for exporter education.
Moreover, Mohammed also stressed that Ghanaian businesses must also form partnerships among themselves, because working as single entities would put them at a disadvantage in their negotiations.
He also urged the Ghana Export-Import Bank to identify prospective businesses that need financing and support them in building capacity to bring their production to scale and be able to meet the demands from the Chinese market.
The Ghana-China Zero-Tariff Forum 2026 was organized by the Africa-China Center for Policy and Advisory and the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), and Sylvia Sinkari, a consultant with CEIBS Africa, urged Ghanaian small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to use the opportunity offered by the zero-tariff policy as a turning point to break away from their slow response to such bilateral partnerships.
With the offer from China, Sinkari said Ghana must begin to move away from the export of raw materials to value addition.
"The policy is actually targeted at exports, and we need to begin to increase our niche manufacturing industry and move away from primary product exports to at least some level of value addition or light production before we move these exports out," she added. ■

Iran calls on UNSC to hold Israel accountable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:16:58 UTC
02:16:58 KST

Iran calls on UNSC to hold Israel accountable
TEHRAN— Iran has called on the United Nations Security Council to take decisive action to compel Israel to fulfill its obligations under international law, end its military aggression across West Asia, and face accountability for serious violations of international law.
Gholamhossein Darzi, Iran’s ambassador and chargé d’affaires to the United Nations in New York, made the appeal on Friday during the Security Council’s open debate on the situation in the Middle East, warning that Israel’s continued aggression, occupation, and destabilizing activities pose a grave threat to regional and international peace and security.
Darzi said the Israeli regime had repeatedly demonstrated disregard for international law and the principles enshrined in the UN Charter, while continuing its military operations and violations despite the announcement of a ceasefire in Gaza.
He pointed to Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip, the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as the two wars launched against Iran by Israel and the United States over the past year, as evidence of the urgent need for international accountability.
“The Security Council must act decisively to address the root causes of this tragedy, end impunity, compel Israel to fully comply with its obligations under international law and relevant UN resolutions, and bring an end to the decades-long injustice inflicted upon the Palestinian people,” Darzi said.
Gaza and Palestine at the center of the crisis
Addressing the humanitarian and political situation in Palestine, Darzi said Gaza remained devastated and subject to continued military attacks, leaving its population to endure immense suffering despite the announced ceasefire.
He also condemned Israel’s continued settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, escalating settler violence, and measures aimed at annexing Palestinian land and displacing its inhabitants.
Darzi stressed that an immediate and permanent end to Israeli aggression was essential, alongside the complete and unconditional withdrawal of Israeli occupying forces from Gaza, the safe and unhindered delivery of sustained humanitarian assistance, and full protection for civilians and humanitarian personnel.
He further emphasized that any political or administrative arrangements for Gaza must respect the inherent rights of Palestinians rather than subordinate them to security conditions imposed from outside.
The Iranian envoy reaffirmed the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and the establishment of an independent, sovereign, and viable Palestinian state, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital and full membership in the United Nations.
He argued that no sustainable solution could be achieved while occupation, settlement expansion, forced displacement, and violations of Palestinian rights continued.
Iran urges an end to Israeli aggression across West Asia
Darzi called on Israel to halt its continued violations of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, withdraw fully from Lebanese territory, and comply with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
He also urged Israel to end its military incursions and attacks on Syrian territory, withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan and other occupied areas, and respect Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The Iranian envoy framed these issues as part of a broader pattern of military aggression and violations of international law, arguing that the Security Council must address the underlying causes of regional instability rather than rely on selective condemnation.
Accountability for international crimes
Darzi described accountability for serious violations of international law, particularly international humanitarian law, as both an indispensable requirement and a legal imperative.
He said that over the past three years, Israel had committed grave international crimes against the peoples of Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran, including genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression.
He also accused Israel and the United States of waging two unjustified wars of aggression against Iran in violation of the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law.
According to Darzi, the two countries had deliberately targeted civilians and critical infrastructure, crossing fundamental legal and humanitarian boundaries.
He stressed that those responsible for such acts, as well as those who enable, support, or facilitate them, must be held fully accountable under international law.
Darzi warned that politically motivated conditions and selective condemnation must not be allowed to undermine the consistent, impartial, and unequivocal enforcement of international law.
Iran rejects allegations over the Strait of Hormuz
In the closing section of his address, Darzi rejected 'baseless and politically motivated allegations' directed against Iran by some speakers, including certain members of the Security Council.
He said such accusations distorted the facts, overlooked the root causes of the current crisis, and sought to reverse the roles of aggressor and victim.
Turning to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Darzi said the current tensions were a direct consequence of the US-Israeli war against Iran, which began on February 28, 2026, and subsequent US actions, including 'an unlawful maritime blockade.'
He reiterated that Iran remained committed to safe and secure navigation and had exercised its inherent right of self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity, population, and vital interests.
Concluding his remarks, Darzi said the restoration of normal and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz required an immediate and permanent end to US aggression, credible guarantees against its recurrence, respect for Iran’s sovereign rights, and the complete lifting of the maritime blockade and all other unlawful coercive measures.

Tens of thousands march in Lisbon over housing and living costs

Unknown Publisher

Tens of thousands march in Lisbon over housing and living costs
LISBON – Tens of thousands of people marched through central Lisbon on Oct 17 to protest against soaring living costs and a deepening housing crisis in Portugal, increasing pressure on the centre-right government.
Portugal’s biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “tens of thousands” packed one of the capital’s main avenues. Police gave no crowd estimate.
Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet in the European Union and NATO member state.
The demonstration followed days of growing unrest, including a tent camp set up by housing activists in the northern city of Porto that police cleared in a pre-dawn operation on Oct 12.
It coincides with protests in France against rising costs and declining public services, and smaller protests in Belgium. There are also mass protests in Albania, where protesters are demanding the prime minister’s resignation.
Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6% in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15% year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.
House prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’s worst housing affordability crises.
The squeeze is most acute in major cities.
Protesters’ concerns
Carolina Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher earning about €1,300 (S$1,870) a month on a scholarship, may lose her home as her rental contract nears expiry.
She and her partner pay €716 monthly for a flat in the Lisbon area, but renewal could push the rent above €1,200 – far beyond their means.
“I’m the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I’ve done, I still can’t make it... Right now, housing in Lisbon is the problem,” Cruz said.
Pedro Penilo, 62, a teacher, said Portugal’s leaders were “out of touch with reality”.
“Life is incredibly expensive… it’s going up brutally. I need to see how my mortgage is going to turn out in the coming months when it’s adjusted. I’m very worried,” he said.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said on Oct 16 that the “government will not yield to shouts from the street” and that concrete measures to address the concerns were already being rolled out. REUTERS

Sabarimala temple opens for Thulam month rituals; CM Satheesan offers prayers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:06:55 UTC
02:06:55 KST

The revered Sabarimala Lord Ayyappa temple was opened on Saturday for the rituals of the Thulam month, drawing numerous devotees eager to pay their respects.
The Sabarimala Lord Ayyappa temple opened on Saturday for the Thulam month rituals, with Kerala Chief Minister V D Satheesan and several other dignitaries visiting the hill shrine to offer prayers.In the presence of Tantri Kandar Brahmadathan, head priest Prasad E D opened the sanctum sanctorum and lit the ceremonial lamp. The sacred fire was then kindled in the Aazhi, located below the 18 holy steps leading to the shrine.
According to news agency ANI, Devaswom Minister K Muraleedharan, Travancore Devaswom Board President K Jayakumar, Keralam State Police Chief Ravada Chandrasekhar, and MLAs Pazhakulam Madhu and C V Shanthakumar were among those, who arrived at the Sannidhanam to seek the blessings of Lord Ayyappa.Despite persistent heavy rainfall, thousands of devotees gathered at the hill shrine to offer prayers.
Temple to open for devotees at 5 am on Sunday
The temple will open to devotees at 5 am on Sunday, marking the first day of the Thulam month. The selection of the new Melsanthies, or chief priests, for the Sabarimala and Malikappuram temples is also scheduled for the day through a draw of lots.
The selection process for the Sabarimala Melsanthi will take place at the Sopanam at 7.30 am, following the Usha Pooja. Sabarimala Special Commissioner R Jayakrishnan and Devaswom commissioner B Sunilkumar will supervise the proceedings.
The draw of lots to select the Malikappuram Melsanthi will subsequently be held at the Malikappuram temple.
Thulam rituals coincide with Mahanavami and Vijayadashami
According to officials, this year's Thulam month rituals are particularly significant as the temple has opened during Mahanavami and Vijayadashami after several decades.The temple will close at 10 pm on October 22, following the conclusion of the Thulam month rituals.

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:04:04 UTC
02:04:04 KST

Either Security Together or Insecurity Together
Iran's FM tells OIC US has deepened distrust after two years of good-faith talks, making new talks impossible without credible guarantees.
TEHRAN – Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi told the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad that lasting security in the region is indivisible: either states build security together, or they will endure insecurity together.
Speaking on Saturday at the OIC ministerial meeting hosted by Iraq under the theme "Dialogue and solidarity, two fundamental pillars for promoting peace and sustainable development," Araghchi laid out Iran's position on the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, Palestine and Yemen.
Araghchi arrived in Baghdad to attend the 52nd session, and was welcomed at the airport by Iraq's Deputy Foreign Minister. Upon arrival at Baghdad International Airport, he paid tribute at the memorial of resistance commanders Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis.
He opened his address by thanking the Government and people of Iraq, "our neighbor and brother," for hosting the meeting, congratulating Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed on his appointment, and thanking Türkiye for its successful chairmanship of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers.
The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice, he said, recalling that its Charter, like the UN Charter, rests on sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference, peaceful settlement of disputes and refraining from threat or use of force. Those principles, he stressed, "belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value."
Aggression instead of diplomacy
Araghchi said Iran has remained steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy over the past two years, while "the United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law."
About 5,000 Iranians have been martyred, including hundreds of women and children, he said. He accused the United States and the Israeli regime of assassinating Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, calling it a grave violation of international law.
Citing documented cases, he listed the killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak in Sirik. The U.S. and Israel, he said, "cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor."
He thanked those member states that expressed solidarity with the Iranian people and called on the Organization as a whole "to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member."
Iran, he added, defended its people, sovereignty and legitimate interests and will continue to do so by any means. "We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the U.S. military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately located in our neighborhood."
There is no contradiction between defending rights and pursuing peace, he said: "We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace. Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all."
"This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation," he added.
Hormuz open until Feb. 28, reopenable in seven days
On the Strait of Hormuz, Araghchi reaffirmed Iran's commitment to safe and secure navigation in the waterway vital to the energy and trade of many OIC members.
"Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States," he said.
"Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal."
He revealed that diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on June 17. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to facilitate safe movement of vessels and immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman. Within two weeks, he said, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level.
Subsequent unilateral U.S. measures and military action blocked implementation and bypassed the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged, Araghchi said.
Over two years, Iran negotiated in good faith and repeatedly was met with military action rather than diplomacy, creating deep distrust about renewed talks without credible assurances, he said.
"Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," Araghchi told the ministers.
Palestine and Yemen
Araghchi called Palestine the central cause of the Islamic world. "We cannot speak of peace while ignoring it," he said, describing Gaza as a victim of genocide and a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians.
Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence, he said, urging the OIC to make ending the killing and blockade and protecting civilians a shared priority backed by practical and coordinated action. He endorsed the proposal by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to designate a Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.
On Yemen, he said the people have endured almost a decade of devastating conflict, prolonged blockade and restrictions on civilian infrastructure, with undeniable U.S. and Israeli roles. Iran supports the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of both Yemen and Saudi
Arabia, he said, and backs a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only sustainable solution.
"There is no military solution," he said. "Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion."
Iran, he added, is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to assist dialogue between the parties on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.
Build security together
Closing his speech, Araghchi delivered his central message to the Islamic world in a direct appeal:
"No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former."
"Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees," he concluded.
On the margins of the Baghdad session, Araghchi held a series of bilateral meetings to explain Tehran's positions on Hormuz, Palestine and the Arabian Peninsula.
U.S. broke its word two weeks after Islamabad MoU
In his meeting on Saturday morning with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, the two sides discussed bilateral relations and regional and international developments.
Araghchi, recalling the founding philosophy of the OIC, described Palestine as still the most important issue of the Islamic world, and stressing the genocide and crimes in occupied Palestine, underlined the need for urgent and joint action by the Islamic Ummah to end occupation and genocide and end the impunity of the Zionist regime.
On the region, he said the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime that began on Feb. 28 and have continued in various forms.
Emphasizing Iran's commitment to diplomacy and peace, he noted that the Islamic Republic has always responsibly adhered to diplomacy to reduce tensions, but the American side has repeatedly broken its promises, and in the latest case violated its commitment only two weeks after signing the agreement on ending the war.
He also briefed his Egyptian counterpart on the latest diplomatic consultations through mediators.
On the Arabian Peninsula, Araghchi announced Iran's readiness to provide any assistance to stop clashes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, stressing that the experience of 12 years of tension and conflict showed there is no military solution or military approach to Yemen.
Hormuz developments reviewed with Fidan
In his meeting with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, the two sides discussed bilateral ties and the latest regional developments, particularly Palestine and the continued genocide.
Referring to the summit theme of dialogue and solidarity, Araghchi stressed the need for Islamic states to focus on Palestine and take practical measures to stop Israeli crimes and help realize the Palestinian right to self-determination.
Both sides, emphasizing stronger cooperation among Islamic countries, also consulted on using OIC capacities to confront challenges facing the Islamic world, including Islamophobia.
The latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz were also reviewed, with Araghchi briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing trends.
Stability in Libya is prerequisite for North Africa
In a meeting with Taher al-Baour, acting Foreign Minister of Libya, both sides reviewed Tehran-Tripoli ties and stressed strengthening consultations.
Araghchi repeated Iran's principled position in support of national sovereignty and territorial integrity and unity, and the need to stop any foreign interference, and stressed that security and stability in Libya is a prerequisite for peace and stability in North Africa.
Both sides also consulted on developments in the region and the Islamic world. Araghchi, pointing to continued occupation and genocide by Israel in Palestine, called Palestine the greatest priority of the Islamic Ummah and the international community and called for urgent and serious OIC action to end the genocide in Gaza and end Israeli impunity.
Araghchi also met his Lebanese counterpart Youssef Raji on the sidelines in Baghdad for talks on bilateral ties and regional developments.

Meta denies favouring Bolsonaro as Brazil court orders equal treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
17:02:58 UTC
02:02:58 KST

Meta has denied favouring Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro after a court ordered the company to treat him and incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva equally ahead of their October 25 runoff.
The company said on Friday that problems affecting Lula’s accounts stemmed from global technical glitches, anti-fraud measures and regulatory compliance, rather than political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it said.
Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported, citing internal messages it reviewed, that Meta employees acknowledged restrictions had hindered Lula’s Instagram accounts while the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and WhatsApp channel.
Lula’s campaign alleged that some of his posts lacked sharing options, had reduced reach and suffered technical problems affecting audio and user interactions.
The campaign also said it would file a complaint with the Organization of American States, accusing Meta of manipulating social media during the election.
Meta said the technical issues were already public and that the internal discussions concerned their severity, not political interference.
The company cited two global disruptions earlier in October: one froze Instagram Reels view counts across more than 100 countries without affecting content distribution, while another temporarily prevented users from creating advertisements from existing Instagram posts through one of its tools.
Its response did not address why Bolsonaro’s Instagram profile and WhatsApp channel had received algorithmic recommendations.
Court orders equal treatment
On Thursday, a justice at Brazil’s top electoral court ordered Meta not to unjustifiably restrict the reach of political content related to either candidate during the runoff campaign.
The ruling also required the company’s chatbot, Meta AI, to avoid favouring either candidate in election-related content.
Meta said it would continue to defend itself in the case.
The dispute follows Bolsonaro’s stronger-than-expected first-round performance, which secured him a place in the runoff against Lula.
Lula’s administration has pursued tighter regulation of technology platforms, including measures targeting illegal content and misinformation.
Irregular political ads
Separately, a study by researchers at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro found Meta allowed at least 1,613 irregular political advertisements between July and September.
The ads, funded primarily from the United States, generated 171 million views and approximately two million reais ($400,000) in revenue, AFP reported, citing the study.
Marie Santini, a communication professor involved in the study, said only political parties, candidates and coalitions were permitted to purchase electoral advertisements in Brazil.
“It is not the first time that Meta is negligent with the electoral law, not the first country. It is a systematic behavior of the company,” she said.

Building friendships is the best education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:58 UTC
01:47:58 KST

In my classroom, you can find students from Vietnam, the Philippines, India and Thailand sharing the same space. I am from Guatemala. Just like the 140,417 international students reported by Study in Taiwan for last academic year, we came for a degree or an exchange program. The first big surprise in Taiwan for me was not eating with chopsticks or using an EasyCard; it was finding myself in a classroom full of young people from many parts of the world.
Taiwan has become a hub offering world-class education, attracting people from diverse continents. This is partly thanks to scholarships and funding opportunities provided by the government and other institutions to connect the world with Taiwan.
Beyond scholarships, there are other elements that make Taiwan and its education system special. According to a study published in 2012 on international students’ perceptions in Taiwan, 36 percent of international students chose to study in the nation because it had a “surrounding suitable for learning.”
In terms of a conducive environment, some people might simply imagine quality infrastructure, modern technology or innovative approaches. However, there is something rarely discussed that is also important for effective learning: collaboration, diversity and inclusion.
The same study identified three main aspects that international students recognized as part of classroom and campus norms in Taiwan. One was that they felt cultural differences were respected at school. The other two aspects were related to academics and their initiative to encourage interaction and efforts to support international students.
After 14 years, I can affirm that this sense of respect, safety, and above all, teamwork remains active and tangible. I was surprised when one of my professors set aside an entire morning just to get to know me and my international classmates, learning where we came from, what we had previously studied, and even identifying what we truly hoped to learn in Taiwan.
On the student side, if there are 30 people in a classroom, I can guarantee that I have heard perhaps up to 12 different accents. In addition to the Asian touch I mentioned earlier, one can distinguish those who come from France, some Caribbean tones from the Americas, and others from Africa. Coming across such an environment proves that these values are not merely reflected in statistics or studies, but are part of the daily language in the country.
Another data point mentioned in the study was that 40 percent of international students wished to have a Taiwanese friend. This remains a significant challenge for those of us who have come to this country. Popping the bubble of feeling like a foreigner is not so easy. Saying “hello” and “thank you” in Chinese is not enough to make friends.
One day, a Taiwanese classmate asked me, in Spanish, whether I spoke Spanish, and I said: “Yes.”
He told me he had learned some words on Duolingo. Ever since, whenever I see him, I greet him in Spanish, and he responds in kind.
In a world filled with technology, we sometimes forget that the best way to connect is still the simplest. Academic prestige and scholarships attract young people from all over the world to Taiwan, driven by the cultural openness and inclusion of its universities. However, it is those small, everyday exchanges — a spontaneous greeting, a smile in the hallway or an attempt to understand each other — that remind us that, at the end of the day, the best degree we can take home from here is a good friendship.
Pablo Mendoza is a scholarship recipient from Guatemala under the Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative studying smart agriculture in Taiwan.

What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. Songshan airport important for defense, researcher says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:56 UTC
01:47:56 KST

The primary value of Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) lies in its role in national defense, while its commercial benefits are an additional reason to keep it operating, Institute for National Defense and Security Research Defense Strategy and Resources Division director Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) said yesterday.
His comments came after Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeking re-election, on Oct. 9 proposed relocating the airport and redeveloping its site as an artificial intelligence hub featuring technology clusters, housing and public green space.
Songshan is a key takeoff and landing site for responding to crises in or around the capital, Su said, adding that it also serves as an alternative landing site and gives the military greater operational flexibility.
Photo: Lu Chun-wei, Taipei Times
The airport supports the Fokker 50 executive aircraft used by the president and other senior government officials. Aircraft carrying visiting US lawmakers, including US Senator Tammy Duckworth, have also landed there, he said.
These functions are part of the airport’s broader role in national defense and security, he added.
Su said arguments for relocating the airport based on the infrequent use of its runways by military aircraft overlook its wartime importance.
Military aircraft use Songshan airport less often in peacetime, because it is primarily designated for commercial aviation, he said.
Songshan is about 66km from the air force’s Hsinchu base. At a fighter jet’s cruising speed of about 900km per hour, or 15km a minute, the flight would take about four to five minutes, Su said.
The airport’s strategic value lies not simply in its location between Dazhi (大直) and Songshan (松山) districts, but in its role as a launch point for air operations over the capital and northern Taiwan, he said.
Su said the “Wan Chun Plan,” which was developed to protect the head of state, was only indirectly related to the debate over Songshan. The plan is intended to protect the president and other senior officials, and escort them to secure command centers to preserve the chain of command during wartime. Whether officials travel by aircraft is not central to the plan, he said.
Songshan’s economic contribution should also be considered, Su said, adding that its everyday benefits could be a more persuasive argument against relocation.
Relocating the airport is open to discussion, but airports allowing passengers to reach a capital’s downtown area within 20 minutes of landing can generate substantial economic benefits, he said.
About 5 million people use the airport annually, including about 3 million people on international routes, and it generates more than NT$60 billion (US$1.86 billion) in tourism benefits, Su added.

2026-10-17

Katie Zacharia is departing as White House press secretary, a person familiar with the matter said on Friday, after a short and rocky tenure that was defined by questions about her professional background and lack of polish in fielding questions from journalists.
The person, granted anonymity to discuss a personnel decision not yet made public, said Zacharia would be transitioning out of the role. The shift comes after US President Donald Trump cast significant doubt on her future earlier on Friday, telling reporters that he would have a discussion with her following his weekend travel — and that if he were her, he would reconsider the job.
Zacharia had come under immediate scrutiny when she appeared uncomfortable during her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, delivering halting remarks touting the president and his accomplishments. Her 14-minute briefing was followed by criticism that the conservative commentator had long called herself a lawyer when she had not passed a bar exam nor was otherwise credentialed to practice.
Photo: AP
Zacharia was a surprise choice when Trump announced her appointment on Oct. 9, as the successor to Karoline Leavitt, the youngest-ever White House press secretary who had been part of Trump’s inner circle for years. The chaotic nature of Zacharia’s appointment and subsequent downfall evoked some of the personnel messes of the president’s first term, which had largely been absent from his second.
In a lengthy exchange with reporters at the White House on Friday, Trump said he told Zacharia that she might want to change her mind about the job, and said he thought she had been treated unfairly by the press.
“I told her, ‘I think you’re better off being happy,’” Trump told reporters on the South Lawn as he left for a rally in Georgia. “I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider.’ I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
Messages to Zacharia seeking comment were not returned on Friday, and the White House did not respond to a request for confirmation.
In his own comments, Trump said he told his press secretary, “’Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this,’” and that he wanted “her to have a good life” and not be subjected to criticism, which he likened to being “brutalized by the media.”
The president said he would make a final determination later, perhaps after his campaign travel on Friday and this weekend, adding, “When I get back, we’re gonna talk.” He was asked who might replace Zacharia, and said that there were a lot of people who wanted the job.
In Zacharia’s first and only briefing on Tuesday, she took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative-leaning or Trump-friendly outlets, and left after only about 14 minutes.
Zacharia has said she wanted to keep her briefing short to ensure Trump had enough time later that morning for his own question-and-answer session with reporters, and that she had not been fully briefed by White House staff beforehand.
She later traveled with Trump when he held rallies on Wednesday and Thursday in Alaska, Arizona and Montana — but did not hold more press briefings.
In an appearance on Fox News Channel earlier on Friday, Zacharia was asked if she had the president’s confidence and responded: “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.” But she also would not say when her next press briefing might be.

China’s panda diplomacy is losing its charm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:51 UTC
01:47:51 KST

During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later. This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as a tool of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.
Perhaps the true message of this “panda diplomacy” lies in the manipulation and exploitation it embodies. While China claims the familiar black-and-white bear as its mascot, one of the species’ primary natural habitats is Wolong, which sits on the steep edge of the Tibetan Plateau. Within a horizontal distance of about 30 miles (48.2km), elevations range from alpine peaks exceeding 17,000 feet (5,181m) to below 1,600 feet (487m), creating a moist, temperate microclimate that sustains the high-altitude bamboo forests where pandas thrive.
Historically part of the Tibetan region of Kham, Wolong is under Sichuan provincial jurisdiction, in Aba Tibetan-Qiang Autonomous Prefecture — and China is all too eager to subsume everything that makes it culturally unique. Since China’s annexation of resource-rich Tibet in 1951, the government has sought to systematically erase Tibetan culture and identity, not least by incorporating the region’s distinctive geography, wildlife and natural resources into mainline Chinese national identity. China’s appropriation of others extends even to cherry-tree cultivation, which it has said began not in Japan or Korea, but in “China’s Himalayan highlands” — that is, Tibet.
Illustration: Tania Chou
The Tibetan Plateau is home to the endangered red panda, a housecat-sized mammal with a long, bushy tail, in addition to giant pandas, which are classified as a vulnerable species. There are fewer than 2,000 giant pandas left in the wild, and China claims ownership of almost all of them. This brings us to a second dubious element of China’s panda diplomacy: it is based on a lucrative “rent-a-panda-pair” program.
While China reaps the soft-power benefits of keeping its endearing mascot in foreign zoos, it charges those zoos high prices: up to US$1.1 million per year for the right to display and breed a pair of pandas. China retains ownership not only of the leased adults, but also of any offspring they produce. The leasing zoo must pay a one-time fee of approximately US$600,000 for each cub that is born during its lease. Facilities also often pay up to US$2 million in additional sponsorship and research commitments.
The fees add up. Between 1994 and 2023, China made almost US$300 million from its panda-rental program. Small wonder the Guinness World Records lists the giant panda as the “most expensive species in captivity.”
The money is just the start. The increasingly one-sided contracts that the state-run China Wildlife Conservation Association signs with zoos allow China to terminate an agreement unilaterally and prematurely recall pandas for a wide variety of reasons, such as the “unauthorized release of relevant information” to the public. China prohibits zoos from using terms such as “lease,” “rental,” “loan,” or “contract,” apparently to obscure the transactional nature of the arrangement.
China uses panda loans to send political messages. China gave a pair of pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972, following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing. In 2010, however, it accelerated the recall of two US-born panda cubs after the White House announced that then-President Barack Obama would not cancel a meeting with the Dalai Lama. In 2023, the three remaining pandas at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo were returned to China, the end of a tradition that had lasted more than a half-century.
And it is not just the US. This year, Japan returned its last two giant pandas to China, leaving it without any for the first time since normalizing relations with China in 1972. By contrast, when China sent a pair of pandas to Qatar before the 2022 World Cup, officials hailed the move as a reflection of the countries’ “depth of relations.”
However, the power of China’s panda diplomacy seems to be waning. While the general public might still find pandas appealing, visits to panda-hosting zoos tend to plateau after the novelty wears off, and conservationists stridently criticize the commercial and diplomatic use of a vulnerable species.
Most importantly for China, political analysts and lawmakers increasingly view panda loans as more of a charming distraction than a meaningful barometer of bilateral relations. This helps to explain why Xi’s “gift” to Zoo Atlanta attracted little US media coverage. As international panda-leasing programs dwindled from 21 countries in 2019 to just 16 today, even Chinese state media are asking whether panda diplomacy has “lost its sparkle.”
Giant pandas can appear cuddly and docile, but they are bears: they have long, sharp claws and a highly developed jaw structure, which delivers a bite force of almost 1,300 Newtons, almost as strong as that of lions. While captive-bred pandas introduced into the wild tend to die because they lack critical survival skills, wild pandas can be aggressive and dangerous. In this sense, perhaps pandas really are an accurate symbol of China: even when it appears harmless, it cannot conceal its teeth.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research and fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin, is the author of Water, Peace, and War:
Confronting the Global Water Crisis.

The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

The Chinese vessels, numbered 3301 and 3303, entered the restricted waters at 3:34pm, the CGA’s Dongsha-Nansha Branch said in a statement issued on Friday night. The confrontation was still ongoing at the time the statement was released.

Photo courtesy of the CGA
The CGA’s Dongsha command first detected the ships southwest of the atoll at about 2pm. Based on their courses and speeds, officials assessed that they might enter the restricted waters and directed the two Taiwanese vessels to respond.
The branch said the CGA had conducted 11 operations this year to expel Chinese coast guard ships from waters around Dongsha, involving 14 vessel encounters.
The branch cited Friday’s incident as Beijing’s use of purported law enforcement activities to expand its authority and create the appearance of jurisdiction over the area.
Taiwan has sovereignty over Dongsha and its surrounding waters, the branch said, pledging to take all necessary measures to defend Taiwan’s national sovereignty and maritime security.

Three jailed for over 158 years in surfer murders
Unknown

01:47:49 KST

A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.
The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.
A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesus Gerardo Garcia, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
Photo: Reuters
Antonio Otanez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” However, he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
The Robinson brothers and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San Jose, about 80km from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.
Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.
Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15m deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.
The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested Garcia, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.
State authorities said Garcia had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.
Garcia’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Angel Jesus “N,” were also arrested in the case.
Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
State prosecutor Maria Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.
“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she said.

EDITORIAL: Prepare for a second ‘Han Wave’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:47 UTC
01:47:47 KST

The official English name for Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign is “the Taipei Current.” It comes from the Chinese term yangliu (洋流), a direct translation of which would be “Ocean Wave,” using the last character of Shen’s name, yang (洋, “ocean”). The Chinese term is a reference to the 2018 campaign for Kaohsiung mayor that swept a hitherto marginal player within the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), who is now legislative speaker, whose successful campaign then was termed the “Han Wave” (韓流).
Shen’s usage of the Chinese term is intentional. He is the underdog in the Taipei mayoral race, taking on the incumbent, Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT. Historically, the DPP has not fared well in the nation’s capital. Just as Han secured an unexpected victory for the KMT in a DPP stronghold in 2018, Shen hopes to ride the “Ocean Wave” to victory on Nov. 28.
Two TVBS polls five months apart show Shen cutting Chiang’s lead from 28 percentage points in May to only 8 percentage points this month. Another poll, commissioned by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association and released on Tuesday last week, showed DPP Legislator Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the party’s candidate for New Taipei City mayor, having a 13.1 percentage point lead over her KMT rival, Lee Shu-chuan (李四川).
The loss of Taipei and New Taipei City would be catastrophic for the KMT. There are indications that some KMT figures have already started to think about the implications for their individual political prospects. It would certainly make sense of Han’s combative Double Ten National Day address last weekend, which last Sunday’s editorial (“Two different National Day speeches,” Oct. 11, page 8) called “a rant against the government” that was “strangely out of place for the context.”
In one interpretation, Han was positioning himself within shifting internal party dynamics, mending fences following his support — much-maligned within the party — of the government’s national defense proposals and his “dark forces” outburst against KMT legislative caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) in August.
The hubris of the Han Wave made Han think he could pursue the presidency in 2020, before he had even served half a term as Kaohsiung mayor. Had he completed his full term, gained the experience in governing and established himself, he might have been prepared for running in 2024. Instead, he was defeated by a landslide in 2020, recalled months later and cast into the political wilderness, until being offered the speakership in 2024. This time he will have more experience and a higher political profile.
There are four main KMT figures who might seek the party’s presidential nomination in 2028: KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文), Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), Chiang and Han.
According to an opinion poll released in mid-August by the online media outlet Z.Media (震傳媒), 20.4 percent of respondents said Chiang was their preferred KMT candidate for the 2028 presidential race, compared with 18.9 percent for Han, 16 percent for Lu and 3 percent for Cheng.
Cheng is not a forerunner for 2028, and if the KMT performs poorly in next month’s local elections, she would almost certainly face calls to resign, even more so if the party loses control of its traditional strongholds of the capital and New Taipei City under her watch.
Defeat next month would free Chiang up for a 2028 presidential run. While the Z.Media poll put him in front, his failure to secure a second term would mean losing control of the capital to the DPP, and Han would benefit from the damage that would cause to Chiang’s prospects. Lu is notoriously reticent about revealing her hand.
At the same time, the party’s loss of Taipei and New Taipei City would elevate the importance of Taichung and Taoyuan: If his colleague Deputy Legislative Speaker Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) is elected Taichung mayor, with Taoyuan Mayor Simon Chang (張善政) — Han’s running mate in 2020 — in place, Han would potentially have two influential allies to support him.
If he maneuvers himself into the right position, Han could even emerge from a potentially catastrophic result for the KMT next month into a relatively strong position for 2028.
In this light, last week’s National Day address could even be seen as laying the groundwork for riding a new Han Wave, with the benefit of having learned the lessons of the previous one.

The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. Soccer referee in Uruguay game tests electronic cards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:45 UTC
01:47:45 KST

A referee raised a phone-sized electronic device to caution a player during a Uruguayan cup match this week, replacing the familiar flash of a yellow card with a digital screen in a trial aimed at modernizing one of soccer’s oldest rituals.
Match official Eduardo Varela used the device during Nacional’s Copa Uruguay match against Rentistas on Thursday, testing a system designed to simplify referees’ administrative work by recording disciplinary decisions digitally.
“We are looking to bring technology to the only thing in football that is still analogue,” said Mauro Sacco, director of REFe, the company behind the project, in an interview with Uruguayan radio El Espectador Deportes on Friday.
The idea emerged more than three years ago when Sacco and fellow director Diego de la Pena watched a match in rainy conditions and considered how referees recorded cautions by hand before transferring the information to digital systems.
The new device logs match incidents with timestamps, with developers aiming to streamline the submission of official records to the Uruguayan Football Association’s COMET platform.
For Varela, the new tool was comfortable to use and its software responded quickly, although he acknowledged that it lacked the drama of the traditional gesture.
“You lose a little of the magic of the quick card, but I think it is something that will help us a lot, especially with the administrative side,” he said.
The first real-world tests have also exposed a problem: visibility. An earlier trial was abandoned because sunlight made the screen difficult to see, while spectators and television viewers struggled to distinguish some decisions during Thursday’s match.
“It’s a project with room for improvement. It looked much better live than it did on TV. The challenge we face now is to improve it for the whole audience,” De la Pena said. “The yellow card has to be yellow, the red card has to be red, and it has to be visible to people at the ground and on television.”
The developers are exploring changes, including LEDs around the device, to make the colors clearer to spectators.
Sacco said the brand had been registered, and the hardware and software patented, with the developers based in China.
The trial has drawn mixed reactions online.
“We have seen all kinds of comments, positive and negative. We have even laughed at the memes,” he said.
“The important thing is that people are talking about it. Any innovation takes time,” he added.
REFe hopes to refine the technology and eventually see it adopted by South American governing body CONMEBOL and world soccer’s FIFA.

Chinese cars a potential Trojan horse for Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:47:44 UTC
01:47:44 KST

Chinese-made cars filmed sensitive information during a Norwegian military exercise, including access codes at secure sites and officials’ comings and goings, raising concerns about the risks posed by connected vehicles.
During a security exercise at Oslo airport on Sept. 14 to 18, waiting soldiers tapping on their vehicle’s screen discovered videos recorded by the onboard cameras, the Dagens Naeringsliv (DN) newspaper revealed.
The recordings showed who was getting in and out of the cars, the routes taken and even the codes used to open gates or doors to military facilities.
Photo: Reuters
In its report three weeks after the exercise, DN said the recordings came from rental vehicles — at least two of them Deepal-brand cars, made by Chinese state-controlled automaker Changan. They were supplied to the army by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by the Chinese auto group Geely.
“Yes, soldiers from the Home Guard found videos from the vehicles’ sensors stored in their systems,” Lieutenant Colonel Per Gunnar Grosberghaugen, Norwegian Home Guard spokesperson, said.
It was not known if the recordings were shared with a third party, notably in China, but the officer could not rule out the possibility.
The case highlights a paradox: While Europe’s armies are bolstering their protection against espionage and hybrid threats, the vehicles they use can collect sensitive information. Even after discovering the leaks, the military continued to use the vehicles until the end of the exercise due to a lack of alternatives and the soldiers deleted the videos, DN reported. Judging that the impact of a general ban on Chinese-made vehicles would be disproportionate to the potential security gain, the military said it preferred security procedures tailored to each site, with possible local bans on vehicles equipped with cameras and sensors regardless of their origin. Hertz Norge stressed that it complies with Norwegian and European regulations.
“Our customers’ data is safe with us,” Hertz Norge marketing and communications director Hallvard Nerbovik said. “No personal data related to our rentals is shared with car manufacturers, our owners or other third parties without explicit legal grounds,” he added, without specifying whether the onboard videos might have been transferred.
Changan group did not respond to AFP’s questions.
Last year, tests carried out for Oslo’s Ruter public transport authority revealed that Chinese manufacturer Yutong could theoretically remotely immobilize its electric buses with their “over-the-air” update system.
Norway could use the buses one day to evacuate the population in the event of an emergency.
Ruter has since introduced mechanisms enabling it to monitor and delay incoming signals in order to control updates, it said.
Modern vehicles are not the only potential Trojan horses. Smartwatches and fitness apps such as Strava, popular with joggers, can also expose sensitive military information.
In 2018, data published by Strava made it possible to identify military sites and soldiers’ routes, notably in Afghanistan and Syria. In March, French newspaper Le Monde was able to locate the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle in almost real time in the eastern Mediterranean, thanks to a sailor on board using the app. The Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) said modern vehicles are “rolling computers that collect information.”
“We don’t know for sure where the information is sent or what it’s used for,” NSM official Andreas Skjold-Lorange said.
The organization, which is responsible for minimizing strategic risks, including digital, said that beyond the data collected, Norway should be wary of excessive dependence on a single country.
Especially if that country does not cooperate with Norway on security matters.
“If we become too dependent on services or products from a given country, that makes us vulnerable, whatever that country may be,” Skjold-Lorange said.
Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak on Wednesday urged so-called middle powers to become a “poisonous shrimp” to carve out strategic economic leverage in a more turbulent global environment. Sunak drew from a metaphor by former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀): A big fish will eat a smaller fish, and the smaller fish will eat the shrimp. Lee made the point a year after the Asian nation’s independence in 1966 that the city-state needed to build up its defense mechanisms — like a shrimp that stings — so it would be left alone by predators. “He was thinking about what Singapore’s

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-18
00:44:57 CST
01:44:57 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked European diplomats in the village of Taybeh, near Ramallah in the West Bank, according to the Israeli police, the military and media reports.
According to Israel's state-owned Kan News, seven masked settlers armed with clubs attacked French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and Palestinian olive pickers at the scene. The assailants also smashed a window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian consulate.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said in a statement that no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack because the call was made to a divisional operations room that handles reports from security personnel, not civilians.
Israeli police said that they had opened an investigation and notified the Israeli Foreign Ministry to help locate the diplomats who were attacked, collect statements, and identify the attackers.
"Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will pursue these investigations to their conclusion, bringing to justice everyone involved in such incidents," the police statement said.
The IDF also condemned the attack. However, it said that the diplomats' tour had not been coordinated with the military.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar condemned in a statement "the serious acts of violence committed by Israeli rioters in the Taybeh area."
He said that his ministry is in contact with the ambassadors of the countries concerned to assist law enforcement authorities, which are working to identify the assailants and bring them to justice.
More than half a million Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in 1967, alongside about 3.4 million Palestinians.
Also on Saturday, Abdul Jawad Joudah, a Palestinian police officer, was killed in an Israeli airstrike targeting a police post in an area of Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, according to Palestinian sources.
Since a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel took effect in October 2025, Israeli attacks have killed 1,511 people, bringing the total death toll since Oct. 7, 2023, to 74,469, according to Gaza-based health authorities on Saturday. ■

Israeli forces, settlers damage 3,522 West Bank fruit trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

Israeli forces and settler attacks damaged at least 3,522 fruit trees and caused agricultural losses exceeding $1.9 million over a period of a week in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture announced.
The ministry's report for the week of 8 - 15 October showed that settlers had intensified their targeting of farmers and their crops during the olive harvesting season. At least 2,667 olive trees - three-quarters of the trees included in the survey - were reported damaged.
The damage varied between cutting down, uprooting, and burning trees, in addition to stealing and confiscating olive fruits, and destroying agricultural facilities and irrigation networks.
The report also noted that Palestinian farmers were prevented from accessing their lands, threatening their ability to harvest crops and compounding their losses during a season on which thousands of Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank depend as a source of income.
The ministry's report added that settlers stole 8,612 kilograms of olives, equivalent to approximately 8.6 tons.
The impact of this theft extends beyond the value of the olives themselves; farmers also lose a portion of their seasonal income and bear the costs of tree care and harvesting without any guarantee of safe access to their land or the ability to market their produce.
Hebron Governorate topped the list of the most affected areas with losses estimated at approximately $455,000, followed by Jenin with approximately $452,000.
The similarity in losses between the two governorates reflects the wide geographical extent of the damage, while the remaining losses are distributed across other areas of the West Bank.
The report comes after a week of even greater losses, with the Ministry of Agriculture's report for the period from 1 - 8 October documenting direct losses of approximately $3,678,000 and damage to 3,192 olive trees in seven governorates, with Jenin being the most affected.
The new report records damage in the following week, indicating continued losses throughout the harvest season.
The olive harvest is a primary source of income and employment in Palestinian villages, supporting tens of thousands of families wholly or partially.
The effects of the attacks go beyond the trees and the harvest, impacting family incomes and activities related to harvesting, pressing, and trade.

After ruling out the possibility of a minority government, Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Lieberman said Saturday evening that "we must get rid of Bibi" and outlined a plan to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and pass legislation that would prevent politicians under criminal indictment from serving as prime minister. 
"Immediately after the 26th Knesset is sworn in, we will work to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and elect a new speaker. After that, we will pass the 'defendant law' through all three readings, and that will be the end of it," he wrote.
Lieberman's remarks appear to signal for the first time that he is considering another election, this time without Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being able to run as Likud's candidate for prime minister. However, it remains unclear whether the proposed legislation, which would bar a person under criminal indictment from serving as prime minister, could withstand a challenge in Israel's High Court of Justice, given concerns that it would be considered legislation targeting Netanyahu personally. The Supreme Court previously ruled that Netanyahu could serve as prime minister despite the criminal indictment against him.
Lieberman has also rejected a proposal by Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar! party, to establish a minority government, with polls generally showing a deadlock between the rival political blocs. Speaking at an Israel Democracy Institute conference, and in a social media post published simultaneously, Lieberman made his position clear: "We will not support any minority government, not even a minority government for a transitional period. We need a Zionist majority government, period."
At the same conference, Lieberman said Likud could become a coalition partner if Netanyahu were no longer leading the party. "Likud without Netanyahu could be a significant partner. With Netanyahu, even if the world turns upside down, we will not sit with him under any circumstances. I know Likud lawmakers who understand the gravity of the moment and would be willing to provide the numbers needed and join a Zionist coalition." His comments, together with Saturday's declaration that Netanyahu must be removed from power, also point to the possibility of forming a broad government comprising what Lieberman has described as "Zionist parties only."
The dispute between Lieberman and Eisenkot has intensified in recent days. On Friday, 11 days before the election, Lieberman published a lengthy and particularly harsh statement titled "Gadi Eisenkot: Benny Gantz 2," accusing the former IDF chief of staff of seeking to establish a government with Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox parties. Meanwhile, Lieberman's second-in-command, Rafi Ben Shitrit, indicated that Yisrael Beytenu would recommend Lieberman for prime minister after the election. "He is the best and most seasoned politician we've had here, with 30 years of experience," Ben Shitrit said.
According to Lieberman, Eisenkot's campaign to make Yashar! the largest party is not intended to attract a single vote from what he called the "draft-dodgers' bloc" to the "bloc of those who serve," but rather to draw votes away from other parties within the same opposition bloc.
"That is completely contrary to the agreements reached between the bloc leaders at their last meeting on September 26. It undermines our unity and raises one simple question: What is behind this move?" Lieberman wrote. "As time passes, the picture becomes clearer. Eisenkot is preparing for the day after the election. What interests him is not being the largest party in the bloc of those who serve, but being larger than Likud and entering negotiations to form a government with Netanyahu from a position of strength."
Lieberman went on to accuse Eisenkot of "working toward establishing a government with Netanyahu, Goldknopf and Deri, while keeping the possibility of a minority government on the table as leverage against Netanyahu so that he can serve first in a rotation agreement."
"When I hear Minister Miki Zohar discussing the possibility of cooperation with Eisenkot, read reports about President Herzog's initiative to establish a Netanyahu-Eisenkot government, and hear the briefings coming from the White House, things begin to fall into place," Lieberman wrote. "The positions taken by Eisenkot's people on military conscription and the constitution only reinforce these concerns."

Tehran seeks rail link to Afghanistan via Uzbekistan as Iran-Kazakhstan freight grows
TEHRAN- The head of the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, on the sidelines of the two-day summit of ministers from Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) member states in Kazakhstan, announced a review of obstacles to Iran-Kazakhstan rail cooperation and the issue of connecting Iran’s rail network to Afghanistan via Uzbekistan.
Jabbar-Ali Zakeri, at the two-day ECO ministers’ summit in Kazakhstan, referred to the development of rail infrastructure and the increase in regional transit capacity and emphasized the need to expand transport cooperation among regional countries.
The head of the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways, referring to the annual holding of the “New Silk Road” conference by Kazakhstan Railways and the country’s Ministry of Transport, described the main goal of the event as developing transport in the region and strengthening international corridors.
Zakeri, referring to the opening last year of the Dostyk route, the second border crossing between Kazakhstan and China, said: “Rail-laying operations are underway on the continuation of this route over a length of 150 kilometers, and the project is expected to become operational next year. This measure can increase the capacity of the East-West corridor.”
The Deputy Minister of Transport and Urban Development, stating that Kazakhstan’s rail transit, despite existing restrictions in Russia’s and Belarus’s communications with Europe, has grown by 20 percent to about 30 million tons, described this trend as a sign of the high capacity of rail transport in the region.
He also cited the digitalization of processes and the elimination of paper documents in exchanges between executive bodies as among Kazakhstan Railways’ important measures, explaining: “This transformation has reduced the time for wagons to cross the border to about 30 minutes.”
According to him, the move by member states of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) toward using an integrated digital system can bring about facilitation of rail transport and regional trade.
Zakeri, emphasizing the importance of Iran’s use of these capacities, expressed hope that, given Iran’s border and transport connections with regional countries, the ground would be prepared for using integrated digital systems as well.
The head of the Islamic Republic of Iran Railways further recalled the long-standing rail relations between Iran and Kazakhstan and announced a noticeable increase in freight movement capacity between the two countries.
He added: “Obstacles and problems in bilateral cooperation, the development of the rail network, border connections, and especially the establishment of a rail link between Iran and Afghanistan via Uzbekistan were reviewed at this meeting.”
Zakeri expressed hope that part of the agreements and decisions made at this summit would enter the implementation phase by next year and provide the ground for strengthening rail cooperation and developing regional transit.

Iranian delegation accompanied President Masoud Pezeshkian in his visit to Kazakhstan during which the two countries Joint Economic Committee meeting also convened.
The Iran Chamber of Commerce signed three memorandums of cooperation, including two with KazTrade and the Kazakhstan Trade Development Council and one with the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs Atameken, covering trade data exchange, business delegations, logistics and green freight transport.
Six additional agreements were signed between Iranian and Kazakh companies in sectors including agriculture, mining, copper production and food processing. One of the deals is valued at more than $1 billion.
An Iran-Kazakhstan business conference convened in the Kazakh capital Astana on Thursday, with the presidents of both countries, senior ministers, private sector officials, and business delegations from the two countries in attendance, seeking to deepen commercial ties.
Officials from Kazakhstan’s National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA) and representatives of Iranian and Kazakh companies also attended the event.
Speaking at the conference, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran aims to build a stable network of cooperation and mutual investment between the private sectors of the two countries, calling the Central Asian nation a strategic partner.
ICCIMA Head Samad Hassanzadeh, for his part, outlined four key obstacles to Iran–Kazakhstan trade and called for joint planning and stronger private-sector involvement to remove them. He said completion of the North–South Corridor infrastructure should be a top priority.
He said the current bilateral trade of roughly three hundred and fifty million dollars could grow several-fold in the short term, given existing potential and political backing.
Hassanzadeh said the presence of senior officials at the forum underscored shared determination to expand economic ties, noting Kazakhstan’s importance as a major Central Asian economy and strategic partner.
He said proximity, stable political ties, and opportunities in energy, agriculture, mining, Caspian shipping, petrochemicals, metals, food industries, engineering services, and pharmaceuticals provide a strong basis for deeper cooperation.
