Videogame developer House House says Big Walk will not release on Xbox due to BDS listing
Melbourne-based videogame developer firm House House announced this week that the popular video game Big Walk would not be rolled out on Xbox due to their compliance with the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement.
The developers said that while in 2026 they had announced that the game would be released on computers and other devices such as PS5 and Switch 2, fans urged them against a future Xbox release.
“We have made the decision not to release Big Walk on Xbox, in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS (Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions) movement’s call to boycott Microsoft, and their designation of Microsoft Games (and Xbox) as a priority boycott target,” the statement from the developers reads.
It calls on fans and readers to read about why Microsoft is being targeted, and how such a targeted boycott has already been proven to be effective. It directs people to the BDS website, which details how Microsoft's technology is being used in Israel’s war on Gaza to carry out potential war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
“It has always been our intention for Big Walk to be played by groups of friends, and we know that keeping the game off Xbox runs counter to those intentions,” the statement from House House continued.
House House expressed regret at not being able to make the game available Xbox, but said it remains firm on the decision until Microsoft and, or Xbox have been removed as BDS boycott targets.
The decision has received widespread praise from activists, with many also calling on them to take their decision a step further by cutting any links they have to SONY, citing their sale of equipment to the Israeli military.
This is not the first time House House has supported the plight of Palestinians. In 2023, the developer released a statement emphasising the Palestinian right to self-determination following the start of Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave.
“Now that we're back on here, we want to express our support for the Palestinian people, and their right to self-determination, safety and happiness. An end to this genocide. An end to apartheid. Free Palestine,” they wrote.
The Big Walk game, which is a multi-player adventure that centres on teamwork, challenges and puzzles, is still available on other apps and platforms, including Steam and Nintendo.

Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
16:34:23 UTC
01:34:23 KST

Pope Leo left the hospital in Rome on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican four days after surgery for lung cancer, an illness that has prompted speculation about how it might affect his 17-month papacy.
The 71-year-old walked unaided to his waiting car, waving to well-wishers outside Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He stopped to speak to a 13-year-old girl named Varvara from Ukraine who has been in Italy for cancer treatment.
He was pictured smiling broadly and waving through an open window when his black SUV left the hospital. He waved again to crowds as he was driven back into the Vatican but did not speak to anyone there before re-entering the world's smallest country.
His doctors had said earlier on Saturday that he was well enough to return home after they carried out the latest blood tests and chest imaging, and that he was able to perform normal daily activities independently.
Leo, who had an operation on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, will hold his first public engagement since surgery when he will lead weekly prayers with pilgrims in St. Peter's Square at noon (1000 GMT) on Sunday.
He has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis for a pope known to be relatively young and energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy as he deals with the illness.
The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
Pope pursues packed agenda
The Vatican signaled on Friday that Leo, known for following a busy schedule, intended to keep up his commitments, as some cardinals began to publicly express concern about the pope's health.
In a sign the pope was back to work, Leo held a phone call on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging a ceasefire to help get vital supplies into the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky.
The Vatican said work on Leo's November 6 to 17 visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, one of the most intense arranged for a pope in decades, was also "going forward." It released a list of journalists accredited to travel with Leo and cover the trip.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, said on Friday that Leo may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health." It is unusual for a cardinal to say openly that a pope might need to modify his routine.
On Friday, the Vatican released the first images of the pope since his surgery, showing him celebrating Mass and standing unaided.

Spain's hard left fails to unite before election, hurting chances of staying in power
MADRID, Oct 17 - Spain's hard-left parties on Saturday presented separate candidate lists for a snap election after talks on a nationwide pact collapsed, reducing Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez' chances of staying in power at the head of a leftist coalition.
Spain's electoral system disadvantages smaller parties running separately, particularly in less populous provinces, where fewer seats are available.
The division could also demoralise left-wing voters, whom organisers hoped to galvanise around housing protests and fear of the far right.
The Broad Front, a platform comprising several parties represented in the minority government, and the other main party on the hard left, Podemos ("We Can"), had been publicly arguing over the leading positions on joint candidate lists for the November 29 election in Madrid and Barcelona, the largest constituencies.
Long-standing animosities between former comrades-turned-rivals did not help.
"These past few days have been very difficult ... some people will be disappointed today, and for that I am sorry," Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor and leader of the Broad Front, said at her platform's launch event in Madrid.
Podemos, whose lead candidate is former equality minister Irene Montero, had proposed open primaries to determine candidates' positions on joint lists.
But the Broad Front refused, arguing there was too little time, and wanted its own preferred candidates to lead the lists in Madrid and Barcelona.
Podemos then made a separate pact deal with the Republican Left of Catalonia (ERC), which favours Catalan independence. REUTERS

Croatian PM meets Chinese FM, voices willingness to expand bilateral cooperation

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
ZAGREB, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi here on Saturday, expressing Croatia's willingness to further expand cooperation with China.
During the meeting, Plenkovic asked Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, to convey his sincere greetings to the Chinese leadership, saying that he looks forward to visiting China at an early date and meeting with the leadership.
Relations between Croatia and China have continued to improve, underpinned by mutual respect and sincere cooperation, Plenkovic said. Chinese enterprises have participated in infrastructure projects in Croatia, including roads, bridges and tunnels, he said, noting that the Peljesac Bridge has played a significant role in improving connectivity between different parts of the country.
The Croatian side highly appreciates these contributions and welcomes continued participation of Chinese enterprises in the country's development, he said. Croatia is willing to further expand cooperation with China in such areas as tourism, photovoltaics and wind power, he added.
The prime minister also welcomes the launch of direct flights between Croatia and China, looking forward to closer exchanges between their peoples.
Stressing that Croatia attaches great importance to cooperation with China under the China-Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) framework and the Belt and Road Initiative, Plenkovic said Croatia is willing to continue contributing to these efforts and looks forward to the early resumption of CEEC-China leaders' meeting mechanism to create new opportunities for closer high-level exchanges between the two sides.
For his part, Wang conveyed the Chinese leadership's good wishes to Plenkovic and welcomed him to visit China at a mutually convenient time.
Wang said China was among the first major countries to establish diplomatic relations with Croatia, adding that bilateral relations have enjoyed healthy, steady and sustainable development under the strategic guidance of the two countries' leaders.
China and Croatia treat each other with sincerity and mutual respect and have established a mature, long-term comprehensive cooperative partnership, Wang said, noting that this has been the right choice made by both sides. China is willing to further elevate bilateral relations on this foundation, he added.
Moreover, Wang said China cherishes its traditional friendship with Croatia and is willing to translate it into a strong driving force for bilateral relations in the new era.
Wang also said China respects the choices of the Croatian people and Croatia's governance model, and is willing to deepen mutually beneficial cooperation to support each other's development and revitalization.
China values people-to-people and cultural exchanges with Croatia and has introduced measures, including unilateral visa-free access and direct flights, to facilitate travel and enhance mutual understanding between the two peoples, Wang stressed.
In addition, Wang noted that China firmly believes that China and the European Union (EU) are partners, not rivals. China supports European integration and Croatia's efforts to achieve faster development through this process, and hopes Croatia will play a constructive role in deepening China-EU cooperation, Wang added.
Meanwhile, Wang stressed that China and CEECs share a practical need to strengthen exchanges and cooperation. Such cooperation is entirely open and transparent and contributes to European integration, he said.
China is willing to strengthen cooperation with interested countries in the region through established mechanisms, Wang said, noting that China appreciates Croatia's positive attitude in this regard and is ready to use the 15th anniversary of the China-CEEC cooperation mechanism next year as an opportunity to reinvigorate mutually beneficial cooperation between the two sides.
The two sides also exchanged views on China-EU economic and trade relations. Plenkovic said that EU countries, including Croatia, have concerns about trade imbalances. Participants at the recent EU summit spoke positively of the consensus reached through the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism and expressed hope that the two sides would continue to strengthen communication and dialogue to properly address their differences, he said.
Wang said that trade issues between China and the EU stem from the international division of labor and market demand. Imports of high-quality, competitively priced Chinese goods benefit European consumers and help curb inflation, reflecting demand in the European market, and there is no so-called "overcapacity" problem, he noted.
China is willing to import more high-value-added products from Europe and hopes the EU will ease restrictions on exports to China, Wang said. China is committed to promoting balanced growth in bilateral trade, with both sides moving forward rather than backward and expanding shared benefits rather than diminishing them, he added.
He also said China is ready to strengthen dialogue with the EU on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, jointly uphold free trade and advance open and inclusive economic globalization.
Meanwhile, Plenkovic briefed Wang on the situation in the Western Balkans. Wang said that China does not interfere in the internal affairs of countries in the region and hopes that all countries will enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust and coexist in harmony through dialogue. China is willing to play a constructive role in line with the needs of countries in the region, he added.

Feature: Uzbek girl connects to China through Tai Chi
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
23:48:50 CST
00:48:50 KST

TIANJIN, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- On a Chinese university campus, 22-year-old Uzbek student Ibrohimkhonova Ezozaxon practices Tai Chi in the dawn light, moving slowly and steadily through the routine.
Ezozaxon won first place in Tai Chi at Uzbekistan's national youth competition. Today, she is studying at Tianjin Normal University in north China's Tianjin Municipality. For her, Tai Chi has become more than a sport.
"Tai Chi connects me with China and helps me understand Chinese culture and Chinese people," she said.
Tai Chi is a traditional physical practice characterized by relaxed, circular movements that work in concert with breath regulation and the cultivation of a righteous and neutral mind. UNESCO inscribed it on its Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020.
In China, about 78.6 million people practice Tai Chi, including 35.1 million regular practitioners, according to an official national survey released in late 2025.
Ezozaxon's connection with the sport began when she was three. Then, her father returned from China, where he had studied Chinese and Tai Chi. She still remembers seeing her father practicing in their yard wearing a white Tai Chi suit. Later, watching films starring Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Jet Li with her family deepened her interest in Chinese martial arts.
In high school, Ezozaxon took up Tai Chi to improve her health. At first, she found the movements "too slow, only for the elderly," and nearly gave up. Her coach helped her see that Tai Chi was about more than slowness: it is performed by controlling breath, strength and movement in slow motion, combining softness with firmness.
The competition victory that followed changed how she saw the practice. "As I delved deeper, I found Tai Chi looks gentle but holds power. It helps me cultivate my character," she said.
Driven by her interest in Tai Chi and Chinese culture, she chose to study in China, where she found martial arts far more diverse than she had imagined.
In the early mornings in Tianjin, many older people practice Tai Chi in public squares, and she joins them. "I see a sense of ease and calm in them, and I read the Chinese way of cultivating body and mind," she said.
The philosophy embodied by Tai Chi also touched her. "No coach taught me to attack others. They always say: first protect yourself, then protect others," Ezozaxon said.
To her, Tai Chi reflects the Chinese temperament -- gentle and calm, embodying the Chinese concepts of peace, harmony and friendliness.
"It helped me understand the Chinese philosophical idea that harmony is precious," she said.
Chinese martial arts, or Wushu, is stepping onto a broader global stage. With the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games approaching, Wushu Taolu (choreographed sequences) will make its debut as an official sport on the Olympic stage. In Tianjin, Ezozaxon has seen athletes from Senegal's national youth Wushu team training in China ahead of the event.
"Wushu originated in China but belongs to the world," said Zhao Qingjian, a coach for the youth team and an associate professor at Capital University of Physical Education and Sports. "We want to further improve their skills and performance."
Through training and competition, Ezozaxon has experienced the exchange and integration brought by Wushu's growing internationalization. She has competed in Wushu events across China against athletes from around the world.
"On the field we are rivals; off it, we become friends," Ezozaxon said. Now she rehearses Wushu routines with Chinese classmates and students from other countries and regions. Wushu has given young people worldwide a new common language.
"Tai Chi has taught me to slow down, to feel strength within softness, and to appreciate the Chinese cultural wisdom in it. I will keep practicing, strive to be an envoy of cultural exchange, and pass on this beauty of harmony rooted in China to more friends," Ezozaxon said. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- China's national flood control authorities on Saturday stepped up preparations for heavy rain across wide areas of the country, as 15 provincial-level regions were forecast to see heavy to torrential rainfall and some areas faced risks of flash floods and geological disasters.

Temperatures across northern China were also expected to fall to their lowest levels since the second half of the year began.
From Saturday to Sunday, temperatures in parts of the northwest, Inner Mongolia, north China, northeast China and other regions were forecast to drop by 4 to 8 degrees Celsius, with some areas seeing declines of more than 10 degrees, Fang Chong, chief forecaster of the National Meteorological Center, said.
The weather could disrupt autumn harvesting and planting, while the rainfall would also help replenish soil moisture in northern China and support the sowing and seedling emergence of winter wheat, Fang added. ■

Prisoners wait for their release in Sanaa, Yemen, on Oct. 17, 2026. Yemen's Houthi group on Saturday released 159 prisoners whom it described as having surrendered during recent fighting, under an amnesty issued by the group's leadership. (Photo by Mohammed Mohammed/Xinhua)
SANAA, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group on Saturday released 159 prisoners whom it described as having surrendered during recent fighting, under an amnesty issued by the group's leadership.
Abdul Qader al-Murtada, head of the Houthis' prisoner affairs committee, announced the release at a press conference in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.
Al-Murtada described the prisoners as fighters who had "voluntarily surrendered without fighting" during recent combats, without identifying the forces to which they belonged or specifying where they were captured.
He said the release was carried out under a general amnesty issued on Sept. 10 by Mahdi al-Mashat, head of the Houthi Supreme Political Council.
According to al-Murtada, Saturday's release was the second batch carried out under the amnesty, following the release of 323 prisoners in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah on Sept. 15. He said dozens of others had also been released in separate operations in Taiz province.
The released prisoners would be returned to their home areas and families in coordination with local authorities in their respective provinces, which would handle arrangements concerning their status, al-Murtada said.
The release comes amid renewed fighting between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government, which is backed by the Saudi-led coalition.
The warring sides have conducted several prisoner exchanges under UN-mediated agreements in recent years.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognized government out of the capital. ■

23:58:27 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- The latest consensus reached between China and the European Union (EU) on hybrid vehicle trade is expected to reduce policy uncertainty, stabilize market expectations and safeguard the interests of businesses and consumers on both sides, paving the way for more predictable and mutually beneficial cooperation in the sector, analysts and industry representatives said.
Guided by the principles of mutual respect and equal consultation, the two sides, in the consensus reached during the latest meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism in Beijing, emphasized and confirmed three basic principles regarding hybrid vehicles: compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, non-discrimination and respect for facts.
Under the arrangement, China retains all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and trade compensation, while Chinese products will not be subject to discriminatory treatment. The arrangement also uses the trade volume recorded in 2025 as a baseline, allowing room for continued growth in Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe.
The consensus comes against the backdrop of rapidly expanding Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the European market. In 2024, the EU imposed additional countervailing duties of up to 35.3 percent on Chinese-made battery electric vehicles, while hybrid vehicles were not subject to the additional tariffs.
Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe subsequently surged. According to Eurostat, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024, with the figure rising to 302,000 in 2025.
Fu Xin, a senior partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm in Beijing, described the outcome as a breakthrough, noting that using the 2025 volume as the baseline accommodates the reasonable concerns of the Chinese automotive industry and its expectations for stable growth.
"Admittedly, quota restrictions will constrain excessively rapid growth by Chinese automakers, but they will encourage companies to compete on quality and pursue higher profit margins through higher-value-added products, in line with China's broader goal of promoting high-quality foreign trade development," noted Shi Xiaoli, director of the WTO Law Research Center at the China University of Political Science and Law.
For Chinese automakers, one of the most immediate benefits of the consensus is a substantial reduction in policy uncertainty surrounding exports to Europe.
Fu noted that growing uncertainty in trade and investment policies in recent years has made it increasingly difficult for Chinese automakers to formulate long-term business strategies.
The latest consensus, he said, will give Chinese companies operating in Europe a more stable framework of rules for the foreseeable future, allowing them to plan exports, investment and production with greater confidence.
Chinese automaker BYD said the consensus has effectively managed trade differences, prevented further escalation and taken into account the realities and legitimate concerns of industries on both sides, creating favorable conditions for sustainable cooperation.
At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li disclosed the company's plans to expand its manufacturing presence in Europe. BYD's plant in Hungary is scheduled to begin large-scale production in the fourth quarter of this year. The company is also planning to establish its second and third manufacturing facilities in Europe, with France among the potential locations.
European automakers have extensive experience in automotive hardware, design and vehicle lifecycle management, while Chinese companies have competitive strengths in battery supply chains, intelligent driving and software technologies. These complementary advantages offer considerable scope for technological cooperation between the two sides, analysts noted.
Highlighting the strong complementarity between the two industries, Chinese carmaker Chery Group said closer cooperation would benefit businesses and consumers on both sides while contributing to the stability of global automotive supply chains.
Cooperation between Chinese and European companies could combine their respective strengths to improve vehicle quality, noted Andrea Levy, president of the Turin Motor Show.
Beyond the immediate benefits for trade, experts said that against the backdrop of rising trade protectionism and growing uncertainty across the global economy, the choice by the two major economies of dialogue over confrontation to resolve differences sends a positive signal in itself.
The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers said managing differences through institutionalized consultations and resolving disputes through cooperation rather than confrontation represented a rational choice that served the fundamental interests of both sides.
Responding to claims that the consensus was the result of EU pressure, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce stressed Friday that the understanding on hybrid vehicle trade is reciprocal and mutually beneficial, dismissing such claims as entirely unfounded.
The purpose of China-EU economic and trade consultations is to properly manage differences and address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, the spokesperson said, calling on both sides to demonstrate sincerity in resolving problems.
The spokesperson also stressed that the EU should not expect to gain benefits by exerting pressure, nor should it underestimate China's determination and ability to safeguard its own interests. ■

American Jews face a bitter dilemma as Israel's election approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:57:45 UTC
23:57:45 KST

Israel's October 27 election is generating intense interest and growing concern among American Jews, as three years of war in the Middle East have deepened divisions over Israel within American society. Those disagreements are increasingly visible in street demonstrations and in the campaign for the U.S. congressional midterm elections in early November.
American Jews remain sharply divided along political, religious and often generational lines over the outcome they hope to see in Israel's election, widely regarded as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The vote is also taking place against the backdrop of the continuing trauma of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, which triggered the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu's supporters, particularly among Orthodox Jews, believe he is defending a country they love and regard as central to their identity. Many liberal and younger American Jews, however, believe his policies have damaged Israel's international standing and generated widespread hostility that threatens to affect them in the United States as well.
The situation is especially sensitive amid rising antisemitism and antisemitic violence. Even some of Netanyahu's harshest critics, whether over the war in Gaza or Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, acknowledge that responsibility for attacks against Jews cannot be placed entirely on the Israeli prime minister.
Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El, a Reform synagogue in Boca Raton, Florida, said many American Jews feel caught between competing concerns. They want an end to attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, while also rejecting accusations of genocide against Israel and what they regard as double standards applied to the Jewish state.
Israel remains central to many American Jews' identity
Levin's large Reform synagogue is among numerous congregations across the United States holding educational programs this fall about the Israeli election. Although most members are not Israeli citizens and cannot vote, Levin said they feel a profound emotional investment in the outcome.
Israel's complex multiparty electoral system makes the October 27 result difficult to predict. Polls suggest a close contest between the political bloc led by Netanyahu and an alliance of his opponents, with neither side assured of forming the next government.
Many American Jews have friends and relatives living in Israel. Beyond those personal ties, supporting Israel remains an important part of Jewish identity for many older Americans, particularly religiously affiliated Jews aged 45 and above, according to a recent poll conducted by The Associated Press and the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
Reform Judaism, the largest Jewish denomination in the United States, places considerable emphasis on progressive values. Many Reform Jews see no conflict between their liberal beliefs and Zionism, which they understand as the Jewish people's aspiration to live freely and independently in their homeland, according to Rabbi Josh Weinberg of the Union for Reform Judaism, an umbrella organization representing more than 800 Reform synagogues across North America.
But Weinberg said many Reform Jews are concerned about the growing influence of ultra-Orthodox parties over Israel's political and religious life, as well as government settlement policies and the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank. They regard those policies as fundamentally inconsistent with their values.
Weinberg warned that another Netanyahu victory could deepen the disillusionment of younger American Jews, some of whom may ultimately decide they have had enough and say, "I'm giving up on Israel."
The generational divide is reflected in the AP-NORC survey. Only about four in 10 religiously affiliated Jewish adults under 45 said supporting Israel was extremely or very important to their Jewish identity. Younger respondents were more likely to place greater importance on other expressions of Jewish identity, including observing Jewish holidays.
Antisemitism remains a central concern
The same survey found that most Jewish American adults consider prejudice against Jews an extremely or very serious problem in the United States today.
With Israel's election approaching, many Jewish communities are concerned that its outcome could affect attitudes toward Jews in the United States. Jonathan Sarna, professor emeritus of American Jewish history at Brandeis University, said some American Jews believe a different kind of Israeli prime minister, one more like previous leaders who frequently spoke about their desire for peace, could change how Jews themselves are perceived in America.
Even Netanyahu's critics, however, do not expect antisemitic attacks to disappear simply because Israel elects a different government. Their concern is particularly acute when anger over Israeli policies toward Palestinians is used to justify violence against Jews regardless of their nationality, political beliefs or connection to Israel.
Weinberg pointed to a protest slogan calling for an intifada and revolution, which he and others interpret as encouraging violence against Jews. He argued that the meaning of such rhetoric changes depending on where it is heard. A slogan shouted in the Palestinian city of Ramallah, he said, carries a different implication when repeated on the streets of Minneapolis. For him, the latter raises an unmistakable concern about antisemitism.
Others believe changes in Israeli policy could nevertheless help reduce hostility. Rabbi Jill Jacobs, CEO of T'ruah, a rabbinic human rights organization, said people who attack Jews in the street or deliberately drive vehicles into synagogues bear full responsibility for their own actions. Such violence cannot be blamed on the Israeli government's conduct.
At the same time, Jacobs warned that the election of another Netanyahu government, particularly one continuing policies she described as expanding the occupation, ethnic cleansing and an endless war, would create a deeply frightening environment for Jews around the world.
Stanley Weinstein, an Orthodox Jew from Florida, rejects much of the criticism directed at the Israeli military and the country's political leadership, particularly given the threats posed by Hamas terrorists in Gaza and other continuing confrontations. These include tensions with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran, even as fragile ceasefires remain in place.
Weinstein considers Israel's security essential, especially as he sees increasingly hostile rhetoric toward Israel and Jews among American political figures on both the right and the left. He has observed those trends even from his home in Miami Beach, which has a large and diverse Jewish community.
He said he was appalled by the growing hostility, both as an American and as a Jew, but added that it only reinforced his gratitude for Israel's existence, declaring, "thank God there is an Israel."
Netanyahu, Trump and elections that could deepen divisions
For American Jews, Israel is also becoming an increasingly important issue in the U.S. midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the next two years. American voters will go to the polls on November 3, exactly one week after Israelis cast their ballots.
From New York to Michigan and elsewhere, support for Palestinians and demands to end American military assistance to Israel have become more prominent issues among Democratic voters.
Both elections could influence the longstanding alliance between Israel and the United States. Relations have been particularly close under the Trump and Netanyahu administrations, although tensions have emerged in recent months, especially over the war the two countries jointly launched against Iran.
Despite growing controversy over some Israeli government policies in the United States, support for Israel itself remains substantial among American Jews, according to Jason Isaacson, chief policy officer of the American Jewish Committee, a prominent advocacy organization seeking to represent a broad spectrum of Jewish communities in the United States and internationally.
Isaacson said there is continued strong backing among American Jews for maintaining the U.S.-Israel relationship, as well as broad agreement on the importance of Israel's continued existence and security.
Yet regardless of political affiliation or religious outlook, some American Jews are most troubled by the possibility that Israel's election will produce even deeper divisions within the country and across Jewish communities abroad.
Levin, the Reform rabbi from Boca Raton, said the upcoming vote could prove one of the most consequential elections in modern Israeli history. He argued that the Netanyahu government's deeply divisive character has created tensions severe enough to threaten the cohesion of Israeli society itself.
Weinstein, the Orthodox Jewish resident of Miami Beach, believes Netanyahu has performed extremely well as prime minister. Nevertheless, he shares Levin's anxiety about Israel's future. For him, the greatest challenge facing the country is the lack of national unity, a problem he considers more important than the outcome of any individual political contest.
His central question is whether Israel can overcome those differences: "Is there a way to unify the country, unify the people?"

A Paid Community is Coming to AIs without Minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:21:09 UTC
23:21:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
This post is about my upcoming paid community tier, a post I’ll pin for future paid subs to read, and where I am laying out what I want the community space at AIs without minds to be. Get comfy and dig in! If you’re interested in an intentionally built intellectual community, on questions of minds and all things AI, this might just be the perfect space for you. ✨
Why a Community?
I’ve talked to my paid subscribers, and others who closely engage with my work and what I have heard most consistently is that folks want a space to think with others, a space to talk to others about all things AIs and minds. So that’s what’s happening.
I am launching a community space as part of the paid tier. I am thinking of this as a broader project, one that I’ll continue working on.
So this is just the first instalment, and I would love to receive feedback and other suggestions from folks who have ideas about what else they would like to see as part of a paid AIs Without Minds community.
The first instalment is a chat for paid subscribers and monthly zooms where we can discuss whatever ideas, thoughts, or arguments are on peoples minds.
Members will be able to start their own conversations/threads about questions related to all things AIs, minds, and everything in between; reply to each other in substantive, respectful, and genuinely curious ways; meet others, and hopefully, through the chat and monthly lives, form substantive friendships around intellectual issues that deeply matter today.
The monthly zooms are deliberately not Substack lives, where only I am visible. They will be held on zoom so folks have the opportunity to talk to not just me, but to engage with and meet others who are interested in similar issues.
What Kind of Community Space Will This Be?
There is a reason I did not open my chat from day one when I started this newsletter. It’s because I knew that if I did ever build a community space here, I would want to do it intentionally, and in a way that would actually be valuable to my subscribers.
As someone who works in academia, I am deeply aware of how important the shared spaces we have to talk about issues are, and I also know that such spaces are rarely accessible to those who do not have the privilege of pursuing higher education or working at universities and similar institutions.
With that in mind, as I choose to build this community, I want to lay some ground rules for how the space operates. Here they are, and I am always happy to update them and welcome feedback:
(1) this is a space for human thinkers: by this, of course I don’t mean that I am here to police your writing style or AI use, rather that AI slop being copy and pasted into a chat won’t be tolerated. We want to learn from fellow humans in this space, and hear what you think, so your thinking can develop. That’s the point of the community.
(2) if you start a thread about a particular idea/argument/question be sure to stick around to engage with those that respond to your thread. This sets up mutual trust and respect that’s needed in engaging in learning together. Please don’t start several threads at once that you cannot / are not willing to consistently return to and engage with. if the chat is flooded with unfinished threads, it wont be a fun space to engage and learn in.
(3) if you link things to the chat, they need to be explained. No linking your own pieces for self-promotion (sorry, but this is not what this chat is about), and no dumping in memes etc, that are not about generating real conversation and learning.
note: the exception of course, is if you’re working on something and want to share it because you’re stuck on an idea, an argument, etc and would appreciate feedback. But even then, do be mindful of giving as much to the community as you receive in terms of time commitment and effort.
(4) be respectful of peoples contributions and don’t screenshot and share things from that chats. I want this to be a welcoming and good-faith space for people to learn, ask questions, and engage. The chat is restricted to paid members partly because I want this to be a smaller, more intentional space for learning than a public feed.
(5) you do not have to agree with my views in the chat, or with anyone else’s. Disagreement is encouraged, so long as it’s respectful and what is being challenged are ideas and arguments, not people.
(6) its okay to come with half formed thoughts and ideas, but don’t dump into the chat incredibly long chunks of writing without yourself first making sure you have been as succinct as you reasonably can.
(7) Please don’t expect this space to be somewhere where I respond to questions on demand. This is somewhere I will occasionally participate and start threads, but the primary benefit is not access to me, its access to a community of thinkers. If you have specific questions for me, the better place for those is in monthly zooms.
If these rules are consistently violated, I may reach out to you and remove you from the chat. this is in the interest of making sure this space is a place where intentional learning happens. For that to happen, we need community cooperation.
The goal of this space is to allow people to learn to how think better, together, and in community. These rules exist to maintain that, and ill update them accordingly if something isnt working.
We launch today! For paid subscribers, you’re already in. If you’d like to upgrade to the paid tier, now’s an excellent time to do that.
Become a part of the community

projection mapping and performances make the night come alive at signal festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
14:15:19 UTC
23:15:19 KST

projection mapping and performances make the night come alive at signal festival
co-founder martin pošta reflects on the origins of the digital art festival that transforms prague’s streets, landmarks, and historic buildings with light, sound, and performance.
prefer designboom on google
Signal Festival co-founder in conversation with designboom
Signal Festival reemerges for a weekend of immersive digital art installations that light up the corners and monuments of Prague. Founded by Martin Pošta, alongside producer and curator Jan Rolník and artist Amar Mulabegovič from the art group The Macula, nearly fourteen years ago, the event has grown from a yearly festival to also include a permanent space, open year-round in the Czech capital. Following the opening night of the event’s fourteenth edition, Dream On!, Pošta catches up with designboom in the recently opened Signal Space in Prague’s city center to chat about the event’s history.
The projection-mapping project that started it all
From the beginning of his career, even before Signal Festival, Pošta was interested in creating things people would love to watch. He started out producing films and documentaries, eventually attending film school in Prague and going on to organize a film festival in the Czech Republic. After leaving the television industry, he was asking himself what he would do next when he met up with some friends in a bar. As they were chatting, they got the idea to transform a local church with projection mapping. This was 2010, the nascent days of the technology, which had even Pošta himself asking, ‘what is video-mapping?’
After discussing the project with the deputy mayor at the time, he suggested that they instead work with the Prague Astronomical Clock (Orloj), which at the time was about to celebrate its 600th anniversary. ‘I went to roam around and to check out what’s the vibe amongst the people,’ remembers Pošta of the crowds that gathered for this first project. He recounts seeing an older gentleman looking up at the clock tower in awe, telling his wife that she ‘must come and see the installation.’ ‘And I literally got tears in my eyes,’ Pošta admits. ‘I was touched… it was the moment when I kind of knew that I found my next calling.’ It was from this first project that he’d go on to champion new media projects.
Bringing light art to Prague with Signal Festival
After that event in 2010, Pošta and his team at The Macula created and produced these types of installations around the world. Seeing all the emerging talents in the sector spread across the world, he began to work on an event that would bring them all to one place. ‘I was lucky enough that the guy who was deputy mayor for culture, was still there. He knew what we were doing, so it was easier to explain to where we were heading towards,’ Pošta reflects on the early days of organizing what would become Signal Festival. ‘And then I was lucky to get introduced to the Ministry of Regional Development. And I got the first funding for the festival… honestly, we hardly knew what we were doing, but that’s how it happened. We had the list of the artists that we really wanted. There was no curation back then – we were just like, OK, we love this guy, this guy, that guy.’
Creating art, community, and performance
‘It’s a huge matrix of the stuff that you have to combine,’ says Pošta of bringing the festival to fruition each year. Not only do they invite artists from around the world, but they also commission new, site-specific works. ‘Some of them are super ephemeral, like with the video mapping projections, there are four nights and that’s gone,’ he says of the installations. Nevertheless, with the newly opened Signal Space, a permanent mainstay in the heart of Prague, some of the works can be seen year-round under Old Town Market Hall. Inside the space, the ceilings open up to reveal some of the turquoise metal supports that hold up the historic building.
Over fourteen years, Pošta has built up a team of what he affectionately calls ‘like-minded lunatics,’ who have come together to create ‘a lot of things that would be deemed impossible.’ These are the coordinators, administrative staff, and tech teams that pull together the festival. They also include the artists who realize the installations, some of whom return for subsequent editions.
Laterna Magika at the 14th Signal Festival
One group that reappears in the dark evenings of Signal is Laterna Magika. Pošta shares a bit about the group’s history in the Czech Republic, saying that ‘they are a faction of the Czech National Theater.’ He describes their technique as one where, ‘They play with the fact that you cannot see people dressed in black against a black stage. You can just see what is lit up, so they created first illusions,’ with this particular technique and projected light and video. He goes on to say, ‘about six years ago, we introduced performative aspect to the festival, and it’s always super interesting to explore with [Laterna Magika] the possibilities of performance, dance, body and visuals.’ This year, they create a live, site-specific performance at the Old Wastewater Treatment Plant in Bubeneč, working from a poem by the Czech author František Vinant.

BANGKOK, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- Thailand cast itself as a "trusted connector" in a fragmented global economy on Saturday as it began wrapping up its hosting of the 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group.
During a concluding press conference on Thailand's hosting of the meetings, Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Ekniti Nitithanprapas said the event had demonstrated the country's capacity to help set the global agenda together with the IMF and the World Bank.

Officials noted that they are not a negotiated international outcome or formal policy recommendations but rather a distillation of themes raised in discussions among policymakers, international institutions, businesses, and other participants.
The document argues that economic fragmentation is happening within countries as well as between them. It says leading firms may gain access to new technologies and markets faster than small- and medium-sized enterprises, while some communities still lack the tools to seize new opportunities. ■

====================================================================================================

Gaza shelter crisis deepens as millions face winter rains, floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Repeated displacement during three years of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has left shelters across the enclave increasingly damaged, while restrictions and funding shortages are undermining efforts to prepare for winter, a senior U.N. migration official said late Friday.
Karl Baker, the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) regional crisis coordinator for the Gaza response, said some Palestinians have been displaced as many as eight times, with each forced move further damaging or destroying tents and other makeshift shelters.
“When they move, all those goods that they currently have or did have either get destroyed, or they have to seek new shelter,” Baker told U.N. News.
Even basic materials such as tarpaulins need to be replaced roughly every six months, but humanitarian agencies have been unable to bring replacements into Gaza at the required scale, he said.
Baker said agencies now need to move beyond temporary solutions toward more durable transitional shelters.
Materials needed for stronger roofing, concrete floors and more substantial walls, however, are subject to Israel’s “dual-use” restrictions, which are imposed over security concerns.
“After three years of war, we do need to improve the level of shelter which is inside, and move further away from temporary and more toward transitional type of shelter,” he said.
Baker said IOM remains in constant contact with Israeli authorities, but some durable materials continue to be denied entry over security concerns.
He also cited funding shortages and disruptions to international shipping as obstacles, saying IOM relies on suppliers in countries including China, India and Pakistan.
Although funding has begun to arrive, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of an estimated 1.8 million to 1.9 million people requiring shelter assistance, he added.
Baker said only around 30% of Gaza is currently accessible to most of the population, forcing displaced Palestinians into increasingly crowded and often flood-prone areas.
“The 30% in which they currently live is a very large displacement camp,” he said.
With winter rains already beginning, humanitarian organizations are working to address flood-prone areas and deploy water pumps. Baker warned, however, that getting displaced Palestinians through the winter would be the biggest challenge.
Earlier this month, IOM said available and incoming shelter supplies covered only 17% of Gaza’s winter needs, while more than half of tents and makeshift shelters were in poor condition.
A cease-fire has been in effect since Oct. 10, 2025, but Israeli attacks and restrictions on the entry of humanitarian aid and shelter supplies have continued.

'Nine murders' claim, then a clarification: How 'Chote Sarkar' has put Nitish, JD(U) on the spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:36:18 UTC
22:36:18 KST

Anant Singh is no ordinary legislator as locals rarely use his given name. They call him 'Chhote Sarkar'.
NEW DELHI: Anant Singh, Bihar's bahubali MLA, who is intensely popular on social media reels for his impromptu one liners in local Magahi dialect, made a jittering claim to prove his loyality and sacrifice for JD(U) chief Nitish Kumar."I got nine people murdered," he said on camera, reviving the distressing memory of Jungle Raj that once besieged Bihar. The statement also had a dramatic irony as he was mentioning the man who ruled Bihar as 'Sushasan Babu', Nitish Kumar.Speaking to reporters about his years of loyalty with Bihar's former chief minister Nitish Kumar, the six-time legislator said: “Who has made so many sacrifices as I have? Nitish Kumar was nothing back then; he used to roam around here and there. At that time, while being with Nitish Kumar, I got nine people murdered.”However, maybe after releasing the political gravity of his remark, the Mokama MLA backtracked and pinned the blame on Lalu Yadav, who was once an ally of Nitish Kumar.
In 2004, Anant Singh weighed Nitish Kumar against silver coins during a public rally in the Barh parliamentary constituency to show his support.
The video went viral and the timing was fatal, because Singh, popular as 'Chhote Sarkar', is already at odds with his party over the Patna Graduates’ MLC election.He is backing the candidate fielded by Prashant Kishor against JD(U)’s Neeraj Kumar, the very man he defeated in the 2015 assembly election.
As criticism came crashing in from the party and the opposition, Singh sensed the backlash and tweaked his remark, saying: “During the Lalu Prasad regime, nine of my associates were killed, and I myself was shot. It was because we aligned ourselves with Nitish Kumar that Lalu had them killed. We have suffered such immense losses. My father also passed away due to a heart attack.”However, the RJD held back the attack as Lalu's party spokesperson Shakti Singh Yadav, said: “Anant has publicly confessed to killing nine persons during the NDA regime. Now Nitish will have to offer explanations.”He went further: “Although he (Anant) has confessed to his involvement in nine murders, the responsibility straightaway goes to Nitish regime...Is paap se chhutkara nahin milekga (There will be no escape from this sin).”
Fate tied to bahubali brother
Anant Singh is no ordinary legislator as locals rarely use his given name. They call him 'Chhote Sarkar', or little lord, because in the Barh and Mokama belt his word has often counted for more than the government’s.His story begins with his elder brother, Dilip Singh. Dilip won as an independent and became a minister in Lalu Prasad’s cabinet during its first term, from 1990 to 1995. Dilip Singh is remembered as the first of the so-called bahubalis, or musclemen politicians, to reach such a post.Anant Singh, who first handled his brother’s election campaigns, took over the family's political reins following Dilip Singh's electoral defeat to rival strongman Surajbhan Singh in 2000.In the next election cycle in 2005, Nitish Kumar, who came to power that year promising to clean up one of India’s poorest and most fractured states, brought Anant Singh into the JD(U). Anant Singh's backing could help the party among upper castes, who did not naturally support Nitish Kumar.However, his allegiance to Nitish began a year before. In 2004, Anant Singh weighed Nitish Kumar against silver coins during a public rally in the Barh parliamentary constituency to show his support.Anant Singh successfully contested the Mokama assembly seat in 2005 on a JD(U) ticket.Once asked why he had embraced a man with such a reputation, Nitish Kumar replied, “There are certain compulsions of politics.”Anant Singh then again contested as a JD(U) candidate in 2010, and the relationship lasted until he quit the party before the 2015 polls.
Pet lover who loves python
Anant Singh keeps a python as a pet, owns an elephant trained to shake hands and rides an antique buggy pulled by expensive horses.Residents describe him holding a durbar where he settles disputes, hears complaints against the police and acts against “miscreants”. Admirers credit him with safer streets and quicker access to services. Critics see a parallel government.
Anant Singh with his horses
Jail, raids and remarkable run at the polls
Aanant Singh has faced around two dozen serious cases, ranging from murder and kidnapping to conspiracy to kill and the possession of illegal arms. But for years none ended in a conviction, as judges died, officers were transferred and evidence went missing.In his last affidavit he filed in 2025 Bihar elections, he mentioned 28 criminal cases involving undue influence or personation at an election, making preparation to commit dacoity, insult intended to provoke breach of the peace, rioting and armed with a deadly weapon, dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person.In 2015, after he was arrested on murder and kidnapping charges, Nitish Kumar cut him loose. The move was widely read as a gesture to Lalu Prasad Yadav, his old rival turned new partner. Nitish JD(U) had snapped ties with the BJP-led NDA over Narendra Modi being chosen as the PM face.Anant Singh, however, fought the election from jail as an independent. His wife, Neelam, campaigned in his name and called him a “rare diamond”. Interestingly, he won comfortably without stepping onto the campaign trail.The pressure returned in 2019 after police arrested three suspected sharpshooters on 15 July, who allegedly planned to kill a contractor, Bhola Singh, and his brother Mukesh Singh.They reportedly told investigators that Anant Singh had given them the contract. He gave a voice sample to the state forensic science laboratory.Soon afterwards, an AK-47 and hand grenades were recovered from his ancestral house, and he was booked under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, or UAPA. Anant Singh disappeared for nearly a week.“The man, whose name once spelt terror, is now running for cover,” a senior IPS officer said at the time. He eventually surrendered in a Delhi court and alleged a “conspiracy by political forces”, an apparent dig at the JD(U).Nonetheless, Bihar politics is never bereft of bahubalis. And 2020 was different from 2015. Nitish was back with NDA with ever-dominant BJP under Prime Minister Narendra Modi. And RJD, which was by then handled actively by Lalu's son Tejashwi Yadav, forged an alliance with the Congress.This dynamic also shifted the allegiance of Anant Singh, who fought on RJD's ticket and Nitish Kumar's party. Still in jail in 2020, he won with 78,721 votes, about 53 per cent of valid votes cast, by a margin of more than 65,000.In 2021, a special court in Patna sentenced him to 10 years in the arms case, which cost him his seat. Neelam Devi then won the by-election for the RJD, showing that the family’s hold on Mokama had not loosened.Nitish again dumped the BJP in 2022 and returned to the RJD's Mahagathbandhan fold. But nothing much changed for Anant Singh.
The fluid loyalty
In February 2024, Nitish Kumar flipped again, leaving the RJD-led alliance for the BJP-led NDA. He won the floor test comfortably with 129 votes, as the opposition walked out. Anant Singh’s wife, Neelam Devi, was one of three RJD MLAs who cross-voted in his favour, a pointed gesture even though the numbers did not depend on it.Months later, Anant Singh stepped out of Patna jail on 15 days of parole in the middle of the Lok Sabha elections. He backed Lalan Singh of the JD(U) in Munger, a sworn enemy whom his wife had challenged on a Congress ticket in 2019. Munger has roughly 3.5 lakh Bhumihar voters, the community to which Singh belongs. The RJD questioned the timing of his release.
A fragile equilibrium
The most dramatic chapter came during the Mokama assembly contest in 2025. Dularchand Yadav, 76, was murdered while campaigning for a Jan Suraaj candidate. Police arrested Singh, then the JD(U) nominee, in connection with the killing. The NDA responded that, unlike under the Lalu regime, no leader enjoys immunity from legal action.The case revived an old rivalry with Surajbhan Singh, another Bhumihar strongman. Surajbhan began in the LJP, later moved close to the RJD, and saw his own electoral influence shrink after criminal convictions. His wife, Veena Devi, kept the family relevant in nearby seats. The two men have long competed for land, contracts and political dominance.The arithmetic made the stakes plain. Mokama has about 2.9 lakh voters. Bhumihars number roughly 55,000 to 60,000, Dhanuks about 45,000 and Yadavs about 40,000.Muslims and Dalits together make up roughly 30 per cent. A shift of 5 to 10 per cent could move 15,000 to 25,000 votes. The killing of a Yadav campaigner threatened to unsettle backward caste voters, while the Bhumihar vote risked splitting between two powerful figures.
Net-net, contrary to Anant Singh' remark, "Chhote Sarkar" has been an ally, an outcast, a prisoner, a convict and a kingmaker, often within a few years. And this time again, he has been vocal against his party's MLC candidate Neeraj Kumar and backing Jan Suraaj's Anuj Kumar Singh.
“Nishant (Nitish Kumar's son) should not have campaigned for Neeraj Kumar. Sometimes he is taken to Barh, sometimes some other places, but there are few people to support him,” Anant Singh said, claiming he would “medically treat” Neeraj in the election.

====================================================================================================

Predictions of Gaza’s death toll were wrong - why is no one being held accountable? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:34:30 UTC
22:34:30 KST

In late September, Gaza’s Hamas-run Health Ministry published its 2025 mortality report, the first since the war began to purport to count every death in Gaza.
Of 24,650 deaths, it attributed 17,286 to “war operations,” without separating combatants from civilians, and 1,584 to accidents. Independent analyst Eirik Schrøder-Bråtane calculated that the remaining 5,780 nonviolent deaths roughly matched Gaza’s prewar annual nonviolent toll. The ministry also recorded 50,227 births.
This was 2025: the year Israel halted aid for 11 weeks after Hamas refused to extend the truce and release more hostages, following a six-week ceasefire during which 25,200 trucks delivered nearly 450,000 tons of aid. Israel said Hamas was seizing and selling supplies to finance its war. By September, Israel counted over two million tons delivered during the war.
It was also the year UN officials warned of babies dying by the thousands and the IPC, the UN-backed hunger monitor, declared famine in Gaza City.
Yet the ministry’s own figures show nothing resembling the mass-mortality footprint those warnings suggested: no surge in nonviolent deaths from hunger, disease, or other indirect causes.
Andrew Fox, a former British Army officer and senior fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, argued in 2024 that Gaza’s war toll was being padded with natural deaths. Now, he wrote, the famine allegations and other claims had been “debunked by Hamas’s own numbers.” The modelers who predicted hundreds of thousands of deaths, he added, “should lose their careers.”
Then he said: “They won’t. They’ll get a free pass.”
That may be the safest prediction anyone has made about this war.
For years, Israel’s accusers have issued confident predictions of mass death and confident counts of massacres. The headlines circle the globe. When the predictions fail, or the numbers collapse, the correction barely travels at all.
On May 20, 2025, the UN’s humanitarian chief, Tom Fletcher, told BBC Radio 4 that 14,000 babies in Gaza “will die in the next 48 hours” unless aid reached them. Within a day, the UN clarified that the figure meant roughly 14,100 projected cases of severe acute malnutrition among young children under age 5.
Not deaths. Not babies. Not 48 hours.
The report does show deterioration: infant mortality of 15.8 per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality of 33.4, both worse than before the war. But in the year of the UN’s warnings, Gaza’s infant mortality roughly matched Egypt’s peacetime rate of 16.1, and both its rates sat below the global average. Worse, yes. Mass death, no.
In February 2024, researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Johns Hopkins projected as many as 85,750 excess deaths in Gaza over six months in a worst-case scenario of escalating war and epidemic disease. Activist outlets ran headlines like “Israel Could Kill 85,000 More Gazans in 6 Months,” and a lead author told US news program Democracy Now! that the escalation scenario was “currently what’s happening in Rafah.” That epidemic never came.
In Sudan’s largely forgotten war, the same London School found the dead going uncounted: some 26,000 violent deaths in Khartoum State alone in the first 14 months, more than monitors had recorded for the entire country, and over 61,000 deaths from all causes.
In Gaza, the alarm far outran the dead. In Sudan, the dead outran the alarm.
In March 2024, the IPC projected famine in northern Gaza by the end of May if fighting and severe aid restrictions continued. By June, its own Famine Review Committee found the evidence did not indicate famine.
The IPC declared famine in the Gaza Governorate in August 2025, over Israel’s objections to its methodology. Somalia’s 2010-2012 famine killed an estimated 258,000 people, including 133,000 children under five. At its peak, it killed about 30,000 people a month.
Incentive to inflate numbers
Gaza’s Health Ministry, an arm of Hamas with every incentive to inflate, reported 455 malnutrition deaths across nearly two years of war, fewer than Somalia’s famine killed in half a day at its height.
By the IPC’s own threshold, two deaths per 10,000 people a day, the declared famine should have killed about 9,000. Hamas’s own ministry counted fewer than 200, across all of Gaza, fewer than the US records in four days.
Rafah followed a familiar pattern. Before Israel entered the city in May 2024, the Palestinian Authority’s Foreign Ministry warned an assault would bring “the annihilation of about 1.5 million Palestinians.” The EU’s then-foreign-policy chief, Josep Borrell, scoffed at evacuating civilians: “Where? To the moon?” Within three weeks, about a million people had evacuated Rafah. There was no annihilation and no apology.
The pattern is older than this war, and it only ever runs in one direction.
In April 2002, during Israel’s operation in Jenin, PA negotiator Saeb Erekat told CNN that Israeli troops had killed more than 500 people. The UN secretary-general’s own report later counted 52 Palestinians dead, at least half of them terrorists, along with 23 Israeli soldiers, and found the 500 figure unsubstantiated. By then, the “Jenin massacre” had entered the world’s vocabulary.
Operation Cast Lead followed the same arc. Hamas initially acknowledged fewer than 50 dead combatants. The since-discredited 2009 Goldstone Report cited a Palestinian Centre for Human Rights tally identifying just 236 of the dead as combatants. Then, in November 2010, Hamas interior minister Fathi Hammad acknowledged that up to 700 men from Hamas’s military wing and security forces had been killed, close to Israel’s count of 709.
Abroad, the dead were nearly all civilians. At home, they were Hamas martyrs.
On October 17, 2023, Hamas’s health authorities instantly blamed Israel for the Ahli hospital explosion and reported nearly 500 dead. American, British, French, and Canadian intelligence assessments concluded that a misfired Palestinian rocket was the likely cause; US intelligence put the toll at a fraction of the ministry’s tally. The New York Times later conceded that its early coverage had relied too heavily on Hamas’s claims.
The progressive Left, which prides itself on following the science, rarely asks why so many catastrophic predictions and claims about Israel fail. A growing faction of the populist Right, the so-called “woke Right,” recycles Hamas figures and UN forecasts it would ridicule on any other subject.
The method works because the claims and predictions do their work before they can be tested. Put Israel in the dock. Push for sanctions or an arms embargo. Pressure Israel, but not those sworn to its destruction. By the time the evidence arrives, the damage is done.
Tom Fletcher still runs the UN’s humanitarian office. The IPC has not retracted its 2025 famine declaration. Newsrooms still headline the forecasts and bury the accounting.
In most fields, predictions this consequential would at least produce an audit. When the subject is Israel, they produce the next failed prediction.
The writer is an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former NYPD officer. He writes widely on Israel, Zionism, antisemitism, and Jewish history. He serves on the board of Herut North America.
