In Pittsburgh, campus antisemitism report’s authors neglected to speak with Jewish students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:34:21 UTC
22:34:21 KST

Can a college campus accurately assess its antisemitism problem without talking to Jews?
That’s the question facing the University of Pittsburgh, where an internal working group on campus antisemitism recently published a report that did not include, and did not appear to solicit, the perspectives of the school’s estimated 1,400 Jewish students, or any other members of the campus Jewish community beyond the group itself.
The July report by Pitt’s working group on campus antisemitism, which is made up of Jews, has divided the campus, drawing criticism from the left for what they perceive as recommendations that would limit speech, and from within the campus Jewish community for not adequately consulting with Jewish students and faculty. Before it was even published, one author of the report said her home was targeted after she was named to join the working group.
Addressing campus antisemitism after Oct. 7
The report has also resurfaced questions about the most effective methods for universities to address antisemitism for Jewish students three years on from the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks that prompted so much uproar across campuses.
The report’s omission of any research on its Jewish community was by design, the working group’s chair recently told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“Our charge from the chancellor and provost was not to provide data as part of our report,” Katherine Blee, a sociologist and the faculty chair of the Pitt working group, said in an interview.
Instead, she said, the recommendations came out of discussions between the group members, whom she characterized as “a very diverse group with a very diverse set of opinions, which is representative of the university.”
The school immediately agreed to take action on the group’s recommendations, which include strengthening its Title VI civil rights law compliance; giving “clear guidance” on free speech and protest policies; reviewing its bias training; and committing to new “Dialogue and Discourse” programming to facilitate constructive conversations around Jews and Israel.
The issue of antisemitism at Pitt became particularly urgent after two Jewish students wearing kippahs were wounded in a violent off-campus attack in 2024 in an incident that preceded the announcement of the working group. The perpetrator, who wore a keffiyeh and had no apparent university affiliation, attacked the students with a bottle as they were on their way to a Hillel Shabbat dinner.
“We recognize that members of our Jewish community have experienced harm, and we take that seriously,” the university said in its press release following the report. The school’s statement went on to quote the Mishnah-era rabbinic sage Rabbi Tarfon: “It is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you at liberty to neglect it.”
This was a heartening development for some of the committee members. But the finished report, along with a strict confidentiality agreement the authors agreed to, has sparked local controversy.
Non-Jewish faculty criticized report's recommendations
The university’s Jewish Studies program director, initially a member of the working group, didn’t sign the final document.
And some non-Jewish campus faculty writ large have criticized the report’s recommendations for, they claim, potentially threatening shared governance principles at the university. The university’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors, the national faculty union that in 2024 ended its longstanding opposition to academic boycotts to allow members to boycott Israel, called for the report to be withdrawn.
Blowback among a more progressive contingent of Jewish personnel at Pitt has led to the proposal of an alternative set of recommendations for tackling antisemitism, including creating a joint Kosher/Halal dining area and emphasizing teshuvah, or the Jewish tradition of repentance, “when a member of the university community does harm.”
This cohort has stronger, more ideological concerns with the report than whether it surveyed Jewish students. “We refuse to let anyone use the pain of antisemitism to dismantle academic freedom, free speech, and open engagement within our university community,” an open letter proposing the new plan reads.
Proponents of the second plan stressed the importance of soliciting perspectives from the broader Jewish community.
“If you’re going to really talk about this, you need to be really thinking more broadly about what the rest of the community thinks,” Harry Hochheiser, a Jewish biomedical professor at Pitt and critic of the report who has helped push the alternative set of recommendations to the university, told JTA.
Pitt’s report, and the response to it, comes as the question of how to respond to campus antisemitism feels less settled than ever. Some campuses are continuing to see fresh threats to Jewish safety: Recent flyers at the University of Oregon targeted that school’s Hillel director, by name, as an “enemy of the people.”
At the same time, the Trump administration’s aggressive response to the issue is starting to see pushback. A recent bipartisan report from the federally mandated US Commission on Civil Rights criticizes the administration’s handling of campus antisemitism cases, as well as its withholding of documents related to the investigations.
In response to a series of emailed questions from JTA, a Pitt spokesperson said the working group “drew on perspectives from across the University community rather than establishing a faculty-only process,” and that the school is “taking next steps on a number of the Working Group’s recommendations.”
The working group includes administrators, a student Hillel president, the lone student named in the final report, and a former director of Pittsburgh’s Jewish Community Relations Council.
The Pitt spokesperson, Jared Stonesifer, also said the school “is in frequent and ongoing discussions with Jewish students about their experiences and their views on the campus environment, and student input was included on the Working Group that produced the report.”
Both Blee and Stonesifer framed the report as the first of many future steps to help Pitt confront campus antisemitism, and expressed hope that future steps would involve talking to Jewish students. One of the report’s recommendations is to “survey antisemitism in the campus environment regularly.”
Pitt’s undergraduate student body is home to around 1,400 Jews, just under 7% of the 21,000 total students, according to Hillel International estimates. The school is served by Hillel Jewish University Center, a local Hillel that also tends to Jewish students at other Pittsburgh colleges, as well as a dedicated Chabad house and a Jewish Studies program that grants an undergraduate certificate.
Julia Jassey, co-founder and CEO of the national Jewish student advocacy group Jewish on Campus, offered a mixed assessment of the Pitt report and of the school’s promise to include students in future decision-making.
“Students should be a part of the process in the implementation, not looking at it as a postmortem,” Jassey told JTA, noting that student input is valuable because “no two campuses are exactly the same.”
Yet, Jassey added, “That doesn’t mean that the report itself is inherently not helpful.”
Tree of Life Synagogue, the site of the 2018 mass killing that was the deadliest act of antisemitism in U.S. history, seen on April 21, 2023, in Pittsburgh, PA. (Jahi Chikwendiu/The Washington Post via Getty Images)
A sensitive climate
That Pitt would commission a campus antisemitism report was, on its own, not unusual.
In addition to the attack on the two Jewish students in 2024, Pitt’s Jewish community also continues to live in the shadow of the 2018 shooting at the Tree of Life worship center, two miles from campus. Many of the university’s Jewish students and faculty have personal connections to it; Pitt has also hosted exhibits about the attack. A local memorial and museum commemorating the attack, now under construction, is scheduled to open to the public in 2028.
Both the 2024 attack and the Tree of Life massacre were part of “the context in which we were writing,” Blee said.
Blee is a longtime member and past president of Congregation Dor Hadash, the Reconstructionist synagogue located inside the Tree of Life building. One Dor Hadash congregant was among the 11 killed in the attack.
In addition, her research specialty is white nationalism and far-right antisemitism: When the perpetrators of the deadly 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, were charged with violations of federal law, Blee was called to the stand as an expert witness.
So when her synagogue became the site of the deadliest antisemitic attack in US history, Blee recalled, “my work and my Jewish life intersected in a really terrible way.”
Blee’s 2025 appointment to chair the antisemitism working group, the Pittsburgh Jewish Chronicle reported, marked the moment the working group “begins to take shape.”
The final report recommends the university form an “advisory group” on Jewish issues and suggests that the local Hillel and Chabad-Lubavitch house, as well as the Pittsburgh Jewish federation, be represented, a recommendation that spurred criticism from pro-Palestinian groups on campus who objected to the federation’s presence.
Additional members of the working group contacted by JTA for this story, including the former JCRC staffer, directed requests for comment to Blee or declined to comment. The director of the Hillel serving Pitt’s campus, after requesting questions from JTA by email, did not respond by press time.
In a statement accompanying the report’s publication, the working group’s vice chair, Jennifer Murshatashvili, wrote, “My goal was to contribute to outcomes that would improve life for everyone at Pitt, not only Jewish and Israeli members of our community.”
Murshatashvili, a professor of Eurasian studies at Pitt, also told the university community that after she was named to the working group, “my home was targeted, and I was subjected to extensive online hatred and harassment.”
Even though the working group was not charged with gathering data, Blee told JTA that one of its instructions was to investigate “how effective” the university’s existing policies on antisemitism were after the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel strained relationships on the campus. There was disagreement among the group about how seriously to take the encampments mounted by pro-Palestinian groups at Pitt, she said.
“Some people were more concerned about the encampments than others,” she told JTA. Drawing on her own research into the far right, she explained, “Everybody would agree that a Nazi rally is antisemitic. Not everyone on the committee, and not everyone at the university, and not everyone in the United States Jewish community, would agree that the totality of the protests after October 7 were antisemitic.”
Blee declined to elaborate on how the working group determined policy effectiveness without gathering data. The confidentiality agreement brokered by the group members also prevented her from sharing more detail on their internal deliberations, she said.
“I can tell you that the committee gathered information that was needed,” she said. “But under that confidentiality agreement, I don’t want to go into exactly how that was done.”
Rachel Kranson, the director of Pitt’s Jewish Studies program, was announced as a member of the working group in 2025 but does not appear on its final report. Kranson declined to comment to JTA.
A flood of reports
Internal reports chaired by Jewish university faculty, officials and students have become part and parcel of the standard university response to campus antisemitism since October 7.
At public and elite private schools alike, the formation and release of an internal antisemitism report has been greeted with considerable fanfare, and no small amount of controversy, directed at everything from the political makeup of committee members to the data-gathering process and final recommendations.
Yet one consistency among such reports has been the presence of at least some polling of the experiences of that school’s Jewish students, which many Jewish groups and Jewish leaders have agreed is a crucial component of any successful campus antisemitism response.
Committees at Harvard and Columbia, two schools figuring prominently into the national conversation on campus antisemitism, each conducted surveys with more than 500 Jews on campus to inform their findings. Harvard’s final report runs 311 pages, while Columbia released multiple reports on the subject.
Stanford’s antisemitism committee report, released in 2024, runs nearly 150 pages and draws on listening sessions with more than 300 people, plus one-on-one interviews with students, administrators, and representatives of national Jewish groups.
The University of Washington and the University of California, Los Angeles, both public universities like Pitt, also surveyed and interviewed Jewish students to inform their own reports. The data itself can sometimes lead to controversy: A contingent of progressive Jews at UW criticized that school’s report for conducting focus groups with only a few dozen Jewish students, among other objections.
Pitt’s report, published two years after the administration committed to forming the working group, runs eight pages and includes no references to interviews or focus groups. It largely praised the university for, its authors said, already taking meaningful steps to combat antisemitism.
“I was surprised at the brevity of the report as the culmination of 1.5 years of work,” Andrea Goldschmidt, a psychiatry professor at Pitt and member of the Pitt Jewish Community affinity group, wrote in an open letter. “This stands in sharp contrast to the very lengthy and thorough reports I have seen come out of other universities.”
Goldschmidt also criticized the lack of “listening sessions or focus groups with the Jewish community during the course of the task force’s work.” She suggested that the lack of such conversations “reflects either that there was so much internal disagreement on the task force that the short report reflects the only areas of confluence among its members, or that the task force was somehow hobbled in its work before it even began.”
The Pitt Jewish Community affinity group’s president, Vicky Davide, echoed those concerns in comments to the student newspaper, telling the Pitt News that she and her colleagues had trouble accessing information about the group’s inner deliberations. They were “really disappointed” by the finished report, Davide, who leads engagement programs at Pitt, said.
Some suggested that, despite the lack of input from Jewish students, the recommendations themselves could still be useful. Jassey claimed that Pitt’s recommendations generally enjoy a “consensus” among Jewish students more broadly, and expressed hope that students would be included in the implementation step.
“I guess the question now is, what’s next,” she said.

Tear gas, clashes between protesters and police hit French cities in cost-of-living demonstrations

2026-10-17
13:34:12 UTC
22:34:12 KST

Police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in several French cities on Saturday as some of the most violent protests in years over living costs and public services drew thousands onto the streets.
French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday and blamed the unrest on what they described as the "ultra-left".
The protests began last month at high schools in Paris' poor northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement focused on inequality, public spending and living standards.
Violent incidents were reported in several cities, including vandalism in Marseille and attacks targeting police, media and public buildings, the Interior Ministry said.
Police were visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of two authorized demonstrations.
Protest echoes Yellow Vest movement
Protesters in high-visibility vests blocked streets, echoing the Yellow Vest movement that marked President Emmanuel Macron's previous term.
In Marseille, the mayor said the town hall had been vandalized, and that additional police were being sent to the city following talks with the prime minister and interior minister.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," said Lola, a 19-year-old protester in Paris.
About 100 people walked towards the start of the protests shouting "All cops are bastards", according to a Reuters witness.
The tourist office of the French city of Lyon was also set on fire amid the protests, French broadcasting network BFMTV said.
Police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in several cities across France on one of the most violent days of protest in years in the country, as demonstrations against rising costs and declining public services drew thousands onto the streets.
Macron, who urged calm on Friday, is entering the final stretch of his presidency amid a fragmented political landscape and growing pressure over the economy.
France's efforts to reduce public debt have failed to reassure investors, pushing government borrowing costs to their highest levels in more than two decades.
Police response under scrutiny
Police tactics have drawn criticism following a series of injuries among demonstrators, including a teenager who lost a hand after picking up a stun grenade. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said more than 900 police officers had also been injured.
The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence. France suspended the use of stun grenades during the student demonstrations, but Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said they could be used on Saturday.
Calls on social media for veterans of previous protest movements to join the demonstrations appeared to have broadened participation, raising the prospect of larger.
The Yellow Vest movement emerged in 2018 in opposition to diesel taxes before expanding into a wider protest against living costs and inequality. The movement subsided after Macron announced billions of euros in tax cuts.
Yannick Maillou, a teacher from La Crèche in western France who participated in the Yellow Vest movement, said local organizers had set up several gathering points for Saturday's protests, and labor unions were also encouraging participation.

The Christian progressive who could flip Texas: James Talarico on Trump, Gaza and a rabbi's lessons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
13:31:44 UTC
22:31:44 KST

Last weekend, a man called Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health treatment facility in Mason, Ohio. Claiming to be a relative of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, he asked whether Talarico had been discharged. Shortly afterward, on Sunday, two influencers from the MAGA movement, which supports President Donald Trump, published what they claimed was a recording of the conversation, suggesting that Talarico had indeed been hospitalized at the psychiatric facility and subsequently released. 
Given that Talarico had been absent from public appearances for nine days because of what his campaign described as a severe case of the flu, this appeared to be the kind of revelation that could destroy the campaign of the first Democrat in decades with a realistic chance of winning in the vast conservative stronghold.
But the Lindner Center of Hope quickly issued an official statement confirming that Talarico had never been treated there. The New York Times reviewed time-stamped images from security cameras at his home showing that he was there between October 1 and October 8. Talarico himself declared, "I've never even been to Ohio." 
Finally, the complete recording of the phone call revealed that the version circulated by the two influencers, Nick Sortor and Rhein Amacher, had been selectively edited. The full conversation showed that the caller, who lacked the required patient access code, supplied a made-up code, while the staff member repeatedly said she could find no record of anyone named James Talarico. The recording provided no evidence that he had ever been admitted to the facility.
By now, of course, none of that seems to matter. Elon Musk has amplified the conspiracy theory, as has Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and one of Trump's most influential advisers. The vast MAGA media machine is demanding that Talarico produce geographical proof that he was not in Ohio during his absence. 
This entire manufactured drama is unfolding because Talarico, 37, is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in the polls and has a genuine chance of winning one of the key races in the November 3 midterm elections. Polling suggests that Democrats could capture not only the House of Representatives but also the Senate, severely complicating Trump's final two years in office.
Midterm elections have historically been viewed as a referendum on the sitting president. His party generally suffers losses and sees its congressional strength diminished. But with polls showing Trump's popularity at a low point, and Republican and independent voters increasingly frustrated by the cost of living and price increases following the war with Iran, Democrats now hope to win even in traditionally conservative strongholds. 
Texas is the most striking example. America's second-most populous state, with approximately 32 million residents, has been considered reliably Republican for decades. Trump defeated Kamala Harris there by 14 percentage points in 2024. The last time Texas elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate was in 1988, a year before Talarico was even born.
Democrats have suffered repeated disappointments in Texas. In 2018, they placed enormous hopes in Beto O'Rourke, whose campaign against Republican Senator Ted Cruz generated tremendous enthusiasm. O'Rourke ultimately lost, although by just 2.6 percentage points, a historically narrow margin in Texas. 
Unlike Talarico, however, O'Rourke had not established a sustained polling lead before the election. That is why Democrats are more optimistic this time, while Republicans are increasingly alarmed, as reflected in the extraordinary sums they are pouring into efforts to rescue Paxton.
The intensity of the contest is reflected in its cost. It has become one of the most expensive nonpresidential races in American history, with spending surpassing half a billion dollars. Republican groups alone have committed enormous sums to defending the Senate seat being vacated by veteran Republican John Cornyn, with approximately $232 million earmarked for the final stretch between early September and Election Day. 
Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton after Trump backed the challenger, regarding the longtime senator as insufficiently loyal. Polling had suggested Cornyn would have been a much stronger candidate against Talarico, and analysts believe the race would not have been nearly as competitive had the incumbent won the Republican nomination. Paxton, by contrast, carries considerable political baggage, including corruption allegations and an impeachment attempt led by fellow Republicans in Texas.
Trump and conservative billionaires are now mobilizing behind Paxton with an aggressive campaign designed to portray Talarico as far too liberal for Texas. They have seized on statements from his past that he has since sought to clarify or distance himself from, including his assertion that God is nonbinary. 
Trump has given him the mocking nickname "TalaFREAKO," while the campaign has been accompanied by false allegations, including the debunked psychiatric hospitalization claim and Trump's repeated assertion that Talarico is a vegan, despite the Democrat explicitly saying he eats meat. 
The attacks may nevertheless be succeeding in bringing moderate and undecided Republican voters back into the party's camp. Recent polls indicate that Talarico's lead has narrowed. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in late September put him six points ahead, but a Marist poll conducted October 8-11 found his advantage had shrunk to just two points, within the margin of error.
‘We have lost the South for a generation’
It is difficult to remember, or even believe, today, but Texas was once a Democratic stronghold. For nearly a century after the American Civil War, Texas was a cornerstone of the Democratic-dominated South. Republicans, the party of Abraham Lincoln, were deeply unpopular across the former Confederate states. 
Then came Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, which helped pull the United States out of the Great Depression, won enormous popularity in impoverished, agricultural Texas and further strengthened the Democrats. Democratic politicians from Texas, including Roosevelt's vice president John Nance Garner and later President Lyndon B. Johnson, emerged from that political system.
The transformation began as conservative white Texans grew increasingly resentful of the Democrats' movement to the left on civil rights for Black Americans and the expansion of the economic safety net. The turning point came after President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964. 
According to a widely repeated account associated with his close aide Bill Moyers, Johnson feared that the legislation would cost Democrats the South for a generation. The remark, commonly rendered as "We have lost the South for a generation," became almost mythical in explanations of the seismic political shift that turned Texas and other Southern states from Democratic territory into firmly Republican strongholds, although historians have questioned whether Johnson actually used those precise words.
In 1961, John Tower became the first Republican senator from Texas since the 19th century. Bill Clements became the state's first Republican governor in more than a century in 1978. During the 1980s and 1990s, the suburbs of Dallas, Houston and Austin experienced enormous population growth. Many of these new residents were affluent white, religious, middle-class business owners and people employed in the oil industry. Attracted by the Republicans' low-tax policies, they shifted their political allegiance.
Democrats managed to hold on for a while, thanks in part to popular figures such as charismatic Governor Ann Richards. But in 1994, Richards lost the governorship to George W. Bush, and four years later Republicans had secured control of every statewide executive office, including governor, lieutenant governor and attorney general, as well as the Texas Supreme Court. 
No Democrat has won a statewide office in Texas since 1994, and the state has not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1988. Over the past decade, however, the growth of Texas's Hispanic population, whose voters historically leaned Democratic, revived hopes of another political transformation. Those hopes have not materialized. 
Now, though, polls suggest Hispanic voters are abandoning Trump amid frustration over the cost of living and his administration's mass deportation campaign against undocumented immigrants. Democrats are dreaming of Texas once again.
Christianity takes center stage: ‘Economic justice appears 3,000 times in Scripture’
Until a year ago, anyone who was not a political obsessive had probably never heard of Talarico. Born in Austin, he is an eighth-generation Texan. His grandfather was a popular pastor in South Texas, and his grandson grew up to become a devout Christian, a Harvard-educated former teacher who continues to study Christian theology at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary alongside his political career. 
Since November 2018, Talarico has served in the Texas House of Representatives, representing districts in the Austin area, the state capital and a Democratic island in an overwhelmingly Republican state.
The first time Talarico's name reached an audience well beyond Texas politics was during an interview former President Barack Obama gave a year ago on comedian Marc Maron's podcast. Maron expressed his frustration with Democratic candidates who, he felt, were unable to connect authentically with voters, relying instead on talking points prepared by political consultants. Obama acknowledged the problem but pointed to a young Texas politician who stood out. He mentioned Talarico, describing him as "terrific" and a "really talented young man."
Since then, Talarico has become a rising star in the Democratic Party. He comfortably defeated his much better-known rival in the Democratic primary, outspoken progressive Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, while building a grassroots campaign that made highly effective use of social media. 
Talarico has carved out an unusual political identity within the party: a progressive candidate who is also a devout Christian and places Christianity at the center of his political work. His message emphasizes social justice, loving one's neighbor, caring for the poor and immigrants, defending the separation of church and state, and opposing Christian nationalism. 
"Economic justice is mentioned 3,000 times in our Scriptures," Talarico has said, arguing that concern for the poor and oppressed is central to the biblical tradition but largely absent from modern Christian nationalism and the religious right. In deeply religious Texas, that message is finding an audience.
Like many Democratic candidates, Talarico has pledged not to accept money from corporate political action committees. Nevertheless, large sums have flowed into his campaign, both through individual contributions and from billionaires supporting outside groups. He has explained that he cannot afford to disarm unilaterally while Republicans benefit from hundreds of millions of dollars in billionaire-funded spending. 
He has also managed to capitalize on attempts by the Trump administration and federal regulators to restrict his access to late-night television programs, whose networks depend on federal broadcasting licenses. Two planned television interviews, with Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel, were kept off their respective CBS and ABC broadcasts amid legal concerns and pressure from the Federal Communications Commission. Both were instead made available online, where they attracted tens of millions of views and helped Talarico raise millions of dollars.
Since Cornyn's defeat in the Republican primary, Talarico has sought to court moderate conservative voters who are disappointed by Paxton's nomination and troubled by the corruption allegations surrounding him. He has repeatedly made clear that such voters are welcome in his campaign. 
According to the New York Times poll from late September, 60% of voters identifying as independents supported him, along with 7% of self-identified Republicans. One of them, Pete Nodecker, an 81-year-old retired restaurant industry supplier who voted for Trump twice, told CNN that he intended to vote for a Democrat for the first time. "I'm rather disillusioned with the Republican Party," he said. "The Republican Party has been hijacked. They're not the Republican Party that I was a member of for all my life."
Netanyahu, AIPAC and ‘the moral test of our time’
Although Talarico is considered a progressive, with a campaign focused on fighting the cost of living, raising taxes on the wealthy, combating corruption and expanding access to health insurance, he has adopted more moderate positions than some of his ideological allies, including on Israel. He emphasizes his support for Israel's right to exist and defend itself, but has sharply criticized the war in Gaza. 
He has said that, if elected to the Senate, he would vote to halt sales of offensive weapons to Israel and oppose the use of American taxpayer money to finance actions that harm civilians. At the same time, in communications with Texas's Jewish community, he has made clear that he supports continued funding for defensive systems such as Iron Dome.
Talarico has described the war in Gaza as "the moral test of our time," accused Netanyahu's government of war crimes and collective punishment, and strongly criticized what he describes as the use of starvation and restrictions on humanitarian assistance. Nevertheless, he has repeatedly declined to characterize Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide, saying the legal question is being considered by the International Court of Justice. 
He has also said Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be removed from power. During a CNN town hall on Wednesday, he was questioned by a Jewish voter about rising antisemitism in the United States. Talarico responded that he had deep love and respect for the Jewish people and Jewish scripture, explaining that he had studied the Hebrew Bible under a local rabbi rather than from a Christian perspective. 
He named Rabbi Neil Blumofe of Congregation Agudas Achim in Austin, crediting him with helping shape his understanding of Judaism. Talarico also said he had stood alongside Jewish leaders in Central Texas in confronting antisemitism and had consistently opposed hatred in all its forms, believing that Texans should feel welcome regardless of their religious beliefs.
When the woman questioning him, Rabbi Holly Levin Cohn of Congregation Beth El Binah in Dallas, asked about the relationship between criticism of Israel and antisemitism, Talarico stressed that his criticism was directed at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, not the Israeli people. Speaking as a former teacher, he said that watching the devastation in Gaza, particularly the suffering of children, "makes me sick to my stomach." 
He also acknowledged that the October 7 massacre was the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust. Talarico reiterated his belief that Israel, like any other country, has the right to defend its citizens, but argued that this right did not give Netanyahu permission to wage war against civilians, impose collective punishment or restrict humanitarian aid. That, he explained, was the conduct he had spoken out against.
Talarico, who supports a two-state solution and calls for a halt to Israeli settlement expansion in the West Bank, has taken an aggressive stance toward the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC. He has accused the organization of discouraging legitimate criticism of Netanyahu by threatening political candidates with massive spending against them, a practice he argues damages the prospects for reconciliation and peace in the Middle East. 
At the same time, he has drawn clear lines against antisemitic rhetoric, more forcefully than some of his progressive colleagues. Among other things, he refused to campaign alongside Maureen Galindo, an extremist Democratic candidate seeking a Texas seat in the U.S. House of Representatives who pledged to turn an immigration detention facility into a prison for American Zionists if elected. Talarico condemned her statements as antisemitic, and Galindo ultimately lost her primary runoff. In any case, Jewish voters account for less than 1% of Texas's population, making their direct electoral influence relatively limited.
Another thing Talarico and a new generation of Democratic candidates are doing is taking their message directly to conservative media audiences. Talarico has appeared repeatedly on Fox News and sat down for a two-and-a-half-hour interview with Joe Rogan, the enormously popular podcaster whose audience is heavily male. 
During their conversation, Rogan told him, "You need to run for president," adding that the country needed someone who was genuinely a good person. All of this has helped put Talarico in a position where he leads by margins generally ranging from one to four percentage points in the polls. It is an advantage no Democrat running for the Senate in Texas has enjoyed in more than 30 years. 
But it is also an extraordinarily fragile lead, underscoring just how conservative Texas remains. That reality becomes even more striking when considering the identity of Talarico's opponent, a politician weighed down by scandals and opposed by many within his own party, yet one who still has a very real chance of winning.
Affairs, a confrontation, impeachment and loyalty to Trump
Paxton, 63, was born in North Dakota to a U.S. Air Force officer. He holds a bachelor's degree in psychology, a master's degree in business administration and a law degree. He married Angela Allen, now a member of the Texas Senate, and the couple have four children. Their marriage has become the subject of highly publicized divorce proceedings, which we will return to later. 
Paxton began his political career in Texas state government. He was among the politicians who rose to prominence through the Tea Party movement, which emerged in response to Barack Obama's election and laid much of the ideological groundwork for Trumpism. Between 2003 and 2014, Paxton served in the Texas House and Senate before being elected the state's attorney general.
He quickly became a Republican star who waged an aggressive legal campaign against Democratic administrations. He filed dozens of lawsuits against the Obama and Biden administrations, particularly over immigration, environmental regulations and the Affordable Care Act, commonly known as Obamacare. He took an uncompromising position against abortion rights and strongly supported gun ownership. 
After the 2020 presidential election, Paxton led a legal challenge seeking to overturn Joe Biden's victory. He also spoke at the January 6, 2021 rally in Washington where Trump addressed supporters before a mob stormed the U.S. Capitol. All of this made Paxton extremely popular with Trump, who has repeatedly praised his loyalty and recently said that Paxton had stood by him more than almost anyone else. That loyalty paid off in this year's Republican primary, when Trump endorsed him against incumbent Senator John Cornyn.
Throughout his tenure as attorney general, Paxton has been dogged by scandals. As early as 2015, his first year in office, he faced securities fraud charges stemming from allegations that he misled investors. The criminal case dragged on for nearly a decade. In 2024, he reached a pretrial agreement requiring community service, legal ethics training and nearly $300,000 in restitution, without admitting wrongdoing. 
The criminal charges were formally dismissed in 2025 after prosecutors said he had fulfilled the agreement's terms. The most sensational scandal surrounding Paxton involved an extramarital relationship with a woman named Laura Olson. What began as a private marital matter developed into a major legal and political controversy. 
According to testimony from former senior officials in his office, Paxton allegedly arranged for a political donor, real estate developer Nate Paul, to employ Olson and, in return, used his public office to help Paul with legal matters. In May 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted to impeach Paxton on allegations including abuse of office and bribery. He was temporarily suspended, but in September of that year the state Senate acquitted him, allowing him to return to office.
Last year, reports emerged that Paxton had been involved in another relationship, this time with Christian influencer Tracy Duhon. An American tourist reported an encounter in London, alleging that Paxton physically confronted him and attempted to seize his phone after the tourist photographed him walking with Duhon. 
Paxton's wife, Angela, had publicly stood by him throughout years of criminal investigations and even sat in the chamber during his impeachment trial, when details of his infidelity were revealed. But last year, after 38 years of marriage, she formally filed for divorce. Nevertheless, this month she appeared in a campaign advertisement urging voters to support the entire Republican ticket, without directly mentioning her estranged husband's name.
No-meat campaigning and a nonbinary God: ‘California doesn't need a third senator’
Paxton is popular with relatively few figures in the Republican establishment, and resentment over his victory against Cornyn, who is also well-liked by many Democrats in Congress, has produced a steady stream of leaks from private conversations, revelations about past romantic relationships and even mockery of his physical appearance. 
An injury he suffered as a child left his right eyelid permanently drooping. Yet the Republican Party is still investing everything it can to save him. Trump has already visited Texas three times in recent weeks, and there is every reason to believe he will return before Election Day. Republicans might be able to live with losing ground in the midterms, as virtually every governing party does. But losing Texas is something they cannot afford.
The Republican campaign has already shown early signs of success. Throughout the race, Talarico has found himself defending statements from his past that Paxton's campaign has repeatedly highlighted as evidence that he is concealing his true political views. Among them are remarks he made in 2021, when he said that God was masculine, feminine and everything in between, describing God as nonbinary. 
In another exchange, he argued that modern science recognized six biological sexes rather than simply male and female, referring to chromosomal variations. Paxton has seized on the remarks, dubbing him "Six-Gender Jimmy." At one rally, Paxton declared, "California already has two senators. It doesn't need a third," suggesting that Talarico would represent the values of California's liberal left rather than conservative Texas.
The false claim that Talarico is a vegan also stems from remarks he made in 2022, when he argued that Americans should reduce their meat consumption and described his campaign for reelection to the Texas House as a "non-meat" campaign. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Talarico sought to distance himself from some of the statements he made just a few years ago, acknowledging that he regretted certain remarks and that others had "missed the mark." 
He accused Paxton of deliberately circulating embarrassing clips taken out of context to distract voters from his record of corruption. Asked whether he still believed there were six biological sexes, Talarico replied, "I know there are two sexes, men and women." He added that a small percentage of people have chromosomal variations and emphasized that they deserve dignity and respect.
And yet, as the campaign enters its final stretch, Trump already sounds as though he is preparing to shift the blame if Paxton loses. In a lengthy post on Truth Social on Thursday, he accused Republican Senator Cornyn, whom Trump himself helped defeat in the primary, and veteran Republican strategist Karl Rove, one of Trump's most prominent critics within the party, of doing everything they could to prevent Paxton's victory. 
Trump described Talarico as a radical left-wing lunatic, calling him "James TalaFREAKO" and "the ANTITHESIS of Texas Values." He went on to argue that any Paxton defeat would be the fault of Cornyn, Rove and other weak, ineffective Republican political operatives who had opposed him throughout his career.

12:59:27 UTC
21:59:27 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that US President Donald Trump’s decision to ease sanctions on Russia could encourage the Kremlin to continue its war against Ukraine, saying he fears further concessions to Moscow.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving sweeping US sanctions targeting Russian energy revenues, prompting concern in Kiev as Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure continue.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy said he feared the move was only the beginning of a broader relaxation of restrictions.
“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue. I believe the ‘diesel deal’ is just the first step,” Zelenskyy told reporters.
He said he still personally hoped Trump would do everything in his power to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, but argued that limiting Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian attacks while easing pressure on Moscow would not achieve that goal.
At least two people were reported killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine on Saturday, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s energy infrastructure
Zelenskyy said the US sanctions decision came on the same day Russia attacked 15 critical power-generation facilities across Ukraine in what he described as one of the largest assaults on the country’s energy grid.
Officials said a Russian attack in the southern city of Kherson killed one person and wounded 22 others, including two children. Another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.
Zelenskyy warned that Russia was seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without electricity and heating ahead of winter, when damage to energy infrastructure could have severe consequences for civilians.
Last winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Ukraine experienced prolonged interruptions to heating and electricity during freezing temperatures.
The Ukrainian president called on Kiev’s allies to increase pressure on Moscow and argued that sanctions were intended to raise the cost of continuing the war.
Kiev urges Washington to maintain pressure on Moscow
Zelenskyy also appealed to the United States to reconsider its approach to sanctions, highlighting the Lindsey Graham Act, which targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, Putin and the so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western restrictions.
The legislation, named after the late US senator who sponsored it, was intended to increase economic pressure on Moscow.
“It is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening,” Zelenskyy said on social media, arguing that the sanctions framework could still help bring the conflict to an end.
He warned that easing restrictions while Russia continued attacking Ukraine risked rewarding the aggressor and encouraging further military action.
Trump’s sanctions waiver followed his announcement of a deal with Putin allowing Russian diesel exports in exchange for sanctions relief.
The US president’s move came shortly after Putin, appearing in military uniform, said Moscow aimed to capture the remaining parts of eastern Ukraine.
Moscow welcomes Trump’s decision as talks stall
Russian officials welcomed the sanctions relief, although the Kremlin and Putin had not issued a direct response to Trump’s announcement at the time of the report.
Kirill Dmitriev, a Putin envoy, described the suspension of the Graham Act as an “important and truly historic moment”. He argued that the legislation would have caused serious damage to the US economy and global markets.
Zelenskyy met European leaders in Brussels on Friday, urging the European Union to continue financing Ukraine’s defence. He said he was standing up for his country amid the dispute with Washington.
As Russian strikes continue and winter approaches, Kiev is pressing its allies to sustain economic and military support while diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.

France rocked by protests over rising prices as Yellow Vests return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

Police clashed with protesters in Paris and other French cities Saturday as thousands demonstrated against rising living costs, stagnant wages and alleged police brutality, reviving the Yellow Vest movement and increasing pressure on President Emmanuel Macron’s government ahead of the presidential election.
Officers fired tear gas and used water cannons in Paris to disperse groups of demonstrators wearing hoods and face masks who threw fireworks and other objects at police.
Riot police were deployed around Place de la Republique, while authorities closed metro stations and banned some gatherings near government buildings.
Windows at the Paris offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 were broken after protesters threw projectiles at the buildings, according to reports from the scene.
The Interior Ministry said authorities had recorded about 140 protest actions outside the Paris region by shortly after midday, involving more than 32,000 people. Police had detained at least 166 people nationwide.
The demonstrations followed weeks of student-led protests over education funding and police conduct, with labor unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement joining calls for higher wages, lower prices and better public services.
The unrest has intensified scrutiny of the government’s response to demonstrations, particularly after several teenagers suffered serious injuries during confrontations with riot police.
In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, masked demonstrators forced their way into the lobby of City Hall after striking the entrance with security barriers.
Some entered the building, and one spray-painted an anarchist symbol on an interior wall before police moved in to disperse them.
Shops and a municipal police station were also damaged. Mayor Benoit Payan described the damage inside City Hall as limited in an interview with French broadcaster BFM TV.
“We’re taking the Bastille,” one demonstrator shouted, invoking the 1789 storming of the Paris fortress that became a defining moment of the French Revolution.
An Agence France-Presse (AFP) photographer also witnessed protesters attacking a police building in Marseille.
“We’re here to protest the deplorable resources allocated to education and against police brutality,” said Aude, a masked student who declined to give her surname.
In the western city of Rennes, about 20 people erected a barricade using trash bins and large wooden pallets near a shopping mall.
Christophe, a 47-year-old carpenter and former Yellow Vest protester, said he was angered by what he considered excessive police force against teenagers during recent demonstrations.
“We’ve reached the point where the repression is targeting our own children,” he told AFP.
In central France, about 300 people, including high school students, gathered in Gueret to protest rising prices and stagnant wages.
“At the end of the month, I have nothing left. Prices are going up but wages aren’t,” said Franck, a civil servant in his 40s who declined to give his surname.
“We can’t take it anymore, we’re suffocating,” he added.
Authorities also reported violence in Paris, Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers, including attempted looting, attacks on police officers, fires involving street furniture and damage to government institutions and media offices.
The demonstrations were organized partly through social media, with supporters seeking to revive the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 in opposition to planned fuel tax increases and broader concerns about economic inequality.
Named after the high-visibility vests worn by protesters, the movement organized months of demonstrations against Macron’s government, drawing support from workers and rural communities who felt the cost of living was rising faster than their incomes.
Organizers called for renewed protests under the slogan “yellow and youth,” urging teachers, students, workers, pensioners and farmers to participate. More than 600 demonstrations were planned across France, according to a website established by organizers.
The mobilization coincided with the start of school half-term holidays, as student groups sought to broaden support for protests that began in mid-September. School blockades and demonstrations have focused on education funding and allegations of excessive police force.
The CGT, one of France’s largest labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services.
Authorities imposed restrictions on demonstrations in central Paris, including near the Champs-Elysees, major railway stations and government buildings. Police detained about 60 people in the capital on Saturday morning, according to AFP.
Macron appealed for calm Friday in Brussels, emphasizing that the right to demonstrate did not justify violence or property damage.
“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”
The demonstrations have unfolded amid growing criticism of police tactics during student protests. Thousands of people have been arrested in recent weeks, while hundreds have been injured and some schools have been set on fire during the unrest.
Some of the most serious injuries have involved teenagers struck by police crowd-control weapons. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of a type of stun grenade against young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
The incidents have become a rallying point for protesters who accuse authorities of using disproportionate force to control demonstrations.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis on Tuesday, bringing further international attention to the student movement.
The government faces the challenge of addressing public anger over household costs while preventing further violence. The demonstrations have also become a political issue as France approaches a presidential election campaign in which purchasing power, public services and law enforcement are prominent concerns.
A survey of 2,000 people published earlier this month found that about 45% of French people were concerned about the cost of living and inflation.
Purchasing power has come under pressure, while fuel prices have climbed since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war earlier this year, adding costs for motorists and businesses.
France is also struggling with mounting public debt, which is projected to exceed 120% of gross domestic product next year, roughly double the European Union’s 60% benchmark.
Economists say significantly reducing the debt will require major reforms, potentially including changes to France’s costly pension system. Such proposals have long been politically sensitive, particularly among workers and retirees concerned about their incomes and benefits.
The unrest has given political parties on both the far left and far right an opportunity to position themselves ahead of the presidential race.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and joined a demonstration earlier in the week. Marine Le Pen, whose National Rally party has led opinion polls in the presidential race, has positioned herself in support of the police.
The competing responses reflect the political divisions surrounding the demonstrations, as protesters demand relief from rising prices and improvements to public services while the government faces calls to restore order.

Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:51:12 UTC
21:51:12 KST

Intl. Archaeology Day: A glimpse of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage and museums
TEHRAN - On 17 October, archaeologists and cultural institutions worldwide mark International Archaeology Day, highlighting archaeology’s contribution to our understanding of the human past. The occasion also invites reflection on the broader role of archaeology in reconstructing human history, investigating changing relationships between people and their environments, and communicating scientific knowledge to the public through museums and other cultural institutions.
In Iran, this day offers a valuable occasion to recognize a heritage that extends far beyond monumental architecture and written records. Long before the emergence of urban centers, human groups inhabited the Iranian Plateau and its mountain ranges, developed stone-tool technologies and other early technologies, adapted to changing climatic conditions, and exploited a wide range of environments. The Paleolithic represents the longest period of this history, and it places Iran at the center of important debates concerning human evolution, hominin dispersals across Eurasia, and adaptation during the Pleistocene.
Situated between Southwest Asia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent, Iran encompasses a remarkable diversity of landscapes and ecological settings. These environments formed part of the geographical context in which prehistoric populations moved, settled, and adapted to changing conditions. Iran should therefore be understood not just as a corridor between better-known prehistoric regions, but as a distinct archaeological landscape with real potential to contribute to future research on the early human occupation, Neanderthal behavior, and the dispersal of Homo sapiens.
The earliest chapters of Iran’s Paleolithic record are documented primarily through stone-tool assemblages recovered from open-air sites and sedimentary contexts. Sites such as Kashafrud in northeastern Iran and Dehtal, north of the Persian Gulf, have contributed to discussions of Lower Paleolithic occupation. Nevertheless, questions concerning chronology, stratigraphic integrity, and the relationship between artifacts and their depositional contexts remain important. Addressing these issues requires carefully designed field investigations, critical reassessment of existing collections, and reliable dating wherever suitable materials and archaeological contexts are available. Darband Rashi Cave is a key example, where modern dating methods and lithics associated with faunal remains in stratigraphic context help advance understanding of Iran’s Lower Paleolithic.
The Zagros Mountains are particularly important for understanding the Middle and Upper Paleolithic in Iran. Caves, rockshelters, and highland valleys preserve archaeological sequences that provide evidence of Neanderthal technology, subsistence strategies, and responses to environmental change. These records are also essential for investigating the arrival and subsequent expansion of modern humans, as well as the cultural and demographic processes associated with the Middle-to-Upper Paleolithic transition. Together, they offer a valuable basis for examining how human populations occupied and adapted to the varied environments of the Iranian highlands.
Over recent decades, Iranian archaeologists have advanced Paleolithic research through independent projects as well as, in some cases, collaboration with international colleagues. Their work has expanded field investigations, strengthened analytical capabilities, and brought Iran’s prehistoric record to greater attention within the international archaeological community.
The contributions of Iranian women archaeologists have been particularly significant, advancing scientific knowledge, broadening research perspectives, and strengthening the foundations of the discipline. Dr Marjan Mashkour has made major contributions to zooarchaeological research, deepening our understanding of past subsistence strategies, human–animal relationships, and interactions between human populations and their environments. Through her teaching and mentorship, she has also trained and helped shape a new generation of Iranian zooarchaeologists, many of whom are now conducting research at institutions across Iran, contributing to the development of the field nationally. Her work illustrates how specialist research can enrich museum collections and exhibitions, helping visitors understand how animal remains recovered from archaeological sites provide evidence of past diets, economies, and relationships between people and animals. Dr Sonia Shidrang has also made important contributions to Paleolithic research and to the international recognition of Iran’s prehistoric heritage, notably through her involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley, which were inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2025. Beyond research and heritage management, her commitment to teaching and organizing workshops at Shahid Beheshti University and other institutions has helped transmit specialized knowledge and practical skills to a new generation of archaeology students. Their work illustrates how Iranian women archaeologists contribute not only to scientific research and international collaboration, but also to the development of national research capacity and the future of the discipline.
Field archaeology matters just as much for heritage management, particularly when development projects threaten archaeological sites and landscapes. The Darian Dam Archaeological Salvage Programme in the Sirwan Valley, conducted in 2015–2016, demonstrated the importance of archaeological investigation in a landscape undergoing substantial transformation. Although salvage archaeology cannot replace the preservation of sites in situ, it can document threatened remains and recover information that would otherwise be lost. The project also underscores why prehistoric landscapes, even when they lack monumental structures or visible architectural remains, must be recognized as integral components of Iran’s cultural heritage.
The Khorramabad Valley occupies an exceptional place within this broader archaeological landscape. Its caves, including Kunji, Yafteh, and Ghamari, preserve important evidence for reconstructing Paleolithic lifeways and investigating the long-term human occupation of the Zagros. In 2025, the inscription of the Prehistoric Sites of the Khorramabad Valley on the UNESCO World Heritage List marked a major achievement for Iranian archaeology. As a member of the nomination team, I witnessed firsthand the importance of a rigorous scientific foundation in securing international recognition for archaeological heritage. This inscription provides an important opportunity to advance archaeological research, strengthen site management and conservation, and communicate the valley’s significance to local communities and international audiences.
My work in Gilan Province similarly brought prehistoric research into dialogue with broader questions of cultural heritage through my involvement in the UNESCO nomination of the Cultural Landscape of Masouleh. This experience highlighted the value of examining cultural landscapes across different timescales, taking into account the environmental and historical processes that have shaped them. Archaeological research can extend this perspective beyond standing architecture and documented history to explore the deeper relationships between people and their environments.
Museums play an essential role in connecting archaeological research with public understanding. In 2001, I led the establishment of the Paleolithic Gallery at the National Museum of Iran to present archaeological evidence in a form accessible to a wider audience. Stone tools may appear simple at first glance, but their technological characteristics, raw materials, and archaeological contexts can reveal important aspects of past human behavior when interpreted carefully. The challenge for museums is to communicate these findings clearly while preserving the scientific context essential to their interpretation.
The establishment of the Zagros Paleolithic Museum in Kermanshah extended this work into the region whose archaeological record constitutes a major part of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Regional museums are particularly valuable because they connect archaeological discoveries with the landscapes and communities from which the evidence originates. More recently, Paleolithic displays developed at the Archaeological Museum of Lorestan in 2024 have further strengthened the presentation of western Iran’s prehistoric heritage within its regional context. Together, national and regional institutions can help audiences appreciate the diversity of Iran’s archaeological record and its contribution to our understanding of the human past.
Museums also play a central role in the responsible management of archaeological collections. An artifact’s scientific value depends not only on its physical characteristics, but also on its provenance, stratigraphic position, and association with other evidence. When these relationships are lost, important opportunities for interpretation and future research are diminished or disappear altogether. Documentation, conservation, and responsible curation must therefore remain integral to archaeological practice.
International Archaeology Day provides a moment to recognize the scientific and public value of Iran’s Paleolithic heritage. Advancing research requires sustained fieldwork, renewed investigation of existing collections, interdisciplinary collaboration, and stronger connections between research institutions and the public. Such efforts can integrate Iran’s archaeological record more fully into international scholarly debates while ensuring that future generations of researchers have the evidence, expertise, and institutional resources needed to investigate it.
As head of the Paleolithic Department at the National Museum of Iran, my experience in field research, museum development, and UNESCO nominations has reinforced the importance of connecting scientific investigation with public interpretation and long-term heritage management. Archaeology achieves its greatest value when discoveries contribute not only to scholarly understanding but also to a broader appreciation of humanity’s shared past. Iran’s Paleolithic record offers an exceptional foundation for advancing that understanding, connecting the history of human adaptation across deep time with the responsibilities of scientific research and cultural stewardship today.

Israeli forces entered an area in the western countryside of Syria’s Daraa province on Saturday, according to the country’s state-run SANA news agency.
A force consisting of two Israeli military vehicles entered the Wadi al-Ruqqad area, SANA reported.

The Syrian government has repeatedly condemned the Israeli incursions as violations of the agreement and demanded Israel’s complete withdrawal from Syrian territory.

Protests sweep France as riots erupt in Marseille, police fire tear gas in Paris | Live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:22:22 UTC
21:22:22 KST

France is bracing for mass demonstrations Saturday as several protest movements join forces against the high cost of living, deteriorating public services and rising fuel prices. Tens of thousands of people are expected to take to the streets in demonstrations bringing together members of the Yellow Vests movement and student protesters, among others.
The student protest movement in France began Sept. 17 and has gained momentum in recent weeks, with students at hundreds of schools, particularly in impoverished, working-class suburbs such as Saint-Denis outside Paris, blocking school entrances, taking over roads, setting trash cans on fire and attacking police officers and passersby. The students say they are protesting neglected school infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. The demonstrations erupted as the French government seeks to pass its 2027 budget, which aims to reduce the deficit.
In central Paris, large numbers of police officers gathered, particularly near the Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe. Police also fired tear gas canisters at demonstrators in Place de la République. Some protesters wore masks and black clothing and launched fireworks.
But the more dramatic scenes, even before the demonstrations officially began, came from Marseille. In the southern city, protesters were filmed smashing windows at a local police station and spray-painting graffiti, including on police flags. Fires were set in the streets, with mannequins apparently looted from stores thrown into the flames.
Dozens of protesters also briefly stormed City Hall, shouting, "This is the revolution — we're storming the Bastille!" Police removed the demonstrators from the building and deployed officers at the entrance to prevent them from returning. Officers in the streets of Marseille also used tear gas, while some images showed arrests taking place.
By midday, French authorities had recorded approximately 140 protest actions involving tens of thousands of people. A total of 166 people had been arrested across France, including dozens in Paris. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he feared that "far-left elements" could inflame the demonstrations and turn them violent during the afternoon.
In a post on X, Paris police said, "We will not back down in the face of rioters and those who come to attack law enforcement officers," accusing "hostile individuals" of carrying out attacks against police.
"We are fighting because the cost of living is too harsh, because the price of fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions," a 19-year-old protester who identified herself as Lola told Reuters.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Thursday that authorities were concerned about possible riots during the protests. President Emmanuel Macron, for his part, called for "calm" ahead of Saturday's demonstrations but stressed that he believed in the right to protest. He urged demonstrators to respect people and property.
Opponents of the protests accused the France Unbowed party, led by radical left-wing leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a staunchly anti-Israel politician, of inciting violence and fueling the unrest. They also emphasized the involvement of immigrants and their descendants in the street violence. The party categorically denied the allegations.
Palestinian keffiyehs and flags were seen at many of the demonstrations. About a week and a half ago, U.S. President Donald Trump weighed in on the issue in a social media post, alleging that the protests were not really about conditions in schools but rather reflected immigration spiraling out of control and an attempt by Islam to take over France.
Police could resume use of stun grenades
Last week, France announced it was suspending the use of stun grenades following an incident in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand. Police said they had faced more than 200 students throwing stones and launching fireworks, and that the boy had picked up a grenade that exploded in his hand. Students, however, claimed he was struck directly after a police officer fired the grenade at him.
In another incident last week, a 14-year-old boy named Eden was struck in the face by a tear gas canister near Paris. According to his lawyer, he lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw.
On Friday evening, however, Interior Minister Nuñez announced that the use of stun grenades could resume.
"If there are clashes, all types of equipment may be used," he said in a television interview Friday.
The wave of unrest in France has erupted just six months before the presidential election, against an already tense social and political backdrop, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls and fuel prices soaring.
Current polls suggest that Le Pen will not win outright in the first round and that she will face radical left-wing leader Mélenchon in the decisive runoff — and defeat him.
Either way, such a showdown would signal that France is abandoning the political center and finding itself forced to choose between two parties widely regarded as extreme.

Israeli rabbi rules settlers can steal Palestinian olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
12:20:13 UTC
21:20:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Israeli rabbi issues ruling permitting settlers to steal Palestinian olive harvests
A prominent Israeli rabbi on Friday issued a religious ruling that would allow Israeli Jews to steal olives from Palestinian land in the occupied West Bank, with several Israeli media outlets affiliated with the religious Zionist movement, including Channel 7, publishing the religious edict.
The ruling, issued by prominent religious Zionist rabbi Dov Lior, said that the olives belong to the Jewish people, and that taking the crops represents the implementation of what he described as the "commandment to occupy the land".
The ruling, titled “In response to numerous enquiries regarding olive harvesting in the groves throughout Judea, Samaria and Binyamin” — biblical names used by Israelis to refer to areas of the occupied West Bank — states that “the people of Israel have never relinquished the Land of Israel, as we express in our daily prayers".
This comes amid escalating Israeli settler violence and terrorism targeting Palestinian farmers in the occupied West Bank, with mobs stealing tractors, setting alight olive trees, and damaging cars.
Lior further claims that "the Arabs never purchased the land from the people of Israel or from any Jew, and therefore it is usurped in their hands".According to his assertion, Palestinians “did not acquire ownership of it by any means, and it has remained the property of the people of Israel".
The rabbi further states that if Palestinian farmers cannot reach their crops for security reasons, it can be assumed that they have abandoned the crops.
“If they planted trees that bear fruit, such as olives, the principle of despairing of recovering them applies to them. Therefore, if they are unable to harvest them for security reasons, it should be assumed that they have given up on them — and all the more so that they have given up on olives that have already been picked," the rabbi said.
He adds that even if the owners of the trees were entitled to compensation for cultivating them, they had already received sufficient produce from them over previous years. He maintains that the land and its fruits should ultimately return to what he describes as the ownership of the Jewish people.
Lior goes so far as to declare that settlers harvesting olives from Palestinian land is “entirely permissible". He adds that this act contains an “additional virtue”, given the security risks supposedly posed by Palestinians approaching settlements and settlement outposts.
His position is not limited to olive harvesting on land adjacent to settlements. He extends the ruling to groves farther away, stating: “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements, in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land, and thereby fulfil the commandment to conquer the land.”
Dov Lior is one of the most prominent rabbis associated with Israel’s religious-nationalist movement. He previously served as the chief rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement near Hebron. Lior is known for his hard-line religious and political positions towards Palestinians and his support for expanding settlements in the West Bank. He wields influence among settlers and religious movements associated with the settlement movement.
Israeli media reported that Lior’s ruling came in response to a religious ruling issued last Tuesday by seven rabbis from settlements in the Gush Etzion bloc, south of Bethlehem. Those rabbis prohibited settlers from stealing olives from Palestinian land, even when Israeli forces prevent the owners from accessing their property for security reasons.
The rabbis, including Ze’ev Whitman, Uri Lifshitz, Avi Bliedstein and Moshe Shifter, argued that preventing Palestinians from reaching their groves does not mean they have relinquished ownership of the harvest. They stressed that seizing the olives constitutes "theft forbidden by religious law and a desecration of God’s name".
The seven rabbis based their position on provisions of Jewish religious law prohibiting the theft of property belonging to non-Jews. They emphasised that even if the landowners were assumed to have abandoned their fruit, this would not make it permissible for others to take it.
The Tzohar movement, which includes prominent rabbis, also joined the opponents of Lior’s ruling on Friday. It stated that “theft is forbidden from any person, whether Jewish or non-Jewish”, and that individuals do not have the authority to confiscate property.
The circulation of the ruling comes amid escalating attacks by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian farmers during the current olive harvest season. These attacks have included beatings, gunfire, the theft of crops, the burning of trees and vehicles, and preventing farmers from accessing their land.
Several areas of the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate witnessed widespread settler attacks on olive pickers on Friday. The attacks targeted the villages of Abu Falah, Turmus Ayya, Burqa and Deir Jarir, causing injuries among Palestinians and resulting in olive trees and vehicles being set on fire.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are considered illegal under international law.
